en: {The Chapter on Direct Perception} Having perpetually bowed before Umāpati, the Lord of all worlds, the Supreme Sovereign who bestows liberation,
and following after all my gurus, I shall set forth this compendium of the true meaning of Nyāya for the sake of attaining final release.

At the beginning of this work, the statement beginning with "having prostrated" (*praṇamya*) serves both for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*) and for the purpose of establishing the connection (*sambandha*), the purpose (*prayojana*), and the subject matter (*abhidheya*). For by means of the auspiciousness produced through prostration—which acts as an obstacle to non-merit (*adharma*)—the obstacles and impediments rooted in non-merit are dispelled; consequently, the completion of the treatise follows. Thus, the prostration is purposeful. Where, however, completion does not occur, one may infer either that the prostration was imperfect or that there is an abundance of non-merit on the part of the author. It is not the case that the prostration lacks efficacy altogether, for it possesses efficacy elsewhere. Indeed, one has never seen a hundred jars of water, though incapable of extinguishing a fire in a blazing elephant stable, to be ineffective elsewhere. Even where the completion of a treatise is observed without an explicit prostration, a mental or physical prostration must be inferred there, or else merit (*dharma*) accomplished by other means. If verbal prostration were the sole requirement, the successful accomplishment of instruction would belong to others as well. Every action, especially by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), must be preceded by prostration to Maheśvara, so that, just as with the completion of the treatise, the attainment of liberation may likewise be free from obstacles. Alternatively, perhaps non-merit—the cause of obstacles—does not exist, or merit exists that acts as an obstacle to them due to prior actions. Nevertheless, prostration must still be performed out of apprehension of such obstacles, just as one carries weapons and the like out of apprehension of enemies and so forth.
The Necessity of Expressing the Relationship and Other Factors.

The statement of the relationship (*sambandha*) and other factors is for the sake of engaging the listener, because it serves as a cause for engagement by way of creating doubt regarding the subject matter. If that were not stated, even doubt regarding the lack of purpose (*anartha*) would become a cause for withdrawal, just as one might refrain from eating when a meal is promised but not actually promised, or refrain from entering a house when it is promised but not actually promised. Nor does this lead to an infinite regress, because engagement can occur even through bodily exertion at the outset, driven by the initial desire to know. However, considering that further effort is required for each subsequent stage of engagement, a discerning person requires the statement of the relationship and so forth. Furthermore, the mere relationship and such are not the sole motive for engagement among those seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); what then? It is the intended purpose (*prayojana*) and the subject matter (*abhidheya*), designated as the means to that purpose and so on. And there is also the relationship of the treatise with both the teacher and the student. Thus says the Sūtra: "From the knowledge of the reality of the instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the rest, the attainment of the supreme good. In this context, the relationship between the treatise, the student, and the teacher is not explicitly stated because it is already established by logic; however, it must be made clear by the commentator. By doing so, the listener engages, thinking: "This treatise is connected to its purpose and so forth; this teacher is competent in explaining this treatise; and I too am qualified to hear it here"—thus, he believes the intended goal will be accomplished right here. If it is asked: "Why is the ultimate purpose, known as the supreme good, which is the remote and primary motive for engagement, not mentioned in the summary?"—the answer is no, because that purpose is already obtained simply by stating the purpose called "awakening" (*prabodha*), since awakening has that [supreme good] as its object. We shall explain later how awakening has that as its object. Alternatively, the knowledge of reality is determined by Vedic scripture and the Sūtras to be the cause of the supreme good; therefore, the inquiry (*jijñāsā*) is directed toward the very cause of that knowledge of reality, and the subordinate purpose is stated in accordance with that.

The term "child" (*śiśu*) is employed to indicate that even those who have approached this [teaching] under other teachers—lacking correct knowledge of the inner self—are to be instructed like sons. (The distinctions of the subject matter.)

In this context, the subject matter (*abhidheya*) is twofold: primary (*pradhāna*) and secondary (*apradhāna*). Among these, the primary is the categories (*padārtha*) such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), while their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) are secondary, because a definition exists for the purpose of determining those [categories]. Even among the means of valid cognition and so forth, the object of cognition (*prameya*) is primary; and even within that, the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*) is primary, because all others exist for its sake. If it is argued that the definition alone must be considered primary—on the grounds that in a *tatpuruṣa* compound the final member is predominant—the answer is no; for we also observe cases where the first member is predominant, such as in the expression “a hundred students were fed” (*chātraśataṃ bhojitam*). Alternatively, let the definition be primary; and thus the author of the Sūtras, having stated that the "true nature" (*tattva*) of the means of valid cognition and so forth is expressed by a genitive case denoting a remainder (*śaiṣikī ṣaṣṭhī*), says: “From the knowledge of the true nature, there is the attainment of the supreme good” (*tattvajñānān niḥśreyasādhigamaḥ*). Furthermore, the true nature of the means of valid cognition and so forth is said to be precisely their definition. The objection that it would follow that the means of valid cognition and so forth are unknowable and indefinable is also not to be raised. For a cow is certainly not left undetermined when its definition—consisting of the dewlap, hump, tail-hair, hooves, and so on—is described; on the contrary, it becomes well-determined. To explain: a definition is called the property that determines things without confusion with one another by virtue of its own capacity for determination. If that [definition] is not determined, the things themselves remain undetermined. Therefore, the definition holds primacy.
{A doubt regarding the lack of purpose for the Cārvāka in stating the definitions of the means of valid cognition, etc.:} Now, it has been said:
"The means of valid cognition are well-known, and worldly practice is carried out by means of them."
"When the definition of the means of valid cognition has been stated, its purpose is not understood."

The same should be stated regarding the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth. By this, the following is said: first of all, the object of definition (*lakṣya*) is not produced by its definition (*lakṣaṇa*), because we observe that in the case of a cow and the like, the possession of dewlaps and other such characteristics and the cow itself exist at the same time, and because the objects of definition such as the Self (*ātman*) are eternal. Nor is the object made known [by the definition], because in the world we observe the cognition of the object even when the definition is unknown, and furthermore, an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) would be difficult to avoid. If it is argued that activity and cessation, verbal discourse, and the practice of sublation and non-sublation (*bādhyabādhaka*) regarding the means of knowledge and so forth cannot be established without a definition, we say no; for even those are already established. In the world, the very characteristic of sublation and non-sublation is indeed established. If it is argued that the technical designation (*saṃjñā*) is not established by rule, we say no; for it is well-known. For instance, even women, Śūdras, and others are seen saying things such as, "Your word is sublated by perception itself. Therefore, the definition of the means of knowledge and so forth is useless.
The refutation of that [position].

In this regard, first of all, regarding the position that [the universal] is produced, the very non-acceptance [of that position] is the refutation. As for its apprehension, however, it is indeed observed through the medium of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), as in the case of a cow and so forth. For instance—even among many cows—one determines one's own cow by perceiving its unique defining characteristic; whereas one who is ignorant of the characteristic remains in doubt. In this way, examples should be understood for all specific cases, whether stationary or moving, such as jewels and the like. If it is argued that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if the defining characteristic itself were to be determined by another defining characteristic, we say no; for a restriction is accepted only with respect to the object of doubt. This restriction is accepted: "Only in the case of a thing where there is doubt is there a determination preceded by the perception of a defining characteristic. Furthermore, doubt does not exist everywhere; for doubt does not arise even regarding specific features such as curvature and the like, in the same way that it arises regarding posts (*sthāṇu*) and the like. Moreover, if that were accepted, it would contradict perception and other means of valid cognition. Now, why is it that doubt occurs only regarding posts and the like, and not also regarding the series of specific features such as curvature? [The opponent replies: Because the causes of doubt exist in the case of posts and the like, but do not exist elsewhere. We say: No, because the challenge remains here as well—why is it that the cause of doubt does not exist even in the series of those specific features? In this matter, the answer must be given in terms of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of things, which simply are so.
Even a property that is non-pervasive and so forth can function as a definition.

We, however, speaking of an object exactly as it has been perceived, do not deserve censure. If it is argued that even in a state of doubt there is certainty due to the perception of a specific feature (*viśeṣa*), and not merely from the perception of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*), we say no; for the words *viśeṣa*, *aṅka*, *cihna*, and *lakṣaṇa* are synonyms. If it is argued that this would lead to the consequence that both the under-extensive (*avyāpaka*) and the over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*) could also be considered definitions, we say no; for even the over-extensive is a differentiator (*viśeṣaka*). When even something like horns is understood through some distinctive mark, it is then accepted as a definition of "cow. Even an under-extensive particularity is accepted as a definition, such as "possessing action" (*kriyāvattva*) for substance (*dravya*); for when "possessing action" is perceived, it does not fail to produce the determination of substance. Indeed, the fault of under-extension is raised only against one who intends that "whatever possesses action is a substance," leading to the consequence that space and the like, being inactive, would not be substances. But for one who intends that "whatever possesses action is necessarily a substance," the definition is faultless. By this, the definitions of the self (*ātman*) as desire and so forth, of the body as the locus of movement, of the mind (*manas*) as the non-simultaneity of cognitions, and of determination (*nirṇaya*) as "having deliberated" and so forth, are explained. As for other instances of the defined (*lakṣya*), such as liberated selves (*muktātman*), even in the absence of the stated definition, the conventional usage of "self" and so forth is established through another definition. Just as in the case of space and the like, the conventional usage of "substance" is established by the definition of "possessing qualities" despite the absence of "possessing action," so too the conventional usage of "self" is established in liberated selves by the property of "selfhood" (*ātmatva*); the usage of "mind" in the internal organs of the dead by "mind-ness" (*manastva*); the usage of "body" in bodies within stones by "bodiness" (*śarīratva*) and "being the locus of sense organs"; and the usage of "determination" in determinations such as those regarding the palm of the hand by the experience of non-deviant ascertainment (*niścaya*). Thus it should be inferred in other cases as well. If it is argued that let there be only a pervasive definition, and that the statement of an under-extensive definition is useless, we say no; for this [under-extensive] is also capable of determining its own specific instance, and because the definition of desire and so forth is indeed sufficient for the cognition of "self-ness" and the like.

If it is argued that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) because, even when a definition is subject to dispute, another definition must be stated [to resolve it], we say no; for such dispute is impossible in every case. How so? If this disputant indeed understands the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the means (*upāya*) and the end (*upeya*), whether sentient or insentient, then by that same principle, any other matter should be established for that particular person. On the other hand, if he does not understand anything at all, then the utterance of specific words directed toward that particular person would be impossible. Why? Because even after seeing a tree or the like, if one were to say just anything, one would be disregarded like a madman.

Nor is this succession of definitions accepted. Why? Because the definition of a definition (lakṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa), by virtue of its exclusion of the entire class of definitions, excludes itself as well. Just as the sentence "All sound is impermanent" expresses the impermanence of itself as well; or as the injunction "The Veda is to be studied" prescribes the state of being studyable for itself as well. If it is argued that it is illogical for the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) to be one and the same in a single action, we say no, because such a thing is observed in some cases, just like the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*). If it is argued that by that very example there would follow non-difference at all times, we say no, because the difference between the cloth, the shuttle, the loom, and so forth, is established through perception and other means. Thus, since it serves as the cause of certainty regarding everything that is a subject of doubt, the statement of a definition is not purposeless. If it is argued that if the definition alone is the cause of certainty, then the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is redundant, we say no, because the definition also possesses the status of a means of valid cognition insofar as it has certainty as its result. Now, is a definition a synonym for the means of valid cognition, or is it one of the [standard] types such as perception, or something distinct from them? Some say it is a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*). We, however, have already stated: "Words such as *viśeṣa* and *aṅga* are synonyms. For this very reason, it is not a synonym for the means of valid cognition, because everything that establishes a means of valid cognition is itself a means of valid cognition; whereas a definition is specifically that which distinguishes a particular object of knowledge (*prameya-viśeṣaka*). And it also receives the designation of "perception" and so forth by virtue of its cooperation with the sense organs and other factors. Its separate mention, like that of the members of a syllogism (*avayava*), is due to its specific utility.
The function of the statement of characteristics as the remover of error.

If it is argued that the definitions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth are already well-known even without a treatise (*śāstra*), and that therefore a treatise for that purpose is useless—since otherwise how could worldly people engage in the practical usage of "means of valid cognition" and so on?—we say no. This is because the treatise provides a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the sake of dispelling error. For those who are deluded and adhered to other philosophical systems (*darśana*) state various definitions in different ways, and thus they cause confusion regarding the means of valid cognition and so forth even in the world. Therefore, by restating the definitions that are already well-known, that delusion is removed, just as the delusion of one who has seen his father mistakenly is removed by a restatement of his identifying marks. To explain: having restated the definitions of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, where deluded persons perceive even correct means of valid cognition as fallacious when their objects are the self (*ātman*) and so on, or perceive non-entities such as presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) and the like as actual entities, there [the treatise] prescribes the truth. Conversely, where they perceive even fallacious means of valid cognition as true means of valid cognition when their objects are non-duality, momentariness, the Vedas being non-eternal, or the non-existence of the self and so forth, or where they perceive non-entities as entities, there [the treatise] prohibits them. Thus, the purpose of the restatement should be understood to apply to the definitions of the self and so forth, as well as to the definitions of doubt and the rest. By this, the following objection is also refuted: "Knowledge of the self and so forth, as well as liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) as the goal, are already established in the Upaniṣads and other Yoga treatises; therefore, this treatise which prescribes them is useless. It is not the case that knowledge of the self or liberation is being prescribed here. Rather, having restated what is already established, the treatise establishes—by way of supporting the self and so forth, and by way of refuting all opposing views—that such knowledge is grounded in the means of valid cognition. This is for the sake of removing the delusion of those whose minds have been captivated by the Buddhist (*Śākya*) and other systems, who perceive the knowledge of the self and so forth as false and a cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), and who perceive liberation as being accompanied by a self and as non-existent. Consequently, once a discerning person has become free from doubt by determining that everything stated in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere is indeed true, he practices the very means already established therein, and the attainment of liberation occurs.
The general definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And thus, having established that the self and other categories are supported by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the venerable author of the Sūtras stated: "by means of the methods of the internal discipline" (*adhyātmavidhyupāyaiḥ*). Now, one might object: "Even those who practice after grasping the meaning of the spiritual science (*adhyātmaśāstra*) according to the maxim of 'Śiva’s Fist'—that is, keeping the essential core secret while giving away the rest—surely attain liberation; therefore, this treatise is useless. This is not so, because it is meaningful for those who seek logical justification (*nyāya*). A treatise is not commenced for the sake of favoring everyone, for it is impossible to favor all persons, owing to the infinity of living beings and their unsettled intentions. Rather, it is for the sake of favoring qualified persons (*adhikārin*). And here, there certainly exist qualified persons who seek logical justification and possess specific doubts regarding particular points; even for them, once they have ascertained the meaning of the spiritual science through mere statements, there may still arise doubt due to some cause when hearing conflicting views. For their sake, it is proper to listen to this treatise, both for the purpose of favoring others and for the sake of maintaining one's own conviction. Thus it has been said: "For the sake of protecting the determination of reality" (*tattvādhyavasāyasaṃrakṣaṇārtham*), and so forth. In this way, all the sūtras consisting of enunciation (*uddeśa*) and definition (*lakṣaṇa*) are for the purpose of restatement (*anuvāda*); however, the sūtras of examination (*parīkṣā*) are to be seen as meaningful through the result of that restatement, which consists of injunctions and prohibitions (*vidhipratiṣedha*). Such is the ultimate purpose of this treatise.

[Objection: But surely, just as those seeking results engage in agriculture and the like, or in the hearing of the scriptures, solely because of doubt regarding the result, so too will it be with respect to the means to liberation; therefore, what is the use of this treatise? [Response: No, because the fruit of agriculture and the like is for the most part seen, whereas liberation is entirely unseen and thus impossible to conceive [prior to practice]. Furthermore, in agriculture and the like, there is no engagement involving the total renunciation of previously acquired wealth, wives, and so forth, nor is there any discrepancy regarding the result; however, in the case of the means to liberation, there is a possibility of error. Therefore, by those who act with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārin*), certainty regarding liberation along with its means is sought as the cause for removing doubt about the lack of benefit. And that certainty arises from the ascertainment of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); the ascertainment of the means of valid cognition, in turn, arises from the ascertainment of their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, the definition itself is stated first.

"A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is that which is the instrument for correct experience. By this, its distinction from fallacious means of cognition (*pramāṇābhāsa*), which are of the same class, and from objects of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth, which are of a different class, is established. In the same way, it should be explained that the definitions of perception and the other [means of cognition] also serve to exclude both similar and dissimilar classes.
[The purpose of the word *samyak* (correct).]

To one who thinks that there are no objects of exclusion belonging to the same class as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), he says: “The inclusion of the term ‘correct’ (*samyak*) is for the purpose of excluding doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*). This means that the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), or removal (*nirākaraṇa*), of doubt and error—which might otherwise be considered results of valid cognition—is the purpose of the term. Alternatively, the meaning is that it is for the purpose of the exclusion (*apoha*), or differentiation (*vyāvṛtti*), of experience from doubt and error. Consequently, the status of being a valid cognition is thereby excluded even from the means of achieving those [doubt and error]. For it is by means of the correctness or incorrectness of the result that the correctness or incorrectness of the valid cognition and its semblance (*pramāṇābhāsa*) can be determined; therefore, the word “correct” is explained as a qualifier of the result—namely, that it is both correct and an experience. Correctness consists in having the nature of a determination of an object as it truly is; incorrectness consists in having the nature of an experience contrary to that.
The definition of doubt.

Furthermore, this [definition] applies to both doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*), because such usage is observed in common worldly practice and in the treatises (*śāstra*). Since it is impossible to abandon or acquire something whose nature is unknown, the nature of these two must be stated. Now, this is said: "Among these, doubt is knowledge that is non-determinative (*anavadhāraṇajñāna*). This means it is both non-determinative and knowledge. If it is argued that this is untenable due to contradiction, we say no; for the word "knowledge" (*jñāna*) has as its cause the universal (*jāti*) [of knowability], just like the word "cow" (*go*) and others. Just as words such as "cow" (*go*) or "lotus" (*paṅkaja*) are not conventionally fixed to their respective meanings by virtue of their etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*), but rather by virtue of having a universal as their cause—so too the word "knowledge" is conventionally fixed to its own meaning by virtue of the universal "knowability" (*jñānatva*). And that universal, "knowability," and so forth, subsists in individuals (*vyakti*) whose natures are either determinate or non-determinate. It has been stated that non-determinate knowledge is "non-determinative. For this very reason, the consequence of non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) being a form of doubt does not arise, since even that possesses a determinate nature. And its determinate nature is inferable from the memory produced by it. To explain: a memory of the form "this object is not there at all," "that object is similar to this one," or "it is greater or less than this"—such a memory indicates that the prior experience was determinate in nature. And that experience from which a non-determinate memory arises is itself a doubt, precisely because it is non-determinate in nature. For memory conforms to the form of the experience; how could it be otherwise? If it is asked: "How can the knowledge arising from the first glance of the sense organ—which occurs without causes such as the perception of specific features—be either determinate or non-determinate? We say no; it arises in that way due to the power of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Otherwise, out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), the perception of specific features that arises without further perception of specific features would itself be non-determinate. If that were non-determinate, then even the possessor of those specific features would remain undetermined, and the entire world would be non-determinate in nature. Indeed, we do not observe a lack of determination regarding a person based on a non-determinate cognition of his head, hands, and other specific features. Furthermore, if you admit the efficacy of unseen merit and the like, let determination arise from that alone; what is the use of a perception of specific features that is itself non-determinate and lacks a valid means of proof (*pramāṇa*)? Thus, since there exists in some cases knowledge that is determinate and in others non-determinate even without causes such as the perception of specific features, the definition—"doubt is non-determinative knowledge"—is faultless.
The divisions of doubt and their definitions.

If the definition of doubt is faultless by this much alone, then is the Sūtra beginning with "from the occurrence of common and multiple properties" (*samānānekadharmopapatteḥ*) redundant? It is not redundant, for it serves the purpose of classification and the purpose of defining the specific [types]. To that end, he says: "And that [doubt] is fivefold," etc. If it is argued that doubt is impossible from the mere presence of common properties and so forth, we say no, because there is no such restriction. For it is not restricted in this way, that doubt arises *only* from common properties; what then? The mention of specific causes—such as the contact between sense organ and object—is for the purpose of excluding those of the same class (*samānajātīya*). However, the exclusion of those of a different class (*vijātīya*) has already been accomplished by the general definition itself and is therefore not repeated here; for the specific definition is to be understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*) of the general definition. By this, the following meaning is established: from common properties included within the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there arises a non-ascertaining cognition (*anavadhāraṇajñāna*); thus, it is a distinct entity from those doubts produced by causal complexes characterized by multiple properties and so forth. This should be explained similarly in other cases as well; therefore, there is no fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*).

The author of the Sūtra, however, included the mention of "the non-determination of perception and non-perception" (*upalabdhyanupalabdhyavyavasthā*) and so forth for the purpose of refuting objections (*kucodya*) and to provide examples of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*); it is not by this alone that the complete causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is established, because internal factors such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and the mind (*manas*) have not been mentioned. Furthermore, the objection here is as follows: "Even the perception of common properties (*samānadharmopalambha*) is not a cause of doubt, because even when that [perception] exists, doubt is not observed in one who is walking among grass and other such things. To this, the reply is: "It is that which requires particulars" (*viśeṣāpekṣa*). That doubt whose cause is a requirement—meaning an expectation or a memory directed toward particulars—is described thus. What is meant? Since the expectation of particulars is the cause of doubt, doubt does not arise in its absence. Nor is something a non-cause simply because an effect is not produced despite its presence due to the absence of auxiliary causes; for if that were so, it would follow that everything is a non-cause.

[Objection: But even so, when one’s beloved is standing at a distance, doubt does not arise even though both [the common property and the desire for particulars] are present; therefore, the common property (*samāna-dharma*), even when accompanied by the desire for particulars, is not the cause [of doubt]. [Response: The answer to this is: “Because of the non-settlement of perception and non-perception” (*upalabdhyanupalabdhy-avyavasthā*). The meaning is: because there is an absence of a cause for certainty in the form of either affirmation or negation. What is meant is this: it is not only the desire for particulars that is the auxiliary cause, but also the non-settlement of perception and non-perception; therefore, even in the absence of that [desire for particulars], doubt does not fail to arise. Likewise, for one moving with great speed, although there is the perception of a common property such as “tree-ness” in *panasa* trees and the like, doubt does not arise because, despite the non-settlement of perception and non-perception, there is an absence of the desire for particulars. Thus, it is accepted that the common property is the cause of doubt only when it is endowed with all its auxiliary factors. Furthermore, since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors are common to other effects as well, their status as auxiliaries is understood even if they are not explicitly mentioned here; this is the intention of the author. Just as with the common property, the same should be explained for the multiple properties (*aneka-dharma*) and so forth, provided they are endowed with all their auxiliary factors. The meaning of this very point has been elaborated upon in the *Parīkṣā*, so there is no redundancy. Regarding the term *samāna-dharma*, two compounds should be understood as alternatives: a *karmadhāraya* and a *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. When it is a *karmadhāraya*, a common (*samāna*)—that is, similar—property characterized by size (*parimāṇa*) and so forth is obtained, which differs with each substratum. When it is a *tatpuruṣa*, a property not differing from one substratum to another, characterized by a universal (*sāmānya*), parts (*avayava*), conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and so forth, is obtained. An example of this is given: “For instance. Verticality (*ūrdhvatva*) is the cause of the cognition of “upward” in a long object situated in a specific direction. Whether that be a dimension (*parimāṇa*), a universal (*sāmānya*), or what is called a property distinct from the six categories (*ṣaṭ-padārtha*), no investigation is made of it here because it is of no use [to the present discussion].

Regarding the phrase “from multiple properties” (*anekadharmāt*): “multiple” (*aneka*) refers to both that which belongs to the intended class and its opposite. A property that distinguishes [an object] from multiple [others], or one that does not belong to multiple [others], or one that is excluded from multiple [others], or one that causes the cognition of multiple [alternatives]—is called a “multiple property” (*anekadharma*) by way of establishing difference (*bheda*). Thus, in all cases, the compound is formed by eliding the middle term (*madhyamapadalopa*). In every respect, what is intended is an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) property. An example is: “Is this sound eternal or non-eternal, because it possesses a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) such as space (*ākāśa*)? But how can an uncommon property produce doubt? For this [property] has never been perceived together with contradictory particulars (*viruddhaviśeṣa*), such that its perception might serve as a cause for the recollection of them. Nor is recollection appropriate when there is no perception of a related object, because that would entail the recollection of all experienced objects at all times. Furthermore, doubt does not arise without the recollection of contradictory particulars, since such a thing has never been observed. Moreover, this uncommon property is itself a particular (*viśeṣa*) of its own substrata; and since doubt is removed by the perception of a particular, how could doubt arise from it? Indeed, a doubt regarding a cow is never observed to arise from the perception of “cowness” (*gotva*). And if it did, it would lead to the consequence of its [doubt’s] never being cut off. That doubt which arises from the perception of a common property (*samānadharmadarśana*) is removed by the perception of a particular; but as for that which arises from the perception of a particular, how will it ever reach destruction? Therefore, an uncommon property is not a cause of doubt.

On this point, some offer the following rebuttal: "Since a specific property (*viśeṣa*) is observed in two ways—both among things of the same class (*tulyajātīya*) and among things that are different in nature (*arthāntarabhūta*)—the non-observation of such a property along with contradictory specific properties does not constitute a reason for the 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason] to be a cause of doubt. What is meant by this is as follows: when impermanent objects are intended to be expressed as being of the same class, then permanent things—which are different in nature—are mentioned. In those things of the same class, such as jars (*ghaṭa*), and in those different in nature, such as the self (*ātman*), a specific property like "jar-ness" or "self-ness" is observed in both ways, meaning it is perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as coexisting with both permanence and impermanence. Now, there exists in sound a specific property, namely audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) and its status as a specific quality of space (*ākāśaviśeṣaguṇatva*). We do not know whether this specific property belongs to sound as something permanent or as something impermanent. This, they argue, is not a cause of doubt distinct from the "common property" (*samānadharmāt*); why? Because the possession of a specific property (*viśeṣavattva*) is a cause of doubt only insofar as it serves as a basis for the recollection of contradictory specific properties. And since this is common to both the permanent and the impermanent—just like the possession of a general property (*sāmānyavattva*)—how could it be a distinct cause? Some say that the previous mention was of the possession of a common property, whereas the present mention is of the possession of an uncommon property; thus, they are stated separately only on account of this distinction. However, we maintain that its status as a cause of doubt is due precisely to its uncommon nature. How so? Exclusion from permanent things is observed only in impermanent things, and exclusion from impermanent things is observed only in permanent things. But this sound, by virtue of its specific properties such as audibility, is excluded from both the permanent and the impermanent. Therefore, we do not know: is it impermanent because it is excluded from permanent things like a jar, or is it permanent because it is excluded from impermanent things like the self? Furthermore, permanence and impermanence cannot coexist in one place, as they are properties established by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthitidharmatva*). Nor does this lead to an infinite regress of doubt, because the auxiliary causes—such as the lack of a definitive perception or non-perception—cannot occur continuously. Nor does it lead to the impossibility of cessation, because doubt ceases upon the observation of specific properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*). Finally, it does not follow that "being produced" and other such properties would also cause doubt simply because they share the status of being specific properties like audibility; for "being produced" and the like have been observed elsewhere to be invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with impermanence. Therefore, it is established that even an uncommon property is a cause of doubt.

Alternatively, it is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "many and that is a property" (*anekaścāsau dharmaś ca*). By this, the status of being a cause of doubt is obtained for a contradictory plurality of properties perceived in a single locus, as in: "Is the mind material because it possesses motion like an arrow, or is it immaterial because it is intangible like space? Now, materiality and immateriality cannot coexist in one place, because they are properties existing in mutual exclusion. Furthermore, the lack of a fixed determination regarding perception and non-perception acts here as a cooperative factor; therefore, there is no consequence of doubt occurring at all times or in all places. If it is argued that when those two [properties] are of equal strength, their contradiction would result in the non-production of a definitive judgment (*nirṇaya*) rather than the production of doubt, we say no, because that very [state of doubt] is established by this fact. For in the absence of a definitive judgment, the person does not remain like an insentient wall, nor does he act erroneously; rather, he is observed reflecting or posing a question. And neither reflection nor the posing of a question is possible without doubt. If it is argued that this is merely a state of indecision (*anadhyavasāya*), [we reply: no.

Now, if you think that when a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*) does not arise, this is a case of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) rather than doubt (*saṃśaya*), that is incorrect; for it would follow that even from conflicting testimony (*vipratipatti*) there would be non-determination. Indeed, there is no distinction whatsoever between this [perception of multiple properties] and conflicting testimony. Furthermore, because it has been established that non-determination is included within doubt, and because in another passage you yourself stated that two contradictory properties constitute a cause of doubt. Thus, having posed the question, "Is 'going-ness' a synonym for 'action-ness' or is it another universal (*sāmānya*)?", and having asked, "From what source do you have this doubt?", you stated that the two properties—the being the cause of a pervasive cognition like 'action-ness' across all [motions] such as upward throwing, and being mentioned separately like upward throwing—are the causes of doubt. Therefore, even a single property that is manifold is a cause of doubt.

Regarding "contradictory discourse" (*vipratipatti*): contradictory discourse is a conflicting report. Upon hearing such [discourse], when the previously mentioned auxiliary conditions are present, doubt arises: "Are the sense organs material (*bhautika*) or non-material (*abhautika*)? "Does a self exist distinct from the body and so forth, or does it not exist? "Is it eternal or non-eternal? Such contradictory discourses are to be understood in this way. Knowledge proceeding by way of affirmation is perception (*upalabdhi*). Knowledge proceeding by way of negation, as well as the non-arising of knowledge, is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). These two have distinct causes for doubt and distinct characteristics of non-determination; therefore, the five-sūtra formulation should be seen here as follows: "Doubt is a deliberation requiring a specific determination, arising from the occurrence of perception and from the non-determination of perception and non-perception"; and "Doubt is a deliberation requiring a specific determination, arising from the occurrence of non-perception and from the non-determination of perception and non-perception. This same logic should be applied to the other cases, such as "from the occurrence of a common property" and so forth. Thus, the objection that "doubt would result everywhere, both regarding the object of perception and the object of non-perception," is untenable, for we do not intend for mere perception or mere non-perception alone to be the cause of doubt here. Granted that this may be so, nevertheless, these two are not different from the "common property. How so? If doubt concerns the very object of perception and non-perception as being existent or non-existent, then "perceptibility" and "non-perceptibility" are the common properties. If, on the other hand, doubt concerns whether things currently perceived or unperceived—such as water or a *piśāca*—are actually present or absent, even then "being manifested by cognition" and "not being manifested" are the common properties. On this point, some offer a rebuttal: "The common and manifold properties reside in the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), whereas perception and non-perception reside in the knower (*jñātṛ*); it is due to this distinction that they are mentioned separately. We, however, say: they are mentioned separately for a specific purpose. How so? By means of non-perception alone, proponents assert the non-existence of heaven, the unseen force (*apūrva*), deities, and so forth; by means of perception alone, they assert the permanence of sound, consciousness in the body, and the non-difference of universals (*sāmānya*) from their substrates. It is for the sake of refuting these views that the mere nature of perception and non-perception is stated to be a cause of doubt.
The non-distinctness of *ūhana* (speculative reasoning) and *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment) from *saṃśaya* (doubt).

By the inclusion of the term "correct" (*samyak*), doubt (*saṃśaya*) and error (*viparyaya*) are excluded. Now, one might object: "By what are conjecture (*ūha*) and non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) excluded? To this, the following answer should be given: "Because they lack definitiveness (*anavadhāraṇatva*). The meaning is that when [conjecture and non-determination] are not distinct entities from doubt, then by the very exclusion of doubt, the status of conjecture and non-determination as results of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) is also excluded, since they are of the same nature as it. Thus, the author of the Sūtras employed the term "determinate in nature" (*vyavasāyātmaka*) solely for the purpose of excluding doubt, and not another term for the purpose of excluding conjecture and non-determination. If it is argued: "Doubt is that which apprehends two objects through an alternative (*vikalpa*), whereas conjecture and non-determination are different from that; so how can they not be distinct entities from doubt?", we say: No. For it is illogical for things subsumed under a single definition to be considered distinct entities merely on account of internal differences (*avāntaravaidharmya*). It is not reasonable to claim that stone is a distinct entity from earth simply because it differs from clay. Just as in common worldly usage the term "earth" refers only to specific portions of the ground, yet in the technical treatise (*śāstra*) earth-ness is accepted even for stones and the like because they share the common property of possessing odor (*gandhavattva*); likewise, because they share the common property of lacking definitiveness, conjecture and non-determination are accepted as being of the nature of doubt.

If it is argued that because there is no difference in their being means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the others would follow as being one, we reply: this is not a fault, because we accept it. This entire category of means of valid cognition is indeed one; its division into perception and so forth is merely internal. Furthermore, the ground for the conventional usage of "perception" does not exist in inference and the rest, nor does the ground for the conventional usage of "inference" exist elsewhere, such that the conventional distinction between perception and the others would cease. By this, the oneness of inference and scripture is also refuted, since there is no difference in their being means for mediate experience (*parokṣānubhava*). Nor is it the case that the ground for the conventional usage of "doubt"—namely, being non-definitive knowledge—does not exist in [the process of] reasoning (*ūha*) and so forth.
And what is this *ūha*? It is a cognition consisting of a state of "it must be so," occurring in the interval between doubt and certainty. For example: "It is a carriage track."

In that case, doubt (*saṃśaya*) [is not a distinct category], because its nature is non-determination (*anavadhāraṇātmakatva*). If you argue that it is not doubt because its nature is non-conceptual (*avikalpātmakatva*)—that is, if you think that doubt consists of conceptualization (*vikalpātmaka*), such as "Is this a post or a person?"—then we reply: This [subsequent cognition] occurs after the suspicion of another alternative has ceased due to a subverting means of knowledge (*bādhakapramāṇa*); therefore, it is not doubt. Nor is it a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), because it arises even in the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhakapramāṇa*). For a definitive conclusion does not arise solely from the negation of the counter-position; as it is stated, "by both the position and the counter-position," and because it is enumerated separately [from doubt and conclusion]. As for the claim that doubt is conceptual in nature, that is not so, because doubt is observed otherwise as well. For instance, one who has understood a specific result may have doubt regarding a specific means: "What is the specific means for this result? Or, having determined that death is certain for one born, but not knowing the specific time, one doubts: "When will my death occur? Although the conceptualization of "today" or "tomorrow" is not explicitly experienced here, it is indeed obtained through reasoning. To explain: first, it must be a person, because one observes an abundance of reasons for the possibility of it being a person. Yet another alternative might also exist, because there is no certainty regarding the absence of every other alternative. If there were such certainty, it would be a definitive conclusion. For the specific characteristic of a person is simply the state of being upright, characterized by the absence of all other alternatives. Similarly, seeing a particular field, someone thinks: "There must be an abundance of crops for the owner of this field," or seeing a particular householder, "There must be food available," and so forth. In these cases, there is no certainty regarding the absence of other alternatives, yet a cognition consisting of a "must-be-ness" (*bhavitavyatā*) is observed. Regarding the reason "because it arises subsequent to doubt": if this is stated with reference to the category [of cognitions], then it is not different from the probandum (*sādhyāviśiṣṭa*), since inferential knowledge (*ūhajñāna*) is also accepted as a specific kind of doubt. If, however, it is intended with reference to individual instances (*vyakti*), then it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), because doubt itself arises at a time subsequent to the occurrence of a doubt-instance. The argument "because it is enumerated separately" is also inconclusive, because the members of a syllogism (*avayava*), though not distinct from the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), are nevertheless enumerated separately. And this is also true for fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) and so on, even though they are included within the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Nor is there any contradiction with the Sūtra for this very reason, since the separate mention is made for the sake of a different purpose. First, the general purpose of doubt is to initiate the process of reasoning (*nyāyapravartakatva*). How so? "Reasoning does not proceed toward an object that is neither unperceived nor already determined; rather, it proceeds toward what is doubted. What is the reason? In the case of the unperceived, there is the consequence of the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhatva*); in the case of the determined, there is the consequence of futility (*vaiyarthyaprasaṅga*). Therefore, reasoning proceeds toward what is perceived in a general way but not determined in its particulars. But what is precisely determined here? If it is that reasoning proceeds only toward a doubted object, that is not so, because its operation is observed even toward what is not doubted. For neither the proponent nor the opponent has doubt when they employ reasoning. If you say this rule applies only to inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), we say no, because we observe the operation of inferring smoke and so on while wandering in a forest for some other purpose. If you then maintain the restriction that reasoning proceeds only toward a doubted object, that too is impossible, because we observe non-operation in some cases due to a lack of interest or other causes. Thus, doubt is not the cause of the initiation of reasoning. This is not correct, because we accept the prior restriction with respect to suitability (*yogyatā*). What is intended is that reasoning proceeds toward an object that is doubted—that is, toward an object suitable for doubt. Suitability consists in a general perception accompanied by non-determination of particulars, as well as disagreement (*vipratipatti*) in debates and the like. This being the case, it follows that error (*viparyaya*) should also be mentioned separately, just like doubt, as a constituent of inquiry (*vicārāṅga*), even though it is included under the categories of "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*) and "objects of knowledge" (*prameya*). For a reason does not attain the status of a valid proof when applied to a subject (*dharmin*) determined through error. Nor is anyone observed acting for the sake of removing error in the same way as for the sake of removing doubt. Even a respondent who acts to remove error does so with the intent of refuting disagreement, for the sake of nourishing his own conviction, and for the sake of instilling conviction in students and others, regarding the object of disagreement. And since that object of disagreement is the object of doubt, it is doubt alone that is stated by the author of the Sūtra as a constituent of inquiry. Therefore, it is established that the purpose of doubt is to initiate the process of reasoning.

If inference (*tarka*) is included within doubt (*saṃśaya*), what then is the purpose of its separate mention? It is said: its purpose is to assist the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The former teachers [state]: "The means of valid cognition, operating upon an object distinct from that of inference, are assisted by inference. We, however, maintain this: inference is taught separately for the sake of qualifying the engagement in debate (*vāda*) and other such activities. How so? Some think thus: "The engagement of a Naiyāyika in debates and the like is not proper. Why? Because for one who investigates, engagement is impossible without certainty. And here there is no certainty [of the form]: 'By this refutation or this proof, I shall defeat or instruct the opponent,' because the intention of another is difficult to discern. For even in the case of one whose wisdom has not been tested at the time, when being instructed by a teacher or the like, non-comprehension or miscomprehension is sometimes observed. Likewise, a teacher too is sometimes found rendered speechless. Therefore, since even the means for one's own comprehension is fallible, and because there is no certainty regarding the means for instructing others, engagement in debates and the like would be untenable; thus, the thorough knowledge of debate and so forth would be useless. To those [who hold such views], the author of the Sūtras, having separately mentioned and defined inference, stated that it is a means for engaging in debates and the like in the words: "The proof and refutation by means of *pramāṇas* and *tarka*" (*Nyāyasūtra* 1.2.1). This is what is meant: in debates and the like, the Naiyāyika must state the proof and refutation either as determined by *pramāṇas* or as brought within the scope of *tarka*, because they serve as the causes for victory and defeat. Why? Because through them, the attainment of the goal and the avoidance of the undesired are possible. When one engages after having ascertained the matter through a *pramāṇa*, then that matter is indeed established for him. Even when one engages with a probable matter due to the occurrence of reasons in the absence of certainty, that matter is nonetheless established for him. If it should fail by chance—just as for a weaver engaged with threads, the cloth [might not appear]—nevertheless, even when challenged by others, a Naiyāyika should not engage in debates and the like until his own capability, characterized by excellence in knowledge and so forth, and the opposite incapacity of the opponent, as well as the capacity of the presiding judge (*sabhāpati*) and the assessors (*prāśnika*) to prevent unjust conduct and their impartiality, have become well-ascertained or well-probable. Furthermore, he who engages merely out of egoism, without investigating his own capability and so forth, is not truly a Naiyāyika, because he lacks the quality of an investigator. Indeed, even one who is very hungry does not, as a prudent person, proceed to eat food without first dispelling the suspicion that it might be poisoned.

If it is argued that even doubt regarding an object (*arthasaṃśaya*) is a cause for engagement—thinking that just as the three cases of doubt, inference, and certainty regarding what is not beneficial (*anartha*) are well-known causes for non-engagement, so too doubt, inference, and certainty regarding what is beneficial (*artha*) are causes for engagement; and how could it be that doubt has no role as a cause for engagement in debates and the like? The answer is: No, because doubt regarding an object is a cause for engagement in a different sense. When someone afflicted by suffering, while doubting among the various means for alleviating suffering, perceives no other means for the cessation of suffering, he engages precisely because of that doubt regarding the object. For one who engages, the cessation of suffering may eventually occur; for one who does not engage, the suffering remains exactly as it was. Likewise, when one doubts among the means for attaining a desired object, perceiving no other means for that desired object, and not anticipating excessive effort or the attainment of something harmful from engaging, he engages precisely because of that doubt regarding the object. Thus, for a discerning person (*vicāraka*), even doubt regarding an object is a cause for engagement, but not in the manner seen in gambling and similar activities. In the case of *jalpa* (wrangling) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), however, a great harm befalls the defeated party, whereas for one who does not engage there is no significant loss. Therefore, a discerning person should not initially engage in debate (*vāda*) out of mere doubt. For one who employs fallacious proofs (*asatsādhana*) and the like would have speech that is not worthy of attention, being reduced to the level of an unintelligent mind. Furthermore, even one who, having first reached a state of uncertainty due to the power of the proof, engages in debate with teachers and others to resolve that uncertainty, is still merely a student, because his intention is the acquisition of knowledge—like one engaged in reflecting on the meaning of a treatise—and is not a "proper debater" (*samyagvādī*). Thus, although it is included within doubt, *tarka* (reasoning) is taught separately for the purpose of qualifying engagement in debate and the like.
Non-ascertainment is included within doubt.

The state of non-determination (*anadhyavasāya*) expressed as "What is the name of this tree? does not differ from doubt (*saṃśaya*). For an object that is the referent of the notion "tree" is seen to be the referent of other notions as well, such as "mango" and so forth. Thus, having inferred a specific name in a general way and recollecting its distinctions—just as in the case of mangoes and the like—one doubts: "What is the name of this tree? Indeed, because both well-known and unknown specific names are numerous, a cognition that explicitly articulates a specific name does not arise, just as in the doubt regarding a post (*sthāṇu*) and so forth. This is just as when it is said, "One of your cows has calved," a doubt arises for even a master of a thousand cows who knows the specific names of his well-known cattle, taking the form: "Which cow has calved? It is not a conceptualization of specific names such as "Bhadra" or "Nanda. By this, the non-determination of weavers (*iṣukāra*) and others due to distraction or lack of interest should be seen as included within doubt. Even in the doubt regarding a post and so forth, there is indeed an intermediate articulation: "We do not know what this is. This alone does not constitute a different category [of cognition], because their defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is one, despite internal differences, just as between determinate (*savikalpaka*) and indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) perceptual cognitions. Thus, it is established that because there is no difference in the quality of being non-determinative (*anavadhāraṇatva*), *ūha* (speculative reasoning) and *anadhyavasāya* (non-determination) are not distinct categories from doubt.
The doubt regarding the non-existence of uncertainty.

But surely, there is no such thing as doubt at all; how then can its inclusion [within other categories] be considered? For instance: what appears in that cognition of doubt—is it the substratum (*dharmī*) or the property (*dharma*)? If it is the substratum, is it real (*tāttvika*) or unreal (*atāttvika*)? If it is real, how can that cognition have the nature of doubt? Because it would have the nature of apprehending a real object, like the certain perception of the palm of one's hand. If, on the other hand, it is unreal, then because its object is unreal, it is merely an error (*bhrānti*), like the cognition of [illusory] hair, and not a doubt. If it is the property—characterized as "being a post" (*sthāṇutva*) or "being a person" (*puruṣatva*) or both? If it is characterized as "being a post," then the same fault applies regarding whether it is real or unreal as before. If it is characterized as "being a person," the same fault applies there as well. If it is both, then the same fault applies to both the reality and unreality of the two. If one is real and the other is unreal, then it follows that the cognition regarding that object is simultaneously erroneous and non-erroneous. Furthermore, if a "doubtful object" appears in the cognition of doubt, does that doubtful object exist or not? Thus, this poor thing called "doubt" has fallen into a thicket of conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*); being neither true knowledge nor error, it is incapable of making itself known as a distinct category.
The refutation thereof.

Thus, this person, attempting to dispel doubt by the logic of the "cow-dung and milk-porridge" (the absurdity of rejecting the obvious for the trivial), is ignored even by ordinary people. For doubt, being essentially a state of non-ascertainment, is self-evident to all living beings; whether its object be the substratum (*dharmin*) or the attribute (*dharma*), whether it be a single cognition or multiple, and whether its objects be real or unreal—can these various alternatives possibly fragment it even by the width of a hair? If one were to deny a difference established by perception, one would have to deny the difference between pleasure and pain. If you say, "That is indeed desired," for what reason? If you say, "Because the destruction of reality (*tattvopaplava*) is established," then from what is that itself established? If you say, "Due to the absence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)," then from what is the absence of valid cognition established? If you say, "Due to the absence of a definition (*lakṣaṇa*)," then if an argument is offered for the establishment of that very absence of a definition, then that very argument constitutes a reality; how, then, can there be the establishment of the destruction of reality? On the other hand, if no argument is offered, then it remains unestablished due to the lack of an argument. Furthermore, if something were established by mere words alone, then every doctrine would be established.

Furthermore, since even the absence of a defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇābhāva*) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by virtue of establishing the absence of other means of valid cognition, how can the non-existence of all means of valid cognition be established? If you argue that we are merely posing a challenge to others and that nothing is being established [by us], that too is incorrect; for if the nature of the opponent is not ascertained, a challenge cannot logically be raised. Since no means of valid cognition are accepted, neither the world, nor its conventional transactions, nor the aesthetic appeal of that unexamined world is established; therefore, everything is mere idle chatter and useless. Some maintain that doubt regarding another object in a subject (*dharmin*) is not logical because one perceives a common property (*samānadharmādi*) belonging to a different object. That too is incorrect, because although there is no difference in their being "other objects," it is observed—as in the case of threads and so forth—that only some things act as auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) and producers (*janaka*) for something, while not everything acts as such for everything. Master Uddyotakara holds that doubt arises regarding that very [object] as a specific feature (*viśeṣa*) upon the perception of what possesses common properties and so forth. Therefore, doubt exists and is produced by common properties and the like.
{The Examination of Perversions}

Error (*viparyaya*) is a false determination (*mithyādhyavasāya*). Its meaning is that it is a certain conviction regarding an object contrary to reality, an overestimation of something as being what it is not. For example: "There are two moons," or the vision of elephants and so forth by one who is asleep. Why is this latter example provided? It is for the purpose of including all types of error and for the purpose of refuting other philosophical views. Some maintain here that dream-cognition is a distinct category from the results of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), memory (*smṛti*), and so on; therefore, its exclusion [from those categories] is established. For it is not logical that something subsumed under the definition of error should be a separate entity from it. Furthermore, even that dream-cognition which is distinct from [ordinary] error is not a different kind of ignorance (*avidyā*). What is the reason? First, whatever consists of non-determination is included within doubt (*saṃśaya*). If it is argued that there can be no doubt for one who is asleep because of the absence of the causes of doubt—such as the perception of common characteristics (*samānadharmādi*) in an object—we say no; for by the word "object" (*viṣaya*), the subject, namely the cognition itself, is intended. And that cognition of common characteristics, whether it be correct or erroneous, is accepted as a cause of doubt when accompanied by auxiliary factors, since the capacity of a cause is determined by the observation of its effect. As for that dream-cognition which manifests merely an experienced object, that is memory (*smaraṇa*). But that which consists of a correct experience is the result of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, such as the awareness of pleasure and the like. Thus, whatever dream-cognition is subsumed under a particular definition must be seen as included therein, just like waking cognition, and not as a separate entity from them. Error is also divided into many kinds according to the difference in its causes, as follows: through similarity, the cognition of a snake in a rope, or a person in a post, and so forth; through contact with another substance, the cognition of redness in a white cloth and the like, or in a crystal and the like, merely due to the proximity of an adjunct (*upādhi*); the cognition of simultaneity in things occurring in succession due to rapidity; the notion of motion in stationary objects due to traveling in a boat and so forth; and the cognition of sorcery (*indrajāla*) and the like through the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth. This should be understood as error-cognition primarily caused by external factors. Now, that which is primarily caused by internal factors: the cognition of yellowness in conch shells and the like due to the dominance of bile (*pitta*) in the eye and so forth; the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) despite the absence of hair due to the defect of cataracts (*timira*); the appearance of multiplicity in a single moon and the like; the appearance of a young woman and the like even when the object does not exist, due to the intensity of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*); the contrary understanding regarding what is not beneficial or regarding improper means due to the study of false scriptures; confusion regarding directions and the like due to the power of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*); and likewise, dream-cognition should be known to arise from the intensity of mental impressions and other factors combined with sleep.

Let the error [of cognition] then be examined by way of its object: (1) is it simply non-apprehension (*akhyāti*)? (2) Or is it the apprehension of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*)? (3) Or is it the apprehension of a well-known object (*prasiddhārthakhyāti*)? (4) Or is it the apprehension of an extraordinary object (*alaukikārthakhyāti*)? (5) Or is it the loss of memory (*smṛtivipramoṣa*)? (6) Or is it self-apprehension (*ātmakhyāti*)? (7) Or is it the apprehension of an object that is indefinable as being either existent or non-existent (*sadasattvādyanirvacanīyārthakhyāti*)? (8) Or rather, is it misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*)? {The Theory of Non-Apprehension and Its Refutation}

In this regard, first of all, non-apprehension (*akhyāti*) is untenable due to the absence of evidence; yet it is not so, for evidence is established. To explain: in a cognition appearing as a mirage, the existence of water cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*), because that would entail the cognition being non-erroneous. Nor does the absence of water appear at all, and thus it cannot be the objective support. For this very reason, even the rays of light are not the objective support; for even if their appearance were admitted, the apprehension of them would entail the cognition being non-erroneous. Furthermore, the claim that there is an apprehension of the rays under the form of water is also untenable, because they are distinct entities. Indeed, the apprehension of one thing, such as a cloth, under the form of another, such as a jar, is never observed. Therefore, erroneous cognitions of water and the like are without an objective support, just like erroneous cognitions in dreams. This [position] is incorrect, because it entails the impossibility of specifying [the nature of the error]. For in that case, neither one's own nature nor the nature of another appears at all; by what distinction, then, could it be designated as "cognition of water" or "cognition of silver"? Moreover, there would be no distinction between the state of error and deep sleep. Indeed, there is no distinction here other than the object appearing [in consciousness], and the object appearing is said to be the objective support of that cognition. How, then, can mere non-apprehension be the error?

*Asatkhyāti* (the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent): Another, however, says—“True, what you have said; nevertheless, when that appearing object is examined, whether it be of the nature of the existent (*sadrūpa*) or the nature of the non-existent (*asadrūpa*), it does not exist. Therefore, *asatkhyāti* alone is accepted. Even in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like, the appearance of white and so forth is not erroneous; rather, it is the appearance of silver. And since that form of silver does not exist there, it is therefore *asatkhyāti* alone. {The refutation of that and the determination of the theory of the manifestation of a well-known object (*prasiddhārthakhyāti*)}: [This follows].

Another [teacher] says that this too is incorrect. Why? Because that which is non-existent, like a sky-flower and the like, cannot appear; furthermore, it would follow that there could be no variety in error. For one who maintains the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), there is no variety residing either in the object or in the cognition, by means of which an error with multiple forms might be perceived. Therefore, even in error, a diverse object appears precisely because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor is that object non-existent when subjected to investigation, because investigation is impossible apart from perception (*pratīti*), and because it is sublated by perception. For even the existence of things such as the palm of the hand is established solely by the force of their appearance, and that appearance exists elsewhere as well. Even if that object does not appear in that way at a later time, nevertheless, when it does appear, it certainly exists at that time. Otherwise, even the existence of lightning and the like could not be established. Therefore, the manifestation of a well-known object (*prasiddhārthakhyāti*) alone is logical.
The rejection of that [position] and the description of the theory of the manifestation of non-worldly objects.

This too is not tenable; for if there were no distinction in the apprehension of objects as they actually exist, there would be no conventional distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous. Furthermore, even when water and the like are absent, their signs—such as the moisture of the ground—would still be perceived. Indeed, unlike lightning and such phenomena, the instantaneous and traceless destruction of water and the like is never observed anywhere; moreover, the perception [of water] would be subject to contradiction by all observers of that location, just as it is with lightning. Furthermore, the relationship of sublation (the sublated and the sublator) would not obtain, because all cognitions would be indistinguishable in having well-established objects as their domain. Therefore, some say: "This object appears in this way as something super-mundane; thus, it is accepted that it is simply the manifestation of a super-mundane object."
The establishment of the theory of the loss of memory (*smṛtipramoṣa*) following the refutation of that [opposing view].

That too is without substance, because that object is unestablished due to the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). First of all, whatever object such as water is established by perception and other means does not appear at all in an error, due to the previously mentioned defects. But how is [the object] established if it is not distinct from what is established by perception and so forth? If it is argued that "because it lacks a means of valid cognition, this [object] is non-worldly (*alaukika*)," we say no; for in the absence of a means of valid cognition, no determination can be logically maintained. Otherwise, every determination would everywhere be devoid of a means of valid cognition, so what would be the use of these imagined *pramāṇas*? If it is then argued that a means of valid cognition called "error" (*viparyaya*) must be postulated to establish that object—[and that] "this object does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), because it is produced by a visual perception, like the moon [in the sky]"—we say no; for that would entail the consequence that it is as non-sublated (*abādhya*) as the perception of the [actual] moon. Furthermore, no sublated thing is ever seen to possess the status of a means of valid cognition, either in the world or in the treatises. Moreover, exactly as an object is perceived through perception and other means, in that very same way it appears even in erroneous cognition; it is not some other non-worldly thing. Therefore, this delusion is called a "loss of memory" (*smṛtivipramoṣa*), because it conforms to a previously seen object, just like the memory of something else—so another [scholar] maintains.
{That refutation}

That too is untenable—for memory cannot have the form "this is silver," because that would entail its being indistinguishable from direct perception (*anubhava*). Nor is memory sublated by another cognition, since its object is a thing already made known by perception. If you argue that this is due to "deprivation" (*vipramoṣa*), what is this so-called deprivation? If it means the production [of memory] with a different object due to a defect of the mind, that is impossible for memory; for if even a slight new element were manifested, it would follow—just as in the case of recognition—that it would not be memory at all. If memory, due to a mental defect, causes a different object to appear under the form of its own object, then you would simply be accepting "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*) under a different name. Furthermore, error does not arise from a mental defect alone, as it also arises from defects such as ophthalmia (*timira*). Therefore, this is not memory. Now, if "deprivation" is said to be the production of memory through non-discrimination (*aviveka*) alongside perception, like milk and water, what is this non-discrimination? If it is the grasping of two distinct things as non-distinct, then it would be misapprehension. If it is a specific kind of conjunction, that is impossible for two cognitions. If it is production in immediate succession, then it would follow that cognitions of inferred word-meanings or Devadatta and the like—which occur immediately after recollection—are themselves cases of "deprived memory. As for the claim that "non-apprehension" (*akhyāti*) itself is deprived memory because of the non-grasping of the distinction between memory and perception, and that a subsequent cognition arises which distinguishes those two objects as distinct without sublatting anything—it is also unreasonable, as it contradicts experience. For instance, when the sublation arises—"That which was previously understood as silver is actually a piece of mother-of-pearl, not silver"—one experiences it thus, and not as "silver was remembered and this piece of mother-of-pearl is perceived. If the cognition "silver" were considered memory despite being experienced as having the same object as the cognition "this," then the cognition "mother-of-pearl" would also have to be considered memory, as there is no difference [between them]. Consequently, that which is perceived as "this" would result in being neither silver nor mother-of-pearl, i.e., a mere non-entity (*anupākhyam*), which is not tenable. Furthermore, if both memory and the cognition of perception, though produced in immediate succession, manifest their respective objects according to how they truly exist, then how could there be the conventional usage of "error" there? It would be like any other cognition that manifests its object correctly. If, however, it manifests it otherwise, then it is "misapprehension."
Self-manifestation (ātmakhyāti)

But another says: Distinctive linguistic usage such as "the cognition of silver" or "the cognition of water" would not be appropriate in the absence of a distinction [between cognitions]. Therefore, a distinction residing either in the cognition or in the object must necessarily be asserted. In that regard, since objects such as silver do not exist [in the present] and are thus unperceived, their status as qualifiers is untenable. For that which has not been determined as a qualifier by virtue of being related to something cannot serve as its qualifier. Even if it were presented by memory, it could only be a qualifier of the prior experience, not of the present one, because it lacks a connection to the latter. If it is argued that the very mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) is the object of the illusion of silver and so forth, that is incorrect; for it would follow that there is no appearance of silver at all. Indeed, it is not reasonable that a cognition whose object is color should manifest taste. If it is argued that it is called an "illusion" precisely because one thing is the objective support (*ālambana*) while something else appears, whereas a cognition in which the objective support is the same as what appears is simply a cognition of reality (*tattvajñāna*)—this is untenable. For there is no other object serving as the objective support of a cognition apart from the object that actually appears, as if it were purchased by some transaction. By what distinction, moreover, does that [unperceived object] possess the status of an objective support? If it is by virtue of being the "object-factor" (*karmakāraka*), how can that status be understood for something that is indistinguishable from other things in terms of being a cause, except through its appearing? If it is argued that it is because the cognition is directed toward that specific place, no; for then even grass and such located in that place would have to be the object-factor. Indeed, there is no reason for the distinction that this person is proceeding toward the mirage itself and not toward the grass situated in that place, unless there is an appearance [of the former]. Furthermore, with respect to a cognition manifesting past or future objects, what could possibly be the object-factor? If it is that very object, it does not exist there.
