If it is something else, then it follows that the cognition is illusory. Consequently, there would be no apprehension of past and future objects. Therefore, whatever appears is said to be both the objective support and the object. Moreover, even if the cognition were qualified by an object such as mother-of-pearl, the linguistic usage "silver appears to me," "this is a cognition of silver," or "this is a cognition of water" would not be logical. Thus, the form of silver and so forth must be admitted to belong to the perception itself. And that [form], due to the power of the affliction of beginningless ignorance (*avidyā*), appears as if external. Furthermore, humans possess various beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that ripen in a sequential order. Therefore, cognitions with multiple forms, which are cognized solely in their own forms, arise sequentially. Hence, it is established that there is only self-manifestation (*ātmakhyāti*).
The Refutation of the Theory of Self-Appearance (Ātmakhyāti)

This too is not tenable. For *ātmakhyāti* (the theory that consciousness perceives itself) would only be established if cognition were both restricted to self-awareness and possessed of the form of the object. We shall refute both of these points later. Furthermore, if all cognitions were indistinguishable in their grasping of their own internal forms, the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous, as well as the relationship between the sublated and the sublator, would be impossible, because there would be no deviation from the cognition’s own form. Moreover, if the form of silver and so forth were perceived while residing within the very nature of the cognition, it would not be apprehended as something external, just like the form of pleasure and the like. Furthermore, the perceiver would not act to acquire it, because it would not be an object of purposeful action due to its instability. If you argue that, by the power of the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*), there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of externality and stability, then surely you are thereby accepting *viparītakhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension), since you admit the determination of an unstable form of the object—which is non-different from the cognition—as being otherwise.
The theory of the indeterminable manifestation (anirvacanīyakhyāti).

But another says: The object of knowledge is not something accessible through instruction or established by inference, such that a contrary object might be imagined. What then? That which appears within a cognition is called its object. And in the cognition of water and so forth, only the object consisting of water and so forth appears, not its opposite, for otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the designation "cognition of water" and so on. That object, such as water, does not exist as a real entity (*sat*), because that would entail the consequence that the cognition thereof is non-erroneous. Nor is it non-existent (*asat*), because that would entail the consequence that it is not an object of appearance or activity, like a sky-flower and the like. Nor is it of the nature of both existent and non-existent, because of the faults of both positions and because of the contradiction between existence and non-existence being a single essence. Even according to the Digambara view, since all cognitions would equally involve the appearance of objects that are both existent and non-existent, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions would be untenable. Therefore, this object manifested by the intellect cannot be defined as being existent, non-existent, or by any other attribute. For this very reason, the dilemma as to whether ignorance (*avidyā*) is different from or non-different from Brahman has no place. Why? Because ignorance is not, in the ultimate sense, definable in any form whatsoever. If it were definable, then it would be reality itself and not ignorance. Since ignorance is accepted by everyone as having the nature of unreality (*atattva*), the theory of the manifestation of an indefinable object (*anirvacanīyārthakhyāti*) is established.
That rejection [of the theory] and the exposition of the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*).

This too is incorrect: that [error] is established only when non-duality (*advaita*) is established, and we shall refute that non-duality. Furthermore, as for what was said—that the object of cognition is not accessible through instruction (*upadeśagamya*) and so forth—surely it has been reached by you yourselves as being accessible through instruction. For instance, in an illusion such as water, an object like water appears with a fixed location, time, and nature, precisely as something real (*sadātmaka*), because one who desires to grasp it is observed to act toward that very place. How could this be "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*)? For such an appearance and such an inclination toward action are not possible if the object were truly indefinable. If you argue that while being investigated, this object turns out to be indefinable in terms of existence, non-existence, and so on, but at the time of the illusion it does not appear as such—then, in that case, because it appears otherwise, it is simply a case of "misapprehension" (*viparītakhyāti*). But surely, even misapprehension is not tenable because it contradicts the actual appearance? No; this is due to a failure to understand our intention. We do not say that the cognition is "this object is the opposite"—rather, misapprehension is defined as the cognition "this is a man" occurring with respect to a post (*sthāṇu*) which is actually the opposite of a man. But surely, in a cognition where a man appears, it is illogical for a post—which is not appearing therein—to be its object, as this would lead to a lack of determinacy (*avyavasthā*) everywhere? This is not so; for in the cognition "this is a man," it is the post itself that appears, not a man. The notion that "this is a cognition appearing as a man" is itself an error, because it is actually the post that appears. To see this, consider what one reflects upon after the sublation (*bādhottarakāla*): "This was a post, but it appeared to me as a man. Furthermore, we observe some people grasping a worthless object under the impression that it is a valuable substance; this too is consistent only with misapprehension. Thus, others, having taken hold of it with their hand, declare: "I have obtained or purchased this gold or silver. Therefore, it is logical that the post and so forth, due to the non-apprehension of its true nature and the influence of demerit (*adharma*) and other factors, are determined (*adhyavasīyate*) in the form of a man and so on.
An Investigation into the Nature of Dream Objects

Now, in the case of knowledge derived from dreams and the like, what then is the "erroneous object"? Some say it is the bedstead and so forth located in that [dream] place. That is not correct, because there is a lack of proof. For an object of cognition is not such merely by virtue of being present; rather, it is that which appears [in consciousness], and this is established even by means of subsequent reflective synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*). Now, no such synthesis exists regarding the bedstead and so forth; therefore, that is not the object. What then? It is that which—whether previously perceived or unperceived, whether existing or non-existing—is synthesized at the time of waking by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pratyaya*), just like a post or similar object. Indeed, that is called "erroneous" because it appears in dream-cognition with a difference in place, time, and nature. To illustrate: having awakened, one says, "Today in my dream I saw my dead father as living," or "my son, who was staying in another country, as being here," or "the blind man as not blind," and so on. Even in the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*), a non-existent mass of hair appears in the form of something real, because it is synthesized as such when the subverting cognition arises. [Objection: But since that which is non-existent cannot be an objective support (*ālambana*), it follows that error is without an object. [Reply: No, because the past and the future, though non-existent, can serve as objective supports. For if it were without an objective support, it would be merely a case of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), and the fault in that has already been stated. [Objection: Since cognitions of the past, the future, dreams, and so forth are indistinguishable in their having non-existent objects as their supports, the distinction between erroneous and non-erroneous cognitions is untenable. [Reply: No; the distinction between true cognition and its opposite arises from the fact that one grasps an object in its own form while the other grasps it in a form other than its own. The division between true cognition and its opposite does not depend on whether the object is existent or non-existent. Rather, when a non-existent object is determined precisely in its non-existent form, then the cognition of that object is indeed a true cognition, because it does not deviate from that form. However, when a non-existent object is conceptually determined (*adhyavasīyate*) through an existent or otherwise contrary form, then it is an error.

By this, what some have said is also refuted: namely, that "this proliferation of water—consisting of real water and unreal water—is like sweet water and so forth. Just as when there is the cognition of real water, unreal water or the absence of water does not appear, so too when there is the cognition of unreal water, neither real water nor the absence of water appears; for cognitions terminate within their own respective objects. Therefore, there is no such thing as a 'contrary' [cognition]. This is also rejected because there is no such thing as "unreal water" per se. Even if such a thing existed, if it were determined as "this is unreal water," then it would be non-erroneous knowledge. But when it is determined in the form of water capable of drinking and so forth, how can it be non-erroneous knowledge? For the determination of a contrary object is universally recognized in both worldly and scriptural treatises as being erroneous. And one who acts in contradiction to that is neither a worldly person nor an investigator; he is simply to be disregarded.
{The objection that there is no evidence for the Cārvāka’s being mistaken}

Now, from what is the erroneous nature of cognition known? It cannot be known through perception (*pratyakṣa*), for if it were, an erroneous cognizer would not act out of a desire for that object. Nor is it perceptible at the time when sublation (*bādha*) arises, because by then the erroneous cognition has already passed. And since the past is not perceived by the perception of people like us, inference (*anumāna*) also does not operate—since there can be no establishment of a pervasion (*vyāpti*) for either sublation or any other logical mark (*liṅga*) when they are entirely imperceptible. Indeed, a pervasion is never grasped here even in a general way, as it is in the case of cause and effect and so forth. Furthermore, if pervasion were grasped everywhere through inference, there would be an infinite regress. By this, the apprehension of non-erroneousness is also refuted. Moreover, what is the logical mark for non-erroneousness? Is it being produced by unimpaired causal factors (*aduṣṭakāraka*), or the non-arising of sublation, or the efficacy of purposeful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*)? First, it is not being produced by unimpaired causal factors, because the eyes, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and other causes are beyond the senses, and thus their lack of impairment cannot be ascertained. A logical mark that is itself unestablished cannot establish the possessor of that mark (*liṅgin*). Nor is the lack of impairment of the causal factors established solely from the specific cognition arising from them, because both would remain unestablished due to the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Nor is the non-arising of sublation its mark, because the non-arising of sublation can occur even due to reasons such as the person not acting, going to another place, or death. Furthermore, the non-arising of sublation for all persons cannot be understood by one who is not omniscient. The non-arising of sublation for the cognizer alone is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since we see that even a few people may be erroneous at various times. That "sublation never arises at any time" cannot be understood by one who is not omniscient. Therefore, the non-arising of sublation is also not a logical mark. Nor is the efficacy of purposeful action [the mark], for the efficacy of action consists in the attainment of the object and the avoidance of the non-object. If that is not understood, how could something unestablished be a means of knowledge? If it is understood, then how is the non-deviation of that understanding known? Thus, the aforementioned series of dilemmas becomes unavoidable. Moreover, the non-erroneousness of the appearance of the moon and so forth would not be established, because the attainment of an object such as the moon is impossible. Nor is the attainment of an object such as water possible once it has appeared, because it is destroyed every moment through the production of atomic motion by wind and other living beings. Since the attainment of an object of the same class is inconclusive, it is not a means of knowledge. If it is argued that the attainment of an object belonging to that lineage is the indicator, no; since ultimate atoms do not produce [gross objects], an object of that lineage is impossible. And as long as that is unestablished, there is no inference whatsoever that "this object belongs to that lineage. Thus, by these and other refutations, the mark for non-deviation is rejected; therefore, there is no apprehension [of truth] even through a logical mark.
The resolution thereof.

To this it is replied: If there were no certainty regarding error and so forth, how then could this worldly convention found in the treatises exist—such as, "I have understood it correctly," or "You have known it falsely"? For such a convention is not tenable without a certainty regarding the actual state of things. If you argue that this convention is preceded by a false certainty (*mithyā-niścaya*), then surely, if the falsity of that certainty is not itself apprehended, how can you know that the convention is preceded by a false certainty? Furthermore, the very means of understanding you propose here would likewise provide certainty regarding error through its opposite, and certainty regarding non-error through its opposite. Thus, how can you claim there is no certainty regarding error anywhere? If you say, "I do not state a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) anywhere, because I am merely demonstrating doubt everywhere," we reply: Doubt also arises only when both possibilities are perceived. Consequently, just as in the case of a post or a person, certainty regarding error and so forth must be admitted in some instances. Once that is established, you must necessarily consider the means of valid cognition that serves as its cause, for the purpose of investigators is precisely to investigate the causes of well-known conventions. Moreover, even the demonstration of doubt is not possible without a means of valid cognition, since that by which it is demonstrated is itself the means of valid cognition; so how is it that no means of valid cognition is stated anywhere? If you argue that doubt is produced in the opponent through various alternatives but not actually demonstrated, we say no; for it is impossible to employ multiple alternatives unless their capacity to produce doubt is certain. Indeed, it is not logical to employ a specific cause toward a particular effect if the cause's efficacy is uncertain, as that would lead to the absurdity of employing just anything. If you say that even in cases of doubt, the employment of threads and so forth toward a specific effect is observed, we say no; for in the case of threads and the like, the capacity to produce an effect such as a cloth is certain, and the non-production of the cloth in the absence of threads is also certain; thus, a restricted employment is logical. For you, however, there is no certainty anywhere, which results in either a total lack of activity or an unstable activity. Therefore, to avoid the charge of incoherent prattle, you must state a means of valid cognition somewhere. And that cannot be stated if it is uncertain; yet such certainty is not possible without a certainty regarding the distinction between the erroneous and the non-erroneous. Hence, there is certainty regarding error and so forth. If you ask, "From what means of valid cognition does that [certainty] arise? We reply: This is something to be considered by both of us. In that regard, one must admit that immediately after the arising of a cognition, a non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpa-pratyakṣa*) grasps that cognition as qualified by error and so forth; otherwise, this convention of "erroneous" and "non-erroneous" would be rootless. Nor does it follow that one who is mistaken would never act, because the apprehension of that error is indistinct, like the perception of a thorn by one who is running. Indeed, a distinct cognition—whether of the nature of memory or direct experience—is seen to be the cause for withdrawing from an undesirable object. Even when the initial apprehension is indistinct, a distinct memory is seen to arise due to a specific cause. For example, at the time of first perceiving a cow, although the universal "cowness" is apprehended indistinctly in its inclusive and exclusive aspects, later on, upon seeing individuals of the same and different classes, a clear memory arises: "I saw something similar to this," "I saw something different from this," "This is its similarity," or "This is its difference. In the same way, after an indistinct apprehension of error and non-error, a clear memory arises due to the causes of subverting or corroborating cognitions: "That was false knowledge," or "That was correct knowledge. Alternatively, the perceptuality of those two occurs immediately after the production of the subverting or corroborating cognitions. If you say that perceptuality at that time is illogical, we say no, because the mind has all three times as its object. Otherwise, even yogins would not possess the apprehension of the past and future. If you argue that for yogins, the perception of the past and so forth is logical due to the power of *yogaja-dharma* (virtue born of yoga), we ask: why is it not logical for people like us as well, in certain cases, due to the power of previously acquired unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) accompanied by a specific cause? For the power of unseen merit is to be inferred from its effects. Or, if you say that error and so forth are determined solely by inference from the production of a subversion, then by whom is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) grasped? If you say by another inference, and that too by another, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) has occurred. What is the fault in that? Since the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless, it is accepted. First of all, just like the memory of food and so forth, the memory of pervasion also arises from impressions (*saṃskāra*) belonging to previous births, aided by unseen merit. If you argue that the proof of the subject at hand fails because it is exhausted by a series of examples, we say no; for the example is already established beforehand. Indeed, no one perceives the relation between fire and smoke in kitchens and the like at the very moment of inferring fire. If you say that at the time of inferring for another, an example must necessarily be proven, then if that other person disputes the example in every case, he would never reach certainty regarding error and non-error based on that example. In its absence, the convention established in the world and in the treatises would cease. For one who denies the apprehension of pervasion in smoke and so forth is refuted precisely by contradiction with worldly convention, and not otherwise. That contradiction is the same here as well; therefore, for the opponent too, an example is established somewhere, and by its force, others are also proven. Alternatively, first someone who perceives everything directly caused some non-omniscient person to grasp the pervasion. They, having grasped the pervasion through the instruction of a reliable authority (*āpta*), taught others: "That cognition which is subverted is erroneous; that which has a subsequent corroborating cognition is non-erroneous. Others were taught by them, and they by others, continuing until people like us, just like the pervasion of jars and divine objects. By this same reasoning, the apprehension of pervasion between cause and effect through perception and inference must also be supported.

As for what was said—that being produced by a non-defective causal complex (*aduṣṭasāmagrījanyatva*) is not a logical mark (*liṅga*) for non-erroneousness—that is indeed accepted. However, the non-arising of sublation (*bādhānutpatti*) is in some cases intended to be a means of cognition (*gamika*), specifically where it is impossible for the non-arising of sublation to occur even for investigators except through the non-perversity of the object as it appears; this is as in the case of a cognizer endowed with specific place, time, state, and so forth, regarding the cognition of the oneness of the moon. Furthermore, that erroneous cognition which, having arisen in such a manner due to the capacity of its own causes, acts as an obstacle to the production of a sublating cognition—its destruction is likewise of that same nature, just like the "correct cognition" desired by others.

That too is incorrect. For it is not accepted by the opponent that right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) acts as an obstacle to the production of a subverting cognition (*bādhakajñāna*); what then? It is the non-contrariety of the object as it appears, or the non-arising of error. Furthermore, no obstruction can be placed upon the arising of anything, whether real or unreal. What then? A cause is obstructed—that cause which, even when its auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*) are present, does not produce an effect due to the presence of something else, but does produce it in their absence; that [something else] is said to be the "obstructor," such as gravity being obstructed by conjunction and so forth. And in the case of the arising of a subversion, what is obstructed by what? Moreover, the destruction of something that is an obstructor of another thing does not itself become an obstructor of that thing; for the destruction of conjunction and so forth is not an obstructor of gravity and the like, but rather an auxiliary condition (*sahakārin*). Therefore, it is untenable to claim that its destruction is likewise [an obstructor]. This is because, in both worldly experience and the treatises, a cognition such as "this shell is silver" is well known to be the subverter of a previously arisen cognition such as "this is silver. To ask "what is subverted therein—the object or the cognition? and to attempt a refutation through various alternatives, merely invokes the "cow-dung-and-milk-porridge" logic (i.e., a futile distinction). Likewise, an investigation into whether this "subversion of cognition" consists in the removal of the object or the removal of the result is of no use anywhere. What is useful is simply the demonstration of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) that subversion occurs only in the case of erroneous cognition and not in the case of valid cognition. Thus, in some cases, non-erroneousness is understood through the non-arising of subversion; in other cases, however, it is understood through the efficacy of purposeful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*), as in the case of a previous cognition of water and so forth, which results in the attainment of the intended object such as water.

Now, it was argued that the attainment of an object as it appears is impossible; this is not so. For some objects, such as stones and the like, which appear, their attainment is indeed possible. In the case of objects such as water, even though they perish, the attainment of what arises in their continuum (*saṃtāna*) serves as the indicator [of the initial cognition]. What, then, is this "continuum"? It is the uninterrupted arising of things similar to that [original object]. It is the cause of the non-contradictory worldly cognition that "this is that very same thing. For one who acts after determining an object through error does not attain the object belonging to its continuum exactly as it appeared. Therefore, the non-erroneousness of the prior cognition is understood both by the attainment of the appearing object and by the attainment of the object belonging to its continuum. By this, the fact of being in that same location is also explained. If it is asked: "In the absence of certainty regarding that [object], how can there be certainty regarding its belonging to a continuum?", we say: no, because that is certain due to non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*). For when the appearing object is either impossible or otherwise, this cognizer—acting after the time of engagement and employing that object in discourse among many groups of people—does not encounter contradiction in the judgment "this is that very same thing. Thus, due to non-contradiction, it is determined that the object is exactly as it appeared.

Furthermore, one who, even without acting, perceives the specific qualities of an object that has appeared, determines the actual state of the object through those very qualities while remaining in that same place, and thereby establishes the non-erroneousness of the prior cognition—either by himself or through corroboration by the words of another person. And thus, as it has been stated, the non-erroneousness of cognitions such as those of the moon would not be established; for it is not restricted solely to the capacity for successful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*), since non-erroneousness, like fire and so forth, can also be inferred from multiple marks (*liṅga*) via conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and is accessible through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Others, however, explain that by the phrase "the efficacy of purposeful activity" (*pravṛttisāmarthya*), what is intended is corroboration by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara-saṃvāda*). And this [corroboration] occurs either through the perception of a specific quality—whether the object that appeared has perished or not—or through the mention by several possible persons. Therefore, for one who accepts that the certainty of non-deviation arises from the efficacy of purposeful activity alone even in every case of doubt, there is no fault whatsoever.

Furthermore, as for this infinite regress that was urged by the argument beginning with "How is the non-deviation of that cognition understood?", that too is untenable because it is sublated by worldly practice (*lokavyavahāra*) which is preceded by certainty. For we observe that speakers act without further expectation once a distinction has been apprehended through a second or third [cognition]. Indeed, the infinite regress has already been refuted; therefore, one should not accept intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) out of fear of infinite regress.
{The Description of Intrinsic Validity} As some have said:
"When there is intrinsic validity, nothing else need be sought;
for falsity is dispelled effortlessly through the absence of defects."

Intrinsic validity (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) means that valid cognitions are independent in their production, operation, and cognition. Invalid cognitions, however, possess invalidity extrinsically (*parataḥ-aprāmāṇya*) because they are endowed with the three types of dependence. For instance, false knowledge becomes invalid when it arises depending on defects of the sense organs and so forth, which are distinct from the collection of causes that produce awareness. True knowledge, however, does not depend on anything other than the causal complex that generates awareness for its being true; this is because the causes [of true knowledge] are pure by their very nature. Even dependence on purity is not logical, since defects are merely adventitious; therefore, dependence on them is appropriate only for invalidity. For this very reason, the function of excellences (*guṇas*) lies in the removal of defects, not in the production of validity. Indeed, validity is not produced in the case of one whose eyes lack defects such as cataracts simply because of the absence of excellences like collyrium. Nor is it logical for something to be a cause by its mere existence when its positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has not been observed, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). From the example of collyrium and others, it should be inferred that other excellences, such as being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), function only in the elimination of defects. Likewise, a valid cognition, while operating toward its own effect—namely, the manifestation of a real object—does not depend on the cognition of itself or on the excellences of its causes. Even in its own cognition, it depends on nothing other than its nature as awareness, lest there be the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Invalid cognition, on the other hand, depends on either the cognition of defects arising from its causes or the cognition of the object being otherwise.
The refutation of that [position] and the establishment of extrinsic validity (*parataḥ-prāmāṇya*).

As for the claim that [the means of knowledge] are independent in their production, that is not so, because they depend on specific factors such as light, location, and the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). For it is not the case that the specific conditions of light and so forth, in whatever state they are, are required by the eyes and other senses for the production of correct knowledge in exactly the same way they are required for the production of false knowledge. Nor is it the case that these [defects] merely remove obstacles; for in their absence, even the production of knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) would be impossible. Furthermore, the knowledge of reality regarding the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, whose capacity has been determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), depends upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other factors for the cognition of the object to be inferred. So how can there be independence for the means of knowledge? As for cataracts, jaundice, and the like, they are merely states of imbalance in the humors (*dhātu*) situated within the eyeball and so forth. How, then, could validity be extrinsic (*parataḥ*) in dependence upon them? For that would entail the consequence that validity is extrinsic in dependence upon the state of balance [of the humors]. Moreover, since non-existence (*abhāva*) is established as a cause through positive and negative concomitance just like existence (*bhāva*), why should the eye and other organs not be dependent in the production of validity even when they depend on the absence of defects—just as in the case of the action of falling and so forth? We shall demonstrate later that non-existence is a distinct entity from existence.

Now, if it is argued that intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is asserted because a cognition does not depend on an additional cause consisting of a real entity, we say no; for this is merely a conventional assertion (*samayamātra*). A convention can be established otherwise as well, so no objective proof is achieved by this alone. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the production of intrinsic validity; rather, the following inference establishes the opposite: validity arises from something else (*parataḥ*), because it comes into being after previously not existing, just like invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Validity is also dependent upon other factors even in its engagement with its own effect, because only the eye and other sense organs—which produce a specific cognition—are considered instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and their dependence has already been demonstrated. As for the state of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), independence exists there even in the case of invalidity, so there is no distinction at all. We shall refute the view that validity belongs to cognition alone; therefore, whether its operation is intrinsic or extrinsic need not be deliberated. As for this example mentioned regarding intrinsic operation—
"A jar depends upon the clay, the wheel, the staff, the string, and so forth for its birth;
however, it has no such dependence for the act of carrying water."

Thus, it remains indistinguishable even in the case of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*). Furthermore, since even a pot depends upon conjunction and other factors, its independence (*nirapekṣatva*) is unestablished. Likewise, the cognition of validity is also extrinsic (*parataḥ*), because there is no means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for establishing validity intrinsically (*svataḥ*). On the contrary, the following inference [proves] the opposite: validity is known through something else, because it is an object of cognition (*jñeyatva*), just like invalidity. If it is argued that validity is established intrinsically simply by virtue of being of the nature of consciousness (*bodhātmakatva*), we say no; for the nature of consciousness is equally present in what is invalid. If it is then argued that the two are established through the principles of general rule (*utsarga*) and exception (*apavāda*), as it has been said:
Therefore, the validity of cognition, which is attained by virtue of its being of the nature of awareness,
is set aside by the knowledge of a defect arising from a cause that results in the object being otherwise than it appears.

This is incorrect, because even false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) would result in being valid (*prāmāṇya*) by virtue of its nature as consciousness (*bodhātmakatva*), prior to its sublation (*bādha*). Furthermore, the arising of sublation is untenable in the case of a consciousness that has already become a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*), for that would entail the consequence of sublation occurring for all cognitions. Nor is it logical for a single cognition to possess both validity and invalidity, since two contradictory natures cannot coexist in one thing. If it is argued that there is no contradiction between these two in a single entity due to a difference in time—just as activity and inactivity can coexist—we say no, because such a thing is impossible given the instability of consciousness; for a property (*dharma*) cannot subsequently belong to a substratum (*dharmin*) that has already perished. Now, if you maintain that the sublation of a cognition’s validity is intended with respect to a future sublation—since it has been said: "That cognition is a means of valid knowledge for which no sublation arises in another place, at another time, in another person, or in another state"—then the mere nature of consciousness is not the determiner of validity. What then? It must be consciousness qualified by the absence of sublation throughout the three periods of time (*traikālika-bādhābhāva-viśiṣṭa-bodhatva*). And this is impossible to determine, for who knows whether sublation will arise for this cognition at a later time or not? For we observe that even what is determined as correct may be sublated through the passage of time, such as days, months, and so forth. The claim that "when the cognition of a defect (*doṣajñāna*) has not arisen, doubt is groundless" is also incorrect, because doubt is only possible once the cognition of a defect has indeed arisen. For when the cognition of a defect has arisen, there would simply be a certainty of invalidity. If it is argued that the doubt regarding invalidity is removed by the certainty of being produced by non-defective causes and so on—we say no, because even the certainty of being produced by non-defective causes becomes an object of doubt, just like the previous certainty. If you argue that in that case too, the doubt is removed by a further certainty of being produced by non-defective causes, we say no; for the certainty that removes it would likewise be an object of doubt, as before. If one continues to demand a certainty to remove the doubt in each subsequent case, how could an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) not occur? But surely the infinite regress was avoided by Bhaṭṭa himself! For he said: [and so forth].
Thus, no further cognition beyond three or four is required; for at that very point, a single cognition attains self-validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) by itself.

From what should it be understood that no further cognition is required? It is because, in all cases, the absence of doubt and the lack of further expectation lead even investigators to be seen engaging in worldly activity. Now, why does this very avoidance of infinite regress—which we are propounding—produce such hostility in you? By whichever means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) the suspicion of invalidity is removed, by that very same means the certainty of validity is also produced, just as in the case of the certainty regarding a post or similar object. This is because we do not experience the operation of two distinct means of cognition; therefore, once the suspicion has ceased, there is no subsequent determination of validity through the nature of being a cognition (*bodhatva*). If you argue that validity was already determined as being due to the nature of cognition prior to the removal of doubt, and that the other means of cognition merely dispels the suspicion, that is incorrect. For the nature of cognition, being indistinguishable from before, cannot produce certainty because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), just like "uprightness" and so forth. Furthermore, certainty cannot arise without a cause. Moreover, since even mere cognition is admitted by your own school to be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) and thus inferable, how could the validity of a specific cognition be perceived intrinsically (*svataḥ*)? If you say that a means of cognition reveals its object while remaining itself unknown, and for that reason validity is called intrinsic—otherwise, if it revealed the object only when itself known, there would be an infinite regress—this has been stated: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, if validity were established by another cognition, one would have to ask: is that second cognition valid by itself or by another? If by itself, then why not accept the same for the first? If by another, then an infinite regress ensues. Therefore, the view that validity is extrinsic (*parataḥ*) is untenable. Consequently, it is established that validity is intrinsic. This concludes the section on the intrinsic nature of validity. Now, the following is said regarding the definition of a means of valid cognition: "A means of valid cognition is that which produces a new, non-erroneous, and determinate cognition. Here, "new" excludes recollection; "non-erroneous" excludes error; and "determinate" excludes indeterminate perception. Thus, the definition of a means of valid cognition is complete. As for the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*), it is derived from the root *mā* preceded by the prefix *pra*, meaning "to measure" or "to determine," with the suffix *ana*. It refers to that by which an object is measured or determined. This concludes the investigation into the intrinsic nature of validity. Now, the following is said regarding the number of means of valid cognition: "The means of valid cognition are two, namely direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Direct perception is that which is produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects. It is of four kinds: sensory, mental, yogic, and self-cognizing. Inference is of three kinds: pūrvavat, śeṣavat, and sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. Pūrvavat is inference based on a previous experience, such as inferring rain from the swelling of a river. Śeṣavat is inference based on what remains, such as inferring the sweetness of the rest of a fruit after tasting one part. Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa is inference based on general observation, such as inferring the existence of the soul from the presence of desire and so forth. These are the two means of valid cognition. Comparison (*upamāna*) and verbal testimony (*śabda*) are included within inference. Thus, the means of valid cognition are indeed two. This concludes the section on the number of means of valid cognition. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of direct perception: "Direct perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpodha*). Conceptual construction is the association of a name with a thing. That which is devoid of this is direct perception. It is non-conceptual because it arises immediately upon the contact of the sense organs with the object. This concludes the section on the nature of direct perception. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of inference: "Inference is the knowledge of an object not present to the senses, arising from a logical mark (*liṅga*) that is perceived and known to be invariably concomitant with the object. The logical mark must be perceived, known, and invariable. Invariable concomitance is of two kinds: positive (*anvaya*) and negative (*vyatireka*). Positive concomitance is the presence of the probandum where the probans is present. Negative concomitance is the absence of the probans where the probandum is absent. This concludes the section on the nature of inference. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of verbal testimony: "Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*). A reliable person is one who speaks the truth out of compassion. Their instruction is verbal testimony. It is a means of valid cognition because it leads to the attainment of the intended object. This concludes the section on the nature of verbal testimony. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of comparison: "Comparison is the cognition of similarity based on the instruction of a reliable person. For example, having heard from a reliable person that a gavaya is similar to a cow, one goes to the forest and perceives the similarity between a cow and a gavaya. This is comparison. It is a means of valid cognition because it leads to the acquisition of the gavaya. This concludes the section on the nature of comparison. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of self-cognition: "Self-cognition is the awareness of the cognition itself. Every cognition is self-cognizing, just as light illuminates itself. This is necessary because if a cognition were not cognized by itself, it could never be remembered later. Therefore, self-cognition exists. This concludes the section on the nature of self-cognition. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of mental perception: "Mental perception is the cognition of the object immediately following sensory perception. It is a means of valid cognition because it is non-conceptual and non-erroneous. This concludes the section on the nature of mental perception. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of yogic perception: "Yogic perception is the clear, non-conceptual cognition of supersensuous objects attained by yogis through the power of meditation. It is a means of valid cognition because it is non-erroneous and non-conceptual. This concludes the section on the nature of yogic perception. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of inference: "Inference is of two kinds: for oneself (*svārtha*) and for others (*parārtha*). Inference for oneself is the knowledge of an object not present to the senses arising from a logical mark. Inference for others consists of the statement of the five members: proposition (*pratijñā*), reason (*hetu*), example (*udāharaṇa*), application (*upanaya*), and conclusion (*nigamana*). The proposition is the statement of what is to be proven, e.g., "Sound is impermanent. The reason is the statement of the property that establishes the proof, e.g., "because it is produced. The example is the statement of a well-known instance, e.g., "whatever is produced is impermanent, like a pot. The application is the connection of the subject with the reason, e.g., "and sound is produced. The conclusion is the reiteration of the proposition, e.g., "therefore, sound is impermanent. This is inference for others. This concludes the section on the nature of inference. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of the fallacies: "The fallacies are the unestablished (*asiddha*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), and the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The unestablished is that whose existence in the subject is not proven. The contradictory is that which proves the opposite of what is to be proven. The inconclusive is that which is common to both the similar and dissimilar instances. These are the fallacies. This concludes the section on the fallacies. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of the refutations (*dūṣaṇa*): "Refutation is the pointing out of a fallacy in the opponent's argument. This is done by showing that the reason is unestablished, contradictory, or inconclusive. This concludes the section on the refutations. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of the rejoinders (*uttara*): "Rejoinder is the response to a refutation. This is done by showing that the refutation itself is flawed. This concludes the section on the rejoinders. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*): "Points of defeat are those situations where one is defeated in debate. These include the failure to state a proposition, the withdrawal of a proposition, the contradiction of a proposition, and so forth. This concludes the section on the points of defeat. Now, the following is said regarding the nature of the victory: "Victory is the establishment
"Even when consciousness has arisen, the object is not ascertained as long as the purity of its causes has not been apprehended through another means of valid cognition."
In that case, the arising of another cognition must be awaited from another cause;
for as long as [the object] has not been determined, its purity is equivalent to non-existence.
"If its cause is also pure, then that cognition would possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*);
yet, since the same [question] would apply there as well, one would never reach a final point."

This is incorrect. For we do not accept that the manifestation of an object (*arthaprakāśakatva*) belongs to a cognition already determined (*niścita*), such that this objection would be meaningful. Rather, the Naiyāyikas accept that the manifestation of an object by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists precisely in its producing knowledge (*jñānotpādakatva*). And that knowledge arises from a means of cognition that is itself undetermined; for knowledge arises not only from a valid means of cognition, but also from an invalid one, provided both are undetermined. Furthermore, a person’s activity—characterized by the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired, preceded by desire and so forth—generally does not depend upon the determination of the distinction between a valid means of cognition and its semblance (*pramāṇatadābhāsa-viveka-niścaya*). However, when one who has acted in such a manner is in doubt due to the attainment or failure to attain the object, a prudent person (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*) acts with a view toward the certain attainment of the object in some cases, and thus depends upon the determination of the means of cognition; it is in this sense that the determination of the means of cognition possesses purposefulness (*arthavattva*). If it is argued: "Just as in the case of mere awareness (*bodhamātra*), there is initially an ascertainment of correctness (*samyaktva-adhyavasāya*) because no other cause [for error] is perceived, whereas an ascertainment of falsity (*mithyātva-adhyavasāya*) never occurs in that way; therefore, the status of being a valid or invalid means of cognition is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) or extrinsic (*parataḥ*)," [we reply: No, because it has other causes. Just as for one who has frequently seen virtuous persons, there is initially an ascertainment of virtue in any person at all, whereas the ascertainment of non-virtue arises from the perception of another cause; likewise, because correctness is generally observed in cognitions, there is initially an ascertainment of correctness in mere awareness for one whose mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) have been sharpened by the practice thereof. An ascertainment of falsity, however, requires the perception of another cause due to the lack of sharpness in those impressions. But merely on account of this cause, the designation of validity or invalidity as intrinsic or extrinsic does not establish the point at hand. Enough of this digression. Thus, since correctness and incorrectness—the objects to be accepted and rejected—are established by the means of valid cognition, the qualification "correct" (*samyak*) in the definition of experience (*anubhava*) is meaningful.

{The purpose of the term *anubhava*}: "In the phrase 'cognition other than recollection' (*smaraṇājñāna*), the status of recollection and non-cognition as results of means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇaphala*)—such as sacrifice and the like—is excluded by the inclusion of the term *anubhava*; for it is not established anywhere that those two, when derived through the suffix denoting abstract state (*bhāva-vyutpatti*), are denotable by the word *anubhava*.
{The function of the term *sādhana*}.

"Regarding the term *sādhana* (means of accomplishment): how, moreover, is such a specific meaning understood from the word *sādhana*, which is not itself qualified? It is because it is distinguished by the inclusion of [only] those factors (*kāraka*) that are intended; for those learned in grammar accept the inclusion of factors based on what is intended. Thus, this word *sādhana*—derived as "that by which something is accomplished"—denotes the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) as intended [by the speaker]. How then could it denote the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*), which are the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karman*), nor the result (*phala*), which is produced by the instrument? For the instrument is that which is most effective in accomplishing [an action] (*sādhakatama*), and the status of being most effective does not belong to the object and the other factors. Now, what is this so-called "most effective" (*sādhakatama*)?"
According to the view of some, the category of instrument (karaṇatva) is as follows:

Some maintain that the activity of the agent (*kartṛvyāpāra*) is produced by all the factors of action (*kāraka*) without exception. Indeed, all the factors of action, having become possessed of their own respective activities and having generated the activity of the agent, become fulfilled; and because the activity of the agent has not yet been fulfilled and because it produces the primary action without mediation, it possesses the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*). Furthermore, the agent, while producing the action through that [agent's] activity independently of the activities of other factors of action, is called "independent" (*svatantra*) and thus an "agent. For if the factors of action were to produce the action by coming together as a group, they would possess equal activity; in that case, what would be the meaning of "most effective means" or "independence"? Such a view contradicts the entire tradition of grammar (*vyākaraṇa*). For this very reason, they state that the activity of the knower (*jñātṛvyāpāra*) is the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). And that activity of the knower is of the nature of consciousness (*bodhātmaka*), because it exists in identity with the knower whose nature is consciousness.
{The refutation thereof}

This is untenable. For if an operation (*vyāpāra*) existing in identity with the agent were to arise, then the agent itself would have to arise. Or, if that [agent] does not arise, then the operation would likewise not arise, or there would be a contradiction of their identity, as in the case of space and water. Furthermore, if the operation were eternal, there would be no cessation of activity. If it is argued that the meaning of the term "identity" is being both different and non-different, this is not so; for the position of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) will be refuted later. Now, suppose the operation is indeed distinct [from the agent]. Is it of the nature of motion, or of the nature of non-motion, or is it the final auxiliary cause (*antima-sahakārin*)? If it is of the nature of motion, then immobile things would lack causal efficacy due to their lack of operation. If it is of the nature of non-motion, is it a cause of the effect or not? If it is not a cause, then what is the use of that which is ineffective for the agent? If it does produce something, does it depend on another operation or not? If it depends on another operation, then that other operation would likewise require yet another operation, leading to the fallacy of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is without operation (*nirvyāpāra*), then the causal factors themselves, being likewise without operation, would produce the effect; thus, an operation need not be postulated, as there is no evidence for it. Moreover, one must necessarily admit that the substratum in which the operation arises is its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), just as a substance is for a quality. Consequently, when that causal factor produces its own operation, does it do so by being "with operation" or "without operation"? If it is with operation, then due to the consequence of an infinite series of operations, the primary effect could not be produced because the agent would be exhausted. If it is without operation, then let the production of the effect belong to the one without operation just as the production of the operation does; what is the use of postulating an operation? Therefore, the claim made by some—that "all causal factors are agents in the production of their own actions, and they take the forms of object (*karman*), instrument (*karaṇa*), etc., in the production of the principal action"—is also refuted. For there is no evidence whatsoever for the existence of an action distinct from the actions produced by the various causal factors, since it is impossible for a single entity to be the producer [of multiple distinct actions].

Nor can the final auxiliary cause be an "operation" (*vyāpāra*), because since no further subsequent moment is possible for it, it would follow that it is devoid of operation, which entails its being a non-cause. Therefore, there is no operation whatsoever distinct from the mutual cooperation of the causal factors themselves. Consequently, since the cognition of an object is established through the sense organs and so forth alone, the presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding the operation of a cognizer (*jñātṛ*) is exhausted. Furthermore, by words such as "cognition" (*saṃvitti*) or "ascertainment" (*pramiti*), no meaning other than consciousness itself is expressed; thus, even though the sense organs and so forth produce the awareness of an object, they would not be "illuminators" of the object due to their insentient nature. Nor is any property of the object—such as "illumination" (*prakāśa*) or "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*)—perceived by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) apart from consciousness (or, apart from light and its radiance), such that its existence could be inferred through the principle of "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) to establish the presence of cognition. Therefore, because its own nature is unestablished and because it lacks a result, it is not the case that cognition alone functions as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

{The Category of Instrumentality according to the Grammarians’ View} Others maintain that "kārakas arise through intention. For example: "The lump of clay makes the jar," "Having obtained the lump of clay, the jar comes into being," "By means of the lump of clay, the potter makes the jar," "From the lump of clay, the jar arises," "The jar is a modification of the lump of clay," and "The jar is produced in the lump of clay.
{Refutation thereof}

They should be asked as follows: "Does a *kāraka* exist even though it is not present merely by virtue of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*), or does the application of a word denoting it occur only after the status of being a *kāraka* has already been established? In the first case, in the production of a jar, the lump of clay would have the status of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and the potter would also have the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*). Furthermore, there would never be the fault of the non-application of a *kāraka* term, because there would be no obstruction to the speaker's intention in any instance. If, on the other hand, the second case is held, then the cause for the distinction between those *kārakas*—their difference in essential nature (*svarūpabheda*)—must be stated, so that when their respective definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) are applied, the application of words would be appropriate, just as in the case of a scale and its various parts.
{The category of instrumentality in the Śākya doctrine}:
Regarding the act of valid cognition (*pramiti*), the Śākyas maintain that the instrumentality belongs solely to the form of the object as it exists within the cognition. Thus, they have stated:
"For [cognition] connects itself with the object not by abandoning its own objective form."
Therefore, the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) for the apprehension of the object of cognition (prameya) is its having the form of that object.

For not everything is the means of accomplishment for every action simply because it is a means; rather, that from which something attains its establishment [is its means]. In this regard, since cognition—which is essentially similar [to its object]—occurs through mere experience, it must exist in that same essential form with respect to every object, so that it may be distinguished for each respective object as "this belongs to this. Furthermore, although a distinction exists among its causes, such as the contact between sense-faculty and object, that distinction does not serve as a regulator by way of differentiation for a cognition whose nature remains undifferentiated across different objects, because the status of being an instrument is dependent upon the action itself. Since there is no difference in that [action], the distinction of the [instrument] is also unestablished; or even if a distinction were present, it would not be a cause because it is not a constituent part of that [cognition]. Therefore, that from which this differentiation arises—namely, that "this is the comprehension of this" due to a specific nature of the self—is the means (*sādhana*) for this comprehension with respect to the object. Nor can this connection of the object with cognition arise from anything other than the similarity of form (*sārūpya*) to the object. For the sense-faculties and so forth, though they possess their own distinctions such as acuity or dullness, do not connect this [cognition] with the object; for in that case, there is no basis for proximity. If it is argued that there is a specific experience produced by the object from which this cognition arises, and not from similarity of form, then why is the form of that [experience], even though it exists, not pointed out? It is impossible to designate this in terms of "this-ness" (*idantayā*). Yet, by means of an undetermined nature, it establishes entities: "this is his," "this is not his. Thus, entities are well-established. Therefore, the means for the comprehension of the object of knowledge is the form of the object within the cognition itself.
{The refutation thereof}

Regarding the statement, "Insofar as it connects this [cognition] with the object," and so forth: if what is intended is that it "connects" means "relates," then that is incorrect. For the relation of the cognition with the object is not produced by the cognition assuming the form of the object; rather, that cognition is produced already related to the object by its own causes. Indeed, a cognition does not arise first and subsequently become related to the object. Nor is the assumption of the object's form the cause of the cognition, for that would entail the consequence of their identity (tādātmya). Alternatively, if what is intended is that "the assumption of the object's form connects the cognition" means "it determines the cognition as being related to the object," that too is incorrect, because such a relation is unestablished. For the assumption of the object's form residing in the cognition has never been observed to coexist with a cognition that is related to the object, such that it could serve as its indicator.

Now, this might be the intention: "The very fact that cognition is produced by an object is its connection with that object, and that [connection] is not something distinct from the cognition itself. Furthermore, since there is a relation of identity (*tādātmya*) between the form of the object and such a cognition, and since cognition is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) because it is self-cognizable, the connection—which is not distinct from it—is also established through direct perception. Therefore, how could there be a lack of proof for the connection? This is not so; for the relation of identity will be refuted in detail during the investigation of inference (*anumāna*). And thus, there is indeed no dispute over the point that "not everything is the means (*sādhana*) for every action," because it is accepted that only a specific type of causal factor (*kāraka-viśeṣa*) possesses the status of being a means.

As for what was said—"But that which attains its establishment from something"—that is incorrect. This is because it has already been examined whether "establishment" (prasiddhi) is characterized by origination or by cognition; however, in the case of that characterized by verbal expression, it is established by the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*), not by the form of the object. Furthermore, the statement beginning with "by mere experience alone" is also incorrect, because even though speech is uniform in nature across all objects and agents, a specific restriction is observed due to the very nature of the utterance—such as "the word *nīla*," "the word *pīta*," "this is Devadatta’s speech," or "this is Jñadatta’s speech"—even in the absence of the actual form of the object [in the speech itself].

As for the claim that "that which is non-self (anātman) belongs to him" and so forth, that too is incorrect; for it is observed that only that which is non-self acts as a regulator, just as a son is regulated by his parents, a servant by his master, or curds and the like by the process of fermentation and so on. Furthermore, the nature of an instrument (*karaṇa*) is accepted as being dependent upon action (*kriyā*).

As for the argument that "since there is no distinction [in the object], a distinction in that [cognition] is also unestablished," this is not tenable, because a distinction in action is possible even due to distinctions among the causal factors (*kāraka*), such as the object (*karman*) and so forth. Therefore, the claim that "this [distinction arises] from a distinction in its own nature" and so on is also untenable, because a distinction within one's own self is impossible; for if there were a distinction, its non-distinct nature would be contradicted. Furthermore, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for [the cognition] being determined by itself; rather, there is an inference to the contrary: "This apprehension must be determined by something other than itself, because it is something determined, like a son and so forth. Since the ascetic (*yati*) is also determined by something other than himself—namely, by knowledge, effort, and so on—the reason is not inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Nor is the claim that "this is not a connection with an object" and so forth tenable, because the connection with an object is possible through the eyes and other sense organs alone.

Now, it may be argued that it has already been stated [by us] that "it is not [due to] sharpness, dullness, and so forth," and so on; but that is not correct, because it is unproven (*asiddha*). To explain: from common usage such as "I see form with the eye," it is understood that the eye and other [senses], aided by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors, bring about the cognition of form and the like. Furthermore, the absence of a basis for proximity is also unproven, since a specific kind of contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) has been established. Alternatively, the very cognition of a knowledge connected to an object—expressed as "this is his knowledge"—is itself the connection. That too is produced by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is assisted by unseen merit and other factors, because the internal organ has both external and internal objects as its domain. Moreover, the connection of knowledge with an object consists solely in its specific production, and not in a nature of physical contact; for when that [connection] is apprehended by the mind, there arises the realization: "this is his knowledge."

As for the objection raised regarding a specific experience—namely, "Now, why is the nature of even that which exists not specified? and so forth—that is incorrect. For there certainly do exist certain such particulars which, although they are perceived, cannot be specified in detail, just like the particularities of tastes and the like. And it has been said:
"There is a great difference in the sweetness of sugarcane, milk, molasses, and so forth;
nevertheless, even Sarasvatī herself would be unable to describe that distinction."

This being the case, the conclusion—"Therefore, the means of the cognition of the object of knowledge is its having the form of that object"—is untenable. Furthermore, how can the form of the object, which is non-different from the cognition itself, be the means [of that cognition]? For it is impossible for an action to operate upon itself, whether in a state of being already established or not yet established. It might be argued that the very answer to this has already been stated, as it was said: "When the means of proof is something other [than the result], the connection of that [means] with the action is not established.
And since that [form] is essentially identical to it, the result is not a separate entity."
And that [cognition], while maintaining that [form] within itself through its nature as the apprehension of an object,
appears as if it were possessed of activity toward its own object by means of that [objective] operation.
"Because of that [dependence], due to its being established by that, it is itself non-agential. Thus [it is said].

As for the claim that "if another means (*sādhana*) is admitted, the relationship between the action and its object, or between the action and the object of that means, is not established"—that is incorrect. For when the means is indeed distinct, the relationship between the action such as cutting (*chidā*) and the object such as a tree, by means of an instrument such as an axe, is well-established; as in the expressions, "He cuts the tree with an axe" (*kuṭhāreṇa vṛkṣaṃ chinatti*) and "the cutting of the tree" (*vṛkṣasya chedanam*). Nor is it established—either in common usage or in treatises—that the axe is non-different from the act of cutting, or that it takes on the form of the tree, even though it is the means for that action. Furthermore, regarding the argument: "That which possesses [the form]—namely, the cognition of the object—while maintaining that [cognition] within itself, appears as if possessing activity toward the object-form as its own objective (*karman*), by means of an activity whose nature is the apprehension of the object; though it is itself devoid of agency, it appears so due to the influence of that object-form, because of the determination of each specific object. This too is unsound, because by this [statement], the status of the means would have to be called figurative (*gauṇa*). And since the figurative is preceded by the primary (*mukhya*), one must state what the primary means is. Indeed, nothing is known in the world or in the scriptures to be a primary means that does not perform an action, whether by way of appearing or by way of arising. Thus, having composed a mere semblance of a treatise with empty words, he deceives those of dull intellect and seeks only gain, honor, and fame like a *ḍiṇḍika* (a mendicant who refuses all gifts), rather than providing even a slight benefit to others. The metaphor "as if possessing activity" (*savyāpāram iva*) is also not tenable, because the distinction between "possessing activity" and "not possessing activity" is impossible in your view, just as it is impossible to distinguish between a cow and a gavaya. For in your system, there is no "activity" (*vyāpāra*) or "agency" (*kārakatva*) for anything apart from the actual being (*bhūti*). Since you admit that both action and the factors of action (*kāraka*) consist of the same being, the activity is everywhere undifferentiated. Even so, the metaphor is not tenable; for one does not say, "This object possessing a dewlap is like a cow. Furthermore, the use of the particle *iti* [to mark the metaphor] is improper, because it is never employed in the treatises on logic (*pramāṇa-śāstra*) nor in worldly usage, and because it serves no purpose. For just as the phrase "like Rāma and Rāvaṇa" conveys an extraordinary excellence of battle through their exclusive engagement, the phrase "as if possessing activity" does not convey any such excellence of meaning.

If it is argued that the purpose [of this definition] is to conform to worldly convention (*lokavyavahārānusāritva*), the following thought might occur: all people in the world, perceiving an axe or similar tool as being "active" through its operation consisting of actions such as raising and lowering, designate it as an "instrument" (*karaṇa*). Following that convention, we have stated that it is "active. What is meant is this: just as people accept the instrumentality of an axe and so forth based on the perception of it as being active, so too have we accepted the instrumentality of cognition—which possesses the form of the object—based on the perception of its activity consisting in the apprehension of the object. This is because worldly convention alone is the authority regarding the meaning of words. Furthermore, even for an axe and the like, there is no operation distinct from itself consisting of actions such as raising; for all entities are momentary and thus cannot serve as a substratum [for a separate action], and because there is no utility produced by such [an external] action. To explain: if that substance has arisen from its own causes already as active, then there is no need for a further action as a separate entity, as it would be redundant. If, on the other hand, it is inactive, then even when a separate action arises, how could it become active? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, just as for an axe and so forth, what is called "action" is simply the arising of a continuous series of moments in adjacent locations—like the shadow of an umbrella—and its status as an instrument is based on the perception thereof; likewise, cognition, which bears various successive forms such as blue, yellow, and so on, is perceived as being "active," and by virtue of that, its instrumentality is indeed primary, just like that of an axe.

First, as for the refutation of the production of an effect distinct [from the cause] by means of the power of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), that is not tenable, because it is a mere wishful thinking. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate later how even an axe or similar instrument, while being non-momentary, possesses activity precisely through an action that is a distinct entity. If the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) were based merely on the cognition of having an operation (*savyāpāra*), then the person who cuts would also be perceived as having an operation, and thus he too would possess the status of an instrument. If, on the other hand, the axe is the instrument because it is the most proximate (*pratyāsanna*) factor in accomplishing the action of splitting a tree or the like, and therefore only it—and not the person—is the instrument; well then, you have effectively accepted that the status of an instrument belongs to that which is proximate and accomplishes the action. Consequently, just like the action of splitting, the action to be accomplished—namely, the cognition of the object's form (*arthākārajñāna*)—must be stated to be distinct from its means of accomplishment. How then can the result not be a distinct entity? Now, if you think that even the axe does not possess the status of an instrument by virtue of accomplishing the splitting, because that would entail the status of an instrument for everything that accomplishes it, but rather that the axe’s production in a specific form upon encountering the cause of the splitting is the ground for the conventional designation "this is its means," and by virtue of that it is designated as an instrument—and you claim the same applies to cognition—that is not so, because momentariness has not been proven. For this process would be plausible only if momentariness were established, and we shall demonstrate its lack of proof later.

Furthermore, with respect to the action of splitting (*dvaidhībhāva*), what possesses the status of the instrument (*karaṇa*)? For an action is not possible without an instrument. Nor is the splitting itself the instrument, because if it consists of the object to be split (*chedya*), it is well-known as the object (*karman*) alone; and even if it consists of the separation from another entity, it is well-known as being of the same nature as the action itself. Therefore, another distinct entity must be stated as the instrument; and since, by that example, a distinction between action and instrument is established everywhere, how could there be non-distinction in any case?

Furthermore, having stated that the relationship of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) is established between the cognitions of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), you have said that the relationship of probandum and probans between two parts of a single cognition is due to their being the basis for a determination (*vyavasthā*). This is an exceedingly eloquent statement! Even though the relationship of probandum and probans between two distinct entities is established through numerous examples, it is not logical; yet, you claim it is logical between two parts of a single cognition even though they do not exist as separate entities by their own nature—who other than one blinded by passion and delusion for his own position could say such a thing? Moreover, that which determines (*vyavasthāpaka*) performs an action upon that which is to be determined (*vyavasthāpya*), just as the property of being a *śiṃśipā* (a specific type of tree) produces a certainty regarding a tree. Therefore, even in the case of a determinant, the probans is not something other than the action itself. However, the object of determination (*prameya*) is not the action. Thus, this rebuttal—that linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) does not reside in the actual nature of things—is also not tenable. For if linguistic convention were entirely devoid of a real basis, it would follow that anything whatsoever could be designated as a probans. Consequently, the effort to establish that only the cognition possessing the form of the object (*arthākāra-jñāna*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by way of excluding other positions becomes futile. Therefore, the state of possessing a specific form (*viśiṣṭākāratva*) alone is the cause for the linguistic convention of "instrument" (*karaṇa*); and that [specific form] is not logical if no action distinct from the entity itself is produced.

But surely, even when no other action is produced, the establishment of factors such as the object (*karman*) is observed merely through the production of something qualified by similarity; for example, "the son resembles his mother," "the son resembles his father. For here, there is no separate action of "resembling" apart from the production of a son who is similar to the father. If [you say] it does not exist, then let the establishment of factors here also not be real, as in cases such as "the *gavaya* resembles a cow. However, in the case of the action of cognizing similarity, the instrument (*karaṇa*) is indeed distinct, namely the eye and so forth. And thus, wherever an action is perceived through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there must necessarily be an instrument distinct from that [action], just as in the case of the action of cutting; otherwise, the action would be accidental. Furthermore, no one understands that "he grasps the form of the father" merely from seeing the form of a son similar to him when the father is not actually present. By this, the example of brothers born at the same time who resemble each other is refuted according to the Vaibhāṣika position.

Furthermore, regarding the form of objects such as blue that appears in cognition, is it common or uncommon? If it is common, characterized by [universal properties] such as existence (*sattva*), then how can the determination of specific objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) be established from it? For its form would be indistinguishable in all cases. If, on the other hand, it is uncommon, characterized by blueness and so forth, or defined by the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyāvṛtti*), then because cognition is connected with that [form], it would follow that cognition is non-conscious (*abodhātmaka*) by nature. Why? Because that which is connected with blueness, or excluded from non-blue things, is invariably perceived to be non-conscious by nature. If it is argued that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because a cow and a gavaya are perceived to be of different species despite having a single identical form, we say no; for that form, characterized by a specific arrangement of parts, is common [to both], since that same form is seen even in wooden figures, paintings, and the like. By this, the example of father and son and so forth is also refuted, because cognition is devoid of color-form (*rūpa*) and the like, and is partless (*niravayava*). Even such a similarity does not exist [between them].
