Nor does the consequence of being non-conscious fail when there is a connection with such a similarity; and thus, if cognition were not cognition and the object were not an object, nothing would exist—like the churning of a donkey’s milk.

If you argue that because all objects consist of consciousness (*bodha*), there is no example whatsoever for anything lacking the nature of consciousness, and thus how could there be the possibility of knowledge being non-conscious by nature—well, we shall certainly dispel even this obsession of yours; do not be distressed. Furthermore, the argument that it is like a mirror with the shape of a face is also incorrect, because that [perception] is erroneous. Even if the cognition of the face itself were non-erroneous therein, the cognition of its identity with the mirror is indeed erroneous. Moreover, is the aspect of momentariness and so forth distinct from the aspect of the object such as blue residing in that cognition, or is it non-distinct? If it is distinct, then it follows that the aspect of the object such as blue would be non-momentary, since non-momentariness is defined by the exclusion of the momentary aspect. Consequently, just as the blueness and other qualities of the external object are established, its non-momentariness and other such qualities would also be established. If, on the other hand, it is non-distinct, then just as the blueness and other qualities of the object are established by that objective aspect, its momentariness and other qualities would also be established by it; thus, inference for that purpose would be redundant. Or, if momentariness and the rest were not established, then blueness and the rest would also not be established from that aspect, because there is no difference in the cognitive connection between those two aspects.

It might be argued: "A means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is held to be that which produces ascertainment (*niścāyaka*). Therefore, even though cognition possesses the form of an object with multiple natures, validity belongs only to that specific aspect in which it generates ascertainment due to the clarity of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and not to all aspects. But then, is that ascertainment with a form (*sākāra*) or without a form (*nirākāra*)? If it has a form, then that form of the object—whether it be the form of momentariness and so forth—is it different from [the cognition] or non-different? In this case, the same dilemma as before arises. Furthermore, if one were to postulate another ascertainment for that [first ascertainment], there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is without a form, then since cognition is indistinguishable across all objects by virtue of being the nature of ascertainment, how could the restriction regarding the object (*karmaniyama*)—that "this is the ascertainment of this particular object"—be established? If the restriction regarding each respective object is established for a formless [cognition] through some cause, then since that would be established elsewhere as well by that very same cause, what is the use of postulating a form? Moreover, if the form of the object in the cognition of an object were the means of valid cognition, then even in the case of an erroneous cognition of hair and so forth, the form of the hair and so forth would have to be a means of valid cognition.

Now, is it not the case that for non-contradictory cognition (*avisaṃvādijñāna*), the form of the object itself is accepted as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), since it has been said: "The means of valid cognition is non-contradictory cognition"? Now, what is this so-called "non-contradiction"? Is it not said to be the capacity to bring about the attainment of an entity capable of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)? As it has been stated: "For one who acts after having determined an object by means of these two [types of cognition] is not deceived regarding purposeful action. Even in common worldly usage, that which brings about the attainment of an object previously indicated is called "consistent" (*saṃvādaka*); likewise, a cognition is also called "consistent" when it brings about the attainment of the object it has displayed. And the capacity of a cognition to bring about such an object consists precisely in its generating activity toward that object, because only when there is activity is that object attained. Furthermore, the generation of activity consists simply in the illumination of the object that is the focus of that activity; for a cognition does not lead a person forward by seizing them by the neck. Therefore, the definition of a means of valid cognition is that a cognition is non-contradictory precisely insofar as it displays an entity capable of purposeful action. That is not correct, because it would follow that inference (*anumāna*) lacks the status of a means of valid cognition, for it does not display an entity capable of purposeful action. This is because it is admitted that inference is erroneous (*bhrānta*) due to having a non-existent universal (*sāmānya*) as its object. Nor is it tenable to say that even an erroneous cognition is non-contradictory because of its connection with a real object, since it is impossible for inference to have a connection with the object it grasps. If, on the other hand, non-contradiction were based on a connection with an object that is not grasped, then cognitions such as those of dreams or magical illusions (*indrajāla*) would also result in being non-contradictory, as they too have some kind of connection with an object. If you argue that non-contradiction is based on a connection with the object as it is conceptually determined (*adhyavasita*), this might be your thought: "The objects of means of valid cognition are of two kinds—the grasped (*grāhya*) and the determined (*adhyavaseya*). Although inference does not possess the capacity to bring about the attainment of an object in relation to its grasped object, it nevertheless brings about the attainment of the determined object; for even by means of inference, fire capable of the purposeful action of burning is determined, since we observe that those seeking such an action proceed from that [inference]. Therefore, just like perception, inference is also non-contradictory by virtue of bringing about the attainment of the determined object.

Furthermore, does this determination (*adhyavasāya*) determine only an object that has been perceived, or even one that has not been perceived? If it were to determine only what is perceived, fire capable of burning and so forth would not be determined by inference, because it is not perceived [at the time of the inference]. Alternatively, if it were perceived, then like perception (*pratyakṣa*), it would not be erroneous (*bhrānta*). If, however, it determines what is unperceived, then there would also be a determination of the three worlds, since there is no difference in their being unperceived. Now, you might think: "Due to the power of memory and superimposition (*adhyāropa*), there is no determination of the three worlds; just as when a lamp is seen, it is a gem that is determined, not the three worlds. This is because such is the very nature of error (*bhrānti*), whereby one thing is determined upon seeing another. If that is so, then even perception would result in being erroneous, because it determines moments distinct from what was actually seen; for the activity of those seeking purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is not possible if they determine a perishable moment. Nor is the blue portion anything other than a moment, wherein non-contradiction regarding activity and so forth could exist. Furthermore, mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) is not non-contradictory, as it is no different in the case of [illusory] hair and the like. It is also not tenable to say that "the very same continuum (*saṃtāna*) which was seen by perception is what is determined," because apart from the moment, the continuum is also impossible in reality. Moreover, it is not accepted that perception has a conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*) object, for that would entail no distinction from inference. If perception is non-erroneous simply because it determines what is perceived on the basis of mere worldly convention, then for that very reason inference would also be such, as there is no difference. Let this great discussion rest for now.

Likewise, even the cognitions of yogins do not possess the quality of revealing objects that exist as real entities, because the past and the future, being non-existent, are incapable of performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Similarly, self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) would also lack non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāditva*), since it does not reveal an object toward which purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) can be directed. Thus, even non-contradiction cannot withstand scrutiny within the Buddhist doctrine. Therefore, since the mere appearance of an object's form occurs even in erroneous cognition, such a cognition lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, is the nature of the external object perceived as being non-cognitive, or not? If it is not perceived, then even the mention of an external object must cease, because its nature—which is distinct from cognition—is not perceived. If, on the other hand, it is perceived by a cognition that possesses its form (*tadākāra*), is it perceived by a cognition having that very form, or by one not having that form? If it were by a cognition not having that form, then let there be perception of blue and so forth by a cognition that does not have the form of blue and so forth; what then is the use of postulating a cognition with the form of blue and so forth? If, however, even though it is non-cognitive in nature, it is perceived by a cognition having that very form, then surely, by virtue of the identity between the form of the non-cognitive nature and the cognition, the cognition itself would also become non-cognitive in nature. If you do not accept that the cognition becomes non-cognitive despite the identity with the form of the non-cognitive, then likewise, despite the identity with the form of cognition, let the form of blue and so forth be considered non-intellectual in nature, for there is no distinction between the two cases. Moreover, since the natures of cognition and non-cognition are contradictory, their unity is untenable. As Dharmakīrti himself has said: "This alone is the difference between entities, or the cause of difference, namely, the imposition of contradictory properties and the difference in causes. Therefore, if difference is not established, there would be no difference between anything and anything else, and the entire universe would be a single substance. Thus, since the forms of cognition and the object are distinct, the identity of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and its result (*phala*) is not tenable in the Śākya (Buddhist) doctrine. And so, as it was stated:

"Though the nature of cognition is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, to those whose vision is distorted.
And this establishment of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and their results proceeds according to such [distorted] perception."
"Even though it does not exist, it is produced for the cognition of the grasped and the grasper."

That is rejected, because the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*), the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), and self-awareness (*saṃvitti*) has been established as real. Furthermore, if the status of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and the result (*phala*) were established—even though non-existent—merely in accordance with erroneous perception, then why would that status not also be established for illusions such as [the appearance of] hairs and the like? For there is no difference in their being erroneous perceptions. Consequently, the distinction between valid and invalid cognition would be untenable. Now, was it not already stated that this objection has its own rebuttal? What is that? It is said: Even the proponent of "representation-only" (*vijñaptimātra*)—perceiving that the conventional practice of one who is unawakened is unreliable due to the defects of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cognitive disturbances and mental intentions—might declare one [type of cognition] to be invalid. He might declare another to be valid with respect to the non-contradiction of worldly practice here, on the grounds that its latent impressions are firm due to an uninterrupted continuity persisting as long as *saṃsāra* lasts. And this nature of valid cognition is appropriate for the merely conventional (*sāṃvyāvahārika*). Yet, even regarding this, others, being deluded, mislead the world; thus, they cultivate wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī prajñā*) so as to bring face-to-face the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) valid cognition, which is stainless through the discrimination of error and is unfailing. This is incorrect. For if all valid cognition established by the world is non-ultimate, from what source is the ultimate valid cognition—stainless through the discrimination of error—ascertained? Not by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because the knowledge of a yogin is not an object of the direct perception of people like us. If you say that self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the ultimate direct perception, even so, the distinction between the ultimate and the non-ultimate cannot be established by it, because it is merely the awareness of its own existence without distinction. Nor can it be established by inference (*anumāna*), since that depends upon the comprehension of a logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*). Now, a partless cognition or object does not possess a real threefold characteristic; if the establishment of a real object were based on an imagined threefold characteristic, then the establishment of a real object could follow from an inference imagined by others as well, since there is no difference. Moreover, since the non-momentariness of objects and so forth is perceived by everyone in the world without contradiction—just like the inference of fire and the like—why is it not accepted? If you argue that it is not accepted because investigators point out subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), we say no; for the subverting evidence will be refuted later. If, on the grounds that investigators provide subverting evidence, one does not accept what is perceived through non-contradiction with worldly practice, then the form of the object residing in cognition (*jñānagatārthākāra*) should also not be accepted, for you yourself have stated the subverting evidence against that. As it has been said: [The passage continues with the cited verse: *...tasmād arthasvarūpam eva svabhāvaḥ...* (Therefore, the very nature of the object is its own essence... (Note: The provided text ends mid-citation; the translation reflects the preceding argumentative prose.)
"Otherwise, how could the forms (*ākāra*) of a single entity that appears in various forms be real? For that would entail the loss of its unity.

If it is argued that this statement is directed against the proponent of the non-duality of the Self (*ātmādvaitavādin*), we reply: no, because the same [objection] applies, as we shall explain later. Furthermore, we will refute in detail later on the claim that cognition possesses the form of the object (*arthākāra*); therefore, even in the Śākyan (Buddhist) system, the object as the most effective means of proof (*sādhakatama*) is not tenable.
The instrument is that which most effectively accomplishes [the action].

Others, however, describe it otherwise: among many instruments (*sādhaka*), that which is most effective is called the "most effective instrument" (*sādhakatama*), according to the rule "the suffixes *tamap* and *iṣṭhan* are used to express excellence. This is true; however, we do not perceive such excellence in any single instrument, because all the factors of action (*kāraka*) participate equally in the performance of a single action. But has not the excellence (*atiśaya*) of the "dark one" (*tamas*) been explained in various ways? How so? It is the possession of that [excellence] by both existence and non-existence: when the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exists, the valid cognition (*pramā*) necessarily arises; but even when the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) exist, it may or may not arise. Or, the excellence is the state of not producing valid cognition despite the presence of the knower and the object, which [non-production] occurs due to the absence [of the means]. Or, it is the final stage of occurrence. Or, it is the immediate succession to apprehension—the meaning being that the excellence is that immediately following which the birth of apprehension occurs. Or, it is the status of being the unique cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*). Or, it is the state of favoring the conjunction that produces valid cognition. Or, it is the state of having its purpose unfulfilled (*acaritārthatā*): while the knower and the object have their purposes fulfilled once the means of knowledge has performed its function, the means of knowledge is called the "most effective instrument" because it produces the valid cognition while its own purpose remains unfulfilled. Or, the excellence is that which possesses [the capacity] by which one cognizes. The teacher, having set out to remove the student's doubt, has instead increased that very doubt by demonstrating these various unsettled positions: "What here is the most effective instrument?"
The final position among the positions stated by Uddyotakara and its refutation.

Some maintain that in all positions, it is intended that only the final cause possesses the status of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). But this is not so; for even objects of cognition (*prameya*), such as pleasure and pain, are seen to exist at the final moment in relation to their own perception, yet no connection (*sambandha*) arises there subsequently. If it is argued that even in that case, the cognition of "pleasurability" (*sukhatva*) and so forth occurs at the final moment, we reply that this is not accepted because non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) is not held to be preceded by the apprehension of a universal (*sāmānya*); as we shall explain later. Furthermore, in the production of color and other qualities belonging to themselves, composite wholes (*avayavin*) do indeed exist at the final moment; however, since they serve as the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), it is not logical for them to function as instruments (*karaṇa*). Moreover, if one does not accept the eye and other senses as instruments in the perception of color and so forth, then their existence could not be established through inference from the nature of action (*kriyātva*). Even in common worldly usage, the status of an instrument is well-known for axes and the like; thus, the establishment of a real object would not occur, as there would be no distinction [from other factors], except for the non-contradiction of worldly convention regarding the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and its contact. Furthermore, due to the contradiction with the *tulāsūtra*, the status of being the final factor alone cannot constitute instrumentality. Rucikāra, considering the intention of the enemy of darkness (Dignāga), stated that everything distinct from the object and the agent possesses the status of the most effective instrument. This is expressed by the phrase: "Or rather, that which possesses those [factors] by which one cognizes is the excellence (*atiśaya*). The meaning is: "That which possesses" (*yadvān*) refers to those auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) which exist for it; when an agent, endowed with those auxiliaries, accomplishes an action upon an object, those very auxiliaries are the most effective instruments, not the agent nor the object. Or, having reasoned it out himself, he stated: "Every causal factor (*kāraka*) distinct from the object and the agent is an instrument."
The causal efficiency belongs to the totality alone, and the refutation thereof.

Others, however, considering that no excellence (*atiśaya*) can belong to the individual causal factors (*kāraka*) merely by virtue of their distinctness, maintain that the status of being the "most effective means" (*sādhakatamatva*) belongs to the totality (*sāmagrī*) alone. For it is the totality that produces the action immediately upon its completion, whereas an individual part does not require anything further; this is said to be its excellence over its parts, constituting its status as the most effective means. That too is incorrect, for the totality is the complete collection of causal factors such as the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and so forth; how then can the totality itself be the instrument? Nor is it logical that the agent and other factors possess the nature of an agent only in their non-productive state, while possessing the nature of an instrument only in their productive state, since the status of being an agent and so forth is also dependent upon the action. Nor can it be that in the productive state they are instruments with respect to the whole, while being agents and so forth with respect to their individual parts, because that would result in their being unreal (*apāramārthika*), like the position accepted by the Buddhists, due to such a distinction being merely conceptual (*kālpnika*). If it is argued that the totality is an entity distinct from the agent and others, and that it possesses the status of the instrument, we say no; for this would entail that the agent and others lack productivity, since it is held that the effect arises from the totality alone, and because this view is tainted by the same refutations already stated against the theory of the final cause (*caramakāraṇa*). Furthermore, even if the totality is accepted as a cause in the sense of being a mere property (*dharma-mātra*), its status as the instrument is still untenable, as it contradicts the definition of being the "most effective means. In that case, let the view of Rucikāra be adopted; but no, for that would entail the absence of causal factors such as the recipient (*saṃpradāna*). If it is argued that the usage of terms like "recipient" and so forth applies to different types of instruments according to the analogy of grass and weeds (*tṛṇolapa-nyāya*), we say no, because there is no such perception. For just as the perception of "grass" is seen in the case of *ulapa* and similar plants, the perception of "instrument" is not similarly seen in the case of the recipient and others. If one were to accept such usage based on mere convention, then the acceptance of the agent and the object as being distinct types of instruments would also be unavoidable. Consequently, there would be no real, ontological determination of causal factors anywhere. Nor is it logical for causal factors to possess excellence merely through their distinctness from the agent and the object, for that would entail that the agent and the object themselves possess the status of being the most effective means, due to their mutual distinctness.
The status of being the most effective means (sādhakatamatva) as conceived by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*.

What, then, constitutes the state of being the most effective instrument (*sādhakatamatva*)? It is the capacity to accomplish an action belonging to that which is not itself to be accomplished, provided it is presided over by the direct agent. This [quality] does not exist in the case of the recipient (*saṃpradāna*) and so forth; for when one performs an action such as the gift of a cow, the teacher and others are not directly presided over. Rather, it is the hand, or speech, or the mind, or some other [organ] that is so presided over. Where this causal condition is absent, the designation "instrument" (*karaṇa*), even if it occurs, is not primary, just like the designation "agent" (*kartṛ*) applied to the object (*karman*) and other factors. Indeed, primary agency is not tenable without independence (*svātantrya*). Independence, moreover, consists in accomplishing an action according to one's own will. And that [independence], in the case of sentient beings, is either figurative or superimposed through conceptual construction, as in the expression, "the wall wishes to fall."

If it is argued that pleasure (*sukha*) and other such objects would also incur the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), since they directly accomplish the act of their own perception while being presided over by the Person (*puruṣa*), we say: no; for [the definition] is qualified by the term "that which is not yet accomplished" (*asādhya*). For here, all three kinds of objects (*karman*) are designated by the word "accomplished"—namely, the produced (*nirvartya*), the modified (*vikārya*), and the reached (*prāpya*). Without the presence of these characteristics, the status of being an instrument cannot be attributed to any object whatsoever. Indeed, among the factors of action (*kāraka*), there may even in reality be a convergence of these characteristics in certain cases; for example, in the act of cognizing one's own self, that very self possesses the status of agent (*kartṛ*), object (*karman*), and locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Thus, since the distinct definitions of the factors of action are established, the conventional usage of "object" and so forth is real; however, when those characteristics appear [in something else], the usage is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). Furthermore, where even a cause for metaphorical application (*upacāra*) does not exist, conventional usage is still possible through the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of those characteristics by means of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). But if there were an absolute absence of reality, there could be no usage even through the superimposition of conceptual construction; for an object never before perceived cannot be conceptually constructed, since even things like horns are only conceptually attributed to the head of a hare after having been seen on cows and the like. Therefore, that which is the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) toward valid cognition (*pramā*) is real; whether its nature is conscious (*bodhasvabhāva*) or unconscious (*abodhasvabhāva*), it is called a "means of knowledge" (*pramāṇa*). In this regard, it is established that by the word *sādhana* (instrument), which denotes that [means of knowledge], the valid cognition, the knower, and the object of knowledge are denoted.

{The definitions of the knower and so forth} The distinction between valid cognition (*pramā*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is not unreal, because their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are real. Thus, valid cognition is correct experience. The knower is the substratum of valid cognition; the meaning is that he is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of valid cognition. The object of knowledge is the object of valid cognition—that is, whatever entity appears within valid cognition is its object, the *prameya*.
{The inclusion of the knower, space, time, and so forth, within the object of knowledge}

If this is so, then in the first aphorism (*sūtra*), since the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) has a characteristic distinct from the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), the cognizer should also be taught separately, just like the object of cognition (*prameya*) and so forth. [Response: No; because the cognizer is established by the very mention of the means of valid cognition. For a means of valid cognition is not possible without a cognizer, and it is for the purpose of making known that they share the same status of success or failure (*tulyayogakṣematva*). By the same reasoning by which the existence of the means of valid cognition and its capacity to produce specific or non-specific results are established, the same applies to the cognizer; therefore, no separate mention of him was made. [Objection: In that case, a separate mention of the object of cognition (*prameya*) would also not be required. [Response: True; however, we do not accept a separate mention of the mere object of cognition in general. A mention of a specific type of object of cognition is made for a particular purpose. We shall demonstrate that purpose later when describing the specific definitions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*). Just as with the mere object of cognition, the mere act of cognition (*pramiti*) is also mentioned by the very mention of the means of valid cognition. But by the term "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*), a specific type of cognition is mentioned for the purpose of making known that it is the cause of liberation (*apavarga*). If, however, a specific type of object of cognition is mentioned by the term "object of cognition," then surely space, time, atoms, and so forth would not be included. Consequently, since the entire cause of the world would not be explained, its status as a treatise on the inner self (*adhyātmaśāstra*) would be untenable. This is not a fault, because everything is included within the mere object of cognition already mentioned through the power of the mention of the means of valid cognition. This being the case, there is nothing here—whether of the nature of existence or non-existence—that is not mentioned, since everything is an object of cognition by virtue of being an object of knowledge. [Objection: Then the separate statement of doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the other categories is useless, as they are included either within the means of valid cognition or the objects of cognition. [Response: No; even though they are included, they are mentioned separately for a specific purpose. Thus, the purpose of doubt has been established as being the cause for the commencement of inquiry (*nyāyapravṛtti*). Indeed, by means of separate mention and definition, the fact that doubt and the others—which have well-ascertained natures—serve separate purposes will become easy to understand. With this intention, the venerable author of the *Sūtras*, disregarding the brevity of the aphorisms, preferred the *daṇḍaka-sūtra* (the list-style enumeration). Among those, the nature of doubt alone has been stated, but its purpose was mentioned previously; however, the purpose of the others [doubt, etc. was not yet stated, and thus it must now be told.
The description of the purpose of the purpose.

Now, as for the purpose (*prayojana*), one might ask: "What is the purpose of the purpose? This question is not logical, because [the purpose] is of the nature of that [purpose]. For a question regarding the purpose is appropriate only in the case of taking up something that is not itself of the nature of a purpose—[asking], "What is the purpose of this? But in the case of something that is already of the nature of a purpose, a question regarding its purpose is inappropriate; for one does not say, "What is the purpose of happiness? No, [that is not so], because of a misunderstanding of our intention. We do not say, "What is the purpose of the purpose? Rather, we ask: "Even though the purpose is included within the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of cognition (*prameya*), what is the purpose of stating it separately? To this, the author of the Commentary (*Bhāṣyakṛt*) said: "By this [purpose], all living beings, all actions, and all sciences are pervaded, and the system of reasoning (*nyāya*) proceeds by depending upon it. However, we do not understand this with the same conviction, because the pervasion by a purpose is well-known elsewhere in both the world and in scripture. For instance, all those learned in the scriptures and all worldly people, while generally understanding that all living beings' actions, sciences, and systems of reasoning possess a purpose, raise inquiries regarding their specific purposes: "For what purpose did this man act? For what aim is this action? For what aim is this scripture? For what purpose is this inference? Therefore, another purpose is stated.

Some here, desiring to refute the knowledge of the Supreme Self as the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), maintain that the Supreme Lord does not exist because His activity is impossible due to a lack of purpose. They do not accept the purpose stated by the Naiyāyika—namely, the characteristic of restraining and favoring all living beings—arguing that it is not logical for the happiness or absence of suffering belonging to one person to be the purpose of another, and that even the restraint of others cannot be the purpose of one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*). To support this [position], the author of the Sūtras sets forth and restates the well-known definition of a "purpose" separately: "That object aiming at which one acts is the purpose. This is what is meant: in the world, when someone acts having resolved, "I shall accomplish or avert this object for myself or for others," that is established as his purpose. Therefore, whatever object the Blessed One acts aiming at, that alone is His purpose. For although the Blessed One is endowed with unsurpassed knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty, He is of such a nature that He acts aiming at the accomplishment of gain and loss for all transmigrating beings in accordance with their karma; therefore, that alone is the purpose of the Blessed One, because it satisfies the definition of a purpose, just like the pleasure and so forth desired by both parties.
The nature and purpose of the example.

Now, what is the nature and purpose of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)? Some say that the locus of external pervasion (*bahirvyāpti*) is the example. Others say that an example is that which possesses both the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), as well as that which is devoid of them, and is distinct from the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*). The *Bhāṣya* states: "An object within the range of perception is the example. The *Sūtra* states: "That in which there is a consensus of understanding (*buddhisāmya*) among common people and investigators is the example. In this context, the phrase "in which" should be supplied to refer to the locus of external pervasion, the illustrative instance (*udāharaṇa*), or that which possesses or is devoid of the properties of the probandum and the probans. "Consensus of understanding"—that is, agreement—among common people and investigators, meaning between the person to be convinced and the person who convinces, is the example. If it is asked: "Since there is no person to be convinced or one who convinces at the time of inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*), how can the example be an object of consensus of understanding? We reply: No; even in that case, for one who reflects upon it, that very [object] possesses both forms (of being both the subject and the locus), just like the author of a treatise. Alternatively, it may be justified by way of potentiality (*yogyatā*), or another definition should be seen for that which is not included by this definition, just as a substance (*dravya*) is not excluded from being "possessing action" (*kriyāvat*) [even when it is motionless].

Others, however, describe it thus: worldly people are those for whom the properties to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) are established, while investigators are those for whom the proving properties (*sādhanadharma*) are established; where there is no disagreement regarding the establishment of the relationship between the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the pervaded (*vyāpya*) among these, that is the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding its separate mention, the author of the *Bhāṣya* stated the purpose: "Inference and scripture have that [example] as their basis; when it exists, inference and scripture may exist, and when it does not exist, they would not exist. The operation of reasoning (*nyāyapravṛtti*) is also based upon it. The refutation of the opponent's position must be stated by means of contradiction with the example, and one's own position must be established through the corroboration of the example. Furthermore, an atheist who accepts an example would abandon his atheism, whereas if he does not accept it, with what proof could he rebuke another? And once the example has been defined, it is possible to state: 'An example is an illustration (*udāharaṇa*) because of its similarity to the property to be proven, wherein the presence of that property occurs, or, conversely, the opposite. However, we have already stated previously: the statement of the definition following the enumeration is for the sake of restatement (*anuvāda*); and in the case of restatement, the purpose is the prescription and prohibition of the example and its fallacies (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*) in order to remove the confusion of those who are mistaken. Therefore, even what was stated by the author of the *Bhāṣya* should be accepted as being consistent with this."
The nature and purpose of the established tenet.

"In that case, the nature and purpose of a *siddhānta* (tenet) must be stated. A *siddhānta* is an object (*artha*) accepted by oneself. The inclusion of the word "object" (*artha*) serves to exclude from the category of one's own *siddhānta* that which one has accepted merely as a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) or out of rhetorical boldness (*prauḍhivāda*), and it also serves to indicate that even what is being accepted at the present moment constitutes a *siddhānta*. The *Bhāṣya* states: "A *siddhānta* is an object that is being admitted as 'this exists. The authors of the *Ṭīkā* state: "A *siddhānta* is an object possessing both general and specific characteristics, which is being accepted through an admission rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). They interpret the *Bhāṣya* in this same sense. In that context, the qualifier "possessing general and specific characteristics" is redundant, as is the mention of "presently [being accepted]," for an object previously accepted is certainly not a non-*siddhānta*. If it is argued that even an acceptance lacking final determination is a *siddhānta*, then let there simply be the term "acceptance" (*abhyupagama*); why the prolixity of words? Furthermore, what is the purpose of the phrase "rooted in valid means of knowledge"? If it implies that the objects accepted by Buddhists and others are not *siddhāntas*, then one should not point out contradictions with their *siddhāntas*; for if no *siddhānta* exists, how can there be a contradiction with one? If it is argued that the word *siddhānta* applies to what merely resembles a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*) just as the word "valid means" does, we say no; for such usage would be mere conventional practice. No one who is sane, even if aware of the situation, points out a contradiction based on a pseudo-means of knowledge. For one who does so would incur the defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) of "failing to point out a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*). Therefore, one must accept that even the objects accepted by Buddhists and others are *siddhāntas* insofar as they are established by their own intention. Accordingly, this common usage exists both in the world and in the treatises: "This is the *siddhānta* of the Buddhists," "This is that of the Sāṃkhyas," "This is that of the Mīmāṃsakas. Moreover, once these are generally recognized as *siddhāntas*, there may also be a distinction between those supported by valid means and those not. The *Sūtra* states: "A *siddhānta* is the establishment (*saṃsthiti*) of a system (*tantra*), a topic (*adhikaraṇa*), or an admission (*abhyupagama*). "Establishment" (*saṃsthiti*) is a synonym for *siddhānta*. Thus, there are three kinds of *siddhānta*: establishment of a system, establishment of a topic, and establishment of an admission. According to the author of the *Bhāṣya*, the *siddhānta* is said to be fourfold in the subsequent *Sūtra* due to the different types of systems (*tantra*). However, the authors of the *Ṭīkā* say: "A *tantra* is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); that which has this as its basis (*adhikaraṇa*) or root for the establishment of the admission of a particular object is thus described. Consequently, they believe that the definition beginning with 'possessing general and specific characteristics' is what is expressed by this [term]. They explain the *Bhāṣya* which mentions the threefold division according to the opinion of a partial school (*ekadeśīya*).

In our view, however, the definition is simply this: "the establishment (*saṃsthiti*) of what has been accepted (*abhyupagama*). How so? By the word *abhyupagama*, used as a noun denoting the object (*karmasādhana*), "the object accepted" is expressed; its "establishment" means its formal determination (*vyavasthā*). The meaning is: whatever object is accepted by someone, that is his *siddhānta*. And that establishment is threefold—distinguished by a system (*tantra*), distinguished by a topic (*adhikaraṇa*), and undistinguished; therefore, the *siddhānta* is of three kinds. The statement of this threefold nature is for the purpose of making known this point: for those who engage in debate without having accepted a specific system (*tantra*), a fallacy of the thesis (*apasiddhānta*) occurs only through contradiction with the acceptance of a topic or a *siddhānta*, not through contradiction with the content of the system itself. However, when there is an intention to distinguish between systems, it is fourfold; for that purpose, the Sūtra states: "Because of the existence of different objects [in the form of] the establishment of the *sarvatantra*, *pratitantra*, *adhikaraṇa*, and *abhyupagama*. If it is argued that the existence of these as distinct objects is unproven, we say no; for they are perceived through their difference in defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). To that end, there are four Sūtras. Among them: "An object that is not contradicted by any system and is relevant to the system is a *sarvatantrasiddhānta*. For example: the establishment of the objects of knowledge based on the means of knowledge; the production of an effect from a cause; and the comprehension of the speaker’s intended meaning from hearing a sentence whose conventional signification is well-known. Indeed, without accepting these, the activity of composing, listening to, or explaining a treatise, or engaging in debate, would not be possible for anyone who is not insane.

"A tenet established in one's own system but not established in another system is a *pratitantrasiddhānta* (tenet specific to a particular system). Some maintain that an example of this type is as follows: for the followers of Kapila (*Kāpilas*), the *Pātañjala* [system] is a common system (*samāna-tantra*), and for the followers of Patañjali (*Pātañjalas*), the *Kāpila* [system] is likewise a common system. However, the commentators (*ṭīkākāras*) do not accept this, considering it to be unproven and lacking authoritative basis. According to their view, the example is as follows: for the Naiyāyikas, the Vaiśeṣika treatise is a common system, and for the Vaiśeṣikas, the Nyāya treatise is a common system. We, however, explain it differently: when there is a single foundational system shared by numerous authors, commentators, and listeners, it is called a "common" (*sāmāna*) or "shared" (*samāna*) system—just as one speaks of a "common house" or "common wealth. Whatever point is established within that shared system, but is not established in some or all other systems, is a *pratitantrasiddhānta*. Thus, it is understood that a point not established in one's own school, even if established in a similar system, does not constitute a *pratitantrasiddhānta*. Consequently, even if there is a contradiction with such a point, the fallacy of "departing from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) does not follow.

"That which, upon its own establishment, results in the establishment of another matter, is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. When the establishment of a certain object occurs by implication through the force of [the argument], and thereby the establishment of another related matter—which is called a *prakaraṇa* because it is being introduced (*prakriyate*)—becomes faultless, that is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. For example, when the fact that the world and other effects have an intelligent creator is established, the establishment of attributes such as omniscience for that creator occurs by implication through the force of the argument and becomes faultless. For one devoid of attributes such as omniscience is not capable of producing effects such as bodies and worlds that correspond to the ripening of the karma of living beings. Thus, an object known to be connected with the probandum (*sādhya*) is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*; or rather, the probandum itself is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. How so? When a probandum is being established, if the establishment of other particulars follows from the very means of proving that [probandum] due to their being part of the context (*prakaraṇāt*), then that probandum, having included those particulars, is established as an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*. "The *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* is simply the meaning of the reason (*hetu*)," says the author of the *Ṭīkā*. How so? When smoke and the like are established, if there is the establishment of fire and the like which are other than it, then that smoke and so forth is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

"Accepting the examination of its specific qualities because of the acceptance [of the subject] without prior examination is the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (tenet by admission). The authors of the *Ṭīkā* state: "The *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is precisely that which is yet to be proven (*sādhya*). How so? Because one accepts sound or other such things as the locus (*dharmin*) without prior examination—that is, without having investigated them in terms of their impermanence and so forth—the specific quality of that locus, such as impermanence, is then examined. Thus, the examination itself is the *abhyupagama-siddhānta*. However, according to the literal meaning of the *Bhāṣya*, the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is the opposite of what has been examined; it is an unexamined matter not belonging to one's own school (*asvaśāstraka*), which is specifically qualified by the act of admission. Therefore, this very aphorism should be analyzed as defining the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* as "the acceptance of what has not been examined. In this regard, if someone asks: "Why would anyone accept a matter not belonging to their own school even while knowing it? the answer is: "Because of the acceptance of what has not been examined, he wishes to perform an examination of its specific qualities"—this must be supplied [to the aphorism]. Is it not possible to examine its specific qualities otherwise? Who says so? If it is argued that for one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) and seeks liberation (*mumukṣu*), the display of intellectual superiority is improper, we say no. For Buddhists and others proceed in this manner solely for the sake of gain, honor, and fame; thus, when they speak in contradiction to the *abhyupagama-siddhānta*, the seeker of liberation may point out their "fallacy of deviating from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*). This is the purpose of defining it. Furthermore, the activity of the learned through the mode of "admission" (*abhyupagama-vāda*) is observed for the purpose of demonstrating that one's own position is fortified by many lines of reasoning (*nyāya*). For example, even while accepting the eternity of the Vedas, their authority is established solely on the basis of the authority of a trustworthy person (*āpta*). Indeed, the comprehension of their meaning does not arise from the Vedas alone without an explanation, and an explanation is precisely the correct understanding of the meaning, even if it is not the primary subject at hand. Moreover, for the learned who employ the mode of admission, the purpose is the avoidance of the charge of "deviating from a tenet. For one who is well-acquainted with the different types of tenets is able to avoid contradictions within his own statements and to expose them in the statements of others. It is for this purpose that all the different types of tenets have been defined. The author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, states this purpose: "Since there are these different types of tenets, debate (*vāda*), sophistry (*jalpa*), and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed; not otherwise."
The essential nature and definition of the members of a formal argument (*nyāyāvayava*).

Now, what is the essential nature and purpose of the members (*avayava*) [of a syllogism]? The author of the *Bhāṣya* has stated the nature of the members as follows: "In whatever collection of words the establishment of the matter to be proven is completed, that collection has five parts—the proposition (*pratijñā*) and so forth. With respect to the whole collection, they are called 'members'. This is accepted by us. Their individual purpose in being stated has also been explained. Among them, there is a convergence of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): the proposition is scripture (*āgama*), the reason (*hetu*) is inference (*anumāna*), the example (*udāharaṇa*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*), the application (*upanaya*) is comparison (*upamāna*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*) is for the purpose of demonstrating the capacity of all [the members] to converge upon a single object. This is the supreme method (*nyāya*). By means of this, formal debate (*vāda*), contentious debate (*jalpa*), and destructive criticism (*vitaṇḍā*) proceed; and based upon it, the determination of reality (*tattva-vyavasthā*) occurs. This is accepted by us without contradicting our own system. However, in our own system, the purpose is the prescription and prohibition, directed toward those who are mistaken, regarding the true nature and the fallacies of the proposition and the other members, following a restatement of their definitions.
An Examination of Reasoning (Tarka)

The nature and purpose of *tarka* (reasoning) have already been determined previously. This aphorism is intended to define it: “*Tarka* is a deliberation (*ūha*) regarding an object whose true nature is unknown, for the sake of attaining knowledge of that true nature, based on the logical possibility of a cause. An object whose true nature (*tattva*)—the specific characteristic that serves as the basis for a definitive conclusion—is unknown, is called an “object of unknown true nature. Regarding such an object, “based on the logical possibility of a cause” means that a deliberation, which is synonymous with *tarka*, arises from the possibility of a subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*). And this is for the sake of knowing the true nature, because it discriminates the object of the knowledge of the true nature; thus say the ancient teachers. We, however, say: the “logical possibility of a cause” is the probability of a means of proof (*sādhana*). If a particular means of proof should ever deviate from its own probandum (*sādhya*), then upon seeing that [deviation], there arises a deliberation concerning the probandum, thinking, “It must be by this [cause] that [the effect] occurs. And this [deliberation] is also for the sake of the knowledge of the true nature by way of human activity; likewise, by way of engaging in debate and the like, it serves to preserve previously arisen knowledge of the true nature and to bring about the knowledge of the true nature of victory and defeat. Furthermore, for one engaged in yoga, when a specific means for the cessation of obstacles or a specific means for the stabilization of the mind is not well-known, deliberation serves indirectly for the sake of the vision of the Self (*ātma-darśana*). Thus, in other cases as well, the fact that deliberation is for the sake of the knowledge of the true nature should be understood through its role in various activities, whether in its own domain or in another domain.
{The Definition of Determination}

“Ascertainment (*nirṇaya*) is the determination of the object through the consideration of the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*); such is the aphorism. Ascertainment is performed by a person after having considered—that is, after having raised a doubt—on what grounds? Through the thesis and the counter-thesis. By the word “thesis,” the proof (*sādhana*) concerning the thesis is meant; by the word “counter-thesis,” the refutation (*dūṣaṇa*) concerning the counter-thesis is meant. What is the purpose of this metaphorical usage (*upacāra*)? It is to establish the distinction between their respective objects: that the proof has the thesis as its object alone, and the refutation has the counter-thesis as its object alone. For if it were stated simply as “through proof and refutation,” one might suspect that they share a single object. “Determination of the object” is a synonymous expression for the same thing. [Objection: It is incorrect to say “after having considered,” because even in the absence of deliberation, perceptual and inferential certainty is observed regarding things like fire in the palm of the hand and so forth. [Reply: No, because the intended definition pertains to the ascertainment of objects beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). Why? Because the scripture aims at the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), and the supreme good results only from the ascertainment of the self (*ātman*) and other such principles; therefore, that alone is being defined. [Objection: Furthermore, the ascertainment of the self and so forth occurs for some people through scripture alone, or through the proof of their own position alone; thus, it is incorrect to say “through the thesis and the counter-thesis. [Reply: No, because the scripture is commenced for the sake of the investigator (*vicāraka*). Since this is a treatise on logic (*nyāya*), the investigator is the qualified recipient of its teaching, and for him, ascertainment must be achieved by way of resolving conflicting opinions (*vipratipatti*). Moreover, such ascertainment does not arise from proof alone, because if both positions were established by proof, there would be the contingency of a "non-deviating contradiction" (*viruddhāvyabhicāritva*). Nor does it arise from refutation alone, because without proof, the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible. What then? It arises from the proof of one’s own position when it is supported by the refutation of the counter-position; hence it is said, “through the thesis and the counter-thesis. However, if the intention is to provide a definition of ascertainment in general, the aphorism should be seen as merely: “Ascertainment is the determination of the object.”

But surely, since *niścaya* (ascertainment) is the fruit of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), its mention [in the definition of the goal] already implies its mention [here]; furthermore, its specific nature has been taught by the term "knowledge of reality" (*tattvajñāna*). So why is this [category of *nirṇaya*] begun separately? No; it is for the purpose of making known that it is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) by virtue of being dedicated solely to that end. The reality (*tattva*)—that is, the definition—of the means of valid cognition and so forth has been stated. From the ascertainment of that [reality], there is the ascertainment of the means of valid cognition and so forth. From the ascertainment of the means of valid cognition and so forth, there is the determination of the self (*ātman*) and other categories. It is through this sequence that knowledge of the reality of the means of valid cognition and so forth is said to be the cause of the supreme good. Even when the very ascertainment of the means of valid cognition and so forth constitutes the knowledge of the reality of the self and others, it becomes the cause of the supreme good only by way of the determination of the self and so forth, and not otherwise. Therefore, the determination of the self and so forth is a cause of the supreme good only when it effects an ascertainment elsewhere; thus, its separate commencement is justified for the purpose of qualifying the knowledge of reality—it is not merely the knowledge of the reality of the self and so forth as taught [in scripture] that is the cause of the supreme good for the investigator. Rather, it is that which consists of ascertainment, which does not waver because it has arisen from well-investigated means accompanied by the refutation of opposing views. The Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), however, states the purpose: "Debate (*vāda*) ends with that [ascertainment]; *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* are for its protection. These two, reasoning (*tarka*) and ascertainment (*nirṇaya*), sustain the course of worldly life."
The purpose of debate and the other [categories].

We shall explain the nature of *vāda* and the other [forms of debate] later on. As for the purpose of *vāda*, the *Bhāṣya* states: "The separate mention [of *vāda*] is for the sake of definition (*upalakṣaṇārtham*). Through that which is thus defined, worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) occurs for the sake of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). It is my view that, having restated the nature of *vāda*, it is prescribed as something to be performed by one who seeks the knowledge of reality, while its pursuit for the sake of gain and so forth is prohibited. And thus says the Sūtra: "One should engage in it with disciples, teachers, fellow students, and the learned who seek excellence, provided they are free from malice. In this regard, one should engage in *vāda* with those of superior wisdom, being humble, for the sake of cutting through doubt, for the sake of obtaining permission regarding what has been determined, and for the sake of understanding what has not yet been determined. For one who engages in *vāda* with those of equal wisdom who act as neutral umpires, there is the ripening of wisdom, the aforementioned result, and the benefit of others as a secondary consequence. Regarding *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*, however, their purpose is said to be the protection of the determination of truth; this we shall examine further below.
The purpose of the points of defeat (nigrahasthāna).

The purpose [of teaching] fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*), quibble (*chala*), futile rejoinder (*jāti*), and points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is their avoidance in one's own statements and their exposure in the statements of others. Furthermore, having restated the definitions of fallacious reasons and so forth, these are prescribed or prohibited for one who is in disagreement regarding their true nature or its opposite. Regarding this, the *Bhāṣya* states: "Fallacious reasons, taught separately from the points of defeat, will be subject to censure in debate. This is not correct, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) [of the rule] is impossible in either case. If, first, those which are taught separately from the points of defeat are those that must be censured in debate, then doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the like would also have to be censured in debate. If, on the other hand, those which are to be censured in debate are those taught separately from the points of defeat, then there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to [the category of] "departure from tenets" (*apasiddhānta*) and so forth; for although these are censurable in debate, they are not taught separately. Some offer this rebuttal: "Those which, while being included within the points of defeat, are taught separately from them, are to be censured in debate, just like quibble and the rest. This is not correct, because no purpose has been stated. Even if quibble and futile rejoinder are admitted to be points of defeat, a purpose must be stated for the separate mention of all three [quibble, futile rejoinder, and fallacious reason] from the points of defeat; yet that has not been stated. Moreover, since the state of being censurable in debate is possible even without a separate teaching—just as in the case of departure from tenets—it follows that the separate mention is useless. It is my view that the separate teaching [of fallacious reasons] from the points of defeat is for the sake of understanding the detailed classification of fallacious reasons by way of the expansion of their specific definitions. For there is no such detailed classification for the "loss of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth, which are not taught separately. Furthermore, the inferent attains great proficiency in discerning the various classifications of fallacious reasons only through this [separate teaching], and not otherwise. If quibble and futile rejoinder are also included within the points of defeat, then this very [purpose of detailed classification] should be seen as the reason for their separate mention.

{Demonstrating the Supremacy of the Science of Logic} This very science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī*), being analyzed through its categories such as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth— [is declared]:
"It is the lamp of all sciences, the means for all actions," [and so on].

"The basis of all dharmas has been examined in the section on the sciences (*vidyā*)," so says the commentary. This is now considered: is the distinction between the sciences due to a difference in their subject matter (*viṣaya*), or rather due to a difference in their purpose (*prayojana*)? If it were due to a difference in subject matter, then there would not be only four sciences, because the fourteen sciences have distinct subject matters; as it has been said: "The Vedas are four, along with their auxiliary limbs (*aṅga*), Mīmāṃsā, and the expansion of Nyāya..."
"The Purāṇas and the Dharmaśāstras—these indeed are the fourteen sciences.
Even this restriction to fourteen is not tenable, because the Śaivasiddhānta and other such systems, as well as the medical science (vaidyaśāstra) and others, possess distinct subject matters.

Now, if the distinction [between the sciences] is based on a difference in their purposes (*prayojana*), even so, there would be no distinction between *Daṇḍanīti* (the science of government) and *Vārttā* (the science of economics), as they share a single purpose; likewise, there would be no distinction between the *Upaniṣads* and *Ānvīkṣikī* (logic). How then could there be four sciences through the division of the *Trayī* (the three Vedas) and so forth? Therefore, the four sciences should be understood according to the distinction between the primary and secondary goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*): namely, the treatises on Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa. Among these, Kāma and Mokṣa are said to be the attainment and avoidance of pleasure and pain, respectively; and their means—Artha and Dharma—are said to be distinguished by being visible (*dṛṣṭa*) and invisible (*adṛṣṭa*). [Objection: If that is the case, then since both the *Trayī* and *Ānvīkṣikī* have liberation (*apavarga*) as their goal, they would result in being non-distinct. [Reply: True. Nevertheless, because its subject matter consists of critical inquiry (*vicāra*) and because it supports all other sciences, it possesses primacy over all other sciences and has internal subdivisions. Its status as a supporter of all sciences is due to its being the *Nyāya-śāstra* (the science of logic). For it is by means of *nyāya* (reasoning) that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of all sciences is established. If it is asked: "Even though perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge are its objects, why is this specifically recognized as the *Nyāya-śāstra*? It is said in reply: Because doubt (*saṃśaya*) and the other categories are presented here through their definitions (*uddeśa*) and so forth, as constituent parts for the purification of the application of reasoning (*nyāyapravṛtti*). For this very reason, although other sciences may deal with inference (*anumāna*), they do not possess the status of *Nyāya-śāstra*. Indeed, in other sciences, the categories from doubt up to the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are not defined in this manner. Thus, because it is dominated by *nyāya*, this alone is the science of logic (*nyāyavidyā*). And because it supports all sciences and is the instrumental cause of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), which is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), it is the most excellent.
Liberation occurs gradually through the knowledge of reality.

Now, does that knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) indeed bring about the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) immediately upon its own attainment? It is said: No; what then? From the knowledge of reality, "upon the successive disappearance of false knowledge, defects, activity, birth, and suffering, there follows the disappearance of each preceding one, and thus liberation (*apavarga*) occurs"—this is the completion of the sentence. Here, the second aphorism is to be understood by supplying the words: "The beginningless causal relationship between suffering, birth, activity, defects, and false knowledge constitutes *saṃsāra*. For it is by means of this aphorism that the possibility of *saṃsāra* and *apavarga* through the non-arising and arising of the knowledge of reality is examined, so that the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), having ascertained the capacity of the knowledge of reality to attain liberation, may apply himself with diligence toward its production. To demonstrate the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra*, the items beginning with false knowledge are stated here in reverse order.

In this regard, false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) concerning the objects of cognition (*prameya*), such as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, exists in many forms: the notion that the real self, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and other such things do not exist; the notion of "self" in what is not-self; the notion of "non-difference" in what is different; the notion of "pure" in what is impure; the notion that another is the agent of one's own produced sufferings; the notion that "I am the agent" regarding sufferings produced by others; the notion of "desirable" in what is loathsome; and the notion of "permanent" in what is impermanent, or "to be accepted" in what is to be abandoned. From such false knowledge arise attachment (*rāga*) toward agreeable objects and aversion (*dveṣa*) toward disagreeable ones. For one impelled by these two and acting through speech, body, and mind, there occurs the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*). How so? One who acts out of attachment toward divine objects to be enjoyed in future births, or toward non-divine objects, accumulates merit by means of performing enjoined sacrifices and the like. Furthermore, one who acts out of attachment toward perceived objects accumulates demerit by means of performing prohibited acts and transgressing what is enjoined. Even from aversion, because the performance of enjoined acts is generally impossible, one primarily accumulates demerit alone. These two accumulations of merit and demerit are referred to here by the term "activity" (*pravṛtti*) because they are the means for activity; through them, birth characterized by the connection with a body and sense organs occurs in the states of gods, humans, and animals. From that, suffering of various kinds—such as dwelling in the womb—and false knowledge arise; and from those, again, the emergence of defects (*doṣa*) and so forth follows. Thus, the uninterrupted causal relationship of false knowledge and the rest is called *saṃsāra*. But when false knowledge departs due to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), then, upon the disappearance of false knowledge, the defects disappear; upon the disappearance of defects, activity disappears; upon the disappearance of activity, birth disappears; and upon the disappearance of birth, suffering disappears, resulting in absolute liberation (*atyantāpavarga*).
An objection regarding the cessation of false cognition and so forth.

Now, what is this "removal" (*apāya*) of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—is it non-arising (*anutpatti*), or is it destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*)? First, non-arising does not result from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), for non-arising, being beginningless, cannot be produced by anything. If it is destruction, that occurs even when the knowledge of reality has not arisen, because all cognitions perish very quickly; nor is any distinction caused by a specific cause perceived in their destruction. Furthermore, the claim that once false knowledge has ceased due to the knowledge of reality, no other false knowledge arises, is also untrue. For instance, although the cognition of a snake in a rope and so forth ceases due to the knowledge of reality, one observes that after some time, the cognition of a snake appears again in that same rope and so forth. Thus, the obstruction of the cause is also without inferential proof. The statement that "upon the removal of false knowledge, there is the removal of defects (*doṣa*)" is also incorrect, because we observe that even those possessing the knowledge of reality are blinded by passion (*rāga*), hatred (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). If you argue that those who are overcome by passion and so forth do not possess the knowledge of reality, then why is the production of the knowledge of reality not possible for those explaining the *Nyāya-śāstra* itself? What, then, would be the means (*sādhana*) for that [knowledge]? Furthermore, the subsidence of passion and so forth is observed for some even when they lack the knowledge of reality for a certain period, yet it is never absolute for anyone; for even in the case of great yogins such as Hari and Hiraṇyagarbha, we hear of their being overcome by passion and so forth regarding certain objects at certain times. Therefore, even the knowledge of reality consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) is not the cause for the subsidence of passion and so forth. The statement that "upon the removal of defects, there is the removal of activity (*pravṛtti*)" is also incorrect, for this living being cannot remain like a stone. And if one does not perform what is enjoined for the sake of avoiding demerit (*adharma*) and does not desist from what is prohibited, then demerit must necessarily arise, since the transgression of what is enjoined and the performance of what is prohibited are causes of demerit, while merit (*dharma*) arises from the opposite of these. How, then, can both be avoided? Thus, since the removal of activity is impossible, there is no removal of birth either; and because that is impossible, liberation (*apavarga*), characterized as the absolute removal of suffering, is not logically established.
The resolution thereof.

To this, the following reply is given: The removal (*apāya*) of false cognition (*mithyājñāna*) consists in the non-arising of that which has not yet arisen and the destruction of that which has already arisen. As for what was said—that because it is beginningless, there can be no arising [of its cessation], and how then could it come about through the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*)? That is not so, because we do not accept that position. We do not say that the non-arising of false cognition—which was previously non-existent—comes about through the knowledge of reality; rather, it is the obstruction of that cause, such as demerit (*adharma*) and the like, which brings about its non-arising, that occurs through the knowledge of reality. Nor is the obstruction of a cause something beyond inference, for one does not perceive the arising of false cognition with respect to an object of true knowledge, such as a post (*sthāṇu*). Indeed, a false determination is never observed to manifest after having sublated a true determination. Furthermore, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of true and false cognitions is also to be inferred, just as it is between the cognitions themselves. For instance, even an impression produced by a single instance of true knowledge, having sublated the entire collection of impressions born of false cognition regarding the same object, generates a memory that conforms to the form of true knowledge and is capable of specific practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, through the practice of true knowledge, the impression born thereof increases day by day, while that born of false cognition decreases until every impression born of false cognition is exhausted. Then, demerit (*adharma*) also—due to the absence of auxiliary causes and being obstructed by true knowledge or its impression—no longer produces false cognition and, due to some cause, eventually perishes utterly. Once that has perished, false cognition never arises again due to the absence of its cause. Thus, the non-arising of false cognition never ceases; when maintained in that state, it is figuratively said to have been "effected" by the knowledge of reality. As for the argument against the theory of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), namely that there is no distinction in destruction, that is incorrect, because it is observed in experience. For although a lamp perishes moment by moment, its effects—the visual perception of objects, the accumulation of collyrium, and so forth—do not cease. However, when its destruction is brought about by water or other means, then all the effects of the lamp cease and the conventional usage of its "absence" occurs. Or, it is like the uprooting of a bulbous root (*kanda*): just as when a plant’s root is completely uprooted with a spade or similar tool, it cannot grow there again, so too, once false cognition along with its impressions is destroyed by the knowledge of reality, it cannot arise again, because it has been uprooted from its very foundation. True knowledge possesses the power to terminate the impressions of false cognition because the impression is opposed by its counter-cognition.

If it is argued that even when false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) has ceased in one instance, its arising elsewhere remains unavoidable, we reply: No, for not all false knowledge is the cause of *saṃsāra*, such that the cessation of every instance would have to be sought. Rather, [the relevant false knowledge] is only that which concerns objects such as the Self (*ātman*). And when that object of cognition (*prameya*), the Self and so forth, is determined in its true nature (*tattvataḥ*), false knowledge does not arise again with respect to it, just as it does not arise regarding a post (*sthāṇu*) once it has been correctly identified. Now, was it not stated that even in that case, false knowledge is observed to manifest at another time? True; it manifests for one who has lost the pursuit of the specific details (*viśeṣa-anusandhāna*), but not regarding the object of the Self and so forth. For the seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), the pursuit of specific details ceases. Indeed, his activity consists in the stabilization of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) day and night out of fear of *saṃsāra*. Thus the Blessed Akṣapāda taught: "For the sake of preserving the knowledge of reality, one should engage in discussion with those who possess that same knowledge," and so on, thereby instructing that cultivation must be stabilized through constant practice. If it is asked: "Since the specific objects of cognition (*prameya-viśeṣa*) are infinite in their individual manifestations, how can there be an absolute cessation of ignorance even in that regard? We reply: No; because when the Self and all else are determined to be such [as they truly are] by means of grasping the generalities (*sāmānya-upādāna*), the ignorance that is the root of *saṃsāra* is ceased. It is not necessary to cease every single instance of false knowledge even regarding specific objects of cognition; rather, [one must cease] that which, by way of being caused by defects (*doṣa*), is the root of *saṃsāra*. If false knowledge regarding the Self and so forth were the cause of *saṃsāra*, then liberation (*apavarga*) would follow upon its impossibility during states such as cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). This is not so, because as long as its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) persist, its absolute eradication is impossible. For this very reason, *saṃsāra* for all embodied beings is caused by false knowledge. However, for a certain person, such false knowledge exists regarding the objects of cognition—the Self and so forth—whether taken collectively or individually, which extends *saṃsāra* by way of being caused by defects. And that [false knowledge] does not occur again once the object of cognition has been determined in its true nature through the grasping of generalities. Just as one who, having determined that nectar and poison are respectively the causes of benefit and harm in one instance, determines that everything of that same class is so, does not act erroneously; likewise, when all objects are determined to be like poison by virtue of the generality of being sense-objects, no further false knowledge caused by passion arises toward them. Furthermore, when it is determined that all things are causes of suffering because they yield the fruits of one's own karma and are thus impossible to avoid, no further false knowledge caused by aversion arises toward them. Likewise, when the transmigrating being (*paralokin*) is determined to be distinct from the body and so forth, and to possess qualities such as existence and permanence, no further knowledge based on [mistaking him for the body] due to delusion (*moha*) arises. Thus, in every specific object of cognition, the removal of false knowledge—which is the root of misfortune—is to be seen as resulting from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
The demonstration that the removal of defects follows from the removal of false knowledge.

Furthermore, as for the claim that because defects such as passion (*rāga*) can still arise even in those who possess knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), the cessation of defects does not follow from the cessation of false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*)—that too is incorrect, because it is observed to be so. Indeed, the cessation of defects upon the cessation of false knowledge is observed here in this world. For example: hatred produced by the false determination (*mithyādhyavasāya*) that a friend is an enemy ceases when, through the knowledge of reality, the cognition of him as an enemy is removed. Likewise, passion produced by the false determination that one’s mother is a beloved woman ceases when, through the perception of reality, that misconception is removed. Many such examples are to be seen. However, the occurrence of passion and the like is never observed in the absence of false determination. And thus it has been said: "Among these, delusion (*moha*) is the most evil, for the others do not arise in one who is not deluded. Now, it may be argued: "But we see that even some who know the meaning of the scriptures are overcome by passion and the like. True; however, in their case as well, an internal defect (*ādhyātmikadoṣa*) is powerful. It overcomes the knowledge of reality and produces the two false determinations—the objectifying of what is attractive and what is provocative. From these two, passion and hatred manifest.
