Moreover, false determination is observed to occur even in one possessing knowledge of reality due to the power of internal defects. For instance: even for someone who has ascertained the directions by means of signs such as the rising of the sun, a confusion of directions (*diṅmoha*) may occur due to the power of demerit (*adharma*). Or, even for one certain of the oneness of the moon, the determination of multiple moons occurs due to the power of defects such as cataracts (*timira*). In this way, false determination produced by defects of the tongue and other senses is also to be illustrated. Just as in that case, a wise person, recognizing "this false determination of mine is due to a sensory defect," removes the defect of the senses and so forth by means of specific medicines, thereby eliminating the false determination; similarly, this seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) who knows the truth of the meaning of the scriptures, realizing "these two false determinations—the objectifying of the attractive and the provocative—manifest in me due to the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) regarding desired and undesired objects," becomes intent on higher discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Through the diligent practice of the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), by means of exhausting the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the unseen, he eliminates even those two false volitions (*mithyāsaṃkalpa*) toward the attractive and the provocative. And thus says the Sūtra: "For that purpose, there is the refinement of the self (*ātmasaṃskāra*) through restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), and through yoga by means of the methods prescribed in the inner discipline. As for those, however, who are afflicted by negligence and laziness, they cannot accomplish even other human goals (*puruṣārtha*), much less liberation. Thus, for one who is vigilant due to the knowledge of reality and intent on higher discernment, the defects are also destroyed upon the destruction of false knowledge. But for those devoid of the knowledge of reality, since they are possessed of delusion (*moha*)—the seed of defects—like children or the insane, how could there be the destruction of passion and the rest? As it has been said: [End of provided text]
"The detachment found in ignorance, and the happiness that depends on others,
perish very quickly— like the shadow of a cloud or a fire of straw. (This refutes the objection that yogis are overcome by passion and other afflictions.)

As for what was also said—that because even yogins are reported to be overcome by passion and the like, even the knowledge of reality consisting of reflection (*cintāmayajñāna*) is not the cause for the subsiding of passion and so forth—that too is incorrect, due to a lack of understanding regarding the true nature of the knowledge of reality consisting of reflection. For it is said that the knowledge of reality consisting of reflection is that meditation which has become firm in four ways—such as the object of knowledge being the self and so forth, in the form of what is to be abandoned and so on—and not merely the cognition of a yogin. Indeed, not all yogins are seekers of liberation or possessors of the knowledge of reality; for many engage in the practice of yoga even with instruction limited to that alone for the sake of attaining supernatural powers (*jñānasiddhi*). Likewise, in the scriptures of Jaigīṣavya and others, many meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) are explained for the purpose of yoga. Furthermore, it is heard that Sanatkumāra, though superior even to Hari and Hiraṇyagarbha due to his excellence in yogic sovereignty, was defeated by the Blessed Akṣapāda when he entered into dispute with the Supreme Lord. Therefore, the possession of the knowledge of reality or the absence of passion and the like is not established merely by being a yogin. Thus, it is established that through the very knowledge of reality as described above, delusion is destroyed, and upon the destruction of delusion, the defects are destroyed.

Furthermore, as for what was said—that even when defects (*doṣa*) have ceased, the cessation of activity (*pravṛtti*) is not logical—that too is incorrect, because the nature of the cessation of activity has not been understood. For here, the cessation of activity does not intend the mere cessation of action; rather, it refers to the non-arising of future *dharma* and *adharma* due to the absence of their cause, the destruction of accumulated [karma] through the exhaustion of its effects and by the fire of knowledge (*jñānāgni*), and their total consumption. Now, it might be argued that the non-arising of future [karma] is illogical because it is impossible to avoid or abandon them; but this is not so, because the avoidance of defects has already been explained. Defect is indeed the primary instrument (*sādhana*); in its absence, *dharma* and *adharma* do not arise even if other causes are present, just as a sprout of rice does not arise in the absence of the rice seed. And thus says the Sūtra: "There is no activity leading to rebirth for one whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been destroyed. There is also the Pātañjala Sūtra: "The latent impression of karma (*karmāśaya*) has its root in the afflictions and is to be experienced in seen or unseen births"; and "When the root exists, its fruition consists of birth, lifespan, and experience. Likewise, an inference is stated here: "A person under discussion, even while acting, is not bound by *dharma* and *adharma*, because he is free from defects, like Maheśvara. Only for one whose defects are destroyed is the extremely pure knowledge of reality capable of removing the stains of *dharma* and *adharma*, not for one whose defects are not destroyed, even if he is a yogi—just as turbid water [cannot reflect an image]. Or, just as even a well-kindled fire does not burn cotton or similar combustibles when they are connected with a specific medicinal herb, so too the fire of knowledge cannot burn karma when it is connected with defects. Furthermore, the fact that karma is combustible is well-known in all Yoga scriptures and the Vedāntas; therefore, it is not without authority.
Regarding the view of some that "action is not exhausted until it has been experienced," and the consideration thereof:

some indeed maintain that the destruction of actions occurs only through the completion of their own effects—expressed as, "Action is not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of kalpas unless it has been experienced. For it is said that a yogi who has attained mastery, having understood this, creates bodies together with their sense organs corresponding to his various states of existence in accordance with his karma, and simultaneously experiences desirable and undesirable enjoyments.

If that were so, then one would have to cease from the actions that bring about the killing of a Brahmin or the horse sacrifice after having produced their effects; thereafter, there would again be an accumulation of karma. How, then, could there be an absolute cessation? Furthermore, the state of having afflictions (*kleśa*) destroyed would not be attained, because one would have to cease from an action caused by passion and the like after having produced passion and the like; this would also result in a contradiction with the rules for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth. Now, if it is argued that unrighteousness (*adharma*), even when aimed at passion and the like, ceases after producing merely suffering, while righteousness (*dharma*) ceases after producing merely pleasure—since, as in the case of threads and other materials, a deficiency in the effect is possible due to a deficiency in auxiliary factors, and because there is no fixed rule regarding the time of the ripening of karma—then this conceptualization is indeed possible and involves no fault. The Teachers say that for one who has accepted the vision of the Supreme Self and is engaged in hearing the scriptures and the practice of the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), dharma and adharma perish entirely after producing only the pleasure and pain born of contentment and exhaustion. The simultaneous liberation through experience (*yugapadbhogamukti*) of the yogin is also accepted on the strength of scripture alone. What offense, then, has been committed against the "burning of karma by the fire of knowledge"? Even though it is established by all scripture, why is it not accepted? As for the scriptural passage, "Karma is not exhausted until it has been experienced," its meaningfulness should be understood as referring to those who do not know reality and have not performed expiation.

If it is argued that if knowledge burns away karma, there would be a contradiction with the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) born of yoga, we say no; for such accumulation is possible during the state when defects (*doṣa*) have not yet been destroyed. Alternatively, there is the cessation of the counter-agent itself, just as in the case of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Just as from the practice of knowledge regarding a single object there occurs both the intensification of its impression and the destruction of the impression of its opposite, so too, for one who desires to abandon transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), through the practice of knowledge of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), there occurs the destruction of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), which are the causes of *saṃsāra* because they are opposed to meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Furthermore, the accumulation of merit that is the cause of *samādhi* continues only until the vision of the Supreme Self is attained. That merit, too, ceases once its own effect has been completed. And because his defects have been eliminated, there is never again the production of future merit and demerit; thus, due to the absolute eradication of their cause, there is the absolute eradication of birth, and from the absolute eradication of that, there is the absolute eradication of sufferings—thus, liberation (*apavarga*) is established.

{The Determination of the Varieties of the Means of Valid Cognition} Now, for the sake of generating knowledge of reality, the number of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is stated first for one who desires to know their specific number and definitions: "It is threefold. The use of the term "threefold" is for the purpose of restriction, because all individual instances of the means of valid cognition are subsumed under exactly these three definitions, namely perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth. Accordingly, we shall demonstrate that analogy (*upamāna*) and the others are included within these very categories. {Refutation of the Cārvāka view that perception is the sole means of valid cognition}

Some maintain that perception alone is the single means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this is incorrect, because through perception alone the distinction between what is a means of valid cognition and what is not cannot be established, nor can the means for achieving pleasure, pain, and so forth be understood. Consequently, neither engagement (*pravṛtti*) nor withdrawal (*nivṛtti*) would be possible, as they are rooted in such understanding. By asserting that there is no means of valid cognition other than perception, yet composing a treatise and uttering sentences for the purpose of instructing others, one mocks one's own activity with one's own words. Oh, how he has revealed his own "excellent" scholarship! {The Refutation of those who hold inference to be the sole means of valid cognition}

The claim that inference alone is the sole means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is also not tenable, because inference cannot arise in the absence of perception. Even if one goes to the furthest extent in asserting the operation of inference through the subject (*dharmin*), the logical mark (*liṅga*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), one must necessarily admit their apprehension by means of perception. By this, the claim that scripture (*āgama*) alone is the sole means of valid cognition is also refuted; for even in that case, if words, sentences, and so forth are not established through perception or inference, the comprehension of the meaning of scripture is impossible. {Refutation of the Jaina position}

If it is argued that [means of knowledge] are of only two kinds, by way of the distinction between direct (*pratyakṣa*) and indirect (*parokṣa*), we say no; for such a conventional usage is not established. Indeed, the conventional expression "I know through the indirect" is nowhere established in the same way as "I know through direct perception," or "through inference," or "through scripture. Furthermore, because it would be purposeless: just as there is a purpose for designating direct perception and the others separately in order to demonstrate distinct means for apprehending their respective validity, there is no such purpose whatsoever in subsuming inference and scripture under the single category of "the indirect. If, however, out of attachment to his own position, someone were to assert the general category of "the indirect" merely to establish a twofold division, and then state that its specific instances—inference and scripture—have distinct definitions, let him do so; who can prevent him? Nevertheless, even this does not negate our stated threefold division, because the three have been demonstrated to possess mutually non-overlapping definitions. Moreover, if the meaning of "direct perception" and "inference" were identical to the meaning of "direct" and "indirect," even then [knowledge] would not be of only two kinds, because scripture (*āgama*) is also a valid means of knowledge and is a different entity from those two. We shall refute the inclusion of scripture within inference later on; therefore, it is not of two kinds even by the distinction of direct and inference. Consequently, it is indeed of three kinds.
Resolution of the Contradiction with the Vibhāga-sūtra

If it is argued that [the number of means of valid cognition] is not three because of a contradiction with the *Vibhāgasūtra*, the following thought might occur: this is the *Vibhāgasūtra*: "Perception, inference, comparison, and word are the means of valid cognition. And the purpose of a classification (*vibhāga*) is the exclusion of numbers fewer or greater than those specified; otherwise, since the fourfold nature would be established merely by the statement of the four definitions, the classification would be redundant. Furthermore, this is not a mere enumeration (*uddeśa*), because they are subjects of investigation. Indeed, the enumeration of the means of valid cognition and so forth has not been investigated; rather, their classification was investigated in the passage beginning with "not four," and so on. Therefore, there are exactly four means of valid cognition.

All of this is untenable because it contradicts the *Ghrāṇādi-sūtra*. For in the *Ghrāṇādi-sūtra*, a classification of the sense organs (*indriya*) is established, and they are examined by such statements as "because there is no difference from the skin" (*tvag-avyatirekāt*). Furthermore, the restriction that there are "only five" is not absolute, since the mind (*manas*) is also admitted to be a sense organ. Even though there is no difference in their being subjects of examination, the *Pratyakṣādi-sūtra* alone serves for the purpose of classification, while the *Ghrāṇādi-sūtra* serves merely for restatement (*anuvāda*). On this point, one must simply drink from the jar [of the text itself], for there is no specific reason [for such a distinction]. Therefore, just as the author of the Sūtras refuted the suspicion that the sense organs were fewer by showing their actual number, so too the acceptance of a greater number is not contradictory; likewise, since the suspicion that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are more than three was refuted, the acceptance of their threefold nature is not contradictory. This is because the fact that both are obtained through reasoning (*nyāya-labhyatva*) is the same in both cases. We shall demonstrate later how the threefold nature of the means of valid cognition is obtained through reasoning without contradicting the Sūtras.

[The Convergence and Distinct Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition] Why is the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) used in the singular? It is for the purpose of making known that even the three [means of cognition] have a single object. For example, having understood fire in mountain regions and the like through the word of a reliable person (*āpta*), one proceeds; then, seeing smoke, one understands that very same fire. Then, being very close, one understands that very same fire through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Likewise, having understood the nature of the self (*ātman*) from the instruction of a reliable person, one understands it again by means of the mark (*liṅga*) such as desire, and further by direct perception through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Thus, the convergence (*saṃplava*) [of the means of cognition] is established.

The separate enumeration of [the means of knowledge] as "perception, inference, and scripture"—sometimes even individually—is for the purpose of making known that each has a restricted domain. For example, regarding the meaning of scripture such as "One desiring heaven should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice," neither perception nor inference is available to people like us. When the sound of thunder is heard, for one like us who has not heard the relevant scripture, only inference operates toward the cause of that sound. When a hand is perceived through perception, there is no operation of inference or scripture due to the absence of any need for them. If it is argued: "The desire for other means of knowledge ceases only when an object is perceived by perception, not when it is perceived by scripture or inference; therefore, those two are not valid means of knowledge," we say no. This is because perception alone, by demonstrating an object characterized by many specific qualities—both those that can be designated and those that cannot—serves as the cause for the cessation of further desire. For an object qualified by as many specific features as is demonstrated by perception is not likewise demonstrated by inference and the rest. If this is so, then since their domains are unequal, the "convergence" (*saṃplava*) of perception with inference and the rest is untenable. This is not the case; convergence is established in view of the subject (*dharmin*) as qualified by certain attributes. For the very same fire, as qualified by a particular place and so forth, is established by scripture, cognized by inference, and perceived by perception. Even though, when an object is perceived by perception, another means of knowledge may operate—whether one desires it or not—insofar as one wishes to perceive it as qualified by some transcendental (*atīndriya*) attribute, nevertheless, this does not happen in all cases. Consequently, where another means of knowledge does not operate, the distinct determination (*vyavasthā*) of the means of knowledge is established; elsewhere, however, there is convergence. If it is argued: "When an object is perceived by one [means], the operation of a second is useless," we say no; because they produce different degrees of pleasure and pain, and because they produce different degrees of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, the operation of the means of knowledge is not dependent on human purpose in every instance, since we observe the operation of the means of knowledge even in the case of useless things like grass, or undesirable things like fetters.
The Buddhist objection concerning the impossibility of convergence [of means of valid cognition], and its refutation.

[Objection: But surely perception has only the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its object, while inference has only the universal (*sāmānya*) as its object; thus, the convergence (*saṃplava*) [of the two] is untenable. [Reply: True; this is indeed the Buddhist wish, but we shall explain later that its object is entirely false. Therefore, there is convergence, and in some cases, there is restriction (*vyavasthā*). The author of the Sūtras also indicated that they have non-different objects by denoting the means of knowledge collectively with a single word, and he indicated that they have restricted objects by denoting them with a plural number. Here, however, convergence and restriction are indicated in another way for the purpose of demonstrating the method of explaining their respective objects. The word *iti* is used to restrict the aforementioned manner—it is determined that [knowledge] is of three kinds in this very manner. Otherwise, since there is no difference in being the instrument for correct experience, it would be of only one kind. However, if one intends to express internal subdivisions, it is sevenfold or even more numerous. Therefore, it is of three kinds precisely through the distinction of perception and so forth.
The definition of direct perception.

Regarding the phrase "therein, correctly" (*tatra samyak*): just as with the word *samyak*, the word *aparokṣa* also forms a *karmadhāraya* compound with the word *anubhava*. What kind of compound is *pratyakṣa*? If it were formed as an *avyayībhāva* based on the rule "it occurs toward each sense-organ" (*akṣam akṣaṃ prati*), then there would be only the substitution of *am* for case endings other than the fifth, third, and seventh; consequently, such usage as "the definition of perception" (*pratyakṣasya lakṣaṇam*), "a perceptible jar" (*pratyakṣo ghaṭaḥ*), or "a perceptible woman" (*pratyakṣā nārī*) would not be possible. Therefore, it is accepted that *pratyakṣa* is a *tatpuruṣa* compound according to the rule "prefixes, *kugati*, and *prādi* [form compounds with a following noun]" (*kugatiprādayaḥ*), meaning "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatam akṣam*). Even so, since the rule "the gender of a *dvandva* or *tatpuruṣa* follows the gender of the final member" (*paravalliṅgaṃ dvandvatatpuruṣayoḥ*) would apply, the forms "a perceptible jar" and so forth would still be untenable. This is not the case; for in the case of a *gatisamāsa*, the application of the gender of the final member is prohibited, and thus the gender of the expressed object (*abhidheyaliṅgatvam*) is intended. Accordingly, there is the statement: "In the case of *prāpta*, *āpanna*, *alam*, and *gatisamāsa* compounds, there is a prohibition of the gender of the final member."
There is a distinction between the etymological derivation and the ground for the application of the term *pratyakṣa*.

But how is it "gone toward" (*prati-gata*) the sense-organ (*akṣa*)? It is so by virtue of being produced from it, by virtue of being its auxiliary cause, and by virtue of having it as its object. First, the result (*phala*) is "gone toward" the sense-organ because it is produced from it; the means of achieving that result (*phalasādhana*) is so because it is its auxiliary cause; and its object (*tadartha*) is so because it has that [sense-organ] as its object. If perception (*pratyakṣa*) is intended as the means of achievement (*sādhana*) by virtue of being an auxiliary to the sense-organ, then surely the status of the sense-organ as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would not be attained, for it is not logical that the very same thing should be its own auxiliary cause. Furthermore, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) would attain the status of perception by virtue of being an auxiliary to the sense-organ, and likewise, doubt and so forth, as well as pleasure and so forth, would incur the undesirable consequence of being results of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*) by virtue of being produced from the sense-organ. [Response: No, because this is merely an explanation of the meaning of the word through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). Etymological derivation itself is not accepted as the basis for the application of words to their fixed meanings. For instance, the fixed meaning of words such as *go* (cow), *paṅkaja* (lotus), and so on, does not depend on etymology, but rather on the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. There is also a difference in definition between the result of the means of valid perception and the perception itself: the result of perception is a correct, immediate experience (*samyag-aparokṣānubhava*), while the means of achieving that is the perception as a means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*).

[Objection: But would this not entail that inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*) are also direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), since their results, like pleasure and so forth, are also immediate (*aparokṣa*)? [Reply: No; for the term "immediate" is intended here as being based on a genus (*jāti*). Pleasure and so forth possess immediacy by virtue of being objects of immediate experience, but there is no such genus as "immediacy" residing in external objects, because that would entail that an object is immediate for all persons, given that a genus is common to all. Indeed, an object endowed with the genus "blueness" is blue for someone, but it is not blue for everyone. However, when it is accepted that only cognition (*jñāna*) is endowed with the genus "immediacy," then the consequence that an object is immediate for all persons does not follow; rather, an object is immediate only for the person whose own immediate cognition has that object as its content. Just as an object is not doubtful for everyone, but is doubtful only for one who possesses a doubtful cognition regarding that object, so too there is no genus "immediacy" in objects as there is the property of "doubtfulness. Thus, although inferential and other types of cognition are indirect (*parokṣa*), they may be termed "immediate" by virtue of having an immediate cognition as their object—just as something is called "doubtful" by virtue of being the object of a doubtful cognition—but not through connection with a genus "immediacy."
The establishment of the generic nature (*jātitva*) of perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*) and other such properties, preceded by the refutation of opposing views.

Even for one who does not admit that there are specific universals (*jāti*) such as "mediateness" (*parokṣatva*) and "immediacy" (*aparokṣatva*) within cognitions, he too must state the ground for the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of those terms. Now, being produced by the contact of sense-organ and object (*indriyārthasannikarṣajatva*) cannot be the ground for the usage of "immediacy," because that [contact] is unestablished so long as immediacy itself is unestablished; and it is illogical for something unestablished to function as a differentiator. Nor is the mere experience of an object its mark (*liṅga*), for a qualified experience is impossible in the absence of the universal of immediacy. Furthermore, "directness" (*sākṣātkāritva*) is merely a synonym for immediacy. Thus, even in the case of the self-experiences resulting from perception and inference, no distinction would be possible if the universals of being produced by contact with the self and of immediacy did not exist. If it is argued that immediacy is a property (*dharma*) of cognition—namely, the manifestation of an object characterized by the distinction between being expressible and inexpressible, rather than a universal—we reply: we do not perceive any such property of cognition called "manifestation" that is distinct from a specific universal. Moreover, a cognition manifesting an object without such qualifiers would lack immediacy. If one admits that a cognition becomes the object of a qualified usage simply by virtue of being produced by its causes, then the usages "jar" or "tree" would also arise from that alone, and not from the universals of jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*) or tree-ness (*vṛkṣatva*). Consequently, the Tathāgatas (Buddhists) would have their desires fulfilled [by denying all universals]. Therefore, even when specific causes are present, one must admit intermediate specific universals (*avāntarajātiviśeṣa*) which serve as the grounds for the inclusive and exclusive usages of individual cognitions—just as in the case of jars, trees, and the like—so that there would be no room even for those who deny the existence of universals. Thus, since the fruit of perception is distinguished from cognitions such as memory and inference by means of specific universals like "experientiality" (*anubhavatva*) and "immediacy," perception—which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*)—excludes itself from both homogeneous and heterogeneous classes. With this intention, the author of the Sūtras stated the qualifications of the fruit itself, such as "produced by the contact of sense-organ and object."
The justification of the universal of immediacy and so forth by means of the words of the Sūtra.

In this context, by the phrase "produced from the contact of a sense-organ with its object," what is intended is that [the cognition] is qualified by being an experience (*anubhava*) and by being immediate (*aparokṣatva*); for since that qualification is established through perception itself, it is logically consistent for it to function as a definition. For if the specific nature of the result were not established, then the contact between the sense-organ and the object would itself remain unestablished; how then could "being produced from that" serve as an uncertain definition? Nor does the non-perception of an obstructed object constitute an inferential mark for the existence of such contact; for if that non-perception were an inferential mark for its absence, then the perception of an unobstructed object would likewise be an inferential mark for its presence.

What is this "obstruction" (*vyavadhāna*)? If it were merely residing at a distant location, then even the sun and other celestial bodies would be obstructed. If, on the other hand, it were the existence of a composite substance such as a cloud or the like in the intervening space, then even that which is separated by glass, mica, crystal, and so forth, would be obstructed. If you say that the very thing situated in between which causes the non-perception of another is its obstruction, then in that case, fire and the like hidden behind a wall would not be obstructed, since they are perceived through inference and scripture.

Now, if the perception produced by the sense-organs (*akṣaja-upalabdhi*) is the mark for the absence of intervention, one might ask: "Is the mind (*manas*) not itself a sense-organ? And is the cognition arising from inference and so forth not produced by the mind? Who says such a thing? However, that [cognition] is called "not produced by a sense-organ" because it is produced by a mind that is not in contact with the object. But even so, would this not lead to an unresolvable circularity (*cakraka*)—namely, that being produced by the contact of a sense-organ with an object constitutes being "produced by a sense-organ" (*akṣaja*), and being produced by a sense-organ constitutes the perception of an unmediated object, and by that [perception], there is the production by the contact of a sense-organ with an object? Thus, if one of these is not established at the outset, all of them remain unestablished.

Furthermore, how could the mind—which is itself an instrument (*karaṇa*)—produce an action toward an object such as an inferable entity (*anumeya*) with which it has no connection? If it were to produce such an action, there would be a contradiction with your own accepted doctrine. If you argue that the mind is said to be "unconnected" because there is no contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth between the mind and the inferable object, we say no; for conjunction and other forms of contact are possible between the self (*ātman*) and the inferable object. If you claim that the self and such entities do not possess the status of being sense-objects (*indriyārtha*) at all, and therefore their relation is not a "contact between sense-organ and object," then the yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*) directed toward those objects would not be produced by contact between a sense-organ and an object. If you maintain that, in relation to yoga, the self and so forth are indeed admitted to be sense-objects, what is the reason for this? If you say it is because the yogic sense-organ produces a specific kind of cognition in that regard, then what is this "specificity" (*viśeṣa*) other than the common quality of immediacy (*aparokṣatva*)? Even "directness" (*sākṣātkāritva*) is merely a synonym for that same quality. If you argue that the distinction lies in the fact that [yogic perception] is not produced by the recollection of a relation (*sambandhasmaraṇājanyatva*), we say no; for even that point remains unestablished.

If it is argued that the ascertainment of an object occurs precisely because it arises upon the non-perception of that [other] object, we say no; for even when [an object] has been cultivated with ease (*āśubhāvitva*), it is possible for there to be a non-perception of the recollection of its relationship [to another]. When, through a formal resolve (*praṇidhāna*), there is a recollection of the relationship such as invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), the direct perception of a certain object may occur immediately thereafter; yet this does not mean that the object is "beyond the senses" (*anindriyārtha*). Therefore, we consider it logical that for a given person, that very object regarding which a cognition qualified by being beyond the senses arises—due to the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth—is indeed an "object of the senses" (*indriyārtha*) for him.
The purpose of the qualification "arising from the object" (*arthajatva*) in the definition of perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣajñāna*).

Although some maintain that the qualification "arising from an object" (*arthajatva*) is introduced for the purpose of excluding memory (*smaraṇa*), this too is not tenable; for even a cognition of an object such as the past, though not arising from [a presently existing] object, is accepted as being the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). Otherwise, since a past or future object lacks the capacity to be a producer (*janakatva*), it would not be an object of consciousness, and thus it would follow that it is simply not an object of knowledge (*aprameya*); for only that which is present can possess the capacity to produce [cognition]. Therefore, an object is not an object of knowledge solely by virtue of being a producer. Furthermore, because it is the object of the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogin, this restriction does not apply even to perception.

Regarding the existence of past and future objects: [Objection] But surely past and future objects are non-entities characterized by destruction and non-arising; since their status as causes is accepted in this treatise, how can it be said that the cognition of them is not produced from an object? [Response] This is not so. For that for whose sake the employment of a cause is undertaken is called "future," and the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not thus, because it is beginningless. Likewise, only that which has already come into being is called "past," and not the posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), because that has not ceased to exist.

What, then, is the nature of that object which is past and so forth? It is not a positive entity (*bhāva*), because it is devoid of existence (*sattva*) and other such properties; nor is it a non-entity (*abhāva*), because it is distinct from prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the other types of non-existence. Therefore, some maintain that it is a third kind of object of cognition (*prameya*). But that is not so, because [the categories of] "existent" and "non-existent" pervade everything—just as with a pot and a non-pot. For whatever is not a pot is necessarily a non-pot, and when that is negated, it must be a pot; there is no other possibility. Likewise, whatever is not a positive entity is necessarily a non-entity; for when two negations are applied, the result is simply the positive entity itself. Furthermore, unlike *adharma* (demerit), non-existence has no specific genus (*jāti*) or defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) by which it could constitute a third object of cognition. Indeed, this is the very definition of non-existence: its being a different thing from a positive entity. And since there is no linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) apart from affirmation and negation, there is no third object of cognition.

What, then, is the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of an object that is past and so forth? It is simply the intrinsic nature of the entity itself. If it is argued that this is untenable because it lacks existence (*sattva*) and other such qualities, we say no; for that [reason] is unproven (*asiddha*). To explain: an object such as a jar is designated as past, future, or present. How, then, could it be devoid of existence and the like? If it is argued that since it is endowed with existence and so forth at all times, it follows that it must be eternal, we say no; for the locus [of the reason] is unproven (*āśrayāsiddha*). The very subject (*dharmin*), the jar and so forth, does not exist at all times; how then can it possess the property (*dharma*) of existence and so on? For it cannot be said that a jar which has perished or one which has not yet arisen exists. But surely it exists in the form of the past and the future. Now, does this jar assume multiple forms like an actor? True. Why is this so? Because it is perceived as such.

Now, if it possesses such a manifold nature (*anekarūpatā*), how can it be said that it does not exist? If you argue that this is because properties such as existence (*sattva*) are absent, then how can that very property—existence and so forth—which, like a jar, possesses a manifold nature before and after [the jar's production], be said not to exist? If you say it is because of the absence of its relation to that jar, we say no; for the objection remains the same here as well. By this, the absence of presentness and the absence of manifestation are also refuted. Therefore, the jar that is unproduced or destroyed is simply non-existent; it does not exist in any form whatsoever.
Because past and other objects are superimposed [upon consciousness], they possess the character of being qualifiers of non-existence.

If it is asked how a jar that does not exist can function as a qualifier for prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, some say: "It is like a rabbit's horn, being superimposed through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Just as elsewhere, having perceived a horn and having conceptually imagined it to have arisen on the head of a rabbit of that same species, one perceives its absence and understands it as "the absence of a rabbit's horn," yet a rabbit's horn does not exist anywhere at all. If, however, it were apprehended as a qualifier [of something real], then its absence would not occur, just as with universals (*sāmānya*) and the like. For this very reason, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding a rabbit's horn is false, but the conventional usage regarding its absence is not; it is like the conventional usage of duality and its absence in the case of the moon and so forth. If the conventional usage of an absence were false, the existence of the positive entity (*bhāva*) itself would be established. Thus, the conventional usage of the prior and posterior absence of a jar and the like is not false, whereas the conventional usage of its presence is indeed false, just as there is a conventional usage of absence when a thing exists. Therefore, the function of qualifying an absence belongs to things such as cloth seen elsewhere, which are here superimposed by conceptual construction, but not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthatas*).
The fact that past and other objects are characterized by non-existence due to their being remembered.

This is not so. For a rabbit’s horn has never been perceived by anyone, in any place or at any time; therefore, it is logical that this absolutely non-existent thing is a mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) and superimposition (*samāropa*). This is not the case for a jar or similar objects, because they are sometimes perceived, and it is precisely of them that we have the cognition of their specific characteristics (*viśeṣaka*). To explain: when a jar was seen, because it has now ceased to exist, there is the cognition "it does not exist"; however, during the time of its absence, there would be a memory (*smaraṇa*) of it, not a conceptual construction. If you argue that memory itself is conceptual construction, who can prevent you from using such a term? In common worldly usage, however, conceptual construction is well known as the superimposition of something unreal, such as the construction of a *garuḍa* within oneself, or the construction of a king or a horse in a painting. But in the case of memory, an object is not constructed otherwise than it was [previously]; for memory consists in the recollection of an object exactly as it was perceived. If you then argue that memory itself is the experience (*anubhava*) of past objects and the like, we say no; for memory cannot exist in the absence of prior experience. How could one who has not previously experienced a certain object have a memory of it at the outset, as in the case of the Pāṇḍavas and others? Furthermore, there is no memory of one object based on the experience of another, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, one must admit that there was an initial apprehension of the object which serves as the cause of the memory.
For an existing entity such as the past and so forth, its "pastness" and so on is the determining factor.

If it is asked, "How can that which is perceived in such a form be past or future?", we say: no, for this is possible due to the intervention of time (*kālavyavadhāna*). Just as that very same pillar, being in such a state, is said to be "distant" or "near" depending on the intervention or non-intervention of space (*deśavyavadhāna*), so too is that very same object "future" because of its intervention by the time of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), "past" because of its intervention by the time of destruction (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), and "present" because of the non-intervention of both those times. If it is argued that there would be the unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) of even an object separated by time performing causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), just like the moon and other objects separated by space, we say: no, because of the absence of a connection (*sambandha*). For indeed, even though the moon and such are separated by space, they possess a connection with persons, eyes, night-lotuses (*kumuda*), and so forth; thus, their causal efficiency is logical. But for an object separated by time, since it does not exist by its own nature (*svarūpa*), there is no connection whatsoever with anything; therefore, it lacks causal efficiency. Alternatively, if it were existent, its separation by time would be contradictory—for it is not logical that what was previously non-existent and what has perished should be "existent. If it is asked, "In the absence of causal efficiency due to non-existence and in the absence of a connection, from where does the rule 'this is the cognition of that' arise?", [the answer is: it is due to the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). Since cognition arises as determined precisely by appearing as that [object], upon seeing that [object], even though it is not a producer, a relationship of "object and subject" (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*) is conventionally designated in relation to that cognition. And that which does not appear in the cognition, even if it is a producer, does not have the status of an object, just like the sense organs and so forth.
[The status of past and other objects as objects of cognition, even though they are not producers:

But surely, one says, "I know a past object"—how can that which is not a producer have the status of a *kāraka* (participant in an action) as an object (*karman*)? No; for we observe the conventional usage of *kārakas* even for non-*kārakas* based merely on the speaker’s intention to speak. Just as one says, "I produce a jar" or "the jar is produced," where the status of being a *kāraka* is superimposed even though it does not exist [in reality], so too the action of knowing with respect to a past object is not unreal.

[Objection: If that were the case, then even the cognition of a sky-flower would not be unreal, and thus the existence of a sky-flower would be established. [Response: This is not so. For if this cognition is "the sky-flower does not exist," then that cognition of a sky-flower is its negator; how could it be its establisher? Or if the cognition is "the sky-flower exists," even that, being erroneous due to its being sublated, cannot establish it. Furthermore, whether that cognition arising from the word "sky-flower" determines its existence, is doubtful, or is its negator—no other kind of object-cognition is perceived. [Objection: Is this not the same as the cognition of past and future objects? [Response: No; for although that cognition determines those objects, it is neither erroneous nor sublated. It is certainly not the case that a past object did not exist or that a future one will not exist. If, however, there were a perception that "that object exists even now," then its erroneous nature would indeed be accepted, because of its deviation from that [past or future] form.
If one does not accept that past and other objects possess the nature of existence, there is a contradiction with the fact that inference has objects belonging to the three times as its domain.

Furthermore, if the cognition of past objects were also incorrect, inference regarding the three periods of time would be contradicted. One might argue: "Inference concerning the future is simply the inference of the capacity of a cause, while inference concerning the past is the inference of a river's connection with a region that experienced rain upstream; therefore, there is no contradiction. If that is so, then if the capacity of a cause to produce an effect and the river's connection with a region that experienced rain upstream are inferred only as currently existing, then the inference would have the present as its object; how then could there be an inference of past and other [future] objects? If, on the other hand, what is non-existent is inferred, then how can that which is not a producer (ajanaka) be an object of knowledge (*prameya*)? If it is argued that once the causal capacity and so forth have been inferred, the cognition of future objects arises by the very force of that capacity, then if one admits a cognition even from a capacity, how can that which is not a producer be an object of knowledge? If you say that such a cognition is merely false, then the inference having the three periods of time as its object is well-established! If it is argued that because specific locations and so forth are the producers, future objects possess the status of being objects (*viṣayatva*) by virtue of being qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) of those [locations], this is not the case. For let the status of being an object belong only to the specific locations and so forth, which are the actual producers, and not to their qualifiers, since they are distinct from them. Indeed, if one thing could be an object of another simply by virtue of the latter being the producer, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

Now, if it is not accepted that past and future objects possess the status of being objects (*viṣaya*), then it would follow that the cognition of them lacks an object and thus fails to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If, on the other hand, it is argued that it is only the specific locations and so forth—subordinate to those [past or future objects]—that become the objective supports (*ālambana*) for the yogin’s perceptual cognition or for inferential cognition regarding things like [past or future] non-existence, this too is untenable. For if the cognition of a past object is held to be a non-valid result due to its lack of an object, then likewise, a cognition of a location or other particulars qualified by that [past object] would necessarily be erroneous, since it arises through the delimitation of a non-existent qualifier. However, just as in cognitions such as "two moons" or "the pillar is happy," if [the cognition of the past object] were not erroneous, one must necessarily admit the grasping of the past object and so forth as a qualifier, because that which is not grasped cannot function as a qualifier. If that is admitted, then it is established that even that which is not a cause can have the status of an object. Furthermore, the cognition of past and future objects is not erroneous simply because it lacks an [external] object, for its grasping of that form is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*). Indeed, a cognition is called deviant only when it grasps an object in a way different from how it exists, even though the object is present—as in the case of the cognition of a person in a post. But when objects, though non-existent, are grasped non-deviantly in the forms "the Pāṇḍavas and others existed" or "pots and others will exist," then that cognition is indeed non-erroneous due to the absence of any sublation, just like the cognition "this is a pot. Nor does the fact that something which is not a cause acts as a cause imply that everyone would become omniscient; for the cognitions of worldly beings arise with restricted objects, being determined by specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. However, that cognition which is not restricted by such a causal complex certainly exists eternally as the cognition of all objects belonging to the Blessed Lord Maheśvara.
Memory, too, is produced by an object.

Furthermore, how can memory (*smṛti*) be said to arise from an object (*anarthaja*)? If it is argued that memory arises even in the absence of an object, then why does that non-existent object not produce memory? If it is replied that it is precisely because of its non-existence (*asattvāt*), then how can the cognition of past and other objects be considered "object-born" (*arthaja*)? Moreover, just as memory—which arises from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*) accompanied by attention (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth—does not conform to the existence or non-existence of its object, we likewise observe that experience (*anubhava*) arising from the cognition of words and so forth accompanied by the memory of a relationship does not conform to the object, since there is no distinction in the comprehension [of the object] whether it is present or absent. If it is argued that only the cognition of words and so forth arising when an object is absent would be erroneous (*bhrānta*), while memory would not, we say no; for error consists precisely in the appearance of an object in a manner other than it actually exists. Thus, memory too, arising by appearing as an object in a manner other than it is, is indeed false. For example, upon seeing someone who resembles an enemy, a false memory occurs: "Do I not remember the harm he did me? In this way, one should see that memory is likewise "other-wise" in cases such as reciting or explaining texts. Therefore, since they share the same logical status (*tulyayogakṣematvāt*), it follows that memory is also object-born, and the cognition of words and so forth is also not object-born. Consequently, it is appropriate that the qualification "object-born" is used there to exclude memory. Thus, the author of the Sūtra intended the definition of the result of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*) to be simply "immediate experience" (*aparokṣānubhavatva*) connected to a single object, by virtue of being produced from the contact of a sense-organ with an object (*indriyārthasannikarṣotpannatvena*).
The definition of direct perception according to [the author's] own view.

Even in this way, the apprehension of the definition is observed—as when, upon the statement "that which is white and moving is a cow," or "that over which this man with an umbrella is seen is a horse," and so forth, speakers understand as the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) precisely that which is indicated by the movement and so on, namely *gotva* (cowness) and the like, which is unique to that [animal] and not shared by others; likewise here too, although it is stated that "that cognition which arises through the presence or absence of the relation between the sense organs such as the eye and objects such as a jar is perception" (*pratyakṣa*), investigators must understand as the defining characteristic precisely the state of being immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhavatva*), which is indicated by its being produced by sensory contact (*sannikarṣaja*) and is unique to that [perception], and not the state of being produced by sensory contact itself, because that cannot possibly be unique to it alone. Thus it has been said.
The purpose of the definition according to the Sūtras.

Why, then, was that very state of being immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhavatva*) not stated directly? It was for the purpose of making known the distinction between types of perception; we shall explain that the perception of those such as ourselves arises solely from the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) between the sense organ and its object. Alternatively, it was for the purpose of raising a discussion regarding disagreements concerning contact and so forth, for when there is disagreement, critical examination (*parīkṣā*) becomes possible, and through that, certainty is attained. Consequently, the proponents of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavādin*) and the proponents of consciousness-only (*vijñānavādin*) would find no ground for subverting the knowledge of reality regarding the self and other categories. Thus, in order to establish their theories of momentary flux and so on, they reject relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and assert instead that distinct things depend upon a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*) as the constraint for producing a single effect. Furthermore, they posit the subject-object relationship (*grāhyagrāhakabhāva*) for the sake of establishing the doctrine of consciousness-only. In that regard, first, in the absence of all [external] contacts, they say the following for the purpose of establishing an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*):
The Buddhist doctrine is that the sense faculties function without reaching their objects.

The eye and the ear do not function by reaching their objects, because they perceive objects at a distance. For if they function by reaching, there would be no perception of the interval between the eye and its object, or between the ear and its sound, just as there is none between an axe and a tree. Furthermore, how does this "reaching" occur? Does the object come to the location of the eye and connect with it, or does the eye go to the location of the object and connect with it? In the first case, there is a contradiction with experience, and it would follow that the eye and other organs would be burned upon seeing fire. In the second case as well, there is a contradiction with experience—for no one perceives the eye as being joined to the object like an arrow. If you argue that it is not perceived because of its subtlety, this is not so; for it is universally recognized by the world that the eye is the eyeball itself, since when that is damaged, there is no seeing of objects. Even if one were to admit its subtlety, is it subtle because it is formless (*amūrta*) like space, or because it is small in size? In the first case, it would have to grasp all objects simultaneously, because it is admitted that a formless substance is all-pervasive. If it is subtle because it is small in dimension, that is incorrect, because we perceive things larger than itself—just as a nail-cutter is observed to perform its action only over the extent of its own contact, it would be impossible for a small-sized eye to grasp mountains and such vast objects. For this reason also, the eye does not function by reaching: because the branch and the moon are perceived at the same time. For if the eye were moving and thus capable of sequential contact, it would be logical for it to perceive them sequentially; yet this is not the case. Nor can the impression of simultaneity be due to rapid succession, because the moon is so extremely distant that its contact must necessarily involve a long duration of time. As for sound, let it be that it is perceived through contact with the ear after arriving via a continuous series (*santāna*); this is not so, because of the designation of direction and place. For if sound were perceived in the location of the ear, the designation of directions such as east or west, or places such as village or forest, would be untenable. Thus, it is established that the ear functions without reaching its object; therefore, by this example, the "reaching" function of all the sense organs should be refuted.
The refutation thereof.

To this, it is replied: As for the argument that "there is a perception of distance," that is not a valid proof because it is unestablished (*asiddha*), since the eye and other sense organs are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). How, then, could the separation of the object [from the sense organ] be grasped by perception? By inference, however, it is understood that the eye and other organs illuminate objects precisely because they are in contact with them, as illustrated by the example of a lamp. As for what was asked regarding how there can be contact (*prāpti*) and so forth, it is replied: The eye itself, proceeding to the location of the object by means of its rays (*raśmi*), becomes connected with it like a lamp. And those rays are not seen because their form is non-manifest (*anudbhūtarūpa*). If it is argued that it is illogical for things with non-manifest forms to illuminate objects, we say no; for such illumination is possible when they are accompanied by the light of a lamp or similar sources. For this very reason, for those whose ocular rays are produced with manifest form through the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), they illuminate objects independently of external light, as is the case with nocturnal animals. Furthermore, the ocular rays of certain nocturnal animals are actually perceived directly by perception.
[The visual rays possess manifest color.

Alternatively, from those constituent parts of light combined with the constituent parts [of the object], visual rays arise that possess only manifest color. For it is observed that in the case of luminous bodies, there is extremely rapid destruction and production, and their color and touch are endowed with the distinction of being either manifest or unmanifest properties. Even though the rays have arisen with manifest color, they are not perceived individually because they merge into another [object], just as the rays of many lamps are not perceived individually when connected to a single object.
[This explains the perception of something larger.]

The argument "because of the perception of something wider" is inconclusive; for a lamp does not illuminate an object only to the extent of its own size, since, by means of its rays, it pervades even what is wider.
[This concludes the refutation of the simultaneous perception of the branches and the moon.]

As for the argument that [the tree] and the moon are perceived at the same time, that too is not a proof because it is unestablished; for there is the misconception of simultaneity due to the rapidity of the process. If it is argued that this is because the moon is extremely remote, we say no; because of their extreme lightness, the rays move with such great speed—just like the rays of the sun—that the sun’s rays, when coming into contact with objects, are not perceived sequentially.
[This concludes the demonstration regarding the designation of direction and location.]

As for what was said—that [the sound's location is known] because of the designation of direction and place—that is not so, because that [designation] can occur otherwise as well. To explain: when one perceives a sound in a region of space delimited by a portion of the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*) that is distinguished by the eastern direction, one then understands that "the sound has arisen in the east. The same should be understood regarding the specific directions of the south and so forth. For the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is the region of space delimited by the parts of the ear-canal, and since those parts exist facing all directions, it is logical that the perception of sound occurs through the delimitation of specific directions. Furthermore, the cognition "the sound has arisen at such a distance" is inferential (*ānumānikī*). How so? Having perceived certain specific qualities of a sound that has arrived via a continuous series (*santāna*) from a certain distance—qualities which arise from the operation of causes previously perceived through direct perception or scripture—one then understands the production of the sound at that same distance, even though the specific qualities of this particular sound are not being perceived. Just as one identifies a conch-shell or a particular speaker by means of certain specific qualities, so too does one infer the distance. However, for one who does not notice such specific qualities, doubt is observed: "Whose is this sound, or from where does it come? And once that specific direction and place have been inferred, one designates the production of the sound in relation to a village or similar location after considering its possibility there; but it is not the case that places and so forth are directly grasped by the auditory organ. Therefore, because they are external sense organs, it is established that the eye and the ear function by reaching their objects (*prāpyakāritva*), just like the tongue and the other senses.
If [the sense organs] functioned without reaching [their objects], there would be the consequence of perceiving all objects.

For in the absence of contact, there would be the perception of all objects; indeed, in the absence of contact, there is no other "capacity" (yogyatā) by virtue of which it could be said that only what is situated in a suitable location is perceived.
Even the magnet and such things function by means of contact.

If it is argued that [the senses act] like a magnet and so forth, we say no; for doubt is not removed by a mere example. Is the non-contacting action (*aprāpyakāritva*) of the senses like that of a magnet, or is their contacting action (*prāpyakāritva*) like that of a wind-instrument (*vāśī*) and so forth? No specific reason is stated here [to resolve this]. Furthermore, a particular substance of air (*vāyudravya*) arises in contact with a magnet within the body, like the vital breath (*prāṇa*); and that [air], having reached the iron, attracts it just as the vital breath attracts water, cotton, and the like. Even though its touch is not perceived, the existence of such an arisen [substance] is understood through its very effect. A mantra also propitiates the very self of the deity with whom it is connected. And that particular deity, having reached [the practitioner], accomplishes the desired object for the reciter; thus, nothing whatsoever acts without reaching its object.
The meaning of the term *prāpyakāritva* according to the opinion of Bhūṣaṇakāra.

If it is asked: "How can there be the property of acting by reaching [the object] (*prāpyakāritva*) in the case of sound, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and so forth, since they produce knowledge of objects such as those in the past which have not been reached?"—we say: no, because of a lack of understanding. Acting by reaching means that a cause produces its effect after having reached an auxiliary factor (*sahakārin*); and this [property] exists even for sound, the internal organ, and so forth. However, it has already been stated that for an object in the past and so on, there is no status as a cause at all; therefore, even though [the sense organs] do not reach it, they are not "non-reachers. Nor does it follow that visual objects and the like are non-producers [of cognition], for their status as causes is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), just like light and other factors. Furthermore, the claim that collyrium and the like, even when reached, are not perceived, is also incorrect. For it is not restricted that whatever is reached by a sense organ must necessarily be perceived; rather, the restriction is that whatever is perceived by an external sense organ has necessarily been reached. What is the reason? Because external sense organs, being material (*bhautika*), illuminate reached objects like a lamp. If it is argued that this would imply the same for the mind (*manas*) because it is also a sense organ, we reply: because it is only in some cases that such is the case. This is a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). But regarding the restrictive position, the contradiction with objects in the past and so forth has already been stated. Moreover, through positive and negative concomitance, it is established that only an existing thing is perceived as a producer by an external sense organ. And just as in the case of causes such as jars, only those things that are mutually connected are the causes of a single effect; thus, sensory contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) is proven, and it follows that knowledge is produced by that [contact].
The purpose of the term "indescribable" (avyapadeśya).

Now, for what purpose is the term *avyapadeśya* (non-verbal)? Some say it is for the purpose of excluding knowledge born from both [the senses and words]; others say that is incorrect because such a thing is impossible. For instance: once the mind, having occupied the ear, has produced the perception of sound and, through the process of action and division, proceeds to occupy the eye, by that time the sound has already ceased; thus, the mind would not be operative [with respect to the sound]. Furthermore, the operation of external sense organs is not possible without being presided over by the mind. Nor can the mind be a simultaneous presider, because of its atomic nature (*aṇutva*). We, however, speak even while granting [the possibility of such a case]: what is this "knowledge born from both"? Is it direct (*sākṣātkārin*) or not? If it is direct, then it is not right to exclude it, because the experience of direct perception is universally established as the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣa*). If it is not direct, then its object is not an "object of the sense" (*indriyārtha*); how then could it be born from the contact of a sense with its object? An object of a sense is not defined merely by being connected to the sense, but rather by being the object of a direct perception. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even some inferable object might be an "object of the sense" simply because it is connected to the sense; thus, another qualification would have to be made to exclude that knowledge. Or how is it understood that a cognition which follows the presence and absence of a word is born from the contact of a sense with its object? If you say "because it arises as 'this' (*idantayā*)," that is not so; for we observe the arising of a cognition as "this" even in the case of fire inferred from touch. Moreover, let that knowledge born from both be the fruit of both, or the fruit of another means of knowledge; why is it called "verbal" (*śābda*) alone? If you say "because it was taught thus by the author of the Sūtras," no; surely objects do not forfeit their own nature out of fear of the author of the Sūtras. And if the word of the Sūtra-author were authoritative without being examined, then the Sūtras concerning critical examination (*parīkṣā*) would be useless. Therefore, the reasoning must be stated for why that which is born from both is verbal. If you say "because it is designated by that [word]," no; for its designation is possible in another way. One who thinks, "This is the meaning to be expressed by this word, and this connection was explained by Devadatta," designates it, saying, "This was named by Devadatta. For otherwise, from where would the cognition of that connection come? And this designation is seen precisely in the apprehension of a connection; for example, someone who does not know the convention, seeing Caitra in a group of people, does not recognize him, thinking "This is Caitra," and asks, "Who here is Caitra? Then someone merely points him out with a finger. Thereupon, having understood the convention from the mere sight of the finger, he designates, "By this person, this Caitra was named for me. And the apprehension of the connection is not born from the contact of a sense with its object; therefore, the term *avyapadeśya* is not for the purpose of excluding that.

But another says: in cognitions such as "cow," the object appears as qualified by its name (*saṃjñā*), and since the qualifier and the qualified are supported by a single cognition, it is not logical that such [cognition] should arise from the contact of the sense organ with the object. Nevertheless, this has been accepted by some; therefore, in order to refute that, he says: "it is non-verbal" (*avyapadeśyam*).

If this is so, what qualification is intended to exclude those who assert that even some inferential knowledge (*ānumānika-jñāna*) is produced by sense-contact (*sannikarṣaja*)? If you say it is simply "being produced by sense-contact" (*sannikarṣajatvam eva*), then let that alone suffice for the purpose of excluding cognitions such as "this is a cow"; what is the use of the term "inexpressible" (*avyapadeśya*)?

Even those who explain the term "inexpressible" for the purpose of refuting the monism of sound (*śabdādvaita*) would have to provide another qualification to refute the monism of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*) and the like, since both cases share the same logical status.
[The purpose of the term "indescribable" (*avyapadeśya*) according to the opinion of Bhūṣaṇakāra.]

Is the term *avyapadeśya* (inexpressible) now indeed useless? It is not useless, because it serves the purpose of defining a specific kind of perception (*pratyakṣa*), much like the definition of certainty (*nirṇaya*). By this [term], that non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) perception is characterized. For that is sought after by all yogis, since the stability of the mind for one possessing conceptualization (*savikalpaka*) is impossible. And it is the root of everything, because in its absence, the operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is impossible. Indeed, in the absence of perception, the operation of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth is not possible. Nor is there the operation of conceptual perception when non-conceptual perception does not operate, because the latter is preceded by the recollection of names (*saṃjñā-smṛti*). Recollection, moreover, arises from the observation of the object and is the cause of cognitions such as "this is a cow," and not mere recollection alone, because its capacity [to function independently] is not established. For when the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation are grasped in their own forms, only then does a cognition such as "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) arise later. Therefore, conceptual perception is necessarily preceded by non-conceptual perception. Thus, the claim that "whatever is perception is all conceptual, because it is a means of valid cognition, like inference"—this is incorrect because its subject matter is contradicted. If it is argued: "Non-conceptual perception is not a means of valid cognition because it is not a cause for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), like indeterminate cognition (*anadhyavasāya*)," we say no, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). To explain: seeing through non-conceptual perception alone the absence of immeasurable undesirable things such as snakes or thorns, one proceeds without fear. Or, having once seen an immeasurable object consisting of a certain state, and subsequently reaching the causes of recollection, one remembers again and again and tells another, "this was seen, this was not seen. Nor is even that [initial] seeing conceptual, because it does not arise in the form "this is blue" (*nīlam idam*). Therefore, because it is a means of valid cognition, the definition of non-conceptual perception is correct. He states this: "*avyapadeśyam*. The meaning is that it is not fit for designation (*vyapadeśa*) such as the cognition "Devadatta" or the cognition "one with a staff."

Even determinate perception (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*) has been indicated in brief by the statements "the qualities of earth and so forth are its objects" and "the individual, the configuration, and the genus are the word-meanings. This is because [in those passages] the object of perception is established as the substantive (*viśeṣya*) and the denotable (*vācya*), and because it is accepted that even an object already apprehended constitutes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Alternatively, determinate perception is already included by the very term "of the nature of ascertainment" (*vyavasāyātmaka*). Thus, while one might simply say "correct" (*samyak*), the fact that he employs the more cumbersome phrasing "non-erroneous and of the nature of ascertainment" (*avyabhicāri vyavasāyātmaka*) indicates that there are only two types of incorrect knowledge—namely, the erroneous (*vyabhicārin*) and the non-ascertaining (*avyavasāya*)—and not four types. This has already been explained at length previously. Since it is well known that only that which is non-erroneous and of the nature of ascertainment is "knowledge," it need not be mentioned separately; this is true. Nevertheless, some claim that the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) is the cessation of ignorance (*ajñāna-nivṛtti*). To dispel that doubt and to ensure the identification of the substantive, "knowledge" is taught separately; thus, there is no fault.

{The Statement of the Twofold Nature of Perception} Having thus stated the definition of perception, this is said for the purpose of making known its divisions without contradicting the Sūtra: "That [perception] is twofold: the perception of yogis and the perception of non-yogis. By the word "and" (ca), it is established that it is also twofold by way of the distinction between conceptual (*savikalpaka*) and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). The mention of "twofold" is for the purpose of refuting a fourfold division, since mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and the perception of internal states such as passion (*rāga*) are impossible [according to our view]. {The Refutation of Mental Perception and Self-Awareness as Accepted by the Buddhists}

For in the opinion of others, mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is a cognition produced by sensory cognition acting as a cooperative cause with the immediately preceding object of its own [sensory] domain. The self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of pleasure and so forth is mentioned for the purpose of demonstrating the clear apprehension of pleasure and the like; however, since the self-cognition of all cognitions is already included by this [definition], both of these types of perception are untenable due to a lack of proof. Furthermore, mental perception is refuted by the negation of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*). Self-cognition is refuted, and the cognition of passion and so forth is also refuted because pleasure and the like are not of the nature of consciousness. Since the mind is itself a sense organ, there is no perception other than sensory perception; therefore, it is only reasonable that perception consists of these two: the perception of yogis and the perception of non-yogis.
An Examination of Non-Yogi Perception (*ayogipratyakṣa*)

Although yogic perception (*yogipratyakṣa*) is mentioned first because it is the most excellent, it is nevertheless understood by people such as ourselves only when non-yogic perception (*ayogipratyakṣa*) is established. Therefore, for the sake of establishing the example, non-yogic perception is first explained within that collection of perceptions, [defined as] "that which grasps gross objects through a specific relation between the sense organ and the object, by virtue of the assistance of light, place, merit (*dharma*), and so forth. "Light" (*prakāśa*) refers to things characterized by lamps and the like, as well as that characterized by the concentration of the mind (*cittasamādhāna*). "Place" (*deśa*) refers to that which stands before one and so forth. "Merit" (*dharma*) pertains to the perception of what is desired; conversely, "demerit" (*adharma*) pertains to the perception of what is undesired. Furthermore, other unmentioned causes (*nimitta*) by the absence of which an object is not perceived must all be understood from the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*). Thus, the "assistance" (*anugraha*) is understood as the cause characterized by light and the rest, since it assists by means of this. Through that assistance, the sense organ (*akṣa*) is the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). This status of being the most effective instrument belongs to the sense organ due to its specific contact (*saṃnikarṣaviśeṣa*) with the object; endowed with that, the sense organ accomplishes the apprehension of the object.

But surely, when one says, "I see by means of a lamp," the lamp also appears to be the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*); and since there is no sublation here, how can it be that only the sense organ is the most effective instrument while the lamp is merely a causal condition (*nimitta*)? True; however, perception is said to be the sense organ with respect to its predominance (*prādhānya*). And predominance consists in the fact that the result is designated after that [instrument], as in the case of a barley sprout and so forth. The lamp also possesses the status of being the most effective instrument because it assists other causal conditions; for the production of the result occurs only through the connection with the object (by this connection). This very connection is called the state of being the most effective instrument. For example, immediately after the conjunction of the eye and the tangible object, there arises the cognition of a substance such as a jar. Although in some cases even a non-final connection serves as a cause for cognition, this statement is made with regard to the majority of instances. In ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), however, that which is indeed the final [factor] is what constitutes the sense organ's status as the most effective instrument, and this is what is expressed by the suffix *-tva*.

If, then, the "most efficient instrument" (*sādhakatamatva*) is defined as the relation (*sambandha*), it would follow that the object is grasped in its entirety, because the object is related [to the sense organ] in its entirety. This is not so, because the capacity of a cause is restricted to a specific domain.
