For an axe does not, merely because of being related, cut space and other things just as it cuts a tree; nor does smoke make known all the properties of fire. Furthermore, in your own position, since you admit the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*), it follows that a cognition produced by an object in its entirety and endowed with the object's form would necessarily determine the object in its entirety. Adhering thus to the logic of the camel and the stick (*uṣṭralakuṭanyāya*), how could one not become an object of ridicule? Indeed, when there is a distinction between the substratum and its properties, only that property or substratum which is capable of being grasped by the sense organ is perceived as being related to the organ. That which lacks the fitness to be grasped by the sense organ is not perceived even though it is related. It is for this very reason that it was stated [in the verse] that [the sense organ] grasps a gross object.
The Refutation of the Whole (Avayavin)

[Objection: But surely [the opponent claims] that the gross object is the apprehender, and not that there is grossness in the form of cognition; therefore, the gross is not something graspable consisting of cognition. [Response: It is even more impossible for the gross to be an entity distinct from cognition. To explain: first of all, it cannot be a single composite (*avayavin*). If that were so, then when its hand or other parts moved, the whole would necessarily move, or else, if it did not move, there would follow the consequence of a separate existence between the moving and non-moving parts, like a cloth and water. Furthermore, if one part were covered, the whole would necessarily be covered because they are non-different; or else, if nothing were covered, it would be seen in its entirety. Even if one accepts that the covering is of the part and not of the whole, then even when half is covered, since it would remain uncovered, there would be the consequence of seeing it just as before. On the view that the perception of the whole occurs through the perception of the parts, there would be the consequence of never perceiving the whole at all, since it is impossible to see all its parts. If the whole is perceived by seeing only a few parts, then just as here, even when the parts are seen, there would be the consequence of seeing only such [a partial whole]. Moreover, if when one part is dyed the whole were dyed, then even a part situated elsewhere would be seen as dyed; if not, then even when all parts are dyed, the whole would be perceived as undyed. Furthermore, the whole does not exist because its subsistence (*vṛtti*) is untenable. To explain: "The horn is on the cow" is common in the world, whereas "the cow is in the horn" is not; therefore, if the parts subsist in the whole, then since the indivisible whole would be occupied by just one part, where would the other parts reside? For corporeal things do not occupy the same location. Nor is there any distinct location for the whole apart from the parts, by which the parts might not be forced into occupying the same space. And if one accepts that a substance subsists in a single substance, there would also be a contradiction with reason. Now, suppose the position is that the whole subsists in the parts. Even there, if it subsisted in one part with its entire self, then the other parts would not be its substratum; and if it had only a single substratum, the substance would be eternally produced and indestructible. If it subsists in one part by way of a single portion, that is not so, because for that indivisible [whole], a location distinct from the parts is impossible. Or, if such a location were accepted, there would be subsistence in those locations by means of further locations, leading to an infinite regress.

Furthermore, the composite whole (*avayavin*) does not exist, because it is not perceived when the parts are mentally analyzed. For when the parts are being separated by the intellect—thinking, "this is a thread, this is a thread"—no composite whole distinct from them appears. By this, the position that the composite whole is merely a property of the parts is also refuted. Therefore, there is no single composite whole that could be the object of the perception of grossness. Nor is the collection of atoms itself the object of the perception of grossness, because such a collection has been discarded according to the same logic applied to the composite whole, as it is nothing other than the atoms. And since individual atoms lack grossness, how could it exist in them when combined? For a red appearance is not perceived in a collection of things that were individually not red. [Otherwise], it would be a mistaken perception, like the appearance of water in a mirage.

Now, it might be argued: "If a gross object cannot possibly be the apprehended object distinct from cognition, then the subtle [atom] itself must be the apprehended object. That too is incorrect, because:
"Through simultaneous conjunction with six [atoms], the atom would have six parts;
if all six were in the same location, the entire mass would be no larger than a single atom."

Thus, for that which possesses form, there must necessarily be a division according to the directions, even into ten parts; and it is impossible to assert the existence of that whose nature is not perceived. Furthermore, because of its penetration by space, the atom would either lack omnipresence or [be non-existent]; therefore, not even an atom exists. Consequently, an external object of apprehension is not logically tenable. As it has been said:
"There is no other object to be experienced by the intellect, nor is there any other experience of that [intellect] itself."
"Due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper, that very [cognition] shines forth by itself.

The collective meaning is this: because it is devoid of a grasped object and a grasper distinct from itself, the cognition—which possesses the forms of both—is itself the illuminator of its own nature, like light. Furthermore: "Because they are necessarily perceived together, there is no difference between the blue and the cognition thereof."

For even though they appear as distinct, the object is not something other [than the cognition], because it is of such a nature that it is experienced simultaneously with the blue, just like the perception of two moons and so forth. Indeed, when one of these two is not perceived, there is no perception of the other; and this would not be logical if they were different in essence, due to the absence of any obstructing cause.
Now, if it is argued that the perception of the object is subsequently experienced by another cognition, that too is incorrect; for:
"For one whose perception is not itself directly perceived, the seeing of the object is not established."

For the apprehension of an object does not occur through the existence of the object itself; rather, it occurs through the existence of its apprehension. And that [apprehension], being unestablished by any means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*), does not sustain the linguistic conventions regarding it that are based upon its existence. If that [apprehension] is not established, the object itself is also not established, and thus there would be the total cessation of all linguistic conventions concerning existence. For even if something exists, it cannot be conventionally designated as "existent" if it is not being apprehended.

Now, if the cognition of an object is itself cognized by another cognition, then that [second] cognition—its existence being unestablished and being as if non-existent—how could it establish anything else? If one seeks yet another cognition for that too, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus no object whatsoever would be established; consequently, the world would be blind and mute. If, however, one accepts a final term somewhere, then since it perceives itself simultaneously in the form of the object, let other things be the same, for there is no reason for distinction. Thus, simultaneous perception is established; from that simultaneous perception, there is non-difference between the object and its cognition. And so, when one says "the perception of blue," what is meant is simply the perception of the nature of blue—that is, consciousness itself arises in manifold forms due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and is perceived, just like a dream-cognition. Moreover:
If cognition possesses a form such as blue and so forth, what is the basis for an external object?
If cognition does not possess a form such as blue and so forth, what is the basis for an external object?

If this blue form appears as an attribute of cognition itself, being identical with its very nature, then there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the existence of an object such as "blue" that is distinct from it. On the other hand, if this is not admitted to be a form of cognition, then how could that cognition—whether it be formless or possess a different form—be the establisher of the blue and so forth? For the establishment of one thing from another thing is impossible without a necessary connection (*pratibandha*), as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If the connection were based on "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), then the eye, the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth would also have the status of objects. Furthermore, if it does not transfer its own form, even the specific quality of being a producer (*janakatva-viśeṣa*) is unestablished. How then, despite the lack of distinction in being a producer, can there be the status of being an "object" (*karma-kārakatva*)? Or is it simply the production of a cognition whose object is itself? It is said in reply: Even for those who, relying on the connection of "dependence on a single causal complex" (*ekasāmagryadhīnatva*), maintain that the relationship of grasped and grasper exists only between things that are simultaneous, even in their view, the eye, the unseen merit, and so forth—which are dependent on that same single causal complex—would necessarily result in having the status of being grasped, since there is no distinguishing feature [to exclude them].

Now, even if the specific characteristic [of cognition] is its having the form of the object (*arthākāratva*), on what basis would there be an external object? Indeed, this single form of blue is perceived, and it is accepted as being of the very nature of cognition; however, a second form is not seen. How could that which is not seen be established as being external? Furthermore, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished, it cannot even be known through inference.
Others, however, read it thus:
"If cognition possesses the form of blue and so forth, what is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for an external object?"
"If cognitions do not have forms such as blue and so forth, how can that [object] be their experience?"

The intended meaning here is this: if cognition (*buddhi*) is formless, the systematic determination of [cognition] according to each respective object is untenable; and if it possesses a form, then the external object lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*). Now, one might argue that the form of the object is perceived solely as the apprehended (*grāhya*), whereas the form of consciousness is perceived solely as the apprehender (*grāhaka*). How can these two be one? For if they were identical, their manifestation would occur even in reverse order. This is not so; for such a systematic perception is established precisely through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless cognitive distortion. As it has been said:
Just as it is perceived by those under delusion as having the forms of the known and the knower,
with distinct characteristics, due to the distortion of the forms of the grasped and the grasper;
"When this [distinction] has been established in such a way— as in the case of the difference between the cognitions of hair and so forth—
then it cannot be challenged as having the characteristic of the grasped and the grasper."

The meaning of this is as follows: although cognition (*buddhi*) does not exist in its own nature with the forms of an object of knowledge (*vedya*) and a knowing subject (*vedaka*), it is nevertheless treated as having been established in that very way by deluded practitioners. By those deluded ones, this [cognition] is perceived as being corrupted by the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender (*grāhya-grāhaka*), which possess distinct characteristics. It is described as such because its corruption consists precisely in the forms of the apprehended and the apprehender appearing as if they had distinct characteristics. Like what? Like the distinction in the cognition of hair and so forth. Just as for those whose eyes are afflicted by cataracts and the like, non-existent hairs and so forth appear as if distinct from consciousness, so too are blue and other objects. When this differentiation of cognition is based solely on ignorance (*avidyā*), then it is not "characterized by an apprehended and an apprehender that can be challenged" (*saṃcodya-grāhya-grāhaka-lakṣaṇā*)—that is, it does not possess an apprehended and an apprehender that are subject to objection (*paryanuyojya*). For an aspect superimposed by ignorance does not deserve to be challenged. Thus, since an apprehended object and an apprehending subject external to cognition are impossible, cognition itself appears in manifold forms due to the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); therefore, it is incorrect to say that [cognition] is the apprehender of a gross object.
The establishment of the whole and its properties, such as grossness and so forth.

To this, the following reply is given: As for the claim that there is no single composite whole (*avayavin*), because if its hand and so forth were to move, the consequence would be that the whole must move entirely—this is incorrect, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished. Indeed, a pervasion has never been observed anywhere to the effect that "for whatever [it is claimed] the consequence is that the whole moves entirely when its hand and so forth move, that [whole] does not exist. Nor has such a pervasion as "for whatever exists, it is not the case that the consequence is that the whole moves entirely when its hand and so forth move" been perceived by the opponent. Furthermore, the capacity of a reason to establish one's own position or refute the position of another is never seen to exist in the absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Even a *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅga*) gains its validity only when a pervasion between both [terms] is established, as in the case of the *reductio* involving light and a lamp. Furthermore, the argument that "if there were no movement, it would follow that the moving and non-moving parts would be established separately" is untenable if external objects do not exist. For no sane person would ever object in this way: "The son of a barren woman does not exist, because if his hand and so forth were to move, the consequence would be that he moves entirely, or else, if he did not move, it would follow that the moving and non-moving parts are established separately, like a sky-flower or a donkey's horn. If you argue that the meaning of the *reductio* is this: "Since there is a contradiction between being moving and non-moving, one who accepts the oneness of the whole must necessarily accept that the whole moves in its entirety; and one who accepts both moving and non-moving states cannot accept oneness," we say no, because this is redundant. For neither a Naiyāyika nor a Vaiśeṣika accepts that a single composite whole possesses both moving and non-moving states toward whom such a *reductio* would be meaningful.

[Objection: But surely, even when one part is moving, there is a state of being moved and unmoved because other parts do not move; thus, difference is established. [Response: What undesirable consequence follows from that? Even if there is a difference between parts due to their being moved and unmoved, what does that have to do with the whole (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity? When the movement of the whole arises, it is not the case that the whole remains unmoved simply because some part is unmoved. Conversely, when [the movement of the whole] does not arise, the whole does not move even if a part is moving. This is because those two—the movement of the part and the movement of the whole—cannot be necessarily simultaneous, since they are produced by different causal complexes (*sāmagrī*). In that case, we do not know whether the whole possesses movement at the time when half of its parts are moving, since a corresponding cognition is possible in either way. Similarly, even when the whole is stationary, the cognition of movement occurs just as it does for color and so forth, provided that the supports (*āśraya*) are seen to be moving. Conversely, even when it is moving, a cognition of stationariness is possible due to the inherence (*samavāya*) of unmoving parts, just as one fails to perceive movement due to causes such as distance. Nor does this lead to a lack of confidence in all cases, for certainty is established when the grounds for doubt are not perceived. Otherwise, the conventional distinction between the moved and the unmoved would be entirely rootless.

Alternatively, since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) involves motion, motion also exists only in a particular location (*pradeśavṛttitva*). Therefore, it is not contradictory for even a single entity to be the object of both the cognition of "moving" and "not moving. If you argue that this is illogical because, when a person is running, motion is observed not to exist in a particular location, then by the same token, since the conjunction of a cloth with water and so forth is observed not to exist in a particular location, it would follow that conjunction itself does not exist in a particular location—which is also illogical.

If it is argued that the misconception of [the whole] as existing without spatial parts (*apradeśavṛtti*) arises because a cloth or similar object is perceived in conjunction with water and so forth along with the conjunctions of all its parts, then the same applies here: since motion is perceived in the whole together with the motions of all its parts, there is likewise merely a misconception of it as existing without spatial parts. We see no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for determining the distinction that when there is a conjunction of a finger with a wall, etc., there is also a conjunction of the body, yet when there is motion of the hand, there is no motion of the body. For the establishment of every doctrine would follow from mere theoretical construction (*prakriyāmātra*). Therefore, since motion also exists in specific locations (*pradeśavṛttitva*), the perception and non-perception of motion in a single whole are not contradictory, just like the perception and non-perception of conjunction. By this, the states of being covered and uncovered are also explained. Furthermore, the perception of the parts or the sensory contact with the parts is not the cause for the perception of the whole; otherwise, if even one part—such as half or a third—were covered, the whole would not be apprehended. What then? It is the sensory contact with that [whole], accompanied by all auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). And that [contact] is inferred from the perception of the [whole]; however, by the non-perception of it, it is merely the incompleteness of the auxiliary factors that is inferred.

If it is asked, "Why is the whole not seen even when half of its parts are covered?", we say: no; for that which has an undivided nature is indeed seen as a complete whole. When that [whole] is thus seen through its parts, doubt is not contradictory, depending on whether one considers the specific or non-specific qualities of the parts and so forth. Furthermore, because the perceptions of its parts and the perception of the whole have distinct causes, there is no rule of their simultaneous occurrence. Therefore, the whole is apprehended even when its parts are not perceived.

As for what was said—"and when one [part] is red," etc.—that too is incorrect. For the whole (*avayavin*) does not become such [red or non-red] by virtue of its parts being red or non-red, because it is a distinct entity from them. Rather, the redness of the whole is simply its conjunction with a red substance, and its non-redness is the absence of that. And since conjunction exists as non-pervasive (*avyāpyavṛtti*), the state of being both red and non-red does not contradict the unity of a single whole. If it is asked, "How can there be non-pervasiveness in one?", we say no; for this is the very nature of conjunction that, wherever the whole is perceived in a part, there the conjunction is not perceived—even when the causes for its perception are unimpaired—just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth. Likewise, wherever space (*ākāśa*) exists, it is not delimited there by the conjunction of space with the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*); otherwise, all sounds would result in being objects of a single sense of hearing due to their inherence (*samavāya*) therein. For this very reason, sound also lacks pervasive existence, as it would follow that even a sound produced in one place would be an object of all ears. This property of conjunction, sound, and so forth is also expressed by the term "local existence" (*pradeśavṛttitva*), yet there are no spatial parts (*pradeśa*) for an impartite entity like space. Even though the parts of a whole constitute its "parts," the conjunction of the whole does not reside therein; otherwise, it would follow that no whole whatsoever could be the locus of conjunction. Furthermore, since an atom (*paramāṇu*) has no parts, it could have no conjunction; consequently, if bodies and so forth were not produced, nothing at all could be perceived. Therefore, just as in your own view, by means of indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*), that very same determinate cognition (*savikalpaka-jñāna*)—which is similar to itself—is somehow produced and somehow not, and thus a "portion" is conceptually constructed for that which is actually undivided; so too it is for the substratum of conjunction and so forth. Thus, the local existence of conjunction and the like is not faulty. Consequently, even for a single entity, being red and non-red is not contradictory.
The impossibility of a variegated form.

If, then, a whole (*avayavin*) is produced from parts that are themselves both colored and colorless, what is its form? Because no specific [form] is initiated, it is simply indefinable in its particulars. For while there is a contradiction in the initiation of specific forms belonging to causes that are mutually exclusive, there is no contradiction in the initiation of a general [form], since the nature of "form" (*rūpa*) is possible in all cases, such as blue, yellow, and so on. Thus, even though a form devoid of specific qualities like blue has arisen, this is understood precisely through the perception of the whole; for it is impossible to perceive a substance lacking form, and if one thing were perceived by means of the form of another, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, that which arises is merely form in itself, indefinable in its particulars. As for the variegated appearance (*citrapratibhāsa*) therein, it is due to the connection with variegated parts, just as the appearance of blue and other colors occurs in a crystal. If this were so, then even the form of a dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) would become indefinable because it initiates mutually exclusive specific forms; consequently, all forms of wholes preceded by that [dyad] would also be indefinable. Furthermore, since the specific forms of subsequent [parts] would be beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), the very designation of specific forms would be utterly destroyed.
The production of variegated form.

This is not so, because every undertaking depends upon the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and the unseen force initiates actions that serve the purposes of the person; however, it is not the case that such an undertaking fails to serve the person's purpose, for if it were always undertaken in such a way, it would contradict the perception of specific forms in all cases. Alternatively, that very form has arisen as variegated (*citram*) precisely because it appears as such without sublation. If it is argued that this is untenable due to the contradiction between being "one" and being "variegated," we say no; for even a single entity can be the locus of multiple properties such as blueness and so forth, and thus it is possible for it to be the object of a variegated appearance. For example, a cloth connected with many colors such as red ochre and others is perceived as "variegated. If it is argued that the co-inherence (*samavāya*) of the universals (*jāti*) of blueness and so forth in one place is not logical because they are contradictory, we say no; for their contradiction is unproven. If it is argued that their contradiction is established by the fact that they are never seen together elsewhere, we say no; for then it would follow that blueness and lotus-ness are also contradictory. If it is argued that there is no contradiction because those two are seen in one place, this applies equally here. Even by reasoning, it is possible for the form of a whole (*avayavin*) produced from parts of different kinds to be the locus of multiple universals, since we observe that the forms of the parts invariably produce a form of the same kind in the whole. Even in the opponent’s view, let the cognition variegated by multiple latent impressions (*vāsanā*) serve as an illustration. Indeed, it is the very differences in universals that are expressed by the terms "difference of exclusion" (*vyāvṛtti-bheda*) and "difference of capacity" (*śakti-bheda*). Whether these are distinct from or non-distinct from their substrata is a separate point of dispute. Therefore, a single form that is the locus of multiple universals is variegated. And although it is of such a nature, when—due to some cause—the non-perception of the multiple universals occurs and it is grasped as qualified by only one specific universal at a time, then it is grasped as "white" or "red," but not as "variegated. This is like the color of a support (the ground). Now, if it is argued that what is grasped as "white" or "red" is only the form of the parts, whereas the form of the whole is held to be perceptible only at the time of grasping it as "variegated," let it be so; we have no insistence on this point, as the refutation of the Buddhist objection is established in every respect.

However, even those who do not accept the existence of a whole (*avayavin*) must state the object of the appearance of variegated colors and the like. If they accept that the object consists of parts distinct from atoms (*paramāṇu*), then that very thing becomes accepted as a "whole. But since atoms are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), they cannot be objects of the senses; for they lack the defining characteristic of an object. For they maintain that the defining characteristic of an object is its capacity to produce a cognition with its own form (*svākāra*). Yet atoms lack the capacity to produce their own forms, because what is experienced everywhere is only a gross form and so forth. Furthermore, if something that produces a dissimilar form were also considered an object, then the eyes and other sense organs would also have to be objects.

Now, if it is argued that atoms possess the capacity to impart forms such as blue and so forth, and that their status as objects is due solely to this, that is incorrect. For the form of blue and so forth is experienced precisely as being of the nature of something gross and so on; no other form of blue and so forth, consisting of unaggregated atoms, appears. Furthermore, on what basis is this distinction determined—that only the form of blue and so forth has an external material cause, and not the form of the gross and so forth? For the proponent of forms (*ākāravādin*) does not perceive even the form of blue and so forth as an entity distinct from the form residing in cognition, in the same way that the form of the gross and so forth is [perceived]. How, then, can the causal relationship between the object and its form be established through perception and non-perception? Moreover, by means of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), the external material cause of the gross form would also be established, since both cases share the same logical status. If it is argued that many atoms situated together appear as something gross, we say no, for this has already been refuted. If the atoms are individually unaggregated and not gross, then a cognition possessing such a form would necessarily be erroneous. Furthermore, do those many atoms impart a single form to the cognition, or a different form for each atom? If they impart a single form to the cognition, then perception itself would have a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object, because it would grasp a common form; moreover, it would be erroneous, since it grasps as a single form those things which are individually distinct in form. Furthermore, there would be no variegated appearance, for a single form cannot be called "variegated. If, on the other hand, the cognition possesses a different form for each atom, that too is untenable; for it is impossible for a single, undivided cognition to have a plurality of forms. If there were a difference in forms, there would necessarily be a difference in the cognition itself, or else a contradiction with its unity (since there is no other alternative). If it is argued that a difference in forms is indeed accepted as implying a difference in cognition, we say no, because it contradicts experience. One experiences a single cognition of a pillar and so forth, not an incalculable number of distinct cognitions corresponding to each atom. And if cognitions terminate in their own individual forms, then—just like cognitions in separate mental continua—their forms would be mutually unknown to one another; how then could there be an apprehension of many things as having a gross form?

Now, if it is argued that no external object exists at all, and that in every case it is only the cognition itself that appears in the form of that [object], that too is incorrect; for how could a single cognition possess a variegated form? If one accepts that what is of a non-different nature can be variegated, then what offense has the "whole" (avayavin) committed, such that even though it is well-established by all the world, it is rejected?

Now, if it is claimed that a single, undifferentiated self does not possess variegated forms, but rather that a plurality of cognitions arising simultaneously with restricted forms is called "variegated," that too is not tenable. Since [cognition] is grounded in self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), only a single form is experienced; a cognition never experiences the form of another cognition. And if there is no such experience, how can a cognition that produces multiple simultaneous forms be variegated, like the multiple forms of cognitions belonging to different mental continua (*saṃtāna*)? If it is argued that a single conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arising from those [sensory cognitions] within one continuum is produced, which determines the variegated forms, we say no; for even a variegated cognition that appears clearly is observed [to be non-conceptual]. Furthermore, you do not accept that conceptual construction possesses clear appearance. If the conceptual construction has only a single form, then how can it determine variegated forms? If it has distinct forms, how can there be distinct forms for that which is undifferentiated? By this very argument, the proliferation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is also refuted.

Now, if it is claimed that multiple cognitions arising simultaneously are mutually cognizable because they are produced from a single material cause (*upādāna*), and that for this reason the perception of multiple forms constitutes a variegated appearance (*citrapratibhāsa*), this is not so. For if a cognition is perceived as assuming the form of another cognition, how could it then be of a single form and devoid of that [other] form? How could there be the cognition of the latter within the former? If that were the case, the same would apply to the object. If, however, a form is cognized that does not constitute the very nature of the cognition, then the postulation of such a form would be entirely without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). {The Proof of Non-dual Variegation (*Citrādvaitasiddhi*)}

Let it be, then, that there is a manifold non-duality (*citrādvaita*). Nor is this the case for the external world, because when it is subjected to analysis, its nature as something distinct is impossible to establish. Nor is such analysis possible for cognition itself; for cognition does not analyze its own self by itself, since it is experienced precisely as having an undifferentiated nature. Nor can it be analyzed by another cognition, because that too consists solely in the self-awareness of its own self. If it is argued that the analysis consists in noting that what is now appearing alone is "other" than the form of the previous cognition which was not so appearing—this is not so, because the previous [cognition] is imperceptible and thus not experienced. And if that is not cognized, how can one realize, "I am distinct from that"? If it is argued that this is known through memory—this is not so, because memory is not a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If it is claimed that it is indeed a means of valid knowledge because it is produced by experience—this is not so, because there is no proof for such production. For memory, without having experienced the original experience, does not know, "I have arisen from that experience. If, however, the experience were being experienced [by the memory], then it would be the experience itself and not memory. By this, inferential and other types of cognition are also refuted, because they too are restricted to self-awareness and lack the capacity to perceive anything else. For if they were to perceive another, then upon assuming its form, they would simply become that very thing. Therefore, since it is impossible to differentiate them, the manifold cognition consisting of the forms of the grasped, the grasper, blue, and so forth, is one and the same; thus, manifold non-duality is established. Since the nature [of things] is apprehended in this way as being a means of valid knowledge, there is no contradiction either.
{Refutation of Variegated Non-duality}

To this it is replied: Since the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*) in its entirety has already been refuted by this very sūtra—“The absolute [monism] of the Sāṃkhyas is not established, because neither the non-occurrence nor the occurrence of a cause is possible”—it is untenable. We shall elaborate on this further below. However, the following point must be questioned here: If the doctrine of the non-duality of the manifold (*citrādvaitavāda*) is indeed your intended position, then for what purpose is this great effort expended in rejecting the Veda? For even there, the ultimate truth is that the Self alone, whose nature is consciousness, is one and takes on the form of the universe. Thus, the Śruti says: “All this is indeed Brahman,” “This Person is a mass of knowledge alone,” and “This is one only, without a second. It would be more appropriate for you to say that this treatise exists precisely for the sake of ascertaining the meaning of such Vedic passages; it is not right to declare their lack of authority, like the authors of the *Śārīraka* (Brahmasūtra) and other scriptures. Otherwise, since your own scripture would have the same meaning as those, it would follow that your scripture is also lacking in authority. This might be argued:

The state of having variegated forms (*citrākāratā*) is also unreal, because it is impossible to apprehend; for indeed, cognition, being self-cognized, is submerged solely in the experience of its own self-cognitive form, and thus there is no experience of another form. If it is asked, "What contradiction is there even in the experience of that [other form]?", [the answer is: there is simply the impossibility of both its own nature and another nature [coexisting]. For it is not logical that such a cognition experiences another form by way of its own nature, since its own nature is established within itself. How can a form situated within its own nature, which is directed only toward itself, know another? If it is argued that "it is directed toward another," then in that case its own self is not perceived; consequently, there would be no perception of two [aspects], just as in the case of perceiving another mental continuum (*santānāntara*). If it is argued that "he who possesses those two directions is one and the same," then who is the one who perceives that "this is a duality"? If it is he himself, then again, a third [factor]—namely, the two directions and self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*)—would follow. From the cognition of these three, yet another self would have to be admitted; from his three directions and self-cognition, a fourth would follow. Again another, again another—an immense series of calamities would ensue. Therefore, cognition is indeed one, and the appearance of difference therein is merely a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*). Even cognition, if unapprehended in its own nature, is non-existent; thus, emptiness alone remains. For it is not possible to apprehend that [cognition] as excluded from other forms by means of something else that does not apprehend it. Nor can it be established that "cognition is cognition because it is excluded from non-cognition" if that exclusion is not cognized. As it has been said: [The verse follows...]
"This is what has come through the power of reality, as the wise declare: in whatever way objects are analyzed, in that very way they fall apart."

If it is the very nature of objects that they cease when examined, then what can we do about that? Furthermore, it is not proper for a proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*) to accept an unexamined entity based on mere appearance, as this would entail the acceptance of even the objects of dreams and the like. How, then, is the nature of perception and so forth established by means of refuting the opposing position? To this it has been said: "of the conventional" (*sāṃvyāvahārikasya*), and so on. Therefore, in this context, non-dual mere appearance, which is empty of all phenomena, is not equivalent to the non-duality of Brahman and other such doctrines.

This too is incorrect, because even in the Veda, due to the restrictive determination that "this is indeed one," neither manifoldness nor substantial transformation is intended. Just as for you [the Yogācārins], properties such as having form (*sākāratva*) and momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) are stated merely in a conventional sense, so too in the Veda are properties such as eternity (*nityatva*) and omnipresence (*vyāpakatva*). And just as non-duality (*advaita*) has been stated by you through the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*), so too in the Veda it is stated in such passages as "without smell, without taste, without form. Now, if what is intended is the void (*śūnya*), in the sense that "nothing at all exists," that is incorrect, because it contradicts the utterance of one's own words. If it is argued that the utterance is itself a cognitive distortion (*upaplava*), even so, that by which something is distorted and that which is distorted must both exist; otherwise, this entire world would be nothing but darkness and space. If, indeed, something exists, what of it? Surely the Veda should not be rejected, since within it both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) are taught. If it is argued that in the Veda non-duality is perceived through the negation of other things, whereas here (in our system) nothing else is affirmed or denied, but rather non-duality arises simply from establishing the falsity of the appearance of difference—that is incorrect. For as long as difference is not negated, how can the falsity of its appearance be established? Is it not the case that the perception of difference is unreal precisely because of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)? To explain: if the perception of self and other constitutes the perception of difference, then it would have to be called "self-awareness" and "awareness of another. In that case, self-awareness is restricted to itself, and awareness of another is restricted to the self of the other; thus, not even one of them is a perception of difference. If, on the other hand, the perception of blue, yellow, and so forth is the perception of difference, that too is false. Since the perception of blue is restricted to the nature of blue and the perception of yellow is restricted to the nature of yellow, every perception is simply self-awareness; what then is the perception of difference here? If a single perception whose objects are multiple things like blue and so forth is the perception of difference, even then, since that very same thing is the perception of blue and that very same thing is the perception of yellow, it would be a mere synonymous designation for a non-differentiated perception. Furthermore, a distinct determination based on a non-differentiated perception is not logical, as it leads to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the appearance of difference is not real.

This Buddhist assertion appears entirely incoherent, like chewing on the air. To explain: first of all, the appearance of difference occurs for everyone; from what, then, is its unreality perceived? Is it from that very same appearance, or from another appearance? If you say "from that very same [appearance]," that is not tenable, because that appearance has difference as its object. Indeed, an appearance such as "these objects are distinct" does not determine its own unreality; for if it were so determined, there would be no activity based on error. If you say that the unreality is determined by another cognition, then how can that other cognition—which is restricted to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*)—know the unreality of something else? If it has both as its object, why is there no apprehension of difference? If there is no apprehension of difference even when both are the object, that is a contradiction of your own words. If you argue there is no contradiction because you are speaking according to the opponent's admission, is that admission of the opponent perceived as non-different from your own admission, or as different? If it is perceived as non-different, then it would simply be your own admission. If it is perceived as different, the contradiction remains exactly as before. If you say this is merely a restatement of worldly convention (*lokavyavahāra*), we say no. Is that worldly convention indeed something other than the vision of reality (*tattvadṛṣṭi*), or is it not something other? If it is not something other, then the vision of reality itself is the worldly convention; therefore, the establishment of difference follows precisely from that convention. If the worldly convention is something other than the vision of reality, then how is it not a case of difference? If you say this is a delusion (*upaplava*), is that too different from the vision of reality, or non-different? In either case, the same logical consequence (*prasaṅga*) as before applies.

It is also not tenable to say that "difference exists conventionally" (*saṃvṛti*), for the following undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains unresolved: is even this convention something other than the vision of reality (*tattva*), or is it non-other? Therefore, for those who advocate non-duality (*advaitavādin*), silence is better and preferable. Furthermore, we shall refute non-duality at length later on. {Refutation of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedanatā*)}

First, the proponent of self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is questioned: by what is the falsity of the determination of the distinction between the cognized object and the cognition determined? It cannot be determined by that very [cognition] itself, because that cognition consists in the determination of a distinction. Nor can it be determined by another cognition, because it is not admitted that one cognition can be the object of another cognition; for if it were so admitted, this reason—namely, "due to the absence of the relationship of grasped and grasper"—would be unestablished (*asiddha*). If it is argued that one cognition is the object of another cognition through error (*bhrānti*), we say no; for error is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). This we shall demonstrate in the section on inference (*anumāna*).

And what is this delusion (*bhrānti*)? Is it merely the apprehension of its own form (*svākāra*)? Or is it the superimposition of its own form upon something else? Or is it the superimposition of another form upon itself? First of all, mere apprehension of its own form is not delusion, because that would entail the consequence that all cognitions are delusory. Nor is the superimposition of its own form upon something else delusion, because such superimposition is impossible if that "other" has never been perceived. Indeed, the superimposition of any form upon an object that is entirely unperceived is nowhere observed. If, then, delusion is the superimposition of another form upon itself, even there one must ask: is it the superimposition of a form already seen, or the superimposition of a form not seen? The superimposition of a form already seen is not tenable, because a false form has never been seen [by you]. For in your view, the falsity of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding the distinction between the grasped and the grasper (*grāhya-grāhaka-bheda*) has never been perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in any instance, such that the superimposition of such a form could occur in another cognition. If, on the other hand, it is the superimposition of an unseen form, that is not so; for the superimposition of an unseen form is never observed. In every case of delusion, it is observed that only a form already seen—such as yellow—is superimposed upon things like conch shells. Even in the case of the moon and so forth, the property of duality and the like is merely the superimposition of what was seen elsewhere. Furthermore, if delusion were the superimposition of an unseen form, then, like the delusion of two moons, it would not be non-contradictory with respect to that form. Consequently, the knowledge of the falsity of the determination regarding the distinction between the grasped and the grasper would be invalid (*apramāṇa*). And if that were invalid, the determination of the distinction between the grasped and the grasper would be correct. Moreover, even in the delusion of an external object, if that external object is entirely unperceived, how can its form be superimposed? Indeed, the form of a specific jewel in a king’s treasury is never seen to be superimposed by someone who has not seen it. Furthermore, in delusion, is the form of the external object superimposed by another cognition? Or is that very [deluded] cognition itself that form? It is not superimposed by another cognition, because that is not its object; for no form is ever superimposed by anyone upon something that is not its object, such as taste and so forth, by means of the eye. Moreover, in your view, one cognition is not the object of another cognition. If it is argued that the delusion itself is that form, that is not so; for it is contradictory for a single, undivided self to possess multiple distinct forms. If it is argued that the multiplicity of forms appears despite being non-existent, that is not so; for that would open the door to universal nihilism (*sarvaśūnyatā*), and a fault has already been stated regarding that. Furthermore, it would result in the doctrine of the appearance of the non-existent (*asatkhyātivāda*), which contradicts your own established tenets (*svakṛtānta*). If it is maintained that the possession of multiple forms is the very nature of cognition, and that there is no contradiction for something with its own nature, then why go so far as to overstep all boundaries? It would be better to maintain that the external object itself possesses that form. For in accepting that, there is neither contradiction with common experience nor contradiction with reason. Indeed, for one who accepts the identity of attribute and substrate (*dharma-dharmin*), it is impossible to avoid the contradiction of a single thing having multiple forms. For if that were accepted, it would follow that there is no contradiction even for a single entity in the acceptance of the nature of the entire world. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever in accepting that the form of a whole (*avayavin*) is indeed a single locus of multiple attributes.
The non-existence of the whole does not follow from its analysis.

As for what was said—that because an external object cannot be analyzed by the intellect (*dhi*), whereas the analysis of cognition (*jñāna*) is possible—that is an unconsidered statement. For, according to the position of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition can indeed sometimes be analyzed since it is capable of being perceived. But how can an external object, whose very nature is absolute non-perception, be analyzed? Indeed, one cannot analyze the ornaments of a king’s inner apartments without having seen them. If it is argued that the analysis is possible because that which is intended as "external" is actually the aspect of cognition (*jñānākāra*) and is thus visible, [we ask]: does its analysis result in the non-existence of that very aspect, or of something else? It is not logical to say it is the former, because that would entail the consequence that cognition is formless (*nirākāra*). And if that were so, there would be a contradiction between the manifoldness and the unity [of cognition]. Nor is it the non-existence of something else, for if the non-existence of another thing were established through the analysis of one, it would follow that the three worlds do not exist. If you say that it is merely the distinctness of that [aspect] from cognition that is denied, we say no; for that is irrelevant. Here, the question of whether it is distinct or non-distinct from cognition is not the topic; rather, the topic is how a single [cognition] can have a manifold aspect. In that regard, it has already been stated that if it were distinct from cognition, the manifold aspect would be all the more untenable. Now, if it is argued that the analysis is untenable because an external object is analyzed by many people, whereas cognition—being merely self-cognizing—ceases once it has known itself to be manifold in aspect, and by whom then could it be analyzed? That is incorrect. For if cognition were not the object of another cognition, there would be nothing but the doctrine of non-duality (*advaitavāda*). Or, if it is somehow an object, then analysis occurs in exactly that same way; so how can analysis be untenable? Furthermore, the claim that the analysis is untenable because an external object is analyzed by many people is also incorrect due to internal contradiction. For how can that which is the object of the cognitions of many people be non-existent? If you say that it is the object of the cognitions of many people only through delusion (*bhrānti*), then the analysis must be delusory; therefore, because it lacks validity (*apramāṇa*), it cannot prove non-existence. If you argue that even a delusion is valid knowledge (*pramā*) because of its connection with a real object, that is incorrect; for there is no connection between a delusion and an external object. Or, if such a connection existed, the object would not be non-existent.

Furthermore, is the whole (*avayavin*) distinguished by means of the cognition of the whole, or by means of the cognition of the parts? It cannot be by means of the cognition of the whole, because it would follow that the non-existence of the whole being thus distinguished is established; for that [cognition] has the nature of apprehending its existence, just like the cognition of blue and so forth. If, on the other hand, its non-existence were established by the cognition of its existence, then its existence would likewise have to be established by the cognition of its non-existence; in that case, the determination would be quite sound. If, however, its non-existence is established while it is being distinguished by the cognition of its parts, let it be so—provided that there exists an unerring cognition of its non-existence. But such a cognition of the non-existence of jars and the like does not occur everywhere; therefore, its non-existence is not established in all cases. If it is argued that its non-existence is established while it is being distinguished by the cognition of the parts, that too is incorrect; for the cognition of the parts establishes only the existence of the parts, and it is incapable of either establishing or negating the existence of the whole, since the whole is not the object of that cognition.

If it is argued that because the whole (*avayavin*) is not perceived while its parts are being perceived, therefore it does not exist at all—then in that case, when odor, touch, and color are being perceived, taste is not perceived, nor is the cognition of another person; consequently, the non-existence of both of those would also follow. If it is argued that they do not [absolutely] not exist because taste is perceived by another sense organ and the cognition of that other person is perceived by another person, then likewise, the whole is not non-existent because it is perceived by a different kind of perception. For instance: the appearance of distinct forms occurs only with respect to the parts, whereas the appearance of the whole is of a non-distinct form. If it is argued that there is no difference [between the two appearances] because they are objects of the same sense organ, we say no; for this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of blue, yellow, and so forth. Furthermore, how is there a difference between the sense organs themselves? If you say it is due to a difference in their appearances, let that same [principle of difference through appearance] apply elsewhere as well; what is the point of invoking a difference in the sense organs? Now, if the whole exists, why is it not perceived by anyone as something distinct from the parts? Who says this? To me, at least, it is clearly perceived. If you say, "This is an illusion on your part," then [we reply: my cognition—which is consistent with the worldly transactions of all people—is indeed an apprehension of non-difference. For example: "This single cloth has been produced by many threads"—how could this be an illusion? Likewise, production [of the whole] is also established, since its impossibility due to momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) has already been refuted. Therefore, the non-existence of the whole cannot be established through analysis (*vivecana*). By this, the claim that the cognition of a cloth is untenable upon the removal of the threads is also refuted. For if "removal" (*apakarṣaṇa*) is intended to mean the disjunction of the threads, then its non-existence is indeed accepted by us due to the destruction of the conjunction. Moreover, that which undergoes destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is not absolutely non-existent, for otherwise it would follow that even cognition itself is absolutely non-existent. As for the "removal of cognition" (*buddhyapakarṣaṇa*) through analysis, it is refuted by the very refutation of that [analysis], since they have the same meaning.
The refutation of the notion that cognition is directed toward itself.

As for what was said regarding "facing oneself" and "facing another" in order to establish self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone—we shall explain that knowledge does not possess self-awareness. Therefore, "facing oneself" is not accepted; however, "facing another" is indeed admitted as a property of knowledge, which is designated as the "relation between object and subject. Even if that [property] is not perceived, there is no infinite regress, because the object is perceived even without it. Furthermore, since there is a distinction between the property and the substratum, we shall explain that the substratum is not divided merely by the division of its properties. And since various objects such as blue and yellow appear within a single, undivided cognition, this [argument of yours] is also untenable. Moreover, it is not logical to establish distinct objects based on a non-distinct cognition, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in a single cognition perceiving multiple objects.
{The Refutation of the Impossibility of Functioning}

As for what was said regarding the impossibility of subsistence (*vṛttyanupapatti*) in the refutation of the whole (*avayavin*): is this an independent proof (*svatantrasādhana*) or a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅgāpādana*)? First of all, an independent proof is not tenable; for in your own position, there is no subsistence of anything whatsoever—either in its entirety or by way of a part—in any locus. Thus, due to the impossibility of subsistence, the non-existence of everything would follow. Nor is it a reductio ad absurdum, because a pervasion (*vyāpti*) is impossible, as in the case of a lamp and its light. Or, if pervasion were admitted, then just as with the lamp, there would be no absolute absence of the subsistence of the whole through either its entirety or a part; for the establishment of the absence of the pervaded is only logical upon the establishment of the absence of the pervader. Furthermore, it is impossible to understand the pervasiveness of a subsistence that is absolutely unperceived. So how can the non-existence of the whole be established from the absence of subsistence? Even if pervasiveness were understood in some cases, the whole would not be absolutely non-existent. If you argue that this is because the opponent admits that subsistence pervades the whole, that is incorrect; for in that case, since the opponent admits that the primordial matter (*mūlaprakṛti*) pervades all effects, upon its cessation, there would be the non-existence of every effect, whether conscious or unconscious. Moreover, the opponents do not admit that the subsistence of the whole occurs either in its entirety or by way of a part; therefore, even the pointing out of a contradiction in the opponent’s admission is untenable. The opponent’s admission is that the undifferentiated whole subsists in the differentiated parts precisely through the relation of inherence (*samavāya*). We shall explain later that inherence belongs to this [whole].

The bamboo stalk also exists upon the pillars by way of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), not by way of occupying a single part (*ekadeśena*), because a single part does not [itself] possess parts. How then is there the cognition that "the bamboo exists upon the pillars by way of a single part"? This is not difficult to explain: for a part of the whole (*avayavin*) is indeed a constituent part (*avayava*); thus, for one who perceives it as conjoined with that single part, such a cognition arises. However, existence [of the whole] in a single part alone is neither the mode of subsistence (*vṛtti*) nor the cause of subsistence, because it would follow that atoms (*paramāṇu*) and space (*ākāśa*) lack conjunction; consequently, no effects whatsoever could ever arise.

Now, if it is argued that what is one exists in only one place—just as color does—and therefore one who accepts the oneness of the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth must not accept its existence in multiple locations, we say no; for they are established by equal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Why is it not accepted that from the very same means of valid cognition by which the existence of color in a single location is established, the existence of the whole and so forth in multiple locations is likewise established? Or, just as there is an inherence (*samavāya*) of the substratum of color together with multiple [qualities] such as odor and taste, so too is there inherence of the whole and so forth with multiple substrata; what contradiction is there in this?

But surely everyone has the cognition that "the branch is in the tree" or "the horn is in the cow"; how then can parts be considered the substrata [of the whole]? No, for that cognition is otherwise explained. When the whole, such as a tree, remains in its state, those who perceive the parts such as branches do not see them fall because their falling is obstructed by the connection with the parts situated below; thus, they form the notion that the branches have the tree as their substratum. However, the status of parts as substrata consists in this: the whole exists only when those parts exist, and it is non-existent when they are absent. By this, the fact that qualities such as color (*rūpa*) are dependent on substance (*dravya*) is also explained. Because they are observed there, even eternal things are conceived as being dependent. Likewise, although universals (*sāmānya*) are eternal, they are perceived only in individual objects (*piṇḍa*); therefore, they do not become objects of linguistic usage when individuals are absent. For this reason, they are conventionally designated as being dependent on them. Therefore—
"There may be a support for water and the like that prevents their movement; but what need have qualities, universals, and actions—which are themselves immobile—of supports?"

This statement, too, expresses a meaning that has not been properly considered; for in the world, a substratum is not known to be merely that which obstructs gravity, but rather in other ways as well—such as a face in a mirror, pain and so forth in the body, or luster in a sword. Therefore, while a specific kind of relation between a single composite whole (*avayavin*) and its many [parts], or between a single substance and its many qualities such as color and so forth, is established with effort, let the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheya-bhāva*) be postulated there according to the circumstances.

Now, if it is not accepted that there is also inherence (*samavāya*) of color and the rest in a substance, then upon what basis does this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) rest—that "whatever is one exists only in one place"? Furthermore, when color produces another color, does it do so by its entire self (*sarvātmanā*) or by a single part (*ekadeśena*)? If color were exhausted in producing another color by its entire self, then it would lack the capacity to produce cognition and so forth; for it has no internal differentiation of self, nor can it exist by a single part, since that which is partless lacks spatial divisions. Moreover, it would follow that space itself would be the producer. As for cognition as well, is it produced from color by its entire self or by a single part? If the cognition produced from color by its entire self were also produced from another cognition, then it would not be possible. Nor could it be produced by a single part, because that [cognition] lacks spatial divisions.

If it is argued that this undesirable consequence does not apply to the proponent of *vijñānamātra* (consciousness-only), we say no; for even in that case, the consequence—that a single cognition is produced by multiple cognitions, produces multiple cognitions, and perceives multiple forms—does not cease. Moreover, if this is not admitted, there would be nothing but non-duality (*advaita*), and the web of faults already mentioned therein will be stated [further] below. By this, one should see that the status of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) and the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) is also untenable. Therefore, for one who rejects the whole (*avayavin*) through the analysis of its modes of existence, even the meaning of their own school’s doctrine collapses. If, however, a single cognition possesses such a nature, then the whole must likewise possess such a nature; since they share the same logical status (*samānayogakṣema*), it cannot be subject to further objection.
"When a fault is equal for both parties and the rebuttal is likewise equal, one should not be subject to censure by the other in such an investigation of the matter."

[The opponent argues: "Therefore, the whole (*avayavin*) does not exist separately [from its parts], because when the parts are not perceived, it is not perceived. Whatever is not perceived when something else is not perceived does not exist separately from it, just as a second moon is not perceived when the [first] moon is not perceived. [Reply: This reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, when one *kṛttikā* star is not perceived, another *kṛttikā* is not perceived; yet there are distinct *kṛttikā* stars. Furthermore, the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*). For instance, even when the parts such as threads are not perceived from a distance, the whole such as a cloth is perceived. Nor can it be assumed that there is a perception of the threads simply because they do not appear in their true form, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Objection: "It is perceived like an army or a forest. [Reply: No, because atoms (*aṇu*) are beyond the reach of the senses. Perhaps this thought occurs to you: "Just as an army or a forest is perceived from a distance—even though the individual forms of elephants, horses, chariots, or trees are not perceived—there is nevertheless a perception of 'army' or 'forest'; likewise, although the forms of the threads and so on are not perceived from a distance, the cognition of a 'cloth' and so on occurs with respect to those very things. But since we do not admit a whole, threads and the like do not exist apart from atoms. How then can there be a cognition of a cloth and so on even with respect to them? If you say, "It is with respect to the atoms themselves," no, because atoms are beyond the reach of the senses. Indeed, even an illusion cannot arise from the senses regarding objects that are beyond the senses. Visual cognition does not occur with respect to tastes and the like. And just as it is not logical for sense-born cognition to be neither erroneous nor non-erroneous regarding atoms that are beyond the senses, the same applies to the qualities and so forth residing in them. Since there would be no parts, there would be no production of sound, pleasure, and so on, and thus there would be no perception of them either. This is exactly what he says: "There would be no perception of anything because the whole is not established. [Objection: "It is like the perception of hair by one suffering from ophthalmia (*taimirika*). If you think: "Just as for one whose vision is impaired by ophthalmia, hairs do not appear individually, but appear when aggregated, so too it is with atoms"; or "just as for one with unimpaired vision, hairs appear even individually, and therefore they are not entirely beyond the senses; likewise, atoms appear individually to a yogin, and therefore they too are not entirely beyond the senses. [Reply: If that were so, it follows that nothing at all is beyond the senses, since everything would be an object of the yogin’s senses. Consequently, all objects, like atoms, might at some time be perceived by the senses by people like us. But they are not so perceived. Therefore, because they are beyond the senses, atoms are not perceived by direct perception by people like us, just like the unseen [*adṛṣṭa*] and so on. However, hairs are not beyond the senses even for one whose vision is impaired by ophthalmia, because of the cognition "this is a mass of hair. But no one has a cognition such as "this is a mass of atoms. Moreover, if everywhere only an aggregate of atoms were seen, then, like the cognition of a "forest" in an aggregate of trees, there would be no cognition of the various distinctions of genus (*jāti-bheda*). If you argue that "because the members of the collection have different forms, there is a grasping of various genus-distinctions in their aggregates," then if the members of the collection—such as the cloth and the threads—are indeed different, it is proven that the cloth and the threads are distinct entities.

Now, if those very constituents that form the cloth are identical to the threads and other parts, how then is there the perception of a difference in genus (*jātibheda*)? For even in the case of a collection such as an army, there is no perception of a characteristic distinct from the [individual] soldiers and so forth. Even by those who loathe the notion of a "genus," a difference in exclusion (*vyāvṛttibheda*) is admitted in its place; yet that too would not exist if a composite whole (*avayavin*) were not admitted. For a collection of hairs does not appear as excluded from the individual hairs in the same way that a cloth appears as excluded from its threads. If it is argued that the difference in appearance follows from a difference in causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), we say no; for a difference in appearance is observed even when such causal efficiency is not perceived.

If it is argued that [the cognition of a forest arises] because of the observation of suitability (*yogyatā*), what indeed is this suitability other than a difference in genus (*jāti*)? If it is claimed that this suitability is that which has a non-different substratum, we say no; for then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the cognition of a cloth and so forth even with respect to its individual parts. If it is argued that this is because such [suitability] is not observed in those [parts], then that suitability must be beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), since it is not perceived even when its substratum is being perceived; and consequently, the cognition of a cloth and so forth would never occur at all. If it is argued that the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) of that [cloth] is accomplished by all its parts together, and therefore that suitability is perceived only when all [the parts] are perceived, we say no; for it is impossible to perceive all the parts. Therefore, it is logical that the application of a word based on a genus occurs precisely because of the existence of a whole (*avayavin*). Thus, when the genus "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is perceived, the designation "forest" (*vana*) applies to the collection of its substrata. Furthermore, the cognition "this is a forest, this is a forest" is justified through linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). For without the basis for that [genus], even a convention could not be established; and in the absence of such a convention, the cognition of a "forest" would likewise not exist.

Others, however, thinking that there is no cognition of non-difference (*abhinnapratyaya*) regarding distinct objects anywhere, claim that even the cognition of an "army" (*senā*) and the like has multiplicity (*bahutvasaṃkhyā*) as its object. Others say its object is existence (*sattā*). First of all, neither multiplicity nor existence appears in the cognition of an army and the like. If [non-difference] is postulated because otherwise the appearance of non-difference would be inexplicable, then let the object of the cognition of a "cloth" (*paṭa*) and the like be number and so forth. If it is argued that there is no sublation (*bādhaka*) even if its object is a whole (*avayavin*), how can it have that as its object when there is no proof (*sādhaka*)? If it is argued that the very difference from the appearance of the parts is the proof, no; for such a difference is possible even if its object were number and the like. Therefore, just as the cognition of a cloth and the like does not have number and the like as its object because of its coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with cognitions qualified by action and quality, so it is also with the cognition of an army and the like. And thus, the author of the Sūtras did not provide a rebuttal to the objection—"the mention of 'armies, forests,' etc., [in the definition of a word]"—by saying that the army and so on are not distinct from the soldiers because they are non-different or because they are different objects; rather, he said, "[it is not so] because atoms (*aṇu*) are beyond the senses. For one who says, "there is no usage of non-difference regarding distinct things," there would also be a contradiction with the Sūtra ending with "those [phonemes] ending in inflections are a word" (*te vibhaktyantāḥ padam*), for it is not stated there that even the parts—the phonemes—are a single word. And if the cognition of such things as "the flowering forest is being cut down" or "the great army is marching" is justified as having number and the like as its object because it is caused by the inherence (*samavāya*) of qualities and actions in a single object, then even a proponent of the category of universals (*jātipadārthavādin*) can certainly justify the coreferentiality in cases like "the white cow is walking" by relying on a specific proximity (*pratyāsatti*). Consequently, the statement "individuals, configurations, and universals are the meanings of words" (*vyaktyākṛtijātayas tu padārthāḥ*) would be without authority. Therefore, in the cognition of an army and the like, it is only the substratum of qualities and actions that appears; the appearance of non-difference therein is merely an error (*bhrānta*), arising from the non-apprehension of difference due to distance, like the appearance of "trees in the village. If it is argued that the cognition of a cloth and the like is also like this, no; for this has already been examined. Or rather, that which possesses color and other qualities and has a non-erroneous appearance of non-difference is precisely the whole. Nor is there error everywhere; for the appearance of non-difference is sublated by the apprehension of difference. Furthermore, it is not logical that the apprehension of difference is real when there is no apprehension of the non-different everywhere, since difference has as its substratum many non-different [parts]. If it is argued that there is an apprehension of non-difference in the atom, no; because it is beyond the senses. Moreover, these cognitions of cloths and the like do not have atoms as their objects, because of their coreferentiality with the cognition of "large," like the cognition of space and the like. Therefore, wherever the cognition of a cloth and the like occurs in something distinct from atoms, that is the whole. Others say that this [cognition] is actually a property of the atoms. Is that [property] endowed with color and the like, or devoid of it? If it is endowed with color and the like and is distinct from the atom, then there is no dispute, as there is no contradiction in an effect possessing the properties of its cause. But if it is devoid of color and the like, then there is a contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa*), since a cloth and the like are perceived by perception itself as being endowed with color and the like. Even in the Sāṃkhya position, since the non-difference of property and substrate is accepted, it is illogical for a property beyond the senses to be perceptible. For if it were perceptible, it would follow that the substrate, being non-different from it, would also be perceptible, or else there would be a reversal of identity (*tādātmya*).
The status of being a whole (avayavin) in the case of temples and similar objects.

If it is argued that the cognition "these two pots are conjoined" does not refer to many atoms or their property [of conjunction], but rather—like the cognition of a temple (*devakula*) and so forth—is merely a specific conjunction of bricks and the like, and that just as a temple or a wall is said to be a particular conjunction of bricks, yet there arises the cognition "the temple and the wall, possessing color and other qualities, are conjoined," so too it is with pots and the like—this is not correct. For even a temple and such are admitted to be composite wholes (*avayavin*). However, the opponent [Tamasāri] stated that the cognition of a temple and so forth has conjunction as its object according to the Sāṃkhya view; this was intended to show that, in every respect, no such example is tenable within the Buddhist position. Furthermore, it is impossible to explain a treatise without contradicting the views of all commentators, because in all scriptures there exists a diversity of commentators with conflicting intentions, and because they present one another's explanations as faulty. Therefore, one must strive specifically to avoid contradiction with valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, if a wall and the like were merely of the nature of conjunction, the aforementioned cognition would not be possible, and there would be no cognition of them as a single unit, because the conjunctions of the bricks and so forth are manifold.

But surely, since only things of the same class (*samānajātīya*) can initiate a substance (*dravya*), how is it that a temple or similar structure initiated by heterogeneous materials such as wood and bricks does not contradict valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding its status as a whole (*avayavin*)? No; for we observe that even heterogeneous things can initiate a body (*śarīra*). If they are somehow of the same class, let there also be a commonality of class for wood, bricks, and so forth, in the form of their being earthy (*pārthiva*) and so on—what here is contradictory? But if they are all equally earthy, why do threads, *vīraṇa* grass, and the like not initiate a cloth? And why is it that *vīraṇa* grass alone, though homogeneous, does not initiate a cloth? If you say it is due to a lack of capacity (*asāmarthya*), then one must simply admit the lack of capacity, not heterogeneity. However, threads and *vīraṇa* grass do possess the capacity to initiate a rope and the like. Therefore, wherever the capacity of homogeneous things to produce an effect has been determined through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), their initiation of that specific effect should be admitted. One should not maintain this dogmatic restriction: that only homogeneous things can be initiators.

[Objection: But in that case, there would be no contradiction even if all five elements were to initiate a single effect. [Reply: Let it be so, provided such an effect is perceived. We do not perceive any such effect at all; therefore, we do not grant this. [Objection: Is it not the case that the body is composed of the five [elements]? [Reply: No; its being "composed of the five" is a mere metaphorical designation based on its having the five as its causes, not because the five are inherent in it (*samavāyin*).
