For instance—since space is all-pervasive and intangible, it cannot be an initiator of a substance at all; if it were its inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*), the body would have to be all-pervasive and devoid of color and other qualities. Even if it were produced from air, it would possess only the quality of touch. Even if produced from fire, it would lack smell, taste, and weight. And if produced from water, it would lack smell. Furthermore, there would be the perception of contradictory colors and so forth, because a composite whole conforms to the color and other qualities of its parts. Therefore, the body is not produced from multiple elements. Moreover, through direct perception, only earthy particles are apprehended; and since moisture, heat, respiration, and so forth are apprehended only as inhering in what is conjoined with them (like in jars and the like), [the body is not made of the five].

Thus, even in the case of the commencement of a fish and so forth, the earth-elements possess the status of inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), while the others possess the status of instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). However, if an effect endowed with variegated color and other qualities is observed, then—as was stated previously—it is indeed accepted that the parts thereof, despite being causes of contradictory properties, originate a single effect. Therefore, in the case of the construction of temples and the like from wood, bricks, and so forth, one must accept—according to what is observed—that some possess the status of inherent cause, some possess the status of instrumental cause, or all possess the status of inherent cause. Thus, it is established that even a temple and such things possess the nature of a whole (*avayavin*).

"In that case, a whole (*avayavin*) characterized by a village and so forth must also be admitted," some say, "True. Others [say] that it is illogical for houses and such, which are not mutually conjoined, to be the originators (*ārambhaka*) of a village and so forth. For if they were originators through conjunction with what is already conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*), it would follow that even parts situated in other locations would be originators. Therefore, the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of "village" and so forth should be seen as applying only to aggregates (*samudāya*) of houses and the like. By this very [argument], the conventional usage of "assembly" (*pariṣad*) and so forth is also explained. It was already stated previously that even such a distinction in conventional usage is not possible regarding aggregates of atoms (*paramāṇu*). Therefore, the whole exists. As for what was said beginning with "by six," etc., for the purpose of refuting the atom—that too is illogical, because it is sublated by the very perception of its effect. Indeed, the existence of an effect is never perceived in the absence of a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). Furthermore, the existence of the whole has been established; it must necessarily have a material cause. That which is its fundamental material cause is the atom; its having parts (*sāvayavatva*) is untenable. For if it had parts, it could not be fundamental at all. If there were no fundamental material cause whatsoever, then everything would be non-existent due to the absence of a foundation. If one does not accept that the succession of parts has a limit, then, since there would be no difference in having infinite parts, there would be no difference in size or weight between a speck of dust and a mountain. Therefore, there is a limit to being smaller, smaller, and smallest; and since its momentariness is denied, its uncreatedness (*akṛtakatva*) is established. For nothing arises without a material cause, nor from a material cause of equal or greater dimension. The claim that "the atom has six parts" is illogical due to contradiction with one's own words, just like saying, "My mother is barren. For that than which nothing smaller exists is called an atom; how could it have six parts? Since its parts would themselves be smaller, it is only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*) that the possessor of parts is called an atom; the primary atom is indeed partless. "The [mass] would be only the size of an atom even if the six [atoms] occupied the same location"—this too is illogical. Because an increase in the dimension of the whole is observed over the dimensions of its parts, it is inferred that even that which is begun by atoms possesses a larger dimension. And since the effect has a larger dimension than the dimension of its [material] cause, how could the mass be only the size of an atom?
{The Refutation of the Atom Having Ten Parts}:

As for what was said—that there are ten parts by way of the division of directions—that too is incorrect; because it is only other substances that are divided by the directions when another thing serves as a limit, such as, for example, "the Himalaya stands to the north of Prayāga" and "the Vindhya to the south," and so forth.

But is it not observed that even that which serves as a limit (avadhi) possesses divisions—for instance, "this is its eastern part, this its western, this its southern, and this its northern"? No; for even in that case, the division of one part from another is established by taking yet other parts as the limits. Furthermore, the atom (*paramāṇu*) is partless; therefore, there can be no conceptualization of divisions such as east and so forth for it.

Now, if that atom is conceptualized as being "eastern," "southern," "western," or "northern" relative to other substances serving as its limits (*avadhi*), then there is no contradiction whatsoever; for we observe that even in a single, undivided entity, different designations arise due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).
{The Refutation of the Penetration by Space}

The argument that [the atom] is "due to being divided by space" (*ākāśavyatibhedāt*) is also not tenable, because it is impossible to divide that which is eternal and partless. If you argue that if there were no space within it, then space would follow as being non-omnipresent (*asarvagata*), we say no; this is due to a lack of understanding of the nature of omnipresence. For instance, a substance is called omnipresent when it has a connection with all corporeal things through its undivided self. This very nature belongs to space, as is inferred from the production of sound everywhere; therefore, space is indeed omnipresent. If you claim it is non-omnipresent because it lacks a connection with the interior of an atom, we say no; for such an interior is absolutely non-existent, like a hare's horn. Indeed, for a single partless entity, there can be no distinction between exterior and interior. Since it is conjoined with every corporeal thing that exists, how could it be non-omnipresent? Therefore, even this [argument] is merely a delusion of an unrefined intellect. Thus, because the composite whole (*avayavin*) and so forth do exist, the reason [adduced by the opponent], namely "due to the absence of the grasped and the grasper" (*grāhyagrāhakavaidhuryāt*), is unestablished (*asiddha*).
{The Refutation of the Simultaneous Apprehension of Cognition and its Object}

As for what was also said—that because of the necessity of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is no difference between the object and its cognition, just like the vision of two moons—this reason is first of all inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For instance, there is a necessity of simultaneous perception regarding the stars of Kṛttikā, yet there is no identity [between them], since their distinctness is established through universal consensus. And just as one who investigates perceives the stars of Kṛttikā with distinction, so too does one perceive cognition and the object. Furthermore, this reason is contradictory (*viruddha*), because the meaning of the word "simultaneous" (*saha*) is possible only when there is a difference; for there is no such thing as the meaning of "simultaneous" in the case of a single entity. If it is argued that the meaning of "simultaneous" exists in relation to error—that you might think that even though they are non-different, they are determined as different by error, and in relation to that, "simultaneous perception" is spoken of, just like the perception of two moons, whereas in reality there is the perception of only one—[we reply: No, because in that case a distinct form is appearing as something superimposed. Therefore, it is not logical to prove the identity of the real form by means of that superimposed form. Indeed, identity between the nature of a conch shell and a yellow form is impossible. For in that case, does the distinctness of form appear as something existing or as something non-existing? In either case, there is a contradiction with the proof of identity. How can there be identity between two things that are ultimately distinct in form? If the distinctness of form is not ultimate, how can there be identity with it in the ultimate sense? Identity is being proved only for those two things that are perceived as having distinct forms. If it is argued that this is because that distinctness of form has the nature of a void (*tuccha*), even so the reason remains inconclusive; for even if distinctness of form is a separate entity, it is perceived simultaneously with the form of consciousness. Or, if it were not a separate entity, then the form of consciousness—which would be identical with it—would also follow as being of the nature of a void. Furthermore, the meaning of the reason "because of perception by one [person] alone" is also untenable due to being unestablished (*asiddha*), since an object is perceived by many persons.

As for the one who says that the meaning of the argument "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambhaniyamāt*) is "because of the apprehension of only one," he too must be asked: Is it because of the apprehension of cognition alone, or because of the apprehension of the object alone? If it is because of the apprehension of cognition alone, then how can there be non-difference from an object that is not being apprehended? For that would entail non-difference even from the three worlds. If one attempts to prove its non-difference with itself, the reason is redundant, since there is no dispute in that regard. By this, the claim "because of the apprehension of the object alone" is also refuted. Furthermore, it is unestablished (*asiddha*), since both cognition and the object are apprehended. If it is argued that at the time of apprehending the object, cognition is not apprehended, or at the time of apprehending cognition, the object is not, and thus the apprehension of only one is established—even so, it would result in a contradiction of one's own tenets and an acceptance of the opponent's position.

Now, if there is only a single apprehension (*upalambha*) of both cognition and its object, then because of this single apprehension, no distinction between them can be established. In that case, does that [apprehension] grasp their difference or not? If it does not grasp their difference, then since they are non-different from it, how can one speak of "cognition and object"? If it does grasp their difference, then why is there no establishment of a distinction between them? If you say it is like the cognition of a double moon and so forth, we say no; for it has already been stated that in those cases, non-difference is untenable due to the superimposed form. Furthermore, by what means is the single apprehension of cognition and object established? Surely it was said: "For one whose apprehension is not itself perceived, the seeing of the object is not established. But what is this "establishment" (*prasiddhi*) of the seeing of the object—is it its production (*utpatti*), or its apprehension (*upalabdhi*)? And what is this "apprehension" such that, while the object is being perceived, the seeing of the object is not established—is it that very seeing of the object, or the cognition that produces it? If that very seeing of the object is the apprehension, and its non-perception implies that its production is impossible, that is incorrect. For when production occurs, it is logical that the seeing of the object becomes perceptible *afterwards*, not *prior* to it. Indeed, nowhere is this sequence observed where the production [of something] occurs after it has already been perceived. If, on the other hand, the apprehension is the cognition that produces the seeing of the object, and the seeing of the object does not arise when that [cognition] is imperceptible, that too is incorrect. Just as with the eyes and other sense organs, it is possible for something to be imperceptible yet still productive of an effect; furthermore, in the awakening from deep sleep caused by a sharp touch or similar stimulus, there is no awareness of a prior cognition. Moreover, even if the seeing of the object were produced by a perceptible apprehension, the rule of the "single apprehension" (*ekopalambhaniyama*) of object and cognition would still not be established. If, then, the "establishment" of the seeing of the object is its apprehension, the meaning of the sentence becomes: "For one whose apprehension is imperceptible, the apprehension of the object is not perceptible. But nothing is thereby proven. If "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) means simply the object—because it is seen—then the sentence-meaning would be: "For one whose apprehension is imperceptible, the object also is not perceptible. This is not correct, because the object is distinct from the apprehension. Nor is it logical that the imperceptibility of one thing entails the imperceptibility of another, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if the apprehension is imperceptible, the cognition "the object is seen" does not occur. This is actually our own position: "An ungrasped qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) cannot be the cause for the cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*). Yet, it is not the case that everywhere an object is grasped only as qualified by a visual perception. In the case of "the white cow is walking," the visual perception of the cow is not experienced here; rather, the cow itself is apprehended as qualified by qualities and actions.

Now, it was stated here: "The apprehension of an object does not occur through the existence of the object; rather, it occurs through the existence of its apprehension. What follows from this? Was it not stated that such [apprehension] is not established by means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇikī*) and therefore does not sustain linguistic conventions based on existence? What is the meaning of this statement? Does it mean that even for an unperceived existence, there is no capacity whatsoever to initiate mere linguistic convention, or that it lacks the capacity to initiate a linguistic convention qualified by itself? The first position is not tenable, because we observe the occurrence of linguistic conventions—such as the designation of "cognition" regarding color and so forth, or the use of terms like "eye"—based on the existence of the eyes and other faculties, even though that existence is not perceived. If it is asked how it is known that these linguistic conventions proceed from those [faculties] when they are unperceived, it is known simply from observing those conventions, just as one determines the nature of seeds and the like from observing sprouts, pain, and so forth. If it is argued that it is impossible for something whose existence is unperceived to initiate a linguistic convention qualified by itself, there is no dispute on this point. However, since we do not observe linguistic conventions qualified by [the apprehension] in all cases, it is not necessarily the case that the apprehension of the object must itself be apprehended. If it is argued that the object remains unestablished if that [apprehension] is unestablished, what is the reason for this? For the apprehension of that [object] does not establish its own object like a logical mark (*liṅga*), such that the object would remain unestablished if the apprehension were unestablished. Rather, by the mere fact of being produced in the form of having grasped that [object], it renders the object fit for linguistic convention. Even if that [apprehension] is unestablished, it is said that the object is indeed established. Furthermore, the apprehension of that apprehension is held to occur at a later time, either through perception or through inference. Nor does this lead to an undesirable consequence, because it is not accepted that every apprehension is itself felt (*saṃvedita*). That apprehension which is felt is said to be cognized by another cognition; it is not the case that an unperceived apprehension simply does not exist or does not perform its own function. This much, however, is reasonable: as long as something is not felt, it is impossible to employ the linguistic convention "it exists," just as in the case of fire and the like. And it is not the case that when fire and the like are unperceived, their effects, such as smoke, fail to arise or are not cognized. Thus, just as in the case of fire and so forth, since the effect characterized by the recollection of the object, its verbal designation, and the movement of the eyes can occur from an apprehension that is itself unperceived, one should not accept self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) merely to avoid contradicting that [fact].
If cognition is not self-cognized, then it follows that its nature is non-luminous; and being itself non-luminous by nature, like a jar or other such objects, how could it illuminate anything else?

What is this so-called "having a non-luminous nature"? Is it the state of not producing cognition (*bodha*), or is it the absence of radiance (*aprabhatva*), or rather, is it having the nature of non-cognition (*abodhasvabhāvatva*)? First of all, the state of not producing cognition is untenable, because the eyes and other sense organs produce cognition even though they are not self-cognized. If, on the other hand, it is the absence of radiance, then that absence of radiance is simply the state of being non-luminous due to its difference from light (*tejas*), and not due to its being self-cognized. If it were the case that it has the nature of non-cognition, that is not so; for even if it is not known, it does not abandon its own nature. Indeed, that which is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of something does not cease to be so merely because it is not self-cognized.

If it is asked, "In the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what else could be the nature of cognition?"—the answer is that the very state of being cognition (*bodhatva*) is the nature of cognition. If it is argued that this [state of being cognition] is itself self-awareness, we say no; for by a mere change in name, the fact that it illuminates its own self is not established. If it is asked, "How can this be the nature of cognition if it lacks the quality of cognizing its own self?"—it is like fire, which has the nature of burning even though it does not burn itself; or like a sickle and such tools, which have the nature of cutting even though they do not cut themselves, or like a lamp, which does not illuminate itself. {Furthermore, there is no rule of simultaneous perception even in the case of memory.}

[Objection: But surely, since there is a recollection of an object characterized by the very act of seeing—such as "I have seen"—how can it be said that there is no rule of the simultaneous apprehension (*ekopalambha-niyama*) of the experience and the object? [Response: This is not so, because we observe the recollection of the object alone. For instance, in such cases as "I served my mother and father," "I have five servants and ten cows," or "Devadatta is at home," it is the object itself that is remembered, not the experience.

[Objection: But surely experience itself is remembered here, since when questioned, he says, "Devadatta was seen by me alone. [Response: No, for that is possible otherwise as well. Even from the memory of the object alone, having inferred its having been seen, he speaks in that manner. If this were not admitted, then there would also be a rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) for the eye and so forth. To explain: when asked, "How was he known by you?", one would say, "He was seen by the eye alone. If it is argued that even so there is a rule of simultaneous perception, we say no, because it contradicts both common experience and our own treatises. For no one has the perception of the eye and so forth within a cognition that grasps objects such as blue; nor is the form of the eye and so forth admitted in our own treatises. Alternatively, there would be the undesirable consequence of a rule of simultaneous perception even for the association with verbal expression, because memory occurs only for that which is associated with it. Indeed, even a well-trained person cannot, through memory, present a pure object, nor can they describe it to others when questioned. Furthermore, if there were an experience associated with verbal expression, there would be a contradiction with [the definition] "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and so forth, and there would be the consequence of the doctrine of the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaitavāda*). Therefore, the rule of simultaneous perception is not established even on the basis of memory.
The Refutation of the Consequence that Cognition Would Be Externalized.

If it is argued that in the absence of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), cognition would result in being external like color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, and would lack its own nature like the cognition belonging to another mental continuum (*santānāntara*), then what exactly is this "externality"? If it means existing in a location outside one's own body, that is incorrect; for even color-form and the like are not external simply because they are not self-aware, but rather because they arise there by the power of their own causal complex (*sāmagrī*). As for cognition, pleasure, and so forth, the causal complex that produces them exists precisely within the interior of the body; therefore, they do not arise externally. By this, the definition of externality as "being perceived as situated outside" is refuted.

Nor is "externality" the state of being an entity distinct from the class of cognitions (*jñānavarga*), because it is impossible for something of that same nature [i.e., a cognition] to be distinct from its own class. However, it is indeed accepted that pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth are external insofar as they are entities distinct from the class of cognitions. Nevertheless, because they arise within the very location of the body due to the power of their own causal complex (*svasāmagrī*), they are not called "external. Alternatively, their non-externality consists in their inherence in the self (*ātmasamavāyitva*); and this inherence in the self is determined by their own causes, not by their being self-cognized (*svasaṃviditatva*). [Thus ends the refutation of the consequence that [pleasure] would not belong to the self.]

As for the argument that [knowledge] would follow as being non-appropriated (*anātmīya*), like the cognition belonging to another continuum (*santānāntara*), that too is untenable. For appropriation and non-appropriation do not depend on whether something is self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*) or not; rather, they depend on its connection with or lack of connection to one's own self (*ātman*). According to your view, however, since all cognitions are self-cognized, there would be no cognition whatsoever that is non-appropriated. If you argue that "whatever does not have a self-cognizer of its own is non-appropriated by it," then in that case, preceding and succeeding cognitions, as well as the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) acquired in other lives, would not be appropriated. This is because, even in your system, there exists no continuum (*santāna*) that persists through all cognitions and could serve as a self-cognizer such that everything belonging to it would be appropriated.

If it is argued that something is called "one's own" (*ātmīya*) by virtue of the relationship between beneficiary and benefactor even though it is not self-cognized (*asvasaṃvidita*), then, alas, one must not say that it is "not one's own" because it is not self-cognized, like the cognition belonging to another mental continuum (*santānāntara*).
[This concludes the refutation of the inference proving self-luminosity.]

As for what was further stated—that cognition illuminates itself because it is luminous, like a lamp—here too, what is the meaning of "illuminating itself"? If what is intended is simply self-cognizability (*svasaṃvedyatva*), then the example is devoid of the probandum (*sādhya*); for even in your own view, a lamp, which consists of its own nature, does not possess self-cognizability. Furthermore, since the lamp’s being of the nature of cognition is unestablished for both parties, it is not a valid example. If, on the other hand, "illuminating itself" is said to mean that it does not depend on another of the same class (*sajātīya*) with respect to its own self-awareness, then tactile sensation (*sparśa*) and so forth would also have to be considered self-illuminating. Nor is self-cognizability established merely by the fact that it does not require a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) of the same class for the production of self-awareness. The independence from a similar class is unestablished even for an illuminator, because its parts and the whole (*avayavin*) act as mutual cooperators, and because [the lamp] depends on the eye and visible form (*rūpa*). Why is this so? Because that which is being illuminated is illuminated by something other than itself, just like a jar and the like.

As for what was further stated here—"The jar is not illuminated by the lamp, but rather there is the arising of something already existing in that manner"—this is not so, because momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) will be refuted later. Even if there were such an arising, since it arises from something else in that manner, the jar's nature as non-luminous is established prior to its arising; and by that same example, [the same applies] to the lamp and to cognition. So how can it be said that "cognition which is not cognized does not exist"? Now, one might argue: "Just as a jar requires a lamp as its illuminator even though the eye and its own color-form (*rūpa*) are present, so too should the lamp [require another]. Or, "If the lamp does not require [another], then the jar should likewise not require one. In this way, [the jar] would not require any other illuminator apart from the eye and so forth. "If you say: 'For the jar, both the lamp and the eye are illuminators, but for the lamp, only the eye is,' then in that case,"
One [cause] may be the illuminator for something else, and two [causes] alone for another;
since it depends on what is possible, let there not even be one for another—what loss is there?
For one who is absolutely incapable, there are two [cases]; for another, one; and for yet another, not even one. This is simply the nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*). What loss is there in this?
Now, if it is argued that there is a contradiction in an action directed toward itself (*svātmani kriyā-virodha*), that is incorrect; as he says:
"When that [action] is its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then how can there be any contradiction?"
"For if there were contradiction by way of its own nature, everything would simply perish.

As for the argument that "one thing [is the cause] for something," and so forth—that is incorrect. Even if in some cases one thing is capable of acting as a cooperative cause and in other cases many things are, nevertheless, an accidental (ākasmikī) action is not logical. For instance:
"There is either eternal existence or non-existence, because of the lack of dependence on anything else in the absence of a cause."
For it is because of dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible.

Furthermore, it is never observed that things such as trees or stones—which lack all auxiliary causes (*sahakārī*)—possess the capacity for actions such as moving their own bodies; yet, the variation in the number of auxiliary causes is accepted because it is observed through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). The claim that "when there is its own nature (*svarūpa*), then there is [the action] for it," and so forth, is also incorrect, because its very nature is unestablished (*asiddha*). Indeed, when both the example and the reason (*hetu*) are untenable, self-cognizing nature (*svātma-saṃvedakatva*) cannot be established. Moreover, what is the meaning of the phrase "because of being illuminating" (*prakāśakatvāt*)? Does it mean (1) because of having a luminous form (*bhāsvara-rūpatva*), or (2) because of being an auxiliary cause for the object of cognition (*vedya-sahakāritva*), or (3) because of having the nature of consciousness (*bodha-svabhāvatva*)? Having a luminous form is unestablished for consciousness. Being an auxiliary cause for the object of cognition is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the eyes and other sense organs. Furthermore, having the nature of consciousness is simply a unique property (*asādhāraṇa*) [of the subject].

Furthermore, it is not logical for a reason to be indicative of an object that has not been determined; for the Buddhists themselves have rejected that something identical merely by virtue of verbal similarity can establish an inference. [This concludes the presentation of the proof for the fact that cognition is cognizable by another cognition.]

If it is asked, "What is the proof for cognition being cognizable by another cognition?", it is precisely what the venerable teachers have stated: "Cognition is cognizable by a cognition distinct from itself, because it is an object of cognition, like color and so forth. To this it has been replied that [if this were true], there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [cognition] being external and non-conscious; for it will be stated later that a [reason] contradicted by a specific [property of the subject] (*viśeṣaviruddha*) is not a valid refutation. In order to avoid the charge of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*), one must either admit that the Supreme Lord possesses two types of cognition, or else that his omniscience exists only insofar as it is distinct from those [two], or else the qualification "while being non-eternal" (*anityatve sati*) must be added [to the reason]. Thus, since self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is unestablished, the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) is also unestablished; therefore, the identity of cognition and its object is not proven.
Consequently, this [position] is also untenable:
"This nature of that [consciousness] consists of blue and so forth, and it is an experience;
thus, while being an experience of its own nature, it is known as the experience of blue and so forth."

Furthermore, regarding this rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), is it established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) or is it devoid of them? It cannot first be the case that something lacking positive and negative concomitance is a means of proof, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, how can the establishment of positive and negative concomitance be perceived in the non-apprehension of difference? For no one is able to perceive positive and negative concomitance within their own self alone. Nor is it logical to establish negative concomitance and so forth based on a deluded perception of difference, as that too would lead to an over-extension. Furthermore, if there were absolutely no perception of difference, even the distinction between delusion and non-delusion would not be possible; otherwise, every doctrine would be established by mere words alone.

Now, if it is argued that only the difference between cognition and its object is not perceived, but not even the difference between two cognitions, that is incorrect. For it has already been stated in the discussion on the analysis of the variegated (*citravicāra*) that, according to the position of self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), the difference between two cognitions cannot be apprehended either. Furthermore, the difference between two cognitions is not grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*), because [each cognition] consists merely in the awareness of itself. Indeed, when another is not perceived, it is not logical to perceive a difference between self and other. And if one were to admit the perception of another, there would be the consequence of contradicting such statements as "there is nothing else to be experienced. Moreover, the argument of "simultaneous apprehension" (*sahopalambha*) would become inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Nor is it logical for one cognition to grasp another cognition without assuming its form; for otherwise, it would follow that even blue and so forth could be grasped by a cognition that does not possess their form. If [the second cognition] did possess that form, it would be identical to the first; how then could the difference between the two cognitions—the grasped and the grasper—be established? If it were established, it would likewise apply to the object and the cognition. Therefore, the difference between two cognitions is not grasped by perception, nor by inference (*anumāna*), since the latter is preceded by the former. Indeed, inference does not establish itself unless the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is grasped by perception in every respect. Thus, for those who maintain the non-difference of the grasped and the grasper, there is no apprehension of another cognition within one's own continuum (*svasantāna*); how then can another continuum (*santānāntara*) be established? Consequently, even talk of another world, Buddhas, and so forth, is cast far away; thus, the entire Buddhist scripture (*śāstra*) is inconsistent. For if difference and so forth are not established, the conventional practice of proof, refutation, and so on, is untenable.
The Refutation of the Distinction Between the Perceptible Object and the Object of Determination.

Now, it might be thought: "The non-difference of the apprehender (*grāhaka*) is admitted only with respect to the apprehended (*grāhya*), but not with respect to the determined object (*adhyavaseya*). But then, what is the difference between the apprehended and the determined? It is said: that form which actually appears in the cognition is the apprehended; whereas that which is superimposed is the determined. Alternatively, that which appears in the cognition is the apprehended, while that regarding which there is the conceit of being grasped even though it does not appear [in the cognition] is the determined. It is precisely from this determination (*adhyavasāya*) that purposeful action (*pravṛtti*) arises. As it has been said: "One acts toward an object by means of one's own appearance [in the cognition] through the determination of the object; even though it is an error, it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because, through its connection with the object, it is non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*) with respect to it. That too is incorrect. For just as the validity of the determination of an external [object] is untenable—since no connection can be grasped between the determination of an external object and an external object that is absolutely unperceived, and thus non-deviance is unestablished—so it is also for the determination of the distinction between cognitions belonging to one's own and another's continuum. If validity is established merely by non-contradiction with worldly convention (*lokavyavahārāvisaṃvāda*), then let the determination of an external object also be the establisher of that object merely by non-contradiction with worldly convention, since they share the same logical status (*samānayogakṣematva*).

Now, if one’s own cognition and the cognition belonging to another continuum (*santānāntara*) are both perceived by that very self, then it is logical that even a subsequent erroneous determination (*adhyavasāya*) arising from them possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). But as for an external object, since it has not been seen by anyone, how can it be possible to establish that a determination of it arises from it and possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge? No; for by that determination, its non-existence is not understood. Just as by a determination of an external object—which grasps only itself—one cannot ascertain whether the external object is self-cognizable or uncognizable, so too it is with the determination of another cognition; for there is no difference whatsoever in this regard. If it is argued: "But memory is indeed a determination; thus, even recollection, which establishes another cognition, does not arise from that other cognition. Since it grasps its own nature through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), why does it not establish the other cognition? [We reply: Then the same consequence applies: since [memory] grasps its own nature as having arisen from an external object, why does it not establish the external object? Furthermore, self-awareness itself does not know this distinction—that "I have arisen from another cognition and not from an external object. Thus, because the establishment of an external object is of equal security (*yogakṣema*) to the establishment of another cognition, there is neither the impossibility of an external object nor the proof of a difference between these two. Consequently, since the reason such as "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*) is the root for understanding the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) [of a valid reason], and since the perception of difference destroys that very root, how could the non-existence of the external object be established from it? By this, the argument beginning with "the cognition's having the form of blue, etc. is also refuted.
For instance:
If one cognition were to appear as another cognition, what would be the means of knowing their distinction?
If it does not have the nature of another cognition, how could it be the apprehender of that [other] cognition? (1)

Just as connection and correspondence are difficult to establish regarding external objects, so too are they [difficult] regarding another cognition for one who maintains that self-awareness is the ultimate reality. (2)
If the diversity of cognitions is established through agreement with worldly consensus, then it follows that the external object is likewise fully established for that very same reason. // 3 //
Just as the establishment of an external object is not perceived even through subtle scrutiny, so too it is with another cognition; thus, the distinction between them is difficult to maintain.
Just as the intellect does not perceive its own difference from external objects that have not been grasped,
so too it does not perceive [its difference] from another intellect, because there is no distinction in their being equally beyond the senses.

If it is argued that the distinction between cognitions is established because a form dissimilar to [the object] cannot otherwise be explained, then why is that same distinction not also established for external objects? (6)
These are the summary verses.
[The fault in refuting the distinction between the grasped and the grasper.]

Thus, by one who rejects the distinction between the apprehended object (*grāhya*) and the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*), non-duality (*advaita*) itself must be accepted. For if that were not accepted, even such statements as "the forms of the cognized and the cognizer [appear] just as they do to the deluded" would be untenable; this is because it has been shown that the apprehension of an external object is of the same logical status (*samānayogakṣema*) as the apprehension of another cognition. Even if non-duality is accepted, the contradiction remains unavoidable—this is what has been called "the logic of the eyeball coming out when a pea is inserted," which has befallen the Buddhists. Therefore, to resolve the contradiction in this way, one must accept that the external object is cognized by a cognition that does not possess its form. Furthermore, that external object is generally perceived with the very form in which it is established; however, in some cases it appears even with a superimposed form due to the influence of cataracts and the like, and thus the distinction between error and non-error is also logical. But this is not the case when there is the awareness of a cognition devoid of all other conditions (*upādhi*).
Refutation of the Inference of Objectlessness (Nirālambanatva)

But another says: "All cognitions that have become the subject of dispute are without an objective basis (*nirālambana*), because they are cognitions, like cognitions in dreams and the like. And just as in the state of dreaming, even though external objects do not exist, there occurs a determination of external objects based solely on the cognition of the form of knowledge alone, and there is a distinction between error and non-error; so too in the waking state, the appearance of difference should be regarded in exactly the same way. Thus, it is only the lack of an objective basis that is being proven, and not the appearance of difference itself denied. Therefore, there is no contradiction with the perception of difference in the inference. Furthermore, even if the appearance of difference is erroneous, since it possesses the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to the non-contradiction of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), there is no failure to establish the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and other logical requirements.

First of all, this reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive due to doubt (*saṃdigdhānaikāntika*), because the contradiction between being a condition (*pratyayatva*) and having an object (*sālambanatva*) is not established. Nor is the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) established merely by the fact that the object of certain conditions is not seen to exist in the way it is determined; for even in your own system, such a thing is not admitted. As it has been said: "Non-deviation in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is not established by mere non-perception, because deviation is possible—just as in the case of rice cooking in a pot."
When the negative concomitance (vyatireka) is demonstrated merely by the non-perception [of the probans] in that [subject],
it is illustrated as "the remainder-like" (śeṣavat), because that [non-perception] is a cause for doubt.

Now, it might be argued that it is not logical for one thing to be the object (*ālambana*) of another. What contradiction is there in this? If you say, "It would follow that everything is an object, because there is no distinction in their being 'other'," we say no; for even given otherness, a restriction is possible just as it is with causes—for smoke does not have its own self as its cause, nor does it have everything else as its cause, despite the lack of distinction in their otherness. Furthermore, even when cognition arises, how could an object that was previously unmanifest become manifest? If you argue, "When that which is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) arises, that very cognition is the manifestation of the object, because its characteristic is light," we say no; for if non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) were established, the object would be manifest precisely through its connection with the manifestation of its own cognition, like a lamp and a jar. Moreover, cognition is not something perceivable by multiple knowers, whereas the external object is the opposite of that. To illustrate: having heard, "The dancer will dance," many people, eager to see her, proceed and perceive her without distinction [among themselves]. If you claim this is also the case in dreams, we say no; for in that case, subsequent corroboration (*uttarottara-saṃvāda*) is impossible. For one who asserts that "all cognitions are without objects" (*nirālambana*), there is a contradiction in the presentation of his own statement. To explain: this statement is presented by you as a means of proof (*sādhana*) for the purpose of informing another; yet you yourself do not possess that awareness of the other. If you do possess that awareness, then since the awareness of the other is itself an object, your argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to that very instance. Furthermore, if the other person has no comprehension, how can the "cognition-ness" (*pratyayatva*) of all cognitions be grasped? A property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) that is not grasped cannot be a prover. Likewise, if the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is not established, there is no proving power; if it is established, then the argument is inconclusive. Similarly, if inference (*anumāna*) also has all cognitions as its object, then that very inference possesses an object; if it does not, then how can the objectlessness of all cognitions be established? If you argue, "This is not a fault, because we accept that all inference is authoritative precisely when it is objectless," we say that is incorrect; for it is illogical for that which is objectless to be an authority. Indeed, the status of cognition as an authority and its objectlessness are not merely conventional terms. Rather, that by which an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is determined is an authority, while that in which nothing appears is called objectless. How then is there no contradiction between these two?

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because even that which has its own self (*svātman*) as its object is said to have another object (*arthāntara*) as its objective support, we say no. Is its status as an inference (*anumānatva*) now established only with respect to its own self? Furthermore, the fact that other objects have an objective support is not established by means of that which has only its own self as its domain, because [those other objects] are not its domain. For that which is not the domain of something cannot be established by it; if it were so established, then that very thing would become its domain, since the definition of a domain is that which is the character of the probandum (*sādhyalakṣaṇa*), like the nature of the self itself. If it is argued that even though it is not the domain [of the cognition], it is established through non-contradiction (*avisaṃvāda*), like a gem, we say no. This is because it is not established that the cognition of the gem, though non-contradictory, has the radiance (*prabhā*) as its domain; or, if it were established, then that itself would be a contradiction—how then could it be non-contradictory? We shall explain later that it is only the subsequent cognition of the gem that is the valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, it was already shown previously that the establishment of external objects through other cognitions shares the same logical status (*samānayogakṣema*). And by that, just as other cognitions are established, the non-conscious nature (*abodhātmakatva*) of blue and other such things is also established. It is improper to conclude that all cognitions of external objects are invalid simply because some cognition of an external object is seen to be a pseudo-means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*); for this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all inferences are pseudo-means of knowledge, using the example of the inference regarding the dream state. What is untenable here? Nothing other than the inference of the absence of an objective support (*nirālambana-anumāna*) itself. If it is asked, "If the inference of the absence of an objective support is also not a valid means of knowledge, how can your purpose be accomplished? we say no, for nothing is accomplished except for the intended purpose [of refuting the opponent]. This might be the case: just as sometimes a cognition of mother-of-pearl (*śuktikā*) sublates a cognition of silver, yet even if that sublater is itself sublated by another cognition, the reality of the cognition of silver in dreams, magical illusions, and the like is not thereby established; similarly, even if the inference of the absence of an objective support is non-existent, it is not logical that the cognition possessing an objective support—which is sublated by it—should be real. What is intended to be said by this? If you mean that the unreality of other cognitions, which are never perceived through either a valid means of knowledge or a pseudo-means of knowledge, is established without a means of knowledge, that is incorrect, because the establishment of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) is impossible without a means of knowledge.

The establishment of the existence of external objects would also follow from that very same principle, because only that which serves as the cause for establishing them is non-erroneous valid cognition (*abhrāntapramāṇa*). Indeed, when there is no error regarding a valid cognition, it does not have "two horns" [i.e., it is not bifurcated]; rather, that alone by which an object is established in its true nature is the non-erroneous valid cognition, just like self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) in your own system. Furthermore, the unreality of the cognition of silver is not established by the erroneous cognition of mother-of-pearl; rather, the unreality of both the cognition of silver and the cognition of mother-of-pearl is established precisely by a subsequent non-erroneous cognition.

Alternatively, if the erroneous nature of the cognition of mother-of-pearl (*śuktikājñāna*) consists simply in its having mother-of-pearl as its object, then its erroneous nature would consist in its having as its object silver qualified by falsity; for in that case, it would be non-discrepant [with respect to that object], and if that which is non-discrepant were erroneous, then even self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) would be erroneous. Consequently, the erroneous nature of cognitions would have to be stated merely as a technical convention (*pāribhāṣika*). Or, if by the example of the cognition of silver and so forth, you intend to prove the total lack of stability (*avyavasthā*) regarding all means and objects of knowledge, then you would be entering the system of Bṛhaspati (*suraguru*). And in that case, the investigation of the next world and so forth, as well as the investigation of the means of knowledge that serve as its basis, would be entirely untenable.

But surely, it is impossible to establish other cognitions that are not established through [your own] perception; for you, who are solely committed to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), do not perceive any other cognition. Furthermore, no one prevents you from establishing that the self, which is known through self-awareness, is without an object (*nirālambana*) or is erroneous; however, the word "all" [in your reason] is meaningless, or else, if other cognitions are understood, the reason is stated to be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or even contradictory (*viruddha*). For instance: all cognitions have an object (*sālambana*), because they are cognitions, like a cognition that has another cognition as its object. If you say the example is unestablished regarding the subject (*dharmyasiddha*), then are dreams and so forth, as well as the cognitions of other persons, not perceived at all now? And if they are not perceived, how can there be linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) with them? Who says they are "not perceived"? Rather, we say they do not become objects (*ālambana*). To say "they are perceived but do not become objects" is a fine statement indeed! For an object is not something other than what is being perceived, otherwise it would follow that even self-awareness is without an object. If you argue: "That thing which appears in its own form within a given experience is its object, not merely that which is perceived; otherwise, it would follow that even a remembered thing would be an object," we say no. This is because the object possesses many characteristics, such as being contrary to or not contrary to [the cognition], or being doubtful, and so on. For "the knowable," "the object," "the referent," and "that which appears in the cognition" are synonyms. Since that which appears in a non-contradictory cognition appears precisely in its own form, why would other cognitions not become objects?

Now, an objection might be raised: "Since other conditions (pratyaya) are cognized only in their general form, how can there be a cognition of their specific nature (*svarūpa*)? For they possess no common nature, and that which is their unique nature does not manifest at all because it is beyond perception (*parokṣa*); therefore, it cannot be the objective support (*ālambana*). This is incorrect; for we shall explain later that even a common form is real, and that its inference is likewise valid.

If it is argued that the very form which appears—being unassociated with other conditions and unreal—is what is proven to be without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*), then this [argument] would be as futile as an inference proving the sharpness of a rabbit’s horn. For it is impossible to establish even an indirect connection with other conditions that are absolutely unperceived, ultimately non-existent like a rabbit’s horn. Furthermore, the example of the jewel is not apt here; because the nature of the jewel is indeed ultimately real and is perceived by that very cognizer after the initial activity, whereas such is not the case for the nature of other conditions. Or, if their nature were indeed perceived, how could that perception not possess an objective basis?
The distinction between dream-cognition and waking-cognition.

As for what was said—that since the distinction between cognitions such as those of waking and dreaming is established through worldly consensus (*lokapratīti*) alone, the practical application of proofs proceeds on that basis, and subsequently, if one who reflects upon them perceives some cause for differentiation therein and thereby establishes non-difference, then even if that were so, what fault would there be for the opponent? For if this were considered a fault, then a fault would also arise in establishing the authority of the Veda. To explain: as long as the Veda is not apprehended as distinct from unauthoritative worldly statements, the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) is not established; and as long as that is not established, its authority is likewise not established, rendering the inference fruitless. Nor is a specific distinction established by the particularity of accents, phonemes, and sequence, because other things as well can possess such mutual differentiation.

Now, there is this argument: "When it is being investigated whether this Veda is authoritative or not, if it turns out to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then it is indeed the Veda; otherwise, we shall discard it as useless. This is the same here as well. When one considers whether the cognition [of the dream] is distinct from its established reality in the dream, or not—if, upon further investigation, the dream-cognition or whatever else is found to be mutually distinct, then we shall grasp that distinction. But if there is no cause for distinction whatsoever, then we shall understand their non-difference. Therefore, what contradiction is there here? Is this merely the prattle of a blind man who speaks of the authority of the Veda? Indeed, people see the world and they know the cognitions thereof; therefore, it is proper to examine the specific qualities, such as validity, of the subject known as the "Veda," which is generally established in the world. You, however, perceive nothing at all apart from your own self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And if the thesis and other members of the syllogism are grasped by a fallacious means of knowledge (*pramāṇābhāsa*), how can a reason whose parts are false be a valid means of knowledge?
The Refutation of the Concentration of the Mine of Wisdom (Prajñākara)

But surely this very objection was raised and refuted by Prajñākaragupta himself in the *Alaṅkāra*. As he said: "If it is argued that the cognition apprehending difference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), let it be so; what is the fault? If it is argued that the distinction between the thesis (*pakṣa*) and other members of the argument would not exist, let it not exist now; what is ruined for us? If it is argued that this very fact—that the proof of non-difference is not a valid means of knowledge—is the fault, then in that case, the cognition of the subject (*dharmin*) which is common to both valid and invalid means of knowledge according to the definition of the Veda would itself be invalid, because it is subsequently sublated by the proof of its validity. Therefore, since the proof of the subject is not a valid means of knowledge, the proof of validity by way of that [subject] would also be invalid; thus, the establishment of the validity of the Veda would not occur. Consequently, the entire practical discourse (*vyavahāra*) concerning the relationship between the probandum and the probans would collapse."

Now, [the opponent might argue]: "Even when there is the apprehension of a common locus (*dharmin*), that which apprehends it is not invalid, because its additional validity is established in that very instance. That too is incorrect, because:

"For when the nature of that very locus (*dharmin*) is its status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*), how can there be valid cognition even when it is apprehended while excluding that [status]? (695)

For the Vedic word is indeed the very nature of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If its opposite is apprehended by another [cognition] and that opposite is subsequently uprooted, how could it not become invalid?

[Objection: A refutation of the distinction between property and property-bearer. Now, if it is argued that this criticism does not apply because one accepts distinct properties (*dharma*), we say no; for it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To explain:

If a property were distinct [from its possessor], there would have to be a further connection with it; and if there were a connection with that [connection] as well, there would be an infinite regress of properties—a total collapse of the system. (696)
If that state of being endowed [with validity] is accepted as the very nature of those two [cognition and its object], then validity is likewise established for us; what contradiction is there? (697)
Even when superimposition has been apprehended through differentiation, is the cognition of non-difference—which arises from its subsequent reflective consideration—not valid in reality? (698)

Nor should it be suspected that for one who perceives no difference [between himself and others], the formulation of a proof cannot proceed through the division of the thesis and so forth; for this is merely a restatement made with regard to the cognition of another, while for oneself there is the application of the proof through the practice of what was previously unknown—thus it is faultless. "It was thus for me as well"—in this way the other person is persuaded.

Thus we see that this person, his vital organs pierced by the thorn of envy, cries out in distress. For instance: if we were to establish that the two characteristics of Dharma—general and particular—are distinct from the Veda, then there would be no room at all for your view.

Even if [the two types of reasons] were based on the exclusion of what is not that (*atadvyāvṛtti*), nevertheless, when the subject (*dharmin*) has been perceived and ascertained as having a similar nature, it is logical that inference proceeds for the purpose of excluding the superimposition (*samāropa*) resulting from the non-perception of other properties (*dharmāntara*). But when the very subjects—characterized as other cognitions—are never within the range of perception, then upon what basis would inference proceed? For even one well-trained in the arts is unable to execute a painting in the sky. If, however, the subjects characterized as other cognitions were perceived in their own form (*svarūpa*), then inference could indeed be conceived as proceeding for the purpose of excluding the superimposition of the non-perception of objectlessness (*nirālambanatva*), by means of an ascertainment of "being a cognition" (*pratyayatva*) arising from the force of that perception. But this is not the case with subjects that are unseen, like *piśācas*.

Furthermore, it has already been stated that for you there is no perception of another cognition apart from self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). As for the argument beginning with "even when [the object] is apprehended as distinct," this is a statement made by one who has forgotten the context; for what is currently undertaken is the proof that all cognitions are without an external object (*nirālambanatva*), not the proof of non-duality (*advaita*). Now, if it is intended that "non-distinction" means simply the lack of differentiation among all cognitions by virtue of their being without an external object, rather than non-duality, even so, if another cognition is not apprehended, inference cannot proceed; but if it is apprehended, the reason (*hetu*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This has already been stated.

Now, if it is argued that by this sequence the exclusion of the superimposition of difference is established for self-cognition itself, no, because this has already been examined previously. Furthermore, is the difference excluded by the very same [cognition] by which it was superimposed, or by another cognition? It is not logical that it is by the same, because there is a contradiction in the identity of the form that performs the superimposition and the form that performs the exclusion.
"If it is by another cognition, there is no distinction from another cognition;
who else but the Venerable One would be able to speak such words?"

If this [cognition] depends upon another cognition, it is a mere restatement; furthermore, the claim that it arises "by its own prior practice" and so forth is indeed untenable, as it contradicts non-duality. Nor is it logical to state that a previously unapprehended cognition and a prior practice can serve as causes. If it is argued that it is perceived without an objective basis (*anālambana*), like the perception of hair-tufts and the like, we say no; for the cognition of hair-tufts and such is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, by one who accepts the two verses beginning with "The forms of the object and the subject are unknowable," as authoritative proof, the Buddhist must necessarily accept non-duality (*advaita*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction. Alas, this monk has fallen into an insurmountable calamity, thinking that the establishment of external objects will occur through a cognition that lacks an objective basis, just as in the case of other cognitions.

Furthermore, if by "objectlessness" you intend the state of having one's own self as its object, then the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), because it is not established that even cognitions such as those in dreams have their own selves as objects; for it has already been stated that there is no proof for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), and it has been proven that cognition is of something other [than itself].

Now, if what is intended is that there is no object (*ālambana*) whatsoever, then, like a jar or other objects, consciousness itself would be unestablished; consequently, this would contradict your own experience, and the entire world would cease to exist. If, on the other hand, what is intended is specifically an external object, that is incorrect; for you have established the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*), and you have demonstrated that even memory has as its object that which is to be remembered. If you argue that [consciousness] has as its object an object appearing [in the mind], just like dream-cognition and the like, then in that case, even though the cognition is illuminated by consciousness, the cognition would not have that [external object] as its object. And thus, just like external objects, consciousness itself would be unestablished; the result is total blindness for the entire world, for if nothing is established in reality for anyone, even the occurrence of error cannot be established, as that would lead to a mere matter of terminology. Now, if you argue that because objects such as hair and so forth—which are perceived as external—are found not to be reached when one tries to grasp them, their non-existence is established; and since the appearance of those [non-existent things] is proven to be without an object, by observing that they share a common form, the lack of an object is established for all cognitions; and furthermore, there is no sublation whatsoever of the view that [cognitions] have themselves as their objects—that too is incorrect. For the observation of a common form is unestablished; indeed, a common form is established only when an object is reached in every instance. But when an object is reached in some cases, how can there be a common form [with those that are not]? If you say there is no reaching of an object anywhere, then how is that [reaching] negated? For it is impossible to negate an object that is absolutely unseen, such as a *piśāca* or similar beings. If you say that its difference from knowledge is being negated, but not the object itself because it is of the nature of knowledge—that too is problematic: how can a difference that is absolutely unseen be negated? If it is seen, then it cannot be absolutely non-existent. If you ask how the negation of a donkey’s horn or *pradhāna* is possible, we say: no; for even there, it is only the emergence of something belonging to the class of "horns" (which is seen) upon the head of a donkey that is negated. Likewise, the fact that pleasure, pain, and delusion are the material cause of the world is negated; or rather, the fact that the inferred material cause of the world—according to the logic of atoms—is composed of pleasure and so forth, and is unitary, is negated. Thus, in other cases as well, it should be understood that what is negated is only something already seen, with respect to its place, time, capacity, and so on. Furthermore, it has been stated that in the position of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), the perception of difference does not exist anywhere.
The refutation of the denial of difference by means of direct perception.

Furthermore, the negation of difference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because its object has already been discarded by perception. For instance, cognition is experienced as having an inward-turned form, instability, and so forth, whereas objects such as "blue" are experienced as being external, stable, and so forth. Moreover, this contradicts the common practice of all living beings; for no one would ever engage in activity for the sake of attaining the desired or avoiding the undesired if they understood that there is only cognition which perishes in a moment. If it is argued that all this is like a dream and the like, we say no; for even those who maintain [the dream-like nature of things] are seen to engage in activity and so forth once a sublation (*bādhaka*) has arisen.

But surely, if the object were distinct from cognition, how could any particular object be seen by that [cognition]? If it is because of a connection with seeing, and if that connection is also a distinct entity, then one would have to postulate yet another connection for that [first] connection, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If, on the other hand, it is not a distinct entity, then how can the object, which is distinct from cognition, be established through perception? Therefore, it is logical that the object is perceived only when it has entered into the interior of consciousness, and not while remaining untouched by it. As it has been said:
Therefore, the externality of an object is not established by means of cognition;
for if it were to exist outside of cognition, that very [externality] could not be established.
If blue is perceived, how can it be called external?
If blue is not perceived, how can it be called external?
"By another [cognition] it is perceived; thus is its non-abiding nature.
And if it were perceived by another, how could this be determined by itself?

This too is untenable—for it has already been established that every object of cognition is cognizable by another cognition. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct entities.
{Avoiding the Fallacy of Infinite Regress}

Furthermore, there is no infinite regress, just as in the case of certainty (*niścaya*). In your own system, for instance, certainty is conceptual in nature; and while it does not ascertain itself, it ascertains another object, yet this does not entail an infinite regress of certainties. Likewise, it is not defective that one thing—whether already known or unknown—establishes the status of another object to be known. Moreover, you yourself have accepted that certainty establishes other objects. For it has been said: "When there is the cognition of [illusory] hair, following the recollection of a previous experience and immediately after such an appearance, there was an attainment. That conceptualization arises with the delineation of grasped and grasper; even that, though devoid of the forms of grasped and grasper in its own nature, is established as such by another. It is not that it is not established by itself. If it is argued that because conceptualization is of the nature of memory, it is entirely without an objective basis (*anālambana*), we reply: let it be so. Nevertheless, its capacity to establish other objects by way of having the nature of the grasped, the grasper, momentariness, and so forth, is indeed accepted. Similarly, let its capacity to establish external objects such as permanence be without an objective basis; we have no objection to this. It might be argued: since conceptualization is of the nature of memory, its validity (*prāmāṇya*) is possible only through its being an establisher of an object exactly as it was experienced. It is logical that validity belongs only to a conceptualization that establishes the properties of a cognition known to itself, and not to one that establishes the properties of an experienced external object.

How is this to be understood? Is it not the case that the nature of the self—such as its momentariness—is not perceived while being experienced by non-conceptual cognition itself? Yet, since certainty (*niścaya*) exists even regarding external objects, how can it be said that [the nature of the self] is unexperienced? Furthermore, in your own system, validity is not accepted for a cognition that apprehends what has already been apprehended, because of the statement that "it is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) since it apprehends an aspect already seen," and because of the qualification "the illumination of an object not previously known.
[Therefore,] even dream-objects are not non-existent.

Furthermore, how is it determined that even in cognitions such as dreams, objects appearing as distinct [from consciousness] are non-existent? If you say it is because of their non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) or the non-perception of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), that is incorrect. For if an object were ever perceived to be pervaded by non-contradiction or by causal efficiency, then the absence of that [pervader] would establish the absence of the object—just as the absence of smoke is established from the absence of fire. But when there is a denial of external objects, no relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) has been established for them with anything else; so how could there be a negative pervasion (*viparyayavyāpti*)? It might be thought: "The absence of objects in dream-cognitions and the like is established for all the world, so we do not need to prove it. No; for worldly consensus (*lokaprasiddhi*) is not accepted as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Or, if it were accepted, then by that very fact the objects of waking cognitions—which are the subject of your argument (*pakṣīkṛta*)—would be established; so how could the lack of a basis (*nirālambanatva*) be established for any cognitions? Furthermore, for one who understands [the argument] himself, it is improper to employ an example based merely on what is established for another, because inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is defined as the illumination of an object already perceived by oneself. As it has been said: "Just as knowledge of the probandum (*liṅgin*) arises in oneself from a three-featured mark (*trirūpaliṅga*), so too the statement of the three-featured mark with the desire to produce knowledge of the probandum in another is 'inference for others. The mention of an object 'perceived by oneself' is used in the sense of the cause being figuratively treated as the effect; it is for the purpose of making known that what is seen by another is not a means of proof, nor is there establishment [of the thesis] through a non-object. Therefore, it is not proper to take dream-cognitions as an example based merely on what is established for another. Moreover, the proofs such as "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*) have already been refuted, so the example is not established thereby. If it were established, then the establishment of the probandum would follow from that alone, making the property of being a cognition (*pratyayatva*) redundant. Furthermore, regarding this form (*ākāra*) of blue and so forth which appears in dream-cognitions, it is precisely its non-existence that practitioners of discourse (*vyavahartṛ*) understand from the subverting evidence (*bādhaka*). If that [form] is not something other than the cognition, then the non-existence of the cognition itself follows. Or else, dream-cognition would not possess the form of blue and so forth. Consequently, the meaning of the inference for the lack of a basis becomes: "All cognitions are devoid of form, because they are cognitions, like dream-cognitions. And when neither a distinct nor a non-distinct form of blue and so forth exists for the cognition, then the total cessation of all worldly discourse (*sarvavyavahāra*) would result. If all cognitions were indeed without a basis, then why is there this rule: that for those engaged in discourse there is non-correspondence in some cases, while in others—even when separated by space, time, and so forth—there is correspondence? If you say it is due to a difference in mental impressions (*vāsanābheda*)—that is, you think that where the cause is weak impressions there is non-correspondence, but where the cause is strong impressions there is correspondence—that is not so, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).
The postulation of external objects alone is superior.

Moreover, it is better to postulate that external objects themselves serve as the causes [of cognition] through their distinction as being either vivid or non-vivid, since it is logical for them to be the objects of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), rather than postulating mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, what is the cause for the vividness of these impressions? It cannot be a vivid cognition, because you do not admit the existence of any novel particular object [to be cognized]. Nor can a specific cognition arise spontaneously from mere consciousness alone. If it is argued that the cause is a cognition of great intensity (*ādara*) or a cognition resulting from repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), we say no, because of the lack of invariable concomitance (*vyabhicāra*). To explain: even in the case of those overcome by passion, grief, and so forth, where there is an intense degree of regard or repeated practice regarding objects such as a beloved woman or a child, one still observes that the cognition of the object is sometimes deceptive. Conversely, in other cases, a cognition may be entirely consistent (*saṃvādya*) even with respect to an object that is utterly unprecedented and astonishing. If it is argued that in the latter case, too, there exists an impression arising from a previous birth, we say no; for that impression can be eclipsed by the repeated practice of a cognition contrary to it. Otherwise, through the practice of [the realization of] selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so on, the impressions of passion and the like would never be eclipsed. Furthermore, if no object exists apart from cognition, there is no cause for the awakening of a specific impression. For when a previous cognition has perished, the present cognition consists of many impressions; how then could a specific manifestation arise from that alone? We shall examine the cause of impressions in the future as well, so let this suffice for now.

For this reason as well, an object such as "blue" is not of the nature of cognition alone, because it is cognizable by both oneself and others. Indeed, it is not possible for that which has the nature of cognition to be cognized by multiple persons. But how is the fact that an object is cognizable by multiple persons known? It is known from signs such as the occurrence of speech and activity that are non-contradictory [with the object]. However, the speech and so forth of two people suffering from ophthalmia (taimirika) are not valid signs because they are contradicted by other persons. Furthermore, if it were impossible to understand another's awareness, then there would necessarily be no engagement in activities such as composing treatises; for even a madman does not explain a treatise solely for the sake of his own understanding, nor does he present proofs and so forth in debate, thereby defeating himself by pointing out the opponent's failure to state a proof or a member of the syllogism.

Now, it might be argued that even in the absence of external objects, there is no fault because [the existence of another] can be inferred from the mark (*liṅga*) consisting of the appearance of linguistic activity and the process of communicating with another; for instance, one infers that the appearances of physical movement and speech arise through the influence of another, independent of one's own internal effort or desire to speak. This is not so; for those who maintain the doctrine of self-cognition alone (*svasaṃvedanamātra*), even the comprehension of another's cognition is impossible—how then could there be comprehension of another’s awareness? This has already been explained at length [in the section on] the proof of the non-existence of other mental continua (*santānāntara*) within the doctrine of the absence of objective support (*nirālambanavāda*).

Furthermore, for one who asserts that all cognitions are without objective support (*nirālambana*), like dreams, how can the existence of another mental continuum (*santānāntara*) be established?
