In this regard, the following is considered: if all cognitions were without an objective support (*nirālambana*) and consisted merely of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what would be the distinction between the perception of a yogin and that of others? If it is argued that the distinction lies in being pure or impure—supposing you think that the perception of a yogin "shines forth clearly, with the web of conceptual construction shaken off"—let it be so for now; nevertheless, its having the Four Noble Truths and so forth as its object is not tenable. For it is not logical to say that the Four Noble Truths and the like have been directly realized by the mere awareness of one's own self, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that it has those as its objects because it possesses their form (*tadākāratva*), has the Sautrāntika position then been accepted? True; yet even so, how can there be an object that is past or future? For that which is non-existent possesses no form whatsoever. If the forms of what has been seen, heard, or inferred appear clearly through the power of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then the perception of a yogin would necessarily be erroneous (*bhrānta*), because it appears in the form of something existing when it is actually non-existent, like the cognition of a dream. If it is argued that it is not erroneous because it is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvāditva*), we say no; for even though that which arises from inference is non-discrepant, it is admitted to be erroneous. Furthermore, if even an erroneous cognition is not authoritative simply because it is non-discrepant, then the definition of perception as being "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) is contradicted. Moreover, non-discrepancy itself is not tenable in your view. For do you intend non-discrepancy to mean: (1) indicating an object that is to be attained, (2) indicating the object toward which activity is directed, or (3) the accomplishment of a causal function (*arthakriyā*) from the object as it appeared? None of these is possible for a cognition of an object that is past and so forth. Even in the case of a cognition of a present object, it is not possible under the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Therefore, the Buddhists' description of the perception of a yogin is entirely inconsistent.
Conceptual perception.

The word "that" refers to yogic perception; and by the use of the word "also," the meaning is that non-yogic perception is likewise twofold. Among these, determinate (savikalpaka) perception is that which arises as the cause for the production of knowledge through the explicit mention of the connection with names and so forth. Because that [determinate perception] is supersensuous (*atīndriya*), it cannot be directly illustrated; rather, its result alone is illustrated—such as "Devadatta is stick-bearer" and so on. The cognition "Devadatta" arises through the explicit mention of the connection with a name alone, while "stick-bearer" involves the explicit mention of the connection with a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); in this same way, cognitions involving the explicit mention of connections with qualifiers such as qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth are also to be illustrated.

Now, does the cognition of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) have the qualified alone as its object, or does it have both the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified as its object? What follows from this? If it had the qualified alone as its object, the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) would not arise in respect to a man who lacks a staff, because even if something exists, if it is not manifested [in cognition], it is as good as non-existent. If it is argued: "How can the cognition of the man, which is produced by a staff qualified by its own cognition, be unqualified?"—that is incorrect. For, in the case of an inferable object and so forth, a cognition is produced by a mark (*liṅga*) etc. that is qualified by its own cognition; yet such a cognition is not perceived arising in the form "this is the smoke-possessor" (*dhūmavān*) and so on. Furthermore, it would follow that the cognition "this place possesses fire" (*agnimān ayaṃ pradeśaḥ*) is a result of perception, since the bare place is in contact with the sense organ. Even if it were to have both as its object, the cognition would be "the staff and the man. Since there is no difference in their being objects of a single cognition, there could be no relation of primary and secondary (*guṇapradhānabhāva*). Moreover, it would follow that [the cognition] would not be in grammatical apposition (*asamānādhikaraṇatva*) with the cognition of Devadatta and so forth.

Others say that [cognition] is according to its appearance (*yathādarśana*). They argue that in cognitions such as "this is a fragrant substance," the qualificandum alone is the objective support (*ālambana*), whereas in cognitions of the inferable (*anumeya*) and so forth, both [qualificandum and qualifier] are the support. This is not correct, because the acceptance of this distinction lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, the cognition of the inferable (e.g., fire) is perceived to be in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the cognition of the mountain and so forth. If it is argued that this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because the cognition of a kingdom or an army is in coreferentiality with the cognition of its ruler, we say no; for even there, it is not accepted that the object of the conventional usage of "kingdom" and so forth is actually the king himself. The cognition "one who has a staff" (*daṇḍin*) does not have the staff as its object, because it is in coreferentiality with the cognition of the person, just like the cognition of Devadatta and others. In this way, all cognitions must be established as not having qualifiers as their objective support. If it is argued that the coreferentiality is erroneous (*bhrānta*), then the Buddhist view (*śākyadarśana*) follows. And in that view, since all conceptual cognitions (*kalpanājñāna*) are without an object, the consideration of an objective support is simply untenable. Moreover, in refuting the Buddhist perspective, just as the cognition "one who has a staff" is non-erroneous, so too the cognition "that same one who has a staff is eating" and so forth is indeed non-erroneous. If it is argued that this is due to the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the whole to a part, then is that metaphorical cognition erroneous or non-erroneous? It is not reasonable to say it is erroneous, as that has already been refuted. If it is non-erroneous, then if the cognition "one who has a staff" is non-erroneous even through metaphorical application and is established as having the person alone as its support, what proof is there here that there exists another primary (*mukhya*) cognition having both as its support? Nor is it logical to assume a metaphorical status for something else when that other primary thing is not established, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that coreferentiality is in relation to the principal element (*pradhāna*), thinking that whatever is the principal in the cognition "one who has a staff" is the same in the cognition of Devadatta and so forth, thus making coreferentiality possible—we say no, because it does not appear so. No one has the intuition that "what is the principal in the cognition 'one who has a staff' is also the principal in the cognition 'Devadatta'. Rather, the intuition is "Devadatta is the one who has a staff" and "the one who has a staff is Devadatta. If you say this is merely a designation of the principal, who is opposed to one who acts favorably? When by the word "one who has a staff" the principal itself is designated, and the principal itself is the support, our desired conclusion is established. Thus, "one who has a staff" is designated as "he who possesses a staff," and cognition occurs according to the designation. As for what was said—that the cognition of the inferable and so forth is produced by a mark (*liṅga*) qualified by its own cognition, and yet it does not arise in the form "this is a possessor of smoke" (*dhūmīya*)—that is incorrect. For the cause for the production of a qualified cognition is not restricted to this much alone. What then? A qualified cognition is produced by the cognition of the qualifier and its relation, assisted by the recollection of convention (*samaya*). This is like following the various conventions of grammar, such as the suffix *matvartha* (possessive). Furthermore, the causes for recollection are stated to be indefinite in the *Praṇidhāna* Sūtra. Therefore, when a convention is applied in many ways to a single object, according to how recollection arises from the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too is a specific cognition produced in that very object by the sense organ acting as an auxiliary. Nor is it the case that smoke located in a place is grasped together with a connection to fire, such that the objection regarding the consequence of it producing the cognition "this place is possessed of smoke" (*dhūmī*) in relation to fire could be raised. As for the claim that the cognition "this place is possessed of fire" would result in being a fruit of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*), if that cognition "this place is possessed of fire" arises from the contact of the sense organ with the object, why is it not accepted as a fruit of perception? If it is argued that it is well-known as inference, we say no, because such renown can exist even through metaphorical application. The place qualified by the fire to be inferred is also called "inferable. Nor does this entail the fault of smoke not being a property of the subject (*apakṣadharmatva*), for the subject (*pakṣa*) is defined as the locus characterized by the property to be proved (*sādhyadharma*). Whether that [place] be called "inferable" or not, the reason residing therein is indeed a "property of the subject" (*pakṣavṛtti*), because it is precisely the fire located there that is being inferred. Nor is there a lack of coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). [Objection: But then a vast chain of cognitions or mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) results, because there is no rule that the apprehension of a qualifier must be preceded by the apprehension of another qualifier. [Reply: No, for we do not accept that the apprehension of a qualifier is necessarily preceded by the apprehension of another qualifier. Therefore, a single cognition whose object is the fire and its relation arises from inference, and it is inexpressible. From that, the cognition "this place is possessed of fire" also arises through perception. Those who think that an object qualified by a supersensible (*atīndriya*) qualifier cannot be perceptual—in their view, determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) would not be possible. For a person qualified by the name "Devadatta" is perceived as "Devadatta. And at that time, the name "Devadatta" is not perceived [as a separate entity], yet it functions as a qualifier, because it serves to differentiate [the person] from others, just as a staff does. Just as one might say, "Having summoned a staff-bearer among the Brahmins, let him eat," where the Brahmin is differentiated from other Brahmins by the staff, so too, in the command "Let one call Devadatta among the men," the man is differentiated from other men by the name alone. If it is argued that the name is merely an accidental indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) like a crow on a house, we say no, because they are synonyms. "Accidental indicator," "qualifier," and "differentiator" are indeed synonyms. If it is argued that this leads to the cognition "Devadatta's house has a crow," we say no, because it has already been explained. Cognition occurs according to convention: a wandering ascetic is indicated by a staff, and Devadatta's house by a crow; there is no difference between these two in their capacity as differentiators. Therefore, whatever differentiates an object from its own kind, from a different kind, or from another state, all that is called a "qualifier. Consequently, the name "cow" and its relation, when being remembered, become qualifiers themselves when they produce a qualified cognition such as "this is a cow. If it is argued that "cowness" (*gotva*) alone is the qualifier there, we say no; for even when cowness is seen, the cognition "this is a cow" does not arise in one who has not mastered the convention. Thus, both [the name and the relation] are qualifiers.

On this point, some say: if [the universal] were a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the name, there would arise the cognition, "This is named 'cow' (*go-saṃjñaka*)," or "This is denotable by the word 'cow' (*go-śabda-vācya*)," and that [cognition] is held to be purely inferential. For "being named 'cow'" is said to be the capacity to produce a cognition of its own object through the power of the cooperation of the word 'cow'; and that [capacity] is indeed beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). Furthermore, the cognition "this is a cow" is produced solely from the qualifier "cowness" (*gotva*), and therefore it is held to be perception (*pratyakṣa*). To explain: "This is a cow" and "This possesses cowness" have the same meaning; the convention (*saṃketa*) is likewise taught and understood in this very way. That is incorrect, because no one perceives or teaches the state of being connected with cowness at the time of the convention; for even without grasping the convention, [the universal] is established by perception. Indeed, one who has not grasped the convention still perceives the similarity among individual objects such as the *śābaleya* cow, which are excluded from buffaloes and the like. Therefore, it is only after having grasped the convention regarding the relationship between the designator and the designated that it is taught by means of any one of several words expressing the same referent, such as: "This is a cow," "This is named 'cow'," or "This is denotable by the word 'cow'. Even by the listener, it is understood in exactly that way. Consequently, for one who wishes to maintain that cognitions such as "this is a cow" are the fruit of perception, one must not admit that the qualifier and the qualified share a single cognitive object (*ekajñānālambanatva*). Nor is it the case that a cognition of the qualified, produced by a qualifier beyond the senses, is itself the fruit of perception. If it is asked: "How then is the cognition of an object qualified by multiple qualifiers—such as the form 'this is variegated' (*citram etat*)—possible? This is not difficult to establish, because we admit the apprehension of the qualifier and the qualified only in succession, but not [the simultaneous apprehension] of the qualifier, its relation, and so forth, since we admit that each of these is the object of a separate cognition. In some cases, even those apprehended in succession become qualifiers when they are made the object of a single recollection (*smaraṇa*). We shall explain how those apprehended in succession can be the object of a single recollection in our investigation of the sentence (*vākya*). Thus, it is established that the cognition of the qualified does not have both [qualifier and qualified] as its object, but rather has only the qualified as its object. If it is argued: "Because it is a conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*), the cognition that joins [the object] with words and so forth is not born of the senses (*akṣaja*), nor does it have the [external] object as its support (*arthālambana*)," we say: no, for there is no contradiction in a conceptual cognition being both sense-born and having the object as its support. As for the arguments you have explained, we shall refute them right away. Thus, it is proven that determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) exists.

{An Examination of Non-conceptual Cognition} For the cognition produced by the initial contact of the sense-organ with its object arises independent of the recollection of conventions and the grasping of qualifiers; therefore, it is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), which is said to be one-pointedness. For the yogin established therein, perception is exclusively non-conceptual, because one-pointedness is untenable if there is conceptualization.
{The Buddhist Theory of Perception}

The Śākyas maintain that whatever is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is exclusively non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Accordingly, the definition stated by Dignāga is that "direct perception is free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*). This should be understood as a restatement of the general definition. By this, it is said that whatever non-contradictory cognition is free from conceptual construction is direct perception. "Free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*) means devoid of, or separated from, conceptual construction; the meaning is that it is devoid of the nature of conceptual construction. Now, what is this conceptual construction? It is the association with name, genus, and so forth; the meaning is the connection with names and the like. In this regard, the association with a name is, for example, "Devadatta"; the association with a genus is, for example, "cow"; the association with an action is, for example, "he goes"; the association with a quality is, for example, "white"; the association with a substance is, for example, "staff-bearer. These five types of conceptual construction are cited according to what is established in the systems of others. However, in our own system, all of these are simply conceptual constructions of names. And thus Kīrti says: "Conceptual construction is a cognition associated with verbal expression. "Conceptual construction is a cognition whose appearance is capable of being connected with verbal expression. Others hold that "connection" (*saṃsarga*) is the merging of the forms of the signifier and the signified within a single cognition by way of being objects of apprehension, rather than a cognition that effects the unification of the name and so forth. By the inclusion of the term "capable" (*yogya*), even the conceptual construction of one who has not yet learned language is included. For even an infant, upon seeing the breast and so forth, attains satisfaction by effecting a unification—thinking "this is that very same thing"—with what was previously seen. Therefore, it is understood that even such a person possesses conceptual construction.

If non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) were perception (*pratyakṣa*), then the cognition of a double moon and the like would also have to be considered perception. This is because that [cognition] is also non-conceptual due to its being produced by the sense faculties (*akṣaja*). Likewise, dream-cognition is also non-conceptual because of its clarity; and since it serves as the cause for the appearance of going, arriving, and so forth, it is also non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādin*). Therefore, it too would have to be considered perception. To exclude such cases, Dharmakīrti formulated the definition: "Perception is free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*) and non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). The state of being erroneous (*bhrāntatva*) means appearing otherwise than it is; the meaning is that it is a distortion regarding the nature of the apprehended object. Some maintain that the error of a double moon and the like is not born of the sense faculties (*indriyajā*). They claim that having seen a single moon, it is conceptually constructed (*kalpyate*) as being two; or that having seen the form of hair existing within the cognition, it is conceptually constructed as being external. The same should be understood for other cases as well. Regarding this, Dharmakīrti states the refutation: "That is not so. Because the conformity with the presence or absence of the sense faculty is the determinant of [its] reality, and that is equal here as well. Furthermore, because there is a transformation when the sense faculty is transformed, and because the stability of the basis [of the cognition] is dependent upon that, it would follow—like the error of a snake—that a mental error (*manobhrānti*) would cease even when the sense faculty is unimpaired. Conversely, it would follow that [the error] would not cease even when the impairment of the sense faculty has ceased. Therefore, even though this [dream-cognition and the like] is born of the sense faculties, it is not perception because it is erroneous.

He shows that Dignāga also intended "non-erroneous" (*abhrāntatva*) as a qualification: by the phrase "for this very reason," he states that distinct from the category of conceptual cognitions delimited by the instrumental case, there is a semblance of perception (*pratyakṣābhāsa*) characterized by the impairment of cataracts (*timira*), namely:
"Erroneous cognition, conventional cognition, inference, that which is derived from inference, memory, and desire—these, along with that accompanied by cataracts, are semblances of perception."
Regarding this, he states its intended meaning:
"Conceptual cognition is of three kinds, arising from a disturbance of the basis;
and there is one non-conceptual [cognition]; thus, that which resembles perception is fourfold."

The basis (*āśraya*) is the object (*viṣaya*); its "affliction" (*upaplava*) is the recollection of something similar to it. Alternatively, the basis is the causal cognition; its "affliction" is a specific latent impression (*vāsanā-viśeṣa*). From this, conceptual cognition (*kalpanā-jñāna*) is threefold: (1) the cognition of a snake, water, and so forth regarding a rope, a mirage, and the like, which is designated by the term "error" (*bhrānti*); (2) the cognition of a jar and so forth, which is designated by the term "conventional cognition" (*saṃvṛti-saṃjñāna*); and (3) inferential cognition (*ānumānika*) and the cognition of the possessor of the mark (*liṅgin*)—both of these are already included within the first two. However, they are mentioned separately as things "seen" (*dṛṣṭa-tattva*) in order to establish that the first two are not produced by the senses (*anakṣaja*). Regarding the third view, namely "recollection" (*smārta*) and "desire" (*ābhilāṣika*), the term "recollection" is used for those conceptualizations of affirmation and negation that arise as "this-ness" (*idantayā*) concerning things not present [at the time]. "Desire" is mentioned separately in order to establish that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is also not produced by the senses. The separate mention of "ocular disorder" (*taimira*) apart from this class of conceptualizations is stated to indicate that it is an exception (*apavāda*) to the quality of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Furthermore, the mention of "ocular disorder" is intended to include all impairments (*upaghāta*); Dharmakīrti says that all cognition produced by impairment is erroneous: "Perception is non-conceptual cognition in which no error has been induced by ocular disorder, rapid motion, traveling in a boat, agitation, and so forth. As for cognitions of hair, moons, and the like, they do not possess the nature of conceptual construction because they appear with vivid clarity (*sphuṭa-pratibhāsitva*). Therefore, it is said:
"One who is bound by conceptual construction does not have the appearance of a clear object. Thus it is also said elsewhere:
"Whether in a state of sleep or waking, that cognition which appears clearly is non-conceptual; otherwise, it is conceptual in both cases."

Thus, he states that the fact that perception is free from conceptual construction is understood by perception itself: "That perception is free from conceptual construction is established by perception alone;
for everyone, the resort known as conceptual construction is personally experienced."
Having withdrawn all thought from every side with a tranquil inner self, even while standing still, he perceives form with the eye; this is cognition born of direct perception.
Furthermore, one does not know through the senses, as was previously stated, that "I had such a conceptualization" while reflecting upon something.

Conceptual cognition (*kalpanājñāna*) is indeed erroneous because it manifests an object that is not as it truly is; nevertheless, it is mentioned separately for the purpose of dispelling misconceptions. For others hold the dogmatic view that even conceptual cognitions such as "this is a cow" are direct perception (*adhyakṣa*) and a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because they are sense-born and [they claim they are] non-erroneous. To refute this, it is said to be "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Indeed, the manifestation of association with names is impossible in sensory cognition, because it arises through the power of the object; being produced by the power of the object, it must conform to that very form. For words do not exist in the object, nor are they of the same nature as it, such that they would manifest when the object manifests. Nor does this [sensory cognition] have the property of not contacting the object or not perceiving it, because it applies those [names] to objects; otherwise, it would follow that objects could never be cognized. Therefore, an object, in producing a cognition upon coming into contact with it, ought to produce one that conforms to its own nature, not one bearing the form of something else. For a blue object does not produce a cognition with a white form or the form of taste and so forth; nor is it logical for a cognition arising by the power of that [object] to pursue something else, like a cognition of taste, because even if that [other thing] exists, it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition of another sense-faculty, and because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Conceptual mental cognition (*manovijñāna*), however, is independent of the presence of an object, is aroused by the latent impressions of conceptualization (*vikalpavāsanā*), and grasps sense-objects without restriction. Due to some connection with experience, it may grasp [an object] either simultaneously or separately.
Moreover:
even when an object is being engaged, if sensory cognition were to depend upon the application of a word through memory,
that object would become mediated.

For it is not possible for one who does not remember the general linguistic form (*abhilāpasāmānya*) existing at the time of the convention to apply it [to the object], just as with other words. Nor is it logical that there should be a memory of a specific word when there is no modification produced by the impact of the object, because if that [modification] were not caused by the object, it would follow that the name of that object would not be grasped. Due to the intervention of that memory, the engagement with the object would not have an immediate operation as its result; and consequently, "that which was previously a non-producer of cognition due to the lack of a distinction in its engagement," would remain so later as well, since there is no difference in its nature and thus no difference in its capacity. It is impossible for a single thing to both act and not act upon a single object. Therefore, "even in the absence of the object, visual cognition would occur," because the object has no direct utility in the production of cognition and is already utilized in the awakening of memory; thus, cognition would not depend on the existence of that which provides no assistance. Furthermore, if the arising of cognition were caused by the impact of the object, there would be no intervening memory of the linguistic expression. [The author] says the following to refute the doubt: "Let it be granted that conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is not born of the senses, but conceptualization of universals (*jāti*) and so forth will still be."
"Having grasped the qualifier, the qualified, their relation, and the worldly convention, and having synthesized these, one cognizes [the object] in that way and not otherwise."

When something is perceived as qualified by something else, it is apprehended through the synthesis of the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the qualified (*viśeṣya*), and their relation, in accordance with worldly convention—just like a staff or similar objects. It cannot be otherwise, for there would be no comprehension of the established relationship between the object and its designation. This [synthesis] is simply impossible in the case of those possessing genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*), because the distinctness of form and the relation do not appear, making a conjunction [of them] untenable. Even in cases where a distinction is perceived—as in the case of milk and water—for one who does not recognize them as such, there is still apprehension [of the mixture].
[This process] consists of the synthesis of what has been seen, employing the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) as its means.
"And how could that [recollection] exist in a visual perception, which is devoid of any consideration of before and after?"

Indeed, this [sensory cognition] is not capable of performing such an operation, because it arises by the power of a present object and is non-discursive (*avicāraka*); for if it were discursive, it would follow that sensory cognition and mental cognition would be identical. If they were identical, there would follow the consequence that there would be no grasping or non-grasping of distinctions regarding past and future things, nor of pondering or non-pondering, nor of dependence or independence upon the existence of an object, and so forth. If it is argued that sensory cognition follows what has been processed (*abhisaṃskṛta*) by mental cognition, we say no; for it is impossible for that which does not grasp [an object] in the manner described to function in such a way. This is because it does not operate upon what is not its object, and because universals (*jāti*) and the like, as well as relations, past linguistic conventions, and so forth, are not objects of sensory cognition. Therefore, sensory cognition does not enter into conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), which is the association of an object with [linguistic] designations.

Furthermore, that cognition produced by conceptual construction would not function according to one's will; it would not require the presence of the object. Moreover, even though this [cognition] has proceeded—having been produced by conceptual constructions such as qualifiers—it could be turned back at will by one who possesses the complete causal complex, just like any other conceptual construction.

For conceptual constructions (*kalpanā*) can indeed be warded off through meditative cultivation (*prasaṃkhyāna*), but not the sensory cognitions (*indriyabuddhi*). Even for one who, while the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is complete, sets aside the cognition of a cow and conceives of a horse, the perception of the cow does not fail to occur; nor would this [sensory cognition] depend upon the presence of the object, for the conceptualization of a cow and so forth does not arise only when the object is present. Therefore, only non-conceptual knowledge is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). In that regard, according to the position that external objects exist, the form of the object (*arthākāra*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the apprehension of that object is the result (*phala*). According to the position of mere representation (*vijñaptimātratā*), self-awareness (*svasaṃvitti*) is the result, and the subjective aspect (*grāhakākāra*) is the means of valid cognition, because self-awareness is established by virtue of that [subjective aspect].

In this case, regarding the cognition whose object is the self, just as the experience of passion and so forth is the very result while being the means of valid cognition— because it is perceived as possessing an operation.
This is the same in both of these two positions. {The establishment of the perceptual nature of conceptual cognition}

To this it is replied: Since the investigation into the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) has already been conducted previously by way of refuting the systems of the Śākyas and others, it is not undertaken here again. Rather, what is established here is precisely the fact that cognitions such as “this is a cow” are produced from the senses (*akṣaja*). As for the claim that whatever arises through the power of an object must necessarily conform to the form of that very object—that is not so, because the presence of the object’s form within the cognition has already been refuted. Furthermore, the argument beginning with “for words do not exist in the object,” etc., is also refuted by the very denial that the qualifier and the qualified can be the objective support (*ālambana*) of a single cognition. Moreover, the word does not appear in the cognition “this is a cow”; rather, it is the object possessing a dewlap and so forth that appears, because of the perception of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in such expressions as “this white, fat, horned [cow] is walking. Furthermore, because a corresponding cognition such as “this is a cow” does not arise with respect to buffaloes and the like. The argument that “this is a false cognition because it is conceptual (*savikalpaka*), like other conceptual cognitions,” is incorrect; for otherwise, one would face the unwanted consequence that it is a non-conceptual cognition because it is non-conceptual, like other non-conceptual cognitions, since the objection and its rebuttal are symmetrical.
And as it has been said here:
"Because the mind's activity is simultaneous— whether in the case of conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions— or because its activity is rapid, the deluded person determines them to be one."

In this regard, the following is investigated: Do the conceptual (*savikalpa*) and non-conceptual (*avikalpa*) cognitions determine as a single unity those two [cognitions] themselves—whether they have arisen simultaneously or successively—or rather do they determine the objects of those two? What follows from this? If there were a determination based solely on the cognition itself, there would be no activity directed toward an object nor attainment of it; furthermore, since a non-contradictory cognition cannot be erroneous, activity and attainment could not result even from error. If, on the other hand, it is held that the conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions determine the identity of their respective objects—as it has been said: "Because one proceeds by determining them through the unification of the perceived object and the conceptualized object"—that is incorrect. For if one were to proceed with the determination "this is a cow" even toward the body of a buffalo or similar animals, it would follow that such activity would be non-contradictory (i.e., successful). This is because the absence of a connection with the phonemes *ga*, etc., is indistinguishable in both cases, and the determination of their identity is likewise indistinguishable in both cases. Furthermore, what was stated by that self-styled scholar—"That cognition which occurs regarding an object present before one, produced by a sensory cognition aided by its own object and the immediately preceding object, is accepted as mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*)"—is an unconsidered statement. For that very cognition "cow" which you accept as conceptual because it has the phonemes *ga*, etc., as its object, must likewise be conceptual because "this" also has the phoneme *i*, etc., as its object, since there is no difference in the appearance of association with words. If you argue that the cognition "this" is not like the cognition "cow" because it possesses a clear form of the object present before one, then some divine insight is required here, as there is no logical reason for this distinction. If you argue that because the cognition "cow" arises even in the absence of an object in certain instances, it does not depend upon an object, then the cognition "this" also certainly occurs in the absence of an object in certain instances. That it is erroneous when occurring in the absence of an object and correct otherwise is the same for both cases. If you claim that the cognition "this" is non-conceptual because it lacks the appearance of association with words such as *i*, etc., then this is a contradiction.

Furthermore, you must also accept that a cognition such as "cow" (*gauh*), which does not manifest as being associated with the sounds *ga* and so forth, is a non-conceptual mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*); for the same logic applies. Consequently, your acceptance of the cognition "cow" and the like as being non-perceptual due to its conceptual nature is entirely untenable.

As for what was also said—"One acts by taking [an object] as 'this' (*idam*); therefore, because it causes one to act, it is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)"—that too is incorrect. For one does not act by taking [an object] as "not this" (*nedam*), but rather, as we shall explain, even a newborn infant acts solely due to the ascertainment of what is desired. Therefore, this alone is the correct response: mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is not a different entity from sensory perception (*indriya-pratyakṣa*). That it is a different entity has been stated merely on the authority of scripture (*āgama*), but there is no proof whatsoever for this.

As for what was said—that even though the [word] exists as that very essence, it lacks the capacity to produce a cognition through another sense organ—that is refuted simply by not accepting [the premise]. For it is not admitted that sound is an object of visual or other sensory cognitions; rather, through the eye or other senses, aided by the experience of convention or aided by the memory thereof, a cognition such as "this is a cow" is produced with respect to its own object alone.

As for what was said—"Even when there is the application of the object," etc.—if it is argued that there is an intervention (*vyavadhāna*) for the object due to its momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) because of its dependence on memory, that is not so, because momentariness is unproven. Even by the proponent of momentariness, it is indeed admitted that a single continuum (*santāna*), due to the difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), produces a distinct effect. Therefore, just as a single fire-continuum is held to be a non-cause with respect to a specific form such as color (*rūpa*)—due to being intervened by another continuum of clay or stone in accordance with a difference in auxiliary causes—so too, after the continuum of the object and the continuum of the sense faculty have produced a non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakajñāna*), they will subsequently produce a cognition with the form of "cow" and so forth once they have acquired specific auxiliary causes. Thus, how can there be an intervention? By this, the argument beginning with "That which was previously a non-producer of cognition... is also refuted. For it is not logical that a fire which was previously a non-producer of a certain form should remain a non-producer of that same form later; [the reason] "because there is no difference in its application" (*upayoga*) is unproven, since the very acquisition of specific auxiliary causes constitutes a difference in application. Furthermore, we shall examine in the context of non-momentariness the claim that "action and non-action cannot coexist in one thing at one time. Moreover, it has already been demonstrated that even that which has not yet performed its effect within a continuum possesses the capacity to produce that effect. Thus, the statement "because the object is not directly applied to the cognition" is unproven. As for the phrase "and because it is applied to the awakening of memory," what is meant by this? It cannot mean that the object is applied to the production of memory, for it is admitted that memory is not born from the object.

Now, if it is argued that [the object] has utility in producing the experience of its own cause, then what of it? If you say, "That which has been utilized here cannot be utilized elsewhere," we say no, because we observe that fire is utilized sequentially in the states of charcoal, ash, and so forth. Likewise, since we observe that an object already utilized in a prior mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) is utilized later as well, there is indeed a subsequent utilization of the object in the mental perception. If you argue, "But that [subsequent cognition] is not born of the sense organ (*akṣaja*)," then the dispute concerns its being sense-born, not its being born of the object. Just as it is accepted that the object possesses efficacy toward the sensory cognition of the object first, and later possesses efficacy toward the mental perception when acting as its auxiliary, so too the sense organ and the object possess efficacy toward the non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition first; why is it not accepted that they also possess efficacy toward the conceptual (*savikalpaka*) cognition once they have acquired specific auxiliaries? What contradiction is there here? If you say, "It would entail [the cognition] having the form of that [object],"—that is, if you think that if cognition is produced by the sense organ and the object even later, then that cognition would necessarily have the same form as the cognition previously arisen—this is not so, for we see that even things produced from a single cause assisted by distinct auxiliaries can have a single form. Otherwise, all cognitions produced by the eye and light would have only a single form. Even if there is some degree of similarity in form, conceptual and non-conceptual cognitions certainly share a common form.

Furthermore, as for what was stated after asserting that there is a qualifier and a qualified, and so forth—namely, that this [distinction] is simply not possible for those possessing genus, quality, or action, because a connection is impossible due to the non-appearance of both the distinction of form and their relation—that too is incorrect, because the claim of "non-appearance" is unestablished. For instance, even one who has not grasped the linguistic convention perceives individual cows such as the *śāvaleyā* (the brindled cow) as distinct from individuals such as buffaloes; and he perceives them as having a single form precisely through the apprehension of the distinct nature of the genus (*gotva*) and its relation [to the individual]. If it is argued that exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is nothing other than that which is excluded, we say no, because the theory of Apoha will be refuted later. Once that is negated, it is established that genus, quality, and action, as well as their relations, are indeed entities distinct from their substrates.

The claim that [the distinction between mixed substances] is unknown to one who does not perceive them as such—like milk and water—is also unproven. For even by one who has not seen milk and water in separate substrates, there certainly arises the cognition: "This is milk-and-water," when milk is mixed with a large quantity of water. Even milk mixed with only a small amount of water certainly appears as such to one who knows it. Furthermore, this is the very nature of things: some objects are mixed together from the beginning, while others remain so for only a certain period of time; some objects, though mixed, appear distinctly to all observers, while others appear distinctly only to those who know them; yet others appear distinctly to people like us only in their unmixed state, but without distinction when they are in a mixed state.

As for what was said regarding "synthetic cognition" (*saṃkalanajñāna*): if, first of all, synthetic cognition is intended to be merely the recollection of multiple objects, that is not tenable, because the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) is experienced as having the form of a direct perception (*anubhava*). Even recollection indicates the prior experience of "the man with a staff"; for if there were only the grasping of the individual essences of the person, the staff, the cow, and so forth, a recollection in the form "the man with a staff was seen" or "the owner of cows was seen" could not possibly occur.

Now, if it is intended that this synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanajñāna*) is indeed an erroneous cognition (*bhrāntijñāna*), that too is incorrect; for like the appearance of blue and so forth, this [synthetic cognition] also arises at all times for everyone without contradiction. Furthermore, since there is no cause for error, the error cannot arise from a defect of the sense organs or from an imbalance of the humors (*vāta*, etc.), because it arises—without being restricted by specific place or time—even for all ordinary people who are in close proximity [to the object]. By this same reasoning, the [theory of] mental impressions (*vāsanā*) is also refuted. Moreover, a cause such as similarity (*sādṛśya*) is simply not possible in this case.

Now, it is indeed accepted that the synthetic cognition (*saṃkalanājñāna*) is preceded by the apprehension of qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*) and so forth, because we admit that only what has been observed to possess causal efficacy can be a cause. Since the capacity of the sense organ (*akṣa*) is determined to be no different from the capacity of the apprehension of the qualifiers, the cognition "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) and so forth is not non-sensory (*anakṣaja*). For it is not the case that where one thing possesses causal efficacy, another must necessarily lack it.

As for the argument beginning with "the recollection of convention" (*saṃketasmaraṇa*) and so forth, that too is indeed untenable, because there is no distinction between being a means for the recollection of convention and being visual (*cākṣuṣatva*). Furthermore, the property of having a proximate object (*saṃnihitaviṣayatva*) certainly exists in cognitions such as "this person is a staff-bearer" (*ayaṃ daṇḍī*), as well as in recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*).

Now, one might object: "Does not the word *sa* (that) refer to something previously seen that is currently absent? No, because it is impossible for that [object] to be present while being non-different from this [present perception]. If it is asked, "By what means is its non-difference apprehended?"—it is by the eye itself. It is apprehended by the eye together with memory as being qualified by the previous perception. The meaning is that the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is produced having that as its object. And in that cognition of recognition, phonemes such as the letter *s* appear; the previous perception does not manifest. Rather, the object itself appears, and in order to exclude others, one utters the word "this is that very same thing"—which denotes that very object—recalling it from memory. This should be understood to apply to cognitions such as "the man with a staff" (*daṇḍī*) and so forth as well.

If, moreover, an object qualified by association with verbal expression and so forth were never apprehended at all, then there would be no utterance of a specific word for the purpose of communicating it to another. Furthermore, one might utter just any word out of error, which would lead to the undesirable consequence that there could be no mutual agreement among all users of language.

Regarding what was stated concerning the lack of prior and subsequent reflection and the non-discursive nature of sensory cognition: what is meant here by "non-discursiveness"? If, by that reason of being of the nature of memory, the status of sensory cognition as having an object qualified by qualifiers is denied, then memory itself must be admitted to have such an object; and consequently, there is a contradiction with the admission that [sensory cognition] is without an object. Furthermore, it is impossible to establish an object for memory other than the object of experience, because memory is everywhere experienced as having as its object an entity previously perceived.

Now, it is not the case that memory either does not have as its object an entity qualified by a qualifier; for if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*). When that qualified object is not made an object of either memory or direct experience (*anubhava*), how could it be possible to engage in linguistic usage regarding something that has not been apprehended? If you argue that this occurs through error (*bhrānti*), we say no, because error has already been refuted.

Now, if the reason [for the claim that perception is not a means of valid knowledge] is "being produced by a reflective judgment (*parāmarśa*) which lacks investigation," even so, it is untenable because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). For what would this "reflective judgment" be: a memory, an inferential cognition, or a form such as doubt? In every case, it has already been established that the sense faculty acts as a cooperative cause in the production of a qualified experience (*viśiṣṭānubhava*).

As for what was also stated—that because of the consequence of non-difference between sensory and mental cognitions if they were both investigative—and so forth, that too is incorrect, because [the distinction] is impossible, just as in the case of their lack of difference regarding non-conceptuality and so on. Just as in your own system, although there is no difference among the four types of perception regarding non-conceptuality and non-erroneousness, there still exists a distinction of internal properties, a distinction of objects, and a distinction of causes; likewise, even though there is no difference in their being investigative, there is no absolute identity between sensory and mental cognitions. Nor does it follow that they would apprehend past and future entities and the like.

As for what was also stated—that verbal usage and the like, which transcend the connection with universals (*jāti*) and so forth, are not objects of sensory cognition—that too is without substance. For the connection with universals and so forth has not been proven to be an object of the senses, and it has been established that qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) has as its objective support only the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) in isolation; thus, there is no consequence of [sensory cognition] having past words and the like as its objects. Furthermore, as for the claim that "it is also [cognition] produced by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)," etc., that too is incorrect, because we observe that even for one possessed by desire and the like, the conceptual construction of an object such as a beloved woman standing before them does not cease even through the will. If it is argued that the conceptual construction of a beloved woman and the like ceases through the practice of *prasaṃkhyāna*, then Patanjali and others have said that the sensory cognitions also cease through the practice of the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*). Moreover, since objects in contact with the senses do not appear to those whose minds are asleep or distracted, the operation of the sense organ itself is not possible independently of the mind.

As for what was said—"because one who, while the causal complex is complete, sets aside the cognition of a cow and conceives [it] as a horse, still sees a cow"—that is merely an incoherent prattle. For instance, when the opponent has stated that the cognition "this is a cow" is not possible even in the absence of either the recollection of the convention or the sense faculty, how could such things as "while the causal complex is complete, having set aside... be of any use?

As for what was said—that one need not observe the proximity of an object, for conceptualizations such as "cow" do not arise only when an object is present—that too is an unconsidered statement. This is because we never observe the arising of a qualified conceptualization in the absence of the proximity of an object. Furthermore, since you yourself have rejected that [conceptualization] is a means of inference on account of its identity with the word despite their lack of difference, [your position is untenable]. Moreover, due to the similarity in being produced by the senses (*akṣaja*), there would follow the absurd consequence that all sensory cognitions, like the cognition of [illusory] hair and so forth, would arise independently of the proximity of an object. Consequently, nothing at all would arise through the causal capacity of an object, and thus the fact that [perception] arises from the capacity of an object would remain unestablished. Alternatively, just as even though there is no difference in being born of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāja*), only the cognition of a yogin is accepted as non-erroneous perception (*pratyakṣa*) because of its non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*), whereas the cognition of disturbances such as dreams is not; so too, even though it is conceptual, the cognition "this is a cow" and so forth is perception precisely because of its non-discrepancy and because it functions toward the direct realization of the object.

As for what was also said—that a word functions toward objects by the power of convention (*saṃketa*), yet that convention cannot be established or grasped either with respect to an individual (*vyakti*) or with respect to a universal (*sāmānya*)—because:
"A difference observed in one place is not seen anywhere else;
therefore, there is no other distinct universal, because of the non-difference of cognition."

That too is incorrect; for we shall demonstrate in detail below how the formulation and apprehension of a convention regarding both the particular (*vyakti*) and the universal (*sāmānya*) is possible. Thus, it is established that even conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is perception (*pratyakṣa*).

By this very same reasoning, one must also prove that doubt and other such states, which concern objects of conflicting views, are born of the senses (*akṣaja*) and have external objects as their domain.

If it is argued that conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) lacks the status of valid knowledge (*apramāṇatva*) because its object has already been apprehended by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), we say no; for it apprehends that object in a different manner. Furthermore, it would follow that the cognition of a yogin regarding objects previously seen, heard, and so forth, would also lack validity. Moreover, since the convergence (*saṃplava*) of means of knowledge has already been established, conceptual cognition is not invalid even if its object has been previously apprehended. Nor does it follow that conceptual cognition is merely memory simply because its object has been apprehended; otherwise, since there is no difference in their being objects of recollection, it would follow that perception and the other means of knowledge are indistinguishable from memory. Enough of this over-extension.
Thus ends the first chapter of the *Saṅgrahavārtika*, composed by the venerable teacher Bhāsarvajña in his *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*.
{The Chapter on Inference} {The Nature of Inference} Now, the nature of inference is being investigated—

"The inference preceded by that [perception] is threefold: *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyato-dṛṣṭa*. This is the aphorism. Regarding this, some maintain that the phrase "inference preceded by that" alone serves as the definition, while the remainder is for the purpose of classification; however, that is a misinterpretation. If, by the word "that" (*tat*), only perception (*pratyakṣa*) were referred to, then the faults of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and under-extension (*avyāpti*) would arise: there would be over-extension to mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by perception and to doubtful cognitions (*saṃśaya-jñāna*) etc., and under-extension to an inference preceded by another inference. Therefore, in order to avoid the fault of under-extension, all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) introduced in the section on classification are referred to. Furthermore, by resorting to a specific grammatical analysis (*vigraha*), the avoidance of over-extension is also established. The analysis is "those and they" (*te ca tāni ca*). By the rule of *ekaśeṣa* (retaining only one of identical forms), the word "they" (*tāni*) is formed. That which has those as its antecedent is "preceded by that" (*tat-pūrvakam*). In that context, by the word "those" (*te*), both the observation of the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-sambandha*) and the observation of the mark (*liṅga-darśana*) are connected. By the word "them" (*tāni*), all results of the means of valid cognition are meant. This is what is intended: that which is preceded by the observation of the relationship of invariable concomitance and the observation of the mark, produced by any one of the means of valid cognition such as perception, is so described. Inference (*anumāna*) is the act of inferring (*anumiti*). For once the definition of the result is established, the definition of its instrument (*sādhana*) is necessarily established as well.

Alternatively, it is inference because it arises from that [perception] as its antecedent, due to the distinction between the object and the agent. When the word "that" (tat) refers specifically to the means of valid cognition such as perception, then one instance of the word "antecedent" (*pūrvaka*) should be understood as having been elided; thus, it should be explained as "that which has as its antecedent that which has [perception] as its antecedent," and so forth.
{The threefold nature of inference}

The mention of "threefold" is for the purpose of restriction—that although inference is infinite due to differences in place, time, genus, state, and so forth, it is nevertheless only threefold. The mention of "pūrvavat" and the others is for the purpose of precluding the suspicion that there might be another way of classifying it into three types. "Pūrvavat" refers to inference based on a cause (*kāraṇānumāna*). How so? Here, by the word "pūrva" (prior), the mark (*liṅga*) known as the cause is expressed; that [inference] which has this as its objective support (*ālambana*) for the cognition that establishes the knowledge of the probandum (*liṅgin*) is "pūrvavat. Alternatively, with reference to the result, that [inference] in which the producer exists prior to the knowledge of the probandum is "pūrvavat."

The same etymological derivation applies here for *śeṣavat* as well. *Śeṣavat* refers to inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*). Among cause and effect, the cause has already been explained; therefore, since the effect remains (*śiṣyate*), it is called the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).

The *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation) is that which, even in the absence of a cause-and-effect relationship, makes known another object because of its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*). An example is a particular odor making known a particular taste and so forth. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that this follows the same logical principle. What is meant is this: the Śākyas maintain that only an effect can serve as a signifier of another object, neither a cause nor something that is neither cause nor effect. In that regard, the principle they have taught for an effect’s capacity to signify—characterized by non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*)—is indicated by the word "and" as being present in the other cases as well. We shall elaborate on this further below.

Alternatively, "pūrvavat" refers to purely positive inference (*kevalānvayi*), "śeṣavat" to purely negative inference (*kevalavyatireki*), and "sāmānyatodṛṣṭa" to positive-negative inference (*anvayavyatireki*). How so? By the word "pūrva," the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is designated, because it is first determined. For as long as the presence of smoke is not determined to occur when fire is present, the absence of smoke—even if observed—cannot be determined when fire is absent; this is because the determination of a negation is preceded by the determination of an affirmation (*vidhi*). That inference for which the "prior" (the positive concomitance) alone exists is *pūrvavat*. That for which the "remainder" (*śeṣa*), namely the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), alone exists is *śeṣavat*. It is said "śeṣavat" rather than "vyatirekavat" to demonstrate that what makes known is the purely negative concomitance as characterized by a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), and not mere negative concomitance. That inference which is observed through the general [application] of the two members of proof, positive and negative concomitance, is "sāmānyatodṛṣṭa. This is what is meant: just as this inference is assisted by the positive concomitance, so too is it assisted by the negative concomitance. The word "ca" (and) indicates that the capacity to make something known belongs to the other two types as well, just as it does to the positive-negative type.

The Śākyas indeed assert that neither purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) nor purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) [reasons] possess the capacity to prove [a conclusion]; this [view] has also been indicated as a refutation, and we shall explain that further below.

In this regard, we do not understand how "having that as its antecedent" (*tatpūrvaka*) alone can constitute the definition of inference (*anumāna*), because mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and so forth also have perception and other means of knowledge as their antecedents. If one were to supply the ellipsis [of the word *jñāna*] such that it becomes "knowledge characterized by non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) and so forth, having that as its antecedent," even then there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to perceptual and scriptural knowledge; and if another ellipsis were resorted to for the sake of excluding those, then the mention of "having that as its antecedent" would be redundant, since the definition would be established by the supplied words alone.

[Objection: But surely, by relying on the analysis *te* (of those two), the exclusion of all deviation (*vyabhicāra*) is already established. For, a cognition of doubt or the like, nor a cognition derived from perception or scripture, can be produced by a cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) accompanied by a memory that imitates the observation of an inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). [Response: No, because they were not previously introduced. Indeed, neither the observation of an inseparable connection nor the observation of the logical mark was previously introduced anywhere such that they could be referred to by the word *te*. If one were to admit a reference to something not previously introduced merely by the force of one's own wish, then there would be a reference only to the specific cognition of the object possessing the mark (*liṅgin*). Consequently, the mention of the word *pūrva* (prior) would be useless, since the definition of inference would be established by the word *tat* alone, supplemented by ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*).
{The definition of inference according to others and its refutation}:
Others, however, describe the definition statement as merely "inference is of three kinds, preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakaṃ trividham anumānam*).

The meaning of this [definition] is as follows: "Inference is knowledge based on the three types of logical marks (liṅga), such as the purely positive (kevalānvayin), which is preceded by means of valid cognition such as perception. This too is not tenable, because it is not accepted that knowledge alone constitutes a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For everything that is an instrument for inferential cognition—whether it be knowledge or non-knowledge—is intended to be inference. Furthermore, even a cognition that produces doubt and so forth, if it is preceded by that [perception] and rests upon the threefold mark, would have to be inference. If [the definition] were to avoid under-extension (avyāpti) and over-extension (ativyāpti) through ellipses (adhyāhāra), then the definition would be established by those very [elliptical additions], making the sūtra redundant.

[The definition of inference according to others: Others, however, explain the terms *pūrvavat* and so forth as having the function of defining [the types of inference]—they say: the "subject" (*pakṣa*) is called "prior" (*pūrva*) because it is prior to the [logical reason's] application; that which possesses this [subject] is *pūrvavat*, and thus the logical mark (*liṅga*) that pervades the subject is so described. "The remainder" (*śeṣa*) refers to the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), because it remains after the aforementioned subject; therefore, *śeṣavat* means "possessing the similar instance."

The phrase "not observed in the counter-example" (*vipakṣe*) is to be supplied [to *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*]. The meaning is that it is not observed in the counter-example in a general sense—that is, it is not observed anywhere within that which is denoted by the term "counter-example. The word "and" (*ca*) conjoins [this] with the properties of having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*) and having an uncontradicted object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). In this way, the logical mark (*liṅga*) possessing five characteristics has been stated. The definitions of the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) and purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) types of inference are to be explained by omitting either the term *śeṣavat* or *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*.
[This concludes] the intended meaning of the sūtra "that which is preceded by that" (*tatpūrvakam*).

Let it be so; let the definition of the mark (*liṅga*) be threefold through this arduous conceptualization. Nevertheless, by failing to state the definition of inference (*anumāna*) which is the subject at hand, and instead stating only the definition of the mark—which is not the subject at hand—you would be guilty of stating something irrelevant. For the mark itself is not inference, since the entire collection of instruments that establishes inferential cognition constitutes inference, whereas a mark that generates doubt and the like is not inference. Furthermore, since inferential cognition can occur even from the knowledge of a past or future mark, the mark is not the cause of inference; how then could the definition of inference be established solely from the definition of the mark? Therefore, the previously stated explanation of the term "threefold" and of the words "pūrvavat" and so forth is indeed superior. And the inclusion of the phrase "preceded by that" (*tatpūrvaka*) was stated both for the purpose of adorning one's own inference and for the purpose of refuting the inferences of others.

{Refutation of the Sāṃkhya Inference} How so? First of all, that inference concerning the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa* which has been stated by the Sāṃkhyas is not tenable; for they themselves admit that inference is preceded by perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet in their own system, perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is not established. This is because it is erroneous, having as its object unreal things, like the cognition of a mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) and the like. And thus it has been said by them: "The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision."
"But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.

Thus, just as inference preceded by the perception of illusions, smoke, and so forth [is invalid], inference regarding the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) and other such entities preceded by the perception of unreal transformations is likewise not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).
{The Refutation of Non-dualist Inference}

Even for the proponents of non-duality (*advaitavādin*), inference and scripture regarding the subject of non-duality are untenable because perception—which grasps positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth—is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Even if it were a valid means of knowledge, they would be sublated by that very [perception]. Nor does perception sublate those two, since their existence is preceded by it; thus should it be construed. {The refutation of the Cārvāka position}

Even those who claim that perception alone is the sole means of valid cognition must, in accepting the performance of actions for their own or others' benefit—namely, the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful—admit that the ascertainment of the capacity of the means to achieve those ends cannot arise from perception. Therefore, inference preceded by perception must necessarily be accepted; thus, [the Buddhist argument] beginning with "because the relation of inseparable connection (avinābhāva) cannot be grasped" is untenable.
{The Refutation of the Buddhist Definition of Inference}

It should be applied that for the Śākyas as well, inference preceded by that [perception] would not be possible. Since the cognition of similarity is impossible through perception, and since the three characteristics [of the logical mark] are impossible in its absence, how could inference proceed? For they define the characteristic of inference as "the seeing of an object from a mark possessing the three characteristics. Furthermore, the ascertainment of the three characteristics is not possible through a perception that grasps only utterly distinct entities; thus, how could there be an inference of the seeing of an object from that which is unascertained and a mere mental construction? To claim that the grasping of the three characteristics occurs through error is also a blind man’s whim, because it would entail the consequence of false inference. Indeed, in the world, one does not observe an inference of a fire capable of causal efficacy based on the erroneous determination of smoke possessing the three characteristics.

Now, if it is argued that the three-fold character (*trairūpya*) is grasped by inference alone, this is not so; for even the inference that grasps the three-fold character must itself depend upon the grasping of a three-fold character. If another inference were admitted for that case as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of inferences grasping the three-fold character, and consequently, the intended object of inference (*anumeya*) could never be established. Indeed, this very intention of the author of the Sūtras has been made clear by others as well. As it has been said:

"Because the signs (*liṅga*), the objects possessing the signs (*liṅgin*), and the inferences are infinite, the comprehension of even a single object possessing a sign does not occur even in many thousands of aeons."

And this objection is actually an ornament for us, who accept that the relation, similarity, and so forth, are objects of perception through the process of *saṃplava* (the convergence of means of knowledge). Thus he says: "Inference is preceded by that [perception]. [Objection:

But since you also accept that inference is preceded by inference and verbal testimony (*āgama*), how is that not an objection? [Reply: No; because even that [inference] is accepted as being ultimately preceded by perception. The conventional usage of "being preceded by that" is seen even in the case of an indirect cause, as in the expression, "the abundance of crops is preceded by rain.
{Perception is not included within inference}

Others, however, maintain that even perception (*pratyakṣa*) is included within inference (*anumāna*). To indicate the reason for refuting that view, it was stated: "Inference is preceded by that [perception]. Accordingly, in the *Parīkṣā*, after establishing the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "perception is inference because there is apprehension through the grasping of a single part," the resolution was stated: "It is not so, because whatever is [apprehended] by perception is also apprehended [by inference]; thus there is no contingency of [all] being inference, because [inference] is preceded by that [perception]. Therefore, the inclusion of the phrase "preceded by that" is for another purpose. [The definition of inference follows] from the word "inference" itself.

If even the inclusion of the phrase "preceded by that" (tatpūrvaka) is not for the purpose of defining [inference], then what is the purpose of this aphorism as a definition of inference? The term *anumāna* itself, along with its etymological derivation, serves as the definition; just as in the statement, "Perception, inference, comparison, and word are the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇas*), all commentators accept that the term *pramāṇa* alone, depending on its derivation, functions as the definition—meaning it is said that a *pramāṇa* is the instrument of valid cognition (*pramā*) because "by this, something is correctly known" (*pramīyate 'nena*). In the same way, from the derivation "by this, something is inferred" (*anumīyate 'nena*), it is understood that inference (*anumāna*) is that by which the act of inferring (*anumiti*) is performed.
The definition of inference.

What, then, is this inference (*anumiti*)? It is "the experience of the imperceptible through a correct non-separation" (*samyag-avinābhāvena parokṣānubhavaḥ*). By the phrase "through non-separation," it is meant "by the recollection of pervasion" (*vyāptismaraṇena*), because the word for the object (*viṣaya*) is used here to denote the subject (*viṣayin*). For example: "The country of Saurāṣṭra has been destroyed. The instrumental case in *avinābhāvena* is used in the sense of the most effective instrument (*sādhakatama*). Although the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other factors also serve as means for inference, nevertheless, this designation is made according to their specific, unique character, like the barley-sprout (*yavāṅkura*). For this very reason, it is not said that either the non-separation itself or its recollection is inference; rather, whatever produces the experience of the imperceptible by means of that unique factor is accepted as the means (*sādhana*) or instrument (*karaṇa*)—that is, all of it is considered inference. It is for this purpose that the definition is formulated as "produced by a correct non-separation. Even for one who possesses the recollection of non-separation, a misconception or doubt may arise due to some cause, as in the case of the materialist (*Lokāyatika*); to exclude that, the word "correct" (*samyak*) is stated.

{The Buddhist position is that inferential cognition is erroneous (bhrānta)}; alternatively, the Śākyas assert that the cognition of the object of inference is indeed erroneous. As it has been said: "Even though it is erroneous, [it is a means of valid cognition] because of its connection with the object. The term "correct" (samyak) is included for the purpose of refuting that [position]. Indeed, it is not logical for an erroneous cognition to possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is erroneous, like the erroneous perception of [floating] hairs and so forth.

[Objection: But if this were the case, then because they are cognitions, all cognitions would result in being invalid—just like the cognition of two moons and so forth. That, however, is undesirable. Therefore, just as not everything is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) despite the lack of distinction in their being cognitions, but rather only that cognition which is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvādi*), so too an erroneous cognition (*bhrānti*) that is non-discrepant would be a valid means of knowledge. [Response: No, because this is contradictory. If it is an error, how can it be non-discrepant? For the meaning of "non-discrepancy" is the absence of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). If there is indeed correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for the cognition of the object indicated by the mark (*liṅgin*), then because of its non-deviation, it is precisely non-erroneous; how then could it be erroneous? [Objection: Is it not said that error is the apprehension of something as what it is not? And that nature belongs to the cognition of the indicated object as well, because it proceeds by determining an object in one's own appearance, even though that appearance is not the actual object. Thus, even for an erroneous cognition, there is non-discrepancy due to its non-deviation from the determined object; therefore, its status as a valid means of knowledge is accepted. Because of its indirect connection with the real entity (*vastu*), only this [inferential cognition] is non-deceptive regarding the object as it is determined, and not even the erroneous cognition produced by a fallacious mark (*liṅgābhāsa*).
Thus it has been said:

"Because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity, they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity]."
"Because those two [objects], though devoid of that form, are determined to have that form,
they are established as errors even though they do not actually deceive with respect to that form.
"For example, when two people run toward the light of a jewel and a lamp, respectively, perceiving them both to be a jewel..."
Even though there is no distinction among false cognitions, there is a distinction with respect to causal efficacy.

"Just as, even though inference and its semblance are both non-correspondent with reality (*ayathārtha*), their status as valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) is established by virtue of their conformity to purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). As for the claim that "error consists in apprehending something as what it is not," that is true; such an error certainly exists, but it does not have that [erroneous] form in the case of the cognition of the inferable fire itself. Furthermore, the proof stated here for its being an error—namely, "because it causes one to act by determining an object (*artha*) within its own non-objective appearance (*svapratibhāsa*)"—is not tenable, because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). For there is a determination of fire precisely with respect to fire, and not a determination of an object within a non-objective appearance of one's own.

[Objection: "In the cognition of the fire to be inferred (*anumeya*), it is the universal form (*sāmānyākāra*) that appears. Yet that [universal] is not the fire itself, because it is apprehended differently by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Moreover, since only the specific form (*viśiṣṭākāra*) possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), it alone has ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*); for it is precisely for that purpose that those seeking causal efficiency act. Therefore, even when there is no appearance of the object, activity occurs through the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object. [Reply: That too is incorrect. Indeed, it is not merely the universal form that appears in the inferential cognition; what then? It is the very object, such as fire, as qualified by the universal. And thus, there is a non-erroneous subsequent comprehension: "This was understood by me through inference.
