If it is argued that "because they have the same object, there would be the consequence of a single uniform mode of comprehension," we say: no; for we shall explain that a difference in appearance is possible precisely due to the difference in the instruments (*karaṇabheda*).

If it is argued that because the appearance of the object of inference (*anumeya*) does not cease even when the object itself has ceased, inferential cognition does not have a real entity as its object—this is not so. For it is accepted that the cognition of a yogin, though arising even when the entity has ceased, grasps that entity and is non-erroneous. Furthermore, inferential cognition is not erroneous because it is non-discrepant (*avisaṃvāditva*), just like perceptual cognition. If it is argued that even perception other than self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is indeed erroneous—this is not so, because it contradicts worldly convention and contradicts one's own treatises. Moreover, either all valid cognitions (*pramāṇajñāna*) would be non-erroneous just like self-cognition, or else even self-cognition would be non-erroneous, as there is no distinction [between them]. This too has been stated: "Of the cognitions of the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*)" and so forth.

{The Refutation of That} Regarding this, the following must be stated: Is the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*) alone the cause for the non-deceptiveness regarding that object, or rather [is it the connection] between those two and the cognitions of them? There is no dispute in the former alternative, since the relation of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is admitted. Whether that [concomitance] is restricted by identity (*tādātmya*) and causality (*tadutpatti*), or otherwise, we shall examine this later.

It should not be said that [the cognition] is [indirectly] connected even through a succession, because it is accepted that there is a direct relation of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between the mark (*liṅga*) and the bearer of the mark (*liṅgin*). Now, if it is argued that those two [the mark and its cognition] do not possess the capacity to bind that [object] because they are indirectly connected to the cognitions of them, we shall reply: even though there is no connection between the cognition of that [object] and a future object such as death or destruction, it is nonetheless non-deceptive regarding that object.

As for what was said—that those two [inference and verbal testimony] are devoid of that form (*tadrūpa*), and so forth—that is incorrect; for it would follow that even perceptual cognitions, which are devoid of the form of objects such as blue and yet function by determining those objects, would be erroneous. Indeed, it has already been explained at length that no cognition whatsoever possesses the nature of the object itself. Therefore, a cognition that does not deviate from the determined object is not erroneous, even if it is devoid of the object's form. For if it were erroneous, there would necessarily be some instance of non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*) with respect to something at some time.

As for what was said here—beginning with "between the light of a jewel and a lamp," and so forth—that too is not well-founded. For instance, after the activity [of reaching out] has occurred, a cognition of a jewel arises regarding the light of the jewel, but not regarding the jewel itself. Does sublation (bādhā) occur for that person or another investigator, or does it not? If it does not occur, how can its having the light as its object be established? [One might argue: "That [cognition] has the jewel as its object because it is non-deviant, since it is a cognition of a jewel, like a cognition of a jewel held in the hand. Now, if sublation does occur, then that cognition of the jewel is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) at all, because its object is sublated, like the illusion of [seeing] hairs and so forth. Furthermore, the quality of being a motivator (*pravartakatva*) exists even for memory, doubt, and error, yet they do not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge.

As for what was said—that [validity] is established in accordance with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)—that too is insubstantial. For memory, doubt, and error, while generating activity, sometimes lead to the attainment of the desired object, yet they do not possess the status of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, there is an inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) argument. If you argue that these lack the capacity to bring about the attainment of the object because they deviate from its location, form, and so forth, and therefore lack validity, then the example of the "jewel-cognition" (*maṇijñāna*) should not have been cited. Indeed, a jewel-cognition produced in relation to light emerging through a keyhole does not cause one to attain the jewel situated in that actual location. Nor is the validity of the cognition under dispute established merely by citing an invalid cognition as an example, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). The example is given only to show that even though there is no difference between them in being false cognitions of an object, there nonetheless exists a distinction [between them].

[Objection: What follows from this? [Response: Nothing, because only a specific distinction (*viśeṣa*) has been established. Now, if you argue that just as this distinction is established despite there being no difference in falsity (*mithyātva*), so too there may be a distinction between being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and not being one, despite there being no difference in their lack of correspondence with reality (*ayathārthatva*), we say: no, because an object cannot be established by mere analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Furthermore, it might be argued as follows: "Just as there is no difference in correctness (*asamyaktva*), yet between two cognitions—one arising in the continuum of one who is about to die and one arising in the continuum of one who is not—there is this distinction: the former is incapable of bringing about the intended purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as burning, while the latter is capable; likewise, even though there is no difference in their correspondence with reality (*yathārthatva*), you must admit this distinction as well, namely, that some [cognitions] are valid and some are invalid."

If it is argued that it is not logical to accept the non-validity of any cognition that corresponds to reality (*yathārtha*) because such a cognition lacks non-correspondence (*visaṃvāda*), then surely, since no cognition that does not correspond to reality (*ayathārtha*) lacks correspondence, its validity should not be accepted either. For there is no contradiction between a corresponding cognition and being non-correspondent to reality, since the very apprehension of non-correspondence to reality is itself the nature of non-correspondence. If it is asked how the attainment of an object can occur from a non-valid cognition, we reply: it has already been stated that if one who acts out of desire proceeds even on the basis of a non-valid cognition, and the object is present there, then he will necessarily attain it. This is not so; for validity is established solely in accordance with causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*). In that case, the cognition of an object for one about to die, or the cognition of an object that cannot be attained, would have to be considered a cognition for a person who has no desire [for that object]. Furthermore, causal efficacy, if not cognized by a valid means of knowledge, is itself like a non-entity and cannot establish the validity of the preceding cognition. If it is cognized by a valid means of knowledge, then in that case, the validity of that cognition of causal efficacy must be established by another cognition of causal efficacy, and that too by this one—leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). To this, he says:
If the validity of the preceding [cognition] is due to the absence of causal efficacy for the subsequent [object],
then why is that same validity not present for the subsequent [cognition], given the absence of causal efficacy at that very time?

"It is said that for that [cognition] whose status as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established even for a preceding one by way of the obstruction of its causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), its own causal efficacy occurring at that very time establishes its validity all the more so, because it is stated in general terms that 'non-discrepancy (*avisamvāda*) is the stability of causal efficacy. This is incorrect, because mere causal efficacy is not the prover of validity, since it is possible even in cognitions such as those of dreams or magical illusions. Rather, you have stated that "non-discrepancy is the stability of causal efficacy. Furthermore, you yourself have provided the explanation: "'Stability' of causal efficacy means its non-fluctuation or its firm establishment. Consequently, the non-fluctuation of causal efficacy is not established merely from the perception of causal efficacy, because even in dreams and the like, there is the mere perception of causal efficacy.

If it is argued that non-deviation (*avicalitatva*) is simply the very nature of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), and therefore, when that [efficiency] is known, how could its nature not be known? Then, in that case, the non-contradictory nature of the previous cognition of the object is also simply its own nature. And since that is known precisely from the cognition of that [object], the examination of it would be useless. If it is argued: "Even though its nature is known, delusion or doubt arises due to the similarity with a contradictory cognition; therefore, examination is performed for the sake of removing that"—then, even when there is a cognition of a non-deviating nature, as well as when there is a cognition of a deviating nature, delusion or doubt certainly occurs due to the similarity with a cognition of deviating causal efficiency. Therefore, for the sake of removing that [delusion or doubt], examination must indeed be performed.
Validity [of cognition] is established by worldly convention; this is the Buddhist position.

It should not be done. Why? Because it has been said: “Validity [is established] through worldly convention (*vyavahāra*); the scripture removes delusion. Indeed, even one who is well-trained is not able to establish validity by means of another valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). To explain: perception (*pratyakṣa*), for its part, does not know its own validity because it is a cognition of its own form alone. For when there is a cognition of the mere nature of a cognition, there is no thought, “This is a valid means of knowledge. For the comprehension of its own form occurs intrinsically (*svataḥ*), not that of another form. Perception is indeed a direct apprehension, and direct apprehension belongs to the form itself, not to the object to be reached which serves as a qualification at the time of attainment. And validity consists in the non-deviation from the object to be reached. Nor is there a grasping of the connection with that object when the object to be reached is not grasped. And that which is not thus determined cannot be determined as a valid means of knowledge. Furthermore, the engagement with the form present before one is common to all cognitions; by that, the inclusion of a connection with a future form is not achieved. Nor is there an inclusion of a connection with a previous form by means of a cognition of future purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, because its nature is the self-cognition of its own form, there is no inclusion of a connection in each individual case, nor is a collective possibility, since the cognition of the means and the cognition of purposeful action occur sequentially. As for the recollection occurring at a later time, proceeding according to experience, it conceptualizes the two as unrelated. But if it abandons the actual experience, it is merely corrupted by that [conceptualization]; therefore, no understanding of the connection arises from it. Consequently, since that connection is not grasped, how could there be an understanding of it later through inference based on similarity to what was seen? Thus, there is no means for the understanding of validity. The comprehension of the form itself occurs intrinsically, but not that of validity. If it is argued that validity is the very form itself—since that which is expressed by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is not distinct from it—that is incorrect.
Validity (*prāmāṇya*) has the nature of cognition and is concomitant with the nature of the object to be attained (*prāpya*).

It is stated that when there is the apprehension of the mere nature [of cognition], that [validity] is not apprehended. (197) For validity is not merely the nature of cognition itself, because its establishment as such depends upon its connection with the nature of the object to be attained. And it has already been demonstrated that this [connection] is not apprehended. Consequently, there is merely the self-awareness of one's own nature, which entails neither engagement nor withdrawal; thus, there is no occasion for the doctrine of duality (*bhedavāda*). Therefore, a discerning person should never engage in activity toward anything, nor withdraw from anything.

How, then, is validity established as being excluded from invalidity? It has been demonstrated that validity is conventional (*sāṃvyavahārika*) by means of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). And when worldly transaction is investigated, it simply falls apart. In that case, if satisfaction is found with this much, then nothing further need be done; for there is indeed liberation from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), since that [cyclic existence] is ultimately non-existent. Alternatively, if cyclic existence is established by worldly convention, then the distinction between valid and invalid cognition also certainly exists; thus, no effort need be exerted to establish validity.

Furthermore, by one who establishes conventional validity (*sāṃvyavahārika-prāmāṇya*), it is effectively stated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the single direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, relying on the well-known relationship based upon inference established merely through worldly convention, one proceeds toward the cognition of the means for touch and so forth, by seeing [the object] as "this is the means for achieving purposeful action" (*arthakriyā-sādhana*). Subsequently, even without inferential habituation (*abhyāsānumāna*), activity occurs from mere appearance alone; thus, even direct perception is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it is a motivator of action. To this, it is replied: "Validity is [established] by way of worldly convention. But surely, by visual perception, only color-form (*rūpa*) is perceived, not the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*); likewise, only the present is [perceived], not the future which is to be attained; and similarly, only what is seen by oneself, not what is seen by another. How, then, can there be validity through the attainment of one thing based on the perception of another? It has been stated in this regard: "The comprehension of its own nature is intrinsic (*svataḥ*)."
Furthermore: From the perspective of conventional usage, the establishment of its status as a means of valid cognition [is justified] because of its unity;
due to the non-difference of place and other factors, the unity of the substance is designated. (199)

This has been stated: "Validity [is established] by means of practical activity (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, relying upon the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) as established by practical activity, there is the designation of validity based on the determination that "whatever was seen is the very same thing that is attained. And that determination of unity arises from the non-difference of place, time, and so forth; that non-difference, too, arises because it is produced by a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) capable of effecting that [non-difference]. Likewise, even in the case of future and past [moments], there is the conceit of unity due to their belonging to the same continuum and because they perform the same purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). From that [conceit], there is purposeful activity; and when the purposeful action is accomplished, the status of being a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is established. Therefore, the establishment of validity occurs solely through practical activity.

"If, then, validity is established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), what is the purpose of the treatises on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? Even that which is indicated by a treatise does not become such merely by the word of the text, but rather only through non-contradiction with worldly convention. If that [non-contradiction] exists, the treatise is useless. To this he says: "The treatise is for the removal of delusion. If the nature of the means of valid cognition is understood from worldly convention, why are there mutually contradictory treatises on their definitions? Consequently, even regarding worldly convention, there is indeed disagreement among those engaged in worldly affairs. For instance:
Not everyone understands validity through conventional usage;
therefore, the definition of the means of valid cognition is characterized by mutual contradiction.
By means of such pramāṇas as direct perception, the next world is not apprehended.
Another says, "This is from scripture," and therefore it is not [established] by means of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*).
Consequently—
through the consideration of worldly convention, the treatise (*śāstra*) brings about the cessation of delusion.
The failure to remember what preceded and followed is prevented by this very scripture.

For this very reason, delusion is dispelled only by the scripture spoken by the Omniscient One, and not by any other; thus, in the ultimate sense, the word of the Omniscient One alone is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The ultimate truth is that the cognition of the Omniscient One alone is the authoritative means of knowledge, and nothing else. Nothing else possesses the status of an authoritative means of knowledge, because it is impossible for it to encompass all objects of knowledge (*prameya*).
"There can be no apprehension of the relationship between cause and effect by means of that which is non-pervasive.

For the relation of cause and effect—consisting of a concomitance that pervades past, future, and present times and places—is certainly not an object of knowledge for one who is not omniscient; because perception grasps only the present and proximate locations, and inference does not apply [in such a case].
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: as for the claim that "validity [is established] by means of worldly transaction" (*vyavahāra*), is that transaction itself a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is not a valid means of knowledge, how can validity be established by it? For nothing whatsoever can be established on the basis of what is not a valid means of knowledge, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Consequently, it would follow that the validity of all treatises (*śāstra*) and the stability of entities such as "permanent" (*sthira*) and so forth could be established, since mere worldly transaction is possible everywhere.

Now, if validity is established by means of worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), which itself has become a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇabhūta*), that is incorrect; for you do not admit any other means of knowledge apart from the two [accepted] means of knowledge. Even if it were included within those two, since conventional practice is already refuted by the very refutation of them, validity cannot be established on its basis.

If, on the other hand, the establishment of validity is based solely on unexamined worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), even so, since mere unexamined practice is indistinguishable everywhere, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result, as has already been stated. If it is argued that the establishment of valid cognition proceeds from that practice which is non-contradictory in all respects, this is not so; for a practice that is non-contradictory in every respect is impossible, and because contradiction (*vipratipatti*) is possible everywhere.

Furthermore, that which is treated as authoritative even by those who have not studied the scriptures is indeed a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). In that case, the Vedas and so forth are certainly *pramāṇas*, because their status as authoritative is well-known to all the world. If you argue that validity is established through worldly practice only for cognitions whose objects are perceptible, but not for cognitions whose objects are the contents of the Vedas and such, then have you now taken refuge in the Lokāyata (Materialist) school? And we shall state its refutation as well. Moreover, the validity of the cognitions of the Buddha and others would not exist [under your view]. Alternatively, if you claim that the reason why users of language treat certain cognitions as valid—namely, those cognitions caused by the attainment or avoidance of the means for pleasure and pain well-known in this world—is a reason found elsewhere as well, then that too is indeed a *pramāṇa*. In that case, validity is treated by users of language precisely where non-doubtfulness and non-erroneousness are perceived; for when the opposite is perceived, one observes the treatment of invalidity. Therefore, validity must be determined elsewhere only through the perception of non-doubtfulness and non-erroneousness, and not on account of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), nor from the connection with an object to be attained, nor from being a motivator; for even in the case of cognitions of objects to be disregarded or of dying persons, although they are *pramāṇas*, causal efficiency and the like are impossible, whereas they do exist even in memories, doubts, and erroneous cognitions, as has been stated. Furthermore, how non-doubtfulness and non-erroneousness are understood through a *pramāṇa* was already explained previously, in the investigation of the general definition of *pramāṇa*.

As it has been said: "In the cognition of the means for [achieving] touch and so forth through perception, people act; subsequently, due to repeated practice, even without inference, action occurs from mere appearance alone; thus, perception is also a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because it causes one to act. To this, it is replied: "Validity is established by worldly convention (*vyavahāra*). That is incorrect; even from extreme habituation, an action toward something else is not possible when one has not seen that other thing. Indeed, no one is ever observed, upon seeing fire, to proceed toward water while seeking water. Therefore, the claim that there is a conventional distinction between the memory of a relation and inferential knowledge—which arise with great rapidity due to extreme habituation and are preceded by perception—because they are indistinguishable from perception, is also false. This is a false conceit of the Śākya (Buddhist), who fails to perceive the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) and thinks that action proceeds from perceptual knowledge alone. Furthermore, if action toward the unperceived means of touch and so forth were possible simply from the sight of color, then who could prevent the Cārvāka from asserting that action toward fire and the like also occurs simply from the sight of smoke and the like?
The refutation of the claim that the unity of the whole is established merely by conventional usage.

As for what was also said—that by relying on the unity of the whole (*avayavin*) as established in conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), the determination that "that very thing was seen, that very thing is attained" constitutes a conventional usage of non-validity (*apramāṇatā*)—that too is incorrect. For if one accepts the unity of the whole, there is a contradiction with its refutation; and if one does not accept it, then the conventional usage of validity (*prāmāṇya*) which is established based upon it would also necessarily not be accepted. Indeed, no person of sound mind, while perceiving the objects of dreams, magical illusions, and the like as false, would then perceive the validity of the cognitions thereof based upon those [objects]. If it is argued that validity is accepted merely through conventional usage and not from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), then is there now no such thing as valid cognition at all from the perspective of ultimate reality? And if so, then just like the whole and so forth, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and other such properties—which are established by means of a cognition that is not ultimately real—would also lack ultimate reality; consequently, the apprehension of them would be entirely useless.

Now, if there exists some ultimate (*pāramārthika*) means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), from what is its establishment [attained]? It cannot be through conventional practice (*saṃvyavahāra*) alone, because for that which is established by such means, there is a contradiction with its being ultimate; or else, it would follow that all means of valid cognition are ultimately real. For this distinction—that "this one has ultimate validity" while "that one is merely conventional"—is not established by conventional practice alone. Nor is there any other means for the apprehension of validity, since you yourself have previously rejected such alternatives. Furthermore, if all conventional practice were real, then every means of valid cognition established by it would likewise be unreal. And if those means of valid cognition were unreal, then the afterlife and so forth established by them would also be unreal, just like the objects established by the means of valid cognition produced by a dream-convention. If the afterlife and so forth were unreal, then the scripture (*śāstra*) would be entirely purposeless.

Therefore, the claim that "conventional practice, when subjected to analysis, falls apart" is also false, because it merely attributes the status of "analysis" to what is actually a semblance of analysis. For analysis is said to be a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and it is not logical for that which destroys its own basis to be a means of valid cognition.
{This is a restatement of the Buddhist position on the nature of validity.}

As for what was also stated—that "the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) consists in the non-deviation from the object to be attained," and so forth—that is incorrect; because every intelligent person, when acting upon the cognition of an object such as a transient lamp, even if that object is not actually reached, nevertheless maintains the validity of that cognition by observing its signs (*taccihna*).

But surely, if this object is not attained and does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*), then there would be no activity at all for a discerning person seeking a result, because the desired object remains uncertain. If, however, one acts out of doubt, then that [cognition] lacks validity, since doubt is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Now, if it is argued: "There may indeed be doubt regarding the goal (*upeya*), but the status of being a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatā*) is not thereby lost; since the means (*upāya*) is certain, why should it not be a valid cognition (*pramā*) on that account? (201)

Indeed, it is not the desire to avoid doubt regarding the goal (*upeya*) that motivates action, for action proceeds everywhere merely through certainty regarding the means (*upāya*). Therefore, once there is certainty regarding the means, let authoritative persons (*prāmāṇika*) proceed like farmers and the like. That is incorrect; because:
"Every person engages in activity or desists from it out of a desire for the goal. If there is doubt regarding that [goal], how can there be valid cognition? (202)

Regarding that for which a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is sought, since there is doubt concerning the goal (*upeya*), what kind of verbal artifice is this [to call it] a "means of valid cognition"? Is it not the case that an object must be made known by a means of valid cognition, but the causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) need not be performed? For how can causal efficacy—which occurs later, arising from some specific collection of conditions—be made known? That too is incorrect: if the undertaking is for the sake of something and that very thing is not accomplished, how can that whose connection to the goal is unestablished be called a "prover" (*sādhaka*)? (203)

A discerning person is intent on investigating the validity of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with the thought, "May I attain the accomplishment of my desired object through this means of knowledge," and not otherwise; for otherwise, it would be nothing but a mere whim. Furthermore, if an object is revealed but does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārī*), how does it differ from the non-object, such as the hairs perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia? If it is argued that at some time a causal function occurs in that case, but not in the instance of ophthalmia and so forth—then how does one who desires that object act? Indeed, one who acts out of doubt has not acted based on a means of knowledge; for a means of knowledge is determinative, not a producer of doubt. If there is certainty regarding the performance of a causal function, then how can there be such certainty when the causal function itself is uncertain? If it is argued that the object which accomplishes the causal function is shown by that means of knowledge, but the causal function does not occur due to some deficiency elsewhere and this is not a fault of the means of knowledge—that too is incorrect.

If it is argued that the non-informativeness of a means of cognition (*māna*) is not a defect, then since there would be no other defect for it, everything would be valid cognition (*pramā*). [Objection:
"That by which something is cognized—that is, determined as a desired object—is a *pramāṇa*; and since that which does not inform lacks the power of determination, it is indeed not a *pramāṇa*."
{The refutation thereof}

This [objection] is untenable. First, as for the claim that there would be no activity on the part of a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*), that is not so; for it has already been stated previously that even for a discerning person, activity is possible through doubt regarding an object and through inference. Therefore, the claim that its validity (*prāmāṇya*) does not exist because of such activity is incorrect, as the two factors are unrelated (*vyadhikaraṇatvāt*). Even if the cognition consisting of doubt regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) lacks validity, what does that imply for the invalidity of the preceding cognition which ascertains the nature of the object? By this, the argument beginning with "because of the desire for the goal" is also refuted. For these two do not possess identity (*tādātmya*), such that the doubt regarding the goal would entail the invalidity of the prior ascertainment of the object.

As for what was said—"That for whose sake this undertaking [is made]," and so forth—that too is not correct; for we observe that those who seek purposeful action engage in the means to achieve it simply by discerning mere suitability, just as those seeking cloth engage with threads and the like.

Furthermore, it is also incorrect to argue: "If an object is revealed but does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyākārī*), how is it different from an illusion such as the hairs perceived by one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*), which are non-objects (*anartha*)? For the object perceived by one with ophthalmia is determined to be unreal by a subverting cognition (*bādhakapratyaya*). However, in this case [of a valid perception], even though no causal function arises, its distinct nature is determined through the observation of other specific features. Thus, how can there be no difference?

As for the objection, "How can there be certainty regarding the means of achieving that [purpose] when the causal efficiency [of the cause] is not perceived?", it is not so; because [certainty] has already been established previously. Once the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been ascertained beforehand—namely, that such an effect occurs only when such causes exist and not when they do not—even a discerning person (*prekṣāvān*) proceeds toward those causes, having determined them to be of such a nature, when seeking an effect of that kind. If it is asked, "How was it established at the beginning?", we reply: no, because there is no beginning; we shall demonstrate that this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) is beginningless.

But surely causes do not necessarily produce their effects, since obstacles and deficiencies are observed in the interim; so how can a discerning person who desires that effect engage in such causes? No; for engagement is possible even from the mere possibility of a result, just as a discerning person who desires life engages in eating and so forth.

For even a discerning person (*prekṣāvān*) is not able to engage in action only after having ascertained the attainment of a result, because there is the possibility of doubting a deviation from the attainment of the result due to the uncertainty regarding the maintenance of the body and so forth. And for one who does not engage, there would be the loss of all human goals (*puruṣārtha*) and misfortune; therefore, a discerning person would become no different from one lacking discernment. Consequently, a discerning person engages by ascertaining the suitability of the means and, while not seeing the absence of obstacles to them, merely conceiving the possibility of attaining the result—not from the certainty of that [attainment] itself.

As for the claim that "the fact that [a cognition] does not make known [anything other than its own object] is not a defect for a means of valid cognition (*māna*) if... and so forth, that too is incorrect, because [a cognition] makes known its own object. For all cognitions possess validity precisely through making known their own objects. In this regard, it is illogical that a cognition should lack validity simply because it does not make known another object; for it is not reasonable to say that a cognition of color (*rūpa*) is invalid because it does not make known touch (*sparśa*). If it were so, all cognitions would be invalid, since there is no difference in their failure to make known other objects. Furthermore, regarding the cognition of a means (*sādhana*), how could it be invalid if it does not make known its result, which is a different object? If you ask, "How can there be certainty regarding its being a means if the result is not ascertained?", we say no; for this has already been addressed by the statement beginning with "because it was already ascertained previously. Therefore, even if there is no certainty regarding the attainment of the result, the cognition of the nature of the means—whether one has acted or not—possesses a validity established by the observation of specific characteristics (*viśeṣadarśana*) and is not invalid. Consequently, the assertion that "validity is established only through a connection with the form of what is to be attained" is entirely without proof. For instance, objects such as the ornaments of a king's wife or the stars cannot actually be attained, yet wise people do not fail to act toward them.

Moreover, it is observed that the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of that cognition is established precisely through the perception of specific qualities and the accomplishment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*). If that were denied, then even the establishment of validity through the attainment of the object would not occur, because there is no difference in the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) in either case. Likewise, a cognition of an object that is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) is not invalid. Even if it is not investigated due to a lack of utility, does it follow from this alone that it simply does not exist? Or rather, for the sake of ending dispute, it is indeed seen that some seekers of knowledge establish the validity of a cognition of an object to be disregarded based on the perception of its specific qualities.
The validity of knowledge regarding that which is to be disregarded.

[Objection: Surely everyone who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) engages in the search for valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), not out of mere habit; how then can knowledge of an object that is to be disregarded (*upekṣaṇīya*) be considered valid cognition? [Reply: This is not correct. For the eyes and other sense organs do not produce valid cognitive knowledge by depending on a person’s pursuit of a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Rather, when the completeness of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, valid cognitive knowledge arises even for a person who does not desire it, and even regarding objects such as useless grass or insects. For the function of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists merely in the apprehension of an object, not in [prompting] activity and so forth, since those depend on desire and the like. It is also incorrect to say that desire and so forth are themselves inference (*anumāna*), because they occur even in the absence of the perception of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so on. However, it is reasonable that in the investigation of valid cognition, the engagement of discerning people (*prekṣāvat*) occurs precisely through their pursuit of a goal, not out of habit. Nevertheless, in order to eliminate the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*) in the definition of valid cognition, knowledge of an object to be disregarded must also be examined in general by discerning people—just as pseudo-cognitions (*tadābhāsa*) are examined to avoid the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*), or just as a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*) examines the inference of a *śiṃśapā* tree and so forth. [Objection: If something is not accepted, it must all be abandoned; therefore, there is no such thing as an object to be disregarded. [Reply: That is incorrect, because three types of objects are perceived according to the distinction of their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). To explain: that which is accepted with the thought that it is a human goal, or with the thought that it is a means to achieve it, is "to be acquired" (*upādeya*). That which is desired to be avoided with effort, with the thought that it is harmful, or with the thought that it is a means to achieve harm, is "to be abandoned" (*heya*). But that for which there is neither the thought that it is a human goal nor harm, nor the thought that it is a means to either, is "to be disregarded" (*upekṣaṇīya*). Therefore, since even knowledge of an object to be disregarded is a valid cognition, being a prompter (*pravartaka*) and so forth is not the basis for the conventional usage of the term "valid cognition."
Refutation of the view that self-awareness is the sole direct perception.

Furthermore, the claim that from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*) self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) alone is the only direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the mere babbling of those with extremely dull intellects; for self-awareness has already been refuted at length. For one who asserts that self-awareness alone is the only direct perception, there is a contradiction with such statements as "the knowledge of the Omniscient One (*sarvajña*) is indeed a valid means of cognition" (*pramāṇa*); for omniscience is not tenable if there is only the awareness of a single present moment of consciousness. Moreover, direct perception is held to be non-erroneous (*abhrānta*). If, therefore, the Omniscient One possesses a direct perception whose object is all things, then the statement "all [cognition] is erroneous regarding its objective support" (*ālambane bhrama*) is likewise the speech of a drunkard. If you argue that there is no contradiction because even the Omniscient One’s cognition of all objects is admitted to be erroneous, then it is truly excellent how the Omniscient One’s omniscience is thus described! Consequently, the authority of the scripture based upon that [Omniscient One] should also be accepted. Thus, this person—being obsessed by attachment to his own side—is to be ignored, for his words are not to be heeded as he reveals the delusion even of the Buddha and other founders of rival sects.
{Refutation of the view that "validity is established by worldly convention"}

Even among those engaged in worldly activity (*vyavahārin*), some transactions have false objects while others have real objects. How, then, can validity be established by means of an unexamined transaction? The examination of that [transaction] consists in the practice of reflecting upon the discrimination between reality and its opposite regarding both types of transactions; for this reason, the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is for the sake of practicing the thorough knowledge of the discrimination between reality and its opposite concerning *dharma* and so forth. As for what was said—that "the scripture (*śāstra*) is the remover of delusion"—that is true: a scripture whose root is non-erroneous knowledge certainly removes delusion. But your scripture has its root in erroneous knowledge; being practiced, it only increases delusion, like an oblation [increasing] the fire. Furthermore, as for what was said—that there is no possibility of a means for attaining validity—that too is incorrect; because such a means has already been shown previously. Moreover, later on we shall explain the means for grasping the relation of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) even between two things occurring at different times. Furthermore, just as in the case of attaining validity, one must follow worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) itself, since there is no other means for attaining the recognition of error either.
In the system of the Sugata, the apprehension of error is impossible.

For instance: perception functions only by cognizing its own essential nature (*svarūpa*); from that, there is no cognition of error. Indeed, upon the mere awareness of the essential nature, the thought "this is erroneous" does not occur. Furthermore, error consists in the inversion regarding the object of apprehension (*grāhya*). And that [error] cannot be cognized as long as the inversion of the object of apprehension is not cognized. Nor does that very cognition arise with the nature of cognizing an inversion regarding its own object of apprehension, because such an inversion does not appear [in the cognition]. For if it did appear, a person who is mistaken would not act out of the conceit of having attained the object already cognized. Nor is error cognized by a subsequent cognition following the activity, because at that time the erroneous cognition has already passed away. As for the claim that "error consists simply in causing one to act toward something other [than the object]," by whom is this known? Certainly, that very cognition does not know itself in this way: "I have acted toward something other than the object of apprehension," or "I am the cause of activity. Nor does a cognition grasping the nature of a single self know any relation to a self; nor is the cognition of a relation possible through the mere awareness of a single form. For instance:
The cognition of a relation between two things does not arise from the perception of a single form;
rather, the awareness of a relation occurs only when there is the grasping of the essential natures of both.

Furthermore, in your view, there is no cognition whatsoever that apprehends two distinct intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*). Moreover, it is by a subsequent cognition alone that error is established. Now, would that subsequent cognition apprehend the opposite of the object to be grasped; or would it be a cognizer that determines a form dissimilar to the form of the object to be grasped; or would it be a cognizer of an activity directed elsewhere? Consequently, because both the error and the subsequent cognition consist in the self-cognition of their own respective forms, there is no apprehension of a relationship between them individually, nor even collectively, since they are separated by time. Furthermore, the memory that arises at a later time conceptualizes the two as unrelated, and because it abandons the actual experience, it is itself corrupted; thus, there is no comprehension of the relationship from it. Therefore, since that relationship is not grasped, how could there be comprehension through inference later on, based on the similarity of appearances?

There is no means of establishing [the status of] error. If that were established through conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), then inferential cognition (*anumānajñāna*) would have to be understood as erroneous; for there is no conventional usage of "error" regarding a correct inferential cognition. Indeed, the conventional usage of "error" is never observed in the case of a non-contradictory cognition. Furthermore, [if one argues that inference is erroneous] because it functions by determining an object in its own manifestation despite the object not being real—this is not a valid proof, as it is sublated by conventional usage itself. Moreover, if that [conventional usage] were accepted, then even validity (*prāmāṇya*) would not exist, due to the reasoning stated previously. Furthermore, since perception too would function by determining the attainment of what has been reached even when it is not actually reached, perception would also be erroneous. Since conventional non-error is common to both, how could inference alone be erroneous? Thus, it is established that the inclusion of the term "correct" (*samyak*) is for the purpose of making known the non-erroneous nature of inferential cognition.
The purpose of the term "indirect" (parokṣa).

But surely, that experience for which the recollection of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva-smṛti*) is the unique cause must itself have a remote (*parokṣa*) form. Why, then, is the term "remote" mentioned [separately]? It is not so, because its purpose is to refute a misconception. Some hold that remoteness resides in the object (*artha*), like "cowness" (*gotva*), and does not reside in the cognition (*jñāna*); this is incorrect. For it would follow that all perceivers would apprehend it without distinction, just as they do with blue and other colors. Consequently, it could not be the case that the very same thing is remote for one person and non-remote for another. Indeed, even in the case of blue and such, it is not experienced by some in the form of blue and by others in the form of non-blue. If it is argued that it is like the conventional usage of "far" (*para*) and "near" (*apara*), we say no; for that has a different cause. The conventional usage of "far" and "near" is certainly not based on a universal (*sāmānya*); what then? It has been stated that it is based on the cognition of the greater or lesser number of intervening conjunctions (*saṃyoga*). Even the state of being "more" or "less" is based on relative dependence (*apekṣā*), as seen in expressions such as "a pillar is farther than a wall" or "closer than a pillar. However, the conventional usage of "remote" and "non-remote" regarding objects is not based on qualities (*guṇa*) and the like; otherwise, there would be no means of understanding the erroneous nature [of cognitions] regarding universals (*sāmānya*) and other categories.

Furthermore, since that [object] is apprehended through non-transactional usage (*avyavahāra*), inferential knowledge should not be understood as erroneous. For there is no establishment of error even in the case of correct inferential knowledge, because we observe the distinction between the "remote" (*parokṣa*) and the "proximate" (*aparokṣa*) in practice. Nor is this distinction dependent on external objects, because it is invariably dependent on the knower, as is evident from such cognitions as "this is proximate for me" and "that is remote for you. If it is argued that "the remote" (*parokṣa*) is that which is beyond the sense organ (*akṣāt paraḥ*), while the "proximate" (*aparokṣa*) is other than that, we say no; for it has already been explained at length previously that even though the mind is the object of the sense organ in the case of an inferable entity such as the self, it is still considered "remote. Therefore, just like the states of being experienced (*anubhūtatva*), remembered (*smṛtatva*), or seen (*dṛṣṭatva*), and just like the state of being undetermined (*anadhyavasitatva*), the "remote" and the "proximate" are based solely on specific qualities of cognition. And there is no fault even if one accepts specific universals (*jāti*) of "remoteness" and "proximity" among individual instances of cognition, just as there are universals such as "doubt-ness" (*sandehatva*) or "memory-ness" (*smṛtitva*). A lack of distinction in cognition is also observed due to the connection with a universal and its possessor. For example: through the connection with the universal of heat, there is a "hot touch"; through its connection, fire is "hot," and a stone is "hot. In the same way, through the connection with the universal of remoteness, an experience is "remote," and through its connection, an object is "remote. Just as with the object itself, there is also the conventional usage of "proximate" even regarding a remote experience when it is the object of a proximate experience; and conversely, there is the conventional usage of "remote" even regarding a proximate experience when it is the object of a remote experience. Thus, everything is well-established. This very point, although already examined, has been examined again after observing the diversity of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), for the sake of easy understanding.

Alternatively, some say that if inference were to apprehend an object already apprehended by perception, it would be redundant; whereas if it were to apprehend an object not apprehended by perception, its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would be impossible due to defects such as being secondary (*gauṇatva*). To refute this, the term "indirect" (*parokṣa*) is included. The meaning is that an indirect experience arising through the power of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is indeed perceived as correct. It is impossible to declare that inference, which is the instrument for that [experience], lacks validity, because that would contradict the practical conventions of all the world. {The invalidity of inference [is asserted] because of its being secondary.}
But how is it that they deny inference, which is well-established for all the world? To this it is said:
"Because a means of valid cognition must not be figurative, the object [of knowledge] is difficult to obtain through inference."

"Because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is non-figurative (*agauṇa*)," this is the reason for the refutation. This is what is meant: the validity of a means of valid cognition is established by virtue of its having a non-figurative object, as is the case with perception (*pratyakṣa*). Now, it is impossible to say that inference (*anumāna*) has a non-figurative object; for instance, the subject (*dharmin*) itself is not the probandum (*sādhya*), because it is already established; nor is the property (*dharma*) alone the probandum, since it is already established elsewhere; nor is their collection (*samudāya*) the probandum, because in that case the reason cannot be shown to be a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), nor can a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with it be apprehended. Therefore, for the sake of apprehending the concomitance, the property (*dharma*) alone must be figuratively treated as the probandum, and for the sake of grasping the "property-of-the-subject" status, the subject (*dharmin*) alone must be treated as the "subject" (*pakṣa*). Thus, it has been stated by the proponents of inference: "The subject is the locus (*dharmin*), because the term for the whole is figuratively applied to the part. And this being the case, it is difficult to obtain certainty regarding an object from an inference that is assisted by a figurative "property-of-the-subject" and a figurative "concomitance. In that regard, the lack of cognitive force (*abodhakatva*) is seen in the case of a figurative occurrence in the subject, such as: "This boy is capable of burning, etc., because he is fire (*agnitvāt*). Likewise, there is a lack of proving power even in the case of a figurative concomitance, such as: "Sound is impermanent, because it is audible (*śrāvaṇatvāt*), like pleasure (*sukha*), etc. Here, the concomitance is established by figuratively attributing audibility to pleasure and so on, based on their being pervaded by the word "audible."
{Invalidity due to the impossibility of the proof-operation}:

Furthermore, the probandum is stated in dependence upon the proof-operation. If that [operation] is already accomplished, the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth is useless, because its purpose has already been established. If it is not accomplished, in relation to what is the determination of the subject and other factors made? If one resorts to the metaphorical treatment of the future as if it were the past, that is precisely the fault of inference being figurative; and since there is no primary inference, the figurative one is also untenable. {Invalidity due to the impossibility of concomitance}.

Furthermore, inference is untenable because the conceptualization of the probandum (*sādhya*) is impossible. To explain: since the locus (*dharmin*) is already established, it cannot be the probandum. If it is the property (*dharma*) that is the probandum, is it of the nature of a universal (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) or of the nature of a particular (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*)? What follows from this? If it is a universal, there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatā*); if it is a particular, there is a lack of positive concomitance (*anugama*). This is because a universal characterized by "possessing fire," "impermanence," and so forth, is already established in some instances; therefore, its proof would be redundant. As for a [probandum] qualified by a specific place and so on, there is non-establishment precisely due to the absence of concomitance. For there is no instance of concomitance anywhere between a fire located on a mountain and an impermanence residing in sound.
Because it is impossible to apprehend invariable concomitance, [the inference] lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge.

Furthermore, inference is not a valid means of knowledge because the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) cannot be apprehended. Indeed, it is impossible for perception to grasp the infinite individual instances of smoke and fire as having entered into a state of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*). If the inseparable connection were grasped between mere universals (*sāmānyamātra*), then the relationship of the signified and the signifier would belong to those two alone; otherwise, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, inference would become useless if its object were merely the universal, since that [universal] is already established and because it does not serve a human purpose (*apuruṣārtha*). Likewise, even the particulars possessing those universals cannot be grasped precisely because they are infinite. Nor is there a comprehension of the pervaded-pervader relationship upon grasping a single instance, for one observes deviation (*vyabhicāra*) even when grasping thousands of cows with their calves. Thus, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not grasped by perception, nor by inference itself, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
Because it is contradictory, it lacks authoritative validity.

Furthermore, because contradictory inferences (*viruddhānumāna*) and contradictions (*virodha*) are possible in all cases, inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Among these, the types of contradiction are first stated: (1) the absence of being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) by the probans (*sādhana*) intended by the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) in the case under discussion; (2) the absence of being the locus of the property to be proven by the probans employed by either the proponent of the proof or the proponent of the refutation; (3) the absence of being the locus of the property to be proven by the probans intended by the proponent which has become an object of the senses for both the proponent of the proof and the opponent; and (4) the absence of being the locus of the property to be proven by the probans intended by the proponent which is connected to a time other than the past and future. These [four] apply universally (*sarvagāḥ*). Counter-probans (*pratisādhana*) are also possible everywhere, as follows: the absence of possessing fire connected to this place and time; the absence of sound being a specific quality of space (*ākāśa*), the absence of its being perceptible by the ear; the absence of pleasure and so forth residing in the self (*ātman*); the absence of residing in a locus that is omnipresent; the absence of the earth and so forth having an omniscient creator as their antecedent; and the absence of having a creator distinct from the body and so forth. In this manner, the types of contradiction are to be seen in all inferences.
It lacks the status of a valid means of knowledge because it contradicts inference.

Now, the contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) is demonstrated: The subject (*dharmin*) is not the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as intended by the proponent of the present argument, because it is either the property or the subject itself, or because it is a constituent part of the meaning of the word "probandum" (*sādhya*), just like the property to be proven. Alternatively, the subject in the present context is not the object [of the inference] characterized by the property to be proven, for the two reasons stated previously, just like the subject itself. It is not either of the two—the subject which is the locus of the property to be proven or the property itself—because it is the subject that possesses the property to be proven, just like a jar (*ghaṭa*) and so forth. This thesis (*pakṣa*) does not possess the property to be proven in the present context, because it is distinct from both the thesis and its counter-example (*vipakṣa*), just like the counter-example; or because it is distinct from the thesis and a donkey’s horn, just like a donkey’s horn. This region is not possessed of fire distinct from the fire regarding which there is a disagreement between the proponent and the opponent, because it is a region, and because of its existence, knowability, and so forth, just like any other region different from it. This region does not possess the fire under discussion, because a donkey’s horn lacks smoke, just like a donkey’s horn. A jar existing at the same time as the establishment of the smoke—which has become the probans (*sādhana*) employed by our opponent at a time distinct from past and future—is not a jar, because it is like a flower in the sky or a lotus leaf. In this manner, the contradiction with inference is to be seen in all inferences.
Non-authoritativeness [of the reason] due to its being a contradictory non-deviant.

Likewise, inference is non-authoritative by virtue of being subject to the fallacy of the "non-erroneous contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārin*). But what, then, is this "non-erroneous contradictory"? Some say that there is a difference between the "non-erroneous contradictory" and the "contradiction of inference" merely in name. That is incorrect, because it would result in the pointlessness of mentioning them separately. Therefore, when an inference stated as a sublater produces the cognition of a sublated and a sublater, it is called a "contradiction of inference. When, however, it is perceived as having identical characteristics and produces doubt, it is the "non-erroneous contradictory. Thus, the difference [between the two] is due to the difference in their effects.
Regarding the contradictory [reason], there is contradiction by inference and so forth, as well as its refutation.

Now, if at some point one were to say that "by means of the method of refutation (*parihāravidhāna*), the proof (*sādhana*) is established as having the nature of a proof," here too the path of refutation is demonstrated: In that regard, first concerning the contradictory [reason], the contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*) is stated as the refutation—[the thesis is]: "The subject (*dharmin*) does not possess the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) as its locus when confronted by a contradictory proof put forward by another, because it is devoid of all entities other than the property and the subject, just like the property to be proven. Nor does this reason prove the absence of the specific quality under dispute regarding the subject in question, because the reason and the subject are distinct from each other, just like the property.

"A pot existing at the same time as the reason that proves the absence of a specific property under dispute which is distinct from the object [of the dispute] is not a pot, because it lacks the horn-ness of a rabbit's horn, like the son of a barren woman. A pot existing at the same time as either the proponent or the opponent of the proof or refutation, delimited by the time of presenting the argument that proves the absence of a specific property under dispute which is distinct from the object, is not a pot, because it is one of the two—existent or non-existent—like a cloth. A pot existing at the same time as either the proponent or the opponent of the proof or refutation, characterized by the time of presenting the argument that proves the absence of a specific property under dispute regarding the subject in question, which is included among all entities known by the cognition of an omniscient being’s intellect, is not a pot, because it does not produce anything other than what exists, like a cloth. Thus, when there is a contradiction between an inference and a counter-inference, there is the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*); and in the case of the non-deviant contradictory, it must be stated as a means of avoiding the contradiction. This is incorrect, because: "If the avoidance is by means of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then there too is a triad, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even in the inferential avoidance, there is the triad of defects such as contradiction; if an avoidance is again performed by means of an inference, there is once more the triad of defects, resulting in an infinite regress. Alternatively, the objection is: "By the phrase 'by means of a *pramāṇa*', if the validity of the inferential avoidance is negated by the three [defects] beginning with contradiction—which themselves function as *pramāṇas*—then the Materialist (*Lokāyatika*) would be forced to admit inference itself, since the triad of contradiction and so forth is of the nature of inference. To this, [the opponent replies]: "In that case too, there is a triad, leading to an infinite regress. Even for the triad of contradiction and so forth, another triad of defects such as contradiction must be stated to negate their status as inference; for that too another must be stated, and thus, by admitting an infinite regress, how can inference be admitted? Therefore, since inference is not a valid means of knowledge, the ascertainment of objects beyond the senses is difficult to obtain.

{The Refutation of the Reason of "Metaphorical Status" in the Critique of the Cārvāka View} To this, we reply: As for the claim that the ascertainment of an object through inference—assisted by metaphorical subject-property (*pakṣadharmatā*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—is difficult to obtain, that is not so; for we do not accept it. Indeed, we do not admit that the subject-property and the positive concomitance of a logical reason are merely metaphorical. This is because a primary (*mukhya*) subject-property and so forth, which are non-different from those [metaphorical ones], are impossible. For a metaphorical usage never occurs where a primary usage is impossible; therefore, the determination of the subject (*pakṣa*) and so forth is primary, since they possess the definitions of the subject and so on that will be stated hereafter.

Now, since that which is not apprehended cannot function as a qualifier, how can the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) be the "thesis" (*pakṣa*)? For if that property to be proven, being unapprehended, qualifies the thesis, then the apprehension of its being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth would be useless; for the probandum would already be established prior to that, through mere cognition [of it]. And how can a subject be qualified by a property to be proven that is itself unapprehended? And a mere subject, unqualified by that, is not the thesis.

Now, if it is argued that the subject (*dharmī*) in which a property (*dharma*) is sought to be known or intended to be established is called the "subject of the thesis" (*sādhyadharmin*) only when it is qualified by that property to be proven, then how could there be a "thesis" in cases where—due to the absence of such a desire to know and so forth—one perceives fire and the like from seeing smoke and the like while wandering for some other purpose? This is not so, because of a failure to understand our intention. We do not say that a subject is a "thesis" only at the very moment it is qualified by the property to be proven. What then? It is so even before that. This is what is meant: that subject which will become qualified by the property to be proven is the "thesis" of that reason even prior to it. If it is asked, "How can there be a cognition of its being a thesis if its qualification by that [property] has not yet been cognized? [we reply: No, because the conventional usage of the term is established through the mere cognition of its fitness (*yogyatā*). For example, those seeking an effect such as a cloth engage with things such as threads as its causes based on the mere cognition of their fitness. Indeed, the cognition of something as a cause is not possible without the cognition of the effect; and if that were impossible, there would be no cognition of the cause, and consequently, those seeking the effect would have no practice of taking up that material, resulting in a world devoid of both engagement and withdrawal. Furthermore, if one were to engage with secondary causes, those seeking cooked food would also have to engage with clay pots and the like. Therefore, just as threads and other materials are conventionally treated as the causes of cloth and the like based on the mere cognition of their fitness—and this is not a secondary usage of the terms "fire" or "clay pot"—likewise, a subject alone is conventionally treated as a "thesis" based on the mere cognition of its fitness to be qualified by the property to be proven. Nor is the presence of the reason (such as smoke) in that subject a secondary instance of "being a property of the thesis" (*pakṣadharmatva*), as it would be in the case of a clay pot. When the auxiliary conditions are met, the intended effect is indeed accomplished from it. Similarly, based on the mere cognition of the fitness for being qualified by the property to be proven, the subject alone is conventionally treated as the "thesis," and the reason residing therein does not possess a secondary status as a "property of the thesis" in the manner of the fire in a clay pot.

[Objection: But surely, just as the production of an effect such as a cloth from causes such as threads is observed, therefore even in those threads where an effect has not yet begun, there exists a fitness called "belonging to that same class" which serves as the basis for the conventional designation of being their cause; however, we do not see any such basis for the conventional designation of being a "subject" (*pakṣa*) in a mere locus (*dharmin*). [Reply: No; for here too, the non-perception of the probandum and its negation is the basis called "fitness. For that locus alone in which neither the property to be proven nor its negation has been perceived becomes qualified by a property that has not yet been attained; therefore, it is the non-perception of the probandum and its negation that is here termed "fitness."

Alternatively, fitness (*yogyatā*) is simply the connection with the inferential mark (*liṅga*). To explain: in whatever locus (*dharmin*) a connection with smoke and so forth—which has been present since beginningless time—is perceived, that very locus is seen as qualified by the fire and so forth established by that smoke. Consequently, even when the locus is not yet perceived as qualified by the fire and so forth, the conventional designation "subject" (*pakṣa*) is applied because one perceives its connection with smoke and so forth, which is invariably concomitant with it. This [designation] is not figurative, because its cause—namely, what is called "fitness"—is not figurative, just like the conventional designation of "producing cloth" applied to threads and the like.

Now, if it is argued that even in the case of threads and the like, the designation of "non-producer" prior to the state of being a producer is intended to be merely figurative (*gauṇa*), we say no; for in common worldly usage, such figurative status is not perceived, as it is not the case with terms like *baṭu* or *māṇavaka*. Or, let it be granted that in the case of threads and the like, the subjecthood (*pakṣatva*) of the substratum (*dharmin*)—just as its being the cause of a cloth—is figurative; what is lost to us? It was argued that the inference based on that [figurative status] would consequently lack validity (*aprāmāṇya*) due to its figurative nature; this is not so. For even if the occasioning factor (*nimitta*) is figurative, its result is not figurative, just like the cloth itself. Just as you have stated that the capacity of those threads purchased for the purpose of producing a cloth to produce a cloth is figurative, yet the cloth produced by those very threads when endowed with specific auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) does not have a figurative "cloth-ness," so too, even if the subjecthood of the substratum is figurative, the inference constituted by that subject when endowed with specific auxiliaries is not figurative. Nor does this lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), because the established order is justified by resorting to the aforementioned "fitness" (*yogyatā*). Therefore, the claim that a determination of the object is difficult to obtain from an inference due to its figurative nature is simply incorrect.
{The refutation of the impossibility of the establishment of agency}

As for what was said—that the "probandum" (*sādhya*) is spoken of in dependence upon the "act of proving" (*sādhikriyā*)—that is not so, because the *kṛtya* suffix is prescribed in the sense of "being worthy of" (*arhati*). Therefore, that which is worthy of being established by a means of proof is called the "probandum. And this "worthiness of being established" is the fitness for accomplishment (*siddhi-yogyatā*). Since that [fitness] exists even prior [to the act of proving], it is not incorrect for there to be the status of being a probandum even before the act of proving occurs. Furthermore, we do not accept the synonymy of the terms "probandum" (*sādhya*) and "subject" (*pakṣa*), as the Buddhists do; nor is the aggregate [of subject and predicate] the probandum. What then? Either the locus (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*) is the probandum, as in "this place possesses fire," or the property qualified by the locus is the probandum, as in "there is fire here because of smoke. In both cases, it is accepted that the locus itself—characterized as the place and so forth—is the subject (*pakṣa*). And for the reason (*hetu*) residing therein, its status as a "property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) is primary, not merely figurative.
{The Refutation of the Impossibility of Following}

Nor is positive concomitance (*anvaya*) secondary, because it possesses the defining characteristics of primary concomitance. To explain: the definition of positive concomitance is "the pervasion of the general form of the probans by the general form of the probandum. In that context, when the subject (*dharmin*) qualified by a property is the probandum, then the generality of the probandum is characterized by such qualities as "possessing fire" and so forth. Even when the property residing in the subject is the probandum, then the probandum itself—when its specific distinctions are not intended—is called a "generality," because it is common to both the subject of the thesis and the subject of the example. The probans is likewise a generality, characterized by such qualities as "possessing smoke" and so forth. The pervasion, or the state of being pervaded, of that general probans by that general probandum is positive concomitance; how then could it be secondary? Therefore, the claim that the ascertainment of an object is difficult to obtain from an inference assisted by a positive concomitance where "property-of-the-subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) is merely figurative is also incorrect.

Furthermore, if the previously stated characteristics of being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and positive concomitance (*anvaya*) are not primary, then other primary ones must be stated; for figurative usage (*upacāra*) never occurs where the primary sense cannot be found. If, however, these two—being a property of the subject and positive concomitance—are primary in another context, then even so, since the validity of inference is established by that very fact, it is not an absolute non-existence.

As for what was said—that because the subject (*dharmin*) is already established, the proof is redundant—that is not so; for that which is qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is not yet established. Even though it is that which is to be proven, there is no lack of positive concomitance (*anugama*), because it has been stated that the concomitance is by way of the generality of the property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*). Indeed, no one accepts or perceives in the world a positive concomitance with a specific instance of the property to be proven. What then? It is perceived in the world that "whatever possesses smoke and whatever is produced is possessed of fire and is impermanent. Regarding the objection that even if the property is what is to be proven—namely, that "if it is a generality, it is proving the already proven; if it is a particular, there is no concomitance"—in that case, it is the generality itself that is the property to be proven. Nor is it a case of proving the already proven, because we accept that the generality, being unestablished in the intended subject (*dharmin*), is what is to be proven. And there is certainly concomitance with that [generality]. For instance, the positive concomitance "wherever there is smoke, there is fire" is well-known even in the world, and since we see the operation of inference based on that much alone, the concomitance with a specific location or a specific relation thereto is irrelevant.
Refutation of the impossibility of apprehending invariable concomitance (avinābhāva).

As for what was stated—that the relationship of inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) cannot be apprehended, and so forth—that too is incorrect. For there certainly exists this non-erroneous, determinative cognition even among worldly people and investigators: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire; in the absence of fire, there is nowhere smoke. Now, if upon investigation any one of the [means of knowledge] such as the senses or logical marks can be determined as the cause of that cognition, then all is well. Even if it cannot, nevertheless, it is not proper to deny the object that has been ascertained simply because its cause remains unascertained, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The view of some regarding the apprehension of pervasion, and its refutation.

On this point, some say: "Inference alone does not grasp the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). On this matter, there is indeed no dispute. Nor is it grasped by mere perception; rather, pervasion (*vyāpti*) is understood through repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*). But what is the meaning of "repeated observation"? It means many observations. Are these restricted to individual objects, or do they have as their object all instances of fire and smoke without exception? If they are restricted to individual objects, then even in a thousand eons it would be impossible to produce an observation whose object is every single individual instance, because individuals are infinite due to differences in place, time, and so forth. And as long as the relationship with every individual instance is not grasped, the suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) does not cease. For the fact that earthy substances are cut by iron is not established as non-deviant simply because it has been observed a thousand times. If, on the other hand, each observation has as its object all instances of fire and smoke individually, then since pervasion is established by just one [observation], the remaining observations are useless. Furthermore, because observations arising in succession are non-enduring, they cannot function collectively. Simultaneous arising, however, is impossible, because such a thing is never perceived.

{The view of others regarding the apprehension of pervasion and its refutation} Others, however, describe mental perception as the grasper of pervasion by the force of elimination (*pariśeṣa*); that too is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that [the knower] must be all-seeing. For it is only when there is the observation of the entire set of similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) that a direct perception of pervasion occurs in the form: "whatever is produced is entirely impermanent, whereas whatever is permanent is entirely unproduced," and not otherwise. And if that were so, it would follow that every person who infers would be all-seeing.

If everything is already seen through perception, what is the use of inference, given its redundancy? One becomes an all-seeing seer (*sarvadarśin*) precisely at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and not at any other time.
