If it is argued that inference is therefore meaningful for a subsequent period, we say no; for that would be nothing more than stretching out one's legs (a superfluous extension). Furthermore, if he were an all-seeing seer even at the time of grasping the pervasion, why then does he—not like a yogi who has emerged from meditative absorption—reflect upon the pervasion by thinking, "I have seen such objects existing in heaven and so forth"? Moreover, there would follow the undesirable consequence that there could be neither disagreement nor lack of understanding regarding the discourse on supersensible matters (*atīndriya*). For even in the case of objects of mental perception, such as pleasure and the like, there is no discourse regarding the supersensible, nor is there disagreement or lack of understanding, since these are not observed [to be supersensible].
The views of others regarding the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), and their refutation.

Others, however, say: "Even when the relationship between two things has not been grasped, the state of being the signifier and the signified arises through the force of their belonging to the same class (*tajjātīyatva*), based on the cognition of the relationship between some related members. This too is incorrect, because it has already been answered by the fact that there is deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the class of being earthen or cuttable by iron; furthermore, there is no difference in the fact that the relationship has not been grasped with those that do not belong to that class. Even if the relationship were grasped between two mere universals (*sāmānyamātra*), there would be neither comprehension nor practical activity regarding the particular (*vyakti*), because particulars are distinct from the universal. Nor is it logical for an inference to result in something other than the object [of the relationship] when the relationship was grasped elsewhere, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, the purpose such as burning is not established by the universal alone, such that the inference directed toward that [universal] would have its goal fulfilled.

[Objection: But surely, "A universal cannot exist without its particulars, like a rabbit's horn. Therefore, when the universal is inferred, the particular is apprehended through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*); from that arises purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*), and upon attaining the object, the effect such as burning is accomplished. So how can it be said that inference, having the universal as its object, is entirely useless? [Reply: This is not correct. For instance, is the particular apprehended through the impossibility of the observed relation otherwise being explained (*anyathānupapatti*) by one who has previously seen that relation, or by one who has not? In the former case, the resulting cognition and the subsequent activity would concern only those particulars of fire and so forth previously perceived; consequently, because there is no distinction from memory—which is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*)—inference would lack validity altogether. Even in the case of apprehension by one who has not seen the relation, the apprehension of particulars such as a donkey would also follow from the impossibility of "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) otherwise being explained. [Objection: But "fire-ness" is said to be the state of being fire, not the state of being a donkey and so forth. Therefore, how could a donkey be apprehended through the impossibility of fire-ness otherwise being explained? [Reply: From what is this determined—that fire-ness is the state of being fire and not the state of being a donkey and so forth? If you say "from worldly convention" (*lokaprasiddhi*), we must investigate which root of authority that very convention possesses. Furthermore, in the world, false conventions are seen just as much as conventions regarding black space and the like. If you say that fire-ness is observed only in specific fires and not in specific donkeys and so forth, [we reply] no; if all specific fires and donkeys have not been grasped, how can the restriction "only in specific fires" be established? Moreover, let a specific fire be established somewhere through the impossibility of fire-ness otherwise being explained; but how is it established in the intended location? For fire-ness is not rendered impossible by the absence of that [specific fire]. If you say that fire-ness as characterized by that specific location is otherwise impossible, then since the relation between them is unestablished, from where is this rule established? Furthermore, in establishing fire-ness as characterized by that location, another undesirable consequence follows: even if the relation is not grasped in that manner, if fire-ness of that kind were established, then fire-ness would be established everywhere.
{The author's own view on the apprehension of pervasion}

Should we now follow the doctrine of Bṛhaspati (the Teacher of the Gods) alone? It should not be followed. Why? Because even in his system, an abundance of contradictions has been demonstrated both previously and subsequently. From what, then, is the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) derived? Is it merely accidental? No; for pervasion is apprehended even through perception (*pratyakṣa*) regarding those things that possess it. To explain: "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire; where that [fire] is absent, smoke does not exist"—this is called inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). And this is apprehended even at first by the eye, which is wide open and connected to both places containing fire and those without fire. At most, repeated observation (*bhūyodarśana*) is sought for the sake of strengthening the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) in those of dull, middling, or small intellect, like the repeated study of a text. But surely, the relation of pervader and pervaded between smoke and fire is called inseparable connection. Since that resides in every individual instance of smoke and fire, how can it be apprehended if all those individual instances are not apprehended? Does that which resides in all individuals not reside in one, two, three, or more individuals, such that it would not be apprehended even when those [few] are apprehended? For instance, although universals (*sāmānya*) and inherence (*samavāya*) reside in infinite individuals, their apprehension is observed at the very time one, two, or three individuals are apprehended. Furthermore, it was already established earlier that a whole (*avayavin*) is not apprehended only upon the apprehension of all its substrates. Nor is it a valid objection that conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would then follow as being apprehended upon the apprehension of only one substrate; for the categories (*padārtha*) possess diverse potencies, and therein, whatever is capable of being apprehended in a certain way is apprehended in that way. And that capacity is understood precisely from the apprehension of that which follows a single [instance], following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of specific causes, just as the eyes and other senses apprehend specific objects such as color-form (*rūpa*).
The external perceptibility of inseparable connection (avinābhāva).

If *avinābhāva* (inseparable relation) were a perceptible connection, then, like inherence (*samavāya*), it would be grasped even at the time of perceiving the two related entities. Alternatively, if pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) and pervadedness (*vyāpyatva*) are specific properties restricted to the respective classes of fire and smoke, they too would be grasped at the very moment one perceives one, two, or three individual instances—just as one grasps "fire-ness" or "smoke-ness"—and would not necessitate the perception of all instances. Furthermore, the example is dissimilar: while the perception of "fire-ness" and "smoke-ness" does not depend on the simultaneous perception of their mutual substrates, such is not the case for pervasiveness and pervadedness. Even so, like "priority," "posteriority," or "intermediateness," [pervasiveness] is grasped simply through the perception of two or more subjects. If, however, it were imperceptible, then even when all subjects are perceived, it could not be grasped through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Due to its absence and the resulting consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*), it cannot be grasped through inference (*anumāna*) either; thus, the non-existence of *avinābhāva* itself follows, and consequently, inference would be utterly non-existent. We shall discuss the faults that arise from accepting such a position later. Therefore, even when all individuals are not grasped, the *avinābhāva* between fire and smoke is indeed grasped by direct perception.

If this is so, let the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) belong only to those two things whose invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped, and not to a previously unknown fire and smoke, because their connection has not been observed. [Objection: But if the relationship of signifier and signified were to exist even between those whose connection has not been observed, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Reply: This is not so, because the connection between the classes (*varga*) of fire and smoke has been observed. If that [connection] has been observed somewhere, then the connection between fire and smoke is not unobserved anywhere. Even if a particular substratum (*dharmin*) has not been observed, what follows from that regarding its property (*dharma*) having been observed? For there is no identity between the property and the substratum, nor is there a difference in the nature of the pervaded and the pervader for each individual instance of smoke and fire. Because they are characterized by the same definition—just like "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) or "inherence" (*samavāya*)—and because there is no specific definition [of difference], they are indeed one. Furthermore, it is not logical that the identical essence itself should be both observed and unobserved. [Objection: But in that case, inherence (*samavāya*) too, being one, would be observed when observed in one thing and thus observed in all, due to non-difference; consequently, upon perceiving an entirely unobserved object, there would follow the inference of everything inherent in it. [Reply: This is not so, because the power (*śakti*) of the relation is diverse. Indeed, the power of inherence is one thing, that of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) another, and that of other relations or other properties yet another. In that regard, it is improper to attempt to equalize other powers based on some similarity, as in the case of uneven paths and the like. However, the capacity of the relationship of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*) is such that, even if it is grasped in one place and remembered in another, it becomes the cause for the relationship of signifier and signified even between two previously unknown instances of those two things. [Objection: Even if it is a property of those things in reality, how can there be a memory of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) that was not observed as a property of those things, based on the sight of an unobserved smoke? If the sight of an unrelated object were the cause of memory, there would be an over-extension. [Reply: No; for the cause of memory is the universal smoke (*dhūma-sāmānya*) which was observed as a property of the same substratum along with that [fire]. [Objection: If all pervaded and pervading things are not grasped, how can there be a cognition through a universal synthesis (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*)? [Reply: No; because that is possible through inference (*anumāna*). How? Those particular instances of smoke that have been observed, or those that are conceived as existing in another place, as past, or as future—all are pervaded by fire because they possess the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*), just like the smoke already perceived. Or else, the places possessing smoke are proven to possess fire because they possess smoke, just like the place already perceived. Therefore, since "whatever is thus, all that is exactly so," there is also a memory through universal synthesis. Since this is the case, one need not say that mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) is the grasper of pervasion by means of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), because the elimination itself is unestablished.
In reality, it is the mind alone that possesses the capacity to grasp pervasion.

If, however, it is impossible to justify the apprehension of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) according to the previously stated method, then mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) itself must be justified on the grounds that it would otherwise be impossible for there to be a non-specific cognition [of pervasion]. If it were the case that every living being, having become a yogi, grasps the pervasion, then even for one whose eyes and other senses have never been operative regarding fire and so forth, there would arise the cognition: "Wherever there is smoke, there is everywhere fire. This is not so, because although the mind has all things as its object, its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are not fixed. Just as in the recollection of an object to be remembered, in some cases a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) alone is the auxiliary cause, while in others—where that impression is weaker—a distinction in auxiliaries such as focused attention (*praṇidhāna*) is observed, which conforms to the degree of intensity of the impressions. Likewise, in the production of perceptual knowledge, in some cases a specific quality (*dharma-viśeṣa*) alone is the auxiliary cause. For that [mind] accompanied by qualities that are weaker or weaker still, there is also a distinction in the state of meditative absorption (*samādhāna*), sensory cognition, place, and so forth, which conforms to those specific qualities. Therefore, the mind, when conjoined with the cognition of smoke as qualified by fire produced by the eyes and other senses, grasps the pervasion through a universal synthesis (*sarvopasaṃhāreṇa*); thus, there is no futility in the operation of the eyes and other senses.
There is no consequence of omniscience in the apprehension of pervasion.

Nor does it follow that [the mind] would possess omniscience, because it apprehends [objects] only by way of their general form (*sāmānyākāra*). Indeed, unlike a yogin, its apprehension does not have every individual instance of smoke as its object, nor does it apprehend them through their mutually exclusive, specific forms—as one might see a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand. What then? It apprehends them only by way of the general forms of smoke, fire, and so forth, just as one standing at a distance perceives trees in a forest only by way of the general form of "tree," and not even by way of specific forms such as *dhava* or other species. Furthermore, regarding the various locations, they too are apprehended only by way of the general form of being the locus of smoke and so on; they are not apprehended by way of specific forms such as "Magadha" or "mountain," because those particular forms do not appear [to the cognition]. For the restriction of the object of perceptual knowledge is not something to be established by inference; rather, whatever object appears in a given cognition in whatever manner, that is its object in that very manner. Thus, even in visual cognitions of a person and the like, that object appears distinguished by some particularity—whether collectively or individually—but not everywhere without distinction. Therefore, since the mind, when regulated by specific auxiliary factors such as prior perception (*dṛṣṭa*), functions as the grasper of pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is no consequence of its apprehending all objects in every respect; for this very reason, inference is not rendered useless. Just as memory follows the mode of apprehension, there is no recollection such as "I saw objects existing in such-and-such a state in heaven and so forth," because they were not apprehended in that specific form.
Nor is there an abandonment of discourse concerning that which transcends the senses.

Furthermore, the absence of both [the cognition of] supersensible objects (*atīndriya*) and of disagreement regarding linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-vipratipatti*) would not be possible, because you do not admit the apprehension [of objects] in their specific forms. For in the cognition "whatever is produced is all impermanent," everything does not appear as impermanent even in its form as *dharma*, *adharma*, and so forth. Nor, in the cognition "wherever there is smoke, there is fire," does every fire appear in its form as being located on grassy or woody mountains and the like. Rather, it appears only in a general form; therefore, in relation to the form perceived therein, there occurs the linguistic usage of "supersensible" and disagreement.
{The objection that such an inference [of momentariness] is based on a general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti), and its refutation.}

[Objection: If that were so, then inference would occur only by way of a general form—namely, "whatever is produced is impermanent" and "wherever there is smoke, there is fire. Consequently, inferences such as "there is fire on the mountain" or "sound is impermanent" would not be established as valid, because the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) has not been grasped in those specific forms. Otherwise, one might also have an inference [of fire] by way of its being neighing or consisting of grass, and so forth. But this is not the case; for it does not follow that "because sound is produced, therefore it is a neighing or a peacock's cry," nor that "because there is smoke here, therefore the fire here consists of grass or leaves. [Reply: This is not so, because the capacity of the means of proof (*sādhana*) is determined for the sake of establishing a specific, restricted [object], just as in the case of the eye and other senses. For the eye, though engaged with a woman, does not grasp every particular feature of her; yet it is not the case that it grasps nothing at all, since it grasps precisely that for which it has capacity. Indeed, the logical mark (*liṅga*) possesses the capacity to establish a specific connection with the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmin*); therefore, it establishes only that. It does not establish particulars such as "consisting of grass," because there is no capacity for that. If it is asked, "What is that capacity?"—it is the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), aided by the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*), from which follows the establishment of the specific connection with the subject of the thesis. To explain: smoke whose invariable concomitance has been grasped produces the cognition of fire only in that very place where it is perceived. If, however, even when smoke exists in the subject of the thesis, the fire connected to it did not exist, then the cognition "wherever there is smoke, there is fire" would be false, or else the existence of smoke there would not be real. And this is not the case. Furthermore, even if particulars such as "consisting of grass" are absent, there is no contradiction in the apprehension of pervasion and the property of the subject elsewhere, such that the establishment of those [particulars] would also follow.

If it is argued: "Let the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) or the apprehension of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) be false; what is lost for us?"—we say: no. For, by the same logic that establishes the truth of [your] true knowledge, the truth of this [apprehension] is also established. Indeed, whatever logic applies to the truth of the knowledge intended by you—whether characterized by non-sublation in other places and times, or characterized by worldly consensus—that same logic applies equally in my view to the truth of the knowledge of the property of the subject and the pervasion. How, then, could this be false? Furthermore, for one who accepts that nothing whatsoever has truth, there would even be a contradiction with his own words. For if this very sentence is true, how can it be that nothing has truth? If it too is untrue, how does it establish the untruth of everything? Therefore, it is not the case that the apprehension of the property of the subject and the pervasion is untrue; and if it is true, one must necessarily accept the establishment of fire as delimited by its connection to the subject. The former teachers [say]: "The establishment of both occurs through the grace of external pervasion (*vahirvyāpti*) and internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*). Since the pervasion of smoke by mere fire is understood in a place outside the subject, such as a kitchen, fire is established from smoke in a general sense. But since smoke is perceived within the interior of the subject, only the specific fire connected to it is established—not [fire produced by] grass and so forth, because no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is perceived for those. However, for one who is capable of discerning a specific kind of smoke that is invariably concomitant (*avinābhūta*) with a specific kind of fire such as that produced by grass, for that knower, there is also inference of the specific kinds like grass-fire. By this, the inference of specific sounds is explained. When only the state of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) is perceived in sound, then from that, only a cause in general and impermanence in general are inferred. That the specific connection to sound is established is also to be seen as due to the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), just like [the establishment of] fire. Thus, the same logic should be seen to apply to other inferences as well. Therefore, it is said that inference is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) because the relationship of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) can be grasped. By this, the following is also refuted: "We do not at all deny the validity of inference; rather, we are refuting those who, abandoning the worldly path, describe a mark (*liṅga*) with three or four characteristics for the sake of the cognition of the object to be inferred."
Contradiction with the world and its refutation.

This might be so if inference occurred for worldly people based on the observation of a logical mark (*liṅga*) that does not possess well-known positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). However, even they infer the pervader (*vyāpaka*) only where they see a logical mark whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been grasped. For worldly people do not, upon seeing smoke in a village, conclude there is fire in the forest. Nor do they infer a cause from the perception of effects such as unprecedented words or sprouts. So how have we abandoned the path of the world? [Objection: But worldly people, having seen smoke, then understand fire; they do not, like you, employ technical conventions such as "being a property of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. Therefore, you are incorrect. [Reply: This is not so. Even if, for the sake of brevity in practice, names such as "subject" (*pakṣa*), "similar instance" (*sapakṣa*), and so on, were applied to mountains, kitchens, and the like—just as the term "existence" (*sattā*) and others are used as designations for cognitions—how does this alone render us incorrect? For the purpose of practice does not change by means of a different name. Nor is the absence of those meanings established merely because the terms "subject" and so forth are not well-known in the world; for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It has already been stated that their meaning is established even in the world. Furthermore, the statement of the definition of inference, though already well-known, is for the sake of restatement (*anuvāda*). And it has been said that the purpose of the restatement is the prescription and prohibition of inference regarding the self (*ātman*) and its opposite. Thus, the rejection of inference concerning objects never before perceived is also not tenable, because it shares the same status of validity as the inference of smoke and the like.

{The Refutation of Faults such as the "Contradiction of the Particular" (viśeṣaviruddha)}: This being so, since faults such as the "contradiction of the particular" would have no scope, they would not constitute defects. For instance—if the fault of the "contradiction of the particular" and others were not accepted as a defect in the inference of smoke and the like, then its universal applicability (*sarvatragatva*) would be contradicted. And its universal applicability has already been established; nor is there any specific distinction by which it would not subvert the inference of smoke and the like, while subverting every other kind of inference.
{If inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), there would be contradiction with common worldly experience and contradiction with one's own words.}

Now, if you maintain that even inference based on smoke and so forth is subject to that same refutation, then there is a contradiction with the practical conventions of the entire world and a contradiction with the operation of your own words. If inference were not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), then there would be no utterance of specific words for the purpose of communicating specific objects. Why do you not utter such statements as: "Inference is not a valid means of knowledge because it is impossible to grasp the relationship of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*)"? Why do you not utter such statements as: "Inference is a valid means of knowledge because it is a cause for the correct comprehension of an object"? Why is inference not a valid means of knowledge? Because the capacity of even the aforementioned statement to produce understanding in another person cannot be ascertained. Likewise, why do you not taste fire, poison, and the like, while you taste milk, molasses, and other things for the sake of pleasure? Similarly, this same line of questioning should be applied to the avoidance of wells, thorns, and the like, and to walking along good paths with one's feet. Indeed, apart from inference, there is no other means of comprehension [to know]: "From this means, happiness will come to me; from that means, misfortune. Furthermore, that by which something is inferred is the "object to be inferred" (*anumeya*); that by which something is correctly determined is called "inference" (*anumāna*). Therefore, to say "inference is not a valid means of knowledge" is illogical due to internal contradiction (*vyāghāta*).

If you argue that there is no contradiction because what was called "inference" is actually not an inference at all, but rather [a form of] inference spoken of according to the opponent's perspective—[we reply: how did you come to know the opponent's intention without inference? Furthermore, in your view, there is no inference whatsoever by virtue of whose similarity the term "inference" could be applied even to what is not an inference, just as the term "perception" is applied to fallacious perceptions. Moreover, by what means do you establish that inference is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*)? For no one is able to apprehend the invalidity of inference through perception, nor to communicate that invalidity to another. Furthermore, you have rejected the validity of inference without exception, and you certainly do not accept the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) and so forth, due to such defects as the doubts regarding truth, falsehood, and uncertainty. Therefore, inference as a valid means of knowledge is indeed devoid of authority, like the speech of a madman. As for what was said here—that the invalidity [of inference] is established without accepting its own validity, but rather by means of what is established for the opponent—and that it is not necessary for a means of knowledge to be established for both parties, since inference consisting of words is not a means of knowledge for the speaker, yet the speaker communicates to the other by means of it, and since the effort is for the sake of communicating to the other, there is a need for what is established for both; and that this point must be considered: does a reason (*hetu*) or example (*dṛṣṭānta*) that is not established for oneself, but is established for the other, produce cognition in that other when employed? Or does it not? And it cannot be said that it produces cognition; therefore, establishment for both is not the cause—this is improper. For if inference were not a valid means of knowledge, from where would you ascertain that it is established for the opponent? Indeed, the intellect is not perceived directly like the body, since doubt is observed regarding the nature of the intellect even when the nature of the body is ascertained. Thus, the fact that the reason and the example are established for the opponent, and that cognition occurs by means of them, is entirely untenable, like the examples of those blind from birth or the white crane.

If you argue that the opponent’s own established position is understood from their words, have you now accepted the opponent’s own statement as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? If you say "no," then alas for the power of your delusion, that such a contradictory statement is uttered in the midst of the wise: that the opponent’s established position is understood from their words, yet those words are not a valid means of knowledge. Indeed, horns do not belong to a means of knowledge; rather, that alone is a means of knowledge by which an object is understood. If the statement merely indicates the speaker’s intention, then the speech itself would simply be an inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, it is not logical to convince an opponent through a reason or an example that one has not oneself realized. For no one who has not realized [the truth] can be a teacher. Indeed, children, cowherds, and the like have no authority in explaining the meaning of the scriptures; just as those born blind and others have no authority in investigating the qualities or defects of color and form. Therefore, the claim that the effort [of debate] is for the sake of convincing the opponent is also untenable.

As for what was said—that the speech of a speaker is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) when it is an inference—that too is incorrect. For if no cognition has been produced by that [speech] in the speaker, then how could that speaker instruct another regarding a statement or a logical mark (*liṅga*) whose capacity is not yet determined? He might as well instruct on anything at all, since there is no difference in the fact that its power is unknown. Nor do we maintain the restriction that only that specific individual instance which produces a cognition in both parties must be taught for the purpose of communicating to another. For instance, having seen a particular object with a lamp, one may instruct another even after the lamp has gone out: "You too, having lit a lamp, see that object. Even a blind man instructs based on the capacity previously perceived [by others]. If you argue: "It might be thought that just as a person born blind has never seen a lamp, nor the other forms illuminated by it, yet he still instructs one with sight, saying: 'See the form by means of a lamp'—in the same way, we too do not know the nature of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, nor the nature of the probandum (*sādhya*) to be inferred; nevertheless, thinking that a great soul (*mahānubhāva*) must necessarily act for the benefit of others, we shall instruct one who knows them using reasons and so forth, even though they are unknown to us. Just as there is no reproach against a great soul who liberates others from fetters and the like while he himself is not liberated, so too for us, who are teaching others despite ourselves being unlearned, there can only be greatness, not reproach," [we reply: Who would believe this—that one who is himself unlearned teaches another through his own greatness? Indeed, it is not proper for one who is merely born to be a teacher. Furthermore, a person born blind is not observed to teach one with sight by means of instruction regarding lamps and such. However, if this much were possible—that the person born blind had understood, through his own intuitive power or from the words of a reliable authority (*āpta*), that a lamp together with the eye illuminates forms and so forth, then he might indeed instruct accordingly—[but this is not the case]. You, however, have not understood in any way the capacity of the reason and so forth, whether as a means of proof (*sādhana*) or as a means of refutation (*dūṣaṇa*), for the purpose of communicating to another. So how, like one merely born and unlearned, do you instruct another? And if you can instruct another by means of a reason whose capacity is not understood, why do you not also instruct [others] regarding the existence of the self (*ātman*) and so forth by means of the logical marks (*liṅga*) such as consciousness (*buddhi*), and liberation resulting from the knowledge thereof? By doing so, your greatness might truly be superior.

If you argue: "We do not accept anything as a means of cognition (*pratipattṛ*) nor do we establish anything; rather, we merely engage in cross-examination (*paryanuyoga*) of others, because even the *sūtras* are for the purpose of cross-examination," then this is trivial. For if you engage in cross-examination for no purpose at all, you are to be disregarded like a madman. Alternatively, if you engage in cross-examination with the thought: "By means of this cross-examination, I will discern the opponent's intention, and whatever answer he gives, we shall understand his intention and examine it for its merits or defects"—then how is it that you do not accept inference (*anumāna*) as a valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the comprehension of another's intention? Furthermore, neither the proponent nor the opponent achieves any goal, victory, or defeat through mere cross-examination or mere replies. What then? It is achieved by stating proofs (*sādhana*) and refutations (*dūṣaṇa*) regarding one's own and the other's positions. One's own position cannot be established and the opposing position refuted by perception alone (or by a student alone). Moreover, if there were uncertainty in every case, even the possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*) of such proof or refutation would not exist; therefore, the presentation of proofs and refutations based on mere possibility is extremely doubtful. Furthermore, are these "contradictory reasons" (*viruddhahetu*) and so forth presented to produce doubt regarding the validity of inference, or to produce certainty regarding its invalidity? If it is to produce doubt, is it for yourself or for others? If for yourself, then the contradictory reasons and so forth are useless, for you already have doubt regarding inference even without them. But as for others, from where did you learn that doubt will arise in them from the contradictory reasons and so forth, such that inference is invalid? If you say: "I present the contradictory reasons and so forth with the very thought that 'perhaps doubt will arise in others,' yet perhaps not"—even so, their presentation is useless, because that same result could occur even without their presentation. If you say: "Even if it is useless, doubt still arises"—then this person, seized by the demon of doubt, who refuses to accept certainty even regarding the causes of doubt, such as the observation of common characteristics (*sāmānyadharmadarśana*), must simply be disregarded as incurable. If, on the other hand, the contradictory reasons and so forth are taught to produce certainty regarding the invalidity of inference, then, since they produce certainty, they possess validity itself. And since they are not unlike inference, they are indeed inference. How then can there be the invalidity of all inference? A means of cognition that brings about the understanding of another is indeed a valid means of cognition, just like the sense organs of another. As for what was said—"In that case too, there are three [reasons], leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)"—that too is incorrect, as it results in the failure to establish the intended object. The intended goal is the establishment of the invalidity of inference by means of the triad of contradictory reasons and so forth; yet that very triad is undermined by the infinite regress and thus fails to prove its point. If even that which is undermined by an infinite regress could establish its own thesis, then the original inference (*mūlānumāna*) would also establish its own thesis.

Now, suppose it is argued: "Just as the triad of fallacies beginning with the contradictory (*viruddha*), which I have set forth, fails to prove its own probandum because they are vitiated by an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), so too the inference of the self (*ātman*) and other categories set forth by you is vitiated by the infinite regress of contradictions and the like; therefore, it is simply not a proof for the self and so forth. This is not so. For the defectiveness of the contradictions and the like set forth by you is established solely through your own admission, whereas that defect has not been admitted by me. How, then, could the inference of the self and other categories be defective? Indeed, one does not experience the suffering of having one's tongue cut off merely because someone says, "I am experiencing the pain of tongue-cutting and so forth, just as you did when you insulted the king," provided that person did not actually commit the insult. Furthermore, because the original inference sublates them, the contradictions and the like are not genuine defects. For example, even though the cognition of a single moon or the cognition of trees coming toward one is produced earlier, it possesses the capacity for universal worldly consensus and practical efficacy, and its validity is certain; thus, despite the lack of difference in being sense-produced (*akṣaja*), it is precisely the sublater of the cognition of two moons and the like. Conversely, the cognition of a single moon is not sublated by the subsequent cognition of two moons. In the same way, the inferential cognition of smoke and so forth—possessing the capacity for universal worldly consensus and practical efficacy and having its validity ascertained—must be accepted as the sublater of cognitions involving contradiction and the like. Otherwise, the relationship between the sublated and the sublater would not be established even among sense-perceptions. Consequently, even perception as a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would not be established, and there would be a total collapse of reality (*tattvopaplava*). The refutation of that position has already been stated extensively above. Therefore, one should see that contradictions and the like, being sublated by an inferential cognition of smoke and so forth whose validity is ascertained, are merely pseudo-defects (*dūṣaṇābhāsa*). Thus, in the inference of the self and other categories as well, contradictions and the like are not genuine defects, as they function in the same manner. Moreover, because they lack the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), reasons such as the contradictory do not sublate the fundamental reason (*mūlahetu*); rather, it is the fundamental reason, being endowed with the force of invariable concomitance, that indeed sublates the reasons such as the contradictory.
{An Investigation into the Nature of Pervasion}

What, then, is this "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*)? It is said: inseparable connection is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the probans by the probandum by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). This restriction established by the very nature of the probandum and the probans—namely, that the probandum is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) and the probans is the pervaded (*vyāpya*)—is what constitutes inseparable connection. Now, while it is the case that the pervadedness of smoke by fire is restricted by its very nature, it is not the case that the pervadedness of smoke is likewise restricted by its nature through the absence of being the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) as intended by the proponent of the refutation (*dūṣaṇavādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*). This is because those [roles of] proponent of the refutation and opponent are themselves unstable. For the status of being a proponent of the proof (*sādhanavāditva*) and the status of being a proponent of the refutation are not fixed within a person. Nor is the state of being the probandum and the probans as stated by them, or the absence thereof, fixed by nature in objects. Otherwise, just as there is the absence of being the probandum of the probans under discussion, one would also have to admit the absence of being the object of negation for the negation stated by the proponent of the refutation under discussion, since the logic is the same. What follows from this? There must be either the negation of being the probandum of the probans under discussion, or its absence. Since neither of these is possible, there is a contradiction with the idea of being established by nature; because of the contradiction of mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*), neither can be established.

By this, the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) of such [reasons] as "because it is one or the other of the two" (*anyataratvāt*) regarding the property (*dharma*) and the subject (*dharmin*) is refuted. For these too possess a relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) merely through conceptual construction (*kalpanāmātra*); there is no pervasion by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) as there is between fire and smoke. For if there were pervasion by way of intrinsic nature, there would be the establishment of a fixed property just like fire from smoke, and not a subversion (*upaplava*). However, a subversion is observed in the case of "being one or the other" and so forth. To illustrate: "Sound is eternal, because it is one or the other of the subject and the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), like the similar instance"—this is the same even if [the reason] were non-eternal. Likewise, "Because it is one or the other of space and sound, like space," or "Because it is one or the other of a pot and sound, like a pot"—there is thus a subversion regarding eternity and non-eternity. Similarly, "The subject (*śabda*) is not the locus of the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) in the proof adduced by the proponent of eternity, because it is one or the other of the property to be proven and the word 'property,' like the property to be proven"—thus there is a subversion consisting of a refutation. Likewise, "The property of the subject is not one or the other of the property and the subject which is the locus of the property to be proven in the present inference, because it is a subject, like a pot, etc."—this being the negation of the previous, "It is not the case that the property to be proven is not one or the other of those two, because it is a subject, like a pot, etc. Likewise, "This subject does not possess the property to be proven in the present inference, because it is one or the other of the subject and the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), like the counter-example; and because it is one or the other of the subject and a donkey's horn, like a donkey's horn. Likewise, "This place does not possess fire distinct from the fire [concerning which] there is no disagreement between the proponent and opponent, because it is a place; and because of [reasons] such as existence and knowability, like other places. This being the negation of the previous, "This place does not lack the fire [concerning which] there is no disagreement between the proponent and opponent, because of the aforementioned reasons, like other places. Or alternatively, "This place does not possess the negation of fire distinct from the fire [concerning which] there is no disagreement between the proponent and opponent, for the aforementioned reasons, like other places. Likewise, "This place does not possess the fire that is the object of the present inference, because it is neither a donkey's horn nor a non-horn, like a donkey's horn. This being the negation of the previous, "This place does not lack the fire [negated by] the present counter-inference, because it is neither a donkey's horn nor a non-horn, like a donkey's horn. Or alternatively, "A pot existing at the same time as the establishment of the probandum—the smoke—which has become the means of proof employed by our intended proponent at a time distinct from past and future—is not a pot, because it is a petal of a sky-flower lotus, like a lotus petal. This being the counter-inference, "A pot existing at the same time as the attainment of the self-nature of that very counter-inference is not a pot, for the same reasons and example. Or again, "A pot existing at the same time as the opposite of the establishment of the probandum—the smoke—which has become the means of proof employed by the intended proponent at a time distinct from past and future, is not a pot, because it is a petal of a sky-flower lotus, like a lotus petal. Thus, because the property to be proven is not established, there is no inseparable connection with the property to be proven for [reasons] such as "being one or the other. For it is never seen that smoke and the like, which are inseparably connected to the property to be proven, have an unestablished property to be proven; for even among worldly people and investigators, we observe the establishment of activity based on the determination of fire and so forth upon seeing smoke and the like, resulting in the accomplishment of purposeful action.

By this, the argument for [the pot] having a second entity (*sadvitīya*) is also refuted, as the Cārvākas have said: "A pot has a second entity, namely either a person characterized by a body in which consciousness is manifest or [another] pot, because it is unproduced, like a wall. The meaning of this syllogism is that the person is merely the body qualified by consciousness, and there is no other transmigrating being. Here too, the aforementioned invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) does not exist, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is not established; for instance: "A pot has a second entity, namely either a person possessing attributes such as eternity or another pot, because it is unproduced, like a wall"; or likewise, "A pot has a second entity, namely either a person who is mere cognition (*vijñaptimātra*) and transmigrates or another pot," for the same reason. Thus, whatever one wishes to prove, all of it would be proven by this [reasoning], and therefore there is an absence of a fixed probandum. Furthermore, this is not a property of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), but rather the state of having a fixed probandum and probans. Since the co-existence of a wall with a pot is observed only with respect to another pot, how can the intended co-existence of the pot with a [transmigrating] person be established by that example? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Arguments based on acceptance (*abhyupagama*) and so forth are also refuted by this very point, because acceptance proceeds from mere desire for that [proposition] and cannot have an essential pervasion (*svabhāvavyāpti*) with a specific object. This is because the acceptance of someone who is not omniscient may even be incorrect. Moreover, omniscience is difficult to know; we shall explain later that an object accepted by one whose omniscience is even suspected is merely the content of scripture (*āgama*) and is not an object of inference. However, we do indeed accept the inference of the mere validity of that person's word on the grounds that it was spoken by an omniscient being. Therefore, there is no other substance apart from the nine substances, because it was not propounded by Kaṇāda. There is no other principle (*tattva*) apart from the twenty-five principles, because it was not propounded by Kapila. (Is there no other principle apart from the twenty principles, because it was not propounded by Kapila? There is no other aggregate (*skandha*) apart from the five aggregates, because it was not propounded by the Buddha, like a sky-flower. In this way, the [alleged] invariable concomitance is refuted. Therefore, it is rightly said that invariable concomitance is the pervasion of the probans by the probandum by virtue of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The varieties of inseparable concomitance (avinābhāva).

It is of two kinds, according to the distinction between positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The meaning is that this is based on the distinction between the cognition of affirmation and the cognition of negation. Positive concomitance is the pervasion perceived by way of affirmation; negative concomitance is said to be the pervasion perceived by way of negation. Now, one might object: "Fire located in a specific place is the probandum (*sādhya*); since that is not yet cognized, how can the pervasion of the probans (*sādhana*) with it be apprehended? Furthermore, if the probandum were already cognized, the grasping of pervasion would be redundant. To resolve this, he says: "The pervasion of the general probans with the general probandum is apprehended as positive concomitance"—this is the completion of the sentence. What is meant is this: there is only one positive concomitance that follows all individual instances of fire and smoke; once it is grasped in one instance, it is indeed grasped in another as well, just like the nature of smoke (*dhūmatva*) and so forth. This definition of positive concomitance has been explained previously in the context of the relevant discussion. Likewise, the completion of the sentence is: "Negative concomitance is apprehended as the pervasion of the absence of the general probandum with the absence of the general probans. The term "general" (*sāmānya*) refers to the probans itself when its specific particulars are not intended. Its "absence" means the absence of smoke in general.

The probandum (*sādhya*) is of two kinds: either the property-possessor (*dharmin*) qualified by a property (*dharma*), or the property qualified by a property-possessor. If it is argued that it is not logical for the property to be qualified by the property-possessor—since the qualifier is the property and the qualified is the property-possessor—we say no; for we intend to designate the property-possessor as such by virtue of its being the locus (*āśraya*) of the proving property (*sādhanadharma*). Furthermore, the status of being a property is intended merely in the sense of depending on another. Alternatively, the conventional distinction between property-possessor and property is made with respect to their past and future characteristics; thus, there is no fault. When the property-possessor is the probandum, then the generality of the probandum is either mere fire (*agnimātra*) or the state of possessing fire (*agnimattva*). But when the property itself is the probandum, then the probandum itself, without regard for specific particulars, is the generality. The negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of that [probandum] by the absence of the generality of the proving property (*sādhanasāmānya*). Alternatively, the generality of the proving property is "smokiness" (*dhūmatva*); by its absence, there is the pervasion of the generality of the probandum, which is "fierness" (*agnitva*). The negative concomitance is as follows: wherever there is an absence of fire, there is the non-perception of fierness; and wherever there is an absence of smoke, there is the non-perception of smokiness. However, since there is no generality for "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth, the previous explanation applies. Or else, the generality of the proving property is mere existence (*astitvamātra*), and this exists even for "being produced" and so forth. Thus, it is stated that the pervasion of the absence of the existence of impermanence and so forth by the absence of the existence of "being produced" and so forth is the negative concomitance. In that context, the generality of the proving property is the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the generality of the probandum is the pervader (*vyāpaka*); this relationship of pervaded and pervader is positive concomitance (*anvaya*). The absence of the generality of the probandum is the pervaded and the absence of the generality of the proving property is the pervader; this relationship of pervaded and pervader is negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). The twofold nature of the relationship of pervaded and pervader is established by the two aphorisms: "The reason (*hetu*) is the proof of the probandum through similarity to the example" and "likewise through dissimilarity."
The varieties of gender markers.

The means of proof (*sādhana*) is the logical mark (*liṅga*); it is of two kinds: the perceived (*dṛṣṭa*) and the generally perceived (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*). The word "and" (*ca*) indicates that it is also twofold according to the distinction between inference for oneself (*svārtha*) and inference for others (*parārtha*). The mention of "twofold" is for the purpose of restricting the types to those already stated. It is restricted to these two modes mentioned, and not to other modes such as *pūrvavat* and so forth. However, in the Sūtra, the twofold nature according to the modes of the perceived and so on—indicated by the word "and"—is to be understood. Some maintain that the twofold nature arises from the distinction between effect (*kārya*) and essential nature (*svabhāva*), whereas non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) is included within this very [category] because there is no other type of necessary connection (*pratibandha*); to refute that, it is said to be "the perceived and the generally perceived," since a necessary connection based on identity (*tādātmya*) is impossible, as we shall explain later. Among these, the perceived is that which makes known an object capable of being perceived through direct observation, such as smoke [making known] fire. The generally perceived is that which makes known an object remote in its essential nature, such as the cognition of color and so forth [making known] the eye and so forth.
The examination of perceived signs.

Furthermore, the fitness for perception is understood precisely through the fact of having been previously perceived. For when an object that was previously seen by perception is inferred—whether separated by space or time—that inference is said to be "perceived" (*dṛṣṭa*) because its object is one that has been perceived. Even though there is a difference between individual instances (*vyakti*), it is said that "that very same [object] which was perceived is the very same one being inferred," because of the reliance on a single universal (*sāmānya*). In some cases, however, that very same individual instance is inferred through a specific effect such as sound or by another specific mark (*liṅga*) not common to others. For example: the inference of a brother or similar person from a specific sound; the inference of a previously seen painter from a specific painting; the inference of a previously seen king from specific signs such as elephants, horses, chariots, or parasols; and the inference of a specific constellation from a specific constellation.
{An Exposition of the Inference Based on General Observation}

In inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭānumāna*), however, there is neither identity of individual (*vyakti*) nor identity of genus (*jāti*), because axes and the like belong to different genera from the eyes and the like, and likewise, perception of such forms and the like do not belong to the same genus as cutting and the like. Nevertheless, since the mere presence of an action is observed to be invariably concomitant with the mere presence of an instrument, inference proceeds; and when a specific [instrument] is established by the force of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context), the conventional designation "eye" and so forth follows. Thus, because the inference arises from seeing only a generality, it is called *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. Although in all inferences there is an observation of concomitance through a generality, nevertheless, that very generality—such as "fire-ness"—by which fire and the like, the objects of inference, are designated in common usage, is what is seen elsewhere; therefore, that inference is said to be "seen."

{The Buddhist objection regarding universals} Now, it is not logical that a universal such as "fire-ness" (agnitva) is apprehended by perception; for perception grasps the intrinsic nature of a real entity (vastu), and a real entity possesses only an excluded form (vyāvṛttākāra), not a recurring form (anugatākāra).
To explain: individual manifestations do not follow one another, and nothing else that follows them appears.
If it were not distinct from cognition, how could it become a different object?

Individual instances do not, first of all, enter into one another, for that would entail the consequence of their becoming a single entity. And if they were a single individual, it could not be a universal (*sāmānya*), just like a jar (*khaṭvā*). Nor does a universal exist as something distinct from those instances, because it is not perceived [separately], like a quality (*guṇa*) in the presence of substances. Furthermore, it is not logical that a distinct designation and cognition should arise with respect to distinct objects based on a different object, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even if a relation existed, one does not observe the persistence of designation and cognition in the substrata of number, wholes (*avayavin*), and so forth, as seen in the examples. Therefore, this appearance of a recurring form in conceptual cognition is constructed by beginningless mental impressions (*vāsanā*) and is not based on a universal. If it is argued that the appearance in cognition itself is the universal, and that its reality follows from its being of the nature of knowledge, this too is not tenable.
For how could that which is distinct from cognition proceed toward another object?

How can the form of cognition be the universal (*sāmānya*) of objects, given that it does not exist within them? Alternatively, how could the form of one cognition belong to another cognition occurring in a different individual (*vyakti*), since it is not distinct from that [first] cognition? And if it does not pervade either the other cognition or the other individual, how could it be a universal? Therefore, this apprehension of a single nature among objects is a false conceptual construction (*mithyāvikalpa*). For they are not similar by means of any nature—whether distinct from or non-distinct from the objects—and thus their apprehension in such a way is nothing but a false conceptual construction.

For this reason as well, there is no universal (*sāmānya*): because of the absence of any other intrinsic nature (*svabhāvāntara*) that is delimited by association with a single [individual] restricted to specific place, time, and state, a single entity subsisting in many cannot be conjoined with another [individual] possessing specific place and so forth. The meaning of this is as follows: "place" (*deśa*), "time" (*kāla*), and "state" (*avasthā*)—these alone are the "specifics" (*viśeṣa*), for they are called "specifics" because they distinguish [an object] from others. That which is "restricted" (*viniyata*) to these and is also "single" (*eka*), its "association" (*saṃsarga*) with that, and the "other intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvāntara*) delimited by that; the "absence" (*viraha*) of that is the logical reason (*hetu*). As for the formal application of the thesis (*pratijñāprayoga*) beginning with "subsisting in many": the "cowness" (*gotva*), which is delimited by association with a body (*piṇḍa*) restricted to the place of Citrakūṭa, the present time, and the state of youth, is not conjoined with a body characterized by a different place, a different time, or a different state. This is because it lacks any intrinsic nature distinct from the intrinsic nature of that [particular] body, just like the essential form of the body itself.
{Refutation of the Buddhist Doctrine}

To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that individuals do not follow one another, and so forth—there is indeed no dispute on that point; an individual does not become the essence of another individual, nor is it conjoined with another individual. Furthermore, there is likewise no dispute regarding the refutation of a universal as a cognition (*buddhisāmānya*). As for the claim that nothing else following [the individuals] appears, that is unproven; for similarity (*sādṛśya*) does appear. The argument that "because qualities are not perceived in things like necklaces, [the universal] does not exist" is incorrect, because all objects appear precisely in their own form (*svarūpa*). If non-existence were established simply because something does not appear in another form, then blue and other colors would also be non-existent, since they do not appear in each other's forms. Moreover, even in the case of necklaces and the like, the non-existence of qualities would follow from their not appearing as such. If it is argued that the non-existence of the desired [universal] is proven because it does not appear as a quality despite being intended to be related to many [individuals], we say no; for in the case of a variegated cognition (*citrādijñāna*), which is intended to be related to many blues and so forth, its non-existence is not proven even though it does not appear as a quality. Or else, the non-existence of a cause intended to be related to multiple effects would be proven simply because it does not appear as a quality. If it is argued that because the nature of the relation differs, there is no non-existence despite the lack of appearance as a quality, we reply that here too there is indeed a difference in the nature of the relation: in the case of necklaces, the quality has *saṃyoga* (conjunction), whereas for the universal, it is *samavāya* (inherence) in its own substrates. If it is argued that because the number of effect-substances and so forth have the same relation, it would follow that they are the cause of a single-form cognition, we say no; because of the difference in the potencies of entities (*padārtha*). Just as, despite the lack of distinction in being effects, a difference in potency is understood through the observation of distinct effects in the case of color and so forth, and despite the lack of distinction in being earthen, a difference in potency is understood in the case of poison, honey, and so forth; so too, although there is no distinction in the fact that both effect-substances, numbers, etc., and the universal reside in many [substrates], it is proper to infer only a difference in potency based on the observation of distinct effects such as cognitions, rather than to conclude non-existence or to assert the unwanted consequence of producing identical effects.

As for the passage beginning with "place, time," and so forth: first of all, the inclusion of "place" and the rest in both the thesis (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is useless. For if the connection of something with another [entity] were established independently of specific place and so forth, then the qualification "possessing specific place and so forth" would be meaningful. Likewise, since it has been stated that [the subject] lacks any other nature excluded by its connection with one [particular], what over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) is there that the qualification of "place and so forth" is employed to prevent? Furthermore, there is a contradiction between the terms of the thesis: the subject is a single entity existing in many places, yet the property to be proven (*sādhya*) is that "there is no connection with another. This is untenable due to internal contradiction, like saying "one's mother is barren"; for existence in many places is not compatible with a single entity lacking connection with other substrates, and even the nature of a universal (*sāmānya*) is impossible if there is no relation to other substrates. Therefore, even a universal cannot be the subject. Now, if the existence in many places or the nature of a universal is accepted as the subject's property only from the perspective of the opponent (*parābhiprāyeṇa*), but not because you yourself accept a universal existing in multiple locations and then deny its connection with other substrates—then, according to your own view, what is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the subject intended? If it is characterized by exclusion (*apoha*), or by particularity (*viśeṣa*), or by cognition (*buddhi*), then in proving the absence of connection with another individual instance, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Nor is there any connection even with a single individual instance for that which is characterized by exclusion and so forth; thus the reason would be unestablished (*asiddha*). For the meaning of the phrase "because of the absence of any other nature excluded by connection with one" is "because of having a nature excluded by connection with one. But surely this was stated as a *reductio ad absurdum* (*prasaṅgasādhana*), so the fault of the subject being unestablished (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) and so forth does not apply. Is this *reductio* an inference (*anumāna*) or not an inference? If it is an inference, how can it establish itself while being devoid of the property of residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and the other requirements? If it is not an inference, how can the property to be proven be established from it, given that you do not accept any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) other than perception and inference?
The refutation of the universal by means of a reductio ad absurdum.

If it is argued that a *prasaṅga*-proof is stated by relying on a subject (*dharmin*) and a reason (*hetu*) that are established through the opponent's own admission (*paropagama*), then is that admission of the opponent supported by valid cognition (*sapramāṇaka*) or not? If it is supported by valid cognition, then the object established by it must be accepted by you as well, because valid cognition is impartial (*apakṣapātitva*). If, however, the opponent’s admission is not supported by valid cognition, then both the property (*dharma*) and the reason are unestablished; thus, the *prasaṅga* based upon them would be entirely invalid. Now, one might object: "At the outset, we do not perceive that [the opponent's position] is supported by valid cognition, nor is there an admission of anything at the time of investigation; rather, there is an admission of what has been investigated. Therefore, first the opponent’s admission itself is investigated as to whether it is supported by valid cognition or not. If it is supported by valid cognition, then this admission belongs to us as well."

If, however, it lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), then only the other [the lamp] is perceived. Whatever meaning follows by the force of reasoning must be accepted by you in its entirety, just as when light is accepted, the lamp must also be accepted. Indeed, no one accepts light while not accepting the lamp.
{The method for establishing the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader.}

In the absence of a fundamental reason (*maula-hetu*), this is the method for establishing the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva*)—namely, by demonstrating the connection between two properties such that "if it were so, this would also be the case, yet both are not [found]. The fundamental reason is the non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of that which is intended to be perceived through its distinction [from others], or the reversal of the reductio (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). The meaning of the reductio—that because of its pervasiveness, there would be no perception [of it] as restricted to a single individual—is what establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the fundamental reason. If it is maintained that [the property] is restricted to a single individual, then one must not admit its connection with another thing possessing specific spatial and other qualities. Conversely, if there is a connection with another, then its restriction to a single individual must not be admitted. It is impossible for both restriction to a single individual and connection with another possessing specific spatial and other qualities to coexist, due to their contradiction. If it is argued: "Let there be no restriction to a single individual, since it pervades all individuals," this is not the case; for: [The original Sanskrit text follows: *naikavyaktiniścayatayopalambhaḥ syād iti prasaṅgārtho maulasya hetor vyāptisādhakaḥ.* *yady evam ekavyaktiniṣṭhatvam iṣyate tadā na deśādiviśeṣavatānyena yogo'bhyupagantavyaḥ.* *athānyena yogas tadā tasyaivaikavyaktiviṣṭhatvaṃ nābhyupagantavyam.* *na caikavyaktiniṣṭhatvaṃ deśādiviśeṣavatānyena yogaś cety ubhayaṃ sambhavati, virodhāt.* *mā bhūd ekavyaktiniṣṭhatvaṃ tasyāśeṣavyaktivyapitvād iti cet, naitad asti; yataḥ —* [Translation of the concluding portion: "There would be no perception [of it] as determined by a single individual"—this is the meaning of the reductio, which establishes the pervasion of the fundamental reason. If it is thus desired that [the property] is restricted to a single individual, then one must not accept its conjunction with another thing characterized by specific location and so forth. Alternatively, if there is conjunction with another, then its restriction to a single individual must not be accepted. Furthermore, neither restriction to a single individual nor conjunction with another characterized by specific location and so forth is possible, because of their contradiction. If it is argued, "Let there be no restriction to a single individual, because it pervades all individuals," this is not so; for: [The final verse: *yadi sarvagatatvaṃ syād ekavyaktiniṣṭhatā kutaḥ | ekavyaktiniṣṭhatve ca sarvagatatvaṃ kuto bhavet ||* "If there were omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*), how could there be restriction to a single individual? And if there is restriction to a single individual, how could there be omnipresence?"* *Note: The final verse is provided here as it concludes the logical argument presented in the prose.*

If that [object] were common [to all], its cognition as being omnipresent would remain unimpaired; for an object cannot be apprehended without error by means of a form other than its own true nature. (67)

If a pervasive universal were apprehended by perception as being indeed pervasive, then certainly an erroneous apprehension would not be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). If pervasiveness is cognized, then there must necessarily be a cognition of all its individual instances (*vyakti*), because it is impossible to cognize the state of being the pervader (*vyāpaka*) without cognizing that which is pervaded (*vyāpya*). Yet, the universal is not cognized in such a manner in its own form; therefore, it does not exist. If this were the established position, there would be the fault of the subject (*dharmin*) being unestablished. This [statement] is merely intended to reveal a mutual contradiction [between oneness and pervasiveness]; we are not capable of establishing such a matter, for no other such thing is observed. Furthermore, inference does not function without an example (*dṛṣṭānta*)."

Now, if it is argued that while pervasiveness is impossible for a single corporeal entity, there is no contradiction between pervasiveness and unity in the case of a universal because it is incorporeal—this is not so; for it would follow that ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*), motion (*karman*), and so forth, would also be pervasive. Alternatively, even the universal would lack pervasiveness due to the absence of [ultimate] particulars. If it is asked, "Let the very nature of being a universal or its opposite be the basis for being pervasive or its opposite; what is the fault?"—surely the fault is simply the absence of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If it is claimed that perception itself is the means of valid cognition, then would it be grasped by perception as pervasive or otherwise?
If it is argued that there is no apprehension of pervasiveness, then perception does not have such a scope as to function with respect to a universal that pervades all individual instances. (70)

Now, if all individuals are not apprehended, then how can a universal, when apprehended as associated with only one individual, be apprehended as being pervasive? And if it is qualified by only one individual, the universal would become a particular, just like that individual. Even if its qualification by other individuals is understood through another mode of expression, how is its oneness established—as in the case of a staff-bearer and so forth? If it is argued that this is due to recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), no; for that is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Therefore, the universal defined by the aforementioned characteristics does not exist at all, precisely because it is not perceived.

How, then, is the non-pervasiveness (*avyāpitva*) of the universal (*sāmānya*) established? For the proof of some property (*dharma*) could only occur if the universal were established as the subject (*dharmin*), and not otherwise. It has been stated here that this is a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum), and not a primary logical reason (*maulo hetu*). If you accept the universal as pervasive, then it must be apprehended as such by a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because acceptance is dependent upon a means of valid cognition. Furthermore, how is it reasonable to accept that it is pervasive when it is perceived as being devoid of any other nature delimited by space and so forth, and restricted to connection with a single individual instance? Even when multiple objects are grasped through perception, the universal is not perceived as being pervasive, nor otherwise; therefore, an acceptance of what is not perceived is not reasonable. Thus, the universal does not exist.
The Refutation of the Refutation of Universals (Sāmānya)

All of this is incorrect: namely, that at the outset neither the state of having a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the state of lacking one is apprehended, nor is there an acceptance of anything at the time of investigation. This is not so; for at the very beginning, the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and so forth must be understood through a means of valid cognition. Otherwise, how could the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) occur by their power? For the status of being a constituent of proof for the subject, reason, and so forth does not arise merely from the acceptance of another; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things like a donkey’s horn would be constituents of proof since they are accepted by some. There is no dispute regarding the fact that what is accepted must have been investigated, and it is not mere acceptance alone [that suffices]. It is also not logical for something that has not been investigated to function as a reason and so forth, because of the consequence of fallacies such as being unestablished (*asiddha*).

As for what was stated—that [the universal] is like light and its illumination—that is not so. Why? Because the relationship of pervader and pervaded (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between those two would only obtain if it were established elsewhere through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might argue that this relationship of pervader and pervaded is indeed established in some cases, since you admit the absolute non-existence of universals and the like. However, if they exist in some cases, then by the force of the reductio (*prasaṅga*), their absolute non-existence cannot be established, just as with a lamp and so forth. {The Refutation of the Method for Proving the Relationship of Pervader and Pervaded}

As for what was said—that even in the absence of a [logical] reason (*hetu*), this is the method for establishing the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*) regarding the fundamental reason (*maula-hetu*)—that too is incorrect. For one who maintains the restriction to only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), what other method could there be by which the establishment of the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader might occur? If inference (*anumāna*) is the method, how could it exist in the absence of a reason? If perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the method, how could its nature be described by such statements as "in space, time, etc. or "the acceptance of light, etc."? And what is this "fundamental reason"? If it is non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), then if it refers to something invisible, how can it establish non-existence, as in the case of a *piśāca* or similar beings? If, on the other hand, this is the non-perception of something visible, then like a jar or the like, it is not an absolute non-existence, because universals (*sāmānya*) are perceived somewhere. Otherwise, how could they possess visibility? If visibility were established merely by the admission of another, then since the Buddha and others are also admitted by some to be visible, their non-existence would follow from non-perception. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate that non-perception is unestablished (*asiddha*).
Refutation of the Reduction to Absurdity and its Contrapositive

Now, the *prasaṅgaviparyaya* (the reversal of the reductio) is the fundamental reason (*maulo hetuḥ*). What kind of reason is this *prasaṅgaviparyaya*? If it is [the argument] "because it resides in a single [locus]," then there is no proof for either [of the two positions]. If, on the other hand, "because it is one" is the reason, where is the pervasion (*vyāpti*) established that "whatever is one is necessarily non-existent"? If you say that "being a pervader by virtue of being one" is what is being proven, then there is no negation of the general property-bearer (*sāmānyadharmī*), because the property is being negated—just as, for example, the properties such as permanence are negated in the case of color and so forth. If you ask, "If its residing in multiple loci is negated, how can the universal exist?", then what is the basis for the reason "because it is one"? By stating, "A reason is a property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) which is pervaded by a part of it; it is of only three kinds," you yourself have accepted that a reason lacking a locus is simply not a reason at all. Therefore, even a fundamental reason is not possible.
