As for the contradiction said to exist between residing in a single individual and being pervasive, that is already refuted by the very fact that we do not accept it; for we do accept that the universal resides in multiple individuals.

As for what was said—that because it [the universal] is common to many, there would be [error], and so forth—that is not so, because the property of pervasiveness (*vyāpitva*) is not apprehended. When the property of pervasiveness is apprehended, there arises a cognition qualified by that [property], not from the mere existence of it. Even when the nature of the self is apprehended as "I," no error occurs because pervasiveness is not apprehended, nor is there error because non-pervasiveness is also not apprehended. If it is asked, "How can there be an apprehension apart from the forms of pervasiveness and non-pervasiveness? [we reply: Just as the self is apprehended in the form "I am happy" and so forth, so too is the universal apprehended in the form of similarity, conformity, and so on. If it is argued that this is not a valid example because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatva*), we say no; for elsewhere the perceptibility of the self has been established. Furthermore, a substance such as a clod of earth, though heavy by nature, is not apprehended as "this is heavy"; in that case, would the apprehension of it even in its form as a clod of earth be erroneous? For an error is defined as a contrary apprehension (*viparītagrahaṇa*). Therefore, if the apprehension of the universal were in the form "this is pervasive," then it would be an error; but when the apprehension occurs through similarity—as "this is similar to that," "that is similar to this," or as a remainder—then how could it be an error? Even if there is an apprehension in the form of non-pervasiveness, still the universal is not thereby established, because it is impossible for the cognition of it to be erroneous in every respect. For example, the cognition of two moons is erroneous only in the aspect of duality and so forth, not in the aspect of the moon itself; therefore, the moon itself is not thereby disproved. And you yourself maintain that conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) is erroneous only in its conceptual aspect, not in its cognitive aspect (*bodhāṃśa*); and the establishment of the cognitive aspect is desired precisely from that [cognition]. Likewise, let the cognition of the universal be erroneous only in its aspect of pervasiveness, but not in its aspect of being a qualifier of a particular instance and so forth. Moreover, the very pervasiveness of the universal is apprehended by indeterminate cognition (*nirvikalpakabodha*). Otherwise, how could the relations of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) be apprehended in the particulars by means of that [universal], given the infinity of individuals? For if it were apprehended elsewhere [than in the particulars], it would be impossible to have a cognition of them through words and logical marks (*liṅga*). Furthermore, if it were erroneous, there could be no rule of correspondence (*saṃvādaniyama*). Therefore, precisely because the pervasiveness of the universal is apprehended, it is logical to apprehend the linguistic convention and invariable concomitance despite the infinity of individuals.

As for what was said—that because the pervaded is not perceived, it is impossible to perceive the pervasion prior to the apprehension of all individual instances—that is not so; for we do not admit that the pervasion qualified by all individual instances is apprehended through perception. Furthermore, the apprehension of the pervasion qualified by all pervaded instances is indeed accepted as occurring through inference.

However, even when only the pervaded (*vyāpya*) is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), you must also, though unwillingly, admit the perception of the pervader (*vyāpaka*); otherwise, there would be no cognition of fire as the pervader of smoke. Nor is the determination of the relation between the pervaded and the pervader based solely on the individual instances of cause and effect present before one; for if that were the case, inference could not function regarding things separated by space and time, since the existence of that relation would not be established. If the establishment of that relation were to depend on inference, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) or the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). Therefore, it is logical that even without perceiving every individual instance of smoke and fire, the determination of the pervaded-pervader relationship among those possessing them occurs precisely through the perception of the two universals (*sāmānya*) that have entered into that relationship. If, however, you maintain that all remaining individuals endowed with the universal alone are grasped through mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), let it be so. But the visual perception of the individual standing before one is assisted by numerous qualifiers; therefore, there is no manifestation of all individuals as possessing that [universal] at once. Furthermore, we shall explain the difference between the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*); thus, even when an individual is perceived, its qualifiers are not necessarily perceived. For this very reason, upon seeing another individual of a seen type—whether characterized as stationary or moving—one determines: "This was previously known by me to be of such a type and such a name. One considers it "seen" only insofar as it depends on those specific qualities, just as one says, "This woman was seen before," or "This man was not seen by me before. What is the use of saying more? Whether there is a perception of all individuals or not, the universal is indeed already grasped at the time of perceiving a single individual; otherwise, how could there be the cognition regarding another individual that "this is of exactly the same type"? And we shall refute the claim that this [cognition] is erroneous.
The apprehension of the pervasiveness of the universal.

If the pervasiveness of the universal (*sāmānya*) was not grasped previously, then it is grasped later by the mind aided by the perception of the various individual instances (*vyakti*) of that universal; what contradiction, then, could there be between these two? [Objection: But surely, the contradiction here is clearly manifested as being characterized by mutual exclusion (*parasparaparihārasthiti*) between pervasiveness and unity. [Reply: No, for there is no contradiction between unity and pervasiveness, just as in the case of space (*ākāśa*) and the like. [Objection: The example is like the thing to be proven (*sādhyavat*). [Reply: No, because that has been established in detail in the *Ātmasiddhi*. Furthermore, you yourself have accepted that even a single cognition of an omniscient being (*sarvajña*) pervades multiple objects of knowledge (*jñeya*), and that a certain cause pervades its multiple effects. And just as one perceives a single effect—such as cognition—in its infinite forms (light, sun, horse-nature, etc.), so too is it an act of extreme audacity to claim that such a thing is not perceived. There is no contradiction when there is a connection with non-causes. Likewise, there is no contradiction when a single universal is connected to multiple substrates (*āśraya*). This being the case, what was stated—"We do not [perceive] an object of such a nature," etc.—is refuted by this very argument. For even in the case of the cognition of an omniscient being and the like, which pervades multiple objects of knowledge, there is no perception of another such thing for the opponent, since there is no dispute regarding the existence of the omniscient being. However, it is an act of extreme audacity to say that although the infinite universals characterized as "cowness," "horseness," and so on, are perceived, no other such thing is perceived. Now, if it is argued that the universal cannot be apprehended because nothing else of that nature is perceived apart from the universal itself, then in that case, you would likewise be unable to apprehend the entity "donkey" or "camel," since nothing of that nature is perceived apart from donkeys and camels. If, on the other hand, the universal is not perceived at all, then one must simply say "because of the perception of that [universal] itself. To say "of another such thing" is redundant. Furthermore, the perception of the universal and the grasping of its pervasiveness have already been established. Nor is the restrictive rule—that whatever is formless (*amūrta*) must necessarily be pervasive—accepted. Therefore, there is no consequence of [particulars] such as atoms (*anu*) or specific qualities (*viśeṣa*) being pervasive. For entities possess diverse powers (*śakti*); thus, despite the lack of distinction in their formlessness and so on, only the universal has the power to pervade infinite individuals, while other particulars do not. Even though there is no distinction in their being material (*mūrta*), fire burns and water does not—what question can be raised against this?
The essential nature of the universal.

Now, [the opponent claims] that the very nature of the universal (*sāmānya*) is unestablished; that is not so, because it is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*). Whether its apprehension occurs through perception as being pervasive or otherwise, there is no fault. As for what was said—"The reach of perception does not extend this far," and so on—that is not correct, because there is no distinction even when mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) grasps a universal that pervades all individual instances (*vyakti*). As for the objection raised regarding the apprehension of [the universal] as associated with only a single instance—namely, "How could it be grasped as pervasive, and yet be non-universal like a particular?"—that is not so; for it has already been stated that even when there is an apprehension associated with a single instance, the apprehension of its pervasiveness may occur either at that same time or subsequently. Indeed, just as a stone, even when its heaviness is not apprehended, does not thereby possess a nature that is light like the wind, so too, even if its pervasiveness is not apprehended, the universal does not become non-universal like a particular.

{The Validity of Recognition} We shall establish that recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which has no other cause, is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By this means, even when there is the apprehension of a universal as being qualified by different individuals, the oneness of the universal is indeed established. This is not because the difference in location, such as a staff and so forth, is perceived [as the cause], nor because the recognition of that [difference] is caused by the universal; rather, there is no further universal within the universal itself. Therefore, the recognition even regarding the substrata of that [universal] is based solely upon the oneness of the universal. {Refutation of the Reductio ad Absurdum Argument}

As for what was said—"This is a *prasaṅga*-proof (*prasaṅgasādhana*): if you accept that a universal (*sāmānya*) is pervading, then it must be accepted as such by means of a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since acceptance is based upon valid cognition, it is not logical to accept something that is not perceived"—that too is incorrect. For who would make an acceptance of something unperceived, toward whom this [argument] would be meaningful? Furthermore, if a universal is not perceived as being pervasive, with respect to what would the terms "inference" (*anumāna*) and "word" (*śabda*) function? Indeed, the very nature of one individual (*vyakti*) does not persist in another individual; and if there were no persistence (*anvaya*), every reason (*hetu*) would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). Moreover, how could a word, even if not conventionally designated, indicate a reason and so forth? For even if a convention has been established, the word "Ḍittha" does not indicate another object, "Ḍavittha. Just as in the case of Ḍittha, Ḍavittha, and others, there is no single recurring cause among the various instances of smoke by which the recurrence of a single word [like "smoke"] could be explained. If it is argued that the application of inference and words occurs through the exclusion of others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*), then is that exclusion of others different from the individuals, or non-different? If it is different, and yet it resides as a single entity in all individuals, then that is simply the "universal" (*sāmānya*); there is disagreement over the name, but not over the thing itself. And if, while remaining unmixed, it is manifold, how can it be the cause of a single designation and cognition only in certain particulars? If, on the other hand, it is not different, then because the exclusion is one, it follows that the individuals themselves must be one. Or, if the individuals are infinite, it follows that the exclusion must also be infinite. And if it is infinite, then due to the absence of a single recurring cause, there can be no grasping of convention, persistence, and so forth.
{The Rejection of the Absence of Intrinsic Nature Based on Exclusion}:
Furthermore, as it has been stated here—
"Because cessation is devoid of intrinsic nature, there is no conceptualization of its persistence or non-persistence."

"In reality, this would not be a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because a positive injunction (*vidhi*) must conform to a real entity. This too is incorrect. For if exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) were devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), then how could there be the apprehension of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), logical concomitance (*anvaya*), and so forth, based upon it; nor could there be the relationship between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*)? Indeed, it is impossible to establish a linguistic convention or to apprehend a logical concomitance among certain particulars by means of something like a donkey's horn. Furthermore, since properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) consist in the form of exclusion, they would consequently be devoid of intrinsic nature; and thus, like a donkey's horn or a sky-flower, the establishment of the relationship between the probandum and the probans would be impossible.
The refutation of a universal that exists in the interval between cognition and its object.

By this, the universal (*sāmānya*) situated between cognition and its object is refuted; for a universal is said to be "the state of being common" (*samānānāṃ bhāvaḥ*). How, then, could it be situated in the interval [between them]? If it were connected to everything, it would be designated as the property (*dharma*) of a specific locus (*dharmī*). If its designation as that property were based on error, there would be no established distinction between the properties of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and "not being produced" (*akṛtakatva*) regarding their status as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharman*) or being unestablished (*asiddha*). For just as you have a firm erroneous conviction in the "producedness" of sounds, so too do the Mīmāṃsakas have a firm erroneous conviction in their "unproducedness"; in this case, which one would truly possess the property of the subject, or which would be unestablished?
Exclusions do not possess a single intrinsic nature.

Let it be then that "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "impermanence" (*anityatva*) are not different from the word itself; because of their identity (*tādātmya*), there is no deviation between them. As it has been said: "For when there is an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*), one thing does not deviate from another. This is not so, because the answer has already been given: if there were no difference between the property (*dharma*) and the subject (*dharmin*), the fault in the definition would have been stated by you previously. Furthermore, there would be synonymy (*paryāyatva*) among words such as "producedness" and so on; consequently, a statement such as "sound is devoid of sound because it is expressible" would be possible, and this [other] statement—"Sound is impermanent because it is produced"—would be just like that. This is not a fault, because:
All things, by their very nature, are established in their own individual natures;
for they all partake in exclusion from both their own nature and the nature of others.
Therefore, from whatever [object] the exclusions (vyāvṛtti) of things arise, based upon those [exclusions],
the various universals (jāti) are conceptually constructed as they penetrate their respective particulars.

Therefore, whatever specific property by which a distinction is perceived cannot be established by anything other than that; thus, the determination of difference is based on that [specific property].

All entities indeed abide in their own nature (*svarūpa*); they do not mix their essence with another, for that would entail the consequence of their becoming one. Nor is the non-mixing of entities based upon a universal (*sāmānya*), because such a universal is unperceived and thus non-existent. Or, even if it were to exist, since it too would be established within its own self, there would be no mixing with anything else; and if one were to postulate a further universal for that [universal] as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, these intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are distinct from both those of their own class and from others, because by their very nature they possess a single form. Consequently, although their intrinsic nature is undifferentiated, they are perceived as possessing multiple properties by taking up distinctions from whatever [other things] they are differentiated. These distinctions are conveyed by words whose application is assisted by the cognition of those specific differences. And while those words may imply all possible differences, because they enjoin only a single difference, they remain restricted to that particular specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). Thus, since that entity is also distinct from even a single other thing, there are as many exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) as there are forms of other things relative to that entity; and as many as there are exclusions, so many are the linguistic expressions (*śruti*) intended for practical usage (*vyavahāra*) by way of excluding what is neither its cause nor its effect. Therefore, even though the intrinsic nature is undifferentiated, a particular distinction or difference that is perceived through a certain property or name cannot be conveyed by any other [word]. Hence, all words do not have the same object. Furthermore, there is no fault such as "lack of concomitance" (*ananvaya*), for it is not the case that a single instance of fire is excluded only from those things that do not perform functions such as burning.
{The Refutation of the Distinction Between Exclusions}

To this it is replied: Let it be granted that objects possess unmixed natures; nevertheless, the claim that [words] are for the purpose of conveying the distinction from whatever [other things they are distinct] and so forth is not tenable. For is this "distinction" (bheda) the very nature (*svarūpa*) of the entity, or is it a different property (*rūpāntara*)? If it is the very nature of the entity, then how could words based upon it not have a single object? And how could that [entity] possess multiple properties? For even if there is a multiplicity of other forms, there is no internal division within its own self. If you argue that this is due to metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), we say no; because there is no basis for such metaphorical usage. Furthermore, it would follow that the relationship between the probandum and the probans (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) is merely metaphorical, since it would be rooted in metaphorical properties, just like the quality of being a "lion" and so forth. If it is argued that "distinction" is postulated as a property but not as the actual object itself, then what other "distinction" exists apart from the object, such that you can say this? Moreover, if the distinction between properties does not exist in reality, then—just as with the cases of "being expressible by words" and so forth versus "impermanence," "producedness," and so forth—the relationship of probandum and probans would not exist, because there is no difference in their being merely conceptually constructed distinctions. Consequently, the words serving as the grounds for those [properties] would be mere synonyms, just like the words "expressible by words" and so on.

Now, if it is maintained that the properties (*dharmas*) are indeed non-different [from the entity], then it has been said: "As many as there are other forms of a single entity, so many are its exclusions (*vyāvṛttis*) in relation to those [others]. This is not correct, because of the absence of a relationship. For there is no relationship whatsoever between an entity and its exclusions from others, since conjunction and the like are not admitted by you yourself. Nor is there a relationship of origination (*tadutpatti*), because exclusions do not have that [entity] as their cause or effect. If identity (*tādātmya*) is admitted, then if the exclusions are manifold, it follows unavoidably that the excluded entity must also be manifold; or if the exclusions are one, then the entity must also be one—this undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) is difficult to avoid. Furthermore, this would contradict the fact that a single entity possesses multiple properties, and it would also contradict the principle that "whatever specific difference is perceived through a certain property cannot be [perceived] by another. Moreover, regarding this exclusion of non-fire (*anagnivyāvṛtti*) which is held to be the cause for the application of the word "fire"—is it one and the same across all individual instances of fire, or does it differ with each instance? If it is non-different, then it is simply a universal (*sāmānya*), because its definition is being the cause of the cognition and designation that establishes a recurrence of a non-different nature across multiple things. If, however, it differs with each instance, then—just like the specific differences of individual things—it would lack recurrence; and due to the absence of such recurrence, there could be no grasping of linguistic conventions and the like, resulting in the total non-functioning of words and inference. Alternatively, if it is maintained that even though it does not recur across multiple things, it still serves as the cause for the functioning of words and inference, then one must admit that words and inference have the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as their object, since they are seen to function by way of affirmation (*vidhimukhena*). Furthermore, the defects such as the impossibility of establishing a convention (*aśakyasamayatva*) apply equally to the theory of exclusion (*apoha*); for if exclusion were of the nature of a real thing (*vastu*), it would be absolutely distinct [from other things], and if it were not of the nature of a real thing, it would not be an object of cognition.

{The suspicion that inference is redundant if its object is a real entity} Now, one might argue that if [inference] has a real entity as its object, it would indeed be useless, because the entity is already determined in all its aspects by perception alone. For instance: "Of a single nature of an object which is itself perceptible..."
What other unperceived portion could there be that would need to be examined by means of the instruments of valid cognition?
If another quality were not joined [to the object] by means of a cause of error—
just as the form of silver is [joined] to mother-of-pearl due to the perception of a similarity in appearance— [then error would not occur].

Just as there is the superimposition of the form of silver upon mother-of-pearl, if the form of non-momentariness and so forth were not superimposed due to causes such as the perception of a continuous succession of similar moments, then the operation of other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would find no scope. However, since all the various extrinsic natures of this [object] arise from their respective specific causes as superimpositions, other means of valid cognition are purposeful insofar as they exclude those [superimpositions], just like the means of valid cognition that excludes the superimposition of silver upon mother-of-pearl. Nor is it the case that other means of valid cognition lack the capacity to produce cognition, for their operation is observed in the production of cognition of their own [specific] parts; and since that which is partless cannot be perceived in a single part.
Therefore, every quality of a perceived entity is indeed perceived;
it is not that it is determined [to be absent] due to error—thus the means of proof proceeds.

It is not only when a thing is seen through direct perception that the absence of other means of valid cognition is established; even when a thing is determined by inference, that same fault applies. Thus he says: "But when a single property is ascertained through a means of knowledge upon grasping an object, the apprehension of all properties follows [in the case of exclusion]; this fault does not apply here."

For when that [the object] is ascertained, it is not logical for its nature to remain unascertained. However, when the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropa*) is effected by means other than inference, then because there is the exclusion of one thing through the exclusion of many, another [means of knowledge] operates for that purpose.

Therefore, the logical mark (*liṅga*) is proclaimed to have *apoha* as its object; otherwise, if the locus (*dharmin*) were already established, what would remain unestablished beyond that? Thus it is said.
The refutation thereof.

This [objection] is incorrect. As for the claim that inference and other means of knowledge would be entirely useless if they had a real entity (*vastu*) as their object—that is not so, because we do not admit the non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*). For this defect applies only to one who admits the non-difference of property and property-possessor. For us, however, there are many distinct properties belonging even to a single property-possessor; thus, although the property-possessor is perceived through one property, it is not cognized as qualified by other properties, and it is for that purpose that another means of knowledge operates. [Objection: But surely that [property-possessor] qualified by those [other properties] is the very same thing. [Reply: True; nevertheless, if the other properties are not grasped, there has been no cognition of it as delimited by them, and thus it is said to be "not cognized" as qualified by them—just as when a single mountain is seen as qualified by smoke, it is not seen as qualified by fire. For one cannot say that simply from seeing the mountain, the fire hidden within its other parts has also been seen. And if that [fire] were grasped, the cognition would be either "this [mountain] possesses fire" or "there is fire here. Therefore, the statement beginning with "of a single nature of an object" (*ekasyārthasvabhāvasya*) is indeed untenable.
The impossibility of the exclusion of superimposition.

As for what was also said—that other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) would be purposeful only if they were eliminators of superimposition (*samāropa*)—that too is incorrect. For when the inference of fire from smoke occurs spontaneously, it does not function to eliminate superimposition, since the superimposition of non-fire is not even conceivable there. Now, was it not also stated here: “If the locus (*dharmin*) is apprehended, then because of its non-difference [from its properties], all properties are apprehended; or, if there is difference, then there is no apprehension of that which is unrelated to it. Therefore, even in that case, for one who perceives it, the non-ascertainment of its nature arises from some error (*viparyāsa*). And how can he, while ascertaining that place in a form distinct from that [fire], be called non-erroneous with a cognition turned away from the cultivation of the state of possessing fire? One who is free from doubt and superimposition regarding that aspect should follow the logical mark (*liṅga*) for its apprehension. This too has been stated without any basis in valid cognition. For it cannot be said that there is non-difference or simultaneous perception between the fire and the smoke, or between the locus and the fire, even though they stand in the relation of property and locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*). Nor can one say, without shame, that because of their difference there is simply no apprehension of the fire there. Furthermore, the statement beginning with “And he, while ascertaining that place in a form distinct from that... is itself unintelligible. For it cannot be said that error or doubt exists even when it is not being perceived. Nor is it observed that immediately after seeing smoke, an inference of fire does not occur in the absence of such [error]. Nor is it certain that error or doubt functions as a cause for inference in the same way that the recollection of a connection [between the sign and the signified] does, by virtue of which their existence could be established even if they are not experienced as distinct. If it is argued that the very ascertainment of the locus as distinct from that [fire] is the error, we say no; for error consists in an ascertainment in a manner contrary to reality. If there were an ascertainment that “this place does not possess fire,” then it would be an error. But when the ascertainment is “this is smoke” or “this possesses smoke,” how can it be an error? And why would one who is free from superimposition and doubt not follow the logical mark? If it is argued that it is due to a lack of purpose, we say no; for the very cognition of fire is the purpose. If it is argued that this is because the [mark] is already established once the locus is established, we say no; for their security of status is unequal due to the presence or absence of an intervention. Moreover, we observe the relationship of the cognized and the cognizer (*gamyagamakabhāva*) even among color and taste, which are objects of a single sense-faculty. Because inference proceeds even against one’s will due to the intensity of habituation, inference does not fail to proceed merely because of the absence of superimposition. Since it has been stated that inference proceeds even toward what is not doubted by virtue of its suitability (*yogyatā*), there is no contradiction. Even in the case of what is doubted, the result of inference is not the cessation of delusion (*bhrānti*), because delusion is absent there and doubt is not itself a delusion. If it is argued that in the case of doubt there is a superimposition of a single property through conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and the elimination of that is the result of inference, let it be so; nevertheless, inference must be accepted as having a real entity (*vastu*) as its object. Otherwise, the cutting off of doubt would not occur. For a certainty regarding one thing does not remove doubt regarding another; otherwise, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). By this very reasoning, it is established that even that which removes error has a real entity as its object, just like direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Just as perception, operating upon a real entity itself, removes both doubt and error, so too does inference.
[The Buddhist position: "It is only conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) that dispels doubt, not perception (*pratyakṣa*). [Objection:

But surely doubt and the like are not dispelled by perception, since we observe doubt and so forth even regarding an object perceived in all its aspects. Rather, their removal comes from certainty (*niścaya*), and all such certainty has only exclusion (*apoha*) as its object. To this he says: "Even when something is seen in some respect, that conceptual cognition which has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its object..."
Not superimposed upon any part, its scope is the exclusion of that alone.

For where there is a superimposition (*samāropa*) of silver, permanence, and so forth, there is no certainty regarding that aspect; however, regarding the aspect of the shell and so on, certainty does arise because of the absence of superimposition. Therefore, it is understood that the operation of certainty occurs with respect to the exclusion of what is superimposed. And this very exclusion of that [superimposed nature] is "other-exclusion" (*anyāpoha*). Consequently:
"As many as are the superimpositions upon the various aspects, so many are the definitive cognitions for their removal; and so many are the words. Therefore, they have distinct domains."
"Otherwise, since a single word would comprehend a single object pervaded [by its property], and since it would have no other object, there would be synonymy. {Refutation thereof}

This too is incorrect, because the existence of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) has already been established. Furthermore, in this way, even direct perception would have exclusion (*apoha*) as its object, since it too lacks any superimposed object. For even direct perception does not manifest things as they truly are when they appear in forms such as duality, which are superimposed by causes like ophthalmia. If it did so manifest them, there would be no room for error, because of the contradiction between correct and false perception.

Now, if it is argued that even when reality (*tattva*) has been seen correctly, the superimposition (*āropa*) of forms such as duality occurs subsequently, and therefore this error is born of the senses because it arises subsequent to the perception—this is not so; for if that were the case, the inclusion of the term "non-erroneous" (*abhrānta*) would be purposeless. Consequently, since sensory cognition (*akṣajajñāna*) also functions toward the exclusion of superimposition, it follows that its object is *apoha*. If it is further argued that while perception (*pratyakṣa*) has the real thing (*vastu*) as its object by virtue of its capacity to exclude others, this is not the case for conceptual determination (*niścaya*), and why? Because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of grasping all aspects (*sarvākāra*)—this is not so, because the answer will be stated later. Furthermore, if an object were grasped by perception in all its aspects, then how could an error regarding silver and the like occur? For there would be no room for error concerning an object of knowledge of reality, or else there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The Buddhist's presentation of the intervention [of space] and so forth regarding difference, and its refutation.

Now, it has been argued here: "Indeed, even if an object is perceived as distinct from everything else, it is not recognized in that very same way, because in some cases there may be an intervention [of error], as in the case of [mistaking] mother-of-pearl for silver. However, where there is no cause for the perceiver’s delusion, then, despite the lack of difference in the perception of that object, a mnemonic certainty arises; this is because there exists a relationship of sublation and sublated between superimposition and certainty. This is incorrect, because it contradicts identity (*tādātmya*). For one who says that there is an intervention in some cases but not in others, the acceptance of identity is contradicted, just as in the case of an object covered by a wall and one that is not. If you mean by "intervention" and "non-intervention" the states of being remembered or not remembered, then identity is still contradicted; for there is a difference between what is remembered and what is not, just like between what is seen and what is otherwise. Otherwise, there would also be a difference based on being seen or unseen. If you say that intervention and non-intervention consist in the presence or absence of a cause for delusion, even then identity is contradicted, because there is a difference between their respective objects, just as between the moon and the earth. If it is argued that there is no fault because it is not accepted that delusion and certainty have real properties as their objects; then it must be said that an object once seen is never recognized at all, and the specific mention of "in some cases" and so forth is useless. Even if you claim that they have the same object through a causal chain (*pāramparya*), the contradiction remains, since we observe that the certainty regarding the water of the Ganges and the certainty regarding mirage-water have different objects even through a causal chain. There is no universally accepted example for something having the same object when there is no difference in the object, for there is no example well-known to both parties of someone having both delusion and non-delusion toward the same thing at the same time. Furthermore, mother-of-pearl cannot serve as an example, because the properties such as "being mother-of-pearl" are also admitted by others to be distinct.
Precisely because certainty has a real entity as its object, it possesses the capacity to sublate error.

Furthermore, if [determination] has a non-real object (*avastuviṣayatva*), then its status as a sublater (*bādhakatva*) would also not be established. For it is not logical that the cognition of two moons should be the sublater of the delusion of four moons. If you say, "It is like a dream," no; because in that case, the relationship between the sublated and the sublater is unreal (*avāstava*). And if one were to accept that [the relationship is unreal], then the validity (*prāmāṇya*) of both [cognitions] having a real object would be untenable, and all determinative cognitions would be useless for human goals (*apuruṣārtha*), being like dreams. Therefore, it is logical that a valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*) arising through the power of reality (*vastubala*) is the sublater of what appears as such (the fallacious). If you ask, "In this way, how is it that determinative cognition does not have reality as its object?"—if you say, "Because it is not directly (*sākṣāt*) directed toward that [reality]," then since even error is preceded by the perception of reality, it would follow that there is no distinction [between determination and error]. If you say, "The distinction is that the determination of mother-of-pearl and the like is a synthesizer (*anusandhātṛ*) of the form as it was seen, whereas the cognition of silver and the like is not," then if it does not have that [reality] as its object, how can it be called a synthesizer of it? And if it does have that as its object, it would follow that it synthesizes all forms, because [reality] is partless (*niraṃśa*). If you say, "There is a metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) of having that as its object because that [perception] prompts activity toward it," no; since the object of activity is also partless, how can it be said that the determination occurs only in a certain part? If you say, "The object is conceived as having many parts because it is excluded from many [other things]," let it be so conceived; nevertheless, it is determined as being exactly partless, just as it was seen. Otherwise, the determination would not be a replica of what was seen, or else that perception itself must be accepted as not being according to reality. Just as in perception the object does not impart its own form in parts because it is partless, so too it is not logical for determination to have the form of the object or the form of the perception in only one part, because of its partlessness. Furthermore, if it were formless (*nirākāra*), the restriction of [cognition] to specific objects (*pratikarmavyavasthā*) would be untenable, or else one would have to conceive of perception itself as being without form. Nor is the relationship of sublated and sublater ever established between two cognitions with different objects; rather, it is established among both worldly people and investigators (*parīkṣaka*) when they share the same object, just as in the case of kings and their subjects.
Even when the objects are identical, the relationship between the sublated and the sublator is untenable.

Now, one might ask: even if two cognitions have the same object, how can there be a relationship of sublated and sublator (*bādhyabādhakabhāva*) between them? For otherwise, it would follow that such a relationship exists between memory and direct experience (*anubhava*), and because it contradicts the principle of the convergence of means of knowledge (*saṃplava*). If you argue that this relationship exists only between two contradictory [cognitions], then it would follow that it could exist between any cognition and another cognition, since they are all mutually contradictory. Furthermore, the seizure of an object (*viṣayāpahāra*) is possible only for things like kings and the like, not for two cognitions. Indeed, the object of one cognition cannot be seized by another cognition, because a cognition merely presents its own object. For this very reason, a cognition that apprehends the non-existence of a cognition or its object is not a sublator, as that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: When one cognition, having functioned by superimposing qualities not belonging to a certain object, is apprehended by another cognition as possessing its actual properties, that other cognition determines the former’s status as a superimposer of non-existent qualities. This alone constitutes the relationship of the sublated and the sublator (*bādhya-bādhaka-bhāva*). Thus, the cognition "This is mother-of-pearl, not silver," becomes the sublator precisely by apprehending the true nature of the thing. Nor is there any contradiction in its having a real entity as its object, such that one would have to assume—on the grounds that it occurs immediately after the apprehension of the entity—that it merely has the semblance of having that as its object. Furthermore, even when multiple superimpositions are negated, the difference between properties does not appear through a positive form (*vidhi-mukhena*), as in: "This is not a donkey, not a horse, not a buffalo, not a gayal; rather, it is a cow. Therefore, as long as determinations are not made through a positive form, however many properties of the distinct object they may be, they must be accepted as being like a staff, an earring, and so forth. Consequently, the fault of [the opponent's view] regarding the apprehension of all properties and so on does not apply; however, for the proponent of identity (*tādātmya-vādin*), this fault indeed exists.
Even in the theory that [the universals] have distinct external adjuncts (*arthāntaropādhivāda*), there follows the undesirable consequence of perceiving everything.

Now, one might object: "But surely that same fault has already been demonstrated even in the position that [the universals] are distinct properties (*bhinnadharma*); for it was said: 'Even for one who thinks that the adjuncts are indeed distinct from one another and from their substratum, and that the linguistic designations based upon them apply to those substrata—or that this [consequence] does not follow in that very case—for him too, when there is the apprehension of the self which is non-different from the powers that are the constituent parts of the assistance provided by the various adjuncts...'"
For that which is to be assisted by its entire self, what undetermined distinction could there be?

Even if the adjuncts (*upādhi*) are indeed distinct as the causes for various words and cognitions regarding an object, that [object]—possessing those [adjuncts]—is apprehended as one. For that which has the nature of a power (*śakti*) that serves as the basis for the assistance of various adjuncts, there is no absence of non-difference within its own self. If it were grasped in its entirety, what distinction among the adjuncts could possibly remain unascertained? This is because it is grasped as the benefactor of all the adjuncts. Indeed, the state of being a benefactor is not something other than its form as it is being perceived; therefore, if it is grasped by way of its own nature, it is likewise grasped by way of its state as a benefactor. Because these two are connected within the self, both are grasped in a single cognition. Since the adjunct and the possessor of the adjunct—which are identical in essence—are grasped in a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakāraka-bhāva*), both are grasped in a single cognition. Thus, when that [object] is grasped even as qualified by a single adjunct, all adjuncts are grasped, because the correct perception of the adjuncts is inseparable from the perception of that [object]. Otherwise, it would not be grasped in that manner either. For there is no such thing as a benefactor of another that is distinct [from the beneficiary] and could remain unperceived. Nor, when the benefactor is thus perceived, can there be a non-perception of the beneficiary, for that would entail the non-perception of the former as well, just like the relationship between property and owner. Therefore, this same logical consequence applies even in the theory that the adjuncts are distinct entities (*arthāntara*).

Now, it might be argued: "The powers are indeed distinct from the possessor of power, and it is by means of them that he assists the limiting conditions; therefore, this undesirable consequence does not follow. [To this we reply:

If there is a difference between the powers that assist the properties and that [possessor], what do those [powers] do for him? If they do not assist him, then they would likewise be non-existent; thus, there would be an infinite regress.

If its various adjuncts (*upādhi*) and benefactors (*upakāraka*) are neither identical with its own nature (*svātmabhūta*) nor do they experience benefit from it, then in what sense can they be said to belong to it? Or, if there were such a benefit, then this single entity, while benefiting those powers through powers that are identical with its own nature, would—when apprehended even by means of a single adjunct—be apprehended in its entirety. For, upon the apprehension of one adjunct, there is the apprehension of the power that benefits it; and upon the apprehension of that [power], the entity which benefits it—including all the benefits of the powers identical with its own nature—is apprehended, thereby causing all the powers and those very adjuncts to be apprehended. Thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) remains.

Furthermore, those capacities that assist [the entity] must themselves be distinct from the entity. For, in this way, since there would be no finality in the series of adjuncts (*upādhi*) and their capacities within ever-higher and lower capacities, their integration would be impossible. That single entity, never grasped by those [adjuncts] as having the nature of being assisted by them, would not be grasped as possessing them. Moreover, if words were to project only the adjuncts, then because the [entity] itself is not included therein, there would be no comprehension of everything through the comprehension of that [entity]. Even then, since the [entity] would not be indicated by the words, there would be no activity directed toward it; thus, the employment of words would be futile.

Now, all worldly practice based on action proceeds through injunctions and prohibitions, and in that regard, limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are ineffective. And since only what is effective is enjoined, what is the use of verbal associations? Consequently, the adjuncts would not be adjuncts at all. For they are so called only in relation to some primary entity with respect to which there is activity toward something else; but since that [primary] is not implied by words, those [adjuncts] do not become parts of anything. If it is argued that there is no fault because of "indication of the indicated" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇā*), the same undesirable consequence follows. That [primary object], being perceived as necessarily connected with those many adjuncts, is perceived in its entirety even by a single indicator; thus the undesirable consequence remains as it was. For what difference is there here? Words might indicate this [object], and the adjuncts would be indicated by them; yet at that time, that [object] is determined [in its totality]. Even when the sun and other such visible objects are perceived, there is no perception of the perceiver or the act of seeing in every case. By this, the following is also refuted: it is not the case that one thing which is not itself perceived can be a helper of another, nor is there a failure to perceive the helped when the helper is perceived in that way, for that would entail the non-perception of the helper as well—just like the relationship between property and owner. For if the sun were perceived, there would have to be a perception of the three worlds (*trailokya*) which are helped by it. For the sun, as perceived in its capacity as a helper, is not something other than the one who helps the three worlds, such that it could remain unperceived. Furthermore, for one who asserts that there is no non-perception of the helped when the helper is perceived—just like property and owner—the perception of the three worlds helped by the sun would be unavoidable. As for what was said: "The state of being a helper, which assists all powers inherent in its own self, causes the perception of all powers and those very adjuncts"—by this, it is indeed claimed that the perception or non-perception of even those indirectly helped is entailed. In this way, however, there is an even greater undesirable consequence: the perception of the entire world. How so? Any given object, such as the earth, wealth, or the sun, when perceived as a helper to itself, is necessarily perceived as a helper to others as well. For its status as a helper to others is inherent in its own nature; and being perceived in that way, it causes the perception of all things it helps, and those others help their own respective things, and those others help still others, and so on. Likewise, the state of being both helper and helped is inherent in the very nature of the object. Therefore, when the object is perceived, that [state] is also perceived; and being perceived in that way, the object such as the earth or wealth causes the perception of all its helpers. Those others help their own respective other helpers, and those others help still others, leading to the undesirable consequence of perceiving the entire world.

Furthermore, the apprehension of form (*rūpa*) as having the nature of form is itself [an apprehension] of its being an auxiliary to taste (*rasa*) and so forth, because the latter is identical in nature to the former. And since form, thus apprehended, causes taste and the rest to be apprehended as well, it follows that taste and the rest would also be objects apprehended by the eye. Consequently, there would be a contradiction with the fixedness of the respective domains of the sense-faculties. Thus, by these reductio arguments (*prasaṅga*), it is the Venerable [Bhadanta] alone who is challenged, not we; for he himself has accepted those very reductios. Our position is that the apprehension of the qualified (*viśeṣya*) occurs precisely through the delimitation (*avaccheda*) of whichever qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is apprehended. However, we do not hold that when something delimited by even one [qualifier] is apprehended, it must be apprehended as delimited by all [of them], because such is not the case in experience. As it has been said: "The very apprehension of this [object] by way of its own-being (*svabhāva*) is also [an apprehension] by way of its being an auxiliary (*upakārakatva*). This is not correct, because the property of being an auxiliary to itself is distinct from that [object]. Or, let us grant the apprehension of its being an auxiliary; even so, what follows from the apprehension of other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are different from that [auxiliary nature]? If it is asked, "If those [adjuncts] are not apprehended, how can its being an auxiliary to them be apprehended?"—well, if others are not apprehended, then [the object] cannot be the maker of those others; this amounts to nothing at all.
In the theory that [the universal] is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) consisting of another entity, there is no consequence of perceiving everything.

To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that the object, whose nature is non-different from its powers which are caused by the assistance of various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is grasped in its entirety [by a single cognition], and that if there were a difference in the assisted [object], there would be a difference in the adjunct due to the lack of certainty—this is not tenable. For if there is a difference, it is impossible for there to be a rule that upon the apprehension of one, the other must necessarily be apprehended; it is precisely for this reason that there is the certainty of difference, since if there were the apprehension of only that one, there would even be a suspicion of non-difference. Furthermore, even when the substratum is apprehended, there is no necessary apprehension of those things residing in it, because even when the earth, mountains, and so forth are apprehended, all things residing therein are not apprehended. If you say that there is an apprehension of a "part" (*ekadeśa*) of them, even so, the argument is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for to whatever extent that part is apprehended, there is no apprehension of all things situated in that much space. Likewise, even when the body is apprehended, there is no apprehension of the ornaments and such things residing in it. Thus, there is no apprehension of it in its entirety (*sarvātmanā*). Nor, however, is another single thing apprehended solely through its own singular nature (*ekātmanā*) rather than in its entirety; for it is impossible for a single nature to be the nature of everything. If you say that "entirety" is spoken of because it is the locus of all its own attributes (*dharma*) which reside in the universal (*sāmānya*), even then, as long as all its attributes are not apprehended, it is not apprehended as "this is the locus of all attributes. But if one speaks thus according to the actual state of things (*vastusthiti*), then even the body and so forth would be apprehended in their entirety, since they too are the locus of all their own attributes.

Now, "as an undivided whole" means "as the self of all [its parts]. Even the body, its own spatial location, and so forth, are apprehended only as an undivided whole, yet there is no apprehension of everything residing within them. Furthermore, the fact that the body and such things possess the nature of a composite whole (*avayavin*) has already been established; therefore, their being an undivided whole is not unproven. Moreover, you too must admit that fire and smoke share a single substratum; otherwise, the logical reason (*hetu*) would be misplaced (*vyadhikaraṇa*). It is not the case that fire is apprehended merely through the apprehension of the substratum of smoke, for if one were to postulate its apprehension even when its form does not appear, then one might as well postulate the apprehension of the entire triple world. Furthermore, upon the apprehension of a dancer, there would follow the undesirable consequence of apprehending the cognitions of all observers, because they are related to her just like one's own cognition. And if that were admitted, it would contradict the statement, "There is no other experience of her," and it would contradict direct perception (*pratibhāsa*); for the perceptions belonging to others do not appear as immediate (*aparokṣa*) to anyone. Just as, even when the dancer—who is non-different from the power of assistance—is apprehended in her entirety, there is no apprehension of all the cognitions that are assisted by her, so too, upon the apprehension of the substrate possessing attributes (*upādhimat*), there is no apprehension of all the attributes. To say that the apprehension of the substrate is inseparable from the apprehension of those attributes is baseless; for the substrate is not observed to be apprehended only when all its attributes are apprehended, nor is it not apprehended at all when even a single attribute is not apprehended. To explain: how can "exclusion" (*vyāvṛttatva*) be apprehended in something qualified by the attribute of its own perception? If one admits the apprehension of what is other than that, then upon the apprehension of a single object, there would follow the apprehension of all objects, since all are "other" than it. Consequently, no further perceptual activity would occur. If it is argued that while the certainty "This is that Devadatta" should not arise when Devadatta is not apprehended, "exclusion" is nevertheless apprehended in its own right even when he is not, then we reply: if this is so, then while the certainty "This is his assistant" should not arise when the assistant is not apprehended, "the state of being an assistant" is nevertheless apprehended in its own right even when he is not. This argument amounts to nothing. If it is asked why there is no simultaneous apprehension of all attributes situated in a single locus, the answer is: due to the deficiency of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), such as unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), which brings about such an apprehension. While such apprehension may indeed occur for some things by means of indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpaka*), determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) requires auxiliary factors such as the recollection of names arising in succession; therefore, it occurs only in that sequence. Thus, in the theory of attributes being distinct entities (*arthāntara-upādhi-vāda*), there is no consequence of apprehending everything. Furthermore, words such as "cow" are not admitted to have the attributes alone as their object. Consequently, the refutation stated against that position is avoided simply by the fact that it is not accepted.
Only in the theory that [the universal] is a limiting adjunct (upādhi) not distinct from the object itself does the consequence of grasping everything follow.

In the theory that [the universal] is a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that is not distinct from the object, the consequence of grasping all limiting adjuncts is indeed unavoidable. Since there is a contradiction between grasping only one part and [the claim of] non-difference, the grasping of all exclusions (*apoha*) is necessarily accepted; if it is argued that the certain determination (*niścaya*) of this does not occur due to error, we say no, because the same consequence applies here as well. Upon the certain determination of one exclusion, the certain determination of all exclusions—which are non-different from it—would follow. For an exclusion does not, in relation to its certain determination, abandon its identity by becoming fragmented. If it is argued that identity is desired for the real entity (*vastu*), but not for the exclusions, we say no, because the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) and the excluded thing (*apoha*) are not different in meaning. Furthermore, the exclusion is not other than the excluded entity; so how could the exclusions not have the nature of being real entities? And if the certain determination does not have the real entity as its object, then the entity would remain entirely undetermined. How can an undetermined thing be made the subject of linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*)? If it is argued that it is grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then is perception not itself doubtful or delusive in nature? If you say it is not, then how is it not determinative?
The Refutation of the Claim that Perception Does Not Determine Particularity (Bheda)

As for what was said—that perception is not determinative of anything, and that whatever it grasps, it does not do so through determination (*niścaya*), but rather through its own manifestation (*pratibhāsa*)—that is not correct; for a manifestation that lacks determination takes the form of doubt (*sandeha*). Indeed, we do not observe a third kind of manifestation. Erroneous determination, however, is error (*viparyaya*), since reasoning (*tarka*) and non-ascertainment (*anadhyavasāya*) are included within doubt. As for memory, it conforms to the form of experience; thus, the twofold nature of even non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) is established in the definition of doubt.

If it is argued that the cognition resulting from memory, verbal testimony, and inference is intended as "ascertainment" (*niścaya*), and that this has only the exclusion (*apoha*) as its object and not the real entity (*vastu*) as its object—this is not so; for its having the real entity as its object has already been established and will be established further. Moreover, if the ascertainment arising from memory did not have the real entity as its object, how could it be called invalid on the grounds of apprehending what has already been apprehended? Indeed, it is not logical to say that a cognition whose object is a different thing or which is objectless is one that apprehends what has already been apprehended. Furthermore, it would follow that it is a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), for it cannot be non-valid, nor can it be included within perception, because, while being consistent with reality, it has exclusion as its object just like inference. Nor is it inference, because it is not produced by a mark possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpaliṅga*), just like perception.

But surely, if difference is apprehended by perception, how can the subsequent memory be a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*)? The determination of all its aspects, however, does not occur due to the absence of auxiliary conditions. As it has been said: "Even though a particularity devoid of parts has been apprehended by perception, that cognition which effects the ascertainment of a specific aspect is recognized as [a distinct] cognition."

Even if an object is experienced as being devoid of parts and possessing a nature distinct from everything else, nevertheless, a certain determination (*niścaya*) does not arise regarding all its differences at once, because it depends upon other causes. For experience produces a determinative cognition (*niścayapratyaya*) according to the habituation of conceptual construction (*vikalpābhyāsa*). Just as there is no difference in the perception of a form, yet there arise the conceptual constructions of it as a corpse, a beloved woman, or food. In this regard, factors such as the acuity of the intellect, the habituation of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and the specific context (*prakaraṇa*) are the cooperative conditions for the arising of a determinate cognition of the non-difference of the experience; and it is due to the distinctions among these very factors—such as their proximity and degree—that a sequence of priority and posteriority occurs. This is just as when one sees one's father approaching, despite the lack of distinction between his being a progenitor and a teacher, one thinks, "He is coming," [and not, "The teacher is coming"].

This too is untenable. For this entity does not fear perception alone, such that it would surrender its own self by becoming partless for that very [perception]. And from where did it learn this spell, medicine, or magic trick, whereby—even though it is partless—it becomes manifold for the sake of a determinate cognition (*niścaya*) and displays only one part of itself? Furthermore, a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakāribheda*) cannot break a partless thing into fragments. Therefore, if there is a difference in determinate cognitions, then even when there is a difference [in cognizers], it is determined in exactly that way because of the difference in the object, as in the case of the sun seen by many people; otherwise, one might as well postulate multiple parts due to a difference in visual perceptions. Indeed, a description of a difference in auxiliary causes is appropriate only when there is a real difference in properties (*dharmabheda*), because distinct things do not share the same acquisition and preservation (*atulyayogakṣematvāt*), like a staff and an earring. The example of the conceptualization of a corpse and so forth is also improper, because the properties such as "corpse-ness" are themselves different. Otherwise, one could argue that here there is a determining factor—such as mental acuity, its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), or practice—while elsewhere it is absent; thus, it would be just like the seeing and non-seeing of a single object.
{The refutation of the impossibility of identity among exclusions (apoha)}

Now, if the identity (*tādātmya*) of exclusions (*apoha*) with the objects of certain cognition is not admitted, then there would be no consequence of grasping everything. In that case, does that certain cognition operate upon the real entity (*vastu*) by way of the exclusion, or is it merely the exclusion itself? If it operates upon the real entity, the consequence follows that all exclusions are grasped. Why? Because if it operates upon that [entity] by way of something that provides no assistance, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And if it does provide assistance, if the real entity’s assistance to the exclusion is the very same as its assistance to all exclusions, then the real entity, though determined as assisting the form-exclusion (*ākārāpoha*), would be determined as assisting all exclusions. Furthermore, as long as all exclusions are not determined, it is impossible to determine the "assistance to all exclusions," just as [one cannot determine] the relation between a thing and its owner; therefore, there is the consequence of grasping all exclusions. And if words have only the exclusion as their object, then through the apprehension of that [exclusion], there would be the apprehension of everything; yet even then, since the real entity is not implied by words, there would be no activity toward it, and thus the employment of words would be useless. For all worldly practice (*vyavahāra*) based on causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) proceeds through affirmation and negation, and the exclusion is incapable of that; moreover, what is capable is not being enjoined—so what is the use of employing words? Consequently, there would be "exclusions of exclusions" (*apohāpoha*), for they are so called because they serve as a subordinate part (*aṅgabhāva*) of something that is being excluded. But since those [exclusions] are not implied by words, they do not constitute a subordinate part of anything; how then can they be called "exclusions"? By this, the view that the meaning of the word "exclusion" is either the form of a cognition (*buddhyākāra*) or something existing in the interval [between things] is refuted. If it is argued that this is due to "indication by indication" (*lakṣitalakṣaṇāt*); the same consequence applies. That [real entity] is indicated as being inseparably connected with those many exclusions; yet, by a single indication, it is indicated in its entirety. Thus the consequence remains as it was. What is the difference here? Whether the words indicate it, or the exclusion indicated by them is determined at that time as "assisting all," there is the consequence of grasping everything.

But surely, for you, the entity is the benefactor of exclusion (*apoha*), because it is impossible for there to be an exclusion of something other than that [entity]; nevertheless, since this would lead to an infinite regress by postulating further exclusions for that which is being excluded, the very exclusion is itself the excluded.

Therefore, the description of the position regarding "possessing that" (*tadvat*) in relation to the object of "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is rejected; for a fault would indeed arise if there were a distinctness between the universal (*jāti*) and its possessor (*tadvat*).

As for what they say—that even if the word-referent is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), because it denotes that which is qualified by it, all the objections raised against the position that the referent is a positive entity (*tadvatpakṣa*) apply equally—this too has been refuted. For in that case, a word that operates upon one thing while taking up another object as its basis is beset by defects such as lack of independence (*asvātantrya*). And the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) is not a different object in this sense.

Thus, this "logic of the glowing iron ball" (*ujvalakaṭanyāya*) has been followed. To explain: when the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is applied to a man by taking up a staff, it does not denote his earrings or other ornaments; yet, for that reason, words such as "earring-wearer" (*kuṇḍalin*) would also have to be meaningful in that same context. But in the case of that which is partless (*niraṃśa*), what could remain undetermined for the sake of which another word might be employed, or whereby there would be redundancy? If it is argued that the difference between verbal cognitions arises from a difference in convention (*saṃketa*) and not from a difference in the denoted object (*vācya*), [we reply]: surely, in the absence of a difference in the denoted object, even a difference in convention is untenable; it would be a synonym, like *ghaṭa* and *kumbha*. This is because, unlike the case of a staff and so forth, there is no difference in the causal basis (*nimitta*). Furthermore, if one were to admit a difference in the causal basis, there would be no non-difference between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmin*). Moreover, there would be no use of the genitive case or the formation of secondary derivatives (*taddhita*)—such as "the state of cows is cowness" (*gavāṃ bhāvo gotvam*)—because there would be no meaning beyond that of the base noun (*prakṛti*).
{The Buddhist position is that even though there is no difference between the property and the property-bearer, words function as if they were distinct.} But has it not been stated here:
"Even when two things are denoted by a single word, the case-ending indicates their distinction"?
It follows as if it were a distinct meaning, due to a slight particularity in the expressed sense.

The application of words does not depend on the actual state of things; rather, it depends on the speaker’s intention. Therefore, having superimposed a distinction, a case-ending is conventionally assigned and becomes the cause for cognition according to that convention. For example, the plural form may be used in the sense of the singular—as in *yūyam* (you), *vayam* (we), or *guravaḥ* (teachers)—for the purpose of manifesting respect and so forth. And in such cases, there is no need for a different convention. As it has been said: "The exclusion or non-exclusion of other distinctions between those two [types of universals] is the fruit of the difference in convention, which follows the desire of the knower."

When, having formed a conceptual cognition (*saṃjñāta*) that does not depend on other exclusions, one wishes to make known to someone who desires to know merely the exclusion of "horse" regarding a specific object, then one employs a word for which a convention has been established according to that [specific] meaning, saying "this has non-horseness. But when one wishes to make that known by rejecting other exclusions, then one says "this is a non-horse. For this very reason, in the former case, because the operation of the word excludes other differences, there is neither grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) nor the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśe�ya-bhāva*), as in the expression "its cowness is white. However, when other differences have not been excluded, it occurs as "the cow is white."

This very distinction exists everywhere between two words—one denoting a substance and the other denoting a state—even when they do not refer to distinct entities; therefore, there is no difference whatsoever in their expressed meaning.
Whether it be by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) or even by a primary derivative (*kṛt*), if one intends to convey a different meaning and expresses something else,
there is no distinction beyond that.
Moreover,
for those whose words are governed by the nature of things and do not depend on the speaker's intention, an objection regarding the genitive case, number distinctions, and so forth, is appropriate.

Even if these words were indeed intended to be employed by persons at some point, this objection— "How can there be a genitive case ending and so forth?"— would only apply if they could not be so employed because of a necessary connection to a real entity (*vastu*), as is the case with smoke and the like. However, when a word is assigned by speakers as a signifier (*vācaka*) in whatever manner they determine it;
That speech which expresses [its object] in such a manner is independent of any external referent.
And for one who maintains that in all cases the distinction in the application of words is based solely on a real entity (*vastu*),

what would be the basis for the establishment of difference and non-difference in such instances as "dārāḥ" (wife/wives), "ṣaṇṇagarī" (the city of six), or "khasya svabhāvaḥ khatvam" (the nature of space is spaceness)? Thus [it is asked].
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that [the exclusion] is due to a specific slight portion of the denotable object—that is incorrect. For how could there be a specific denotable object even in a slight degree for that which is partless (*niraṃśa*)? Indeed, no differentiation of properties (*dharmabheda*) is admitted in any respect, because the position of non-absolutism (*anekāntapakṣa*) is not accepted. If it is argued that it is so called through a convention based on the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of difference, then such a cognition would necessarily be false. If you say, "Let it be so," then in that case, the terms "soundness" (*śabdatva*) and "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) would be synonyms, because they are non-different from the word itself; and consequently, just like soundness, producedness would also lack positive concomitance (*anvaya*) in jars and other things. As for what was also stated—regarding the rejection or non-rejection of other differences—we shall explain later how the property of "cowness" (*gotva*) exists even apart from the exclusion of others. Furthermore, if other differences are not distinct entities (*arthāntara*) from the thing being excluded, then how can there be a non-rejection of them? For even by one well-trained, a cloth cannot be grasped while abandoning its own nature. And the state of synonymy remains exactly as before. If, however, they are distinct entities, then if the object qualified by them is denoted, you have arrived at the status of eating vomit—since you are now accepting the very position previously rejected. For what is the distinction here: let the object possessing universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth be denoted, or rather, let it be denoted as qualified by exclusions (*apoha*)? If, on the other hand, only the other differences themselves are denoted, then the employment of words is useless, because that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*) is not denoted; this has already been stated. Moreover, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) would not exist, because—as with words like "jar" and "cloth"—there is no connection to a single referent. If it is argued that there is a connection to a single entity through a lineage (*pāramparya*), then the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of coreferentiality and so forth would apply even to words like "jar" and "bowl," since they too are connected to a single potter through a lineage. If you say, "Because there is no determination (*adhyavasāya*) of those [words] toward that [single entity]," then why does the determination not occur? If you say, "Because the convention (*saṃketa*) does not apply to them there," then in that case, they would directly have that as their object, producing a non-erroneous certainty only where they are conventionally established. Why then speak of "through a lineage"? Furthermore, even through a lineage, if there is no connection to distinct qualifiers but only a connection to the mere thing, there is no example established for both parties regarding the occurrence of coreferentiality. However, in the case of a connection to distinct qualifiers, the fact that words such as "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) function in that way is well-known to all the world; thus, there is an example.

As for the argument beginning with "desiring to make known," that too is incorrect, because it fails to understand the opponent's intention. We do not say that words such as *kṛt*-suffixes, *taddhita*-suffixes, and so forth, ever denote a single [identical] meaning. What then? If they were to denote a single meaning, they would be mere synonyms, just like the words "difference" (*bheda*) and "distinctness" (*bhinna*). Consequently, the utterance of another word would be redundant, there would be no distinction between the subordinate (*guṇa*) and the primary (*pradhāna*), and there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with "cowness" (*gotva*) as there is with "whiteness" (*śuklatva*). Furthermore, if one accepts a difference in properties (*dharma*), how could there not be some distinction within the sentence?

By this, the view of those who claim that "words are dependent upon things" (*vastuvaśā vācaḥ*) and so forth is also refuted. For we do not maintain that all words are bound to real entities; rather, only those that function as means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are so considered, just like sensory cognitions. It is precisely because both modes of usage are observed that the matter is investigated. Expressions such as *dārāḥ* (wife/wives) and *ṣaṇṇagarī* (the six cities) are also not instances of an unspoken censure [of our position], for we do not accept a restrictive rule such as "the plural must be used for many. This is because we accept that the application of words follows conventional agreement (*samaya*). Thus says the Sūtra: "Because the comprehension of meaning from a word is based on convention. Nor is the plural number accepted in the sense of a single object in the case of *gavām* (of cows); nor is the genitive case used where there is no distinction, since the universal "cowness" (*gotva*) is perceived when many individuals, such as Śābaleya and others, possess a single property. Furthermore, one cannot say "cowness exists in many," because that would entail the non-existence of cowness in the state of plurality.
