For this very reason, this is not an instance of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*) suffix applied in its own primary sense (*svārtha*), as in the case of *rākṣasa* from *rakṣas*, because there is no such linguistic usage. While there is usage such as "Rakṣas is a Rākṣasa" in coordination with Rāvaṇa and others, there is no such usage as "this individual is cowness."
Refutation of the General Critique of the Sugata’s Teachings

Furthermore, as for what was stated here—that there is no such thing as a universal (*sāmānya*), but rather a cognition based on words arises through the power of beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, creating even unconnected properties; and that by virtue of the appearance of that [cognition], a universal and co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) are established—this is incorrect. For it would follow that inference is false, like dreams and the like, since there is no difference in the absence of a real connection with the object. Moreover, even if one grants the distinction that [inference] is preceded by the perception of a real entity, it would follow that steam and the like, when determined to be smoke, could also serve as inferential indicators of fire. Furthermore, the absence of similarity to previously perceived smoke is equally present in other instances of smoke; or else, you must admit a universal, since it is precisely similarity that is designated by the word "universal. If that [similarity] were absolutely non-existent, from what source would this distinction arise: that the cognition of similarity here is reliable, while it is not elsewhere?
Regarding the Buddhists' conceptualization of the two truths:

if it is argued that there is a distinction made between the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) and the non-conventional, the following thought might occur: "Where the universal (*sāmānya*) is conventionally real, there conventional practice (*vyavahāra*) is consistent, but not elsewhere; for that which is superimposed by mere conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) is unreal even conventionally. [The author] now demonstrates the nature of that convention and its universal:
"That by which the form of another is concealed by means of one's own form through cognition..."
Based on entities that appear as having a single object, despite being distinct, [a conceptual cognition arises].
By which conventional reality, with its various distinctions concealed,
diverse entities themselves appear as if non-distinct through some particular form.
By virtue of her intention, the universal (sāmānya) is proclaimed to exist;
yet it is non-existent in the ultimate sense, just as she had imagined it.

Indeed, cognition (*buddhi*), arising in dependence upon objects that are excluded from others, being conceptual (*vikalpikā*) and conforming to the nature of its own latent impressions (*svavāsanā*), conceals their diverse forms—which are the causes consisting of the exclusion of non-cows and so forth—and having determined its own undifferentiated appearance, it presents those [objects] as conjoined. This is "concealment" (*saṃvṛti*), because by means of it one's own form conceals the form of another. And these various instances of concealment, though themselves distinct, appear through some form as if they were non-distinct. Therefore, for those who follow this appearance of cognition, the "universal" (*sāmānya*) is said to be the grasping of specific features of entities that exist only within cognition, which flash forth as if external. How, then, is the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*) the universal? It is precisely that exclusion; and while grasping that very [exclusion], that [cognition] appears to grasp a real entity due to the natural delusion of conceptualizations. For, since it arises only with respect to things distinguished from others, it is understood to have distinction as its object.

[Objection: But surely outsiders (*bāhya*) are undiscriminating, and for them there is no activity of conceptual construction (*vikalpavṛtti*); how then can [the universal] exist for them? [Response: It is indeed the commentators who analyze in this way, not those engaged in worldly practice (*vyavahartāraḥ*). They, however, considering only their own objective support (*svālambana*) to be fit for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāyogya*), proceed by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object. It is solely due to their intention that it is said thus. Because they produce [cognition] as such, they convey through words things as distinct from those that do not produce it; yet, because of the difference in appearance and so forth, those who contemplate reality (*tattvacintaka*) do not admit non-difference. If one follows the intention behind the cognition, let it be that even "exclusion of others" (*anyāpoha*) is not the universal, for the cognition does not occur in that way. Nor is the cognition merely "thus"; nor is its form—whether distinct, non-distinct, unitary, eternal, or all-pervading—the cognition itself. Rather, a cognition arises with a non-differentiated form. What is the basis (*āśraya*) of that [cognition]? It is called "exclusion of others," because it exists in real entities (*vastu*) without contradiction, and because worldly practice based on words is observed to function in that manner. However, there is no such thing as a "universal" that exists in the way this cognition appears.
{The refutation thereof}

This is incorrect, because the notion of an object-form within cognition has already been refuted at length [in the previous section], and because perception involving conceptual construction (*savikalpa-pratyakṣa*) has been established. Therefore, it is untenable for the cognition of similarity regarding brindled cows (*śābaleya*) and the like to be erroneous. Furthermore, there is an absence of any cause for error. First of all, this is not an error caused by defects in the sense organs, because it appears to all persons at all times, just like the perception of blue and so forth. Nor is it caused by similarity, because there is no other similarity [to serve as its basis]. Nor is it caused by association with something else—as in the case of a blue crystal—because, given the impossibility of a universal (*sāmānya*), association with anything else is impossible. Nor is it caused by a disturbance of vision due to distance—as in the case of the blue sky—because that universal appears even when the brindled cows and such are nearby. Furthermore, the possibility of being on a boat or similar movement is simply not present here. Nor is latent disposition (*vāsanā*) the cause here, because no capacity for the production of such an error is perceived in that disposition when it is devoid of its usual accompaniments, such as sleep and so forth. If you argue that it is like the error of a woman and so forth in one who is overwhelmed by passion, then in that case, it would not occur universally and without distinction, but only for some specific individuals. Indeed, the error of a woman and so forth does not occur universally for everyone; rather, it occurs only toward specific objects. Moreover, in the absence of the perception of such an object, a latent disposition capable of producing an error of identity through mere instruction alone is impossible. And if that object is not seen, a cognition produced by a latent disposition as an identity cannot possibly be non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādin*).

As for what was said—that [the conceptual cognition] arises depending on objects that are excluded from others (*tadanyavyatirekiṇaḥ padārthān*), and so forth—regarding that, are those objects excluded from others mutually dissimilar (*asamāna*) or similar (*samāna*)? If they are dissimilar, then the unitary cognition based upon them, which conforms to the reality of smoke, wind, and so forth, would not be consistent. If, however, they are similar, then a universal (*sāmānya*) must be admitted for them; otherwise, how could they be similar? For you maintain that objects are by their very nature (*svabhāvena*) of a dissimilar essence. And how could a cognition of similarity regarding things that are dissimilar be consistent, like the cognition of yellow in a conch-shell and the like? However, a non-deviant unitary cognition is observed even among dissimilar things due to a single relation, such as "king's man, king's man" in the case of those accepted by a single king, or "seen, seen" in the case of blue and other colors due to their connection with a single act of seeing. Even where there is a difference in the acts of seeing, the common factor is simply "not being unseen. But in the absence of a cause residing in the object as a whole (*avayavin*), the arising of such a cognition is impossible. How, then, could it be that through this [cognition] the forms of others are concealed by one's own form? Consequently, even a conventionally real (*saṃvṛtisat*) universal would not be established. For if the perception of similar objects were the natural disposition (*vāsanāprakṛti*) [of the mind], then the conceptual cognition following it would be a memory; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, in the absence of a universal, they cannot be called "similar."

{Refutation of the Universal as the Form of Exclusion from Others} If it is argued that the universal is simply the exclusion from others (*tadanyavyāvṛtti*), we say no; for that exclusion is not common to all individuals and thus lacks continuity (*ananvaya*). If it were common, it would be indistinguishable from a genus (*jāti*). Just as a linguistic convention is grasped regarding objects that are continuous by virtue of a single genus, so too could it be grasped regarding objects continuous by virtue of a single exclusion; for what difference is there here? Consequently, the fault stated against the position [that the universal is] "possessing that" (*tadvat*) applies to you as well.

Granted, let there be such a fault; let there be no other universal (*jāti*). For even by one who accepts a universal, a distinction between entities must necessarily be admitted, so that words and the like may apply to objects qualified by that [universal]. Since it is impossible to avoid the fault in every respect, the employment of words is for the sake of excluding what is unintended; thus, it has exclusion as its result. To illustrate: when "bring it" is said, there might be doubt regarding another substance also fit to be brought; to exclude that, the word "ghee" is used. Otherwise, the mention of "ghee" would be redundant. Similarly, the mention of "bringing" is for the sake of excluding other actions, and the mention of "Devadatta" is for the sake of excluding other persons. Thus, in all cases, exclusion is the meaning of the word.
Now, even if one asserts that [the word] denotes a genus (*jāti*), the exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) is not investigated. Regarding this, it has been said:
"If there is an exclusion for this [word], yet this much is not its purpose;
why then, in that case, would there be another general term (*sāmānya*) or the like?"

To this it is replied: If a tree is defined as that which is excluded from non-trees, and a non-tree as that which is excluded from trees, then this mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) is unavoidable. For instance, if the category of non-trees is not apprehended, there can be no apprehension of the category of trees through its exclusion; and if that [category of trees] is not apprehended, there can be no cognition of the category of non-trees through its exclusion. Consequently, since even the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) would not exist therein, there would be a total absence of practical usage (*avyavahāra*). If you argue that this is equally true for us as well, we say: No, it is not equal. For one who maintains that a real universal (*sāmānya*) exists does not posit anything through the exclusion of something else. What then? Having pointed to a single object standing before one, the convention "this is a tree" is established. At the time of the convention, having understood that object as being endowed with the universal (*jāti*), one also understands its subsequent usage. But surely, even in this case, the convention is untenable because one cannot say, "This is a tree, and this too is a tree"; no, for it is possible in both ways. Without regard for particulars, one may say, "This is a tree, and that other one is also like this. But with regard to the universal, one is trained to think, "Only this is a tree," and wherever one does not perceive treeness, one oneself understands that very thing to be a non-tree, because what is contrary to what has been seen is easily known. This is not possible for the proponent of exclusion (*vyavacchedavādin*). In the case of a cumulative position (*samuccayapakṣa*), exclusion is not established; but in the case of a restrictive position (*avadhāraṇapakṣa*), since the perceived [tree] lacks concomitance (*ananvaya*) anywhere else, there would be no cognition of "tree" even in another individual instance.

{The Exclusionary Nature of Causal Efficacy and its Refutation} Now, it may be argued: all things that perform a single causal function, such as cognition, are indeed excluded from those that do not perform it; therefore, a convention (*saṃketa*) is established based on that exclusion even with respect to a single instance. Consequently, at the time of practical usage (*vyavahāra*), there is also the cognition of the exclusion of non-performers. What is inconsistent in this? How can a non-different effect arise from distinct things in the absence of a universal (*sāmānya*)? This is the very nature of entities, since: "In the accomplishment of a single purpose, such as a single reflective awareness or a single cognition of an object..."
Even though there is diversity, some things are determined by their own intrinsic nature, like the sense faculties and so forth.
"Just as certain medicinal herbs are observed to pacify fever and other ailments either collectively or individually, while others do not, even though they differ in their various properties."

To this it is replied: First, as for the claim that "the capacity to perform a single purposeful action (*ekārthakriyākāritva*) is the cause for the non-distinction [of individuals from a universal]," that is not so. For we observe the cognitions of "cow," "fire," and so forth, even when no such purposeful action as carrying or burning is perceived. Nor is it logical to say that something possesses the capacity to perform an action simply because it does not perform it, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that "capacity itself is what constitutes performing that action," then what is this "capacity"? It cannot be the essential nature (*svarūpa*) itself, because that nature lacks persistence (*ananvaya*); and if it lacks persistence, then another individual (*vyakti*), being excluded from that nature, would also follow as not being that [universal]. Furthermore, one would have to determine the capacity to perform that action merely from seeing the essential nature of something never seen before. If, on the other hand, capacity is a property (*dharma*) of that thing, then if it is not a distinct entity (*anarthāntara*), it is simply its essential nature, and the refutation stated there applies. If it is a distinct entity (*arthāntara*), then that is precisely the universal (*sāmānya*); there is no dispute about this. By this, the claim that "capacity is what performs the action" is also refuted. As for the argument beginning with "some things are restricted despite their difference," that is not so. It is logical that the sense organs, light, and so forth—which fall within a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*)—should produce a single effect. However, individuals separated by space and time do not fall within a single causal complex. And falling within a single causal complex is a specific relation belonging only to those assisted by a restricted genus (*jāti*). Why? Because we do not see things that are unconnected or connected to a different genus producing that particular effect. Indeed, the eye does not produce cognition through a form (*rūpa*) that is unconnected, nor through touch (*sparśa*) and so forth, even if they are connected. By this, the fact that medicinal herbs produce a single effect is explained. There too, the connection to a single effect follows from the persistence of a commonality such as "guḍūcī-ness. But in the case of milk, curd, and so forth, because that [commonality] is absent, they do not possess the capacity to produce that [single] effect.

Now, it has been argued here: “If the effect, such as the alleviation of fever, were to arise from the universal (sāmānya) alone, then because that [universal] is without distinction, there would be no difference—such as slow or rapid subsidence—and no gradation of quality, even when there are differences among the individuals, such as the nature of the patient's constitution (*kṣetra*) and so forth. This statement is incorrect. For it is not the case that wherever one universal exists, there is no other particular universal or some specific auxiliary cause (*sahakāryantara-viśeṣa*) by which the disparity of the effect would not occur. Nor is it accepted that the universal alone is the cause of that effect; what then? It is the individuals (*vyakti*) conjoined with that [universal], and these are endowed with intermediate particular universals (*avāntara-sāmānya-viśeṣa*). Endowed with intermediate particulars, they produce effects of that kind; however, when endowed with different auxiliary causes, they produce entirely different effects. Thus, the inference that “from a cause of such a kind, accompanied by such auxiliary factors, an effect of such a kind arises” is also established. But if the universal were absent, since even the various auxiliary causes of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) would be absolutely distinct, how could there be positive concomitance (*anvaya*)? In its absence, how could there be inference? Consequently, those seeking a specific effect would simply not engage with specific causes. Furthermore, if the property of being the producer of that effect were common [to all], then because it is distinct from the uncommon [particulars], it is said to be the very universal. Moreover, there is no certainty regarding the production of that effect even when the effect is not observed. For even when a potter is certain in one instance, there is no certainty regarding him in other cases, such as potters and weavers, where that effect is not seen. Just as for one who is proficient in one case, there is certainty regarding poison, fire, and so on in other cases—even though their effects have not been seen—simply through the non-loss of their essential nature (*svarūpa*). And if a word also applies to those things that produce that effect by way of exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) from those that do not, then a single word would apply to things like lamps and light, which perform the same function, due to their exclusion from non-producers; furthermore, there would be no usage of distinct genera (*jāti*) for the various sub-varieties like *śābaleya* and others. If it is argued that the usage of distinction arises from the difference between other effects, this is not so; since a difference between other effects is possible for every individual, the usage of a universal would be destroyed. Nor is any effect produced by the eye alone, such that the word ‘eye’ could be applied to it specifically by its exclusion from non-producers, because an effect is observed to arise from a collection of causes belonging to both the same and different classes; therefore, the word is applied to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) itself.

Now, if the cause is indeed the specific [particularity] of each individual, then even though a jar is produced from multiple causes, its nature as clay arises solely from the lump of clay (*mṛtpiṇḍa*), while its specific configuration arises solely from the potter; thus, since these are the very essence of the jar, how could that specific [configuration] not be produced by multiple causes? Or else, the jar itself would not be produced by multiple causes. But if they are distinct, then the admission of their identity (*tādātmya*) is lost. Furthermore, why is it not accepted that the nature of being clay is created by the potter, while the configuration is created by the clay? If you say, "Because there is an absence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)," how can there be such an absence? If you say, "Because even in the absence of a potter, the nature of being clay is perceived in things like anthills," then since that is perceived even in the absence of every other cause of a jar, the lump of clay itself would not be its cause. If you say, "There is another clay there that is the cause," then even when that other exists, how can the lump of clay be the cause of something distinct from it? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If you say, "The property of being clay (*mṛttva*) exists there too," this is the story of one who has forgotten his horse while mounted upon it. Since jars, bowls, and the like possess mutually exclusive natures, how could there be a universal (*sāmānya*)—such as the capacity to produce a single effect or the exclusion of what does not produce that effect—among the clays that are their material causes? For proponents of universals, however, it is only when a cause of the same class as clay exists that something of the same class as clay is produced; in its absence, even jars and anthills would not belong to the class of clay. Thus, through positive and negative concomitance, it is logical to establish the causal relationship specifically for the particularities. In the absence of a universal, however, there would be no recognition or cognition of a single form even among things that are utterly distinct.
{The capacity for causal efficiency as the determinant of the convention of non-difference, and its refutation}: Furthermore, it has been stated here—
“Having observed various instances of causal efficiency, such as cognition and so forth, which they perform distinctly...”
Together with the sounds whose objects are the exclusion of everything other than that [referent].
"One should indeed perform recognition by connecting [the past and present] upon seeing another [object]."

That is the manifestation of extreme ignorance; for the cognition of a single form does not arise merely upon seeing a causal function (*arthakriyā*). As has been stated, this is because a single form is perceived even in the case of cows, fires, jackfruits, and so forth, despite the non-perception of their specific causal functions. Furthermore, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) does not occur solely through the association with a name; for even one who is unacquainted with linguistic conventions recognizes that "the form of this is the very same as the form of that" regarding mobile beings of the same species who are situated together in one place, even though they have no names.

[Objection: But surely, for one who perceives a single causal efficiency (arthakriyā), such as cognition and so forth, there arises a false cognition (*mithyāpratyaya*) upon the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*); otherwise, there would be no cognition possessing both difference and connection, as in the case of men with staffs. For in that case, even when there is a connection with a single staff, the thought "this is that very same [man]" does not occur; rather, it is "that is here. And recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is not like this; rather, it is "this is that very same thing. [Reply: No, because that is unproven. For indeed, a recognition "this is that very same thing" does not occur regarding another individual (*vyakti*). What then? It is either "this form of his is the same as his," or "this form of his is the same as his," or "this belongs to the same genus as that. Furthermore, there is no sublation (*bādhā*) here, therefore this is not an error. If recognition were to determine a non-different nature in things that are different, then it would be false, as in the case of lamps and the like. However, just as a staff appears as the locus of that [person], or as "this is his," or as a qualifier of him, so too the universal (*sāmānya*), which is denoted by words such as "form," "nature," or "similarity," appears as the locus of that, or as "this is his," or as a qualifier of him. [Objection: If this cognition of a single form occurs regarding non-universals, such as water-mirages, then it is an error. [Reply: No; even there, the cause is merely the universal. How then is it an error? Because of the superimposition (*adhyāropaṇa*) through memory—aided by factors such as merit and demerit—of "water-ness" and so forth, which was previously seen in conjunction with that universal. [Objection: But that very form is not a universal, so how could there be no error? Nor is it the case that everywhere the superimposed form of a universal appears, for there is no sublation of that [universal] in those cases. Furthermore, since something never before perceived cannot be superimposed—like a donkey’s horn—it is impossible for there to be a superimposition of that [universal] if the universal were not apprehended along with it, as in the case of the form of a donkey in mirages. Therefore, even if one does not wish it, the universal must be accepted. [Objection: One must accept that individuals possess a power (*śakti*) to produce a single effect; let them, being distinct from others, produce such a cognition. What is the use of a universal there? [Reply: This is not so. Because the universal itself is the power called "capacity" (*yogyatā*). For instance, when their commonality is observed, threads and the like are determined by those seeking a cloth to be "capable of producing a cloth," and thus they are employed. If, however, the final capacity were grasped [at the outset], then since the effect would already be established, those seeking it would not engage in activity toward it. Nor is the inherent nature (*svarūpa*) itself the capacity, because even when the nature is grasped in cases where the effect is not yet seen, there is no certainty regarding its efficacy. [Objection: If you say there is no certainty due to error, from what is the error removed? [Reply: If you say "by seeing the effect," then how is it so regarding the objects of engagement? For the nature is not the same in other individuals, such that if it were certain in one, it would be certain in another, as in the case of a universal. Moreover, if the capacity for one effect were determined by the perception of another effect, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). [Objection: If the capacity is determined everywhere by the perception of a cognition with a non-different form, then this is precisely what has been raised: how can a cognition of a non-different form regarding different things be non-contradictory (*avisaṃvādi*)? [Reply: If you say "due to the power of the real entity (*vastusāmarthya*)," then the distinction between the forms of entities is destroyed. Then a cognition of blue, yellow, and so forth, occurring only among white things, would be non-contradictory due to the power of the real entity—this would be a case of "stretching out the feet" (a lazy, absurd conclusion). Furthermore, unity is improper even for cognitions that differ according to each object. Unity by way of a genus (*jāti*) is also impossible, because a genus is not admitted even there. Thus, since other causal efficiencies have mutually exclusive forms, how and from what source could the causes of those [efficiencies] have the performance of a single causal efficiency as the basis for the linguistic usage of non-difference? As it has also been said: *(Note: The original text ends mid-sentence regarding the citation.)*

"Because it is the cause of a single unifying cognition, the intellect is non-different; and by virtue of being the cause of that single cognition, the individual manifestations are also non-different."

That too is without substance, for how can even the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) possess unity? Is it by virtue of the individual instance (*vyakti*), or by virtue of the universal (*jāti*)? First, it is untenable on account of the individual instance, because multiple instances are perceived in a temporal sequence, and because that [awareness] differs with each person; furthermore, it is impossible for past, future, and other such cognitions to be produced by a single [instance]. Nor is there unity by virtue of the universal, because the existence of a universal is not admitted. Even if one were to postulate that it is the cause of a single reflective awareness, there would be an infinite regress; consequently, since its capacity would be exhausted merely in establishing the unity of the cause, there could be no cognition of non-difference regarding the original individual instances. Therefore, the conventional usage of non-difference regarding individual instances is based solely upon the apprehension of the unity of the universal. And as for what was said—
"Since the difference [between universals] is equal, let that very proximity by which a universal extends to some [individuals] and not others be the basis for words and cognitions."

This too is a faulty objection. For it is not the case that by whatever proximity a staff, a string, and so forth extend to a certain place and not elsewhere—that very same proximity should serve as the basis for the conventional usage of "one with a staff" (*daṇḍin*) or "one with a string" (*sūtrī*) in relation to a person, a crystal, and so on; what need is there for the staff, the string, and the like? Furthermore, an effect possessing a specific genus arises due to the restriction of the causal complex (*hetusāmagrī*). Nor can that very same complex—which would have to follow all stable individual instances—be the cause for the determinate words "cow" and so forth, because a qualified conventional usage depends upon the apprehension of a qualifier. Now, do individuals act as causes for a qualified cognition or not? If they do, what is the use of a universal (*sāmānya*)? If they do not, then there would be no activity toward them based on the cognition of that [universal].
If individual manifestations, accompanied by a single entity, are the cause of cognition,
then why does that single entity not eliminate the diversity of those manifestations?

Now, if difference (*bheda*) is not opposed to production, what then? Rather, it is isolation (*kaivalya*); accompanied by that very [difference], [the universal] certainly produces [the cognition]. How, then, is the capacity of individuals understood? Because even when they are individually absent, [the cognition] occurs provided that [the universal] is present; and because [the cognition] exists only when the universal exists. This is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Even when any one of the blue and other [colors] is removed, the visual cognition is produced, but the blue and others are not produced when the eye is removed; nevertheless, it is not the case that those [colors] lack capacity. As for what was also said: "If that [universal] is capable only in dependence on any one of them, and not alone..."
If those [atoms] could assist that one [cognition], why then could they not assist a single cognition?

If distinct [particulars] also assist a non-distinct universal, then let them likewise assist only the cognition of capacity (*śaktijñāna*); what is the use of that superfluous (*antargaḍu*) universal there? That too is incorrect; for it does not follow that: "By whatever capacity blue and other [colors] assist the eye, let them produce only a specific cognition by that [same capacity]; what is the use of the eye? Likewise, "Let the person produce only the cognition 'one with a staff' (*daṇḍin*) through the capacity that assists the staff; what is the use of the staff? For in this way, there would be the rejection of all auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*). [The objection regarding the exclusion of linguistic convention (*śabdasaṃketa*) and its resolution: [The opponent objects: Even if the particulars are capable of producing a cognition of their own form, they cannot produce a cognition of a single form without depending on a single cause, because they are diverse. Therefore, a single universal must be admitted as the cause of the cognition of a single form. [The author replies: This is not so. Even without a single cause, the cognition of a single form arises from the particulars themselves, due to the restriction of their own nature (*svabhāvaniyama*). Just as the cognition of a single form arises from the particulars despite their diversity, so too does the application of a single word arise from the particulars themselves, due to the restriction of their own nature. Furthermore, the application of a single word is observed even in cases where no universal is perceived, such as in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*), "one who has been," or "one who will be. Therefore, the application of a single word is established solely through the restriction of the nature of the particulars. Consequently, the universal is not the cause of the application of a single word. But how, even through the power of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), can a word apply to real entities? For it has been stated: "Words express that which has been conventionally designated (*saṃketita*) for the sake of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*);
at that time, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) does not exist, and therefore no convention applies to it."

For that particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) upon which a convention (*saṃketa*) is established for the sake of linguistic usage does not exist at the time of that usage, because it is not encompassed by differences of place, time, and individual manifestation. Therefore, there can be no convention regarding that [particular], nor can there be one regarding a universal (*sāmānya*), because that would be fruitless. For what purpose is there the employment of words if the object capable of causal efficiency—such as carrying or burning—is not denoted by the word? If it is argued that activity toward particulars occurs simply because the universal is denoted, due to the connection between the universal and the particulars, we say no. Even though such a connection exists, when it is said, "Cut the staff," one does not see activity directed toward those who possess the staff (the persons). Nor does activity toward the particular occur merely because of its possibility; for if it did, it would be a case of incoherent prattle, resulting in activity toward something other than the intended object, like the command to "milk a bull. Furthermore, since a universal cannot exist without a substratum, it is impossible. If it is argued that the denotation of the particular follows from the denotation of the universal, we say no; for when the particular is absent, the universal alone cannot persist. Moreover, from a command to drink milk and water, it would follow that one is commanded to drink their substratum (the cup). Furthermore, there would be no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with words for actions, qualities, and so forth, nor could there be the relationship of qualifier and qualified.

To this it is replied: This fault must indeed be pointed out by us against those who claim that words such as "cow" (*gaur*) and so forth denote only the universal (*jāti*). We, however, maintain that words like *gotva* (cowness) denote the universal, whereas words like "cow" denote the individual qualified by the universal; it is precisely there [in the qualified individual] that the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is established. If it is argued that if the word applies to individuals, the universal would be purposeless, we say no; for it is impossible to establish a convention regarding infinite individuals taken alone. If it is argued that even when [the convention is made] regarding individuals qualified by the universal, infinity remains unavoidable, we say no; for in that case, infinity is not a relevant factor. By grasping the convention in the form, "Whatever possesses this cowness is all a cow," one understands that whatever possesses cowness—be it separated by place, time, or form—all that is a cow. On the other hand, in the absence of a universal, as with words like "Yudhiṣṭhira," a convention established in one instance would not be a cause for cognition in another instance; therefore, one would not establish such a convention. For those who deny the existence of a universal, there is no single, non-different basis (*nimitta*) common to all individuals.
{Description of the grounds for the application [of terms] in cases such as "cook," etc.}

If a convention (*saṃketa*) is established in this manner, one might ask: what is the non-differentiating cause (*nimitta*) in the case of "cook" (*pācaka*) and similar terms? It is the action (*karman*) qualified by "the state of cooking" (*pacanatva*) and so forth. Thus, the convention is made such that whoever is the agent (*kartṛ*) of an action of this kind is called a "cook. Consequently, the objection raised—that how can a universal (*jāti*) residing in an action be the cause of a cognition regarding a different object—is refuted, because it is a cause through a mediated succession (*pāramparyeṇa*). There is a connection (*anvaya*) with actions through the universal, and through that connection, there is a connection with the agents of those actions. An action that has passed away is either remembered or understood from a word as a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*); even a future [action] is apprehended through inference. If it were not apprehended, there would be doubt: "Is this person a cook, or not? If it is asked how that which is non-existent can be a cause, we say no; for it is the cognition having that as its object which is the cause. If it is argued that let there simply be cognition [of the qualifier] in all cases, we say no; for if a cognition of a qualifier were to function as a cause without an object, it would follow that the cognition of the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) is false, like the cognition "the man has horns" and the like. Furthermore, a cognition of the qualificand produced by a cognition of a past or future qualifier becomes veridical (*saṃvādika*) precisely by being delimited by that form of the qualifier—as in "this person was a cook" (he cooked) or "this person will be a cook" (he will cook). Otherwise, if it were understood differently, it would indeed be an error.
{The description of the grounds for the application [of words] in cases such as universals and particulars.}

In that case, what is the cause for the application of words such as "universal" (*sāmānya*) and "particular" (*viśeṣa*)? Regarding this, there is a single defining characteristic: the universal, being of a unitary nature, is the cause of a recurring cognition through its own delimitation across infinite particulars; or else, it is the inherence in multiple locations while being of an eternally non-different nature. The definition of particulars is their being the cause of a cognition of exclusion by way of being qualifiers. Or rather, the state of being a substratum of a universal is established—by means of being devoid of both universals and particulars, or by being the object of a cognition arising from that delimitation—on the grounds of being like a post (*sthāṇu*) and so forth. Furthermore, in that case (the post), there is no particularity consisting of parts, because it is partless and possesses identical properties. Once it is established that [the post] is a final particular (*antyaviśeṣa*) despite having identical properties, then by the aid of that example, it is established that even eternal substances which do not have identical properties possess final particularities, on account of their being eternal substances.
The acceptance of specific categories [of existence] is the absence of dogmatic attachment.

If, however, someone were to demonstrate that even in the absence of ultimate particularities (*antyaviśeṣa*), things possessing common characteristics could nonetheless possess distinctness through some other specific difference—just as in the case of sound, cognition, and so forth—then we would have no need for ultimate particularities. We shall apply the designation "ultimate particularity" precisely to those uncommon distinctions existing in eternal substances; this is the meaning. Thus it is established that words applied to universals function by means of the cause that is their universal-characteristic, while [words] applied to particulars function by means of that same characteristic. In this way, words such as "category" (*padārthavarga*) and so forth, as well as words such as "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*) and so forth, are to be understood as functioning by means of their respective specific characteristics.
According to the view of some, even in universals and the like, there exists a universal through a mediated succession.

Now, if that which is characterized as a universal (*sāmānya*) and so forth were to inhere in multiple things, then it too would necessarily be a universal; consequently, the admission that there is no universal in universals and the like would be contradicted. Alternatively, if it does not inhere [in multiple things], then how could the application of a single, non-different term occur with respect to distinct things? On this point, some say: The cause for the application of a single term to all distinct things is indeed a universal. And that [universal] is sometimes affirmed and sometimes negated; sometimes directly and sometimes indirectly. In the case of universals and the like, it occurs only indirectly; therefore, there is no contradiction with our own tenet.
In reality, there is an absence of universality within universals and the like.

Alternatively, there exists in universals (*sāmānya*) and the like some property that is a semblance of a universal (*sāmānyapratirūpaka*), by virtue of which the word and cognition of "universal" and so forth occur as recurring even with respect to distinct entities. If it is asked: "Why is there not the existence of a universal, given that there is a recurrence of words and cognitions?"—we say: No; because this would lead to an inconclusive argument (*anaikāntika*) due to the recurrence of words and cognitions such as "inactive" (*niṣkriya*) and the like. From what, then, does the distinction between a universal and its semblance arise? From the difference in the recurrence of cognitions. For that recurrence of cognition which occurs even in one who is unlearned (*avyutpanna*) is based on a universal. That which is different from it, however, is based merely on a property (*dharma*). Indeed, even in the case of universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and in the case of absences (*abhāva*) and particulars (*bheda*) such as "blue" (*nīla*) and so forth, there is no apprehension of a single form for one who has not mastered linguistic convention (*aprasiddhasamaya*), as there is in the case of [actual] universals. Furthermore, doubt would arise regarding things that possess a universal; therefore, a particular (*viśeṣa*) must be postulated in them to eliminate that doubt. If one were to postulate a universal even in those particulars, doubt would arise again, and to eliminate that, another particular would have to be postulated in them, and yet another universal in those—thus there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, there is no universal in universals and the like. If, however, the designation "universal" is applied to every property whatsoever on the grounds of the recurrence of words and cognitions, then let there be a universal even in universals and the like; what contradiction is there? It has already been stated, however, that a *distinct* universal does not exist therein. Moreover, since many properties exist even in a single substratum (*dharmin*), just as many words motivated by those [properties] are applied to it. So how could there be an impossibility of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth?
{The Buddhist position is that linguistic co-referentiality occurs only with respect to an object that has been conceptually constructed.}

Now, it might be argued that grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is defined as the occurrence of two words with distinct grounds for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) upon a single substratum, yet this is not possible in reality because there is no conventional linguistic agreement (*saṃketa*) to that effect. For the word "lotus" has not been conventionally established to denote the referent of the word "blue," nor has the word "blue" been established to denote the referent of the word "lotus. Furthermore, a word cannot signify its object independently of such a convention, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, if the object were already cognized from the word "blue" alone, the word "lotus" would be redundant; if it is not cognized, then the word would have multiple meanings. Indeed, it is not logical to say that something which is not cognized from a word is the meaning of that word. Therefore, it is the object established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)—which appears as if external, as if one, whether performing a causal function or not—that is the basis for this usage of coreferentiality and so forth. It is precisely within that [conceptual] domain that the usage of property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) is also elaborated, being inexpressible as either identical to or different from one another. And since that usage pertains to a false object, the [opponent's] reductio argument does not apply equally to our position.
The refutation thereof.

To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that because there is no convention (*saṃketa*) in that manner, words such as "blue" (*nīla*) and so forth do not have a single referent—that is not so. Because the convention is established with respect to that which possesses those [qualities], the word "lotus" (*utpala*) denotes an object qualified by the property of lotus-ness (*utpalatva*), and the word "blue" denotes an object qualified by the quality of blueness (*nīlaguṇa*). Consequently, wherever there is a connection with both qualifiers, both words apply. Nor is either one redundant, because since they denote the object through the delimitation of distinct properties (*dharma*), their referents are not identical. However, with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*), there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). Now, if this were the case, the word "lotus" would denote even red lotuses and the like, while the word "blue" would denote even crows and the like; so how could the two have a single referent? This is not a fault. We shall explain that although a word has its convention established in a general sense, it is restricted to a specific referent by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors. For this very reason, the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣya-viśeṣaṇabhāva*) is also logically consistent. For the word "blue," having been observed generally with respect to an object endowed with many particular properties, while conveying that object in that same way, generates an expectation for a specific detail. Therefore, the word "lotus" is employed for the sake of cognizing that specific detail. Likewise, the word "blue" is employed for the sake of cognizing the specific detail of the referent of the word "lotus."

As for what was said—that the referent of a word, established by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is precisely there that the linguistic usage of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is non-correspondent to reality—that is incorrect. For when [the referent] is related solely to its own nature or established by conceptual construction, it is not possible for disputants to engage in the presentation of proofs and refutations, mutual agreement, activity, and so forth. If such a state were due to delusion, there would be no distinction from dreams and the like; consequently, even the composition of treatises by those possessing discernment would be useless. If it is argued: "Even though conceptual constructions arising in dependence upon that [object] do not have that [object] as their manifest content, they are nonetheless non-contradictory with respect to the real entity, just as the illusion of a jewel in a light is [non-contradictory] with respect to the jewel," we say no; because this is unestablished. Non-contradiction does not arise merely from the attainment of an object. Rather, if an object appears in a certain place, time, and form, it is only if it is attained in exactly that way that there is non-contradiction. Otherwise, even the cognition of a mirage might be non-contradictory, since water is somehow attained from it. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "arising in dependence upon that": what is this "dependence" (*pratibandha*)? It cannot be characterized by identity (*tādātmya*), whether with a real or a superimposed capacity of the conceptual construction. Moreover, identity with its own form is common to all cognitions. If it is "arising from that" (*tadutpatti*), since the existence of the universal form appearing in the conceptual construction is not admitted, how could there be an arising even through a lineage (*pāramparya*)? Furthermore, for proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), an arising from an object that is to be attained is impossible for anything whatsoever. Moreover, it would follow that the cognition of silver is non-contradictory because it arises from the object, such as mother-of-pearl, which is to be attained. Now, if the cause of non-contradiction is arising from an object as it is determined (*yathāvyavasita*), then in the case of the cognition of a jewel, is it the universal form that is determined? Or is it the form of the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)? If it is the universal form, how can there be an arising from it? For it is admitted that, being a non-entity (*avastu*), it lacks causal efficacy. If it is the form of the particular characteristic, then is it the form of a previously perceived [particular], or is it the form of another particular characteristic? If it is the form of a previously perceived [particular], how can that which does not exist elsewhere be a producer [of the cognition]? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

If it is argued that its production is from that [object] because it arises through a sequence of latencies (vāsanā) deposited by the perception of it, then the cognition of a jewel in a light would also have to be produced from that [light], since that too originates from a latency for it.

Now, if it is argued that where there is activity (*pravṛtti*), that [object] is determined (*adhyavasīyate*), and that its production occurs without interval [from that determination], we say no; because that [object] has not been experienced. For an object that is absolutely unexperienced—like a *piśāca* or similar being—cannot be determined. If it is argued that even the form of a tuft of hair and so forth, though previously non-existent, is determined by being superimposed upon something through memory, and the same applies here as well—we say no; in that case, production would arise from the form determined by that [memory]. Furthermore, determination is nothing but conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and it is an established tenet that this does not have an external object as its support. Therefore, how can there be determination with respect to an external thing, and how can something that does not have that as its object be determined by it? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

As for what was said—that commentators indeed analyze it in this way, but practitioners do not; rather, considering their own objective support (*ālambana*) alone to be capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), they act by unifying the perceived object and the conceptualized object, and it is on account of that intention (*abhiprāya*) that it is stated thus—what is the meaning of "unifying" in that context? Does it mean superimposing the form of the perceived object onto the conceptualization, or does it mean superimposing the form of the conceptualization onto the perceived object? In the first case, the one seeking the perceived object would have to act by facing toward the conceptualization itself, just as one seeking mother-of-pearl acts by facing toward silver. In the second case, however, action toward the actual object would not occur; for no one is observed to act by superimposing the form of silver or the like onto an unperceived mother-of-pearl or similar object.

Furthermore, even one who, when commanded by a master to "bring ghee," brings oil or the like, would not be unskilled; for there is no difference between the two cases, as both involve engaging with what is not the word's meaning by superimposing a conceptualized form upon it. Indeed, a word does not function—even indirectly—with respect to an object that is unfit for the intended purposeful action, because a linguistic convention cannot be established for such a thing.

As for what was said—that just as someone establishes a convention (*saṃketa*) regarding form, light, the eye, and so forth, for the sake of linguistic convenience, saying "the barley is the cause of the cognition of form" or "the rice is," and likewise other things that accomplish some single [effect] or are not accomplished by others, these too are called words such as *vrīhi* (rice) established by convention for the sake of a single cognition—this comparison is flawed. For in that case, it has been stated that cognition alone may be the single basis for grasping the convention; however, among the infinite individual instances distinguished by place and other factors, there exists neither a non-different effect nor a non-different cause.

As for what was also said—that "in that very context, these objects capable [of being denoted] must be indicated by him, and they may be indicated by a single word or by many; here, the speaker has autonomy"—that too is an unconsidered statement. For it is not the speaker’s autonomy that is being precluded here; rather, [the question is]: since the word "cow" (*go*) has its convention established with respect to a brindled cow (*śābaleya*), how can it have its convention grasped with respect to the Bāhuleya and other individuals without some non-differentiating cause, as [it does] among the Mahiṣa and other [individuals]? And how could it produce a cognition if its convention were not grasped? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is it observed that the brindled cow, the Bāhuleya, and so forth, perform a single effect, or are produced by a single means, such that the word could function on the basis of a single objective (*sādhya*) or a single instrumental cause (*sādhana*). Furthermore, if one resorts to "capacity" (*yogyatā*), then a universal (*sāmānya*) is merely desired under another name; otherwise, capacity would remain as indeterminate as the form of the individual itself. Therefore, it is logical that a single [entity] residing in many [individuals] brings about a single verbal expression and generates a cognition of concomitance (*anvaya*).
The objection that a universal must reside in multiple instances.

Now, what is this "subsistence" (vṛtti) of that [universal] in multiple locations? Is it being supported (*ādheyatā*), like a jujube fruit in a bowl? Or is it manifestation (*vyakti*)? It cannot be being supported, because that which is eternal cannot be assisted; what could a substratum (*ādhāra*) possibly do for that which is eternal? If it is argued that it is a substratum because of its inherence (*samavāya*) therein, then what is this inherence? It is the relationship of locus and located between things that are not established separately. We do not admit such a state of being a locus for that which provides no assistance, for fear of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, even relations between real entities—such as inherence, conjunction (*saṃyoga*), and inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*)—do not differ from the relation of cause and effect. Nor is the substratum merely that which supports; for how could something be a supporter if it provides no assistance? Furthermore, since a universal is eternally pervasive, it exists at all times; thus, a separate location is impossible, and if there were a separate location, the supporter would be redundant and the universal would be non-eternal. If it were to exist separately, it would lead to an infinite regress. If it is argued that the subsistence of the unmanifested universal in those [individuals] is called "manifestation" by means of the individuals, we say no; for if it does not produce a form (*rūpa*), the manifestor would be useless. Therefore, those things which depend on another for their own cognition necessarily acquire their own nature through it; however, no acquisition of its own nature is possible for a universal from anything whatsoever. Consequently, it cannot be manifested by anything. Moreover—

"And if it is maintained that universals possess the state of being universalized by their manifestors, then a lamp or other illuminator would likewise possess [the universal] 'cowness' and so forth. {This is the objection; here follows the resolution:}

To this it is replied: "Occurrence" (*vṛtti*) is the state of being supported (*ādheyatā*), and manifestation (*vyakti*) is both; and both of these belong to the universal, for that [relation] is its very inherence (*samavāya*). As for what was said—that it is not logical for that which provides no assistance to be a substratum—that is not so, because the lack of assistance is unproven. For the effect, namely the qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) accompanied by that [substratum], is itself the assistance; moreover, an assistance that is identical with the essence of the thing is never perceived. Indeed, there is no established rule that whatever is produced by something X is assisted by X. Nor is the producer alone the substratum, since a bowl (*kuṇḍa*) is the substratum of jujube fruits (*badara*) even though it is not their producer. Now, it might be argued: "By its very nature, a heavy substance has the property of producing an effect in a location different from itself; the state of producing an effect in the same location is brought about by the substratum. Therefore, the bowl is called the 'substratum' when, acting as a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*) with the preceding moment, it produces the effect of the jujube fruit in that very place. This is not so, because momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is unproven, and we shall refute that later. Therefore, the bowl and such are the substrata of jujube fruits and the like only as preventers of falling (*pātapratibandhaka*); and the prevention of falling is simply a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃyogaviśeṣa*), for in the absence of that, falling occurs. We shall explain later that the power (*śakti*) of causal factors consists in the completeness of their auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) or the incompleteness thereof. Thus, when a particular conjunction exists, falling does not occur due to the deficiency of the auxiliary cause that constitutes its absence; therefore, the bowl and such are called the "preventer" (*pratibandhaka*) of that [fall]. Alternatively, why is this conjunction between those two [the bowl and the fruit] alone? Because of the capacity of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), it arises as inherent (*samaveta*) in those two alone. If it is asked, "Why is inherence (*samavāya*) also between those two alone?"—it is because the inhering factor is produced as a property of that [substratum], determined by the capacity of its own causes; however, in the case of eternal things, it is their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). But in the case of one of the two being eternal, the restriction of inherence occurs as the case may be, through the production of the support or the supported by the power of a particular auxiliary cause. We shall explain later how even an eternal thing can have a particular auxiliary cause as the case may be. Furthermore, the conjunction of the bowl, the jujube fruit, and so on, appears even to perception. To disparage that [conjunction] would invoke the logic of the "cow-dung and milk-porridge" (i.e., a baseless denial). Therefore, the relation of substratum and supported is not merely the relation of cause and effect; rather, the bowl and such are the substratum of the jujube fruit and so on precisely as the preventer of falling. If it is then argued that for a universal (*sāmānya*) there is no substratum because it lacks falling, we say no; for otherwise, we would have to deny the substratum of universals, qualities, actions, and so forth, as will be discussed in the examination of the whole (*avayavin*).

Or, let there be the state of being a "supporter" (*sthāpakatva*), characterized by pervading all supports; how so? In that regard, first, the stability (*sthiti*)—characterized by the cessation of motion—of falling objects such as jujube fruits is produced by vessels and the like. Furthermore, for wholes, qualities, motions, and so forth, stability consists in their successive manifestation of their own nature and the performance of other effects; this occurs through the power of their support, for in the absence of a support, the destruction of impermanent things is indeed their "motion. As for the universal (*sāmānya*), its failure to reach [other locations] is achieved only when a support exists; thus, the support is called the "stabilizer. By the example of qualities and so forth residing in a jar, one should understand that even for those residing in eternal substrata, the capacity to perform multiple effects successively—denoted by the term "stability"—is due to the power of the substratum. Nor does another auxiliary cause serve as the motive for the production of all those effects; therefore, the undesirable consequence of [everything] being a support elsewhere does not follow. Moreover, the support manifests what resides within itself and not through some other cause; consequently, the claim that a lamp or the like possesses "cowness" and so forth is incorrect. Even if, by the very nature of things or the power of their own causes, only a certain thing is the support of a certain other thing and not of everything, nevertheless, since the perception of the relation of container and contained—as in "this is here" between a vessel and jujube fruits—is seen to be inseparable from a connection, the same is established for substances, qualities, and so forth, even if it is based on a connection. And that connection, because it is distinct from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the rest, is called "inherence" (*samavāya*). Therefore, the existence of the universal in its own supports is by way of inherence.

{The Implication of the Pervasiveness of the Universal} Now, is the universal omnipresent like space and so forth, or does it reside only in its own substratum? If it were omnipresent, then being manifested in one place, it would necessarily be manifested everywhere because its nature is non-different; consequently, there would be no non-perception of it anywhere, and there would follow the undesirable consequence of a confusion of entities (*vastu-saṅkara*), since all universals would exist in every individual (*piṇḍa*). If it is argued that "only a certain individual is the manifestor of a certain universal, and therefore the fault of confusion does not follow," we say no; for there is no cause for such a restriction. Furthermore—
"For when the manifestor is not apprehended, the manifested is not cognized.
Why, then, is the opposite [the case] for the universal and its possessor?
It follows that the universal alone must be the manifestor. Now, if it is argued that [the universal] resides only in its own substratum, that too is impossible; for instance:
"For that which exists elsewhere, when it is born in a place other than that [original one],
it is illogical to say that it functions elsewhere without moving from its own location.
Moreover, the entity does not even become connected with that place where it is said to exist."
"It pervades that which possesses location; how truly marvelous this is!
It does not go there, nor was it there before, nor does it exist there afterwards, nor is it composed of parts.
It does not abandon its previous substratum—oh, what a succession of calamities! Thus [it is said].
For some, that is the rebuttal.

On this point, some offer the following rebuttal: the universal (*sāmānya*) is indeed omnipresent within its own substratum, because it is perceived precisely there. Furthermore, in the absence of relations such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), it is impossible to designate the universal as existing in the intervals between individual instances (*piṇḍa*). As for the argument that "it exists elsewhere while remaining in one place," etc., that is not correct; for the nature of a thing established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be discarded merely through mockery. Indeed, the potencies (*śakti*) of entities are diverse; thus, the universal possesses such a potency that, while an object is being produced by specific causes, it remains present without moving from its previous location. For if it were to move, its former location would become empty of it. As for the highly extraordinary doubt raised by the passage beginning with "wherever it resides," etc., even that is not extraordinary, precisely because of the diversity of the potencies of entities. For example, a weapon consecrated by mantras and the like cuts a specific disease residing in the stomach, but does not cut the stomach itself; or a thread and so forth, when consecrated by medicine, is not burned by fire, yet it cooks the rice placed in a vessel upon it; and a pigeon, while standing on the roof of a house, places its feet in curds and other substances situated inside. In the same way, the universal possesses such a potency. Cowness (*gotva*) is connected only with the individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*), and not with its parts or those locations. If it is asked, "How can a universal situated in one place be connected with a substratum arising in another place?"—it is due to the efficacy of the very causes that produce that substratum. This is simply the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*): by the efficacy of the causes that produce conjunction with another location, a material object comes to exist in another location; by the cause that brings about the cessation of the previous conjunction, it does not exist there [in the old place]. But in the case of the universal, it exists in the new location due to the cause that produces its substratum, and it does not exist there [in the old location] due to the cause that ceases that substratum. Thus, the fact of being devoid of both destruction and production is the same in both cases; the only difference is the distinction between the causes of connection and non-connection.

Furthermore, as for the claim that a relation is observed only between things possessing parts when they occupy different locations—such as light and a rope, or a bamboo and a staff—and that a universal does not possess parts: this too has already been answered by the refutation of the theory of composite wholes (*avayavin*) and by the critique regarding the [absurd] consequences concerning space, time, and so forth.
{The determination of the existence of the universal in the state of dissolution}

But surely, at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), when all jars and such things have perished, where does the universal (*sāmānya*) such as "jar-ness" reside? Nowhere. But has it not perished? No; because it is eternal. What kind of statement is this—that something which exists eternally does not exist anywhere? The explanation is that it exists precisely without a substratum at that time; however, with respect to its past and future substrata, it is still called a "universal" even then. Nor does it become non-existent simply because it is not being designated [by a particular instance]. Furthermore, there is no proof for the claim that all jars and so forth perish simultaneously. Now, one might object: "In the *Purāṇas* and other texts, both dissolution (*pralaya*) and great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*) are heard of. True; however, dissolution is the destruction of the three worlds, while great dissolution is the destruction of the fourteen abodes along with the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*). But there is no simultaneous destruction of all cosmic eggs; therefore, jars and other things exist within other cosmic eggs. Moreover, if there were a destruction of all cosmic eggs, then upon the cessation of all activity, the scriptural statement—"And nights of the same duration"—would be contradicted. For time cannot be measured without activity. Thus, enough of this digression.
Even though the universal is all-pervasive, it is not perceived everywhere.

Or, let it be that the universal (*sāmānya*) is all-pervading; yet, unlike space (*ākāśa*), it is not conjoined with everything, nor is even "cowness" (*gotva*) and the like inherent (*samaveta*) in everything simply because of its existence. What then? It exists everywhere by virtue of its mere presence (*sannidhi*). And as for the claim that it is non-existent elsewhere—that is not so; for even while existing everywhere, it is only where it is inherent that it is capable of being perceived. Therefore, by means of that inherence, the substratum is called both the locus and the manifester (*vyañjaka*). Thus, there is no confusion of universals (*jāti-saṅkara*). But [an objector might ask]: if that very [universal] is perceived in one individual (*vyakti*), does it not also exist elsewhere? Why then is it not perceived elsewhere too? Who says that it is perceived elsewhere than where it is being perceived? What then? Because of the intervals between individuals, there is no manifestation (*vyañjakatva*) there, just as there is none in the case of its [actual] substratum. Consequently, the misconception of perceiving it there does not arise. Furthermore, since the cognition "this is that" is dependent upon the grasping of the substratum and its relation [to the universal], such a cognition does not occur when [the universal] is not grasped.
The Refutation of the Fault of Not Perceiving the Manifestor.

As for the argument that "because [the manifestor] is not perceived," etc., that is not correct, because there is no such restriction. This is not a rule—that the perception of the manifested must necessarily be preceded by the perception of the manifestor; rather, the rule is simply that the perception of the qualified object (*viśeṣya*) is preceded by the perception of its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Consequently, if an object such as a jar were itself a qualifier of light and so forth, it would have to be apprehended even before them. However, in the absence of a relationship between qualifier and qualified, the apprehension of both the individual (*vyakti*) and the universal (*jāti*) occurs either without a fixed order or simultaneously. Furthermore, a manifestor is not defined as something that causes the cognition of another only through its own cognition; for sense organs and the like are manifestors even when they themselves are not perceived. Therefore, a manifestor is simply a real entity which, due to some deficiency, was previously unperceived; and it is never the case that an individual is devoid of a universal, such that the universal alone could be the manifestor of the individual.
Refutation of the Non-Perception of Universals (Sāmānyānupalabdhi)

Furthermore, as for the argument that because this [universal] is not perceived despite being intended as perceptible, it must be non-existent—and that if it were imperceptible, there could be no recognition of words (*śabda-pratyabhijñāna*) and so forth based on its observation—that is not correct, because its non-perception is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, one might object: "Even though the universal exists, its perception is not observed among the individuals (*vyakti*). For that [perceived thing] is conceived as possessing the form of color and configuration (*varṇa-saṃsthāna-ākāra*), whereas the universal is not like that. Nor does any other form appear therein, such as a staff appearing in those who possess staves (*daṇḍin*). And even if a difference in form does not appear, it is not logical to establish a difference in the entity itself, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). This is not so. For it has been stated that the universal appears by way of a common form (*samānatā-ākāra*), and not as an individual. As for the fact that it does not appear like a staff, that is due to the mutual dissimilarity (*itaretara-vaidharmya*) of entities. Precisely for this reason, the universal is a distinct category (*padārthāntara*); if it were to appear like a staff, it would simply be included within the category of substance (*dravya*). As for the reasons such as its not being grasped through spatial distinction, these have already been refuted previously in the examination of the whole (*avayavin*); therefore, non-existence is not established on that basis either.
The suspicion that the universal is useless, and its refutation.

[Objection: If individuals (*vyakti*) are similar by their very nature (*svabhāva*), what is the use of another universal (*sāmānya*) there? It would be useless. Or, if they are not similar, how could there be a universal among them? For a universal is said to be the state (*bhāva*) of those things that are similar; it is not the case that they are made similar by the universal itself, because that [similarity] has the universal as its cause. [Response: It is said: they are similar by their very nature. Their own being (*sva-bhāva*), their own property (*svakīya-dharma*), which is inseparable from them, is precisely what is called the "universal. Since they appear and are designated as "similar" only when conjoined with that [property], how can the universal be useless? [Objection: If you mean by "by their very nature" "without a recurring property (*anvayi-dharma*)," then even in the absence of that [property], how could they be similar? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, it would follow that even a staff and so forth are useless, for people would be "staff-bearers" (*daṇḍin*) and "crest-wearers" (*kuṇḍalin*) by their very nature. Moreover, perception itself would be useless, for objects would be seen even in the absence of that [perception]. [Response: If that were the case, then just as those who are not staff-bearers by nature become staff-bearers through connection with a staff, so too it would follow that things which are not similar by their own form (*svarūpa*) become similar through connection with a universal. But this is not so, because a universal is connected to all its individual instances (*vyakti*). If one asks why this is so: it is because it is the very nature of things (*vastu-svabhāva*), like the diverse natures of burning, coldness, fluidity, and so on. If the universal is not perceived, what could one rely upon to achieve the cognition of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) by means of a universal inclusion (*sarvopasaṃhāra*)? [Objection: One relies upon "exclusion" (*apoha*). [Response: No, because that has already been refuted. Furthermore, since that [exclusion] is intended to be perceived but is not actually perceived, it is non-existent; or, if it is imperceptible, then words, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), and the like—which depend on the observation of that [exclusion]—would not exist. Nor is it logical for that [exclusion] to serve as a substratum (*āśraya*), like a staff in the case of staff-bearers, because it is not perceived as having a distinct form. And it is not proper for that which is merely superimposed by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and is non-existent—like a sky-flower—to be a substratum. [Objection: Since activity proceeds by the exclusion of others, the meaning of a word (*śabdārtha*) is simply the exclusion of others (*anyavyāvṛtti*). [Response: Since activity proceeds toward a real thing (*vastu*), why is the real thing itself not the meaning of the word? Even when grasping a real thing, as in the case of perception, activity proceeds precisely by the exclusion of what is other than it. And you yourself accept that activity follows from perception, as you have stated: "For one who acts after determining an object by means of these two [perception and inference] is not deceived regarding purposeful action (*arthakriyā*)."

As for the objections against the view that the object itself is the word-meaning, those have been refuted and will be refuted further on. Furthermore, the word-meaning is of two kinds: the denoted (*vācya*) and the implied (*gamya*). Among these, for words such as "cow" (*gauḥ*), the denoted meaning is the object qualified by the universal (*jāti*), while the exclusion of what is other than that (*atadvyavaccheda*) is the implied meaning. For words such as "not a non-cow" (*nāgauḥ*), however, the denoted meaning is the exclusion of what is other than that qualified [by the object], while the universal is the implied meaning. It has already been stated that if that universal were absolutely non-existent, even the distinction between the class of similar things and the class of dissimilar things would not occur. Therefore, the comprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) regarding infinite individuals is based upon the apprehension of the universal.

Thus, it stands established as follows: inference is observed to be that which infers an object qualified by a perceived universal, even when there is a difference between individual instances. On this view, the inference of the sun’s motion and so forth is indeed observed, because motion belongs to an undifferentiated genus despite the diversity of its relata, just as the genus "fire" remains the same despite the diversity of mountains and other substrates.

Others, however, say: "Inference based on what has been seen (*dṛṣṭam anumānam*) is that where the object of inference was previously perceived and can be perceived again at a time subsequent to the activity [of inferring], provided it has not perished; or, if it has never been perceived by persons who share the same nature as the cognizer, that is *dṛṣṭam anumānam*. That which is dissimilar to this is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭam*. According to this view, even the inference of the motion of the sun and so forth is indeed *sāmānyatodṛṣṭam*. What is the mark (*liṅga*) here? It is the reaching of another location (*deśāntaraprāpti*). Is this "another location" a point of space (*digdeśa*), or simply a place (*deśa*)?
