Neither is perceptible, nor is the conjunction occurring therein—just like the conjunction of wind with a mountain—perceptible. How, then, can motion be inferred from that which is unestablished (*asiddha*)? One merely sees the solar orb; there is nothing actually denoted by the term "another location. There is no fault, for the reaching of another location is itself established through inference. How is the sun possessed of the reaching of another location? Because, while being a substance, it is not the object of notions of decrease or increase, and while being perceivable by one facing east, it becomes the object of a notion of having turned back even without the movement of feet, just like a gem and so forth. If this were so, then for one who perceives the disk of the sun or moon as stationary and facing a single direction, there would be no cognition of its rising at intervals such as half a *ghaṭikā*. Therefore, some other specific property (*dharmaviśeṣa*) of the sun and so forth must be stated as the inferent of a specific reaching, or the reaching itself must be perceptible in relation to a different spatial region such as the directions, so that the cognition of half a *ghaṭikā* and so on may occur. Nor is it non-perceptible simply because it occurs between the perceptible and the non-perceptible, like the reaching of wind or a mountain. For there is nothing that is impossible when it is actually perceived. And from what does the non-contradictory cognition of half a *ghaṭikā* and so on arise? If some other cause is proposed elsewhere that accounts for it, let that be so; we have no insistence [on our own view]. Furthermore, that [inference] is of two kinds, distinguished as for one's own sake (*svārtha*) and for the sake of others (*parārtha*); and of these, one kind—*dṛṣṭam* and *sāmānyatodṛṣṭam*—is each twofold.
An Investigation into the Distinction between One's Own Welfare and the Welfare of Others.

In this regard, some claim that inference independent of instruction from another is for one's own sake (*svārtha*), while that which depends on such instruction is for the sake of others (*parārtha*). This twofold division is not tenable, because the distinction between "one's own" and "another's" sake is impossible. From the perspective of the speaker, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*); yet from the perspective of the listener, it is simply for one's own sake. Furthermore, what difference is there here [between these cases] as to whether the mark (*liṅga*) is apprehended through perception, inference, or verbal testimony? That is not correct, because the distinction is established by the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of the different types of perception such as "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) and so forth. For this very reason, the argument beginning with "not from the perspective of the speaker" is untenable. Indeed, inference is not called "seen" (*dṛṣṭa*) or "generally seen" (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*) based on the perspective of either the speaker or the listener, but rather based on its defining characteristic. Alternatively, let it be that it is "for the sake of others" from the perspective of the speaker, precisely because the speaker has no need for it since he is merely restating what he already knows; therefore, it is presented by him for the purpose of making another understand, and thus its status as "for the sake of others" is established. Or, let it be "for the sake of others" from the perspective of the listener: because he is confused regarding the recollection of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and so forth, he lacks the capacity [to infer] on his own and obtains the object—the purpose known as inference—from another who explains it to him; thus it is called "for the sake of others. As for the objection raised—"What is the difference here?"—the response is: "But instruction from another is a statement consisting of five members (*pañcāvayava-vākya*). What is meant is this: for one who asserts that the word itself, like the eye and other senses, is the mark (*liṅga*) by its own nature alone, [that inference] is indeed for one's own sake from the speaker's perspective. It is not that the other person uttered the word for the sake of inference; rather, it was for the sake of making known smoke and so forth that were previously unapprehended. Nor does the listener, being confused about the recollection of pervasion and so forth, depend on another. However, when someone, even while grasping the mark, is confused regarding the recollection of pervasion and is awakened by a five-membered statement, the inference dependent on that statement is said to be "for the sake of others," distinguished by its specific function of removing that confusion. Here, "confusion" (*moha*) refers specifically to the failure to recall the state of things (such as pervasion) even though they have been grasped; thus, even for one who is doubtful, that which awakens them is inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*).
The status of a sentence as inference is figurative.

But surely, since it is stated that "this is the supreme method (*nyāya*)," the sentence itself must be the inference; why then is it said to be "dependent upon that"? No; for the sentence is designated as an inference only figuratively (*upacāreṇa*). A sentence is not a direct means of inferential cognition (*anumiti*), because its purpose is fulfilled simply by making known the capable reason (*samartha-hetu*). If it is argued that there can be no figurative usage due to the absence of a cause (*nimitta*) or a motive (*prayojana*), we say no; for both are established. To explain: first, as for the cause—whether it be the state of being for that purpose (*tādarthya*) or the state of being a means (*sādhana*)—the sentence is called by that [inference’s] name either because it prompts the activity toward it or because it establishes it. Even though the means of inferential cognition already exists previously, it is rendered potent (*śaktimat*) by the sentence. As for the motive, we shall explain it right here under the statement, "This is the supreme method. Furthermore, it is said to be "dependent on the instruction of another" in order to make known that the secondary depends upon the primary.

But has it not been stated thus: "Instruction by another consists of a statement with five members"? What, then, is meant here by a "statement" (*vākya*)? Why is there doubt? Because of conflicting views—[namely,] the doctrine of *sphoṭa* and its refutation.

Some here say: "There exist words whose nature consists of *pada*s and *vākya*s distinct from the phonemes (*varṇa*s). Just as they clarify their own meaning, they receive the name ‘*sphoṭa*’. This is not so, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). For there is no evidence for the existence of such words. It is not that there is none, because perception (*pratyakṣa*) and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) are possible. First of all, by perception itself—namely, through a cognition of an undivided form—the *pada* and the *vākya* are apprehended. Nor is it logical that a non-erroneous cognition of identity could occur regarding things that are distinct, even in the case of the perception of a whole (*avayavin*); this same principle applies here, so why is it not accepted? Furthermore, in the absence of the *sphoṭa*, there would be no comprehension of meaning, for neither phonemes taken collectively nor individually possess the capacity to convey meaning. If it is argued that a collection (*samudāya*) is impossible, we say no; for it has already been stated that in its absence, there would follow the consequence of not perceiving anything at all. Moreover, nothing undesirable follows from the absence of the *sphoṭa*. Or rather, just as there is a cognition of a whole even when its parts are not perceived, why should there not be a cognition of a word and so forth even when the phonemes are not perceived? Furthermore, since the learned have designated the term ‘word’ (*pada*) precisely for those phonemes that end in an inflection (*vibhakti*), according to the rule "a word ends in a nominal suffix (*su*) or a verbal suffix (*tiṅ*)" and "those [phonemes] ending in an inflection are a word," the cognition of a word occurs with respect to the phonemes themselves in accordance with that convention. Therefore, the *sphoṭa* is not perceivable by the senses. Nor is it established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the comprehension of meaning, since the comprehension of meaning arises from the phonemes alone. If the comprehension of meaning were to arise from the *sphoṭa*, the utterance of phonemes would be useless. If it is argued that it is not useless because they manifest the *sphoṭa*, we say no; for the fault is the same. Whatever faults apply to the phonemes in being manifestors of meaning, how would they not apply in being manifestors of the *sphoṭa*? Therefore, by whatever means the manifestation of the *sphoṭa* is desired, let that very means be used for the manifestation of meaning itself; why resort to such effort?

{The fault in the position that a word is initiated by a series of phonemes} Those who say: "A word is initiated by phonemes existing in a series in space, and a sentence is [initiated] by words"—that view also must be refuted by the same logic used for the refutation of *sphoṭa*, because every position that maintains the distinctness of phonemes is identical to the *sphoṭa* theory.
{The faults in the collection of phonemes}

A collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) is a word (*pada*); a collection of words is a sentence (*vākya*); a collection of sentences is a section (*prakaraṇa*); a collection of sections is, according to the occasion, a quarter (*pāda*), a lesson (*āhnika*), or a chapter (*adhyāya*); and a collection of these constitutes a treatise (*śāstra*). But how can a collection of phonemes, which are momentary, be possible? It is not intended here that they form a collection while remaining present together, as in the case of a forest; rather, it is through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), like a collection of ritual actions such as sacrifices.

But how is it that a collection of phonemes (*varṇasamūha*) is the cause of the cognition of a word-meaning, and how might it not be so? [The opponent argues: Because the cognition of a word-meaning does not arise when the final phoneme is not heard, and because at the time of the final phoneme the preceding phonemes have vanished, they cannot be the cause. Nor can the final phoneme alone be the cause, for that would entail the uselessness of the preceding utterances. On this point, some say: "Even perished things can be causes, just as the preceding actions are causes for reaching a desired location at the time of the final action. This is not correct, because it is unproven. In that case, the final action itself is the cause, not the perished actions; for there is no proof that perished things can be generators. [The opponent continues: "In that case, the word is simply the final phoneme. And the preceding ones are not useless, because if they were not uttered, the status of being 'final' would be impossible—just as the final action cannot occur if the preceding actions do not occur. [The author replies: "This comparison is flawed. For in the case of someone situated at a distant place, as long as contact with each successive preceding location is not possible, contact with each subsequent location cannot occur. Therefore, the actions directed toward contact with each subsequent location are helpful by way of the preceding locations. However, one who is already situated in the location immediately adjacent to the intended destination reaches that destination without performing further actions. But here, even if the preceding phonemes are not uttered, it is not impossible to utter the intended phoneme, such that its utterance would necessarily be meaningful."

If it is argued that the final phoneme, depending on the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the preceding phonemes, constitutes the word (*pada*), we say no; for the capacity of an impression to produce a direct experience has not been established. Otherwise, even the inferential mark (*liṅga*) and words would bring about the comprehension of meaning by depending solely on impressions; what then would be the use of the imagined recollection (*smṛti*) of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*)? If [the opponent replies]: "In that case, the preceding impressions generate recollections, and together with these, the final phoneme is the word," we say no; because the simultaneous occurrence of cognitions is prohibited. If [the opponent suggests]: "Then let them generate a single, variegated (*mecaka*) recollection, and together with that, the final phoneme is the word," we say no; because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If the connection were based on their inherence in a single self (*ekātmasamavāyitva*), then it would follow that impressions produced at different places, times, and regarding different objects would also generate a single recollection. By this, the conceptualization that "a single impression arises from those [phonemes], and from that a single recollection" is also refuted. These same conceptualizations should be formulated and refuted regarding the position that the sentence (*vākya*) is the unitary entity, as the logic is the same.
The position that there is a sequence of successive phonemes, each distinguished by its preceding phoneme.

Others, however, say: the second [syllable] is perceived as qualified by the first; the third as qualified by the second, and so on until the final syllable. And thus, when this is done even for a sentence—where the word is [perceived] along with such a qualified experience—then the final word, being qualified by words whose meanings have not yet been understood, would constitute the sentence. Therefore, the following conceptualization applies here: at the time of the cognition of the word-meaning, the cognition of the first word is in the process of perishing (*vinaśyattā*), while the cognition of the second word is in the process of arising (*utpadyamānatā*). Then, at that same moment, the cognition of the second word arises as delimited by the meaning of the preceding word, the memory of the convention (*saṃketa*) of the first word perishes, and the cognition of the third word begins to arise. Thereafter, the cognition of the third word occurs as qualified by the meaning of the second word. This should be applied in the same way even up to a hundred words. There is no contradiction between memory and direct experience (*anubhava*), because they are of different kinds (*vijātīyatva*); therefore, it is said that the destruction of a memory is caused only by another memory, and that of an experience only by another experience.

Alternatively, by means of the cognition of the first word, which is in a state of perishing precisely because it has recalled the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), there is produced a cognition of that word’s referent as qualified by that word. By that [cognition], there arises a cognition of the second word as delimited by that word’s referent; this process should be applied even in the case of a hundred words. Thus, the final word, so qualified, is called a "sentence" (*vākya*). Furthermore, there is no need here for the recollection of the preceding words, because the purpose served by them is already accomplished simply through the production of a cognition of the final qualificand, which is not explicitly stated as such, being qualified by the meaning produced by those [preceding words]. {The refutation thereof}

This too is incorrect. For the cognition of the subsequent word (*uttarapada*) arises through a sequence of experiences of multiple phonemes (*varṇa*); how then could that cognition of the subsequent word be produced by the cognition of the preceding word—which is in a state of perishing—and by the cognition of its meaning, since the former has already perished immediately after the experience of the first phoneme? Furthermore, when there is an excessively delayed pronunciation of what has not yet served its purpose, the comprehension of the word-meaning and the sentence-meaning still occurs; even when one performs actions such as sneezing or spitting during the intervals between phonemes or between words, the cognition of the meaning nevertheless takes place. Therefore, there is no relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva*) between the preceding and succeeding phonemes or words.
Or, [this is] the formulation of the statement by others.

Others, however, having established that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) can serve as the cause of another impression through the power of repeated practice of the Vedas and so forth, interpret the sentence differently: by the cognition of the first word, a latent impression is produced. By the cognition of the second word, together with that [first impression], a different, qualified latent impression is produced. In this manner, one should consider the production of qualified latent impressions for each subsequent word up to the penultimate word. That latent impression, immediately after the experience of the final word, produces a single recollection (*smṛti*) regarding the preceding words. Together with that [recollection] and the experience, the final word constitutes the sentence. As for the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), it is not considered here because a convention cannot apply to a sentence. If that is so, how does it work in the case of a word? In that case too, immediately after the experience of the final phoneme, a single recollection arises regarding the preceding phonemes and the linguistic convention.
The fabrication of speech by others.

Others, however, fearing the consequence that even words whose meanings are not well-known would constitute a sentence, postulate a different process for the sentence: a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) is produced by the refinement of the word and the cognition of its meaning; another [refinement] is produced by the cognition of the second word together with that [first], and another by the cognition of the third word together with that [second], and so on until the penultimate word. Then, as before, the final word—accompanied by memory and direct experience—is the sentence. Since the meaning of the final word alone constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) regarding it has not even been considered there.

Others hold that there is a single memory regarding both the meanings of the preceding words and the conventional designation of the final word; such is the formulation of the sentence according to others.

Others, however, do not accept that the meaning of the final word alone constitutes the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*), because the sentence-meaning must be the principal element. Nor can the final word alone be considered the principal, since the relationship between the subordinate and the principal is not fixed. Indeed, even in the first or middle words, something principal is perceived—whether it be called an action (*kriyā*), or designated as an agent (*kartṛ*), or something else. They, however, postulate this: through the cognition of the meaning of the final word, accompanied by the preceding mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), another distinct impression is produced. Then, due to the power of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), while the final word remains present, there arises a direct experience (*anubhava*). From that, a single recollection (*smṛti*) occurs regarding all the word-meanings; and the final word, distinguished by both that recollection and the direct experience, produces a qualified comprehension even regarding the meaning of the first word, and is thus called a "sentence. This is highly implausible, for it implies that destruction does not occur despite the presence of causes for destruction, simply due to the power of the unseen merit. Why then is such a thing not postulated for cognitions (*buddhi*) themselves? Others propose that instead of recollection, one should postulate a mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*), since its object pertains to the three periods of time (past, present, and future), and specific auxiliary factors like the unseen merit prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Even the proponent of recollection must admit the initiation of a specific impression; therefore, it is better to maintain that it is indeed a mental perception, as this has already been accepted in cases such as the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*).
The formulation of another's statement and its refutation.

But another says: "Let that [cognition] arise from a non-mental [source] for one who depends on the apprehension of pure words and word-meanings; however, from the apprehension of the entire sentence, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning arises. Therefore, immediately after the apprehension of the final word, there occurs a mental perception called *adhyavasāya* (ascertainment) regarding the words and word-meanings accompanied by the connection between action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*). That final word, accompanied by this [perception], is the sentence. This too has been stated without due consideration. Why? Because it would entail the establishment of the very object intended by the opponent. If such a perception is accepted, then what is the use of a postulated sentence? Let the comprehension of its meaning proceed from mental perception itself, which depends on the apprehension of word-meanings; thus, for one who claims that every sentence is like the phrase "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*), the intended object would be established. For what distinction is there here by which a mental perception is accepted only for the connection between action and its factors, and not for the specific object intended as the sentence-meaning? Furthermore, if the sentence is not of the nature of sound (*śabda*), it would follow that it is a separate means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*). But if it is of the nature of sound, how can there be a comprehension of meaning from it independently of convention (*saṃketa*)? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), and it would contradict the Sūtra. Moreover, there is no convention regarding a sentence, since we observe the comprehension of meaning even from a sentence never heard before.

Furthermore, since even the final word has perished at the very moment the cognition of the final word-meaning occurs, there can be no verbal comprehension of the sentence-meaning, nor is it cognized by means of the final word-meaning. In that case, even though the cause of destruction exists, one would have to assume the non-destruction of the preceding words as well due to the power of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because the logic is the same. Therefore, if the designation "sentence" is indeed accepted, it is merely for the sake of conventional usage; the cognition of the meanings as qualified by their mutual connection is purely mental. A word, moreover, is not the final phoneme dependent on the memory of the preceding ones, because sequence is not an object of the external senses, and if that sequence is not grasped, there is no cognition of the status of a word. Thus, according to the Tausala, a word is those phonemes existing in space in a continuous series, distinguished by sequence and simultaneously experienced by the mind. Is this simultaneous experience dependent on the auditory organ, or independent of it? If it is dependent on the auditory organ, it is not tenable because phonemes do not coexist simultaneously [in the ear]. If it were independent of the auditory organ, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that it could occur anywhere, the auditory organ would be useless, and deafness would be impossible. If it is argued that one grasps each phoneme with the auditory organ and then grasps them simultaneously with the mind, we say no; there is no evidence for this. That [impression of simultaneity] is a false conceit arising from rapid succession, like the perception of a hundred petals being pierced. Moreover, when phonemes are uttered slowly or rapidly, such a conceit does not arise, yet the perception of sequence is still present. Therefore, sequence is grasped by the external sense organ aided by the prior apprehension [of the preceding sounds]. If it is asked how something qualified by time can be grasped by an external sense organ, we say no; for it is possible, just as a smell-qualified object can be grasped by the eye.

As for what was said—"If the sentence consists of sound, how can there be comprehension of meaning from it independently of convention?"—that is not correct, because we do not admit the absence of convention. For a sentence has been described as a collection of words (*padasaṃūha*). When there is the grasping of convention for those [words], how could there be an absence of it for the sentence? Indeed, even when all the trees are subject to cutting, flowering, and so forth, it is not possible for the forest itself to be devoid of them.

As for what was said—"There is no convention regarding a sentence, and therefore there can be no comprehension of meaning even from a previously unheard sentence"—that is not correct, because it is unproven. For if that were so, it would follow that even those who are unlearned (avyutpanna) could comprehend the meaning of the Vedas and other scriptures. Furthermore, as for what was said—"By mere worldly usage (*vyavahāra*), the designation 'sentence' is intended to apply only to words"—that too is incorrect; for the designation is applied because [a sentence] conveys a meaning characterized by a specific relation (*saṃsarga*). If it is asked: "Since a convention is not established for such a related meaning, how can that meaning be comprehended from the words? We reply: It is through comprehension in the same manner as an inferential mark (*liṅga*). Just as an inferential mark whose connection has been perceived in a general way, when apprehended as delimited by a particular location and so forth, proves the probandum (*sādhya*) as delimited by that very particularity; likewise, a word whose connection has been perceived through its mere meaning, when heard in proximity to another word, conveys a meaning precisely as delimited by the relation with that other word's meaning. For in this way alone does a word possess meaningfulness. Otherwise, like proving what is already established in the case of a generality, this [sentence-meaning] would suffer the fault of futility, since a meaning of that magnitude alone is already comprehended at the time of the convention. Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the Sūtra. Just as an inferential mark whose connection is grasped in a general way is not said to be independent of pervasion (*vyāpti*) even while it establishes a particularity of place and so forth, so too a word, though having its convention grasped in a general way, is said to be based on convention (*sāmayika*) even while it conveys a meaning as qualified by the meanings of the other proximate words.

[Objection: But surely, in the case of a logical mark (*liṅga*), its connection is well-established as being "wherever [the mark] is, there [is the probandum]. Therefore, it causes one to infer its own pervader (*vyāpaka*) only in that very place where it is perceived, such as a particular location and so forth. However, the word does not function in this manner; for if it did, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that one could understand a specific meaning from a single word without depending on other words, just as one understands a specific object from a logical mark without depending on other marks. [Reply: This is not sound. For we shall explain that the word is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); therefore, it does not share every characteristic with the logical mark. If it shared all characteristics, the word would simply be a logical mark. It was cited as a logical mark only by virtue of certain common features. Furthermore, it has been stated that "the word is the instruction of a reliable person" (*āptopadeśa*). No one is called a "reliable person" merely because they communicate isolated word-meanings through words; rather, it is one who instructs the truth regarding what is to be avoided and what is to be adopted, along with the means thereto. Nor can that be instructed by words that do not express a specific relation (*saṃsarga*). Convention (*saṃketa*) is generally grasped for words that have attained the status of a sentence (*vākya*). For example, in grammar, the linguistic convention (*samaya*) is understood to apply to words expressing actions and factors of action (*kāraka*) even when they refer to specific objects distinguished by their mutual relations, and likewise to words like *nīla* (blue) and *utpala* (lotus) even when they refer to objects qualified by each other. Similarly, in worldly practice, noble persons acquire the convention from children, elders, Kaṇāda, and others. Thus, one whose intellect is refined understands the sentence-meaning through intuition (*pratibhā*) and deliberation (*ūha*), even if the sentence is otherwise arranged. Even for one who has grasped the convention for a single word in some context, when that word is used in the midst of words that have attained the status of a sentence, he understands its qualified nature through intuition and deliberation. Just as one understands the meaning of a word whose convention is not yet known when it is used among words whose conventions are known, at that very moment he grasps the convention there through intuition and deliberation and understands its meaning. If you argue: "But surely, there is no comprehension of meaning from that which lacks a convention," then why is the same not left unestablished for the sentence as well? For instance, where one is unable to grasp the convention through intuition and deliberation, one requires an explanation regarding the sentence-meaning even when the word-meanings are well-known. Now, what is this "intuition"? It is a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*) born from practice in a previous life, awakened by some cause, serving as the basis for memory; it is this that is intended here as "intuition," and not the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a seer (*ārṣa*). "Deliberation" (*ūha*), however, is the intellectual power (*bauddhī śakti*) or reflective consideration (*parāmarśa*). If this were the case, then the meaning of the sentence would not be connected to it; therefore, the reflective consideration is: "This is the meaning of this [sentence]. [Objection: But if that is so, the word has already perished before the reflective consideration occurs; how then could it convey the meaning? Moreover, even a collection of words such as "ten pomegranates" (*daśadāḍima*) would convey a sentence-meaning. Therefore, a sentence is not a mere collection of words; rather, words cease after conveying their respective meanings, and the sentence-meaning is understood from that collection of word-meanings—so say others.

That too is not more sound, for even a collection of word-meanings does not necessarily exist, since the objects such as the Pāṇḍavas, the actions such as the Agnihotra sacrifice, and their results are not present [at the time of understanding]. How, then, can there be comprehension of the sentence-meaning from that? If it is argued that the means for this is knowledge whose object is the collection of word-meanings, why is knowledge whose object is the collection of words not likewise [the means]?

Furthermore, why would even a collection of objects such as "ten pomegranates" not convey a sentence-meaning? If you argue that this is because the necessary conditions—such as mutual expectancy (*apekṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*)—are absent there, then this same rebuttal applies equally to a collection of words; moreover, it would follow that [the sentence-meaning] would have to be established by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For a collection of word-meanings does not fall within any one of the [other] means of valid cognition, such as perception. If you argue that a collection of word-meanings understood from words conveys the sentence-meaning, and therefore it is included within verbal testimony (*śabda*), then by the same logic, since words and logical marks (*liṅga*) understood through perception convey their own respective objects, they too would necessarily be included within perception. Furthermore, there is no such cognition [of the sentence-meaning arising from word-meanings]; for there is no cognition such as "this is a sentence among the word-meanings," or "I have understood the sentence-meaning from the word-meanings."
The Theory of the Expression of Related Entities (Anvitābhidhānavāda)

Nor is there the theory of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of what has been expressed), because the connection exists even prior [to the utterance]. For "connection" (*anvaya*) is defined as the specific mutual relation among the action, the factors of action (*kāraka*), the qualifiers, and so forth. And that [relation] exists even before [the sentence is uttered]; for it is one who perceives it who utters a sentence in order to communicate it—such as: "A dark man cuts down a large tree on a mountain with an axe. If you argue that the connection of the word-meanings is perceived only after they have been expressed, and therefore it is called *abhihitānvaya*, then does that [connection] subsequently arise through the power of the meaning (*arthasāmarthya*) or through the power of the words (*śabdasāmarthya*)? If it arises through the power of the meaning, then by the power of the meanings—even though they have been expressed by words such as "dark," "axe," "man," "mountain," and "large tree"—the connection would be perceived as: "The axe [cuts], the man [cuts], on the mountain, the large tree [is cut]. For the power of the word-meanings is not removed by being expressed otherwise, nor does their nature change.

Furthermore, in works such as poetry and treatises, it is observed that for the sake of understanding the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) after the meaning of the words has been cognized, some require a commentary. Moreover, if the syntactic connection were not denoted [by the words], how could there be the designation: "this sentence is connected" and "this one is unconnected"? If it is argued that the connection is subsequently cognized through the inherent power (*sāmarthya*) of the words, is that [connection] independent (*svatantra*)? Or does it reside in the word-meanings (*padārtha*)? It cannot be independent, because such a cognition does not occur and because it would contradict the principle that "the connection belongs to those [meanings] already expressed. For this very reason, it does not reside in other word-meanings, as there is no means of cognizing it [in that way]. Nor does it reside in the word-meanings as they have been expressed; for when the word *śyāma* (dark) functions according to its conventional usage, it expresses even a non-human being, and the word *puruṣa* (man) expresses even one who is not dark; likewise, the word *kuṭhāra* (axe) expresses merely the axe. And no syntactic connection occurs between word-meanings of such a nature.

Now, words such as "dark-complexioned" (*śyāma*), when uttered to denote objects qualified by mutual association, express those very same qualified objects while depending upon the cognition of their mutual meanings. Conventional usage (*samaya*) is likewise; for those [words] which depend on context and so forth are not general terms (*sāmānya-śabda*). Since this is understood both from instruction and from linguistic usage, the theory of the expression of the related (*anvitābhidhāna*) is thus established.

As for what someone has said—"This cognition of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is sublated by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because, while having another means of proof, it is a cognition of a qualified entity (*viśiṣṭapratīti*), like the cognition 'my brother will come tomorrow'"—that is not so, because the qualification is unestablished (*asiddha*). For we shall explain that there is no sublation whatsoever against its being produced by a sentence. Furthermore, the example "my brother will come tomorrow" is unestablished, as such a cognition does not exist for anyone [in the same way]. If it is argued: "But it exists for some children; how did you know this? If you say, "Because their speech is non-contradictory," we say no; for even one who speaks at random may have a truthful statement, and the non-contradiction of some utterance can occur by chance (*kākatālīya*), like that of a madman; yet this much does not establish a certainty regarding the object for them. Or else, like the cry of a crow, the speech of children might be a mere inferential mark (*liṅga*) indicating an object as an omen; if, however, the cognition of the sentence-meaning were a mental perception, then that [cognition] would occur regarding sentence-meanings even when the word is not heard, just as it occurs regarding pleasure and the like. If it is argued that it does not occur due to a deficiency in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), is the cognition of the word the auxiliary cause, or the cognition of the word-meanings? If it is the cognition of the word, why is the cognition of the sentence-meaning not born from the sentence itself? For it is precisely that which is born from the cognition of a collection of words that is called "born from the sentence. Just as the cognition of an inferable object, though born from the cognition of a past inferential mark, is not called mental perception but is called inferential (*laiṅgika*). Now, if the cognition of the collection of word-meanings is the auxiliary cause for the mind, then the position of *abhihitānvaya* (the connection of expressed meanings) would be established, and the mass of faults already stated therein would apply. Moreover, even the proponent of *abhihitānvaya* does not deny the causality of the mind, since the mind is the cause of all cognitions. Nor is something a mental perception simply because it is produced by the mind, for that would entail the consequence that all cognitions are mental perceptions. Mental perception is the result of an immediate experience (*aparokṣānubhava*) not produced by the external senses; and an immediate experience of a sentence-meaning such as the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) or God is not possible for people like us, as that would entail the lack of distinction between the ordinary person and a yogi. Furthermore, there would be no difference in the nature of the cognition between the sentence-meaning and the perception of pleasure, pain, and so forth, since they would both equally be mental perceptions.

Furthermore, one must also assume that the cognition of word-meanings (*padārtha*) arises from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), as the same logic applies. Upon close examination, even the apprehension of word-meanings is not verbal (*śābda*). For by the third moment, the word itself must necessarily perish—either through conjunction with a material substance (like space) or due to its own effect, the sound. And yet, the knowledge of the word-meaning does not occur at the third moment; for even the recollection of the linguistic convention (*saṃketa*) is impossible then. Nor can it be maintained that the word persists despite the presence of causes for its destruction, on account of some unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); otherwise, it would follow that the entire collection of words might persist through an unseen force until the comprehension of the sentence-meaning occurs. In some cases, however, one perceives the word-meaning after recalling the convention only after a long time, aided by focused attention (*praṇidhāna*), merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth. Similarly, in the case of written letters, one mentally reconstructs the words, recalls their conventions, and thereby understands both the word-meanings and the sentence-meaning. Thus, since the cognition of word-meanings shares the same status (*yogakṣema*) as the cognition of sentence-meanings, it follows that the former is also mental. Consequently, the means of valid cognition called "verbal testimony" (*śabda*) ceases to apply here. Indeed, even in the cognition of word-meanings, the word never acts as a direct cause, since it has already been stated that the word perishes even while being heard. Since the understanding of the meaning is possible otherwise, the persistence of the word cannot be established even by the principle of "presumption" (*arthāpatti*). Therefore, the comprehension of the sentence-meaning is called "verbal" (*śābdī*) only because it arises from the mental reconstruction of the word in its form as a sentence. Primarily, however, the cognition of both word-meanings and sentence-meanings is produced precisely through the mental reconstruction of the word, depending upon convention and other factors. In that context, when there is a reconstruction of the word and so forth, the status of being a "word," a "sentence," or "verbal testimony" is secondary (*gauṇa*), whereas its status as a "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is primary. When the word is not primary, its status as a means of valid cognition is merely secondary, because it does not directly accomplish the knowledge of the object. The speech of an unreliable person (*anāpta*), however, is not a means for correct experience even indirectly, and is thus called "not a means of valid cognition. The speech of a reliable person (*āpta*) is not like this, for it serves as a means for determining the object even indirectly. Therefore, there is no lack of distinction based on being secondary; and since the capacity to determine the object indirectly belongs to all phonemes (*varṇa*) and all words (*pada*), it is not the case that only the final phoneme is a word, nor that only the final word is a sentence. This is consistent with the rule: "Those [phonemes] ending in an inflection are a word," and the *Bhāṣya*: "In whatever collection of sounds the object to be established [is expressed]," and so forth. Furthermore, parts (*avayava*) are said to be portions of a sentence, and propositions (*pratijñā*) and so forth are not portions of the final word alone. Therefore, it is established that a sentence is simply a collection of words.

{Definition of the Members [of a Syllogism]} Are the parts [of the syllogism] merely the words? It is said: No; what then? The members are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). The meaning is that even a sentence expressing a constituent part of the proof is a member of the great sentence [of the syllogism]. {Definition of the Proposition}

In this regard: "The statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) with the desire to communicate [the probandum] is the proposition (*pratijñā*). Even one who merely desires to know might utter the statement of the thesis for the sake of inquiring about the means of proof; therefore, so that even such a case does not become a proposition, the qualification "with the desire to communicate" is added. Alternatively, for the purpose of resolving an objection, the aphorism states: "The indication of the probandum (*sādhyanirdeśa*) is the proposition. In that context, when the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are stated by another means of proof with the desire to establish them, then that [statement] should be accepted as a proposition. For it is not intended here that "probandum" refers simply to what is unestablished for the opponent; rather, whatever is desired to be established by the proponent at a particular time is the probandum, because it is a probandum only in relation to the stated means of proof. What, then, is determined here? If the definition is restricted such that "only the indication of the probandum is the proposition," then the indication of the probandum would be undetermined, as it could exist otherwise [as something other than a proposition]; thus the definition would be over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*). On the other hand, if the definition is restricted such that "the indication of the probandum is only the proposition," then the proposition would be undetermined, as it could exist otherwise [without being an indication of the probandum]; thus the definition would be under-extensive (*avyāpaka*). "No," says Tāmarī, "because there is no fixed rule. There is no such rule that every sentence must be restrictive (*sāvadhāraṇa*). For example: "This is the path; go to Srughna. (In this case, the restriction is on the path, not on the act of going.)
{The position of restricting the fame}:
Here too, there is indeed a restriction, because of the fame [of the following]:
"Non-connection, connection with others, and absolute non-connection..."
The particle, being a separator, distinguishes the property.
Whether explicitly uttered along with the qualifier, the qualified, and the action,
or even when not employed due to the speaker's intention, this meaning of it is understood.
A statement has exclusion as its result, as for example: "Caitra is an archer," or "Pārtha is an archer," or "The lotus is blue."

"In those cases as well, the exclusion of the counter-correlative (*pratiyogivyavaccheda*) is understood regarding the objects, due to established usage, logical necessity, and the conformity of the speaker's intention with the sound.

Therefore, here too, when there is a doubt that he might go by another path, the restriction is "this very [path]"; when there is a doubt that he might go to another village, the restriction is "to Srughna alone"; and when there is a doubt that he might not go as far as Srughna, the restriction is "he is indeed going."

{The Refutation of That} On this point as well, the opponent has said: "We do not see an object for the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). For a restriction is desired to prevent over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) when there is a general statement; for where there is scope for a qualification, there too is scope for a restriction. Nor is there any occasion for resorting to a restriction for the purpose of exclusion when a cowherd instructs one who merely wishes to know the nature of the path, saying, "This is the road that goes to Srughna," or when it is stated that "the proposition (*pratijñā*) is the indication of what is to be proven" (*sādhyaniṛdeśa*).

In the case of the statement "Pārtha is the archer," restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is appropriate for the purpose of excluding others, since there might otherwise be a suspicion among other disciples—on account of their being students of Droṇa—that they too were archers equal to him; otherwise, it would indeed be inappropriate. For how could it be possible to say that Pārtha alone is the archer and that no one equal or superior to him exists?

In the statement "Caitra is an archer," restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) is inappropriate, because the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is already established by the very injunction of being an archer, since injunction and prohibition cannot coexist in one and the same place. However, it is appropriate for the purpose of excluding [the property's] occurrence in only a part [of the locus], as in "The sons of Pāṇḍu are indeed brave. Even when a property occurs in only a part [of the locus], the designation of its "occurrence" still applies, as in the expression: "Hornedness exists in the heterologue (*vipakṣa*)."

It is also not tenable to say, "The lotus is indeed blue," because the absolute exclusion of non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) is already established by the word itself. Furthermore, the view that a sentence has exclusion as its primary fruit has been refuted and will be refuted further. Indeed, it is accepted that even for a word denoting a real entity (*vastu*), the establishment of exclusion occurs through its inherent capacity (*sāmarthya*).

Regarding the statement "the formulation of the probandum (*sādhya*) is the thesis (*pratijñā*"), by implication it is understood that the formulation of what is not the probandum is not the thesis. This being so, fallacious theses (*pratijñābhāsa*) are also excluded, and we shall provide examples of them later in connection with the relevant context. Here, the term "probandum" refers specifically to the locus (*dharmin*) as qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*); therefore, "the formulation of the probandum is the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacana*)" has one meaning. However, the Teachers maintain that the mere formulation of the property to be proven is not the thesis. Alternatively, let it be granted that here the term "probandum" includes even the property as qualified by the locus; even the formulation of that would be the statement of the subject, for from the words "fire is here," it is not the case that a place possessing fire is not understood. Nor is it said that only the locus when being qualified is the subject; rather, it is also [the subject] by virtue of its fitness (*yogyatā*). If that were so, the mention of the locus alone would also constitute a thesis; but it is not, because it would be redundant. For no intended object is established thereby; such a statement, being a non-member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), would be a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
{The suspicion that the thesis is redundant}:

If that is the case, then the thesis itself should not be stated, because its establishment—whether directly or indirectly—is impossible. First of all, no statement whatsoever is a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana*). For it has been said: "Since the understanding of the matter [the probandum] arises from the matter [the reason] itself, the statements of the thesis and the reason have no power [to establish it]."
"Therefore, for those two, there is no establishment of proof by way of their own nature.
Nor is the statement of the thesis sufficient [to prove it], because it merely names what is to be proven;
the statement of the reason, though itself incapable, indicates that which is capable."

Even for one’s own sake, only this much is observed to be useful: the perception of the subject (dharmin) as connected with the mark (liṅga) and the recollection of the pervasion (vyāpti). Therefore, with the desire to bring about the comprehension of another just as one has achieved it for oneself, only internal pervasion (antarvyāpti) and external pervasion (bahirvyāpti) need to be made known. If it is argued that even when the reason (hetu) is thus established, it does not produce the comprehension of another without a thesis (pratijñā), then why, now that you seek the welfare of others, do you seek a price like a Brahmin at a festival? Furthermore, when it is stated, "Whatever is produced is all impermanent, like a pot; and sound is produced," the fact that "sound is impermanent" is understood by implication alone. Thus, setting aside your stubborn attachment (ḍiṇḍikarāga), close your eyes and consider for a moment whether the comprehension of the meaning occurs through this much or not. Since there remains doubt, there is no certainty of the meaning from the thesis; therefore, the thesis is not a constituent part of the proof.
The resolution thereof.

To this it is replied: As for the claim that the statement of the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not a direct means of proof (*sādhana*), there is no dispute on that point. It has been stated that it is a means of proof even indirectly, because it expresses the probandum (*sādhya*); otherwise, the reason (*hetu*) would be "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*). If it is argued that it is not "uncommon" because it expresses the probandum which is assisted by the reason—just as the expression of the reason itself is not uncommon—it is not so. For then the expression of the reason would also follow as not being a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), just like the expression of the reason when it is unassisted by other members of the syllogism. If it is argued that [the thesis-statement] is not uncommon because it indicates that which possesses the capacity [to prove], we say no; for the statements of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would then be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), since they too indicate the capacity of the members of the proof. Furthermore, the statement of the thesis also possesses the quality of indicating a capacity, because it points out the object of the proof. Indeed, no one teaches a means of proving something without first pointing out its object, just as one does not instruct, "See the jar sitting in the house with a lamp. By this, the argument beginning with "like one's own cognition" (*svapratipattivat*) is also refuted; for if one were merely teaching the means of one's own cognition, one should have taught only, "In the house, see with the eye and the lamp," and yet, by not teaching in that way, the intended meaning is not fully communicated. Moreover, the consideration of the merits and defects of the proponent and the opponent occurs in inference for others (*parārthānumāna*), not in inference for oneself.

And that [inference] is rooted in the knowledge of the distinction between the *pakṣa* (the subject) and so forth. Without a thesis (*pratijñā*), there can be no knowledge of the distinction between similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*asapakṣa*). In the absence of that, there would also be no distinction between those who assert contradictory realities. For without the statement "whatever is produced is impermanent, like a jar," there would be no difference between the two [positions]. [Objection: Is the thesis then being asserted by you merely for the sake of revealing yourself as a proponent of a contradictory view? [Reply: It is not so. What then? It is for the sake of removing the suspicion of a specific contradiction or sublation (*bādhā*). For without a thesis, even doubt might arise among the judges (*prāśnikas*). [Objection: If the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being produced" with both permanence and impermanence is stated, the distinction between the proponents of contradictory views is established. [Reply: No; because it is improper to point out a fault or a merit when the specific property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) has not been understood. For if "impermanence" is what is to be proven, then even if the pervasion of "being produced" with "permanence" were stated, it would not be proper to point out a contradiction. Only the fault of stating a reversed pervasion should be pointed out against the speaker. And if "permanence" is what is to be proven, it is not proper to point out a lack of contradiction even if the pervasion of "being produced" with "impermanence" is stated. [Objection: How could a sane person, intending "permanence" in the case of sound, demonstrate the pervasion of "being produced" with "impermanence"? [Reply: How then does a sane person state the pervasion of "being produced" with "permanence"? [Objection: It is due to delusion (*bhrānti*). [Reply: That is equally true in the other case as well. However, a thesis will not be asserted in such a way. [Objection: Even if formulated thus, there would still be no confidence. [Reply: No; because the speaker's possession of such qualities is revealed through the examination of the merits and defects of the sentence, just as the presence of merit or defect in the author of a painting is revealed by the painting’s own quality or flaw. Furthermore, the activity of the wise is not for the purpose of deceiving others, such that they would not utter a clear sentence communicating their own intention. For if the *pakṣa* were not stated, listeners of dull or mediocre capacity, failing to grasp the intended object of proof, would be confused regarding both the similar and dissimilar instances. Therefore, to avoid this, the statement of the *pakṣa* must be made. As for what was said—"Whatever is produced," etc.—that too is incorrect. For no one, having entered the midst of an assembly, would deserve the ridicule of the wise by making such an irrelevant presentation as "whatever is produced," etc., without prior reflection, like a sudden eruption of vomit. And if the statement of the *pakṣa* is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*), why do you yourself teach it—such statements as "the statement of the *pakṣa* is not sufficient even indirectly," or "one thing cannot be connected with another that possesses spatial distinctions, though it occurs in many places"? [Objection: It is taught in the treatises for the sake of instructing the ignorant (*bāla*). [Reply: How can the ignorant be instructed by a statement that is not a member of the proof? On the contrary, it would result in a lack of refinement. Or, if it does produce instruction, how can it be "not a member of the proof"? [Objection: Let it be a member of the proof for the ignorant. [Reply: No; because there is no difference, since there is no difference in its being presented as an inference-for-others (*parārthānumāna*). Nor is anyone observed even in formal debate (*vāda*) who does not state the object of proof. Even if one does not state it in the original formulation, or in the second or third stage, it is not enough to avoid it; for one must necessarily investigate one's own position at great length, saying "this is thus" or "this is not thus"—that itself is the statement of the *pakṣa*, and the adducing of the reason (*hetu*) is for the sake of establishing that meaning.

As for what was said—that the statement of the thesis (*pakṣavacana*) is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*) and not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*)—that too is incorrect. For instance, if it were a mere restatement, what would be the point of saying it, since it would be purposeless? Furthermore, it would constitute a ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Nor is it reasonable to claim another purpose, because that would be irrelevant to the context. If, on the other hand, its purpose is the establishment of the object through a mediated process (*praṇālikā*), then how could it not be sufficient even indirectly?

As for the objection that this would entail that even the desire to know (*jijñāsā*) and the other [limbs] possess the status of being members of a syllogism, because they serve as the causes for the operation of the statement of the reason (*hetu*) just like the thesis (*pratijñā*), that is incorrect. For only that which possesses the nature of a single sentence (*ekavākyabhāva*) has the status of being a member of a sentence. It has been stated that members are indeed parts of a sentence. However, the desire to know and the others do not have such a nature. To explain: the desire to know is the wish to understand a specific object; doubt is the convergence of conflicting attributes; feasibility is the possibility of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that determine the intended object; purpose is the ascertainment of that object; and the removal of doubt is the refutation of opposing positions. Since these are not of the nature of verbal statements, there is no consequence of there being ten members.

Furthermore, as for what was said by the Venerable [Vasubandhu]: “If statements such as ‘This has been desired to be known by you’ and ‘In this matter you have a doubt’ were to result in being members [of a syllogism], then it would follow that a statement must have ten members”—that is not correct. For members do not become so merely by virtue of being statements; rather, they are so because they are parts of a probative statement (*sādhakavākya*), and these [statements] are not parts of a probative statement. [Objection: In that case, the thesis (*pratijñā*) is also not a part of a probative statement, because it causes doubt. [Reply: No; for even the statement of the reason (*hetu*) and so forth, when not assisted by other members, causes doubt. [Objection: There is no doubt regarding its own meaning (*svārtha*). [Reply: No; for there is doubt even regarding its own meaning. Is this meaning of the reason probative or non-probative? And to whom does it belong? Thus, there is doubt even regarding the mere subject (*dharmin*) which is the object of the thesis. Moreover, there is no consensus among all people regarding the meaning of the reason and so forth; since the statement of that [reason] also produces doubt in some, it would not be a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*) and would thus incur a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). For the thesis-statement is not a cause of doubt for everyone in the same way that the statement of the reason and so forth is not a member of the proof once certainty is later attained regarding them. Therefore, the statement of the subject (*pakṣavacaḥ*) is likewise [not a member of the proof].

Another [scholar] maintains that the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is obtained from the context (*prastāva*). What is this "context"? It is the acceptance of the thesis and counter-thesis by the two disputants. But is that not the very same as the proposition? Furthermore, there is no rule that one must employ all five members [of a syllogism]. What then? It is simply that a sentence consisting of all five members is the means of proof. In that case, if some member is not employed because its meaning is already understood from the context or in accordance with the intelligence of the person being instructed, there is no fault whatsoever. However, the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "deficiency" (*nyūna*) occurs only when one is unable to explain a constituent part of the proof even though it is desired to be known. For example, even when asked, "What is the probandum (*sādhya*) here?", a Buddhist, fearing contradiction with his own tenets, is unable to specify the probandum; instead, he might say, "You should know it by implication," or, "If you can know it by implication, then you are still uneducated—go back to the schoolhouse where the alphabet is taught! What right do you have to debate? Such responses are improper for the virtuous. Therefore, one who is engaged in the task of enlightening another must indeed state the thesis; thus, the proposition is not a non-constituent of the proof.

{Investigation of the Reason (*hetunirūpaṇam*):} The statement of the logical mark (*liṅga*) that makes known its status as a means of proof is the reason (*hetu*). That which ends in either the fifth or third case-ending, by which the status of the logical mark as a cause for the establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) is made known—that statement is metaphorically designated as the "reason" because it possesses those [characteristics]. Primarily, however, the logical mark itself is the reason, precisely because it alone possesses the properties such as being a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). The statement that "it is of three kinds," and so forth, should also be explained according to this primary and secondary distinction. Furthermore, the mention of "positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatirekin*) and so on is intended to refute the threefold classification asserted by others, but not to refute the categories such as *pūrvavat* and the rest.
{The Buddhists' exposition of the three types of evidence}

For another has said this: there are three types of logical reasons (*hetu*), characterized as effect (*kārya*), essential nature (*svabhāva*), and non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). For example: "There is fire here, because of smoke"; "This is a tree, because it is a *śiṃśapā*"; "In this place, there is no jar, because of the non-perception of that which has reached the conditions for perception. All three of these possess an essential connection (*svabhāvapratibandha*); according to other opinions, others do not function as valid reasons. The reason of essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) is of two kinds: dependent on an adventitious attribute (*upādhyapekṣa*) or pure (*śuddha*); as in the case of "producedness" (*kṛtakatva*) and "existence" (*sattva*) regarding destruction. For an entity that depends on the operation of another is called "produced. Non-perception (*anupalabdhi*), however, is of two kinds based on the distinction between the non-perception of the perceptible and the imperceptible. Among these, the non-perception of the imperceptible establishes merely the negation of the conventional usage of existence, but it does not establish non-existence itself, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). The non-perception of the perceptible, however, establishes the absence of an entity.

And that [non-apprehension] is of eleven kinds: therein, (1) non-apprehension of the essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) has been cited previously. (2) Non-apprehension of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), for example: "The causes of smoke, whose capacities are unimpeded, do not exist here, because of the absence of smoke. (3) Non-apprehension of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), for example: "There is no *śiṃśapā* tree here, because of the absence of trees. (4) Apprehension of what is incompatible with the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*), for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of fire. (5) Apprehension of the effect of the incompatible (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*), for example: "There is no sensation of cold here, because of smoke. (6) Apprehension of what is pervaded by the incompatible (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*), for example: "Destruction is certain for anything that has come into being, because it does not depend on another cause [for its destruction]. (7) Apprehension of what is incompatible with the effect (*kāryaviruddhopalabdhi*), for example: "The causes of cold, whose capacities are unimpeded, do not exist here, because of fire. (8) Apprehension of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), for example: "There is no sensation of frost here, because of fire. (9) Non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*), for example: "There is no smoke here, because there is no fire. (10) Apprehension of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*), for example: "He does not have such particularities as horripilation, because of the presence of a particular fire. (11) Apprehension of the effect of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhakāryopalabdhi*), for example: "A person possessed of particularities such as horripilation is here, because of smoke. Whatever negation there may be, all of it is non-apprehension; this is the established rule (*samaya*). Therefore, even the apprehension of the incompatible and so forth is said to be nothing but non-apprehension.
{In that regard, there is the refutation [of the opponent] by means of the non-perception of intrinsic nature.}

In this regard, first of all, the reason based on essential identity (*svabhāvahetu*) is untenable, because a necessary connection of identity (*tādātmyapratibandha*) is impossible. That impossibility follows from the fact that it has been established that properties (*dharma*), as well as properties and their substratum (*dharmī*), are distinct entities (*arthāntara*). For the same reason, non-perception of essence (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*) is also not a valid reason. For if absence is already established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), then non-perception is redundant. Furthermore, if absence were established through non-perception, there would be an infinite regress of examples (*dṛṣṭānta*). If one were to admit that in some cases absence is established by direct perception, then how could it be said that "whatever negation there is, it is all due to non-perception"? If it is argued that "conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is being proved for the sake of a deluded person," then if that usage consists in verbal expression or in activity and the like, the means [of proof] for its production would not be a valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, however, it is the indicator of that [usage], then the consequence follows that it must be proved by something else, and thus there would be no identity between the probandum and the probans. If even conventional usage characterized as memory is what is indicated, then the same fault applies. If, on the other hand, it is produced [by the reason], then again it is not a valid cognition, because it would follow that even the mental application (*praṇidhāna*) and so forth which produce memory would be valid cognitions. If it is argued that "fitness for conventional usage" is what is being proved, is that fitness something different from the object or not different? If it is different, then how can the reason be of the nature of that [object]? If it is not different, then since that [fitness] is established simply by the establishment of the reason, inference is useless. It is not logical for a thing to have identity with the reason if it remains unestablished even when the reason is established, just as smoke is not identical to fire. Identity with the substratum (*dharmī*) alone would be the only possible necessary connection; for even in the case of smoke and fire, the substratum—such as a particular location—is a single entity.

If it is argued that even when the object to be proven (*sādhya*) is already established, inference merely performs the exclusion of superimposition (*samāropavyavaccheda*), then what is this "exclusion of superimposition"? Is it non-arising? Or destruction? Or the ascertainment of its unreality? Or is it a cognition opposed to it? First of all, non-arising and destruction are not the fruit of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). If it is the ascertainment of its unreality, then there is no identity (*tādātmya*) between the object and its unreality; therefore, the object cannot be the proof for the unreality of the superimposition. Now, if the "exclusion of superimposition" is said to be a cognition opposed to it, is that [cognition] one that apprehends an object, or one that does not apprehend an object, or is it without an object (*nirviṣaya*)? If it apprehends an object, then since inference would be apprehending what has already been apprehended, it would result in being invalid, just like another instance of memory. Alternatively, it would follow that all means of producing memory are themselves valid cognitions. If, on the other hand, it does not apprehend an object, then how can there be identity between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*)—which are respectively apprehended and unapprehended—any more than there could be between a jar and a *piśāca*? If it is without an object, then inference is not tenable; for there is no validity independent of an object, and this would contradict the principle: "The validity of both [perception and inference] has a real entity as its object. Even if [inference] were to have a real entity as its object indirectly, since the determinations of the sign and the signified would share the same object, one of them would be redundant, just like two determinations of the same thing, such as "this is smoke" and "this is smoke. Therefore, an essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not a reason (*hetu*) for itself, nor is the non-perception of an essential nature. Furthermore, we shall explain that the cognition "there is no jar here" is simply the fruit of perception (*pratyakṣaphala*).

It has been stated that even when the object of proof (*sādhya*) is a conventional reality (*vyavahāra*), an essential nature (*svabhāva*) cannot serve as the logical reason (*hetu*), because it would then be proving something other than itself. Therefore, the threefold division of reasons is based solely on the distinctions of *pūrvavat* and so forth; the various types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) are, however, included within these very categories such as *pūrvavat*. Furthermore, the example cited by the opponent for the apprehension of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*) is not tenable, because even a moment of a jar or similar object that is destined to exist must depend upon other causes. Rather, the correct example is this: "Destruction does not depend on another cause, because it is perceived precisely through a difference in time."

{The Buddhist's Defense of the Essential Nature as a Reason} If the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is not a reason with respect to itself, then it follows that the effect (*kārya*) alone is the only reason; consequently, everything else would be a non-reason due to the absence of a necessary connection (*pratibandha*). As it has been said: "Either from the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) or from an essential nature (*svabhāva*) acting as a regulator..."
The rule of invariable concomitance is established neither from non-perception nor from perception.

What is the rule regarding the necessity of occurrence? It is the impossibility for another [property] to arise otherwise through other [causes], or when a property has a different object as its cause, like dye on a cloth.
Therefore, a nature that is related to its own constituent elements, or a cause, would exclude the entity itself or its effect respectively, because of their non-deviation.

An intrinsic nature (svabhāva), when excluded, excludes the entity (bhāva). For example, a tree excludes a *śiṃśapā* tree, because it is well-established that the latter is a specific [type] possessing branches and so forth; that is its intrinsic nature. And how could an entity exist if it were to abandon its own intrinsic nature? Furthermore, a cause, when excluded, excludes the effect; otherwise, it would not be its effect at all. Since the established relation of cause and effect restricts the intrinsic nature, in both cases exclusion occurs solely through dependence on the intrinsic nature.
Otherwise, how could the exclusion of one thing result in the exclusion of another?
Just because a mortal does not possess horses, must he necessarily not possess cattle as well?
"By the mere proximity of one thing, how can there be the proximity of another? Would a mortal necessarily possess horses simply because he possesses cows?

Therefore, a logical reason (hetu) makes known the probandum (sādhya) solely through an essential connection (svabhāvapratibandha). And that [connection] is characterized either by identity (tādātmya) or by origination from that (tadutpatti). That very inseparable relation (avinābhāva) is demonstrated by means of the two types of examples (dṛṣṭānta). Consequently, due to the absence of an essential connection, neither a cause nor something that is neither cause nor effect can function as a logical reason.
The refutation thereof.

To this it is replied: Is it that being an effect (*kāryatva*) is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvitva*) with [fire], or that being an effect is [established] by way of its inseparable connection with [fire]? It cannot be that being an effect is inseparably connected with fire; for while fire has the quality of being an effect produced by the friction of fire-sticks (*araṇinirmanthana*), it does not possess an inseparable connection with that [specific cause], because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Fire is also produced from the striking of stones and so forth. If it is argued that there is no deviation regarding a specific [type of fire], such as that arising from seeds or bulbous roots like the plantain tree (*kadali*), we say no; because such a distinction is impossible to ascertain. No one is able to determine: "Fire born from the friction of fire-sticks is of this kind, fire born from the striking of stones is of that kind, and fire born from a sun-crystal (*sūryakānta*) is of such-and-such a kind. Nor can one postulate that a distinction exists even when it is not perceived, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Alternatively, if it is argued that being an effect is established by way of its inseparable connection with fire, then since the inseparable connection is established even when the state of being an effect of fire is not yet established, there is a circularity (*itaretarāśrayatva*): as long as smoke's status as an effect of fire is not established, its inseparable connection with fire is not established; and as long as its inseparable connection with fire is not established, its status as an effect of fire is not established. Furthermore, inseparable connection is not merely the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), for otherwise it would follow that properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) would lack such a connection. Moreover, the growth and so forth of a certain living being are seen to result from a particular diet, yet a particular diet cannot be inferred from the growth and so forth of another. Whether it be the mother’s milk, rice-gruel, or any specific variety of *kodrava*, meat, bulbs, fruits, and so on—in all cases there is deviation. There is no specific bodily change caused by a specific diet that is free from deviation, because specific qualities such as complexion and beauty are themselves subject to deviation. Therefore, even upon observing a specific effect, there is no inference of a specific diet.
{The Buddhist's doubt}:

Even though a specific type of food is not the cause of a specific type of body, nevertheless— "Whatever is observed through positive and negative concomitance to be the follower of something [is its cause]."
"His own nature is the cause of that; therefore, there is no arising from what is different.
For that which exists without another cannot have that other as its cause. [This refutes that position.]

If food were not the cause, why would it be required by all living beings who seek the growth, maintenance, and so forth of the body? If you argue that while food in general is the cause, it is a specific kind of food that is not the cause, then does the general category [of food] become the cause? In that case, your contradiction with your own established doctrine and logic is unavoidable. Therefore, it is only a specific kind of food that is the cause of bodily growth and so on. Furthermore, a specific medicine or treatment is the cause of the healing of a wound, yet an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of the effect with that specific cause is not grasped; thus, the argument from "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is not non-deviant (*avyabhicāra*).

As for what was said—that the establishment of the causal relation occurs through seeing and not seeing even once, and that its cognition does not arise otherwise because positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) consist in the complete seeing and non-seeing [of the cause and effect]—that is incorrect; for it has already been demonstrated that the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance is possible even without complete seeing and non-seeing. Even if there is an occasional erroneous apprehension in some instances, it does not follow that it is so in all cases; otherwise, if the apprehension of color and other qualities were occasionally erroneous, it would follow that it is erroneous in all cases.
