Furthermore, why would there not be a suspicion of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the causal relation even when it is seen only once? Is it not true that this was already addressed here?
Smoke is the effect of fire because it follows the properties of the effect;
if it were to exist in the absence of that [fire], it would overstep its status as having a cause.
(Even from a single observation, the causal relationship is determined.)

When something is perceived whose characteristic is unperceived, and that [characteristic] is not perceived even when one of its [constituent] parts is absent, then that is the effect of the former; and if it were to exist without its own cause, it would lack causality altogether. Consequently:
"An uncaused thing must either exist eternally or not exist at all, because it does not depend on anything else;
for it is through dependence that the occasional occurrence of entities is possible."

This is not so. For just as the growth of the body and other such effects do not arise without a cause, since they arise from a specific distinct cause of that very nature, so too it is with smoke; thus, the suspicion of another cause remains unrefuted. Furthermore, just as with fire, the determination of grass as a cause is based on its simultaneous presence and absence; yet smoke does not fail to exist in the absence of that [grass], because it arises even from ghee, grain, wood, and so forth. If it is argued that smoke does not exist from fire alone, and that since smoke exists from wood and so forth even in the absence of grass, grass cannot be its cause—then by the same logic, since smoke arises from grass even in the absence of wood and so forth, wood and the like would also not be its causes. If grass, wood, and the rest were not causes, they could not possess the status of being auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) to fire, for it is contradictory for non-causes to function as auxiliaries. And since fire alone is not the cause of smoke, it follows that smoke is indeed causeless. If it is argued that grass is the cause of only a specific kind of smoke, and not of smoke in general—asking whether there is some smoke other than those produced from grass, wood, and so forth, of which fire alone would be the cause—we say no. If you argue that the observed causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is inferred from its effect, we say no, because the causal complex is perceived differently in different cases. The causal complex for smoke in a kitchen (*rasavatī*) is not the same as that in a fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*). Likewise, in one case it is characterized by wood, in another by grass and so forth; similarly, the causal complex for bodily growth and the like must be seen as varying from instance to instance, because the causal complex differs according to variations in place, time, and other factors.

Now, if it is argued that only that specific effect which is ascertained to be pervaded by a specific cause can serve as its logical mark (*liṅga*), then how can such a certainty arise from a single observation alone—that fire is the pervader of smoke *together with all its specific variations*, and not [the pervader] of grass or wood? For even after many observations, some see smoke being produced only by grass and fire, while others see it produced only by wood and fire. So how can there be a certainty that fire alone is the pervader? Furthermore, just as smoke produced by fire accompanied by other auxiliary causes does not cease to be smoke merely because it is not produced by wood, so too smoke produced by wood or grass accompanied by other auxiliary causes will not cease to be smoke merely because it is not produced by fire. Consequently, the following argument is refuted: "If even the head of Śakra (Indra) produces smoke, then it must be fire; if it is not fire, then how can it produce smoke? [Objection: But surely, that specific kind of smoke produced by grass which exists when grass is present certainly does not exist in its absence; thus, there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*). [Response: If that is so, then let the specific smoke produced by fire not deviate from fire, but another specific kind of smoke might well deviate. And if the distinction between these two—smoke that deviates and smoke that does not—is not perceived, then how can fire be inferred from smoke, any more than one infers a specific diet from the nourishment of the body? [Objection: Surely a specific kind of smoke not produced by fire is never observed, just as smoke not produced by grass is never observed. Therefore, due to non-observation, it simply does not exist; so how can there be no non-deviation? [Response: How can one who is not omniscient be certain that it is not observed anywhere? Just as smoke produced from wood and the like—which was unobserved at the time of observing smoke from grass—is later observed, and just as smoke produced from ghee, coconut, grapes, and so forth, is not always observed by some people like the Kirātas yet is not non-existent because it is observed by others elsewhere, so too smoke not produced by fire may be observed by some somewhere, or perhaps by people like us at some time. Thus, smoke does not have the nature of being produced solely by fire. Moreover, since smoke is observed in things like a cowherd’s water-clock (*gopālaghaṭikā*) even long after the fire has ceased, smoke possesses the nature of being produced [by fire] through a causal chain (*pāramparya*); thus, bodies and the like are also produced by fire. Nor is smoke the only thing produced by fire, for ashes and the like are also produced by fire.

Nor is fire itself necessarily of the nature of producing smoke, because even in states such as a red-hot iron ball or charcoal, it is fire despite not producing smoke. Nor is fire necessarily that which produces smoke, for otherwise it would follow that fuel and the like would also be fire. Furthermore, we shall explain later that the relationship of cause and effect cannot be established under the doctrine of momentariness.
[The relationship of pervaded and pervader between smoke and fire.]

Furthermore, is fire known through smoke as something already past, or as simultaneous with it, or as something to be reached (*prāpya*)? If it is known as something already past, then inference is useless, for no purpose whatsoever is accomplished by means of what is past. This would contradict [the principle that] "everyone seeking causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) relies on both valid and invalid means of knowledge," for [such efficacy] does not arise from these two. Thus, there is no contradiction [in our position], and therefore it is not logical for a valid means of knowledge to inform one of something past. By this, the inference of fire simultaneous with the smoke is also refuted, because even fire simultaneous with the smoke, being impermanent, cannot be the object of purposeful action or attainment. According to the doctrine of momentary flux (*kṣaṇabhaṅgavāda*), however, no object simultaneous with its cognition can ever be the object of purposeful action or attainment; thus, all cognition of a present object would result in invalidity. Nor is there a causal relationship between two things existing at the same time, and you certainly do not accept that a sign (*liṅga*) can be something other than an effect. Since that which is to be reached (*prāpya*) is likewise not a cause, it cannot be inferred. If it is argued that the object to be reached is a cause because it belongs to the same class or to the same continuum (*santāna*) as the cause, then it is only a figurative cause (*gauṇaṃ kāraṇam*) and not fit to be inferred; for a work such as a poem or treatise composed by Devadatta does not lead to the inference of his son or grandson.

Furthermore, even ashes are the result of the fire-rite (*agnikārya*), yet they do not lead one to infer the fire that produced them at the same time or by means of reaching it, because of the possibility of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). By this, the following [argument] is also refuted:

"The cognition of a non-existent thing such as color, which depends on the same causal complex (*sāmagrī*), occurs through the inference of the property of the cause, just like the transformation of fuel in smoke."

Just as smoke, produced by fire through the cooperation of the transformation of fuel, inferring such fire, also infers the transformation of the fuel; likewise, taste, produced from color through cooperation, inferring that very taste, also infers color. By this, the inference of rain from the swarming of ants or the agitation of fish is explained; for even there, a certain transformation of the elements is itself the cause of the ants' agitation and so forth, which is the cause of the rain. If that were the case, then rain would have to be simultaneous with the swarming of the ants and so on, because they would depend on the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatvāt*), just like color and taste. Consequently, the rain would be directly perceived, since its mark [the ants] exists at that time and there is no cause for its non-perception. Furthermore, when inferents infer a future rain by means of the mark of the ants' swarming, it is illogical for those two to depend on the same causal complex. Nor does dependence on the same causal complex entail either invariable concomitance (*avyabhicāra*) or a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), because it would follow that twins, who also depend on the same causal complex, would likewise possess such a relationship. Moreover, by the rising of the sun, one infers the future setting—which is not its cause and is not identical to it. Likewise, the daily increase of the moon during the bright fortnight and its decrease during the dark fortnight; or the destruction of bodies and jars, which is termed "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) or defined as the production of a dissimilar moment. Those skilled in omens (*ariṣṭa*) also infer death by calculating the duration of time. And those learned in astrology infer an eclipse of the moon or other phenomena upon seeing a certain sign. Such inference does not deviate even in the absence of a necessary connection based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). If one suspects it might sometimes deviate, then there would be a lack of confidence (*anāśvāsa*) everywhere. Furthermore, there can be neither identity between the accomplished and the unaccomplished, nor can the unaccomplished arise from the accomplished. Thus, the future cannot be included within the categories of "essential nature" (*svabhāva*) or "effect" (*kārya*). For one who asserts that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding a future object, there is a contradiction with these very inferences.

Furthermore, why would the activity of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*)—aimed at the attainment of what is desired and the avoidance of what is undesired—not occur? For if there were no certainty regarding the inevitable occurrence of results such as *dharma* and so forth, it would not be reasonable to abandon established wealth, wives, and other objects for their sake. Indeed, if they were abandoned, there would be no distinction between them and those who lack discernment. Another, however, says: "That which pervades another object is the cause (*kāraṇa*), and that which is pervaded is the effect (*kārya*). Therefore, between two things that stand in a mutual relationship of pervader and pervaded—whether existing at the same time or at different times—there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect. But where there is an asymmetrical pervasion, as in the case of fire and smoke, there is no relationship of cause and effect either; because only that which is mutually pervaded is the effect. This is not correct, because it is merely your own technical convention. For nowhere in the world or in the treatises is the causality of anything—whether coexistent or future—established by mere pervasion alone. What then? That which generates something is its cause. And there is no mutual relationship of producer and produced; for since both would be unestablished relative to one another (*itaretarāsiddhatva*), it would follow that neither could arise. If even an unestablished thing were a generator, then a thing would also be the generator of itself, since there is no difference in its pervasiveness. Therefore, when something arises immediately after the operation of another, the latter is the cause of the former.

As for what was said—"The conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that arise in one who has been asleep for a long time and has just awakened would not be produced from previous habituation, because they lack immediate succession"—we shall explain in that regard that their production occurs from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) assisted by resolution (*praṇidhāna*) and other factors. Let this fault belong to you, since you do not admit even a stable [entity] such as a latent impression. [This concludes Prajñākara’s account of the causal relationship.]

As for this further point: "The operation (*vyāpāra*) and the arising (*utpāda*) are not other than the essential nature (*svarūpa*); therefore, it follows that [the effect] is from the essential nature itself"—this is not so, because it is a different argument (*vādāntara*). There is indeed this common understanding among worldly people and investigators: "This is excluded from that," and "This has arisen from that. Now, whether that operation and that arising are distinct entities (*arthāntara*) or non-distinct, this is a different argument. [Objection: If causality were based on immediate succession (*anantarabhāvitva*), then everything in the three worlds that occurs immediately after would be a cause. Furthermore, there is no relationship (*sambandha*) that acts as a regulator, because they exist at different times. Indeed, at the time of the cause, the effect does not exist in its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); nor, at the time of the effect, does the preceding cause exist in its own nature. Only the state of being inseparable (*avinābhāvitva*) exists even in the case of what is yet to be. If you say that only that which is seen or has occurred is a cause by virtue of pervading [the effect], and not that which is yet to be—here it is replied: *(Note: The provided text ends abruptly here.)*

The pervasiveness of that which is perceived is cognized by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*); this same [pervasiveness] would also belong to a future entity by way of its superimposed form (*āropita-rūpa*).

For that which is being seen is not pervasive merely by that much, because at that time the pervaded (*vyāpya*) has not yet been cognized. And when there is the cognition of the pervaded, then [the pervader] is pervasive by way of the form it will have in the future; otherwise, if its future nature were not grasped, there could be no pervasiveness. Now, if it is argued that pervasiveness is cognized by the very same nature by which it was seen, and not by way of its future form—that is incorrect; for: *(Note: The following verse is implied by the commentary but not explicitly provided in the source text.)* The pervasion of the fire is established by the smoke, even though the fire is not present at that time. If the pervasion were not established by way of the future nature, then the cognition of pervasion would be impossible. Therefore, the pervasion of the effect is indeed established by way of its future nature. Thus, the argument is refuted.
If the future form is not perceived, pervasiveness is not perceived; for pervasion that is merely partial is not true pervasion—it would be non-pervasion. (208)

For a cause is recognized as such precisely by its pervasion across the past and future times, and not otherwise. And that pervasion is the same for what has been seen and for what is yet to be seen. [Objection: How can there be causality in what is yet to be seen? For even what has been seen is non-existent at that [future] time. [Response: How so? It is the same [for both]. [Objection: Because of its existence [at the time of its own occurrence]. [Response: Then that [existence] belongs to what is yet to be seen as well. [Objection: In that case, it is not [a cause]. [Response: This too is the same. [Objection: It is because of its priority. [Response: What difference is there in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) between the prior and the posterior? Since both are apprehended through an imputed form (*āropitākāra*) and not through any other, there is no distinction. Furthermore, if one is imputed as having a prior form because it was seen, and the other is imputed as having a posterior form because it is yet to be seen, then by that reasoning, neither of the two possesses causality.
The mutual inseparability (*avinābhāva*) of those two is equal for both;
however, what use have we for any further internal subdivision therein?

(209) That without which something else does not occur is the cause of that [latter]. Just as the effect does not occur without the prior existence of the cause, so too the cause does not exist without the subsequent existence of the necessarily occurring effect; thus, the basis for the relationship between cause and effect is the same.
Because the characteristic mark (*nimitta*) is the same for both, there is a relationship of cause and effect between the two;
this is because the inference of a future life (*paraloka*) is established through pervasion (*vyāpitva*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).

Indeed, we do not perceive any other basis in this world apart from pervasion and negative concomitance. And that [basis] exists for the effect as surely as it does for the cause; therefore, there is a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the two.
{The refutation thereof}

This is merely the activity of great delusion increased by the study of false treatises. For no one of sound intellect—who has not lost their sense—conceives that a son is produced by parents who are either yet to come into being or already destroyed. Nor does one consider other contemporaneous factors to be the cause in the same way as the parents, simply because the relationship between the producer and the produced is perceived along with that son. Since the perception of this relationship is no less free from contradiction than the perception of the parents themselves, it cannot be an error. Now, is this relationship a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) or not a distinct entity? This is another debate. At any rate, you yourself accept the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). And that [relation] is established through worldly convention (*vyavahāra*), not by mere technical terminology. Furthermore, those engaged in worldly practice recognize that only what is presently existing can be a cause; for those seeking a result do not employ causes when they have not yet arisen or when they have already perished, thinking that the result will not be produced. If past and future things were to produce an effect, why would those seeking a result strive to bring the causes into the present? Therefore, only present causes produce an effect. Causes certainly exist at the very moment the effect is being produced; as for whether they continue to exist at the time the effect has already arisen, let it be so or not. Since the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is not proven, there is no contradiction in the persistence of the cause even at the time of the effect.
The fault in [asserting] that what is not present can be a cause.

Furthermore, if that which is future were a cause, there would be the undesirable consequence of the effect being produced from it at all times, because its nature would remain unchanged throughout. Likewise, if even that which has perished were a producer, there would be the consequence of the effect being produced from it at all times after its destruction, since its nature remains unchanged. Moreover, it possesses efficacy precisely by virtue of that [future or past] nature, and for that which is efficacious, delay is impossible. If it is argued that its status as a producer depends upon the requirement of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), this is not so; for the past and the future cannot be assisted, and thus auxiliary causes would be useless. If they were indeed assistable, then because the assistance is non-different from the thing assisted, those two (the past and future) would result in being present, due to their production from the auxiliaries. Furthermore, since you accept that a real entity is defined by causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), the past and future would exist by virtue of being producers. And if they exist, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) follows. Consequently, they would exist for only a single moment, and yet be past or future, just like the present, because of their momentariness. Moreover, having produced the effect in its future state, it would produce it again in its present state; thus, a single entity would be both object and agent. This would entail the acceptance of non-momentariness, for the very fact of a single entity being both object and agent constitutes non-momentariness.

As for what was stated—that a cause is perceived only as pervading both past and future time, and not otherwise—that is not so; for no one perceives a cause in such a manner. Furthermore, it has been argued that this would lead to the absurd consequence that even the self (*svātman*) would be a cause. Moreover, Kīrti says that the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is not established without the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*); you, however, have imagined the reverse. Thus, if the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) were first perceived, then the cognition of invariable concomitance would not be based on the cognition of the causal relation. On the other hand, if the invariable concomitance is not perceived at the outset, then the pervasiveness and its exclusion cannot serve as the grounds for establishing causality.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "a cause cannot exist without the other-nature (*parabhāva*) of its effect," that is incorrect. Even when the effect, which is a distinct entity, has not yet arisen, how could the cause—which has already arisen—not exist without it? For it is not logical that something which, while arising, does not depend upon the existence of another thing, should be considered the cause of that thing. Indeed, fire is not a cause merely by virtue of being pervasive or merely by its prior existence; rather, even when other causes are present, one perceives the efficacy of fire in that smoke does not arise there as long as fire is absent. And such efficacy is not perceived in the case of a future [cause]. If it were merely by being pervasive, even a tree would be the cause of a *śiṃśapā* tree. Therefore, the qualification "provided it is distinct" need not be made. Let that which is pervasive even of itself be simply the cause. If you argue that the cause of itself is not accepted because it is not established among common people or investigators, then the future and so forth should likewise not be accepted as causes, for there is no established recognition of causality even in those cases. Therefore, the future is not a cause; thus, the inference of the future world and so forth is included within the category of inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*).
Even in the absence of identity, there exists the relationship between the signifier and the signified.

Nor is there identity (*tādātmya*) between "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*) and "śiṃśapā-ness" (*śiṃśapātvādi*), according to the reasoning already stated. And yet, there exists the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamya-gamakabhāva*). Furthermore, the relationship of signifier and signified pertains to two universals (*sāmānya*), and there is no identity between them; for if there were identity, the ascertainment of "śiṃśapā-ness," "produced-ness" (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth, would itself be the ascertainment of "tree-ness," "impermanence" (*anityatva*), and so forth. Indeed, identity is not logical for two things that have distinct fortunes (*yogakṣema*). Moreover, even if there were identity in a real entity (*vastu*), it could not be the object of inference, because the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the mark (*liṅga*) and the marked (*liṅgin*) are impossible therein. Or, if they were possible, the ascertainment of the mark would be the very same as the ascertainment of the marked, since their objects would be non-different. And by whatever mode [one argues] there is a difference of objects, by that same mode there is no identity either, and thus there would be no inference.

Furthermore, since there is no difference in the identity (*tādātmya*) between a tree and a *śiṃśapā*, the relationship of the signifier and the signified (*gamyagamakabhāva*) would exist even in the reverse case. For identity is not partial. If it is argued that even though identity is undifferentiated, only the pervading part (*vyāpakāṃśa*) is the object of cognition (*gamya*), while only the pervaded part (*vyāpyāṃśa*) is the signifier (*gamaka*), we say no; for a single entity is partless, and if it were to have parts, there would be a contradiction with its being a single identity. That one thing must be either the pervader or the pervaded. By this, the restriction is refuted that the state of being a specific tree, the nature of being a tree, or the necessary concomitance with that alone belongs to the *śiṃśapā*, whereas the state of being a specific tree, the nature of being a tree, or the necessary concomitance with that alone does not belong to the tree. If it is argued that "the tree deviates [from the *śiṃśapā*], but the *śiṃśapā* does not," then if there is deviation even when identity exists, what hope is there that the *śiṃśapā* will not deviate? If you say the tree deviates because there exists a tree whose nature is not that of a *śiṃśapā*, do you have the vision of every single instance [to prove] that there is no *śiṃśapā* whose nature is not a tree? For that too might be suspected of having both natures, just like the tree. Just as in a certain place only blue lotuses exist, and therefore those born in that place establish that the lotus has the nature of blue simply because they see no other kind of lotus—yet it is not necessarily so. Therefore, the statement "either from the relation of cause and effect or from essential nature" (*kāryakāraṇabhāvād vā svabhāvād vā*) is indeed incorrect. Likewise, the statement "otherwise, by the exclusion of one"—and so forth—is also not correct; for upon the exclusion of the pervader, the pervaded is excluded, and through the presence of the pervaded, the presence of the pervader occurs. Yet, there is no relation of pervader and pervaded among cows, horses, and the like. If it is argued that, as in the case of cows and horses, if there is difference (*bheda*), the relation of pervader and pervaded does not obtain for any of them, then even if identity exists, it would not obtain anywhere, just as in the case of "blue lotus-ness" and the like. Furthermore, if there were difference, as in the case of cows and horses, the causal relation between fire and smoke and so forth would also not exist. Even though there is no difference in their being distinct entities (*arthāntaratva*), some things are restricted by their own nature such that only a certain thing is the pervader of another, and not everything of everything. Enough of this digression. Thus it is established that the mention of "positive and negative concomitance" (*anvayavyatireka*) and so forth is for the purpose of refuting the threefold classification intended by others, and not for the purpose of refuting the distinctions of cause and effect and so forth.
Doubts regarding the inference of an effect from a cause, and their refutation.

But how, then, is the effect inferred from the cause? For causes do not necessarily possess their effects, since obstacles or deficiencies may arise in the interval. Nor can there be inference even at the time of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because the effect is produced immediately after the perception of the mark (*liṅga*); thus, at that moment, the effect would simply be perceptible. Furthermore, it is impossible to ascertain a cause as being distinguished by a non-obstructed causal complex, and an unascertained mark cannot be a constituent of proof. To this it is replied: As for the claim that "causes do not necessarily possess their effects," that is not so; for some causes necessarily possess their effects. Indeed, we do not say that all causes are indicators of their effects. Rather, when a cause, in its specific state, does not deviate from a particular effect, then by that very cause in that specific state, that effect is inferred. For example, those who know the specific characteristics of clouds infer rain from a cloud characterized by such features. Nor does the deviation of an unqualified [cause] imply the deviation of a qualified one, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, through repeated practice, interest, and conviction, there is an inference of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the effect of those [states]; or, when the life-span is determined by that impression, future memory is inferred. Likewise, the production of demerit (*adharma*) occurs through acts such as violence, and the production of suffering in another occurs through specific acts such as burning or cutting their body; in these and other cases, the inference of the effect from the cause should be understood accordingly. As for what was further said—

"When the production of an effect is inferred from a complete set of causes, that [inference] is described as being based on essential nature (svabhāva), because it does not depend on any other factor."

That is spoken out of delusion; for the production of an effect is a property of the effect—how could that be the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the cause? Indeed, identity (*tādātmya*) between cause and effect is not logical; rather, the capacity to produce an effect is inferred even from an incomplete cause. If it is argued that the non-deviation (*avyabhicāritā*) from the effect belongs only to a complete [cause], then that [capacity] necessarily leads to the inference of the effect as well; thus, the inference of the effect by means of the cause is established. For example, there is the inference of past rain and so forth by means of the effect consisting of a river’s flood, and the inference of future rain by means of specific signs such as the movement of ants carrying their eggs; such are the various types of inference based on cause and effect.

{An alternative explanation of the sūtra’s term *pūrvavat*:} Alternatively, *pūrvavat* refers to an inference of something occurring at a later time based on what was previously established, even if there is no causal relationship. An inference based on the opposite of that is called *śeṣavat*. In this case, "the common" (*sāmānya*) refers to the single time [of both the sign and the signified]; that which is perceived through that is *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*, meaning it is perceived as being simultaneous with the mark (*liṅga*). According to this view, the inference of rain from ants [moving up their mounds] is indeed *pūrvavat*; however, the examples of *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* are the inference of taste from form, or the inference of impermanence from the fact of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), and so forth.

Alternatively, "pūrvavat" (the "as-before") is that which possesses an object of inference already previously established; for example, the inference that rain has occurred based on seeing a river in flood. The inference of rain from ants [carrying their eggs] is "śeṣavat" (the "as-the-rest"). "Sāmānyatodṛṣṭa" (the "as-generally-observed") is precisely that same type. It has been explained that the distinctions such as "kevalānvayi" (purely positive) are also meanings included within "pūrvavat" and the others. Now, this [classification] is presented in order to reveal the essential nature of these through definitions and examples. {The Determination of the Five Forms}

In that regard, the [reason] possessing five forms is the "positive-negative" (*anvayavyatirekī*). Its five forms are: (1) presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), (2) existence in the similar class (*sapakṣe sattva*), (3) exclusion from the dissimilar class (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*), (4) having a non-sublated object (*abādhitaviṣayatva*), and (5) having no counter-argument (*asatpratipakṣatva*). Among these, the subject (*pakṣa*) is the locus qualified by the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*). The reason’s presence in that [subject] as a pervading occurrence is "presence in the subject. That is to say, it exists pervasively in that subject and not merely in one part of the subject; this means it is a pervading occurrence, i.e., it pervades the entire similar class (*sapakṣa*). The similar class (*sapakṣa*) is the locus possessing a property identical to the property to be proven. The existence of the reason in all or in some part of that similar class is "existence in the similar class. The dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*) is the locus possessing a property excluded from the property to be proven. The non-occurrence of the reason in every instance of that dissimilar class is "exclusion from the dissimilar class. The reason’s occurrence in the meaning of the proposition when it is not contradicted by valid cognition is "having a non-sublated object. The reason’s lack of the three forms [of a valid reason] regarding both the property to be proven and its opposite is "having no counter-argument. That [positive-negative reason] is of two kinds. This positive-negative reason is of two types based on the distinction of whether it occurs throughout the similar class or in only a part of it. For example: "Sound is impermanent because it is a product"—this is a pervader of the similar class. "Because, while possessing generality, it is perceptible by the external senses of people like us"—this occurs in only a part of the similar class. The "purely positive" (*kevalānvayī*) reason is that which pervades the subject, occurs in the similar class, and for which no dissimilar class exists. It is of two kinds, as before, meaning it is of two types based on the distinction of whether it occurs throughout the similar class or in only a part of it, just like the positive-negative reason. For example: "The unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are perceptible to someone because they are knowable (*prameyatva*), like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of the hand"—this is a reason that pervades the similar class. Regarding that same proposition, for the Mīmāṃsakas [who hold that such things are not perceptible], the reason "because they are not perceptible to us, like our own pleasure and so forth" is a reason that occurs in only a part of the similar class.
{The doubt regarding the purely positive inference}

But surely, in the absence of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there could be no inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) for this [reason]. For "not existing without that" is precisely what constitutes negative concomitance. The counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is indeed the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*); therein, the non-existence of the probans (*sādhana*) must necessarily be demonstrated, otherwise there would be the fallacy of the "doubtful inconclusive" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*). Now, since things such as a sky-flower, which are the absence of the probandum, lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it is untenable for them to function as a locus (*adhikaraṇa*), an ablative (*apādāna*), or the like. Therefore, the probans cannot exist there, nor can it be excluded from there. If you then ask, "In that case, should there be presence [of the probans]?"—if you say "No," then [we reply]: No; in that case, should one remain mute? Thus he says:
If there is no activity of the reason with respect to that [object], why is its cessation desired?
Furthermore, this cessation is not a negation; why then is it being negated?
Apart from affirmation and negation, there is no other verbal usage; and since that [usage] does not exist regarding non-existent things, it follows that one must remain silent in this matter.
"There is no negation of existing things, nor does it exist in non-existent things.
By this principle, the meaning of the negative particle has vanished from the world.
Therefore, in the case of a dissimilar example (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta), a substratum is not necessarily required here."
"And because that [reason] is understood even from the statement 'in its absence,
that [property] is not,' there is no purely positive reason.
This is the resolution of that [objection].

This is incorrect. As for the claim that there could be no "inseparable connection" (*avinābhāva*) in the absence of "negative concomitance" (*vyatireka*), that is not so; for inseparable connection is defined as the relationship between the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). And this exists even in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*). If one were to negate a meaning merely because a certain etymological derivation is impossible, it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); for instance, because the etymology "that which has gone toward the sense-organ" (*pratigatam akṣam*) is impossible, the three types of perception such as mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) would not be considered "perception," and a cow that does not move would not be a "cow. Therefore, the inseparable connection is said to be the pervasion of the means of proof by the object to be proven, established solely on the basis of the definition; and that certainly exists here as well.

As for what was said—that the absence of the reason (*hetu*) when the probandum (*sādhya*) is absent is indeed the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), and that if this is not demonstrated, there is the fallacy of the "inconclusive due to doubt" (*sandigdhānaikāntika*)—that too is incorrect. For if a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) existed, one might indeed have the suspicion: "Does the reason exist there, or does it not? But here no counter-example exists, because it is accepted that everything, whether in the form of existence or non-existence, is perceptible. Furthermore, if things such as a sky-flower were perceived either as having the nature of existence or the nature of non-existence, they would simply be objects of proof (*sādhya*); if, however, they are not perceived at all, how can their status as a counter-example—the absence of the probandum—be established? Nor is it logical for something lacking valid cognition to function as a counter-example. Furthermore, in such a case, one does not even consider whether the reason exists or does not exist. Indeed, wise people do not take the trouble to deliberate on whether a reason exists or not when a herd of elephants is situated on the tip of a fingernail. If, on the other hand, the designation "negative concomitance" is applied to the fact that the reason does not exist in unproven things like sky-flowers, let it be so; yet, by means of such a negative concomitance, this [reason] is called "purely positive" (*kevalānvayin*) precisely because it lacks exclusion from a counter-example characterized as previously described. Moreover, the inclusion of the "subject" (*dharmin*) in the definition of a counter-example is intended to exclude that which is merely imagined; for in the world, an object supported by valid cognition is well-known as being either a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) or a counter-instance (*vipakṣa*). Therefore, that [reason] for which there is an absence of a counter-example defined as above is "purely positive."

If there is cessation [of the entity] after that moment, then the aforementioned undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) applies to your own system: if the entity ceases after a moment, its identity with itself is contradicted; if it does not cease, its momentariness is contradicted; and if neither is accepted, then the refutation beginning with "affirmation and negation" (*vidhānaṃ pratiṣedhaṃ ca*) applies. Furthermore, the very meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) has perished for you, since you do not accept the non-existence of an existing thing. Moreover, for a reason whose capacity to convey knowledge rests on the strength of its negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), a dissimilar instance (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) must necessarily be resorted to; otherwise, the negative concomitance would not be understood through mere words. Or, if it were understood, then one need not even resort to a similar instance (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), because the understanding of it would arise from the statement alone that "when this exists, that exists. Therefore, since there is no dissimilar instance supported by valid means of cognition, a purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) reason is neither a negative reason nor a non-reason; for, while pervading the subject (*pakṣa*), it possesses an uncontradicted object and lacks a counter-argument, and thus exists in the similar instances (*sapakṣa*), just like a reason that is both positive and negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*).
An Examination of the Exclusively Negative Reason (*kevalavyatirekihetau*)

A purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is one that lacks a similar instance (sapakṣa), pervades the subject (pakṣa), and is excluded from the dissimilar instances (vipakṣa). For example: "Every effect is preceded by an omniscient creator, because it is occasional; for whatever is not preceded by an omniscient creator is not occasional, as in the case of space and so forth. Likewise: "The living body possesses a self, because it possesses breath and so forth; for whatever does not possess a self does not possess breath and so forth, as in the case of a clod of earth. Or it is employed by way of a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga): "This living body is not devoid of a self, because it would follow that it lacks breath and so forth, like a clod of earth."
The Buddhist objection regarding the negation of selflessness in a living body.

But surely, a property observed in the subject of the example (*dṛṣṭāntadharmī*) is either affirmed or denied in the subject of the thesis (*sādhyadharmī*) by means of a reason (*hetu*) that pervades it. Now, the self (*ātman*) has never been observed anywhere as being the pervader of breath and so forth (*prāṇādi*). So how can the self be established in living bodies based on the perception of breath and so forth, or how can the absence of breath and so forth in jars and the like follow from its absence? If you argue that the absence of self (*nairātmya*) is seen in jars and the like as being pervaded by the absence of breath and so forth, and therefore the absence of self follows from the removal of the absence of breath in living bodies—this is not so. Since non-existence cannot be established through the non-perception of the unobservable, the absence of self in jars and the like remains unestablished. If you claim this is established through the opponent’s own admission, then how can the self be established for the opponent, since it too lacks any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)? And how then is the absence of self established? If its establishment were based merely on an admission, then the self would be understood as something based on scripture (*āgamika*), not as something inferable (*ānumeya*). Therefore, since the absence of the self is not established even when it is not perceived, and since the connection (*pratibandha*) of breath and so forth with it is unestablished, the cessation of breath and so forth is not established solely upon the cessation of the self; thus, [the reason] is not a prover (*agamaka*).
The resolution of certain [objections] and their refutation.

Regarding this, some offer the following rebuttal: "In the case of jars and the like, what is intended by *nairātmya* (absence of self) here is merely the lack of a connection with a self, not the total absence of a self. Since the self is eternal and all-pervasive, its existence is established there [in jars] by means of desire and so forth; rather, in the living body, a specific kind of connection capable of producing breath and other functions is being proven. The meaning of the statement ‘it is not soulless’ (*na nirātmakam*) is not that it lacks a mere connection, for that would entail the absurd consequence of being devoid of breath and the like, just like jars. Furthermore, in jars and such, the state of being soulless is already certain precisely because breath and the like do not arise. However, they should be asked this: Does the non-arising of breath and the like indicate the soullessness of jars and such through the power of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), or through the power of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)? What follows from this? If it were through positive concomitance, then soullessness would apply everywhere, because—just as in the case of a specific connection with a self—the connection is not observed anywhere else, and thus no positive concomitance is established. There would be an infinite regress due to having to rely solely on inference. Moreover, since there is no example of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), soullessness cannot be established even through negative concomitance. If the living body itself is taken as the example, then there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If it is argued: "By the non-production of effects such as breath, the absence of a cause capable of producing them is inferred—just as the absence of a specific connection with an axe and wood entails the non-production of cuts and the like—and therefore there is no fault of mutual dependence," then we reply: In that case, by the production of effects such as breath, a cause capable of producing them would be inferred through positive concomitance alone—just as a specific connection with an axe and wood is inferred when cuts and the like are produced. Thus, the argument based on negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) would be redundant.
The resolution according to [the author's] own view.

To this it is replied: It has been stated that “an example (dṛṣṭānta) is that object regarding which there is a consensus of understanding among ordinary people and experts. Now, regarding the matter of selflessness (nairātmya) and the lack of vital breath and so forth in jars and the like, there is indeed agreement between you and us. So why is this not an example? Why? Because [it is known] through a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). What is the use of this inquiry? Let it be from scripture or from something else. For even by means of inquiry, agreement must be established; if that [agreement] is already established even without that [inquiry], what is the use of inquiry? For if one were to inquire into what is already agreed upon, there would be an infinite regress (anavasthā). Furthermore, if the cognition of selflessness in jars and the like were false, then let the state of having a self (sātmakatva) be correct. But that too is undesirable.
The distinction that the vital breaths and so forth exist in a living body but do not exist elsewhere is nothing other than the doctrine of a self (ātman).

If there were either the state of having a self (*sātmakatva*) or the state of being without a self (*anātmakatva*) in both cases [the living body and the jar], then what would cause this distinction—that the occurrence of breath and so forth exists in one but not in the other? If you say it is due to its very nature (*svabhāva*), we say no; for that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that existence or non-existence must be eternal, and so on. If you say it is caused by the presence or absence of consciousness (*buddhi*), we say no; because breath, exhalation, opening and closing of the eyes, life, movement of the mind, modifications of the other senses, consciousness, pleasure, pain, and so forth, are all designated by the term "breath and so forth" (*prāṇādi*). If you say that since the omnipresent self (*vibhu*) exists everywhere, it would follow that even jars and the like possess a self, we say no; because "having a self" is defined specifically as being presided over by a self, and that [presiding] is established precisely through the fact that breath and so forth would otherwise be impossible. If you ask what causes the distinction between having a self and not having one, it is caused by a specific unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*). That specific force, in turn, is caused by the specific breath and so forth produced in a previous birth. That too was produced in a previous birth; thus, the solution is that the series is beginningless (*anāditva*). Furthermore, without a specific unseen force, the distinction whereby some whose breath has ceased are reborn, while others who have been born experience the cessation of breath after two days, half a month, a year, or other durations, would not be possible. This is because no such distinction is perceived among the causal factors, such as the parents. It might be argued: "Consciousness itself, regulated by a specific prior unseen force, arises only in certain places. As long as it persists, breath and so forth arise and endure accordingly. What need is there here to postulate a self, when the power of the unseen force alone suffices? This is not so; for since consciousness is perishable, we shall explain later that it cannot be a traveler to the next world nor a connector of past experiences. Therefore, that which travels to the next world and connects past experiences is the self. It is only when the body is presided over by that [self] that breath occurs, and not otherwise. And thus, the existence of things like sky-flowers is not established [by this argument]; for even regarding the production of breath from sky-flowers, the capacity [of the self] is not proven by a counter-argument, and if it were proven, that very thing is the self—so there is no dispute.

{The suspicion of positive concomitance and its refutation} Now, one might object: "In that case, the cause is inferred from its effects such as the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and since it is observed that effects such as pots possess causes, there is indeed positive concomitance (*anvaya*); so how can this be a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*)? No; because there is no positive concomitance with the specific probandum (*sādhya*). For the cause of the vital breaths and so forth possesses attributes such as eternity, and no positive concomitance is established anywhere for that which is not of the same nature as the probandum. {By the mere establishment of a general [concomitance], the specific [probandum] is not established here}.

When the general property (*sāmānya*) is established, by the force of the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the conclusion established by the context), only a specific relation such as spatial connection is established, but not specific qualities such as eternity, because the probans lacks the capacity for that. If it is argued that once the mere general property is established, the intended specific quality is established through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), what is this elimination? "Elimination is the cognition of the remaining [alternative] when all applicable [alternatives] have been negated and no other possibility remains. From where does the cognition of the remaining [alternative] arise? The reasons for the negation of the applicable [alternatives] have fulfilled their purpose simply by establishing the things to be negated. However, the primary reason (*maula-hetu*), aided by those [negations],—not requiring a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) with such a probandum—becomes a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) while establishing that specific quality.
The reasons that establish the pervasion of the fundamental reason.

The other reasons serve to establish the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of that [probans] with its own probandum (*sādhya*). To explain: by the fact of being an effect (*kāryatva*), which proves the mere existence of a cause, the causelessness of breath and so forth is refuted. By the principle that "unseen impressions (*adṛṣṭasaṃskāra*) produced by one [agent] do not bear fruit for another," the fact of having a cause distinct from the body and so forth is refuted. By the principle of "the connection with memory practiced in a previous life" (*pūrvābhyastasmṛtyanubandhatva*), etc., the fact of having a cause produced by effort (*kṛtaka*) is refuted. Thus, through these reasons which refute opposing positions, the pervasion of breath and so forth with the specific probandum is established in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself, according to the maxim of "not seeing a crow on the riverbank. If it is argued, "Let this be the case; nevertheless, since there is no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) of this [probans] elsewhere than in the subject, it has been stated to be a negative-only (*vyatirekin*) reason," we reply: even if that were granted, a negative-only reason cannot be a valid reason merely by the non-observation of the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because it would then follow that [the name] "Ḍittha" and so forth could also be established as a reason. Furthermore, in the absence of an omniscient creator, the very nature of being an effect would be impossible. For we shall explain later that the insentient does not function without being presided over by a sentient being. Even where a potter or similar agent exists as a presider, he alone is not the sole agent, because he lacks the capacity to preside over causes such as the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*); nor does the unseen merit/demerit and so forth function without being presided over by him, and a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) lacking that [presiding agent] is incapable of producing an effect. Indeed, an effect is never produced when even a single causal factor fails to function. Therefore, just as a staff and other tools presided over by a potter operate toward the production of a jar, so too do the unseen merit/demerit and so forth presided over by an omniscient being. Thus, like the potter, the Omniscient Being is the agent even in the case of jars and the like; hence, it is established that every effect is preceded by an omniscient creator. In this same manner, other negative-only reasons are also to be supported.
Commentary on the Sūtra on the Characteristics of Causes.

"The reason (*hetu*) is that which establishes the probandum (*sādhya*) through similarity with the example (*udāharaṇa-sādharmya*), and likewise through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This is the aphorism defining the reason. Here, by the word "example," the instance based on similarity (*sādharmya-dṛṣṭānta*) is meant; "similarity" is understood from the context as being with the probandum. In this way, there is the exclusion of the contradictory (*viruddha*), the common (*sādhāraṇa*), and the unestablished (*asiddha*) types of reasons. By relying on the restrictive particle "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "by the example alone," the inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reason is also excluded. To exclude the partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*), one should state "similarity with the probandum alone. Regarding this, Tāmariri says: "In this way, the two types of positive reasons (*anvayin*)—those with two characteristics and those with three—are obtained"; but this is not so, because it would follow that the mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and the counter-balanced (*prakaraṇasama*) would also be considered reasons. If it is argued that the term "establishing the probandum" (*sādhyasādhana*) is included to exclude those, then let there simply be the inclusion of "establishing the probandum," for by that alone the exclusion of all fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) is established, since they lack the quality of establishing the probandum. True, this is so; nevertheless, the words beginning with "example" were composed for the purpose of providing specific definitions. "Through similarity" (*sādharmyāt*) is the definition of the positive (*vīta*) reason, and "through dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyāt*) is the definition of the negative (*avīta*). Thus, the reason is of only two kinds: for the positive reason, the definition is the establishment of the object by its own nature, while for the negative, it is by the negation of the opponent's position. Alternatively, "through similarity" refers to the positive (*anvayin*), "through dissimilarity" to the negative (*vyatirekin*), and the combination of both to the positive-negative (*anvaya-vyatirekin*). Likewise, "through dissimilarity" means the reason is that which establishes the probandum through dissimilarity with the example; here, the "example" is the instance based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). With respect to the definition of the reason as an objective entity (*arthātmaka-hetu*), the words "similarity" and "dissimilarity" should be seen in the nominative case. However, with respect to the reason as a verbal expression (*vacanātmaka*), they are put in the ablative case, because the definition is primarily given in the context of the members of the syllogism (*avayava*). If it is argued that what is being spoken of should be the object (*karman*) and thus the genitive case is appropriate, we say no; for what is intended is the sense of being a cause (*nimittatva*). When the object exists, its perception occurs, and from that, the production of the word follows according to the speaker's intention. When the aphorism concerning the "preceding" (*pūrvavat*) and so forth is for the purpose of defining the positive and other types of reasons, then this [present] definition should be seen as a restatement (*anuvāda*) for the purpose of defining the members of the syllogism. But when that aphorism serves another purpose, then the definition of the positive and other types is prescribed here as a secondary consequence (*anuṣaṅga*). One must supply the words "that statement which [arises] from similarity with the example," or the term "statement" (*vacana*) is governed from the preceding aphorism on the proposition (*pratijñā*). Or, the inclusion of the word "statement" in the definition of the conclusion (*nigamana*) should be seen as applying everywhere. If it is argued that since the word "means of proof" (*sādhana*) denotes the logical mark (*liṅga*), the ablative case would follow just as it does for the words "similarity" and so forth, we say no; for the sense of denoting the statement is also intended. It is not merely a statement produced from similarity with the example that is the reason; rather, the meaning is that it is that which establishes the probandum and makes known its status as a means of proof. This has been explained further below.

{The Examination of Fallacious Reasons (Hetvābhāsa)} By this, it is stated that fallacious reasons lack the status of being valid reasons. Fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are those which, though appearing like valid reasons, are devoid of the defining characteristics of a reason. The *Sūtra* states: "Fallacious reasons are the erratic (*savyabhicāra*), the contradictory (*viruddha*), the equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*), the identical with the probandum (*sādhyasama*), and the mistimed (*atītakāla*). For the sake of summarizing its meaning, the statement "unestablished (*asiddha*), contradictory (*viruddha*), inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), unascertained (*anadhyavasita*), mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), and equal to the point at issue (*prakaraṇasama*)" has been arranged differently for the purpose of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). For if they were all presented in that [original] order, the listener would be considered a mere follower of Vedic style (*chāndasa*). {1. The Unestablished (Asiddha)}

"In this context, 'unestablished' (*asiddha*) refers to that reason whose presence in the subject (*pakṣavṛtti*) is uncertain. Uncertain means either doubtful, contested, or determined to be non-existent. That reason for which such a presence in the subject exists is described as such. Regarding the aphorism: "That which is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhya*) is 'equal to the probandum' (*sādhyasama*) because it is itself something to be proved," the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of being "not distinct from the probandum"—namely, the state of not being an object of established consensus—is too broad (*vyāpaka*). Alternatively, the phrase "because it is something to be proved" (*sādhyatvāt*) may be a mistaken reading of the definition for the internally unestablished (*antarāsiddha*), or it may be redundant due to [the inclusion of other types of] establishment.
{2. Contradictory (*viruddha*):}

A contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is that which exists only in the similar class (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar class (*vipakṣa*). The aphorism states: "Having accepted a tenet (*siddhānta*), that which contradicts it is contradictory. The meaning is that the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is characterized by the acceptance of a tenet; having accepted that [tenet], a reason whose nature is to contradict it—that is, one which pervades its opposite—is contradictory. How can a non-conscious reason accept anything? This is done figuratively (*upacāra*): it is figuratively said that the reason accepts what is accepted by its employer, or what is accepted by the reason itself through the power of that [employer]. And the purpose of this figurative usage is the exclusion of the "contradictory to a specific qualification" (*viśeṣaviruddha*).

{3. Anaikāntikaḥ} "The [reason] that occurs in all three positions is the inconclusive (anaikāntika)" and "the inconclusive is the deviant (savyabhicāra)" is the aphorism (*sūtra*). Here, the synonyms constitute the definition, as in the case of *buddhi* and *upalabdhi*, or the etymological explanations serve as mutual definitions.
{4. Anadhyavasitaḥ}

"The *anadhyavasita* (unascertained) is that which resides in the subject (*pakṣa*) itself and does not prove the probandum (*sādhya*). Some hold that the inclusion of the term "not proving the probandum" is for the sake of excluding the purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reason, and that this [type of reason] is included within "deviation from the probandum" (*sādhyavyabhicāra*). For just as the presence of a reason in both [the similar and dissimilar instances] is deviation, so too is its exclusion from both [instances] a deviation. And just as there is no presence in one extreme, so too there is no exclusion from more than one extreme; thus, like the common (*sādhāraṇa*), this uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). [Objection: Then how can that which lacks a dissimilar instance (*asadvipakṣa*) and the unascertainable (*anupasaṃhārya*) be inconclusive? For example: "Everything is eternal because it is produced by something eternal," or "Everything is impermanent because it is knowable"? [Response: Nor are these two included within the "equal to the point at issue" (*prakaraṇasama*), because they lack its defining characteristic. For if even that which lacks its defining characteristic were included therein, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Therefore, the Sūtra beginning with "the deviating and the contradictory" (*savyabhicāra-viruddha*) is not intended to restrict the number to five, but rather for the sake of illustration—the meaning being that just as these are fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), so too any other thing that appears to be a reason while lacking the characteristics of a reason should be understood as a fallacy of the reason.

{5. Kālātyayāpadiṣṭaḥ} "A reason that exists when the thesis has been sublated by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*. The sutra states: "*Kālātyayāpadiṣṭaḥ* means *kālātīta* (one whose time has passed). Following the presentation of the stated thesis, there is a specific time for the presentation of the reason; that which is presented after that time has passed is *kālātīta*. {6. Prakaraṇasamaḥ}

"Even when both one's own position and the opponent's position are being established, a reason possessing the three characteristics (*trirūpa*) is *prakaraṇasama*. It is called "equal" (*sama*) because it is equal in its possession of the three characteristics regarding the establishment of both positions—the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*). And the three characteristics are: presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), existence in similar instances (*sapakṣe sattvam*), and exclusion from dissimilar instances (*vipakṣād vyāvṛttiḥ*). The *sūtra* states: "That [reason] for which there is an inquiry regarding the topic (*prakaraṇacintā*), and which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*), is *prakaraṇasama*. Because, due to the non-perception of specific qualities such as permanence or impermanence, there arises this inquiry into the topic—namely, "Is this permanent or impermanent?"—that non-perception of specific properties is stated as the reason and is thus *prakaraṇasama*. For example: "Sound is permanent because the properties of the impermanent are not perceived," and "Sound is impermanent because the properties of the permanent are not perceived. [Objection: In that case, the *viruddhāvyabhicārī* (the contradictory non-deviant) would also be *prakaraṇasama*, since there too there is a non-perception of the property of the opposite side. [Reply: It is said in response: even so, the non-perception of a property of the opposite side, such as existence (*sattva*), is unestablished for both parties (*ubhayāsiddha*), whereas the non-perception of a specific property is unestablished for one or the other (*anyatarāsiddha*). Now, if one is unable to point out the lack of proof (*asiddhatā*) regarding the non-perception of "unproducedness" (*akṛtakatva*) and so forth, then this *prakaraṇasama* pertains to that case. But then why is the status of a separate fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsāntaratva*) not desired for those who cannot point out any other defect in the *viruddhāvyabhicārī*? Furthermore, how is the inclusion of "being either the subject or a similar instance" (*pakṣasapakṣānyataratva*) and so forth achieved by this definition? It is replied: Since an inquiry into the topic arises from the perception of something without distinction even when the counter-position is being established, "that is *prakaraṇasama*"—this much alone is the comprehensive definition. The phrase "adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion" is for another purpose. Even for other fallacies of the reason, that which is adduced for the sake of a definitive conclusion constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) only for that person, and not merely because it was adduced by the opponent or the arbiter for the sake of restating the argument.

{The Elaboration of the Subdivisions of Fallacious Reasons} Now, the internal subdivisions of these [fallacious reasons] are elaborated through their simultaneous illustration: [An objection is raised]—"Indeed, they are infinite due to differences of place and time; even by means of subtle analysis, fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are infinite due to differences in their essential nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, how can their subdivisions be stated in detail? It is replied: "Even though their subtle distinctions cannot be stated because of their infinity, nevertheless, relying on a coarse perspective, several subdivisions are shown for the sake of instruction.
{The Subdivisions of the Unestablished (*asiddha*)}

The varieties of the unestablished (*asiddha*) reason are as follows: (1) **Unestablished by its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*):** This is that whose own nature is unestablished. For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible" (*cākṣuṣatvāt*). Now, one might object: "Since visibility exists in color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, it is more appropriate to call this a case of being 'unestablished due to a different locus' (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*). No, [this is not correct], because visibility has not been presented as having color-form etc. as its locus; furthermore, visibility as stated in the subject (*dharmin*, i.e., sound) does not exist there by its own nature. Alternatively, visibility as the object of the eye derived from *ahaṃkāra* is unestablished by nature for one who is blind from birth. (2) **Unestablished due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is eternal, because a cloth is produced" (*paṭasya kṛtakatvāt*). This is both "of a different locus" and "unestablished. Now, one might object: "But isn't 'being produced' present in sound as well? True; however, it has not been presented in that way. Nor does something established elsewhere become established in another place. Or, for one of the two parties, it is unestablished due to a different locus. Another, however, says: "There is also a reason of a different locus that is indicative, such as: 'This person is a Brahmin, because his parents are Brahmins. If this were so, why does it not establish the Brahminhood of actors and others? If you say, "Because their parents lack Brahminhood," then in that case, how can the reason—which is connected to the subject through a causal relationship—be considered "of a different locus"? Or, by the power of the necessary connection (*pratibandha*), even if expressed otherwise, one understands the meaning of the reason as "he is a Brahmin because he is born of Brahmins," and thereby understands the probandum. (3) **Unestablished in its qualificand (*viśeṣyāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is visible while possessing generality" (*sāmānyavattve sati cākṣuṣatvāt*). (4) **Unestablished in its qualifier (*viśeṣaṇāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it possesses generality while being visible" (*cākṣuṣatve sati sāmānyavattvāt*). (5) **Partially unestablished (*bhāgāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it follows immediately after effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*). Now, one might object: "Since sounds such as those of the wind are also preceded by the effort of God (*Īśvara*), how can this be partially unestablished? This is not so; what is intended by "following immediately after effort" is the occurrence of a sound immediately after a state of effort such as intensity or dullness. And the effort of God has no such states of intensity etc., because it is eternal. Or, with respect to one who does not accept God, it is partially unestablished. (6) **Unestablished in its locus (*āśrayāsiddha*):** For example: "Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) exists, because the universe undergoes transformation. (7) **Unestablished in part of its locus (*āśrayaikadeśāsiddha*):** For example: "Primal Matter, the Spirit (*puruṣa*), and God are eternal, because they are unproduced. (8) **Unestablished in its useless qualificand (*vyarthaviśeṣyāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced while possessing generality. Now, one might object: "Since the definition of the unestablished is absent here, this is not unestablished. True; however, it was stated according to the view of certain [teachers]. But the fault of "uselessness" certainly remains, though it is not "unestablished. However, for one for whom "being produced" is unestablished in sound, it is also called "unestablished in respect to the subject" (*pakṣāsiddha*). (9) **Unestablished in its useless qualifier (*vyarthaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*):** For example: "Sound is impermanent, because it is produced while possessing generality. This is both "having a useless qualifier" and "unestablished. The "unestablished in its useless qualificand" is to be explained in the same way. Or, when atoms etc. are made the subject, the "unestablished in its useless qualificand" and the "unestablished in its useless qualifier" are to be seen. (10) **Doubtfully unestablished (*sandigdhāsiddha*):** For example, when there is no certainty in distinguishing between smoke and vapor, someone says: "This place has fire, because it has smoke. (11) **Doubtfully unestablished in its qualificand (*sandigdhaviśeṣyāsiddha*):** For example: "Even today, Kapila is possessed of passion and other defects, because, despite being a human, he has not yet produced the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). (12) **Doubtfully unestablished in its qualifier (*sandigdhaviśeṣaṇāsiddha*):** For example: "Even today, Kapila is possessed of passion and other defects, because, despite being a human, he is always devoid of the knowledge of reality. These varieties of the unestablished are "unestablished for both parties" (*ubhayāsiddha*) when they are intended as being unestablished for both disputants; but when they are intended as being unestablished for only one disputant, they are "unestablished for one or the other" (*anyatarāsiddha*).
"Some say that the fallacious reason characterized by being unestablished for one of the two parties is not [a fallacy]."

Some maintain that there is no such thing as a "reason unestablished for one of the two parties" (*anyatarāsiddha*) as a fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For instance, when the opponent points out that [the reason] is unestablished, if the proponent does not present a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to prove it, then due to the absence of proof, it remains unestablished for both. If, however, he does present a means of valid cognition, then because a means of valid cognition is impartial, it becomes established for both. Otherwise, even the probandum (*sādhya*) would never be established if it were unestablished for one of the two, and thus the presentation of the means of valid cognition would be useless. If it is argued that a reason is "unestablished for someone" only so long as it has not been proven to that person by a means of valid cognition, then this "unestablishedness" is merely figurative (*gauṇa*). Just as an object such as a jewel, while not being perceived in its true nature for some time, is not the primary reality but rather a mere semblance (*tadābhāsa*) during that period. Furthermore, it has been stated that a fallacy of the reason is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); therefore, when the "unestablished for one" is a fallacy of the reason, the proponent would be defeated at that moment. It is not logical for one who is already defeated to be undefeated later. Nor is it appropriate to provide a justification for the reason after the fact, since a debate concludes with defeat.
{The refutation of that}:

Here it is said—if a proponent, even while recognizing the validity of his reason (*samyagdhetu*), is unable to inform the opponent or the judges due to forgetting the logic for its justification and the like, yet does not admit that it is unestablished for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), then he is defeated precisely on account of that *anyatarāsiddha* status. A reason presented as being accepted by oneself but established only for the other party is called *anyatarāsiddha*, which is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
{The varieties of the contradictory (*viruddha*)}.

The remainder [of the statement] is that the various types of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*) are now being illustrated. When a similar instance (*sapakṣa*) exists, there are four contradictory reasons: (1) That which pervades both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*): for example, "Sound is eternal, because it is produced" (*kāryatvāt*). Here, "being produced" (*kāryatva*) means inherence in its own cause. Some maintain that "eternality" (*nityatva*) is existence characterized by two limits [beginning and end]. According to that view, even the non-existence prior to production (*prāgabhāva*) is eternal; thus, this is rightly cited as an example of a contradictory reason. Otherwise, "being produced" would not pervade the dissimilar instances. However, when "being produced" is taken to mean simply "having a beginning," then since destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) is eternal yet is also produced, this reason would be inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), not contradictory. (2) That which occurs in a portion of the dissimilar instances but pervades the subject: for example, "Sound is eternal, because, while possessing generality (*sāmānya*), it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves. Since verbal suffixes (*kṛtya*) can denote fitness (*arhati*), "perceptibility" (*grāhyatva*) here refers merely to the capacity for being grasped; therefore, this reason also pervades the subject. (3) That which occurs in a portion of both the subject and the dissimilar instances: for example, "Sound is eternal, because it follows immediately upon effort" (*prayatnānantarīyakatvāt*). (4) That which occurs in a portion of the subject but pervades the dissimilar instances: for example, "Earth is eternal, because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*).

When there is no similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there are four types of contradictory reasons (*viruddha*): (1) Pervading both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*); for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is knowable (*prameyatva*). (2) Occurring in a portion of both the subject and the dissimilar instances; for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it follows immediately after effort (*prayatnānantarīyakatva*). (3) Pervading the subject and occurring in a portion of the dissimilar instances; for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is perceptible by an external sense organ (*bāhyendriyagrāhyatva*). (4) Pervading the dissimilar instances and occurring in a portion of the subject; for example: "Sound is a specific quality of space, because it is not composed of parts (*apadātmakatva*). Now, an objection is raised: "There are only four varieties of the contradictory reason, namely those that pervade the subject, and not others which occur in a portion of the subject, because those [latter] possess the defining characteristic of the unestablished (*asiddha*). For the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has only three possible courses: it is either a valid reason (*hetu*), a contradictory reason (*viruddha*), or an inconclusive reason (*anaikāntika*). This is not a fault. Because they possess the characteristics of both, they are objects of both designations, just as a scale is designated as both a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and an object of knowledge (*prameya*). For example, a weighing scale is a *pramāṇa* because it is the instrument for determining the quantity of gold and other substances. Yet, when it is itself measured by another scale, or perceived directly in its own form, it becomes a *prameya*. Likewise, those reasons occurring in a portion of the subject are *asiddha* because they possess the characteristic of the unestablished. Furthermore, they are designated as "contradictory" or "inconclusive" because they possess the respective characteristics of those fallacies, even if they are not definitively established as such.
