As for the statement that the property of the subject has only three courses, we shall explain later that the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) and the "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) reasons are also included within the courses of the property of the subject.
The varieties of the inconclusive [reason].

The various types of inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) reasons are also illustrated: (1) Pervading all three positions (*pakṣatrayavyāpaka*): for example, "Sound is impermanent, because it is knowable (*prameyatvāt*). (2) Pervading the subject (*pakṣa*), but occurring in only one part of both the similar (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar (*vipakṣa*) instances: for example, "Sound is eternal, because it is perceptible (*pratyakṣatvāt*). Here, "perceptibility" is intended merely in the sense of being capable of being grasped by the sense organs of persons such as ourselves. Consequently, it does not follow that this reason either pervades all three positions or occurs in only one part of the subject. (3) Pervading the subject and the similar instances, but occurring in only one part of the dissimilar instances: for example, "This [animal] is a cow, because it has horns (*viṣāṇitvāt*). (4) Pervading the subject and the dissimilar instances, but occurring in only one part of the similar instances: for example, "This [animal] is not a cow, because it has horns. (5) Occurring in only one part of each of the three positions: for example, "Earth is eternal, because it is perceptible. Here, "perceptibility" should be understood as being an object of the senses that are incapable [of perceiving it]. (6) Occurring in only one part of the subject and the similar instances, but pervading the dissimilar instances: for example, "Space, time, and the mind are substances, because they are formless (*amūrtatvāt*). (7) Occurring in only one part of the subject and the dissimilar instances, but pervading the similar instances: for example, "Space, time, and the mind are not substances, because they are formless. (8) Pervading the similar and dissimilar instances, but occurring in only one part of the subject: for example, "Space, time, direction, self, and mind are not substances, because they lack momentary specific qualities (*kṣaṇikaviśeṣaguṇarahitatvāt*)."
Those whose distinctions have not been determined.

The varieties of the *anadhyavasita* (uncertain) reason are now illustrated: (1) That which lacks both similar instances (*sapakṣa*) and dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*), yet pervades the subject (*pakṣa*): e.g., "Everything is impermanent, because it exists. (2) That which lacks both similar and dissimilar instances, yet occurs in only a part of the subject: e.g., "Everything is impermanent, because it is a product. (3) That which possesses both similar and dissimilar instances, yet pervades the subject: e.g., "Sound is impermanent, because it is a specific quality of space (*ākāśa*). (4) That which possesses both similar and dissimilar instances, yet occurs in only a part of the subject: e.g., "Every substance is impermanent, because it possesses motion. (5) That which lacks dissimilar instances, possesses similar instances, and pervades the subject: e.g., "Every effect is eternal, because it has the property of arising. (6) That which lacks dissimilar instances, possesses similar instances, and occurs in only a part of the subject: e.g., "Every effect is eternal, because it has parts. [Objection: Why have the two varieties of *anadhyavasita*—that which lacks similar instances but possesses dissimilar instances, and that which pervades the subject while occurring in only a part of it—not been illustrated? [Reply: If you say it is because those two are purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*), then [we reply]: in that case, such arguments as "All effects are preceded by *pradhāna* (primordial matter), and all things are preceded by *ḍittha* (a specific person), because they arise" or "because they possess form," would also be valid purely negative reasons. This is not so, because they suffer from the fallacies of being *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (mistimed) and *bhāgāsiddha* (partially unestablished). These two are indeed varieties of *anadhyavasita* for you, since you do not accept a complete illustration [of a purely negative reason]. For the definition of the purely negative reason is to be understood as being formulated by restating the general definition of a reason; thus, it does not become over-extensive (*ativyāpaka*).
The varieties of the "mistimed" (kālātyayāpadiṣṭa) fallacy: "As for the varieties of the mistimed," [the example of that which is contradicted by perception (pratyakṣaviruddha) is as follows].

(1) *Pratyakṣaviruddha* (contradicted by perception) means that its object is sublated by perception or that its object is refuted by perception; these have the same meaning. For example: "This fire is not hot, because it is produced. {Example of contradiction by inference} (2) "Contradiction by inference (*anumānaviruddha*) is as follows": "Atoms are impermanent, because they possess form (*mūrtatvāt*)."

{The Non-acceptance and Refutation of Inference Contradicted by Inference} Others, however, do not accept an inference that is contradicted by another inference, because it is logically untenable for one to be sublated [by another] regardless of whether their strength is equal, greater, or lesser. If they are of equal strength, which one could be said to be the sublater and which the sublated? Indeed, that which is sublated must be the one with lesser strength, not the one with equal strength. Furthermore, that which has greater strength would be the sublater, not the sublated. But as for that which has lesser strength, it is already defective due to its very inferiority; what need is there for a sublater of it?

In that case, even a [reason] that contradicts perception would not be [considered] such, because that which is endowed with the characteristics of inference is incapable of being sublated, whereas that which lacks them is defective for that very reason; thus, sublation by perception would be purposeless. Now, if it is argued that a [reason] possessing the three features is deficient in the characteristics of inference precisely because it is sublated by perception—well then, a [reason] such as "possessing form" (*mūrtatva*) is deficient precisely because it is sublated by inference, and not otherwise.

But surely, a [reason] such as "possessing form" is defective because it is established otherwise (i.e., redundant), since impermanence is established by "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and not by "possessing form."

No; for we do not accept a restriction regarding the means of proof (*sādhana*), since it is accepted that multiple means of proof are capable of establishing even a single [property]. Otherwise, even such reasons as "having parts" (*sāvayavatva*) would be "established otherwise" (*anyathāsiddha*) in the proof of impermanence. Furthermore, if one were to accept that even those [reasons] which contradict perception and scripture are "established otherwise," what could possibly be said? A reason established otherwise is neither subsumed under the definition of the "unestablished" (*asiddha*) nor under the definitions of the "contradictory" (*viruddha*) and so forth. Thus, you would merely have given another name to a specific variety of the "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
How, then, can there be the relationship of the sublated and the sublator, given that both are equally characterized as inference?

No; because of the distinction between strength and weakness, that which appears strong when investigated is the sublater (*bādhaka*) of the inference, while that which is weak is the sublated (*bādhyam*). In reality, in a case such as "fire is hot," the perception (*pratyakṣa*)—which proceeds by the force of its object due to the absence of any other cause—is the sublater of the inference, and not the perception of water as hot or the perception of a fire-brand wheel (*alātacakra*) and the like. For in those cases, the inference possesses greater strength. Thus, the inference of impermanence is sublated by the inference establishing the nature of atoms, or else [the inference] has its locus unestablished (*dharmyasiddha*). Furthermore, atomhood does not exist in impermanence. In the refutation of the doctrines of momentary destruction (*kṣaṇabhaṅga*) and primordial matter (*pradhāna*), it is established that for a substance, only that which is of minimal dimension is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). How could that [minimal dimension] belong to atoms? For that which is beyond which there is nothing smaller is called an atom. If the state of being "smaller" were without limit, then because there would be no difference in terms of being produced by infinite causes, there would be no distinction between things like a mote (*truṭi*) and a mountain in terms of weight and dimension. Thus, the inference establishing atoms has greater strength because it is not contradicted by impermanence, whereas the [inference] regarding corporeality (*mūrtatva*) has less strength because it is not contradicted by permanence. And this is the inference establishing atoms: "The state of being increasingly minute must terminate somewhere, because it is a state of increasing dimension, like the state of being increasingly large."
Thus, in all cases, the relationship of the sublated and the sublator between two means of valid cognition is to be determined by ascertaining their relative strength and weakness.
{An example of contradiction with scripture}

(3) "An example of [inference] contradicted by scripture (*āgamaviruddha*) is as follows": "Wine and the like should be drunk by a Brāhmaṇa, because they are liquid substances, like milk. Here, it is not mere drinking that is being proven; what then? That which is the cause of sin is to be understood solely through scripture (*āgama*), and is not within the domain of inference (*anumāna*). For it is not possible for people such as ourselves to ascertain through any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that even the drinking of milk is a cause of sin or a cause of merit (*dharma*). Therefore, an inference that operates upon what is not its proper object is sublated by scripture. However, the inference of a formless, all-pervading self is not sublated by a scripture that describes the Person (*puruṣa*) as having the color of the sun and being the size of a thumb. For that inference operates within its own proper domain, whereas the scripture has a different purpose.

(4) An example of [a reason] contradicted by a portion of perception (*pratyakṣaikadeśaviruddha*): "For example, that which is contradicted by a portion of perception is as follows: 'All fire is non-hot, because it possesses form.
An example of [a reason] contradicted by a portion of inference (*anumānaikadeśaviruddha*).

(5) "An example of [a reason] contradicted by a part of the inference (*anumānaikadeśaviruddha*) is as follows": The fluidity, color, taste, smell, and touch residing in all eternal substances are eternal, because they reside in atoms while possessing the property of originating a homogeneous [substance] that does not exist in spatial parts (*apradeśavṛtti*), like the unity (*ekatva*) and so forth residing therein. The inclusion of the term "residing in what does not have spatial parts" (*apradeśavṛtti*) is for the purpose of excluding conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and disjunction (*vibhāga*), both of which originate homogeneous [substances] and reside in atoms. The inclusion of the term "originating a homogeneous [substance]" (*samānajātyārambhakatva*) is for the purpose of excluding plurality (*anekatva*) as a number (*saṃkhyā*) and dimension (*parimāṇa*), which are held to be originators [of substances]. In this context, by means of the inference, only the eternity of fluidity produced by external causes (*naimittikadravatva*) and of color and other qualities born of cooking (*pākaja*) is contradicted, but not the inherent fluidity (*sāṃsiddhikadravatva*) or the color and other qualities of the eternal atoms.

(6) An example of [a reason] contradicted by a portion of scripture (*āgamaikadeśaviruddha*): "For example, a [reason] contradicted by a portion of scripture is as follows: 'The bodies of all the divine sages (*devarṣi*) are composed of earth, because they are bodies, like our own bodies. [This is contradicted] because it is heard in scripture that Varuṇa, Āditya, Vāyu, and others possess bodies made of water, fire, and air. Furthermore, if one does not accept the authority of that [scripture], the very existence of the subject (*dharmin*) would not be established."

"But surely these [faults], such as contradiction with perception and so forth, are defects of the proposition (*pratijñā*) alone, not of the reason (*hetu*). "No," say some, "because the nature of the action remains the same; for even if one expresses it otherwise, fire does not become something else. Likewise, 'being produced' (*kṛtakatva*) does not become something else either; thus, there would be no such thing as a defect of the reason. "True. Every means of proof (*sādhana*) is capable within its own domain. If that [means] is employed by a person outside its domain, it does not effect the establishment of the object. Therefore, the person alone is at fault, who, through lack of understanding, employs it where it is not applicable; but there is no reproach whatsoever for the insentient means of proof itself. Rather, the fault of the person is pointed out by way of that [means]. Just as, for example, the fault of the creator is pointed out by way of his work, such as a painting. "If that is so, then since there is no harm in pointing out the fault of the speaker by way of the proposition as well, the faults of the proposition should also be stated. Indeed, those contradictions with perception and so forth were intended to be pointed out by way of the proposition; therefore, they are [classified as] defects of the reason."

But surely there are other defects of the thesis (*pratijñādoṣa*), such as contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) and so forth; why have they not been mentioned? Because they are included within contradictions with perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of valid cognition. Since the restriction to three means of valid cognition is accepted, there can be no contradiction with what is not a means of valid cognition. The statement "sound does not convey meaning" is a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*). For the Sāṃkhya, the claim "the effect is non-existent [in the cause]" is a contradiction with his own treatise (*svaśāstravirodha*). For one who proceeds having accepted a treatise as authoritative, there is a contradiction between the thesis and the treatise, or between the treatise and the thesis. The statement "the moon is not the hare-marked one" is a contradiction with common consensus (*prasiddhivirodha*). The statement "the reason is ineffective" is a contradiction between two members of the thesis itself. These contradictions should be understood as being included within either contradiction with scripture (*āgamavirodha*) or contradiction with inference (*anumānavirodha*).

{The example of the "equal-to-the-issue" (prakaraṇasama):} Since there are no sub-varieties of the equal-to-the-issue, its example has been stated in general terms. Some maintain that the "non-deviating contradiction" (viruddhāvyabhicārī) is the occurrence of two contradictory reasons with identical characteristics regarding a single subject (*dharmin*), as follows: "Sound is non-eternal, because it is perceptible by the external sense organs of persons like us, like a jar; [and] sound is eternal, because it is audible, like the nature of sound (*śabdatva*) and so forth.
{The suspicion that the non-deviating contradiction is not a fallacy of the reason (ahetvābhāsa)}

Regarding this, they say: "This is not a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) because the simultaneous application of both [reasons] together and individually is impossible. Since the combined form cannot exist elsewhere, it would be an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason; and if one person were to employ them individually, he would be a madman. If two disputants were to employ them simultaneously, there would be no comprehension of the meaning. If, however, they are employed sequentially, is the defectiveness or non-defectiveness of the first already known? If it is defective, how can it be non-deviant (*avyabhicārin*)? If it is non-defective, then once its object has been established, a contradictory reason could not even arise, just like a reason contradicted by perception."
The refutation of that [position] and the establishment of one's own view.

To this it is replied: This fallacy of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) depends upon a particular person, like the *anyatarāsiddha* or the *prakaraṇasama*. As for what was said—that there is either defectiveness or non-defectiveness in the first [reason]—that is not so. For the opponent employs the second [reason] precisely to reveal its specific nature, based on the observation of mere non-differentiation, just as in the case of a conflicting dispute (*vipratipatti*). Indeed, if no specific distinction were stated, doubt would be appropriate here rather than the ascertainment of one side or the other; such is the intention. Just as a conflicting dispute arises when there is no certainty regarding correctness or incorrectness, so too does it arise even in the case of a non-deviant [reason]. Furthermore, the non-deviance of both [reasons] is from the perspective of the two disputants and not in an ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*); therefore, the consequence of establishing both sides does not follow. When the proponent is unable to establish the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*) of his own reason with the probandum by means of a sublation of the counter-example (*vipakṣabādhaka*), while the opponent merely points out that it is "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*), then it is called the "non-deviant contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) fallacy of the reason.
The definition of an example.

An example (*udāharaṇa*) is the statement of a valid illustration (*dṛṣṭāntābhidhāna*). It is of two kinds: the example based on similarity (*sādharmyodāharaṇa*) and the example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇa*). Among these, an example based on similarity is the statement of an illustration by way of positive concomitance (*anvaya*). For instance: "Sound is impermanent because it possesses qualities such as intensity; whatever possesses qualities such as intensity is observed to be impermanent, just like pleasure and so forth. An example based on dissimilarity is the statement of an illustration by way of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*). For instance: "Whatever is not impermanent does not possess qualities such as intensity, just like space. Thus, the twofold nature of the example is stated in the Sūtra itself. As it says: "An example is an illustration [which,] through its similarity to the probandum (*sādhya*), possesses that property (*taddharmabhāvī*); or, conversely, the opposite [is an illustration] through its dissimilarity to that. The similarity of the probandum with the example has been explained under the definition of the reason (*hetu*). That which possesses the property of the probandum—that is, where the property of the probandum exists—is an illustration possessing that property (*taddharmabhāvī*). "Through its dissimilarity to that" means that an illustration which, through its dissimilarity to the probandum, does not possess that property is an example based on dissimilarity. The explanation of this is similar to the previous one. Here we observe the meaning of the ablative case (*pañcamī*). From the similarity to the probandum, does the illustration possessing that property arise, or is it known? It certainly does not arise, because some things arise from other causes and some are eternal. Nor is it known, because it is already ascertained through perception or other means of proof. Therefore, it is explained otherwise: here the specific definition (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) of the illustration is being stated. Its general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), however, was already stated previously in the passage beginning with "the common person, the investigator," etc. By way of restating that, the similarity and dissimilarity mentioned here should be understood as the specific definition. The ablative case is used for the purpose of establishing its divisions. This is what is meant: the previously mentioned illustration is of two kinds—possessing that property and not possessing that property; that is to say, possessing similarity and possessing dissimilarity. Regarding this, he asks: "How is the former to be understood as distinct from the latter? He replies: "By virtue of its similarity to the probandum. The same explanation applies to the second case as well. Since the definition of the illustration itself ought to have been stated right there, its mention here is for the purpose of establishing the definition of the example along with its divisions. How is the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in the phrase "the illustration is the example" to be understood? One view is that it is by supplying the word "being stated" (*abhidhīyamāna*). Alternatively, since in other treatises the terms "illustration" and "example" are used interchangeably, it is stated here that "the illustration is the example" by way of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) in order to indicate that such usage is secondary. The purpose of this metaphorical usage is that the merits and defects of the example belong to the example [as a statement] by virtue of the merits and defects of the illustration. It has been said that "members" (*avayava*) are parts of a sentence; however, the meaning [of the illustration] is not a part of a sentence, therefore only the verbal expression is primarily the example, not the illustration itself. Or rather, one must supply the words "the statement of that" (*tadvacana*). If it were simply said that "the statement of the illustration is the example," then pseudo-examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) would be excluded, because they are not statements of a valid illustration. So why include the term "valid" (*samyak*)? It is not unnecessary, for it serves to exclude defects in the verbal expression as well, as we shall explain later. Pseudo-examples are those which appear to be examples but are not. The qualification "lacking that definition" should be understood here just as it is for pseudo-reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, even in some cases, what is not actually an example appears as one; the term is included to exclude those.
Fallacious examples.

These pseudo-examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) are of many kinds, such as those lacking the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), those lacking the probans (*sādhanavikala*), and so forth. There are eight defects of meaning (*arthadoṣa*) and four defects of expression (*vacanadoṣa*); these twelve varieties have been accepted by many teachers and should be understood as they were introduced at the beginning [of this work]. Thus, for the sake of understanding their distinctions, exactly twelve examples are stated here. Among them, in order to avoid excessive length of the text, all the examples are discussed within the following formal argument (*prayoga*): "The mind is impermanent because it is corporeal. 1. "Whatever is corporeal is seen to be impermanent, like an atom (*paramāṇu*). This is *sādhyavikala* (lacking the property to be proven), because the atom lacks the property of impermanence which is to be proven. 2. "Like action (*karman*). This is *sādhanavikala* (lacking the probans), because action lacks corporeality, which is the probans. 3. "Like space (*ākāśa*). This is *ubhayavikala* (lacking both), because it lacks both impermanence and corporeality. 4. "Like a donkey's horn. This example is devoid of a locus (*āśrayahīna*). Since the substratum itself does not exist, upon what could the pervasion (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) between the properties to be proven and the probans be perceived? If that pervasion is not perceived, or if it is perceived merely through words, what is the purpose of an example? Furthermore, the negation of [the existence of] *pradhāna* and other such principles cannot be accomplished by an unproven example; rather, it must be done through the logic of establishing atoms and the like. For the establishment of *pradhāna* and so forth is not possible simply by asserting that pleasure and the like reside in a self, or that atoms and space are eternal. The negation of the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding them should also be conducted thus: "The linguistic usage that 'pradhāna and so forth exist' should not be employed by discerning persons; because its object is not perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), just like the linguistic usage that 'a sky-flower exists. If this is the case, then there is no defect such as the "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) for the reason (*hetu*) or the example. And the fact that the objects of the reasons cited by others—such as "concomitance" (*anvaya*) and "dimension" (*parimāṇa*)—are not perceived through valid means of knowledge should be established by means of refutation.
The view of those who do not accept the aforementioned refutation.

Some indeed maintain that the statement "like a jar" (*ghaṭavat*) constitutes a fault of the word due to a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). They argue that pervasion is communicated only by means of the distributive repetition "whatever... whatever" (*yad yad... tat sarvam*), and not otherwise. Others, however, do not accept this criticism, because such usage is observed in all treatises. The speech of the opponent is not an independent means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); rather, it is supported by other means of valid cognition. Therefore, if the pervasion is established through perception and so forth, then even the formulation "sound is impermanent because it is a product, like a jar" is understood [as valid]. But if it is not established by perception and so forth, then it is not understood even by means of the distributive repetition or the term "all. For the statement of an example serves to restate what is already established, not to enjoin what is unestablished.

"To state that whatever is impermanent is seen to be corporeal" is an expression of inverted pervasion (*viparītavyāpti*). For the probandum (*sādhya*) must be predicated by way of restating the probans (*sādhana*), so that the capacity of the probans for establishing the probandum may be demonstrated. Otherwise, it would be a statement of what is not a constituent part of the proof. Indeed, smoke is not understood from the word "whatever possesses fire possesses smoke" to be pervaded by fire; such is the case here. These two verbal defects are known as "expression of non-pervasion" and "expression of inverted pervasion. Together with the four preceding defects of meaning, these six are called fallacious examples based on similarity (*sādharmyodāharaṇābhāsa*).
Fallacies of the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmyodāharaṇābhāsa*).

Now, the fallacious examples of dissimilar instances (*vaidharmyodāharaṇābhāsa*) are stated. In this very same argument—"The mind is impermanent because it is corporeal"—the example "like an atom," namely, "whatever is eternal is not corporeal," is one where the probans (*sādhana*) is not excluded [from the example]. Or rather, with respect to the fallacious examples, the masculine gender of terms such as "deficient in the probandum" (*sādhyavikala*) and so on should be understood. It is called thus because the probans, corporeality, is excluded from that atom. "Like action" is an example where the probandum is not excluded; the probandum, impermanence, is not excluded from action. "Like a jar" is one where both are not excluded; it is called thus because neither the probandum nor the probans is excluded. "Like a sky-flower" is one lacking a locus (*āśrayahīna*). Some do not accept the absence of a locus in a dissimilar instance as a fault; to refute that, it is stated here as well that it is "lacking a locus. For it was said in the discussion on purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*): "Where establishment is desired by the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), there the locus of a dissimilar instance must necessarily be accepted, because if pervasion were established by mere statement, it would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). "Like space" (*ākāśavat*) is an expression of non-exclusion; corporeality and impermanence are excluded from space. Yet, since this is not expressed by that word [in the way it should be], this is a verbal fault (*śabdadoṣa*). For the suffix *-vat* is heard in the sense of "equality"; how then can there be a cognition of exclusion from that? Furthermore, without the distributive repetition (*vīpsā*) and the word "all," the exclusion of the probandum and the probans from all counter-instances (*vipakṣa*) is not cognized; therefore, this is an expression of non-exclusion here. "Whatever is incorporeal is not impermanent, like space" is an expression of inverted exclusion; for the probans should be predicated as excluded following the restatement of the exclusion of the probandum, so that the pervasion of the probandum by the probans and the pervasion of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the probans might be cognized. But when the probandum is said to be excluded following the restatement of the exclusion of the probans, that is an expression of inverted exclusion and is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*). For it does not follow that "wherever smoke is absent, fire is absent everywhere. Therefore, in this case too, there are two verbal faults and four semantic faults, such as "non-exclusion of the probans" and so on; thus, there are six fallacious examples of dissimilar instances.
Examples of fallacious illustrations by way of doubt.

Others, however, describe eight other fallacious examples (*udāharaṇābhāsa*) by way of doubt: (1) *Sandigdhasādhya* (doubtful in respect of the probandum): For example—"This person will exercise great sovereignty because he is born of the Lunar dynasty (*somavaṃśa*), like a royal official [currently] intended [as an example]. (2) *Sandigdhasādhana* (doubtful in respect of the probans): For example—"This person is not omniscient because he possesses passion and so forth, like a man on the street. (3) *Sandigdhobhaya* (doubtful in respect of both): For example—"The person intended [as the subject] will go to heaven because he has accumulated pure merit (*śukladharma*), like Devadatta. (4) *Sandigdhāśraya* (doubtful in respect of the locus): For example—"This person is not omniscient because he speaks much, like the future son of Devadatta. (5) *Sandigdhasādhyavyāvṛtta* (doubtful in respect of the exclusion of the probandum): For example—"Whoever will not exercise great sovereignty is not even born of the Lunar dynasty, like another royal official. (6) *Sandigdhasādhanāvyāvṛtta* (doubtful in respect of the exclusion of the probans): For example—"But whoever is omniscient is free from passion and so forth, like one who is proficient in all the scriptures. (7) *Sandigdhobhayāvyāvṛtta* (doubtful in respect of the exclusion of both): For example—"Whoever will not go to heaven is not even one who has accumulated pure merit, like a wicked man. (8) *Sandigdhāśraya* (doubtful in respect of the locus): For example—"Whoever is omniscient does not speak much, like the future son of Devadatta."
{An Exposition of the Upanayana}

The *upanaya* (application) is the statement that, by means of the comparison with the example, demonstrates the pervasion (*vyāpti*) in the subject (*pakṣa*) of the probans whose inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*) has been established in the example. It is of two kinds: "And so, sound is endowed with properties such as intensity" is the *sādharmya-upanaya* (homologous application); "And so, sound is not not endowed with properties such as intensity" is the *vaidharmya-upanaya* (heterologous application). Likewise, the Sūtra states: "The *upanaya* of the probandum is the application [to the subject] as 'it is so' or 'it is not so,' depending upon the example. That which depends upon the establishment of the inseparable connection in the example is "depending upon the example" (*udāharaṇāpekṣa*); the meaning is that its inseparable connection is well-known in the example. By the phrase "it is so" (*tathā*), it is expressed "by means of the comparison with the example. It is an "application" (*upasaṃhāra*) because it is applied as a relation to the probandum; it is called an "application" (*upasaṃhāra*) in the sense that it is applied in consideration of the nature of the object. The meaning is that it is the reason being demonstrated as pervading the subject. And thus, it is called *upanaya* because "it is applied" (*upanīyate*). In this context, the etymological definition based on the sense is incidental. However, in consideration of the definition of the members of the syllogism (*avayava*), it is an *upanaya* because "it is applied by this" (*upasaṃhriyate 'nena*) or "it is brought near by this" (*upanīyate 'nena*); in both cases, the derivation is from the instrumental case (*karaṇa-vyutpatti*).
The suspicion that the introduction (upanaya) is redundant, and its refutation.

Now, an objection may be raised: the statement of application (*upanayavacana*) is useless, because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has already been established by the example (*udāharaṇa*) alone. If you argue that it is for the sake of establishing internal pervasion (*antarvyāpti*), we say no; for that is already established by the statement of the reason (*hetuvacana*). If you argue that this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the same result could follow from stating "visibility" (*cākṣuṣatva*) and so forth, we say no; for that is a statement of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*). Furthermore, even from the application "and sound is visible," its status as a property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) is not perceived. Moreover, since the statement of the reason would otherwise become redundant, the meaning [of the reason] would be established by the application alone. Consequently, the cognition of sound being produced by effort (*śabdakaraṇatva*) would also arise [from the application]. If you argue that the statement of the reason expresses the cause in general, whereas the application expresses it as having an ascertained capacity and as qualified by the subject, we say no; for the mere mention of an unqualified cause serves no purpose. It is also incorrect to say that the application states the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that ascertains the property of the subject, because like the statement of the reason, this too is merely a verbal statement, and no specific means of cognition is perceived from it either. If you argue that it is for the sake of summing up the result of that [means], we say no; because there is no necessity, let the statement of the reason itself serve that purpose. Otherwise, another member of the syllogism would have to be formulated to sum up the result of the means of cognition used to support the meaning of the example. Others claim that its purpose is seen in the case of inference for oneself (*svārtha*), because in one's own inference, after the recollection of pervasion, there arises the "subsumptive reflection" (*parāmarśajñāna*)—"and so is this"—and immediately thereafter the cognition of the probandum (*liṅgijñāna*); this sequence is observed and must necessarily be stated, since inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) is intended to demonstrate the means of one's own realization. We say no, because there is no proof for the existence of such a subsumptive reflection. If you argue that this leads to the redundancy of the application, then that is a fine proof! And furthermore, there would be mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). Moreover, when the mark (*liṅga*) is already known through inference or scripture, how does the subsumptive reflection arise? If you say it is from mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), that is incorrect; because there is no proof for it. Furthermore, if you admit the operation of perception even regarding supersensible things (*atīndriya*), then inference and other means would become useless. A cause is postulated upon seeing an effect. But the effect called "subsumptive reflection" is not certain, nor is anything observed to be contradicted in its absence that would necessitate its postulation. For there is no contradiction in the operation of inference—such as "this possesses fire"—arising from the observation of the mark and the recollection of pervasion. Furthermore, even if a person of weak intellect requires repeated observation, why must it be taught repeatedly even in the case of inference for others? If repetition were required in some cases due to the need to recall pervasion, it would follow that the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) should also be stated repeatedly. Therefore, only the members that constitute the means of proof (*sādhanāṅga*) should be stated. There is no fault in the view that the application is for the purpose of demonstrating that the object of the reason is not sublated (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). How so? Just as a pot or similar thing, being produced, is seen to be impermanent and is not sublated by perception and other means, so too is sound produced; and sound, being produced, is perceived as impermanent and is not sublated by perception and other means. Nor is it the case that "sound is not produced"—the meaning of this is: just as space and the like are perceived by valid means to be eternal and unproduced, sound is not so; for it is certainly not unproduced, since production is perceived, nor is it perceived by valid means as being eternal even while being produced. Therefore, being produced is invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*) with impermanence.
The suspicion that the state of having an uncontradicted object constitutes the nature of a logical reason, and its refutation.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "the definition characterized by [the presence of the reason in the subject] would itself be refuted when there is sublation (*bādhā*), and therefore, because sublation and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) are contradictory, 'having a non-sublated object' is not a form of the logical reason (*hetu*)," this is incorrect. For if one who asserts that the three-fold nature (*trairūpya*) is the definition of a logical reason were to have that definition refuted, what loss would that be to us? We, however, maintain that the definition of a logical reason consists of five or four forms; so how can this criticism apply to us? Moreover, invariable concomitance does not terminate in only three forms; rather, it resides in five or four. Therefore, you have stated "because of the contradiction between sublation and invariable concomitance" without even knowing the true nature of invariable concomitance. For who would assert sublation of that which is endowed with invariable concomitance? It is only in the case of the three-fold reason that sublation has been shown. If it is argued that "since the probandum (*sādhya*) is established by non-sublation alone, the logical reason is useless," we say no; for non-sublation is a property (*dharma*) of the reason, just like sensory perception (*akṣajñāna*). Just as when there is doubt regarding the reality or unreality of sensory perception, the objection that "sensory perception is useless because the probandum is established by non-sublation alone through the ascertainment of non-sublation" is not tenable—since non-sublation is a property of that perception—likewise, let the ascertainment of invariable concomitance occur through the ascertainment of the reason's non-sublation. It is not, however, useless. Furthermore, if the form "having a non-sublated object" were not accepted, then [a reason such as] "fire is hot because it is produced" (*kṛtakatvāt*) would result in being a prover (*gamaka*), even though it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*). If it is argued that this is not the case because "the subject (*pakṣa*) is defined as that which is intended by the proponent himself and is not refuted, and since the 'produced-ness' (*kṛtakatva*) and so on do not subsist in such a subject as defined, it is a non-prover precisely because it lacks the property of being a feature of the subject"—then, in that case, if the probandum were established simply from the ascertainment of the subject being "not refuted," the logical reason would be useless. But if that is not ascertained, how can an unascertained property of the subject be a factor in proving? If, even upon the ascertainment of the subject being "not refuted," the establishment of the probandum cannot occur without the logical reason, then why say "the logical reason is useless because the probandum is established by non-sublation alone"? For the words "non-refuted" (*anirākṛta*) and "non-sublated" (*abādhita*) are synonyms. The status of being a subject depends solely on the proponent’s own acceptance; thus, most disputants agree that a logical reason is a "feature of the subject" (*pakṣadharmatva*) only when it subsists in that subject. It is with this intention that "having a non-sublated object" is stated as a distinct form of the logical reason from the "form of being a feature of the subject," and the statement of the application (*upanaya*) is made for the purpose of making that known.
{An Examination of the Conclusion}

After the *upanaya*, the *nigamana* (conclusion) must be stated; that is now being explained: the *nigamana* is a statement similar to the *pratijñā* (proposition), accompanied by the reason (*sahetuka*). It is "accompanied by the reason" because it is joined with the reason as it is restated by the word "therefore" (*tasmāt*). It is "similar to the proposition" (*pratijñāvat*) in the sense of being equal to it, but not the proposition itself; for since the *nigamana* has a different meaning, it lacks the defining characteristics of the *pratijñā*. Alternatively, if they had the same meaning, there would be the fault of redundancy (*punaruktatva*). The aphorism states: "The *nigamana* is the restatement of the *pratijñā* following the indication of the reason (*hetvapadeśāt*). Some say that "following the indication of the reason" means following the *upanaya*. We, however, maintain that the "indication of the reason" is the restatement of the reason by the word "therefore. Since the rule would normally require the instrumental case in the phrase "together with the indication of the reason," the ablative case is used here to prevent confusion; otherwise, one might suspect that the restatement of the *pratijñā* should have been employed even before the example (*udāharaṇa*), rather than after the indication of the reason. The comparison "like the restatement of the *pratijñā*" should be understood merely as a simile. It is called *nigamana* because by it the *pratijñā* and the other members are concluded (*nigamyante*) and established as having a single purpose.

Now, what is the purpose of this [conclusion]? Some say it is for the sake of completing the sentence (*vākya-parisamāpty-artham*). That is incorrect, because there is no purpose in its completion. For here, the object is intended to be established by means of inference; therefore, only a mark (*liṅga*) that is inseparably connected (*avinābhāvin*) must be stated, so that the proponent himself understands the probandum (*sādhya*) from that. If it is argued: "If a meaning already understood is not explicitly stated, then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of not stating the example (*nidarśana*) and so forth," let it be so, provided that the establishment of the probandum occurs even without them. For it is not a mere whim that the sentence must necessarily be completed even when the object is already established. Moreover, it has been said: "For the learned, only the reason (*hetu*) is to be stated. If the purpose for which the example is stated is already established, what is the use of stating it? The statement of the example is appropriate for those who have not yet grasped the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*); and once the inseparable mark is perceived, the cognition "therefore, this is thus" indeed arises—what then is the use of the conclusion (*nigamana*)? This too is incorrect, because this [conclusion] is not purposeless, as it indicates the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that demonstrates the absence of a counter-proposition (*pratipakṣa*) contrary to the probandum. This is what is meant: if the absence of a counter-proposition were not demonstrated, the inseparable connection itself would remain unestablished, just like the property of being a characteristic of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so on, since the absence of a counter-proposition is also a form of the reason. And the conclusion is for the sake of demonstrating that. For instance, in the case of "therefore, it is impermanent," the commencement [of the word "therefore"] conveys a restriction: "it is impermanent, therefore, and not permanent"; thus, the non-existence of the counter-proposition called "contrary" (*viruddha*) is understood. Consequently, it is established that this is neither a "non-deviating contradictory" (*viruddhāvyabhicārī*) nor a "neutralized" (*prakaraṇasama*) reason. Now, one might argue: "In establishing the absence of a counter-proposition, another means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) must be stated, not a mere statement called the conclusion, because for one who is in disagreement, a mere statement is not a means of valid knowledge. If that is the case, then in establishing the property of being a characteristic of the subject and so on, another means of valid knowledge alone must be stated, not a mere statement of the reason, example, and so forth. If you say: "It is not a mere statement because it is a cluster of means of valid knowledge for proving the property of being a characteristic of the subject etc.," then the conclusion also is not a mere statement, because it indicates the means of valid knowledge that establishes the absence of a counter-proposition. If it is argued: "The determination of the probandum (*sādhyāvadhāraṇa*) is the topic at hand; let that alone be done. What is the use of demonstrating the absence of a counter-proposition contrary to the probandum? This is not so, for the determination of the probandum is not possible without demonstrating the absence of a counter-proposition. Thus it has been said: "Determination (*nirṇaya*) is the ascertainment of the object through the thesis and the counter-thesis. Its explanation was provided previously. If the formulation of the conclusion is accepted as not being a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), then for the sake of establishing momentariness and so on, only the proofs such as existence (*sattva*) and being produced (*kṛtakatva*) should be stated. The subverting proof (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) such as "non-momentary things are non-existent, because of the contradiction with succession and simultaneity" should not be accepted. For if you accept that, you fall into a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Why? Because the subverting proof serves the purpose of the conclusion. For both [proponent and opponent] intend the refutation of the opposite consequence (*viparītaprasaṅga-pratiṣedha*), which is the support of the inseparable connection of the reason by way of refuting the counter-proposition. Now, if the opponent disagrees regarding the purpose of the conclusion even after it has been stated, he can be enlightened by the subverting proof itself, not by a mere statement; therefore, only the subverting proof should be stated. This is incorrect. For the presentation of the subverting proof is appropriate only when the purpose of the conclusion is being disputed, just as the presentation of the proof establishing the reason and so on is appropriate when there is disagreement regarding their meaning. Otherwise, the members of the proof such as the reason should also not be stated; instead, only the presentation of the proof establishing their meaning should be made. One could then argue that even that need not be made, but rather whatever other proof can enlighten one who disagrees regarding its meaning should be stated—this leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, whenever the opponent disagrees regarding the meaning of a particular member of the proof, at that very time another means of valid knowledge—either subverting or establishing—is stated for the sake of supporting the meaning of that member. Enough of this digression.
{An Investigation into the Categories of Discourse}

Why is this supreme *nyāya* characterized by five members (*pañcāvayava*)? Because it instructs a person who has fallen into error, and because it is the cause for the commencement of discourse (*kathā*). What, then, is this discourse? It is said: discourse is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis by a proponent (*vādin*) and an opponent (*prativādin*). The mention of "proponent and opponent" is intended to prevent the definition of discourse from being merely the adoption of a thesis and counter-thesis devoid of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*). It is of two kinds: (1) discourse among those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*), and (2) discourse among those desiring victory (*vijigīṣu-kathā*). In that discourse where one free from passion engages with another free from passion for the sake of determining truth through proof and refutation, that is called "discourse among those free from passion" (*vītarāga-kathā*); it is designated simply as "debate" (*vāda*), and there is no other specific name for it. For example, while "debate" (*vāda*) is the general name for discourse among those desiring victory, "wrangling" (*jalpa*) and "cavil" (*vitaṇḍā*) are its specific names. In all three types of discourse, the name "debate" (*vāda*) is well-known through common usage, whereas the name "discourse" (*kathā*) is established by the Sūtra. Although the term "discourse" (*kathā*) is not explicitly mentioned in the list of terms (*daṇḍaka-sūtra*), it certainly exists by implication; otherwise, how could the author of the Sūtra employ the term later on in the expression: "Deflection (*vikṣepa*) is the interruption of discourse due to attachment to other business"? For the activity of this author of the Sūtra is indeed diverse. Thus, having provided the general designation "discourse" in the list of terms (*daṇḍaka-sūtra*)—just as he did for "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—he did not subsequently provide the specific designations "debate," "wrangling," and "cavil."
{An Analysis of Debate}

The specific definition of *vāda* (debate) is also explicitly stated. Thus it has been said: “*Vāda* is the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis, characterized by the employment of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and reasoning (*tarka*), not contradicting established tenets (*siddhānta*), and consisting of the five members [of a syllogism]. A thesis (*pakṣa*) and a counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) are two contradictory properties residing in a single substratum (*ekadharmi*), such as: “Sound is non-eternal” and “Sound is eternal. Contradiction (*virodha*), however, is the impossibility of coexistence; that is to be understood according to observation. In this regard, properties such as being corporeal (*mūrta*) and incorporeal (*amūrta*) cannot possibly reside in a single substratum even at different times. Furthermore, while activity (*sakriyatva*) and inactivity (*niṣkriyatva*) can coexist in corporeal objects at different times, there is no contradiction. Likewise, existence (*sattva*) and non-existence (*asattva*) are not contradictory in things like jars when distinguished by time or place, but they are contradictory in things like space (*ākāśa*). Thus, contradiction and non-contradiction elsewhere are also to be understood according to observation. The mention of “residing in a single substratum” is for the purpose of knowing that there is no contradiction between properties residing in different substrata. Since the nature of thesis and counter-thesis exists in all three forms of discourse (*kathā*), he states—specifically to define *vāda*—“characterized by the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning. By the inclusion of the terms “employment of means” (*sādhana*) and “refutation” (*upālambha*), it is distinguished from *vitaṇḍā* (destructive criticism), for in *vitaṇḍā* neither proof nor refutation is asserted. To exclude it from being indistinguishable from *jalpa* (wrangling), the inclusion of “means of valid cognition and reasoning” is made; because in this [discourse] both proof and refutation are carried out by means of *pramāṇas* and *tarka*, it is called “characterized by the employment of means of valid cognition and reasoning. Here, by implication, refutation should be seen as occurring either against the thesis or against the counter-thesis. In that case, when the counter-thesis is indeed the primary focus, one of the two instances of the word “proof” (*sādhana*) should be seen as elided. It should be understood that there is both proof by means of *pramāṇas* and *tarka*, and refutation (*sādhanopālambha*) arising from that.
The purpose of including the term "means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) in the definition of debate.

The mention of "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) need not be made, because it is already understood. For instance: that by which something is established is a "means of proof" (*sādhana*); that by which one is reproached is "reproach" (*upālambha*). A statement consisting of five members is performed precisely by means of those members which are themselves means of valid cognition. Since the application of the term "means of valid cognition" occurs within those very members, the fact that they are rooted in valid cognition is already obtained; therefore, the mention of "means of valid cognition" is redundant. It is not redundant, because its purpose is to indicate the rule regarding the employment of various [members]. For in a formal debate (*vāda*), the members such as the thesis (*pratijñā*) and so forth—which reside in the intellect as being rooted in valid cognition—must be employed by the proponent for the sake of proof or reproach, since a debate is a discussion among those free from passion (*vītarāga*). Furthermore, those free from passion do not proceed on account of the opinions of others. [Objection: But even in a contentious debate (*jalpa*), someone might employ fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) without knowing them. [Response: True; nevertheless, when a correct argument initially employed with right understanding is later shown to be a fallacy by an opponent, the debater (*jalpāka*) strives again to justify it. Because he desires victory, he does not desist. In a formal debate, however, the proponent desists because he is free from passion. Moreover, seeing his own defeat, the contentious debater employs even fallacies for the sake of proof or reproach, thinking, "Better a doubt than a certain defeat. But one who is free from passion does not act thus. Therefore, this rule of employment is not established without the mention of "means of valid cognition. It is through the rule of employment that a formal debate is distinguished from a contentious debate; thus, the mention of "means of valid cognition" is not purposeless.

This is another purpose for the mention of *pramāṇa* (means of valid cognition). It is to show that even without a connection to the members (*avayava*) [of a syllogism], the means of valid cognition establish or negate an object. The meaning of this is as follows: the mention of *pramāṇa* is made to indicate that even when the establishment or refutation of some object is carried out by independent means such as perception (*pratyakṣa*), etc., without a connection to members like the thesis (*pratijñā*), it is still considered a "debate" (*vāda*). The mention of *tarka* (reasoning) is also made to indicate that this is a discussion among those free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*). For reasoning functions by way of what has occurred previously; thus, only that which is supported by reasoning—namely, inference for oneself (*svārthānumāna*)—should be stated, and not something that one has not personally realized oneself, as is done by the Lokāyatikas. This has been explained according to the opinion of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*). In our own system (*svamata*), however, it is said that any one of the means of valid cognition, such as perception, is the proof (*sādhana*) for establishing one's own position, while the refutation (*upālambha*) is for the purpose of undermining the opposing position. These two—proof and refutation—are to be stated in debate by the Naiyāyika as having their capacity determined by *pramāṇa* (inference) or as having their capacity established regarding the scope of negation and affirmation through *tarka*. The mention of both *pramāṇa* and *tarka* is therefore made. This should also be understood to apply to *jalpa* (wrangling), because of the inclusion of the term "endowed with what was stated" (*yathoktopapanna*). It also applies to *vitaṇḍā* (cavil), because of the reference to "that" (*saḥ*) [in the definition]. Thus, there is no room for the objection that the Naiyāyika’s engagement in debates such as *vāda* would not be possible due to the fear of failure; for that objection and its resolution have been elaborated upon in the context of explaining the purpose of mentioning *tarka* separately.
The fruit of grasping that which is not contradicted by the established tenets.

Regarding the statement that [the argument] must not contradict the established tenets (*siddhānta*) and must possess the five members (*pañcāvayava*), some say this is for the purpose of restricting the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Because points of defeat are prescribed in debate (*jalpa*), they are prohibited in philosophical discussion (*vāda*); however, certain [of those prohibitions] are permitted. Therein, by the inclusion of "not contradicting the established tenets," the point of defeat called "falling from a tenet" (*apasiddhānta*) is permitted; by the inclusion of "possessing the five members," the five fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*), as well as "excess" and "deficiency," are included—thus there are exactly eight points of defeat in *vāda*. If other [points of defeat] are also pointed out, what would be the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for that? If one suggests it is the cessation of being free from passion (*vītarāgatva*), we say no, because there is no proof for it. Even when the eight points of defeat beginning with "falling from a tenet" are pointed out, freedom from passion does not cease. But if one suggests that freedom from passion ceases upon the pointing out of other points of defeat, there is no proof for this. Furthermore, it would follow that in *vāda*, things such as the "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*) and "irrelevant" (*apārthaka*) or "meaningless" (*nirarthaka*) speech would not be defects; or, if they were defects, how could there be a restriction on the points of defeat, since any defect would simply be a point of defeat, just like "falling from a tenet"? If you argue that the pointing out of "meaningless" or "irrelevant" speech is for the sake of abandoning [the argument] and not for the sake of defeat, then why is the pointing out of "falling from a tenet" and so forth for the sake of defeating teachers and others? Indeed, in *vāda*, there is no defeat other than the abandonment resulting from the realization that the argument is irrelevant to the subject at hand. As for defeat characterized by things such as being mounted on a donkey, even in *jalpa*, such defeat is not accepted by the wise, as it is a cause of demerit (*pāpa*).

Others, however, explain it thus: the mention of "not contradictory to one's own tenets" (*siddhāntāviruddha*) and so forth is for the sake of illustration; all *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna* should indeed be employed even in *vāda*. However, they are employed in *vāda* for the purpose of relinquishing [faults], whereas in *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* they are employed for the purpose of victory and defeat. It is for the sake of making known this distinction that the subsequent sūtra specifically mentions *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*, and not the first one. Alternatively, the author of the sūtras instructs his students that *vāda* must be conducted in a manner not contradictory to one's own tenets and endowed with the five members (*pañcāvayava*). Some dry logicians conduct *vāda* even in contradiction to their own tenets—for example, "The knowledge of God is non-eternal, because it is a quality of a pervasive substance," and so forth. To refute such views, the phrase "not contradictory to one's own tenets" is included. And so it has been said:
"He who investigates the instruction on Dharma given by the Ṛṣis with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures—he, and no other, knows Dharma.

Thus, debate (*vāda*) should be conducted as perfected by these five members: the proof of one's own position, the refutation of the opposing position, the support of the proof, the justification of the proof, and the avoidance of verbal defects. By this, the establishment of the intended object occurs; "avoidance of verbal defects" means the avoidance of defects such as the meaningless, the incoherent, the use of unintelligible expressions, and speaking too rapidly.

Alternatively, debate (*vāda*) is also of two kinds: that preceded by the acceptance of a treatise (*śāstra*), and its opposite. In that regard, having accepted a treatise, one should conduct a debate that is not inconsistent with its established tenets (*siddhānta*); consequently, whatever contradicts that treatise must be pointed out by him as a fault. Without accepting a treatise, one should conduct a debate endowed with the five members (*pañcāvayava*); however, contradiction with a treatise should not be raised as a defect against him, but rather, whatever contradicts the possession of the five members must be raised as a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

Discourse concerning one free from passion (*vītarāga-kathā*) is also of two kinds: that which possesses a counter-position (*sapratipakṣā*) and that which is itself a counter-position (*pratipakṣā*). Thus says the Sūtra: "One should not engage even in a discourse devoid of a counter-position, unless there is a specific purpose. In this way, when the intention to specify internal subdivisions is intended, there are four types of discourse, not three. However, in common usage, discourse exists only through the three specific designations; therefore, only those three specific designations have been indicated. Alternatively, let there be only three; for we shall explain that even *vāda* (debate), when devoid of a counter-position, is indeed nothing but *vitaṇḍā* (cavil). On the other hand, that discourse which is undertaken by one desiring victory, together with one seeking victory, out of a desire for gain, honor, and fame, is *vijigīṣu-kathā* (discourse between those seeking victory).

Now, one might object: since the attainment of gain and the like is contrary to the path to liberation, discourse for that purpose is not appropriate. True; this [discourse] should not be undertaken by one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), but rather it has been described as something to be avoided once it is understood. However, when one who is free from passion (*vītarāga*) is challenged by one desiring victory (*vijigīṣu*) and is unable to avoid the debate due to the pressure of others, then that dispassionate person should engage in that very fourfold debate with that seeker of victory for the sake of favoring others and for the sake of protecting the sprout of knowledge. For otherwise, that seeker of victory cannot be enlightened. Thus it is said: "Wrangling (*jalpa*) and cavil (*vitaṇḍā*) are for the sake of protecting the determination of truth, just as the covering of thorny branches is for the sake of protecting the growth of seeds. The sprout of the determination of truth, having arisen within oneself or within the self of a disciple and so forth, might be devoured by the deer-like followers of the Śākyas and others if no protection were provided by the covering of thorny branches in the form of wrangling and cavil. Furthermore, it has been stated that even one free from passion should engage in wrangling and the like for the sake of favoring those disciples and others who have not yet produced the knowledge of truth, as well as their opponents. And this favor occurs by way of generating faith in the scriptures of liberation, the teachers, and so forth.
{An Examination of Discourse}

In that case, the definitions of *jalpa* (disputation) and *vitaṇḍā* (cavil) must be stated. They are stated as follows: "Disputation (*jalpa*) is the employment of proof and refutation involving the previously mentioned *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*. The phrase "endowed with what has been stated" (*yathoktopapanna*) means endowed with all the characteristics of debate (*vāda*). Even though they possess the characteristics of debate, *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā* differ from *vāda* due to the addition of certain members and the omission of others. The mention of *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna* is for the purpose of demonstrating the additional members of *jalpa*. Thus, there is no fault of over-extension regarding the definition characterized by general rules and exceptions. Others, however, consider this to be an elliptical expression of one of the two words "endowed" (*upapanna*). The meaning is this: *jalpa* is the employment of proof and refutation through *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*, which is "endowed"—that is, possessed—of that which is applicable within the aforementioned characteristics of debate. Objection: But it is impossible for anyone to achieve proof or refutation by means of *chala* and the rest, because they are improper rejoinders (*ayuktottara*). Furthermore, their purpose is heard to be refutation both in the general definition and in the specific definitions. Response: It is not the case that these lack the capacity to establish a point simply because their purpose is refutation; for there is no establishment of anything whatsoever that is not based on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Moreover, since the purpose [of proof] is already established by the mention of "refutation" (*upālambha*), the mention of "proof" (*sādhana*) would be redundant. Some say that their status as "proof" is intended for those who are deluded. For when confusion is produced by *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna*, these are called "proofs" because they are determined as such by the intellect of that person. Or rather, for him, they are so called because they appear to be proper rejoinders (*saduttara*). Thus, even their character as refutations is only from the perspective of a deluded person and not in reality; for *chala* and the rest do not possess the power of refutation either, because they are improper rejoinders.

But surely, it is not the practice of the virtuous to cause confusion in another by means of quibbles (*chala*) and the like. If you argue that one should meet evil with evil, then in that case, one would also have to inflict harm upon him by using kicks, slaps, poison, weapons, and so forth. This is not so, because it is impossible to deny what is actually observed. For those seeking victory are indeed seen employing even quibbles for the sake of proof and refutation; consequently, the notion of proof and refutation is seen to arise even among those who do not understand them. This being a restatement of what is observed, it does not constitute a fault. Furthermore, the purpose of such a restatement is to exclude [the use of these means]; seekers of liberation (*mumukṣu*) should not act like those seeking victory. And for those engaged in the aim of benefiting others, they are unable to cause confusion through quibbles and the like as those seeking victory do. However, it is certainly not the case that quibbles and the like are here enjoined as things to be employed by seekers of liberation.

Others, however, maintain that even for Naiyāyikas whose intellects have been confounded by others through the employment of *chala*, *jāti*, *daṇḍaka*, *toṭaka*, and so forth, there is a period during which they may employ *chala* and the like—specifically, as long as their memory regarding correct proofs (*samyaksādhana*) has not returned. Otherwise, if *chala* and the rest were not employed, opponents who argue falsely might secure victory by merely pointing out points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) such as *apratibhā* (inability to respond). The author of the *Bhāṣya*, however, says: "It is not intended that *chala* and the rest are directly the causes of proof or refutation. What then? When proof and refutation are being carried out by means of valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) alone, if *chala* and the rest are not pointed out when employed by an opponent to obstruct them, then—even though the *pramāṇas* exist—the proof would not be a proof and the refutation would not be a refutation, because they would appear to be defective. Once *chala* and the rest are pointed out, they are recognized as 'these are genuine refutations'; thus recognized, they become auxiliary factors (*aṅga*) to the *pramāṇas* which are the causes of proof and refutation. For it is from faultless *pramāṇas* that proof and refutation arise. Thus, "the employment of *chala* and the rest in debate (*jalpa*) is as auxiliary factors, not as independent ones."

{The Definition of Vitandā} "Vitandā is that [form of debate] which lacks the establishment of a counter-position (*pratipakṣasthāpanāhīna*). According to others, the word "that" (*sa*) refers specifically to *jalpa* (disputational debate). Thus, *vitandā* is of two types: the *vitandā* of one desiring victory (*vijigīṣuvitaṇḍā*) and the *vitandā* of one free from passion (*vītarāgavitaṇḍā*). By the phrase "even though it lacks a counter-position, for the sake of a purpose," he speaks of the *vītarāgavitaṇḍā*. Here, for the *vaitaṇḍika*, his own position is called the "counter-position" (*pratipakṣa*) in relation to the opponent's position. The "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) is the proof (*sādhana*) thereof; a debate or *jalpa* devoid of that is called *vitandā*.

[Objection: But surely, due to the absence of a proof (*sādhana*), the non-existence of the counter-position (*pratipakṣa*) follows. For that which is being cooked (*pacyamāna*) is called a "position" (*pakṣa*). However, in the absence of a proof, there is no manifestation; therefore, it lacks the status of a position. Consequently, it should be stated that such a [position] devoid of a counter-position is "cavil" (*vitaṇḍā*). Thus, the mention of "establishment" (*sthāpanā*) is useless. [Response: This is incorrect, because a "position" is so called by virtue of being accepted by the proponent (*vādin*). A "counter-position" is so called by virtue of being accepted by the opponent (*prativādin*) as being contradictory to that [position], and not merely by virtue of being "being cooked. If it were otherwise, there would be only one single position, and consequently, the consequence of the absence of dispute (*vivāda*) would follow; for a dispute between two proponents is never observed with respect to a single position. Furthermore, if "sound is eternal" were not a position, then the contradictory or inconclusive nature of properties such as "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) or "being knowable" (*prameyatva*), which reside in that [subject], could not be asserted. This is because of the accepted principle that "the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) has three possible courses. Therefore, the status of being a position is established by the mere acceptance of the proponent, and not solely by virtue of "being cooked."

[Objection: But surely, just as in the definition of *nirṇaya* (ascertainment), the word *pakṣa* (thesis) was used to denote the proof (*sādhana*) directed toward that [thesis], so too here, even though it is said that *vaitaṇḍika* (the caviller) is one who lacks a counter-thesis (*sapratipakṣahīna*), it is already understood that he lacks the establishment (*sthāpanā*) of a counter-thesis. Therefore, the inclusion of the term *sthāpanā* (establishment) is unnecessary. [Reply: No; it is for the purpose of refuting the opinion of others. Some believe that the caviller has no thesis at all, for they hold that *vitaṇḍā* is merely refutation (*dūṣaṇamātra*). To refute that, the term *sthāpanā* is included. As to how the *vitaṇḍā* intended by the opponent is not possible, it is stated as follows: "A *vaitaṇḍika* is one who proceeds by means of *vitaṇḍā*. If, when questioned about his purpose, he accepts one, then that becomes his thesis (*pakṣa*), and he abandons his status as a caviller. If, on the other hand, he does not accept one, then it follows that he is neither a worldly person nor an investigator (*parīkṣaka*), and consequently, he should be disregarded like a madman. Furthermore, if he were to state that his purpose is to make known the refutation of the opponent's position, this too would be exactly the same. If he accepts this fourfold set—namely, the one who makes known, the one who knows, the means by which he makes known, and that which is made known—then he abandons his status as a caviller. If he does not accept it, then his claim that his purpose is to make known the refutation of the opponent's position is untenable. Moreover, *vitaṇḍā* is a collection of statements devoid of establishment. If he accepts the meaning of what is expressed therein, then that becomes his thesis to be established. If he does not accept it, it becomes mere senseless chatter, and its character as *vitaṇḍā* ceases. Therefore, *vitaṇḍā* is not merely the refutation of a non-existent thesis. What then? It is that discourse in which one of the two disputants does not state the establishment of his own position, but—considering his own position to be established by default—states only the refutations of the opponent's position. That is *vitaṇḍā*.
The six characteristics.

It has been stated that *chala*, *jāti*, and *nigrahasthāna* constitute the means of proof (*sādhana*) and refutation (*upālambha*). However, it cannot be said that *chala* and the others, whose specific natures are not determined, can serve as causes for proof or refutation; nor is it possible to avoid them in one's own speech or to point them out in the speech of another. Therefore, the specific nature of *chala* and the others must also be explained. To this end, it is said: "Quibble (*chala*) is the subversion of a statement by means of the introduction of an alternative meaning. That which constitutes a subversion of a statement through the introduction of an alternative meaning is *chala*. "Subversion" (*vighāta*) means rejection or refutation (*dūṣaṇa*). "Alternative meaning" (*arthavikalpa*) is the conceptualization of a different sense; its "introduction" (*upapatti*) is its possibility. An example should be sought in the specific definitions (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*), just as in the case of fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*). For there is no example of a general definition other than the examples of the specific ones.
"The sixfold divisions [of sophistry] are:

'That [sophistry] is threefold—verbal sophistry (*vākchala*), general sophistry (*sāmānyacchala*), and figurative sophistry (*upacāracchala*)'. The threefold nature [of the first type] arises from the threefold nature of its definition. Just as there is a threefold division of sophistry based on the threefold nature of its definitions, so it is stated:
*vākchala* (verbal sophistry).

(1) "Quibble regarding speech (*vākchala*) is the imagining of another meaning from a statement whose meaning has been expressed without specification, based on the speaker’s intention. Here, the inclusion of the term "meaning" (*artha*) is for the purpose of making known that the negation applies to the meaning of the statement, not to its verbal form itself. A word or sentence that expresses multiple meanings is "without specification"; when such a thing is employed to express a particular meaning, that is what is called "the meaning expressed. When, while that [meaning] exists, there is an obstruction of the statement caused by imagining another meaning based on the speaker’s intention, that is quibble regarding speech, which has speech as its cause. [Objection: But surely other types of quibble also have speech as their cause. [Response: True; nevertheless, in other cases, there is primarily a cause such as a general property (*sāmānya*), and thus they are designated by that alone. For example, when it is said, "This boy has nine blankets," the proponent of the quibble asks: "From where does he have nine blankets? What the speaker intended was a connection with a brand-new blanket, but the quibbler, superimposing upon it a connection with blankets delimited by the number nine, refutes it on the grounds of impossibility. In this case, he should be questioned: "Do you offer this negation after having understood the meaning of the word, or without having understood it? If he says "after having understood it," then how did you determine this specific meaning from a general term? For it is not proper for a general term, dependent on context and so forth, to establish a specific meaning. When a general term is used, the speaker himself should be asked regarding the specific meaning: "What is your intention? Then, having understood his intention, it is proper to either accept it or refute it, not according to one's own whim. In the case of a perceptible object and the employment of a word, the perception of the object itself is the regulator. For example, when it is said, "A white thing is running," if no white object is seen but a dog is seen, the understanding arises: "The dog is running this way"—this alone is understood to be the speaker’s intention. Similarly, when the speaker utters the words "This boy has nine blankets" upon seeing a brand-new blanket, it is logical to understand that a brand-new blanket is what the speaker intends here. If that is not understood, then the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) characterized by non-comprehension (*apratipatti*) should be declared. If, however, the understanding is "he has nine blankets," that is a contrary understanding (*vipratipatti*); therefore, the point of defeat characterized by misconception should be declared. Alternatively, if you offer the negation without even understanding the meaning of the word, then the point of defeat is still characterized by non-comprehension.
