Or, if you say: "I have indeed understood the speaker’s intention to be 'his blanket is new' (*navaḥ kambalo 'sya*)," yet the opponent must necessarily state some reply, and so you say: "From where does he have nine blankets?"—even so, because of the failure to understand the reply, the point of defeat is characterized by non-comprehension. Furthermore, if the meaning is understood, then [if you claim otherwise] there would be the proving of what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*). Thus, the proper reply would be: "Indeed, if the meaning is understood, then [your objection is redundant]. For when it is said, "The pond is full of water," the reply "Where is the fire here? is not appropriate. Or else, it is the point of defeat of misconception, because of the contrary understanding of the reply. Or, if the understanding of the number arises here due to the similarity of the word "new" (*nava*) [to the word for nine], even so, it is the point of defeat of misconception, because of the contrary understanding.
{Quibble regarding the general}

(2) “Sāmānyacchala” (quibble regarding generality) is the postulation of a non-existent meaning based on the application of an overly general sense to a possible fact. A person intended to be a “knower of Dharma” (*dharmajña*) is possible by virtue of the intention [to denote] characteristics such as being conversant with the four Vedas; this is what is expressed by the word “possible. Transcending that, when a term applies even to those who do not possess that specific attribute—such as *vrātyas*—it refers to a generality characterized by “Brahmin-hood” (*brāhmaṇatva*). That is an “overly general” (*atisāmānya*) sense. Because of the connection of that overly general sense with a possible fact, there arises a basis for postulating a non-existent meaning wherein the statement is subverted; that is *sāmānyacchala*, because it is caused by a generality. For example, when someone says, “Oh, how wonderful! This man is a Brahmin conversant with the four Vedas,” the proponent of logic (*nyāyavādin*) asks, “What is so marvelous about this? When it is thus stated that “being conversant with the four Vedas is possible in a Brahmin,” the quibbler, having made the false assumption that “Brahmin-hood” has been stated as the logical mark (*liṅga*) for being conversant with the Vedas, offers a refutation: “This is not a valid reason, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the *vrātya*. He argues: “If Brahmin-hood is the cause, then since Brahmin-hood exists in a *vrātya* as well, he too ought to be conversant with the Vedas. In this case, as before, the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) must be stated: Is the refutation made knowingly or unknowingly? If it is made unknowingly, then “non-comprehension” (*apratipatti*) is the point of defeat. If it is made knowingly, then because of a misunderstanding of the facts, “misconception” (*vipratipatti*) is the point of defeat. Or, if one insists that even when understanding the facts correctly, one must necessarily state some rejoinder, and therefore I have stated such a rejoinder, then even so, because of a failure to understand the proper rejoinder, “non-comprehension” is the point of defeat; or else it is “misconception” due to a perverted understanding. Why? Because the status of being a “reason” was not intended. For here, Brahmin-hood was not stated as a logical mark (*liṅga*), which would allow for the objection of inconclusiveness. Nor was it stated that Brahmin-hood is the actual producer (*janaka*) of Vedic knowledge, which would lead to the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) you mention. What then? The intention is that, given Brahmin-hood, the fact that one is conversant with the four Vedas is not a cause for wonder, because it is commonly observed; it is like the fact that a fertile field is fit for a harvest of rice. Just as a fertile field is understood to be fit for a rice harvest, yet it is not called unfit even if a rice harvest fails due to some deficiency in the causal conditions; likewise, it is not correct to say that certain Brahmins are unfit simply because they fail to acquire Vedic knowledge due to some deficiency in causal conditions. Or rather, this is a statement of praise (*praśaṃsāvāda*). Just as a field is praised by saying “rice grows in this field” so that farmers will be motivated to work there, so too a Brahmin is praised by saying “knowledge and conduct are possible in a Brahmin” in order to inspire faith and avoid contempt. From this, the accumulation of merit (*dharma*) and the avoidance of demerit (*adharma*) are established.
{Quibble regarding figurative usage}

(3) “The indication of a distinction in the application of a term (*dharma-vikalpa-nirdeśa*), the negation of the actual existence of the object (*artha-sadbhāva-pratiṣedha*), is quibble based on metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*). The property (*dharma*) of a designation is its application according to the primary meaning (*yathārtha-prayoga*). A “distinction” (*vikalpa*) therein is the application elsewhere of that which was seen in one place, by means of a cause such as co-occurrence (*sahacaraṇa*). When there is an indication of such [usage], the negation of the actual existence of the object occurs through the superimposition of the primary sense onto the metaphorical. What is meant? Quibble based on metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*) is the negation [of a statement] by imagining a primary meaning when a metaphorical usage has been employed. Negation (*pratiṣedha*) is the obstruction of speech (*vacana-vighāta*) by means of the impossibility of the primary meaning. For example, when it is said, “The benches (*mañca*) are shouting,” the quibbler says: “It is men who are shouting, not the benches, because they are insentient (*acetana*). For shouting is not possible for insentient aggregates of wood. Therefore, what you have said—‘the benches are shouting’—is incorrect. Regarding this, his point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is as before: is the negation made knowingly or unknowingly? If unknowingly, then the point of defeat is non-comprehension (*apratipatti*). If knowingly, then the point of defeat is misconception (*vipratipatti*) due to a contrary understanding. This is because the use of words is observed in both ways—in the primary and secondary senses—in both common worldly usage and in the treatises (*śāstra*). Therefore, a speaker employs a word either primarily or secondarily according to his will. In that case, when a primary word is used, permission or negation applies only to the primary meaning; but when a figurative usage is employed, it applies only to the figurative meaning. When a speaker employs a word in a secondary sense, yet another person, having superimposed the primary sense upon it, negates it, that negation is merely based on his own whim and does not constitute a valid reproach against the other. “Quibble based on verbal expression (*vāk-chala*) is the same as quibble based on metaphorical usage (*upacāra-chala*), because there is no difference between them. [Response: No, because the nature of the “other meaning” (*arthāntara*) differs in each case. In one case, the imagination of another meaning occurs when there is a statement of non-distinction; in the other, it occurs when there is a figurative statement, by imagining a primary meaning. How then can there be no difference? Or, if there were no difference, then by some commonality (*sādharmya*) there would be the consequence of there being only one type of quibble. For the commonality—that the speaker imagines a meaning not intended by him, or that there is an obstruction of speech—is present in all three types of quibble; thus, the consequence of their non-distinction follows, and the accepted two-fold division of quibble would also be overturned. Therefore, due to the difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bheda*), quibble based on metaphorical usage is indeed a distinct category.
{The doubt regarding the absence of figurative designation}

Another [scholar] maintains that there is no such thing as figurative usage (*upacāra*) at all, so how could there be a "quibble based on that" (*tannimitta-chala*)? For instance: does the word "platform" (*mañca*) produce a cognition of men by depending upon convention (*samaya*), or is it independent of that? If it depends on convention, then it is not figurative (*gauṇa*), because its application there is established by convention, just like the word "platform" itself. Even in cases of multiple meanings, a word is primary (*mukhya*) when it is conventionalized for them, just like the word "cow" (*go*). If, on the other hand, it were independent of convention, how could it produce a cognition? A word does not convey an object through mere suitability (*yogyatā*) like a lamp or similar things; rather, it does so by the power of grasping a relationship (*sambandha*), like a logical mark (*liṅga*). Furthermore, if it were independent of convention, figurative words would not require an explanation (*vyākhyā*). This would also contradict the Sūtra: "The comprehension of an object from a word occurs because of conventionality. Moreover, the dilemma between being an error or not an error is untenable: if it produces an erroneous cognition, then it is not a word at all, because it is a pseudo-word (*śabdābhāsa*). For a word is defined as the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*); a reliable person does not utter a word for the sake of error. If, however, it produces non-erroneous knowledge, then it must be primary, since it possesses the defining characteristics of a word. If it is argued that the word "platform" is figurative with respect to a man because it is not directly related (*sākṣāt-sambaddha*) to him, what is this "direct relation"? First, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) cannot belong to words because they are qualities (*guṇa*) and thus lack it with anything. Inherence (*samavāya*), moreover, belongs to all words only with the ether (*ākāśa*). Convention, however, is indeed direct even with respect to a person; otherwise, as stated, no cognition would arise. For we do not observe a cognition of trees and such things situated on the ground arising from the word "ground" merely through a "related-to-the-related" connection. Furthermore, if it produces a specific cognition even through a "related-to-the-related" connection, then it is not a figurative word; for a sense organ is not called "figurative" when it produces a specific cognition regarding qualities and so forth, even though it acts through a "related-to-the-related" connection (with the substance). If, on the other hand, it produces a non-specific cognition, then one must simply say that the word is invalid (*apramāṇa*), not that it is "figurative," just like a deceptive word. Therefore, there is no such thing as a figurative word.
The resolution thereof.

This [objection] is merely a delusion for those of unrefined intellect; it does not please the minds of the wise. For even in the world, the usage of words is well-established through the distinction between primary (*mukhya*) and secondary (*gauṇa*) application. Regarding the determination of word-meanings, it is indeed the users of language who are the experts; therefore, it is from usage alone that the meaning of a word must be established as being either primary or secondary. Indeed, a word applied to a particular object through one cause is called primary, while through another it is called secondary. For example, with respect to a single mountain, words such as *bhūdharas* (earth-bearer) are action-words (*kriyāśabda*); *śveto mahān* (white, large) are quality-words (*guṇaśabda*); *parvataḥ* (mountain) are genus-words (*jātiśabda*); and *savṛkṣaḥ* (with trees) are substance-words (*dravyaśabda*)—thus words receive different designations by proceeding according to different causes. Or again, the same word may be called technical (*pāribhāṣika*) in one sense and causal (*naimittika*) in another, despite there being no difference in their dependence on convention or their capacity to produce specific knowledge. Convention (*samaya*) is indeed of two kinds: common (*sādhāraṇa*) and uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*). Among these, that which is the cause of usage in many scriptures and in the world is common, such as when the word *vṛddhi* denotes increase or growth. That which is the cause of usage in a specific scripture or in a specific part of the world is uncommon, such as when the rule "vṛddhir ādaic" (Pāṇini 1.1.1) uses the word *vṛddhi* to denote a specific vowel. Furthermore, in the world, names are assigned to sons and others according to one's own intention in every house; and new words are coined for cattle and other things by those engaged in secret dealings with their own associates for the sake of clandestine communication. In this regard, those words that depend on an uncommon convention produce the cognition of the object exactly as intended in whichever meanings they have been assigned; they are indeed primary in those cases. Even those depending on a common convention are indeed primary when they are assigned by taking up causes such as genus (*jāti*), etc., in objects possessing those causes. A word like *vyoma* (sky), though independent of a cause, is indeed primary in the sense to which it has been technically defined. However, those assigned by taking up causes such as association (*sahacaraṇa*), etc., are well known as secondary (*bhākta*) due to their beginninglessness.
The ten distinctions of signs regarding metaphorical designation.

Thinking that such a beginningless convention cannot be transgressed, the author of the Sūtras provides a restatement of what is well-known in all the world and in the scriptures: “The metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of a word occurs—due to companionship, location, purpose, function, measure, support, proximity, conjunction, means, and sovereignty—with respect to a Brāhmaṇa, a bedstead, a mat, a king, barley-meal, sandalwood, the Gaṅgā, a cloth, food, and a person, even when the primary object is absent. The meaning is this: a word that applies to things like a Brāhmaṇa—which are not by nature a staff and so forth—in the same way as it applies to a staff and so forth, is called a metaphorical application. (1) Regarding “companionship” (*sahacara*): in the expression “Feed the staff,” the Brāhmaṇa who accompanies the staff is denoted. (2) Regarding “location” (*sthāna*): in “The beds are crying out,” the persons [on the beds] are meant. (3) Regarding “purpose” (*tādarthya*): in “He makes the grass for a mat,” one says “he makes a mat. This is incorrect, because “makes” (*karoti*) and “produces” (*utpādayati*) have the same meaning, and it is not logical for grass that has already been produced to be produced again. Furthermore, this contradicts the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), and there is no sublation of the primary sense [of production]. If it is argued that there is a contradiction with its being an object (*karman*), we say no; for while “is born” (*jāyate*) implies agency, it is called an object merely by name. It is said that there are three kinds of objects: that which is to be brought into being (*nirvartya*), that which is to be modified (*vikārya*), and that which is to be reached (*prāpya*). Grammarians do not intend for everything that produces something to be an object; rather, for the sake of generating case-endings like the accusative, the designations of object and so forth are applied by mere intention even to things like a donkey’s horn, as in “he names a donkey’s horn. Therefore, it is explained otherwise: someone uses the metaphorical expression “the mats are being brought” when the grass for the mats is being brought, just as one might say “the wood for the sacrificial post is being brought. (4) Regarding “function” (*vṛtta*): “This king is Yama,” or “This king is Kubera,” because he behaves exactly like them. (5) Regarding “measure” (*māna*): “He eats an *āḍhaka* of barley-meal,” meaning he eats barley-meal measured by an *āḍhaka*. (6) Regarding “support” (*dhāraṇa*): Sandalwood held on a scale is called “the scale. (7) Regarding “proximity” (*sāmīpya*): “Cows are grazing in the Gaṅgā. (8) Regarding “conjunction” (*yoga*): “A blue cloth. (9) Regarding “means” (*sādhana*): “Food is indeed life. (10) Regarding “sovereignty” (*ādhipatya*): “This man is the family,” and “this man is the lineage. By stating that there is a metaphorical application even when the primary object is absent, the distinction between the secondary (*gauṇa*) and the primary (*mukhya*) is stated: a word is secondary when its application falters, and primary when its application does not falter. For instance, when “The beds are crying out” is said, the initial application is to the wooden structures themselves; when that is blocked by the literal denotation, the application subsequently shifts to the persons. Thus, a word is secondary when, having faltered in one place, it causes an application elsewhere. But when “The persons are crying out” is said, there is no faltering anywhere. One should not argue that a sequential operation of words is impossible because of their momentariness, for this has already been established in the investigation of sentences. Moreover, there would be no determination of meaning preceded by the investigation of a sentence. If a word depended solely on convention (*saṃketa*), what meaning would the word “cow” convey? Since none of the [etymological] meanings—such as speech and so forth—are perceived anywhere, and since convention functions without distinction, it is said: [...Sanskrit text omitted... (Note: The final Sanskrit fragment provided in the source appears to be a partial citation from the *Mahābhāṣya* regarding the etymology of *go*.)
A wise person should understand the word *go* as referring to nine meanings: speech, direction, earth, ray, thunderbolt, cattle, eye, heaven, and water.

And when it is said, "the cow has been milked," how is it that only an animal is to be understood? If you say it is due to the context (*prastāva*), then surely your view—that cognition of meaning does not arise solely by the force of the context—is contradicted. Furthermore, there is no specific distinction inherent in the word "cow" itself such that, upon perceiving it, one would remember that this word "cow" is conventionally fixed (*samita*) to an animal and thus understand only an animal from that word. Therefore, in the cognition of a word's meaning, all factors such as context, place, time, and the proximity of other words must be admitted as causes, and not convention (*samaya*) alone. Even the author of the Sūtras did not state that convention alone is the cause, for if he had, there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra regarding the cognition of meaning through context and so forth. If mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) were admitted, the means of knowledge called verbal testimony (*śabda*) would be abolished—since the linguistic usage of words is observed to have specific objects as its domain, and if those specific objects are grasped by mental perception alone, what is the use of verbal testimony? Nor does even a trustworthy person utter a word merely for the sake of a non-specific cognition of meaning; therefore, a word does not convey its meaning through convention alone. Moreover, because the cognition of meaning from a word occurs sequentially depending on context and other factors, the cognition of a person [in the case of "The platforms are crying"] should not be accepted as inferential either, since no inferential mark (*liṅga*) is perceived for the person being on the platform. Rather, the cognition of the person on the platform arises from the word "platform" itself when accompanied by the word "crying. And this is the distinction between the primary (*mukhya*) and the secondary (*gauṇa*): the word "person" (*puruṣa*), when employed in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with a common action—as in "there is a person" or "the person is crying"—denotes the person itself and is thus called primary. The word "platform" (*mañca*), however, when employed in coreferentiality with common actions such as "the platforms stand" or "the platforms exist," does not convey the person; rather, the action is not possible in the platforms but is possible in the persons. Being employed in coreferentiality with that [action], it conveys the person. Therefore, it is called secondary (*bhākta*) in that case. Thus, even in the employment of coreferentiality based on qualities (*guṇa-sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the distinction in the generation of cognition between the primary and the secondary should be observed.

Now, it might be argued: "Has it not been stated that cognition which apprehends something as what it is not is erroneous? Therefore, the cognition of a 'bed' (*mañca*) with respect to a person who is not a bed is indeed erroneous, and its cause—the figurative word (*gauṇa-śabda*)—is consequently invalid. This is not so, because there is a cognition through discrimination (*viveka*). Here, the person is expressed by the word "bed" through metaphorical application (*bhakti*); how could this cognition through discrimination be erroneous? For a cognition is erroneous when it occurs without discrimination, such as [thinking] "this is a person" regarding a post, or "this crystal is blue. However, if one understands it thus: "This is indeed a post, but due to causes such as distance it appears in the form of a person," or "This crystal is white, but under the influence of a blue adjunct it appears in the form of blue"; then it is simply a correct cognition, not an error. Thus, the definition should be understood as follows: a figurative word is the cause of erroneous cognition consisting in the apprehension of something as what it is not.

Furthermore, that which is directly designated (*sākṣāt saṃketyate*) in a particular sense is called the primary (*mukhya*) meaning therein. For example, the word "staff-bearer" (*daṇḍin*) is designated with reference to the staff, yet it is the person who is intended, not the staff; when there is an obstacle to its application to the person, the designation applies to the staff. However, the word "platform" (*mañca*) is directly designated for platforms themselves with reference to the state of being a platform (*mañcatva*); when there is an obstacle to its application to the platforms, it applies to the persons [standing] upon them by virtue of their location (*sthāna*), which is the occasioning cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, there is a distinction between the primary and the secondary (*gauṇa*). Thus, since such metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) is possible, the "quibble" (*chala*) based upon it is also logically tenable.

{The general definition of *jāti* and *nigrahasthāna*:} "When a reason has been adduced, a *jāti* is a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) intended for the purpose of leveling [the opponent's position]. Leveling (*samīkaraṇa*) is the demonstration of non-distinction by means of a counter-position. And that reductio is performed in two ways: through similarity (*sādharmya*) and through dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). For this reason it is said: "A *jāti* is a counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) by way of similarity and dissimilarity. Counter-objection (*pratyavasthāna*) means censure; the meaning is refutation (*pratiṣedha*). We shall state the examples in the specific definitions.

The ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is the cause of one's own loss. That, too, is briefly of two kinds, as it has been said: "Misapprehension (*vipratipatti*) and non-apprehension (*apratipatti*) are the grounds for defeat. Misapprehension is either a perverted or a contemptible apprehension. Non-apprehension, however, is the failure to undertake what ought to be undertaken. Having accepted a position (*pakṣa*), one does not establish it; or, having been established by another, one does not refute it; or, having been refuted, one does not rescue it. "And there are many subtle subdivisions of these two. There are many uncountable subtle subdivisions—that is, intermediate distinctions—of these two, namely *jāti* (futile rejoinders) and *nigrahasthāna*. Accordingly, it has been said: "From their various classifications, there is a multiplicity of *jāti*s and *nigrahasthāna*s. From the classification—that is, from the intermediate distinctions—of those two types of *jāti* and those types of *nigrahasthāna*, there arises a multiplicity of *jāti*s and a multiplicity of *nigrahasthāna*s. Here, "multiplicity" is intended to mean being uncountable; otherwise, since the twenty-four and twenty-two subdivisions have already been mentioned, the mention of "multiplicity" would be redundant. Therefore, since it is impossible to state exhaustively all those infinite subdivisions of *jāti* and *nigrahasthāna*, only a few subdivisions are demonstrated here through definitions and examples for the sake of sharpening the student's intellect.

{The varieties of futile rejoinders (*jātibhedāḥ*):} Now, the varieties of futile rejoinders are elaborated as follows: "Equalization by similarity (*sādharmyasama*), equalization by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*), equalization by superiority (*utkarṣasama*), equalization by inferiority (*apakarṣasama*), equalization of the commendable (*varṇyasama*), equalization of the non-commendable (*avarṇyasama*), equalization by alternative (*vikalpasama*), equalization of the provable (*sādhyasama*), equalization of attainment (*prāptisama*), equalization of non-attainment (*aprāptisama*), equalization by consequence (*prasaṅgasama*), equalization by counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*), equalization by non-origination (*anutpattisama*), equalization by doubt (*saṃśayasama*), equalization by the topic under discussion (*prakaraṇasama*), equalization by the non-reason (*ahetusama*), equalization by presumption (*arthāpattisama*), equalization by non-distinction (*aviśeṣasama*), equalization by possibility (*upapattisama*), equalization by perception (*upalabdhisama*), equalization by non-perception (*anupalabdhisama*), equalization by the eternal (*nityasama*), and equalization by the non-eternal (*anityasama*), and equalization by the effect (*kāryasama*). The word *sama* (equalization) is connected with each [term]—*sādharmyasama*, *utkarṣasama*, and so on; this should be applied in all cases.
{(1) The definition of equalization by similarity (*sādharmyasama*) and (2) equalization by dissimilarity (*vaidharmyasama*):}

Regarding this, [the Sūtra states]: "When a conclusion is drawn through similarity (*sādharmya*) or dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*), because the reversal of that property is possible, there arise the two [futile rejoinders] called *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama*. The meaning is as follows: when a conclusion is drawn—either by way of similarity (*sādharmya*, i.e., positive concomitance) or by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*, i.e., negative concomitance)—in the formulation of an example, the "reversal of that property" means the reversal of the property of the example; that is, it becomes a property of a counter-example. Because such a reversal is possible, two fallacious arguments (*prasaṅga*) arise, which are the *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama*. In this regard, when a conclusion has been drawn through similarity, such as: "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a cloth," the opponent offers an objection: "If it is held to be impermanent due to its similarity with the impermanent cloth, why is it not held to be permanent due to its similarity with the permanent ether (*ākāśa*), characterized by formlessness? For there is no distinction here by which it must be impermanent due to similarity with the impermanent, but not permanent due to similarity with the permanent. Furthermore, if it is held to be impermanent due to similarity with the impermanent cloth, then why is it not held to be permanent due to dissimilarity with it? And there is indeed dissimilarity: the cloth possesses color and other qualities, whereas sound is different from that. Yet there is no distinction here that it must be impermanent due to similarity with the impermanent, but not permanent due to dissimilarity with the impermanent. Likewise, when a conclusion is drawn through dissimilarity, such as: "Whatever is permanent is seen to be unproduced, like ether; but sound is produced, therefore it is impermanent"—here too, the objection is twofold: "If it is held to be impermanent because of its dissimilarity with the permanent (unproduced nature), why is it not held to be permanent because of its dissimilarity with impermanent things like cloth, characterized by formlessness and so on? There is no distinction here that it must be impermanent due to dissimilarity with the permanent, but not permanent due to dissimilarity with the impermanent. Furthermore, if it is impermanent due to dissimilarity with the permanent, why is it not permanent due to similarity with it? There is no distinction here that it must be impermanent due to dissimilarity with the permanent, but not permanent due to similarity with the permanent."
The refutation of the arguments based on similarity and dissimilarity.

The answer to these two [objections] is as follows: "Because it is accepted that both similarity (*sādharmya*) and dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) are logical reasons (*hetu*) only when they are invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvin*), there is no such undesirable consequence (*aprasaṅga*), just as in the case of smoke and so forth. Just as the fact of possessing fire is established in a mountain or similar locus solely from smoke—due to its similarity with what possesses fire and its dissimilarity with what does not possess fire—and not because of its similarity with what does not possess fire or its dissimilarity with what possesses fire (such as through connection with a tree, etc.), since that [latter] lacks invariable concomitance; likewise, only the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*) and the like, which are invariably concomitant with impermanence and dissimilar to permanence, are the means of proof, but not formlessness (*amūrtatva*) and the like, even if they lack invariable concomitance. Therefore, the claim that permanence would also be established from similarity with the permanent and dissimilarity with the impermanent is not a valid undesirable consequence.

Nor is it unestablished that there is no distinction here, because the distinction between being invariably concomitant (*avinābhāvitva*) and lacking that [concomitance] has already been stated. And thus says the Sūtra: "Its establishment is like the establishment of a cow from 'cowness' (*gotva*). But how can a cow be established from "cowness," which is not distinct from the probandum (*sādhya*)? There is no fault, for what is being established is the *usage* (*vyavahāra*) of the term "cow. Alternatively, by the word "cowness," its invariably concomitant mark (*liṅga*), such as the dewlap and so forth, is expressed; that very thing—being both the similarity (*sādharmya*) to a cow and the dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) from a non-cow—becomes the means of establishing the cow, because it is invariably concomitant with it, whereas mere similarity such as "animality" (*prāṇitva*) and so forth does not.
(3) *Utkarṣasama* (balancing by addition):

"The [fallacies] of balancing by addition (*utkarṣasama*), subtraction (*apakarṣasama*), praise (*varṇyasama*), blame (*avarṇyasama*), and balancing the alternative (*vikalpasama*) arise from the diversity of properties in the subject (*sādhya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), and because both are to be proven. Since the definitions of these six are stated here, exactly six statements are to be understood. Balancing by addition (*utkarṣasama*) is the consequence of an undesired property for the subject based on the example; for instance, in that very inference of the non-eternality of sound, an opponent objects: "If sound is non-eternal like a jar because it is produced, then like a jar, it must also possess parts. This is balancing by addition.
(4) *Apakarṣasama* (balancing the subtraction):

Now, if it is maintained that sound, despite being produced, is not admitted to be composed of parts, then likewise it would not be non-eternal either, because there is no distinction [between the two cases]. Furthermore, since a jar is observed to be both unhearable and produced, it follows that sound, by virtue of being produced, must also be unhearable; or else, due to the absence of any distinguishing feature, one should not admit it to be non-eternal. This is *apakarṣasama*. (5) *Varṇyasama* (balancing the subject) and (6) *Avarṇyasama* (balancing the non-subject).

If sound is described as impermanent by means of the inference from its being produced (*kṛtakatva*), then in that case, a jar too would have to be described by that very same inference from its being produced. Now, if—out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—the jar is not described as impermanent by that inference, then sound likewise would not be so described, because there is no distinction between them; thus, these are the "equalizing" [objections] of the describable and the non-describable (*varṇyāvarṇyasamau*). These two differ from the "equalizing" objection regarding the probandum (*sādhyasama*) merely in their mode of expression, and are therefore explained within that same summary. (7) The Equalizing Objection through Alternative Possibilities (*vikalpasama*).

Now, [the fallacy of] "balancing the alternative" (*vikalpasama*) is as follows: even though there is no difference in being produced (*kṛtakatva*), just as there is a distinction of properties such as some things being corporeal (*mūrta*), some incorporeal (*amūrta*), and some solid (*kaṭhina*), so too there would be this distinction that some produced things are eternal and some are non-eternal, because there is no difference [in the reason].
This is (8) "balancing the probandum" (*sādhyasama*).

Now, the "equal-to-the-probandum" (sādhyasama) fallacy: If both [the reason and the probandum] are impermanent because of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), then it follows that both must be the probandum (*sādhya*), or else neither would be; for if, despite being produced, both are not the probandum, then both would also not be impermanent, as there is no distinction between them. [The refutations of the six types beginning with "equal-to-the-excess" (*utkarṣasama*) follow: 1. **Equal-to-the-excess** (*utkarṣasama*): If by the production of sound, its impermanence is established, then by the same logic, one might produce its audibility (*śrāvaṇatva*) as well. Since audibility is not established, impermanence is not established either. 2. **Equal-to-the-deficiency** (*apakarṣasama*): If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then since it is also devoid of form (*mūrti*), it should likewise be devoid of impermanence. 3. **Equal-to-the-doubt** (*saṃśayasama*): Just as the production of sound causes doubt regarding its impermanence, so too does it cause doubt regarding its audibility. 4. **Equal-to-the-counter-example** (*prakaraṇasama*): If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then the ether (*ākāśa*) is eternal because it is intangible (*amūrta*). Thus, the very same reason leads to two opposing conclusions. 5. **Equal-to-the-unproven** (*adhyavasitāsama*): If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then the production itself is unproven until the impermanence of sound is proven. Therefore, the impermanence of sound remains unproven. 6. **Equal-to-the-eternal** (*nityasama*): If sound is impermanent because it is produced, then the property of being produced must exist eternally in sound, just as the property of being produced exists eternally in the reason itself. Thus, sound would be eternal. These are the refutations of the six types of futile rejoinders.

The answer to these six [objections] is: "Because the application [of the reason] is established through some similarity, there is no refutation on account of dissimilarity. For example, it is observed that the establishment of an application occurs due to some similarity between two locations, such as a kitchen and a mountain, characterized by the presence of smoke and so forth. "Application" (*upasaṃhāra*) means that which is applied; it refers to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the probandum (*sādhya*), or the reason (*hetu*), according to the etymological derivation based on the object of the action (*karma*). Its "establishment" (*siddhi*) is the determination of its existence. This establishment is seen even when there is a difference in properties between the probandum and the example—such as between a mountain and a kitchen—and is well-known to all the world. It is not the case that every property of the kitchen is established in the mountain, nor does the non-establishment of those [properties] imply the non-establishment of fire. Nor does a property unobserved in the kitchen cease to exist simply because it is not seen on the mountain. Furthermore, just as there is a difference in other properties among things possessing smoke, there is no such difference regarding their possession of fire. Nor is it the case that both locations are simultaneously objects of inference and non-objects of inference. This established rule is well-known to all practitioners and is accepted even in the treatises (*śāstra*); to deny it would contradict common worldly experience, contradict the treatises, and result in the invalidation of all inference, since factors such as excellence or deficiency are possible in all inferences. Therefore, since the application is established through some similarity between the probandum and the example, a refutation based on dissimilarity is not logical. Moreover, an example is appropriate precisely because it serves to illustrate the probandum; it is not logical for the example itself to be the probandum. Thus, that which is universally recognized and used to extend the probandum is properly called an example, and it is not correct to treat it as something yet to be proven.
(9) Equal by attainment (*prāptisama*) and (10) equal by non-attainment (*aprāptisama*):

"Because there is no distinction between the reason and the probandum whether they have attained or not attained [each other], and because that which has not attained cannot be a prover, there are the [fallacies] equal by attainment and non-attainment. Does the reason prove the probandum by attaining it or by not attaining it? First, it cannot prove it by attaining it, because there would be no distinction between the two due to their mutual attainment; for example, in the case of two fingers, which one is the prover and which is the probandum? Nor can it prove it by not attaining it, for fire does not burn wood that it has not reached, nor does a lamp illuminate a jar or other objects that it has not reached.
The answer regarding acquisition and non-acquisition:

The answer to these two [objections] is: "Because we observe the production of jars and the like, and because there is affliction through malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), there is no negation [of causality]. Even though the lack of contact (*aprāpti*) is the same [in both cases], we see that it is the lump of clay alone that is being made into a jar by the potter and others, and it is that which is illuminated by the lamp; the reverse is not observed. Even though the lack of contact is the same, malevolent magic is perceived as causing affliction. Therefore, the negation is untenable in either case. "For even though the lack of contact is the same, these properties such as the relationship between the probandum and the probans are seen to function only with respect to specific objects; they cannot be rejected, because that would contradict all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)."
(11) the equal-to-the-consequence [fallacy] and (12) the equal-to-the-counter-example [fallacy].

"Because no reason is stated for the example, and because of the counter-objection by means of a counter-example, there are the two [fallacies] of the 'equivalence by consequence' (*prasaṅgasama*) and the 'equivalence by counter-example' (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*). One must also state the proof for the example itself. In the case of "a pot and so forth, being produced, are indeed impermanent," no reason has been stated here; yet there can be no establishment of a point without a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). An objection raised on the grounds that this leads to the consequence that a proof would likewise have to be stated for the probandum (*sādhya*) is the "equivalence by consequence. For example: "Just as the property of soundness (*śabdatva*), which is perceived by the ear, is seen to be eternal, so too should sound be eternal; for there is no distinction here such that it must be impermanent like the example of a pot and so forth, but not eternal like the example of soundness. An objection raised by means of a counter-example is the "equivalence by counter-example. In that regard, the difference between the "equivalence by consequence" and the "equivalence by the probandum" (*sādhyasama*) lies merely in their formulation, while the difference between the "equivalence by counter-example" and the "equivalences by similarity and dissimilarity" (*sādharmyavaidharmyasama*) lies in their nature. Therefore, these two are not mentioned separately in the summary [of the *jāti*s], and there is no fault, as it was not promised to enumerate every single variety. Thus, it was said: "How many varieties will be demonstrated? Regarding that, he first states the response to the "equivalence by consequence": "Just as the consequence regarding the acquisition of a lamp [is removed when the darkness is gone], so too is its removal. *(Note: This refers to the standard Nyāya response where the consequence is shown to be irrelevant once the object of the consequence—darkness—is removed, just as one does not need to seek a lamp once the darkness has vanished.)*

{The refutation of *prasaṅgasama*}: Just as when a lamp is employed to illuminate a jar or similar object, the consequence of employing yet another lamp is useless, because the lamp is perceived without depending on another lamp; likewise, since perception itself is established without depending on another example, the consequence [of requiring one] is useless.
{The refutation of *pratidṛṣṭāntasama*}.

He states the response to the objection regarding the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭāntasama*) as follows: "And when the counter-example functions as the reason, the example is not the reason. You have merely stated a counter-example; there is no defect whatsoever in the original example. Therefore, because there is no defect, the example does not cease to be the reason even when it is being designated as having the counter-example as its reason.

Alternatively, with what intention was this counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) stated? Is it that just as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is a means of proof, so too is the counter-example a means of proof? Or is it that just as the counter-example is not a means of proof, so too the example is not a means of proof? In the first case, [the Sūtra states]: "If the counter-example functions as a reason, the example is not a reason. If it is accepted that the counter-example functions as a reason just like the example, then you yourself have effectively admitted that the example functions as a reason for establishing impermanence; consequently, since we have reached an agreement on that point, our position is established. As for the counter-example, however, there remains disagreement even now. In the second case as well, by saying that the example is not a means of proof just like the counter-example, you yourself have admitted that the counter-example is not a reason, while the status of the example remains to be examined. Thus, when the non-provative nature of the example is established, the Sūtra—"if the counter-example functions as a reason, the example is not a reason"—is applicable to both positions.

(13) *Anutpattisama* (the equalizing by non-origination): "The *anutpattisama* occurs because of the absence of a cause prior to origination. When it is stated that "sound is impermanent because it is a product," the opponent objects: "Prior to its origination, sound lacks the property of being a product, which is the cause of its impermanence; therefore, it follows that it is permanent. And the origination of what is permanent is untenable. To counter-argue on the basis of non-origination is *anutpattisama*. {The response to *anutpattisama*}

The answer to this is: "Because that which has arisen exists in such a manner, and because its cause is established, there is no refutation. Indeed, a sound that has not yet arisen does not exist at all; of what, then, could one consider properties such as permanence? For it is only when a sound has arisen that it becomes a "sound," and at that time, the property of being an effect—which establishes its impermanence—is logically established. Therefore, the claim that "the arising of a permanent thing is impossible" is not a valid refutation.
(14) *Saṃśayasama* (The Equal-to-Doubt).

"Because the commonality (*sāmānya*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) are equally perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*), [the fallacy] is 'balancing the doubt' (*saṃśayasama*) due to the similarity between the permanent and the impermanent. Even when the reason (*hetu*) called "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) exists, doubt regarding sound does not cease because the cause of doubt is present. And the cause of doubt is the similarity between the permanent universal (*sāmānya*) and the impermanent jar (*ghaṭa*), namely their being perceptible by the senses; this [quality] exists in sound as well. Now, if it is argued that doubt is not accepted even when the cause of doubt exists, then let there also be no certainty even when the cause of certainty exists, since there is no distinction [between the two cases]; such an opposition based on doubt is "balancing the doubt."
The response to the sophistry of doubt (*saṃśayasama*).

The answer to this is: "When there is doubt due to similarity (*sādharmya*), there is no doubt [to resolve it] because of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*); or, if there were doubt in both cases, it would lead to the consequence of perpetual doubt. Furthermore, since the universal (*sāmānya*) is not admitted to be eternal, it cannot be denied. Even if there is doubt because of similarity—namely, being perceptible by the senses (*aindriyakatva*)—doubt is not tenable because of dissimilarity, namely, being produced (*kṛtakatva*), since that [property of being produced] is a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa*). Therefore, upon perceiving that, let there be certainty of impermanence (*anityatva*) itself. If, however, one maintains that there is still doubt even from that, then, when doubt is admitted to arise from both similarity and dissimilarity, it leads to the consequence of perpetual doubt. For how could such doubt ever cease?

Regarding what was stated—that even though sound possesses the property of being produced (*kṛtakatva*), doubt regarding it does not cease because a cause for doubt exists—the author replies: "Because permanence is not admitted," and so forth. The meaning is that this refers to the universal (*sāmānya*), since it is not admitted that it acts as a source of doubt at all times. For indeed, even when specific features such as the head and hands are perceived, a doubt arising from the universal of "uprightness" (*ūrdhvatva-sāmānya*) is never observed. Therefore, the [opponent's] refutation is untenable. However, this point is not mentioned in the summary (*saṃgraha*) in order to avoid excessive prolixity. (15) *Prakaraṇasama* (The Equal to the Question):

"Because the establishment of the process [of proof] occurs through the similarity of both, it is the 'equal to the point at issue' (*prakaraṇasama*). The meaning is that "similarity of both" (*ubhayasādharmya*) refers to the two similarities. It is called "process" (*prakriyā*) because it is carried out (*prakriyate*); thus, the thesis (*pakṣa*) and the counter-thesis (*pratipakṣa*) are expressed. In that regard, the establishment of the thesis occurs through similarity with the impermanent, while the establishment of the counter-thesis occurs through similarity with the permanent. The mention of "similarity" (*sādharmya*) is for the purpose of illustration; it is the same in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) as well.

"Because the [opposing] process is established through the dissimilarity of both, it is called *prakaraṇasama*. This too differs from *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama* merely in its mode of expression. However, if *prakaraṇasama* is defined as a counter-argument based on a three-fold similarity—just like the *viruddhāvyabhicārī*—whereas *sādharmyasama* is said to be a counter-argument based on mere similarity, then this distinction also exists. [The response to *prakaraṇasama*:]

The reply to this is: "Because the subject matter is established by the counter-argument, the negation is untenable, since the counter-argument is valid. Here, the first [position] is the counter-argument (*pratipakṣa*) in relation to the second position. Therefore, because the subject matter—the first position—is established by that counter-argument, which is the first proof, the negation is untenable; the meaning is that the second position does not arise. Why? Because the counter-argument is valid; the meaning is that the first proof is faultless. (16) *Ahetusama* (the fallacy of the non-reason).

"Because the reason (*hetu*) is not established in any of the three times, there is the 'equal to the non-reason' (*ahetusama*). The reason is the means of proof (*sādhana*). Is that [means] prior to the thing to be proven (*sādhya*), or posterior to it, or simultaneous with it? If the means of proof is prior, then in the absence of the thing to be proven, of what is it the means? If the means of proof is posterior, how could the thing to be proven have arisen previously without the means of proof? How can that which is yet to come and does not yet exist be a means of proof? If the thing to be proven and the means of proof are simultaneous, then in that case, which one is the means of which? Because both are equal in their state of existing, the reason is not distinguished from a non-reason. This kind of counter-argument is the "equal to the non-reason."
The response to the argument regarding the absence of a cause.

The answer to this is: "No, because the probandum is established through a probans (*hetu*). Indeed, nothing that is to be produced (*nirvartya*) or made known (*jñāpya*)—that is, any *sādhya*—is established without a probans. Rather, the establishment of a *sādhya*, such as a jar, is observed to arise from a probans such as a lump of clay and a potter, or from a lamp, the eye, smoke, and so forth. [Objection: Since these too are equally unestablished across the three times (*traikālya*), they would result in being non-probans (*ahetu*). Consequently, if all probans were thus rendered non-probans, no one would ever engage in or desist from anything, and the world would become blind, mute, and devoid of all activity; yet this is not the case. Therefore, the establishment of the *sādhya* occurs precisely through a probans. Furthermore, the relationship of priority, posteriority, or simultaneity must be accepted according to what is observed: in that regard, every productive probans (*nirvartaka-hetu*) necessarily precedes the *sādhya*. However, some indicative probans (*jñāpaka-hetu*) precede it, such as the eye, the sun, and so forth, for things currently arising. Some follow after, such as smoke, sound, or desire, for fire, space, the self, and so forth. Some are simultaneous, such as color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest for touch (*sparśa*) and the rest. Even when the *sādhya* is absent, the designation of a "means of proof" (*sādhana*) is applied by inferring its capacity (*yogyatā*); and even when the probans is present, the designation of a "probandum" (*sādhya*) is likewise employed.
{Another response to the charge of being groundless}

"And because negation is untenable. Is this negation prior to the object to be negated, or subsequent to it, or simultaneous with it? If it is prior, then since the object to be negated does not exist, of what is this the negation? If it is subsequent, then since the negation does not exist, how can there be an object to be negated? If it is simultaneous, then—just like the horns of a cow—the relationship between negation and the object to be negated is untenable. Thus, since negation cannot be established in any of the three times, negation is untenable; and since that is untenable, the reason (*hetu*) is established as being beyond reproach.
(17) Equal by Presumption (arthāpattisama).

"Arthāpattisama [the equalizing by implication] occurs because the opposite side is established through implication (arthāpatti). If it is maintained that sound is impermanent because of its similarity to the impermanent—namely, its being a product—it follows by implication that it must be permanent because of its similarity to the permanent; for sound also possesses a similarity with the permanent, namely, intangibility (*asparśatva*). In this way, opposition based on implication should also be understood in the case of an application of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). This [fallacy] differs from *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama* merely in its mode of expression. Alternatively, when the conclusion is reached through similarity, opposition by means of similarity itself is *sādharmyasama*: if sound is impermanent due to its similarity to the impermanent, it follows by implication that it is permanent due to its similarity to the permanent. When the conclusion is reached through dissimilarity, opposition by means of dissimilarity itself is *vaidharmyasama*: if sound is impermanent due to its dissimilarity to the permanent, it follows by implication that sound is permanent due to its dissimilarity to the impermanent. Even when the conclusion is reached through dissimilarity, opposition by means of similarity is *arthāpattisama*; thus, there is a difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The response to the sophistry of presumption (*arthāpattisama*).

The answer to this is: "The establishment of the loss of the thesis (*pakṣahāni*) from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is [untenable] because the [thesis] has not been stated. For one who desires the proof of the unmentioned thesis of eternity through presumptive testimony, the loss of that very thesis of eternity follows. Why? Because the loss of the thesis has not been stated. Furthermore, such is not the nature of presumptive testimony; what then is it? Presumptive testimony is said to be that which, when something is impossible without another thing, causes that [impossible thing] to be postulated as the means of making that [other thing] possible. And it is not the case that the proof of non-eternality is impossible without the proof of eternality through the similarity to eternal things, such that presumptive testimony would postulate the latter. "And because presumptive testimony is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Indeed, that presumptive testimony which arises solely from the reversal of the meaning of a sentence is inconclusive; for when it is said, "the falling of a solid stone," it does not follow by implication that "there is no falling of liquid waters."

(18) *Aviśeṣasama* (the equalization by non-difference): "Because of the occurrence of a single property, if there were no difference [between things], it would follow that all things are non-different; thus, because existence occurs [in all things], it is the equalization by non-difference. If you do not accept non-difference between a jar and the word [for it] on the grounds that the occurrence of a single property called "being an effect" establishes their impermanence, then surely, in that case, it follows that all entities are non-different, since the occurrence of the single property called "existence" is found everywhere. {The response to *aviśeṣasama*}

In this regard, it is said: If it is being proven that all things are entirely without distinction in every respect, then there is a contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition (*pratyakṣādivirodha*). If, on the other hand, they are without distinction in some respect or another, then since one accepts that all things are without distinction by virtue of such properties as being objects of knowledge (*prameyatva*), the argument results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, the lack of distinction among all things is asserted in terms of either permanence or impermanence, then there is likewise a contradiction with inference and other means of knowledge; thus he says: "Because that property is possible in some cases and impossible in others, there is no negation [of the distinction]. This means that because that property—impermanence—is possible and perceived through a means of valid cognition in some cases, such as a jar (*ghaṭa*), and because it is impossible and not perceived through a means of valid cognition in other cases, such as space (*ākāśa*), there is no negation; that is, there is no contingency of the total lack of distinction among all things. Alternatively, it means that in some cases, such as impermanence, a property that proves it—such as being an effect (*kāryatva*)—is possible as a logical reason (*hetu*). But in the case of the total lack of distinction among all things, no property—whether existence (*sadbhāva*) or something else—can possibly function as a logical reason; therefore, as before, there is no negation.
(19) Equalization by means of proof (*upapattisama*).

“Equivalence by demonstration” (*upapattisama*) occurs because both [contradictory] reasons are equally applicable. If the impermanence of sound is accepted because the reason for impermanence is applicable, then surely, since the reason for permanence—its being intangible—is also applicable, why is permanence not also accepted? To oppose an argument by means of such a demonstration is *upapattisama*; for here there is no distinction [between the two cases]. This [fallacy] differs from *sādharmyasama* and *vaidharmyasama* only in its mode of expression, not in its underlying substance. If it is argued that this would lead to an infinite number [of fallacies] due to the diversity of expressions, there is no fault, because such a position is accepted; for the purpose of the aphorisms (*sūtra*) is to provide detailed examples and to facilitate the understanding of various methods of refutation.

{The refutation by way of proof (upapattisama):} The answer to this is: "There is no negation because the cause for proof has been admitted. By stating that both [types of] causes are established, you have effectively admitted that impermanence is established through the establishment of the cause of impermanence; and it is not logical to negate what has been admitted. Furthermore, we do not accept the establishment of both types of causes, such that a contradiction or a reductio ad absurdum could be leveled against us. This is because the quality of being intangible (*asparśatva*) is not a cause [for permanence]. {The sophistry of perception (upalabdhisama)}:}

"The equalization by perception (*upalabdhisama*) occurs because [the property to be proven] is perceived even in the absence of the stated reason. This means that although the reason called "possessing parts" (*sāvayavatva*), which was stated to establish the "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) in earth and so forth, is absent in the case of cognition (*buddhi*) and other such things where "being an effect" is nonetheless perceived, this reason is actually non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). To counter-argue on the basis of such perception is *upalabdhisama*. {The refutation of *upalabdhisama*}

"There is no refutation [of our position], because smoke and the like are observed to be indicators even when they reside in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*). Here, by the term "a portion of the similar instances," the logical reason (*hetu*) is used figuratively due to its association with that place, just as the word "bench" refers to the people sitting on it. Alternatively, it is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "that of which a portion belongs to the similar instances. Indeed, there is no such thing as a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*) called "non-probative" (*aprayojaka*) distinct from the unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth, because it lacks a defining characteristic that distinguishes it from them. Furthermore, the property of residing in only a portion of the similar instances is present even in reasons such as smoke. Nor is "non-probative" status here simply equivalent to partial non-establishment (*bhāgāsiddhatva*), because the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth do not constitute the subject (*pakṣa*); for it is not intended to prove that the intellect possesses the property of being an effect by means of its having parts. If this were the case, then the proof of the intellect's being an effect would be impossible; therefore, he says: "There is no refutation, because that property [of being an effect] can arise from other causes as well. Just as fire that is currently without smoke is not unestablished—since it is established through perception or other signs—likewise, since the property of being an effect is established in the intellect and so forth by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is no refutation of its establishment therein. What, then, is the proof in this case? It is stated: "The intellect and so forth are effects, because they are not perceived before or after [their production] provided that the causes of non-perception are absent, just like a cloth."
(21) Equal to non-apprehension (*anupalabdhisama*).

"Because the non-existence [of the effect] is established through the non-perception of its non-perception, the occurrence of the opposite of that [non-existence] constitutes the *anupalabdhisama* (balancing the non-perception). The non-perception of that effect, such as cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth, is itself not perceived. If it were perceived, it would simply be a perception; therefore, because of this non-perception of that non-perception, the non-existence of that [effect] is established. And when that [non-existence] is established, the opposite of non-perception—the perception of cognition and so forth—is logically entailed. Consequently, the intention is that the existence of cognition and so forth will be established both prior to and after [the moment of observation]. Yet, there is no distinction here: that the non-perception of cognition and so forth establishes their non-existence, but the non-perception of that non-perception does not. Opposition based on non-perception is *anupalabdhisama*.
The response to the sophistry based on non-apprehension (*anupalabdhisama*).

To this, the reply is: "Because its nature is non-apprehension, non-apprehension is not a [valid] reason. Non-apprehension is the cognition that "it does not exist. Since that [cognition] is personally experienced (*pratyātmavedya*) precisely by virtue of having that [non-existence] as its own nature (*svabhāva*), the non-apprehension of that [non-apprehension] is unestablished; such is the intended meaning. Even when non-apprehension is defined as the absence of apprehension, even then, because the absence of apprehension is personally experienced, the non-apprehension of that [absence] is unestablished. For instance, one experiences [the state] precisely as a non-apprehension: "I do not have the cognition of pleasure," or "I do not apprehend the cognition of pleasure. Therefore, since it is being experienced, its status as an apprehension should not be suspected; for non-apprehension is not experienced in the same manner as an apprehension that arises through a positive mode (*vidhimukha*).
(22) *Anityasama* (the equalization by means of non-eternality):

"Because of similarity, since a common property is established, there follows the consequence that all things are non-eternal; therefore, it is *anityasama*. For one who asserts that sound is non-eternal because of its similarity to a non-eternal jar, the non-eternality of all entities follows as a consequence. For indeed, all entities possess a similarity with the jar, such as existence (*astitva*) and so forth. And there is no distinction here by which, due to similarity with the jar, non-eternality belongs to sound alone and not to all entities. Opposition based on non-eternality is *anityasama*. {The refutation of *anityasama*}

The distinction between the various formulations of the *aviśeṣasama* (balancing through non-distinction) is due to the difference in their expressions; therefore, the answer stated in that context should be understood here as well. For the sake of further clarification, he states another point: "Because [the opponent's] proof is not established through similarity, the refutation is not established, since it shares the same characteristics as that which is to be refuted. Why is the consequence of the permanence of all things raised? For the impermanence of sound is not unestablished simply because the consequence of the impermanence of all things follows. Now, if you argue that a conclusion is not accepted when it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as in the case of a mere statement, then—surely this being so—you must accept that the reason for the impermanence of sound is unestablished (*asiddha*) because it shares the characteristic of being a mere statement, which is not a means of proof (*asādhaka*). What follows from this? Furthermore, if you admit that a reason is unestablished because it shares a characteristic with something that is not a means of proof, then the refutation you have stated also becomes unestablished. Why? Because there is a commonality between the refutation and the object to be refuted, such as both being expressible (*abhidheyatva*) and so forth. Therefore, the refutation is untenable.
(23) *Nityasama* (the "eternal-equivalence" sophism):

"Because the property of non-eternality exists eternally [in the subject], and because eternality would thus be established for that which is non-eternal, it is called *nityasama*. Since the property of non-eternality (*anityatva-dharma*) exists eternally—that is, at all times—the substratum (*dharmin*), namely sound (*śabda*), must also exist at all times. Otherwise, how could there be a property when its substratum does not exist? If the substratum is established as existing at all times, then non-eternality cannot belong to it. Alternatively, if the property of non-eternality does not exist at all times, then too, due to the absence of non-eternality, sound is eternal. This counter-argument based on eternality is *nityasama*. {The refutation of *nityasama*}

To this, the following reply is given: “Because the state of being impermanent [is asserted] eternally regarding that which is to be negated, and because permanence would thus be established for the impermanent, there is no negation. By saying, “because the state of being impermanent [is asserted] eternally regarding the word, which is the object to be negated,” the proponent has admitted the impermanence of the word. Consequently, since impermanence is established, a negation is not tenable. Alternatively, if impermanence is not admitted in the case of the word, even so, the negation is untenable because the reason—“because the state of being impermanent [is asserted] eternally”—is unestablished (*asiddha*). Now, if it is thought: “I am not negating impermanence, but rather I am establishing that permanence exists,” that too is incorrect; thus he says: “And because of the contradiction between the permanent and the impermanent. For injunction and prohibition cannot coexist in one and the same thing. If they did coexist, there would be no fixed rule for engagement or withdrawal from specific means by those who seek to obtain desired results (seen or unseen) or to avoid undesired ones. Furthermore, impermanence is cessation (*pradhvaṃsa*); when that exists, the existence of the word is not possible. [Objection: But if this is so, then since cessation is absent at the time of the word, its permanence would follow. [Reply: No; because that property is future, the future destruction is accepted as its impermanence. For that which will undergo destruction is called “impermanent,” or rather, impermanence is the fitness for destruction. It is this very fitness that is figuratively expressed here by the term “cessation” (*pradhvaṃsa*).
(24) The fallacy of the "equivalence of the effect" (kāryasama).

"Because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort, [the rejoinder] is 'equal to the effect' (*kāryasama*). When it is stated that "sound, consisting of phonemes, is non-eternal because it follows immediately upon effort, like a jar," the opponent objects: "because of the multiplicity of effects produced by effort. It is observed that the birth of jars and similar things occurs immediately after effort; however, in the case of obstructed things, there is manifestation through the removal of the obstruction. In this regard, it is not known whether sound acquires its own existence (*ātmalābha*) immediately after effort, or rather, whether it is manifested. Furthermore, there is no specific distinction here by which it could be determined that sound alone acquires its own existence immediately after effort. Opposition based on the difference in the nature of the effect is *kāryasama*.
The response to the *kāryasama* (balancing the effect) fallacy.

The answer to this is: "In the case of a difference in the effect, effort is not the cause [of that difference], because the causes of non-perception are possible. For where a cause of non-perception, such as an obstruction, is possible, it is logical that when there is a difference in the effect other than mere manifestation—that is, when there is actual production—effort is not the cause. However, no cause of non-perception for sound, such as an obstruction, is ever perceived. Therefore, effort is indeed the cause of sound's acquisition of its own nature (its production). Alternatively, the meaning may be: "Why is effort not the cause of a difference in the effect, namely, of a manifestation of sound distinct from its birth? One must supply the words: "Because the causes of non-perception are possible," meaning that elsewhere it is observed that effort serves as the cause of manifestation. Yet, there exists no cause of non-perception for sound by which its manifestation could result from effort. Furthermore, because sound possesses degrees of intensity and dullness corresponding to those of effort, this is logical only on the theory of production; for gold and the like, even when manifested with great effort, do not become large simply because they were small [before]. Therefore, since sound conforms to the properties of desire and effort, just like velocity, upward throwing, and so forth, sound is produced immediately after effort.
The aforementioned categories serve as indicators for other categories.

By this exposition of the manifold varieties of *jāti* (futile rejoinders), the methods for refuting them are also easily elucidated. [Objection: If there are other varieties of *jāti*, why are they not cited? [Response: Because it is impossible to cite all of them. Why? Because it is impossible to cite all *jātyuttaras* (pseudo-refutations) due to their infinity (*ānantya*). Nor does the admission of their infinity contradict the Sūtras, because the Sūtras themselves are intended merely as illustrations. How is it known that the Sūtras are intended only as illustrations and not as a definitive restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) stating that there are only this many varieties of *jāti*? It is known from the fact that a further variety of *jāti* is used to formulate a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*). If a restrictive enumeration were intended, then the author of the Sūtras, while formulating the prima facie argument, would not have mentioned a *jāti* distinct from the twenty-four. And another variety of *jāti* has indeed been stated, as follows:

*Ananyasama* ("the non-different-equivalent"): "Because one thing is not different from another due to its non-difference, there is no state of being different" (NSū 2.2.31). In the examination of the non-eternality of sound, having established the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) that "[the word is eternal] because of repetition," [the proponent] refuted it with the statement: "Even if there is difference, [the term 'repetition'] is used figuratively. Again, the proponent of the prima facie position says: "Regarding this which is called 'different'—is it different from the self (*ātman*) or non-different? If it is different, then because it would have abandoned its own nature (*ātman*), it does not exist at all. If, on the other hand, it is non-different, then precisely because of its non-difference, it does not become 'different'; thus, there is an absence of difference. This is the *ananyasamā* fallacy.
{The sophistical refutation based on parity of application}

Likewise, [it is said]: "And because there is agreement even in the face of disagreement. If disagreement is not agreed upon, then how do you know that "it exists"? If, on the other hand, it is agreed upon, then since it is agreed upon, that is simply agreement (*sampratipatti*); it is not disagreement. Alternatively, if its meaning is not agreed upon, then—like a barbarian tongue—it cannot be a cause for doubt because its meaning is not understood. If the meaning is agreed upon, nevertheless, since it causes its own meaning to be understood, it is simply agreement. This is the fallacy known as "Agreement with Agreement" (*sampratipattisama*).
{The equality of established order}

"Because non-determination is established in a self that is not determined. Here, if the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is intended, the word "non-existence" (*abhāva*) must be supplied; if the ablative case (*pañcamī*) is intended, "no doubt" (*na saṃśaya*) is to be supplied. If it is not established in a self that is not determined, then it does not exist at all, because it would have lost its own nature. On the other hand, if it is established in a self, then because it is established, it is indeed a determination—thus this is the *sādharmyasama* (balancing the homogeneity) fallacy. Therefore, the author of the Sūtras did not intend to restrict the number to exactly twenty-four, but rather provided a rebuttal for others such as the *anyūnasama* (balancing the deficiency): "Because when another name is applied to an object due to some other cause, it is impossible to deny its actual state [of being what it is]. For instance, when the term "cause" is applied to an effect because it produces another effect, its status as an "effect" does not cease. Nor does the status of being a "cause" of its own effect cease when the term "non-cause" is applied to a cause because it does not produce itself, space, and so forth.
An Examination of the Points of Defeat (Nigrahasthāna)

The varieties of *jāti* have been stated. Now, the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) are being discussed. Since these too are not enumerated exhaustively due to the infinite variations of misconception (*vipratipatti*) and non-comprehension (*apratipatti*), they are explained here in brief: "(1) Abandonment of the thesis (*pratijñāhāni*), (2) substitution of the thesis (*pratijñāntara*), (3) contradiction of the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*), (4) renunciation of the thesis (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*), (5) shifting the reason (*hetvantara*), (6) irrelevance (*arthāntara*), (7) the meaningless (*nirarthaka*), (8) the unintelligible (*avijñātārtha*), (9) the incoherent (*apārthaka*), (10) mistimed (*aprāptakāla*), (11) deficient (*nyūna*), (12) redundant (*adhika*), (13) the repetitive (*punarukta*), (14) failure to restate (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), (15) lack of understanding (*ajñāna*), (16) lack of ingenuity (*apratibhā*), (17) distraction (*vikṣepa*), (18) admission of the opponent's view (*matānujñā*), (19) neglecting to censure when one should (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*), (20) censuring when one should not (*niranuyojyānuyoga*), (21) deviating from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*), and (22) fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*)—these are the points of defeat. Points of defeat such as the abandonment of the thesis and so forth, although consisting of verbal statements, are said to be grounds for defeat because they serve as indicators (*liṅga*) of misconception and non-comprehension.
(1) Abandonment of the thesis.

In this context, "the abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñāhāni*) is the admission of a property of the counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*) in one's own example (*svadṛṣṭānta*). If, in one's own example such as a jar, one admits the property of permanence belonging to the counter-example such as space, then the deficiency of the example regarding the probandum (*sādhyavikalatva*) would itself be the cause of defeat, not the abandonment of the proposition. Now, if it is thought: "By admitting the property of the counter-example, one abandons one's own example; and by abandoning the example, one abandons the entire thesis up to its conclusion; thus it is called the 'abandonment of the proposition,'" [we reply: in that case, it would simply be the abandonment of the example that is figuratively called the abandonment of the proposition. This is not a fault, because here the word "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) denotes the thesis (*pakṣa*). How so? Tāmarī says: "The *dṛṣṭa* is the subject, while the counter-subject is the *pratidṛṣṭānta*. We, however, say: the thesis is here figuratively designated by the word "example" due to its similarity in being the locus of the proof (*sādhanādhikaraṇatva*), and so forth. If it is argued that this is incorrect because the grounds for such figurative usage (*upacāra*) are not stated in the *Sahacaraṇādi-sūtra*, we say no; for that sūtra is intended merely as an illustration. There is no restrictive rule there, since figurative usage occurs even otherwise—as in "the boy is a lion," "the student is fire," "the pond is the ocean," or "the village is burnt" when only a part of the village is burnt. If it is argued that there is no figurative usage because of a lack of purpose, we say no; for figurative usage is observed even in the absence of a specific purpose—as in "the stick eats" or "the beds cry out. Furthermore, there is a purpose here: to show that even if one does not admit the property of the counter-example, if one relinquishes the matter proposed, it is indeed the abandonment of the proposition. The abandonment of the proposition occurs when one admits in one's own thesis a property of the counter-example that contradicts the probandum. For example: when the argument has been made, "Sound is impermanent because it is produced, like a jar," the opponent says: "If sound is held to be impermanent due to the common property of being produced, why is it not held to be permanent due to the common property of being incorporeal, like space?
