There is no difference between the two cases. Thus, being confounded by the opponent’s application of a futile rejoinder (*jāti*) or otherwise, the proponent says: "Let sound be permanent. By his admission of permanence, the proposition of impermanence is abandoned; therefore, the abandonment of the proposition is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

If it is argued that this is not so because [the opponent] does not accept it—supposing someone might think, "I do not accept any point of defeat (nigrahasthāna) at all"—then in that case, there would be neither victory nor defeat for anyone, and thus engagement in debate would be futile. Now, if there is some ground on account of which one is called defeated or a speaker of what is incorrect, is that not itself a point of defeat? How can one be a speaker of what is correct by abandoning one's own proposition? And how can there be no defeat?
{Dharmakīrti’s objection and its refutation}

But surely, having himself accepted that sound is impermanent, how can one who is composed accept it as permanent? If he were to accept it, he would be rendered doubtful by the observation of even the properties of the impermanent; this is not so. For one who does not recognize the fault in the opponent's statement, whose mind is captivated by the fact that [the argument] proves what is already established, accepts permanence. This is because error is a property of persons and because its causes are not fixed. Furthermore, no ground for defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) is possible for a wise person who is composed in mind, since grounds for defeat are characterized by either misconception (*vipratipatti*) or non-comprehension (*apratipatti*). Even a disputant who is in doubt does not manifest his own doubt, because of his desire for victory. Moreover, what is the use of saying more here? When someone, for whatever reason, admits a property belonging to a counter-example or otherwise abandons the matter previously asserted, for him there is the ground for defeat called "abandonment of the thesis" (*pratijñāhāni*).
(2) Shifting the thesis (pratijñāntara)

"When the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) is refuted, the statement of another purpose through a modification of the property (*dharma*) is 'shifting the proposition' (*pratijñāntara*). When the stated thesis—"Sound is impermanent because it is perceptible by the senses"—is refuted due to its deviation from the property of existence (*sattā*) and so forth, one makes a shift to another proposition by means of a modification of the property: "Just as a jar is non-omnipresent, so too sound is non-omnipresent and impermanent. The phrase "for that purpose" means for the sake of establishing the probandum; thus, the mention of "non-omnipresent" is the [new] statement. Some maintain: "This too is merely a proposition, and a proposition is not capable of proving another proposition; therefore, this is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) due to the employment of what is ineffective. This is incorrect, for this is actually a different reason (*hetvantara*), not a shifting of the proposition, because "non-omnipresence" is employed as a qualification of the reason. Furthermore, a proposition stated for the purpose of proving a proposition does not become a "shifting of the proposition"; rather, it is any one of the [other members] such as the reason, because it is employed for the sake of proving the probandum. Indeed, a proposition is defined as a statement made with the status of the probandum (*sādhya*). However, a statement made with the intention of a proof—even if it is unestablished—is not a proposition, as in: "Space is corporeal because it possesses color and other qualities."

Therefore, it is explained otherwise: when the meaning of the proposition (*pratijñā*) has been refuted in the argument "everything is impermanent because of existence" due to the absence of an example, there is a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of that property (*dharma*) characterized by being the subject of dispute—namely, its non-statement previously as a qualification of the proposition and its statement afterwards. In the phrase "for the sake of that" (*tadartha*), the word "that" (*tad*) refers back to the refutation, and the word "sake" (*artha*) signifies cessation (or purpose), as in the expression "this smoke is for the sake of mosquitoes. Thus, the meaning is that "for the sake of that" means for the sake of the cessation of the refutation. "Nirdeśa" (specification) refers to the statement with a qualification, namely: "Everything under dispute is impermanent"—this is a different proposition (*pratijñāntara*) and a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), like a different reason (*hetvantara*). For example, when a reason stated without qualification has been refuted, one who desires a qualification [offers] a different reason; likewise, here too, when a proposition stated without qualification has been refuted, one who desires a qualification should be seen as offering a different proposition, because the logic is the same.
(3) Contradiction of the Thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*):

"Contradiction between the thesis and the reason is contradiction of the thesis. For example: "Substance is distinct from its qualities, because it is not perceived as a separate entity from [qualities such as] color and so forth.
{The faults propounded by Kīrti and their refutation}.

If it is argued that there is no contradiction because distinctness exists even when the distinction between remote entities is not perceived, we say no; for this merely exposes a defect in the speaker’s argument. If you do not perceive the individual as one [with its qualities], how can you, being ignorant of it, make a proposition (*pratijñā*) in order to instruct another? For there is no instructor who is unlearned. Or, if you do perceive the distinction between quality (*guṇa*) and substance (*dravya*), then the reason (*hetu*) "because the distinction is not perceived" is self-contradictory. Thus, due to the contradiction between the statement of the proposition and the statement of the reason, there is a "contradiction of the proposition" (*pratijñāvirodha*). Furthermore, contradiction with perception and other means of valid cognition should also be understood here as a "contradiction of the proposition," since the mention of the "reason" is intended as an illustration.

As for what was said—that in cases such as "the ascetic is pregnant," the pointing out of a contradiction with one's own words (*svavacanavirodha*) in the thesis (*pratijñā*) is not proper, because it is useless, since it is already subsumed by the employment of a thesis that is not a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*), and because there can be no further defeat for one who is already defeated, like a fire that has been reduced to ashes—that is incorrect; for it has been previously established that the thesis is indeed a member of the proof. Thus, whether the analysis of the compound is "contradiction of the thesis" (*pratijñāyā virodhaḥ*) or "contradiction by means of the thesis" (*pratijñayā virodhaḥ*), there is no fault in either case. An example of a contradiction between the thesis and the reason (*hetu*) is: "A single entity does not exist, because the word 'entity' is applied to a collection. For a collection is not possible in the absence of a single [constituent], since a collection is indeed a unification of ones.

If it is argued that there is neither the employment of a thesis (*pratijñā*) nor of a reason (*hetu*) here, but rather this is merely a statement of conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*) for what has been established by another reason, and therefore there is no contradiction here—then what kind of statement would the statement of the thesis and the reason be? Furthermore, for one who maintains that there are only two members [of the syllogism], even the statement of conclusion is not a member of the proof (*sādhanāṅga*). For you do not accept any statement other than inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) as a member of the proof. And you maintain that inference for others is restricted to two members. Moreover, the statement of conclusion is not included within the statements of the reason or the example. Therefore, even the statement of conclusion is simply a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for you.

As for what was said—that no one who asserts that "the one does not exist" intends a collection (*samūha*) in the form of a synthesis (*samuccaya*)—that too is incorrect. For the entire world is not perceptible to you, and living beings are seen to possess diverse intentions; therefore, it is possible that someone might intend such a thing even in this way. Furthermore, one must employ words in debate according to their meanings as established in common worldly usage. Consequently, it should not be claimed that the word "collection" has some entirely different meaning.

As for what was said—that because contradiction resides in two things, there is no difference in meaning between the separate examples of the sublation of the reason and the sublation of the thesis—this is true, but not in reality; rather, the distinction is accepted from the perspective of the speaker's intention (*vivakṣā*). When one wishes to establish the thesis as the authority, then there is a contradiction of the reason by the thesis; but when one establishes the reason as the authority, then there is a contradiction of the thesis by the reason. Thus, the distinction arises from a difference in intended meaning. If it is argued that this is a case of "unestablished due to a different locus" (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddha*) because the term denoting the state (*bhāva-śabda*) is applied to a collection [of reasons], and therefore it is not a "contradiction of the thesis," we say no. This is because we accept the convergence of fallacies (*doṣa-saṃplava*), just as we accept the convergence of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-saṃplava*). Indeed, even in common worldly experience, one observes the mention of multiple defects regarding a single object. Furthermore, when multiple defects have been ascertained, whichever one is recalled at a particular time is the one pointed out then. Therefore, the rule that "only one defect must be stated" is not accepted in this treatise.

Even those contradictions with the thesis (*pratijñāvirodha*) that are included within the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) have their distinctions stated according to the speaker’s intention for the purpose of pointing them out, in the context of the examples of the "mistimed" (*kālātīta*). Therefore, there is no separate mention of contradiction with the thesis [as a distinct point].
(4) Abandonment of the Thesis (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*).

"Abandonment of the proposition (*pratijñā-saṃnyāsa*) is the withdrawal of the meaning of the proposition when the position [of the opponent] has been refuted. The withdrawal of the meaning of the proposition is its denial; for this reason, it is distinct from the "loss of the proposition" (*pratijñā-hāni*). In that case, one abandons the meaning of the proposition due to incapacity, but does not deny it by saying, "I did not indeed propose such a thing. Here, however, when the statement "fire is not hot" has been refuted because it is contradicted by perception, the proponent denies it out of fear of the ground of defeat consisting in a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*): "Look, O neutral witnesses! This is an unfounded reproach; I do not say that fire is not hot. This is the ground of defeat characterized as the abandonment of the proposition. The form *sampaśyadhvam* (you should look) is derived by adding the suffix *ātmanepada* according to the rule: "It should be stated that [the suffix is added] after the root *dṛś* as well, following the rule *sama-gamy-ṛcchi-pracchi*," etc.
The refutation stated by Kīrti and its rebuttal.

"Now, for one who has been defeated by a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), what is the need for recourse to the 'rejection of the proposition' (*pratijñāsaṃnyāsa*)? That alone is the proper point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*); why mention other [points] which are impossible to distinguish and are merely the behavior of the incoherent chatter of a eunuch? For in this way there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If one remains silent when the thesis is refuted, that silence is a point of defeat. One could likewise have to state 'fleeing,' and so forth. Therefore, this too is irrelevant. This is incorrect; because by the principle that "when the cause ceases, the effect also ceases," he wishes to avoid the fault of the fallacious reason by means of the denial of the proposition—just as one avoids the suffering caused by poison by abandoning the poison. To him it is replied: If you abandon the proposition, then for you the rejection of the proposition is the point of defeat; if you do not abandon it, then the previously mentioned [fallacious reason] applies. Furthermore, even when a correct proof is employed, someone might, being confounded by sophistry (*jāti*) and the like, deny the proposition; for him too this would be a point of defeat, or rather, it is a cumulative [point]. It is not that this is the only point of defeat for him. Or, speaking by way of concession (*abhyupagamavāda*): let that not be his point of defeat; nevertheless, by this rejection of the proposition, you are defeated. When the thesis is refuted, since silence and the like are already accepted by him, the refutation of that [proposition] occurs; therefore, nothing else is raised against him, and there is no fault because an exhaustive enumeration was not admitted.
(5) *Hetvantara* (Shifting the Reason):

"When a reason has been stated without qualification and refuted, [the proponent] shifting to a qualified reason is *hetvantara*. For example, when the argument "The Vedas are eternal because their author is not remembered" has been refuted by the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) of such examples as dilapidated wells, and the proponent then seeks to qualify the reason by adding "provided there is no interruption in the tradition," this is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called *hetvantara*, because he has resorted to a previous reason that was unproving.
{Kīrti’s critique and its refutation}

If it is argued that a second reason (*hetvantara*) is useless once [the first] has been defeated by the very fact of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), we say no; for the inconclusiveness is subsequently supported. [The proponent might argue: "This reason, when accompanied by a qualification (*saviśeṣaṇa*), does not deviate"; thus, having removed the inconclusiveness, he says: "First, the qualified reason was not stated; but now, even though a qualification has been added, it constitutes a different reason (*hetvantara*). However, its inconclusiveness remains exactly as it was before, because there is no difference between the qualified and the unqualified [reason]. If the qualified one possesses efficacy, then for what purpose was the unqualified one previously employed?

(6) *Arthāntara* (Irrelevant Matter): "A statement whose meaning is unrelated to the subject under discussion is *arthāntara*. For example: "Sound is eternal, because it is intangible"—this is the reason (*hetu*). And a reason is a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, derived from the verbal root *hi* with the suffix *tu*. Having thus introduced the fact that words are of four types—nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles—one proceeds to explain nouns and the others. Then, by way of digression and further digression, one teaches other irrelevant matters; since these do not serve the purpose of the subject at hand, this constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). {This is the restatement for the sake of praising and approving [the opponent's] fame.}

First, for the proponent, when it is necessary to provide a justification for the proof (*sādhana*) that has been presented, failing to do so and instead stating something else—whether relevant or irrelevant—is a ground for defeat (*parājaya-sthāna*). For the opponent as well, to introduce another point after merely pointing out a fault in the opponent's argument is likewise a departure to an irrelevant matter (*arthāntara*).
(7) *Nirarthaka* (The Meaningless).

"Meaningless (*nirarthaka*) is like the instruction of the sequence of letters. The "instruction of the sequence of letters" is the recitation of the established alphabet (*mātṛkā*); that which is similar to this is "like the instruction of the sequence of letters. That in which even the meaning of the words is not understood by both the judges (*prāśnika*) and the opponent (*prativādin*) is meaningless. For example: "Sound is eternal, because *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* are like *ja-bha-ḍa-da-śa*, [and] like *jha-bha-gha-ḍha-dha-ṣa*. {The faults mentioned by Kīrti and their refutation}

Even though words such as *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, and *ā* may have meanings in certain contexts, nevertheless, when used in this manner, not even a single word-meaning is well-established. Furthermore, one must employ words with meanings well-known to the judges (*prāśnika*) and others in debate. Since you are speaking using words whose conventions are unknown to them—just like the words of the Karṇāṭas and other regions—it fails to convey meaning; therefore, it is a "statement of a non-member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*), which is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). If it is argued: "This is saying too little; for then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even things like 'cheek-beating' (*kapolavāditaka*) or 'striking the side' (*kakṣapiṭṭanaka*) would have to be expressed [in debate]," we reply: No; because the sūtras are intended as illustrations, there is no prohibition against those [other things].
(8) Its meaning is not understood.

"Unintelligible meaning (*avijñātārtha*) is that which, even though stated three times by both the assembly and the opponent, is not understood. That which is to be said, even when stated three times, is not understood by the assembly and the opponent due to causes such as unintelligible usage, rapid pronunciation, and so forth; this, stated for the purpose of concealing one's ignorance, is the point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) called "unintelligible meaning. For example: "A cloth, which is a substance accompanied by sentient beings such as the Jain *tīrthaṅkara*s—[a cloth] which is the substratum for the grasping of objects by the pure cognition of the Tathāgata (who is the substratum for the cognition of the senses grasping all objects that are distinct entities)—is not a pot, because it does not produce a hare’s horn, like a cloth."
The Refutation of Faults Stated by Kīrti.

If it is argued that *nirarthaka* (the meaningless) does not differ from *ajñāna* (ignorance) because there is no distinction in their failure to convey meaning, we say no. In this case (*nirarthaka*), even when one attempts to connect the words and their meanings extensively, the meaning is not understood; nor is it non-different from *apārthaka* (the irrelevant), for in the latter, the sentence-meaning itself is impossible. Here, however, the sentence-meaning is possible, yet it is not understood due to causes such as being uttered too rapidly. If that is so, then the claim—"Because of stupidity, the assembly and others do not understand; therefore, the learned man does not deserve defeat"—is incorrect. For the adjudicators (*prāśnikas*) must be agreed upon by both parties and must not be stupid. Furthermore, it has been stated that [the speaker] cannot inform even the adjudicators because of causes such as the use of unfamiliar terminology or uttering words too rapidly; yet he is still called "learned"—oh, what learning! As for the further argument—"If he lacks the capacity to make the assembly understand, he would not be the victor, nor would he be subject to defeat"—that too is incorrect. Since one person possesses the capacity to make the assembly understand while the other does not, how could there be no victory or defeat? If he is incapable of making the assembly understand, why does he enter the debate at all? And who, and in what way, can recognize his status as a "speaker of reason" (*yuktavāditva*)?

(9) *Apārthaka* (the meaningless): "That which lacks a connection between preceding and succeeding parts due to the absence of a logical sequence is *apārthaka*. Where there is no connection between several words or sentences through their sequential arrangement, and thus a lack of coherence in meaning is perceived—that is called *apārthaka* because the collective sense of the whole is lost. For example: "Ten pomegranates, six cakes, a goat-skin, a lump of meat, a maiden’s drink from Roruka; her father has not yet eaten. This very same disconnected sentence or disconnected expression is what is meant by this term. (10) *Aprāptakāla* (out-of-order).

"Speaking with the components [of a syllogism] in reverse order is 'untimely' (aprāptakāla). The statement of the thesis and the other members in a sequence contrary to that required by the force of the meaning is a point of defeat (nigrahasthāna).
[These are faults imputed to the proponent]."

[Opponent: Even so, the meaning is established. [Proponent: If you argue that this is "like something devoid of words" (*śabdāpeta*), we say no. It might be thought thus: just as the word *goṇī* used for the meaning of the word *gaur* produces a cognition, but not directly—for instance, from the word *goṇī* there arises a memory of the word *gauḥ*, and from that word *gauḥ* brought forth by memory, the cognition of the object possessing a hump and so on occurs—so too, from the statement of the reversal of the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the other members, one grasps the sequence, and through that, the meaning of the sentence. [Response: This is unproven; you are attempting to prove something with what is itself unproven. That the cognition of meaning occurs from a correct word (*sādhuśabda*) through the cognition of a corrupt word (*apaśabda*) is precisely what is unproven, for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for such a process. Furthermore, while someone who knows both the word and the corrupt word might understand in this way, women, *śūdras*, and others do not know the distinction between correct words and corrupt words; how then will they grasp the word from the corrupt word and subsequently grasp the meaning from that?

Furthermore, it is observed that even for those who do not experience [the meaning] directly, there is no cognition [of the meaning] through a traditional lineage [of usage]. Moreover, that which is incapable of [producing cognition] regarding the object is likewise incapable of generating cognition regarding the word; for the capacity to convey (bodhakatva) is nothing other than the very act of generating a cognition whose object is that [meaning]. If an incorrect word (*apaśabda*) could generate cognition regarding the word itself, why would it not generate it regarding the meaning? Indeed, we perceive no difference between this [incorrect word] and the correct word such that one might exclude the former. Furthermore, because it fails to generate cognition even regarding the word for one who has not established a linguistic convention—since this incorrect word does not naturally produce cognition even regarding the word, as is never observed—if it were to generate [cognition] by virtue of convention, why would it not generate it regarding the meaning itself? In this way, the laborious effort of a continuous tradition of comprehension is avoided. And because the opposite is observed: people are seen to be mostly taught by means of incorrect words alone when they wish to understand the meaning from the word; thus, the grammatical analysis (*anvākhyāna*) of words is useless.

If it is argued that [the study of grammar] is not useless because it serves the purpose of deriving *saṃskṛta* words, what is this "refinement" (*saṃskāra*) of words? For we do not perceive in them any refinement such as wisdom or extensive learning; nor do they possess absolute musicality; nor is there any superiority in their capacity to convey meaning; nor do they serve as a means for achieving *dharma*, since unrighteousness arises even from refined words when they enjoin toward false conduct, while righteousness arises even from corrupt words (*apaśabda*) when they consist of pleasant, beneficial, and truthful speech. Furthermore, those who know logic do not honor mere verbal expression as scripture. Therefore, there is no such thing as a word called "refined."

If it is argued that "usage by the learned" (*śiṣṭaprayoga*) constitutes linguistic refinement (*saṃskāra*), then who are the "learned"? Those who possess qualities such as having known what is to be known. But what is this base persistence, independent of any excellence of quality, whereby they employ only these particular words and not others? Furthermore, there is no trustworthy witness with direct perception here, by virtue of whom we could determine with certainty: "These people, indeed, are the learned who employ [these words]. Indeed, not perceiving any superior quality (*guṇātiśaya*) nor any refinement (*saṃskāra*) in certain words, we do not approve of the effort to provide their grammatical derivation (*anvākhyāna*). Even if a superior quality were present, no effort toward derivation should be made, because that very nature [of the word] is established through other means, just like the Prakrits, Apabhraṃśas, Dravidian, Andhra, and other vernaculars. For there is no grammatical treatise (*lakṣaṇaśāstra*) for the various regional dialects; nevertheless, by force of tradition, the world understands them exactly as they are, as well as their corruptions. The understanding of Sanskrit words will likewise occur in this way; therefore, this engagement with grammar is merely the activity of the dull-witted.

Moreover, even in the world, when one states a logical argument (*nyāya*) using any word whatsoever regarding a subject of dispute, victory is observed even if there is a slip of the tongue; defeat is not seen. Therefore, an ungrammatical word (*apaśabda*) is not a ground for defeat.

Furthermore, if their connection is not perceived when the members [of the syllogism] are transposed, then this [transposition] is no different from "meaningless" (*apārthaka*) speech. But if the connection is indeed perceived, then why should it constitute a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*), even though there has been a statement of the members of the proof? For there is no such convention here that the members must be employed in this very order despite there being no difference in the resulting comprehension. It is precisely this sequence in which they are situated that allows the connection to be perceived. Indeed, there is no fixed rule regarding the order of words in a sentence, as in the cases: "the king's man" or "the man of the king. Therefore, there is no such thing as a point of defeat called "inappropriate timing" (*aprāptakāla*).

{The refutation of that} is stated: "This is like [the case of] a corrupt word (*apaśabda*). This is its meaning: just as a corrupt word is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) only within the context of a formal debate (*niyamakathā*), so too is [an argument] out of its proper time (*aprāptakāla*). Some seekers of victory are seen engaging in debate after having made a restriction regarding specific meters such as *sragdharā* based on their pride in their own knowledge. For them, the fault is precisely the failure to maintain what was promised. For once a rule has been established, the very manner in which it was spoken is the cause of victory or defeat, just as in games of dice and the like; there is no other principle involved therein. (11) {Deficiency (*nyūna*)}

"Deficient by even one of its members is [the argument] lacking. Since the establishment of the probandum is impossible in the absence of the means of proof (*sādhana*), and since the status of all five as members of the proof was established in that very discussion on the whole (*avayavin*), it has been stated therein how deficiency constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).
(12) *Adhika* (Redundancy).

"Exceeding [the required number] of reasons or examples is 'excessive' (*adhika*). Since the purpose is accomplished by one, the others are useless. This too is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) in a formal debate governed by rules (*niyamakathā*), but in a free-flowing discussion (*prapañcakathā*), there is no fault because such rules are absent; however, if one accepts the principle of convergence (*samplava*), this fault certainly does apply.
(13) *Punarukta* (Redundancy).

"Repetition (*punarukta*) consists in the restatement of word and meaning, except in the case of restatement for the sake of confirmation (*anuvāda*). That which is a purposeless utterance of a word or an expression of a meaning through a synonym should be understood as repetition. In this regard, "Sound is eternal, sound is eternal" is a repetition of the word. "Sound is eternal, sound is imperishable" is a repetition of the meaning. However, when there is a restatement of a word or a meaning by virtue of a specific purpose, that is not repetition, because it is a restatement for the sake of confirmation (*anuvāda*); as, for example, in a conclusion (*nigamana*). Therein, the phrase "therefore" (*tasmāt*) is a restatement of the meaning of the reason through a different word. "Sound is non-eternal" is a restatement of that very same meaning using that very same word. "The cow, the cow, the wish-fulfilling one" is a restatement of the word alone. In the same way, in cases such as distributive iteration (*vīpsā*) or the repetition of a sense, one should see that it is merely a restatement of the word.
{Dharmakīrti’s objection and its refutation}:

Now, if this is the case, then only one kind of repetition should be mentioned—namely, repetition of meaning (arthapunarukta)—since there is no such thing as repetition of words (śabdapunarukta) distinct from that. This is true; nevertheless, for the sake of the instruction of beginners, and with the intention of providing examples of its internal subdivisions, the subsequent sūtra is also commenced:
{another type of repetition}.

"Repetition (*punarukta*) is the restatement, by its own word, of that which has already been established through implication. For example, once the example based on similarity (*sādharmya-udāharaṇa*) has been stated, the statement of an example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-udāharaṇa*) is redundant, because the meaning is obtained through logical necessity (*nyāya*). Indeed, an example is for the purpose of establishing pervasion (*vyāpti*), and since that [pervasion] is demonstrated by one example alone, a second one is useless. Furthermore, if one [example] were insufficient, there would be no establishment of pervasion for purely positive (*kevalānvayin*) or purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) reasons. Even for one who holds that a reason must possess both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is no negative concomitance without positive concomitance, nor positive concomitance without negative concomitance; thus, since the second is established by the mention of the first alone, its separate statement is useless. If it is argued that both are stated for the purpose of making known the state of being both positive and negative concomitant, what is the use of such knowledge? For that knowledge is not a constituent part of the proof (*sādhana-aṅga*). Rather, it is non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). If that exists, it is understood by a single example alone. If it does not exist, then even both together are not a proof, just like the examples of space and a jar for the reason of "incorporeality" (*amūrtatva*) when proving "eternality" (*nityatva*).
Faults as they are censured by fame, and their refutation.

But how is repetition (*punarukta*) a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*)? Because it obstructs the conclusion of the discussion and because what has been done by one [speaker] becomes useless for the other. This too is a point of defeat only in a formal debate (*niyamakathā*), not elsewhere; for when explaining, one might even repeat oneself again and again before witnesses and others out of fear that they have not heard or understood correctly—therein there is no quibble (*chala*). If it is argued: "This is neither a teacher nor a student, therefore he need not be explained with effort," we say no; for witnesses must be explained with effort, and faults are stated if they are not so explained, and it is declared that "what has been stated three times" [is authoritative]. If it is argued: "This [repetition] does not differ from 'excess' (*adhika*)," that is true; however, just as with verbal repetition, excess is mentioned separately despite its internal sub-classifications. Nor was brevity of the aphorisms intended by this Sage; rather, it was the expansion of the student's understanding. And that occurs through a threefold statement: in some cases a summary, in some cases an elaboration, and in some cases a middle course.

(14) *Ananubhāṣaṇa* (Non-reproduction): "The failure to reproduce what has been understood and stated three times by the assembly is *ananubhāṣaṇa*. It is a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) for the respondent; for, not reproducing [the argument], upon what basis could one state the refutation of the opponent's position?
[This concerns] Dharmakīrti’s objections and their refutation.

[Objection: Surely there may be someone capable of providing an answer, but not of repeating [the opponent's argument] word-for-word. He does not deserve defeat for that reason alone; rather, his lack of confusion is understood precisely by means of a correct answer (*saduttara*). What is the use of repetition? [Reply: No; because it would follow that the answer would be without a subject matter (*nirviṣayatva*). Furthermore, it is contradictory to say that one provides a correct answer while not repeating [the argument]. Nor is this being asserted: that everything must first be uttered and only afterwards should the answer be stated. Rather, the answer should be stated after having restated [the argument] in some way or another; otherwise, it follows that the answer would be without a subject matter.

If it is argued: "Even if the opponent is unable to utter the discussion—which has been expanded excessively through incidental digressions (*prasaktānuprasakti*)—what impairment of his capacity for the reply that consists merely of the basis of the dispute is there by which he should be defeated? It is said in response: If the proponent (*vādin*) has made an elaboration such as the recitation of verses or the like, which is useless for proving the thesis (*pakṣasādhana*), or if he has made a difficult presentation, then it is the proponent himself who incurs the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) of "shifting to another subject" (*arthāntara*) or "unintelligible meaning" (*avijñātārtha*). In that case, there is no fault even in the opponent's failure to repeat [the proponent's words], provided the witnesses (*sākṣin*) so consider it. However, if the witnesses understand the presentation to be useful for the proof and not difficult, then how could the opponent’s failure to repeat it not be the point of defeat of "non-comprehension" (*apratipatti*)? In this regard, if the debate is restricted by the rule that "what has been stated twice need not be spoken," then there would necessarily be a fault in repeating everything beforehand; for one who intends to refute must repeat [the argument] again in order to demonstrate the specific fault, saying "this is the scope of this particular fault," whereby the previous repetition would become redundant. Conversely, if there is a rule that "everything must be repeated beforehand," then there is the fault of failing to repeat beforehand. But when the debate is unrestricted (*aniyamakathā*), then there is no fault even in repeating according to one's own preference.

But surely, what is this restriction that non-reproduction occurs only after [the statement] has been uttered three times? If the activity is for the purpose of making the opponent understand, then it should be stated even a hundred times in such a way that understanding arises. If, on the other hand, the activity is for the purpose of tormenting the opponent, even then why is it uttered only three times? The proponent should whisper into the ears of the witnesses and harass the opponent with difficult, unintelligible, or excessively concise statements, so that he becomes bewildered in formulating a reply and falls silent. Indeed, in a process intended to torment another, there is no principle whatsoever by which [utterances that are] difficult, unintelligible, or spoken too rapidly would be prohibited, nor by which uttering [the statement] three times would be enjoined. [Response: No; the mention of "three times" is for the purpose of indicating the permission of the assembly. For as long as the judges have not determined the incapacity of either party, they must continue to speak. Once the wise have examined both sides and authorized the witnesses as authoritative, it is not proper to later render them unauthoritative.

It is also incorrect to claim that there is no distinction between ignorance (*ajñāna*) and non-reproduction (*ananubhāṣaṇa*), because they are both equally characterized by a lack of comprehension; for their distinction is stated on the basis of a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*). Furthermore, [if one were to argue] that the meaning is already obtained through implication (*sāmarthya*), that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), which contradicts the intent of this detailed exposition (*prapañca-adhikāra*). If, however, there is a preference for brevity, then even that summary is indeed established through the two categories of misconception and comprehension; yet the undertaking of this detailed exposition is directed toward those who prefer elaboration, so there is no fault. (15) Ignorance (*ajñāna*) [is defined as follows:]

"And ignorance is the non-understanding of the meaning. When a statement has been uttered three times and its meaning is understood by the assembly, yet the opponent, even while repeating it, does not correctly comprehend the meaning, that is called "ignorance" (*ajñāna*), a point of defeat for the opponent.
(16) *Apratibhā* (Inability to Respond).

"Silence after having accepted the debate is *apratibhā* (lack of ingenuity), which is a point of defeat for both the proponent (*vādin*) and the opponent (*prativādin*). Now, one might object: "The sūtra states that *apratibhā* is 'the failure to perceive a reply' (*uttarasyāpratipattiḥ*)," and this is true; however, the meaning of this very [sūtra] has been stated by the words "after having accepted the debate," etc. How so? The mention of "reply" (*uttara*) is intended as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*); the intention is that the failure to perceive even the initial presentation (*pūrvopanyāsa*) is *apratibhā*. Furthermore, what is intended here by "failure to perceive" (*apratipatti*) is not merely a lack of understanding; rather, it is the inability to determine how to speak. The meaning is that *apratibhā* occurs when one remains silent due to such indecision. Alternatively, the speech of the first speaker is also called a "reply" (*uttara*) here. How? When the assembly or the opponent asks, "What is your position? What is your proof? or when there is an inquiry such as, "You yourself must state it first," the statement of the position and so forth constitutes the "reply. When, while that ought to be spoken, one remains silent due to indecision, then it should be declared that the proponent suffers from *apratibhā*. As for the opponent, however, it is possible—even after having repeated the argument—that he fails to perceive a reply, given the observation of the diversity of capacities. But even if he does not repeat it, silence on his part constitutes *apratibhā*. Even if one points out *apratibhā* to someone who remains silent, the repetition (*anubhāṣaṇa*) is not without a subject. For if someone says something else without repeating [the argument], but does not remain silent, then his failure to repeat (*ananubhāṣaṇa*) is the point of defeat.
(17) Distraction.

"Diversion (*vikṣepa*) is the interruption of the debate due to attachment to some other task. One who interrupts the debate by citing some task is indeed worthy of defeat, for while the debate ought to end with the defeat of one of the two parties, he himself brings the debate to an end. [Objection: If he is overwhelmed by suffering such as fever or by some urgent necessity, and thus does not speak now but will speak on another day, what fault would there be in that? He might have announced his suffering or necessity even before the assembly had gathered. However, announcing such things once the members of the assembly have already gathered surely reveals a malicious intent—namely: "The members will not gather again and again; therefore no debate will take place; consequently, I shall have equality with the learned, and not defeat. If, however, the suffering from quartan fever or the like occurs at that very moment and the witnesses acknowledge it, then there is no fault in that. Nor does this fall under the category of "irrelevance" (*arthāntara*). "Irrelevance" consists in speech that is useless to the context of presenting a proof (*sādhana*), whereas diversion is specifically the statement, "I shall present the proof later"—this is the distinction.
(18) Admission of the Opponent's Position (*matānujñā*)

"Accepting a fault in one's own position [and thereby] attributing it to the position of the opponent is 'admission of the opponent's view' (*matānujñā*). For example, when it is said, 'You are a thief, because you act with the desire to seize another's property,' the opponent replies, 'You too are a thief in this same way. If it is argued that there is no fault here because the point of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) is being exposed under the guise of a reductio (*prasaṅga*), that is incorrect; for the intention of the speaker is understood from his words. Without an explicit statement exposing inconclusiveness—whether before or after—it cannot be known that 'this person spoke thus with the intention of exposing inconclusiveness. Furthermore, even in formal debate (*vāda*), one should not speak using sentences whose meaning must be inferred through interpretation. Moreover, it is only logical that a reason is inconclusive if it occurs in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) based on what is established for both parties. And as for the claim that 'my activity [of desiring another's property] does not exist,' [if the opponent says] 'it is unestablished for me as well,' then one should simply state its lack of establishment; why resort to attributing a fault to the opponent? If it is argued that it is a reductio according to the principle 'that which belongs to both,' etc., we say no; for the equality of the security and vulnerability (*tulyayogakṣematva*) of both positions has not been proven by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, even when the avoidance of a fault in one's own position has been stated, if the opponent does not understand it due to delusion, then in order to remove that delusion, it is appropriate to employ a reductio such as 'that which belongs to both,' etc., after first establishing the equality of the security and vulnerability of one's own logic with the logic accepted by the opponent. However, he who does not avoid even the slightest fault in his own position but merely attributes a fault to the opponent's position—saying, 'You too are a thief'—is indeed, by speaking thus, admitting the opponent's view. And for one who admits the opponent's view, this very ground of defeat called 'admission of the opponent's view' (*matānujñā*) occurs. Why? Because he accepts his own fault, whereas the opponent does not."

(19) Overlooking the censurable (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇam*): "Overlooking the censurable is the failure to censure one who has reached a point of defeat. One who is censurable (*paryanuyojya*) is one who ought to be challenged because a ground for defeat has arisen; overlooking him means failing to challenge him by saying, "You have reached defeat. [This concludes the removal of the fault stated by Kīrti.]

When the assembly is asked, "Whose defeat is this?", they must state [the answer]. Indeed, one who has incurred defeat should not expose his own private parts (*kaupīna*). If it is argued that determining victory for one who has incurred defeat is improper, and because of its absence, defeat is also improper—since defeat depends upon victory—[we reply: no; it is improper for neither of them, because [in that case] the assembly would be indifferent due to their ignorance of what is proper and improper, and thus the defeat here consists precisely in the fact that his speech is not attended to. If, however, he points out some fault, then even if he does not point out every other fault of the opponent, he is indeed the victor; there is no defeat for him, for it is not the case that "he is defeated" simply because of that. All faults should be stated, or else there is defeat if they are not stated, because even a single one establishes that proof, just like the statement of a single means of proof (*sādhana*). Just as when many means of proof exist for a single object, the object is established by even one means of proof, so there is no requirement to employ all of them, nor is there a failure to state a member of the proof. However, in a debate where there is a rule that one must point out all possible faults, then even if only one is pointed out, the neglect of what ought to be questioned (*paryanuyojyopekṣaṇa*) is properly considered a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*).

(20) *Niranuyojyānuyoga* (the accusation against one who is not to be accused): "The attribution of a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) where there is no point of defeat is *niranuyojyānuyoga*. The meaning is: the pointing out of a fault where there is no fault. For example, when the provability of the effect-nature of earth and so forth is being established by means of their having parts, an opponent might say: "This is a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), specifically one that is non-probative (*aprayojaka*). This constitutes for him a point of defeat characterized by a false accusation. For there is no such thing as a fallacious reason called "non-probative" distinct from the unestablished (*asiddha*) and others; because [a reason] that subsists in only a portion of the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) is indeed a prover, just like smoke and the like. {The refutation of the fault stated by Kīrti}

If it is argued that this is not distinct from *apratibhā* (inability to respond), because it is simply the failure to provide a reply due to the subsequent argument being untenable, we say no; for *apratibhā* has been explained as having the essential nature of remaining silent. Furthermore, what is intended there is merely a reply, and not necessarily a valid one.
{21} *Apasiddhānta* (Deviation from an Accepted Tenet).

"Deviation from a tenet (*apasiddhānta*) is the occurrence of a debate by not adhering to a rule after having accepted a final doctrine (*siddhānta*). For example—having accepted the Mīmāṃsā system, someone says that the *agnihotra* sacrifice is a means to attain heaven. He is then questioned as follows: "But how can the act of the *agnihotra*, once it has perished, become a producer of heaven? Being thus questioned, and seeing no other way out since he does not accept *dharma* as a quality of the self (*ātman*), he says: "The Supreme Lord, propitiated by that action, bestows the fruit, just like a king. Because he does not accept [the existence of] God (*īśvara*), this is also a defeat-ground (*nigrahasthāna*) due to deviation from a tenet. However, some explain the meaning of the Sūtra thus: "Deviation from a tenet is to be understood as the occurrence of a debate by one who asserts the contrary of a matter already promised. This is incorrect; for the contrary of a promised matter is indeed "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*), not "deviation from a tenet. Therefore, deviation from a tenet is when, having accepted a treatise (*śāstra*), one carries on a debate in contradiction to its meaning. Alternatively, "abandonment of the proposition" refers specifically to the contrary of the meaning of the proposition made within a proof-statement (*sādhanavākya*). But "deviation from a tenet" refers to when a proposition is made merely by accepting an established fact, and one then carries on a debate by asserting the contrary of that meaning through some incidental argument (*prasaṅga*).
(22) Fallacious Reasons (hetvābhāsas)

"And the fallacies of the reason (*hetvābhāsa*) as they have been described. Are the fallacies of the reason points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*) by virtue of possessing a different definition, like the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of valid cognition (*prameya*)? No; what then? They are points of defeat as fallacies of the reason precisely by the definition of the fallacies of the reason as it has been described. This is the meaning. The word "and" (*ca*) includes the fallacies of the example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāsa*). Furthermore, the aphorisms do not intend to provide an exhaustive enumeration of the points of defeat; rather, they serve as illustrations for the detailed exposition of their definitions and examples. Therefore, by this collection of aphorisms, one should understand that things such as "difficult speech" (*durvacana*) constitute points of defeat because they are useless for the proof (*sādhana*). However, in a formal debate (*niyamakathā*), even ungrammatical words (*apaśabda*) and the like are included.
The refutation of Dharmakīrti’s established doctrine.

But Raktāmbara says: "The failure to state a member of the proof (*asādhanāṅgavacana*) and the failure to point out a fault (*adoṣodbhāvana*) are the two points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). Any other [point of defeat] is not tenable; thus [we] do not accept [them]. In this regard, the failure to state a member of the proof is a point of defeat for the proponent (*vādin*) alone, whereas the failure to point out a fault is for the opponent (*prativādin*) alone. Success (*siddhi*) is the ascertainment of what is to be proven by the proof; a "member" (*aṅga*) is that which brings about this [success]. The statement of such a member is the "statement of a member of the proof" (*sādhanāṅgavacana*). Not stating it is the "failure to state a member of the proof" (*asādhanāṅgavacana*), whether due to silence from lack of ingenuity after having accepted the debate, or due to failing to support a member of the proof. This is a point of defeat for the proponent because he fails to establish the matter he has undertaken. Even if he employs a proof that is factually capable, it is so because he fails to demonstrate its capability; for there is no establishment of the probandum (*sādhya*) from a proof that has not been supported. Alternatively, "proof" (*sādhana*) is that by which something is proven—the collection of statements regarding the three-fold reason (*trirūpahetu*). A "member" of that is the statement of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharma*) and so forth. Not stating even one of these is the "failure to state a member of the proof. Or again, it is the statement of that which is not a member of that very proof—such as the thesis (*pratijñā*), the application (*upanaya*), and so on—which are not members of the proof. Or else, since there is no establishment [of the probandum] by the expression of only one of the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) or negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), the other is ineffective; thus, the statement of even that which is not a member of the proof is a point of defeat, precisely because it is a useless statement. Or again, "proof" is the establishment [of the probandum], and a "member" of that is the property belonging to the subject of dispute which is the cause for introducing the debate. That is a "member of the proof. Apart from that, the introduction or proclamation of another unasked-about particularity under the pretext of relying on a treatise (*śāstra*) and so forth—for the sake of deluding the opponent, or to obstruct the power of his response—is also the "failure to state a member of the proof," a point of defeat, because it is a statement of what is irrelevant (*aprastuta*). For a relevant connection (*prasaṅga*) is never not applicable, since even dancing, singing, and the like can occur by way of a relevant connection. For example, some proponent of selflessness might say: "There is no self; we Buddhists say so. "Who are the Buddhists? "Those who have accepted the teaching of the Buddha. "Who is the Buddha? "He whose teaching the venerable Aśvaghoṣa took up when he went forth [into the religious life]. "Who is the venerable Aśvaghoṣa? "He whose play is the *Rāṣṭrapāla*. Having made this series of connections, he might then recite "Then enters the Stage Manager" and so forth, and dance and sing. The opponent would be defeated because he is unable to repeat that entire series of connections; therefore, like the digression into dancing and so forth, the proclamation of matters resulting from a succession of irrelevant connections and from one's own actions is merely "shifting to another matter" (*arthāntara*). However, if there is a desire to know [the details], there is no fault.

"Non-exposure of a fault" (*adoṣodbhāvana*) means the non-exposure of a fault; that is, the non-exposure or non-communication of faults such as fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). This occurs because the proof (*sādhana*) is faultless. Or, even if it were faulty, it might be due to the opponent's ignorance of that fault, or due to an incapacity to demonstrate it. For a fault, even if it exists, does not become a cause for defeat (*parājaya*) unless it has been demonstrated. Alternatively, the exposure of a non-fault as if it were a fault of the proof is a point of defeat for the opponent, because of the utterance of a false rejoinder (*mithyottara*). This is the correct definition of a point of defeat. However, other points of defeat mentioned by the Naiyāyikas, such as the "abandonment of the proposition" (*pratijñāhāni*) and so forth, are not tenable and are therefore not accepted. Just as Kīrti stated that the abandonment of the proposition and the like are untenable, I have already explained this individually while presenting the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding their definitions. By refuting them right there, Kīrti’s lack of full understanding has also been revealed. Furthermore, his delusion—when he attempted to justify the status of the proposition, the application (*upanaya*), and so forth, as being limbs of the proof—is made manifest here when it is claimed that stating the proposition, the application, and so on, constitutes a point of defeat. As for those points of defeat shown by the Sage (the Buddha) which are merely stated in different terminology, they are indeed accepted; for even when expressed in different terminology, there is no contradiction with the fact that the meaning remains the same.
The second chapter, the Chapter on Scripture (*Āgamapariccheda*), in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, a Compendium of Explanations (*Saṃgrahavārtika*) composed by the venerable teacher Bāsarvajña, is completed.

Inference has been concluded; now the definition of scripture (*āgama*) is stated: "Scripture is that which, by the power of convention (*samaya*), is the means for correctly realizing the imperceptible. That instrument—whether consisting of words or not consisting of words—in which the predominance of convention is understood through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) as the means for realizing [the object], and which brings about realization through the efficacy of convention, is called scripture. We observe a distinction between convention (*samaya*) and invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*); therefore, the over-extension [of the definition] to inference is precluded by the inclusion of the term "convention. Furthermore, because doubt and error sometimes arise even through the efficacy of convention, the term "correctly" (*samyak*) is included. The term "imperceptible" (*parokṣa*) is included to exclude conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*).

{Establishing Non-contradiction with the Sūtra Definition} Now, one might object: "The definition of verbal testimony (śabda) in the Sūtra is 'verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person' (āptopadeśaḥ śabdaḥ). True; however, this very meaning has been clarified [in the commentary] as follows: that by which an object is taught is called "instruction" (upadeśa), which refers to a means of cognizing an object that depends upon convention (samaya). For an object known through perception or inference is not said to be "cognized through instruction. Nor is an object that is doubtful or erroneous said to be "taught" [by instruction].

Alternatively, it should be understood that the two terms *avyabhicāri* (non-erroneous) and *vyavasāyātmaka* (determinate in nature) are carried over from the *Sūtra* on perception (*pratyakṣa-sūtra*) here as well; consequently, there is no possibility of [the definition] applying to doubt (*saṃśaya*) or error (*viparyaya*). In this way, the inclusion of the term *āpta* (reliable person) is not for the purpose of defining [verbal testimony], because there is nothing to be excluded by it; rather, it is intended to indicate the reason—namely, being spoken by a reliable person—for establishing the validity of statements whose objects are not perceived. Or, let it serve as a definition, provided that the carrying over of the terms *avyabhicāri* and so forth is not accepted here. Furthermore, since the word *upadeśa* (instruction) is seen even in the case of false instruction, the inclusion of *āpta* is meaningful. For a "reliable person" (*āpta*) is said to be an instructor free from defects such as ignorance and passion; his instruction is indeed valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus it has been said:
For tradition (āgama) is the word of a reliable person (āpta); they know reliability to be the destruction of faults.
One whose faults have been destroyed would not speak an untrue statement, because the cause [for doing so] is absent. Thus it is said.

If it is argued that [the definition] is not a valid characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*) because it is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*), we say no; for the destruction of defects (*doṣakṣaya*) is also twofold, due to the distinction between the inferior (*apara*) and the superior (*para*). Among these, the inferior destruction of defects belongs to those such as ordinary reliable persons (*āpta*), Śākyas, and Mlecchas, because their cessation of ignorance and so forth is restricted to specific objects. However, the superior destruction of defects belongs to the supreme reliable person (*para-āpta*), such as Īśvara, because of the absolute eradication of ignorance and so forth regarding all objects. Now, one might object: "Even the instruction of a reliable person (*āptopadeśa*) may fail to produce [valid] knowledge, or may even produce doubt and the like, due to deficiencies in the listener’s intelligence and other factors. Therefore, how can the instruction of a reliable person be considered a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in an absolute sense? We reply: No, because that [usage] is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). For there is no established convention anywhere that a word which does not produce knowledge, or which produces a doubtful cognition, is called "the instruction of a reliable person. Rather, when a reliable person teaches a matter and thereby causes others to ascertain it, he is called "the instruction of a reliable person" in the primary sense (*aṃjasā*) because he effects an unerring ascertainment of the object for others.

Alternatively, it is "instruction" (*upadeśa*) that has been "obtained from a reliable person" (*āpta*). Just as one who speaks while failing to produce knowledge, or producing doubt or error, is not called a "reliable person" even in common worldly usage, but rather one who causes the determination of an object exactly as it is (*aviparīta*) is known as a reliable person; so too, verbal testimony (*śabda*) is called "reliable" when it effects the determination of an object without error. [Objection: In that case, the definition should be made more concise as simply "the speech of a reliable person" (*āptavāk*). [Reply: No; because this would fail to include non-verbal forms of communication such as gestures (*ceṣṭā*). However, by including the term "instruction," everything by which an object is communicated—whether through a gesture of the finger or other means based on convention (*samaya*)—is obtained as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called "verbal testimony. It is for this very reason that the exclusion of memory (*smṛti*) and perception (*pratyakṣa*) is also secured. For there is no established consensus that an object remembered after hearing a word, or an object perceived through conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*), is ever designated as "instructed by a reliable person. Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is precisely this: *Āgama* is the means for the correct experience of an imperceptible object (*parokṣa*) by virtue of convention.
{The Buddhist restriction to two types of valid cognition} Now, if sound has as its object an imperceptible thing, it follows that it is not distinct from inference. And thus it has been said:
"Indeed, the means of valid cognition is twofold because the objects of cognition are twofold, due to [the senses'] capacity and incapacity."
"In purposeful action, there is no object [in the case] of hair [nets] and so forth, because of the conviction that they are non-objects."

The proof of the twofold nature of the means of cognition (*māna*) has as its reason the twofold nature of the objects of cognition (*meyadvaividhya*). As for the twofold nature of the objects of cognition, the reason is their capacity (*śakti*) and incapacity (*aśakti*). Capacity is the ability to produce a cognition that bears its own form directly; incapacity, however, is the lack of such ability through indirect succession, understood by way of exclusion (*paryudāsa-vṛtti*). Among these, the object that is capable is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), because it is characterized by its own nature, and it is the object of perception (*pratyakṣa*). The other, however, is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because it is cognized in a general form, and it is the object of inference (*anumāna*). But as for things like [illusory] hair, which are not within the scope of the two means of valid cognition, they possess neither direct nor indirect capacity toward causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); therefore, they are not real objects. Consequently, because there is a conceptual determination (*adhimokṣa*) of them as non-objects, the cognition thereof is not a valid means of knowledge, since there is no comprehension of a real object due to the determination of what is not an object. In another treatise, he states this very same point: "The object is indeed twofold—perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and imperceptible (*parokṣa*). Therein, that which causes the appearance in cognition to conform to its own presence and absence (positive and negative concomitance) is the perceptible; it is the unique, real form of the thing, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). The other, however, lacks the capacity to directly impose its own nature [upon cognition] and is merely an improper apprehension. It is not logical to imagine one thing when seeing another, because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*); rather, it would occur through an invariable connection (*nāntarīyakatā*). For that [inferential mark], being a connected nature, indicates the proximity of a thing of a certain kind exactly as it is established. And since inference is the cognition of a related object by way of a general property (*sāmānya*), there are only two means of valid cognition, because otherwise cognition would be impossible.
{The refutation of that}

To this it is replied: By what means is the twofold nature of the objects of cognition (*meyadvaividhya*) known? If it were known by the very twofold nature of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇadvaividhya*), there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If, on the other hand, it were known by perception (*pratyakṣa*) alone, then inference (*anumāna*) would be useless, because even that which is beyond the senses (*parokṣa*) would be established by perception alone. Furthermore, it is not logical for that which is grasped by perception itself to be "beyond the senses. And if it is not grasped [by perception], the twofold nature of the objects of cognition cannot be established through perception. Nor can the twofold nature be established through inference, because inference is preceded by perception. If it were established by another means of valid cognition, there would be a contradiction, since a third category would also be possible. The argument based on "capacity and incapacity" (*śaktyaśakti*) is also incorrect—by what is the distinction between capacity and incapacity understood? Thus, the same undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows as before. Therefore, since the twofold nature of the objects of cognition is unestablished, how can it serve as a proof?

As for what was stated here—"The twofold nature of objects is accessible through perception. For the cognition of similarity and dissimilarity is a property of cognition itself, and that is established by the perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*)"—this is the speech of one who is utterly deluded. For it is not the case that a property of cognition is itself the object of knowledge (*prameya*), since [the object] is defined by its capacity or incapacity [to produce a cognition]; nor does a property of cognition, which is not a distinct entity, possess the quality of generating a cognition, whether directly or indirectly. Furthermore, how can a property of cognition be called "similarity" when it is common to others? Because it does not occur elsewhere, it is characterized by dissimilarity. Moreover, a superimposed form (*samāropitākāra*) is not an object of perception; and it is illogical for even that which is an object of the perception of self-awareness to be "remote" (*parokṣa*), like passion and other such states. If it is argued: "By self-awareness, the property of remoteness is grasped. But the remote object is grasped by another sensory cognition that perceives the substratum (*dharmin*). From that, there is the cognition of the relation; then, although the property of remoteness is perceived through perception, the thing itself is cognized through inference. To this we reply: we do not understand how a remote object could be perceived by sensory perception. Even if one accepts the identity (*tādātmya*) of the property and the substratum, no one but a person of impaired intellect would claim that they are apprehended by different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Because there are two kinds of objects of cognition, the establishment of two kinds of means of valid cognition is not proven.

Furthermore, even if there were a twofold division of objects of cognition (*prameya*) based on the distinction between the perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) and the imperceptible (*parokṣa*), how could it be established that there are only two means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), namely perception and inference? This is because [the reason] is irrelevant (*vyadhikaraṇatva*) and because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is not proven. Moreover, the distinction between means of valid cognition is intended to be established through a distinction in their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*). Yet, you have not even now stated that the definition of a specific means of cognition is "having a specific object of cognition" (*meyaviśeṣaviṣayatva*), by which the absence of other means of cognition would be established due to the absence of other objects of cognition. Nor can verbal testimony (*śabda*) be subsumed under the definition of perception—as being "free from conceptual construction" (*kalpanāpoḍha*)—or under the definition of inference—as being "born from a three-featured mark" (*trirūpaliṅgaja*), such that the reason "because it is included within these very [two]" would not be unproven (*asiddha*). Now, you might say: "It was stated that otherwise comprehension would be impossible. True, this was stated; however, what was stated is incorrect. For instance, from words such as "the ocean water is salty" or "Mount Himālaya stands to the north," there arises a comprehension of an object, yet this is neither born of perception nor born of inference, because the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth are not perceived. Therefore, verbal testimony is a distinct means of valid cognition.

{The statement that a word is an indicator of intention} Now, it might be argued that only a word that indicates a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*) possesses the status of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) due to its non-deviation from the object, and that such a word is exclusively an inference for others (*parārthānumāna*). As for other words, they do not possess validity at all. As it has been said:
"Because there is no necessary connection (*nāntarīyakatā*) between words and real entities..."
Therefore, there is no establishment of the object [from them], for they merely indicate the intention of the speaker.

For when a relation exists, one object makes another object known, as smoke [makes] fire [known], or a *śiṃśapā* [tree makes] a tree [known]. However, words do not possess even one of these two types of relations with real entities; therefore, there is no establishment of the object from them. The meaning is that there is no establishment of the object from those words. But words are preceded by the speaker’s intention; therefore, they indicate the speaker’s intention. {The refutation of that}

To this it is replied: as for the claim that [verbal testimony] is not a separate means of knowledge because of the absence of *nāntarīyakatā* (invariable concomitance), what is this *nāntarīyakatā*? Is it merely a relation, or is it inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*)? First, there certainly exists a mere relation between word and object, since the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācyavācakabhāva*) is established. Now, if it is inseparable connection, then precisely because of its absence, it is said that verbal testimony is a distinct means of knowledge, like perception. If, by virtue of being inseparably connected and thus conveying an object, the word were nothing but inference, who would say it is a separate means of knowledge? On the other hand, if it is argued that because of the absence of inseparable connection, there is no capacity to convey an object at all—that is not so, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) seen in the case of the sense organs. It is also incorrect to say that their capacity to cause the cognition of objects is inherent, since they depend on lamps and other factors. Just as the sense organs establish an object by depending on specific auxiliary conditions such as lamps, so too words establish an object by depending on specific auxiliary conditions such as the recollection of conventions. For causes have non-fixed auxiliaries; therefore, one thing may be the auxiliary for another. Thus, even in the absence of *nāntarīyakatā*, it is illogical to claim that words lack the capacity to establish an object.

It might be thought: "Even for perceptual cognitions, the establishment of their own form occurs through identity (*tādātmya*), whereas the establishment of the external object occurs through origination from that (*tadutpatti*). Since the sense organs (*akṣa*) also possess the relation of origination from the objects, all [cognitions] establish the object precisely by way of being invariably concomitant with it. In this regard, because the restriction to these two types of relations has been refuted and because momentariness is unestablished, the origination of the sense organ and the object from one another is unestablished.

Furthermore, what connection can there be between the cognitions of a yogi and objects that are past or future? For it has already been stated that those objects lack the capacity to produce [cognition]. If it is argued that [the cognition] arises from them through a causal series (*pāramparya*), we say no; for future objects do not possess the capacity to produce [anything] even through a causal series. Indeed, no cognition has been directly produced by them such that one could postulate the production of subsequent cognitions through a causal series via the arising of their respective latencies (*vāsanā*). If it is argued that there is the capacity to produce [cognitions] of the same class (*tajjātīya*), we say no; because that which is the producer is itself past. Moreover, a cognition produced from one thing of a certain class does not determine another object, as this would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). It would follow that a cognition produced from a single object—such as a woman or gold—would have the capacity to determine all women, all gold, and so forth.

Furthermore, why is it not postulated that sound (*śabda*) also arises from the object (*artha*)? For that too arises through the sequence of impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the cognition born of the object. If it is argued that this is not accepted because of deviation (*vyabhicāra*), the following thought might occur: if there were a necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between word and object characterized by "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), then the word would never deviate from the object, since deviation and necessary connection are contradictory. If that is so, then one must likewise not accept a necessary connection between the excellence of mental cultivation (*bhāvanāprakarṣa*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) with respect to the object, because they also deviate from the object. To explain: first, the sense organ produces a cognition manifesting hair and such objects even when those objects are non-existent. Likewise, the excellence of mental cultivation generates a cognition manifesting women and such even when those are non-existent. Therefore, a necessary connection with the object must not be accepted for either the cognition born of the excellence of cultivation or the sensory cognition. If you say: "Not all sensory cognition and cognition born of the excellence of cultivation is held to be connected to the object; rather, only that which does not deviate from the object is held to be connected to it," then we reply: surely the necessary connection is sought for the sake of establishing non-deviation. If that [non-deviation] is established even without the establishment of a necessary connection, what is the use of proving a necessary connection? If non-deviation is established only through the establishment of a necessary connection, there follows the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

Furthermore, even regarding verbal cognition (*śabdajñāna*), why should there be no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) for that which is erroneous, while for that which is non-erroneous with respect to its object, a connection with the object is not accepted? If [you claim] there is no connection because of the error of what is similar to it, then it would follow that sensory cognition (*akṣajādijñāna*) and the like would also lack a connection due to the error of what is similar to them. Just as those who know those cognitions distinguish between the erroneous and the non-erroneous among sensory cognitions and the like, so too [should they do] for verbal cognitions; thus, everything is the same.

As for what was stated—that [words] "indicate the speaker’s intention"—that is incorrect, because it would entail the consequence that there is no engagement with actual objects. For engagement with things not themselves perceived is not possible through the cognition of something else, as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, if engagement occurred through error, it would entail the consequence that there is no rule governing engagement with a specific object based on a specific word, and it would also entail the consequence of a lack of correspondence (*asaṃvāda*).
{The refutation of the theory that the cognition of the object occurs by way of the speaker’s intention}

If it is argued that the meaning is understood from the word once the speaker’s intention (*vivakṣā*) has been apprehended, we say no; for there is no necessary connection between the intention and the object, since we observe that an intention arises even when the object does not exist. What, then, is this "intention"? Is it merely the desire to utter a sound, or is it the mental resolve (*abhiprāya*) "I shall communicate this specific meaning by means of this specific word"? What follows from this? If one were to understand only the desire caused by the word, then neither speaker nor listener would engage with treatises and the like; for no sane person would exert themselves to compose or listen to a treatise or another sentence merely to convey the desire caused by the word. Furthermore, all sentences would become indistinguishable from such strings as "ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa" or "ten pomegranates," because they would all equally lack distinction in being mere indicators of the desire arising from their own source. Now, if "intention" is defined as the resolve "I shall communicate this meaning by means of this word," and words are called inference because they indicate that [resolve], even so, words are not inference due to fallibility (*vyabhicāra*). For parrots, starlings, madmen, and others do not utter sentences with such a [specific] resolve. Moreover, does such a sentence convey that resolve independently of linguistic convention (*samaya*), or dependent upon it? If it were independent of convention, it would follow that everyone could understand it, and no one would be ignorant of a particular language. But if the word depends on convention, why does it not convey the object itself? For the word does not fear the object, such that it would fail to apply directly to it. Nor is it experienced that the understanding of the object occurs through an intermediate step of understanding the resolve. Furthermore, the logical principle regarding the non-application of words to objects where a convention is impossible applies equally to the resolve; thus, there would be no comprehension of the resolve from words either. Or, if words apply to a specific resolve in a certain manner, let them apply to the object itself in that same manner—why resort to an indirect succession that contradicts actual experience?
