{There is a fault in the word’s direct application to the object}. Now, for one who desires the word to apply directly to the object, there is a contradiction with its producing a non-manifest form, just as in the case of the sense organs. For it is not logical that there should be a difference in cognition when the object is not different; yet there is a difference between knowledge born of the senses and knowledge born of words. Therefore, the objects are not identical. As it has been said:
"That which is grasped by the senses is one thing; the range of the word is another."
One with impaired vision understands [the object] from the word, but does not perceive it through direct perception.

In this regard, the proposition is stated in the first half [of the verse], and its proof is stated in the second half. The meaning is that even one whose sense organs are impaired understands an object from a word, but does not perceive it as one does through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). He clarifies this very point:
"A burnt person conceives of the sensation of burning differently when it arises from contact with the sense organ;
the meaning of burning is understood quite differently by means of the word 'fire'."
Therefore, the word does not function with respect to the object of the sense-faculty.
{The refutation thereof}

This is incorrect because, in this case, the difference in cognition is not caused by a difference in the object (*viṣaya*), but rather by a difference in the instrument (*karaṇa*). If it were caused by a difference in the object, then the subsequent activity (*pravṛtti*) preceded by those cognitions of water and fire would not have a non-different object, just as [an activity] preceded by the cognitions of water and fire [does not]. Furthermore, there would be no correspondence (*saṃvāda*) for a cognizer who has acted upon the cognition born from the word "fire" when he actually attains the fire through his sense organ. Indeed, even in the world, the establishment of correspondence is never seen in the case of a cognition that is objectless or one whose object is something else when there is the attainment of a different object. Due to the absence of such correspondence, no one would possess the status of a speaker of truth. Moreover, there is a contradiction between the two terms of the proposition; for instance: how can that object which is expressed by the word "something else indeed is perceptible by the senses" not be within the range (*gocara*) of the word? If you say it is not its direct range, then does a cognition of that object arise from the word through an indirect succession (*pāramparya*) or not? If it does not arise, then it is not its range even indirectly. If it does arise, is it identical to the cognition produced by the sense organ, or is it different from it? If it is identical to it, then there is a contradiction with the statement, "But it does not perceive it directly. If it is different from it, then the difference in cognition cannot be the proof for a difference in the object.

And what meaning is expressed by the word "burning" (*dāha*)—is it fire, or hot touch, or a specific color, or a blister, or the pain thereof? What follows from this? All these meanings are understood exactly as they are from a word whose convention has been established for each respective object. However, the word "fire" has its convention established only for fire; therefore, it does not denote a blister and so forth. And fire is understood from that [word]. If this is so, why does it not become a blister or that pain? No, because it has a different causal function. Indeed, blisters and the like are not the effect of the cognition of burning; rather, they are the effect of a specific relationship between the fire and the body. This is because blisters and the like are seen due to a specific relationship with the fire even when there is no cognition of the fire during states such as deep sleep, whereas they are not seen by one standing at a distance even when the fire is cognized by the eye. Likewise, the objection that "if the pain were cognized from the word 'pain,' it would follow that the speaker is himself pained" is also refuted. For being pained (*duḥkhitva*) consists in the inherence (*samavāya*) of pain [in oneself], not merely in the cognition of pain. For one who holds that being pained is nothing other than the cognition of pain, it would follow that he is pained even upon knowing the pain of another. Consequently, even a Buddha would be pained, or else he would not be omniscient. Yet, the direct cognition of all objects is accepted for the Buddha. And that [cognition], by directly assuming the nature of the object, becomes the grasper of the object. Thus, for a Buddha grasping the pain of another through direct perception, it would follow that he is pained because the other's very form of pain would arise [within him]. By this, the consequence of [the Buddha] possessing passion and so forth should also be understood. Therefore, even though the object is non-different, a difference in cognition must be accepted due to a difference in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*). Consequently, the cognition arising from a word regarding a sensory object is not in every respect identical [to the sensory cognition]; thus, the consequence that a blind man would become non-blind is also untenable.
A word requires context and other factors in order to convey its own meaning.

[Objection: But if [the word] is the object of an injunction (*vidhi*), then the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of words such as ‘pot’ with the two words ‘is’ and ‘is not’ would not be possible, because the word ‘is not’ would contradict the injunction, and the word ‘is’ would be redundant. [Response: This is not a fault, because a word that does not depend on context and so forth performs merely the restatement (*anuvāda*) of its own meaning. For this fault would apply to one who says, “Even a word independent of context enjoins its own meaning. However, when it functions as a mere restatement of a general object, since both [affirmation and negation] are observed, doubt may arise: “Is this an injunction or a prohibition? In that case, if there is a desire to express an injunction, one says “the pot is”; if there is a desire to express a prohibition, one says “it is not. Even then, when there is doubt as to where it is or where it is not, one employs a word specifying a particular place and so forth to determine it. Furthermore, when one desires another qualification, one employs a word expressing that other qualification, until the expectation (*ākāṅkṣā*) is satisfied. Thus, the meaning is conveyed without doubt by the sentence alone; therefore, that [sentence] alone is the actual means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). As it is said: “A word, however, is not distinguished from a mere reminder (*smāraka*) because it lacks anything additional. There is no fault even in its being a means of valid cognition, because it denotes the general object alone. Just as when a vertical object is determined from afar by the eye, yet because specific qualities like being a post (*sthāṇu*) are not determined, approaching it and observing the details is not in vain for the sake of certainty—so too, although a word denotes the general object alone, since one observes it as having either affirmation or negation depending on the variation of time, place, and so forth, doubt may arise; therefore, a word such as ‘is’ becomes meaningful for the purpose of determining it as possessing the specific quality desired by the person to be informed. Nor is there any contradiction with the coreferentiality of the word ‘is not’: for it is precisely that [object] which is said to be ‘not’ elsewhere or at another time. If it is asked, “What is the status of the statement ‘a sky-flower is nowhere, never’?”—here too, the very flower seen [in experience] is absolutely prohibited by way of its difference from non-existence. [Objection: But this meaning is already established from the word ‘sky-flower’ itself, for a flower consisting of space (*ākāśa*) never exists anywhere. [Response: True; nevertheless, for one who has been deceived by someone or for some other reason does not understand it at all, another word is meaningful. The same principle applies here to the statement “space exists everywhere, always.”
The suspicion that exclusion (apoha) is the meaning of words, and its refutation.

Now, if another word is desired for the purpose of removing doubt, then exclusion (*apoha*) alone would have to be seen as the meaning of a word. What is this exclusion? It is that which is cognized from the word. What is cognized from the word? Nothing at all; the intention is that [the cognition] is mere illusion. This is incorrect; for when one acts after determining an object through words, and there is no discrepancy due to the correspondence with the causal efficiency of that object, the illusoriness—which is pervaded by that [discrepancy]—is removed. This same principle applies to the non-illusoriness of perception as well. Furthermore, it has been stated that there would be the undesirable consequence of the absence of the distinction between true and false worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). If it is argued that the distinction between true and false worldly practice pertains to the conventionally real and the conventionally unreal, we say no; for the lack of being conventional (*asaṃvṛtatva*) has already been refuted at length. Moreover, it was established in detail that words apply even to real entities, both in the justification of conceptual perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) and in the justification of real universals (*vastu-sāmānya*). Recalling all of that, it should be said; enough with this digression.
{Establishing the Distinction of Verbal Testimony from Inference}:

Thus, when it is established that verbal testimony and other specific means of knowledge are valid because they convey their objects, their distinction from inference is proven: verbal testimony is not inference, because it does not depend on the apprehension of the "property of the subject" (pakṣadharmatva) and so forth, just like perception.

Others maintain that this reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*), for instance: "The subject (*dharmin*) is the word 'cow' (*gośabda*); the property to be proven (*sādhyadharma*) is that it conveys an object possessing a hump and so forth; because it is the word 'cow'; like the word 'cow' perceived at the time of the linguistic convention (*saṅketa*). Similarly, one would have to prove that words such as 'Indra' convey objects such as Indra. But this is incorrect; for if the capacity to convey an object were established [only] at the time of the convention, there would be no corroborating example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, even if the property of signifying meaning is established as a characteristic of the word, how is the object qualified by place and so forth established? For the eye, which perceives color, does not establish a specific color merely through the inference "this is an eye because it possesses the nature of being an eye"; for if it did, it would follow that perception itself is a form of inference. Nor does anyone employ an inference such as "this smoke signifies fire because it possesses the nature of smoke" in order to establish fire in a particular location. What, then, is the case? It is: "this location possesses fire because it possesses smoke. Even when smoke is made the subject (*pakṣa*), fire is established in a particular location only upon the establishment of its connection with a fire situated in that same location, and not merely from the proof of the word's capacity to signify fire in general. Moreover, it is impossible to perceive a pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a word with an object located in the same place. Nor is a pervasion possible for the word "cow" with an object delimited by a specific time—such as the rising of the moon—which causes the tide of the ocean to rise. The word "cow" conveys its meaning as delimited by place and so forth only by depending on the proximity of other words, context (*prakaraṇa*), and the like. An inferential mark (*liṅga*), however, conveys an object delimited by place and so forth even without depending on another mark, context, and the like; furthermore, [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the word "cow" used to signify speech and so forth. If it is argued that there is no deviation (*avyabhicāra*) regarding a specific [word], what is this "specificity"? If it is argued that it is simply context and so forth, we say no; for unlike the upward movement of smoke, a property such as context is not observed to be invariably concomitant with all words "cow" that signify an object possessing a hump and so forth, since such a property is not seen to be uniform across them.

Furthermore, even a logical mark (*liṅga*) produced by an unreliable person does not deviate from its own probandum; however, a word produced by an unreliable person would be nothing but false in meaning. Moreover, the non-deviation of a logical mark is ascertained solely through the determination of its presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth; whereas for a word, it is ascertained solely through the determination that it was spoken by a reliable person and through its efficacy in prompting action, but not through the determination of its presence in the subject and so forth.
Thus, there is a distinction between verbal testimony and inference due to the difference in their modes of making known [the object].

Furthermore, a logical mark (*liṅga*) conveys its object by virtue of an invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), whereas a word conveys its object through mere convention (*saṃketa*). If it is argued that this [convention] is itself the invariable concomitance, we say no; because there is a distinction between being inherent and being dependent upon a person. For the relation of invariable concomitance is inherent, whereas convention follows the will of a person. Moreover, there is a difference due to the distinction between contradictory and non-contradictory objects: for a word, having its convention established even for things contradictory to its primary object—such as "speech" (*vāk*) and so forth, or other things—produces a cognition when it is employed. A logical mark such as smoke, however, never produces a cognition through invariable concomitance with water and the like, which are contradictory to fire and the like, even from some contextual occasion. Therefore, verbal testimony is not inference. Furthermore, by the definition of being the instruction of a reliable person (*āpta*), it is distinct even from perception.
{Doubt regarding the status of being spoken by a reliable person}

But how is the fact that a word was spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) ascertained? Since it is possible for all persons to speak either truth or falsehood given the occurrence of knowledge or ignorance, doubt and so forth do not cease. If its ascertainment were based on the efficacy of successful action (*pravṛttisāmarthya*), then such ascertainment would be useless, because action occurs even in its absence; or else there would be a circularity (*cakraka*): as long as there is no ascertainment that it was spoken by a reliable person, there is no ascertainment of its validity; in the absence of that, there is no action; in the absence of that, there is no efficacy of action; and in the absence of that, there is no ascertainment that it was spoken by a reliable person. If it is argued that the validity of the scripture composed by him is ascertained because one who is omniscient and entirely free from passion cannot possibly speak untruth, we say no; for the existence of such a composer is difficult to establish. Even if such a person exists, how is it ascertained that "this scripture was composed by him"? If you say it is from that very scripture itself, no; for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): as long as the validity of the scripture is not established, the fact that it was composed by that specific person is not established; and as long as the fact that it was composed by him is not established, the validity of the scripture is not established.
The resolution thereof.

To this it is replied: This fault would indeed arise if the validity of every scripture were established solely on the grounds of its being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*). However, [we hold] that some [scriptures] are valid because they are spoken by a reliable person, while others are valid because of their efficacy in prompting action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*). Nor does the establishment of validity through efficacy involve a circular argument (*cakraka*). Why? Because it has been stated that even when validity is not yet ascertained, activity proceeds precisely from doubt regarding the object. Furthermore, such ascertainment of its validity is not useless; for in the case of other [scriptures] where validity is established through being spoken by a reliable person, this serves as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). If it is argued that once validity is ascertained through efficacy, a further ascertainment through being spoken by a reliable person is redundant, this might well be so if scripture were of only one kind. However, since it is of two kinds, distinguished by whether its objects are perceptible (*dṛṣṭa*) or imperceptible (*adṛṣṭa*).
The authority of those [scriptures] whose objects are both seen and unseen.

In that regard, the authority of statements concerning perceptible objects is generally understood through their efficacy in prompting action. For even when authority is not yet ascertained, a seeker may engage in action despite physical hardship. However, in the case of heaven and such things, since they are entirely beyond perception, there is not even a possibility of attainment; therefore, for one who investigates, action is impossible unless authority is ascertained. Consequently, having ascertained the authority of statements concerning imperceptible objects by virtue of their being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*), discerning individuals proceed toward their objectives.

But how can it be understood that sentences whose authors are absolutely unseen possess the status of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*), even in the absence of seeing such an author? It is said in reply: The authority of sentences such as "One desiring rain should offer the *kārīrī* sacrifice," "One desiring cattle should sacrifice," and "One desiring a son should sacrifice," is inferred through the efficacy of their application (*pravṛttisāmarthya*). Here, "application" refers to the fact that, because of an intense desire for results such as rain, and because no other certain means is perceived, one engages in Vedic instructions whose efficacy is not yet certain—just like a sick person. It has been stated that this occurs out of a desire to know, even if it involves some slight suffering.
Doubts regarding the lack of authority in Vedic statements and their refutation.

If it is argued that the ascertainment of validity is not tenable because, even when a rite is performed, its results—such as rain—are generally not perceived, we say: "No; this is due to defects in the ritual action (*karman*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the means (*sādhana*). In this context, a defect in the ritual action (*karmavaiguṇya*) consists in performing it incorrectly; a defect in the agent (*kartṛvaiguṇya*) consists in the lack of knowledge or the failure to perform expiatory rites on the part of the sacrificer or the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); and a defect in the means (*sādhanavaiguṇya*) consists in the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) being unrefined or defiled, the mantras being deficient or redundant, or their accents and phonemes being corrupted, or the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) being ill-obtained, insufficient, or censurable. Even if there is a defect in any one of these, the result is not produced. However, since the production of the result follows from a ritual action, agent, and means that are free from defects, there is no lack of validity. In the world as well, there is the sentence: "One desiring fire should rub two pieces of wood together. Here, a defect in the ritual action is rubbing them incorrectly; a defect in the agent is negligence regarding wisdom or effort; and a defect in the means is using wood that is wet or hollow. In such cases, even with a single defect, the result is not produced. Yet, this does not imply a lack of validity, for we observe the production of the result when the qualities [of the factors] are present. Thus, just as in worldly matters, the validity of Vedic sentences concerning perceptible objects is inferred from the observation that the result is produced when there is an absence of defects in the ritual action, agent, and means. Having inferred this, the supreme reliability (*paramāptatva*) of the author of those [Vedas] is determined by virtue of his perception of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*). For it is impossible for one who is ignorant to be a teacher of things as they truly are. Furthermore, the relationship of means and end (*sādhyasādhanabhāva*) between specific sacrifices and their specific results is not within the range of our perception. If perception does not operate there, inference also cannot operate, because inference is preceded by perception and because a general pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established here [without it]. If that [relationship] were known through another scripture, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), which is untenable due to the lack of a further means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If, however, one accepts a foundational speaker in some instance, he is understood to be precisely the perceiver of supersensible objects. Consequently, since there is no cause for invalidity in all the sentences composed by him, their validity is inferred.
The prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) is that the threefold nature of the Vedas is established as authoritative because it is corroborated by perception and other means of valid cognition.

But another says: If validity is asserted in this manner, then there would follow the consequence that even those scriptures which declare the slaughter of Brāhmaṇas and others to be a means for attaining heaven or liberation would possess validity, since even in those cases, agreement with respect to some part [of their content] is possible. Likewise, there would follow the consequence of validity for the Āgamas of the Jinas, Buddhists, and others, because of the existence of agreement with respect to some part of them. Therefore: (1) only those Vedic statements for which agreement with perception or inference is possible possess validity; (2) but those for which there is disagreement lack validity. And these should be seen as the sentences of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*); thus, even the fact of being spoken by a reliable person (*āptoktatva*) is not contradicted. (3) However, regarding matters such as the seven continents, for which there is neither agreement nor disagreement, there is no certainty of validity nor certainty of invalidity; rather, there is only doubt in that case. Thus, Vedic statements should be viewed in these three ways. Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of validity even for statements such as "The Person is thumb-sized," "This is one only, without a second," and "The one unborn female"; and consequently, there would be a contradiction such as: the Person is sun-colored yet devoid of form and so forth, he is all-pervading yet thumb-sized, and he is non-dual yet manifold. Therefore, the establishment of validity is logical only through agreement with perception and inference. In that regard, in the case of sacrifices for those desiring cattle and the like, cattle and other results are obtained after the performance; from that, it is inferred that "Dharma arises from that performance. How so? Cattle and the like are attracted by the quality of the sacrificer, because they approach the sacrificer, like rice, soup, and so forth. By the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), Dharma is established. Once that is established, it is inferred that Agnihotra and other rites are also means for accomplishing Dharma. For instance: the performance of the Agnihotra produces Dharma, because it is a performance undertaken with faith, like the performance of the sacrifice for those desiring cattle and so forth.
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: as for what was said—that the authority of even the *Ṭaka-śāstra* and similar texts would follow because of the occurrence of partial correspondence—that is not so, due to a misunderstanding of our intention. We do not say that everything is authoritative merely by virtue of partial correspondence. Rather, we say that where there is partial correspondence, it establishes—by the reasoning previously stated—that the author of that work is a seer of supersensible objects (*atīndriyārthadraṣṭṛ*). Because of the absence of any cause for non-authority in such a case, its authority is affirmed. Furthermore, even the correspondence regarding statements such as "eating food" does not prove that one is a seer of supersensible objects, because of a lack of capacity [in those statements] and because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

But surely, the knowledge of the *culikāmāsa* and so forth is divine, and it makes known that its teacher was a seer of supersensuous objects (*atīndriyārthadraṣṭṛ*). True; however, it makes known the status of being a seer of supersensuous objects only for the original teacher (*mūlopadeṣṭṛ*), not for every teacher in general, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). And the original teacher is none other than the author of the Veda; thus, that knowledge is included within the science of astrology (*jyotirjñāna*), which is a limb (*aṅga*) of the Veda. For astrology consists of four categories (*cāturlakṣya*), and therein is found all calculation regarding substances, lifespan, the characteristics of women and men, the planets (*vaura* = graha), and so forth. Therefore, having understood the matter from that [Vedic source], he taught the knowledge of the *culikāmāsa* and so forth using different terminology. Yet, being afflicted by passion and the like, he composed the *ṭaka-śāstra* and other such works for the sake of visible worldly gain.

However, the Jinas and others—deceived by a false conceit born from the beginningless habituation to ignorance, as well as by attachment to their own schools—understood the meaning from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas and taught the *Gāruḍa* and other such texts in a different dialect in order to produce conviction in their own systems. If it is asked why this is not the case [with the Vedas], we say no; for even though they are not taught therein, one finds corroboration here in the teachings regarding types of sacrifice yielding results such as pacification (*śānti*), nourishment (*puṣṭi*), and malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), as well as in other forms of astrology. Furthermore, since those statements in the scriptures of the Jina, Buddha, and others that express matters not taught in Vedic doctrine are indeed contradictory, how can the omniscience of their authors be established?
The Veda being composed by an omniscient being.

If the Veda were composed by one who is not omniscient, then it would not be praised as authoritative among the countless scriptures such as the Purāṇas, just like the scriptures composed by the Jina and others. Even in the world, the authority of news concerning events in distant lands is observed to be valid despite doubts regarding the virtues or defects of its speaker, because of the corroboration of abundant reports; furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence of [the Veda] being impossible to memorize. For one who is not omniscient cannot compose many thousands of texts without depending on books. And if those [texts] he composed were not authoritative, they would not have been accepted by innumerable people in every country, due to the great amount of effort required and the absence of any perceived benefit for visible worldly ends.
The discrepancy between the Jaina and other scriptures and the Vedas.

[Objection: But surely the scriptures of the Jina and others are also accepted by many even without a visible purpose; therefore, their authority must also be admitted. [Reply: No, because they were accepted for other reasons. Having heard that the study and teaching [of the Veda] confer great merit, some Śūdras became eager to study and so forth. Being ineligible [for Vedic study], they were unable to study the Vedas; thus, the Jina and others—desiring fame—described a superior fruit in the study of the scriptures they themselves composed and incited them [to study those]. They, in turn, incited others of a similar kind, and they also incited others, including some Brāhmaṇas who were dull-witted and tormented by the suffering of poverty. Having enticed them with the instruction on the destruction of suffering, they were set in motion. In this way, those scriptures gained currency. [Reply continued: This is not so. Unlike the Veda, they are not committed to memory even by forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*) who are excluded from all [Vedic] scriptures, nor do they gain currency by being taught by Brāhmaṇas alone or recited by only the three [higher] castes. Therefore, the authority of the scriptures of the Jina and others does not follow as a consequence of being like the Veda. Furthermore, as for what was said—that Vedic sentences are of three kinds: authoritative, non-authoritative, and of doubtful authority—that is untenable. For while the lack of authority might occasionally be suspected in the case of sentences composed by one who is not omniscient, it is impossible in the case of those composed by an omniscient being, because there is no cause for a lack of authority. And so it has been said: *... [omitted verse] ...*
Because he is seized by defects such as passion and ignorance, one might speak untruth;
since those do not exist in the Lord, how could he speak otherwise?

The claim that [the Veda] is for the purpose of stating a prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) is also untenable; for if its refutation and the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) were not stated, it would be impossible for the scripture to state a prima facie position. Otherwise, because it would produce confusion among listeners, the author of it would face the consequence of being untrustworthy (*anāpta*). Furthermore, in treatises on reasoning (*yukti-śāstra*), the presentation of a prima facie position is made. But the Veda is taught as being established by authoritative command (*ājñā-siddha*), like the words of a father and so forth; no object is established here by means of reasoning. Therefore, this assertion—that certain Vedic sentences are for the purpose of stating a prima facie position—is merely the prattle of one who has fallen into error through the practice of dry logic (*śuṣka-tarka*).
The manner in which Vedic statements containing contradictory meanings and so forth possess authority.

How, then, can sentences with contradictory meanings possess authority? They do not; for there is no actual contradiction. For one who does not discern the true meaning of Vedic sentences, a contradiction appears to him, just as it does in the case of the sentences regarding the [sacrificial] oblation at sunrise and so forth. For example: having prescribed, "The oblation is to be offered after sunrise," "The oblation is to be offered before sunrise," and "The oblation is to be offered when the sun has half-risen," the text then expresses a censure for the purpose of prohibiting those [other times]: "A black dog devours his oblation, he who offers it after sunrise"; "A brindled dog devours his oblation, he who offers it before sunrise"; "Black and brindled dogs devour his oblation, he who offers it when the sun has half-risen. To resolve this apparent contradiction, [the author] says: "Because the statement of a fault is made only by assuming a deviation from the accepted time. This is what is meant: for whomever a specific time has been accepted, if he offers the oblation at another time by transgressing that time, then this fault is stated. Likewise, the explanation of other scriptural passages must also be made without contradiction. For even other treatises, when explained by those of corrupt intellect, do not convey their intended meaning as they truly are.

In this regard, those statements that express non-duality (*advaita*) are authoritative as having the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) as their referent. However, a statement such as "the one unborn Prakṛti" (*ajāmekām*), which expresses primordial matter (*prakṛti*), is authoritative because its referent is the atoms (*paramāṇu*). For atoms, endowed with qualities such as redness and so forth, being themselves unborn, produce effects—both similar and dissimilar—that possess infinite divisions, such as the stationary and the moving. Primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is the inherent cause (*samavāyi-kāraṇa*); it is designated as feminine (*strīliṅga*) in relation to that [cause], while it is called "one" (*ekām*) in reference to the aggregate. Otherwise, since the Primal Nature (*pradhāna*) also consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), its oneness would be untenable. Likewise, passages such as "measured by a thumb" (*aṅguṣṭhamātra*) are authoritative as denoting the subtle, radiant body (*taijasa-śarīra*) used for transmigrating. It is observed that the word "person" (*puruṣa*) is applied even to the gross body; how much more so, then, to that which is internal? Alternatively, the Supreme Self itself is figuratively described as "having the color of the sun" (*ādityavarṇa*) because of its extreme purity. Although not measured by a thumb, it is figuratively so described because it is perceived by yogis within the region of the heart through the restraint of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, the meaning of other statements must also be diligently understood in a way that avoids contradiction; one should not conclude they lack authority due to poverty of wisdom or laziness when one is unable to grasp the true meaning.
In the case of the validity of scripture, there is no dependence upon corroboration by perception and other means of knowledge.

Furthermore, the claim that the authority of scripture (*āgama*) is established solely through its corroboration by perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*) is untenable; for it would result in the loss of authority for those portions of scripture that teach about heaven, specific unseen results, deities, and so forth. Moreover, heaven is not merely pleasure—what intelligent person, having rejected pleasure already at hand, would engage in the great exertions of asceticism, sacrifice, and the like, for the sake of mere pleasure occurring in another birth? Furthermore, since the specific pleasure that is the cause of engagement and which is indicated by scripture lasts uninterruptedly for many thousands of years, perception and inference do not operate there; thus, in the absence of corroboration, it follows that those seeking heaven would simply not engage [in such practices].

Furthermore, there would be the consequence of invalidity for scripture (*āgama*) which teaches specific means toward a particular unseen result (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), and which teaches distinctions such as pure and impure, because it lacks corroboration by perception or inference. To illustrate: the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and so forth are a means to dharma for a householder, yet they are a means to non-dharma for an ascetic (*yati*). Something that is pure for one person is impure for another. Even acts such as violence are described in some instances as a means to dharma and in others as a means to non-dharma. Regarding such a classification of the objects of scripture, no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) operates for people like us. If [you argue that] being practiced while embraced by faith (*śraddhopagṛhītatve saty ācaraṇatvam*) were to establish [the validity of scripture] merely in a general sense, even that is not tenable. For it is possible that something which is actually a means to non-dharma might be embraced by faith by someone who has been deceived by some untrustworthy person (*anāpta*). If that too were a means to dharma, there would be no distinction between a scripture composed by a deceiver and one composed by a non-deceiver, and this is not logically consistent.
The fallacious nature of the probans used to establish the example:

Furthermore, as for the proof stated for the sake of establishing the example—"animals and the like approach Devadatta because they are drawn by his qualities"—this too is not tenable. It is because it is inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*). For it is observed that even one impelled by the qualities of another may approach toward that other; and there is no subverting evidence here by which the approaching of animals and the like toward Devadatta could not occur even when they are impelled by the qualities of another. [Thus, the quality cannot be established as the means of action.]

Furthermore, from what source is the fact that [the action] is a means to merit (*dharma*) to be understood? For *dharma* is well-known as a specific means to pleasure; therefore, it is not known whether [the attraction] is drawn by *dharma* or by *adharma*. Moreover, let the tenth quality be established for this very reason. Even if the fact of being drawn by *dharma* were established, the establishment that [the action] produces that *dharma* does not follow, because it is possible for *dharma* performed in another life—which is indifferent to the means of *adharma*—to yield its fruit. This is seen in the case of those who perform rites such as sorcery (*abhicāra*) or summoning, those who observe vows involving extremely censurable acts like cruelty, theft, and sexual misconduct according to the *Ḍākinī-tantra* and similar texts, and those who, at the command of a lord of wealth, kill even a Brahmin or other person after gaining their trust, or those who commit acts of theft and the like. Likewise, the reasons stated by others to establish the specific causes of *dharma* and *adharma* should be seen as having either the fallacy of being inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) or the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātīta*). For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of a reason is not established merely by the non-observation of its presence in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), in the absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the opposing side; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To illustrate: "He is dark-skinned because he is his son, like the other sons observed"; "Those fruits are ripe because they grow on this branch, like the fruits already eaten"; "The diamond is scratchable by iron because it is earthy"—such reasons as these would also become valid.

The claim that a reason (*hetu*) becomes "mistimed" (*kālātīta*) due to contradiction with the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend the subject (*dharmin*), the reason itself, or the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), whereas in their absence it would be a correct reason—this too is a false dogmatic attachment. For this would lead to the absurd consequence that even [the reasons] such as "being his son" (*tatputratva*) would be correct. Indeed, there is no sublation (*bādha*) of "being his son" and so forth by any of the means of valid cognition that apprehend the subject or the other factors; rather, such sublation occurs at a later time through the perception of the son's physical form, the tasting of the fruit of that action, the observation of the result of employing iron, or through the word of a reliable authority (*āpta*). Thus, it is impossible to ascertain that [a reason] is uncontradicted in every respect.

Furthermore, it is impossible for one who is not omniscient to ascertain that there is no sublation (bādha) of anything whatsoever; moreover, since sublation may occur for those who perceive [the truth] directly, even if no sublation arises from the perspective of a non-omniscient person, the defect of the reason—either its being inconclusive due to doubt (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*) or its being "mistimed" due to doubt (*sandigdhakālātyayāpadiṣṭatva*)—is not thereby removed. Nor is the condition of having an unascertained, unsublated object a constituent part of the probans, because it is merely a property of the reason (*hetu-rūpatva*), just like the property of residing in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth. Therefore, in order to ascertain that the object is unsublated, one must demonstrate the contradiction between the probandum and the means of proof, or else provide corroboration through a possible scripture; otherwise, it would be nothing more than mere inference.
The refutation of the claim that sentences such as "the seven worlds" have a doubtful meaning.

Furthermore, as for the claim that these scriptures (*āgama*) which establish the seven worlds and so forth possess a doubtful meaning because there is an absence of either proving or refuting evidence (*sādhaka-bādhaka-pramāṇa*), and because other scriptures are seen to be of both kinds—that is incorrect. For it would follow that sensory cognition and the like would also have a doubtful meaning, since they too are seen to be of both kinds and lack proving or refuting evidence. If you argue that doubt is removed in those cases by the perception of a specific distinction (*viśeṣadarśana*), we say no; for such a specific distinction is also seen to be of both kinds, and since proving and refuting evidence are likewise seen to be of both kinds, there would either be a state of doubtful meaning or an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Now, if it is held that a certain determinate cognition (*niścaya-jñāna*) produced by such eyes or such a logical mark (*liṅga*) is determined to be non-erroneous due to its efficacy in purposeful action (*pravṛtti-sāmarthya*), then a determinate cognition produced by exactly such eyes or such a logical mark is established as the fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-phala*) merely through the non-perception of any cause for error. Even though others may be seen to be of both kinds, that [specific cognition] does not have a doubtful meaning, nor does it entail an infinite regress. If this is so, then even though other scriptures are seen to be of both kinds, it is incorrect to claim that the determinate cognition produced by Vedic statements explained in a way that avoids internal contradictions has a doubtful meaning—even in the absence of corroboration by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara-saṃvāda*). This is because not even a trace of a cause for falsity is perceived, and because there is no counter-example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*) to show that the cognition produced by Vedic statements explained according to their true sense is not correct with respect to perceptible objects.
The Mīmāṃsakas [maintain] the non-human authorship of the Vedas.

Others, however, describe the authority of the Vedas as being due to their lack of human authorship; for if they were of human origin, the ascertainment of their authority would be difficult to achieve, since doubt regarding them would not cease because humans are the locus of defects. As it is said:
"It is established that the emergence of defects in a word depends upon the speaker."
"The absence of that [defect] is established in some cases by virtue of being spoken by a virtuous author.

However, in the case of the Veda, a virtuous author is difficult to know; therefore, even the absence of defects cannot be ascertained. But in the absence of an author, it is easily ascertained. For instance:
"Whether defects exist or do not exist is appropriate to inquire regarding human compositions."
"Indeed, because there is no author of the Veda, there is no suspicion of defect whatsoever;
for a person is the locus of defects, so in his absence, how could there be any suspicion of defect? This is incorrect, because—{the refutation thereof}:
The validity of a word is indeed determined as dependent upon the speaker;
likewise, its absence [invalidity] is also established everywhere through the absence of a virtuous speaker.
And therefore:
"Whether validity exists or not is appropriate to discuss regarding human compositions; for in the Veda, since there is no author, even talk of that matter is difficult to find."

For just as a person possessed by passion and other defects is seen to be a speaker of falsehood, so too one endowed with thorough knowledge, compassion, and the like is a speaker of truth. Consequently, just as the falsity of a word depends on the speaker, so too does its truthfulness; thus, when that [falsity] is removed, truthfulness is also removed, and the word would result in being meaningless (*ānarthakya*). If it is argued that the qualities of the speaker merely counteract those defects while validity (*prāmāṇya*) is intrinsic (*svataḥ*), we say no; for the theory of intrinsic validity has already been refuted. Furthermore, it is improper to assume otherwise the causal status of qualities toward validity—which is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)—for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, it is not easy for one who speaks thus to turn back from the position that the defects of the speaker merely counteract those qualities while invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) is intrinsic.
If it depends upon convention, then its lack of human authorship is indeed pointless.

Furthermore, even if it were authorless (*apauruṣeya*), the Veda would necessarily depend upon a convention (*samaya*) established by a person to convey its meaning; otherwise, even children and cowherds would understand its meaning merely by hearing the recitation of the Vedas. Nor are words ever observed to denote a meaning when they have not been assigned a convention. And if that convention were made by an unreliable person (*anāpta*), then the Veda, in conveying its meaning by depending on such a person, would result in a lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*). If, however, it were made by a reliable person (*āpta*), then surely the authority of the Veda would be admitted precisely because of the authority of that reliable person. Consequently, the description of it as being authorless is redundant, and it contradicts the denial of any specific person [as its author].
Even if one disregards the connection, that same fault remains.

If it is argued that words denote their objects by the force of an inherent relation (*sambandha*) without depending on convention (*saṅketa*), then is that relation also impermanent or permanent? If it were impermanent, the same fault would apply as in the case of convention. If it were permanent, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that all those who hear the recitation of the Veda would simultaneously comprehend its meaning. If it is argued that this does not follow because [comprehension] depends upon linguistic proficiency (*vyutpatti*), one might think: "The relation between this signifier and its signified is eternally established; convention merely illuminates it, just as the relation between father and son is already established and is simply made manifest by convention. This is not so, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). While the relation between father and son—characterized as that of progenitor and progeny—is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), there is no such evidence for the existence of a specific relation between word and object.

The establishment of an intrinsic relationship between word and meaning is not non-existent, because such a fixed order is observed. The fixed order—that the word alone is the signifier and the object alone is the signified—is not tenable if no relationship exists. If it is argued that this order is merely produced by convention (*saṅketa*), we say no; for in that case, the status of signifier and signified would result in the opposite as well. For a convention could indeed be made in this way: "this is the meaning of this word," or "this word is the signifier of this meaning," and "this word is the denotatum of this meaning. Thus, the relationship must be intrinsic.

And because it would lead to the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*): if a word conveys its meaning solely through the power of convention (*saṅketa*), that convention cannot be established by a word that is not itself expressive; for the expressiveness of the very word that serves as the cause for the convention would depend on the power of another convention, leading thus to an infinite regress. Therefore, there exists an intrinsic relationship (*svābhāvika-sambandha*) between word and meaning. {The Refutation of the Intrinsic Relationship Between Word and Meaning}

To this it is replied: as for the claim that [the relationship is natural] because a fixed restriction (*vyavasthā*) is observed, that is not so; for such restriction is caused by expressive power (*śakti*). Since that expressive power which belongs to these words does not exist in the objects [themselves], this restriction [of usage] occurs. Otherwise, since a fixed restriction is observed among all causal factors (*kāraka*) and manifestors (*vyañjaka*), it would follow that they possess an inherent connection with their respective effects and manifested objects.

As for what was said—that it would lead to an infinite regress—that too is incorrect. For no such restriction is accepted; this restriction is not admitted that a convention is made only by means of a denotative word, but rather in other ways as well—such as when one points with a finger or touches with the hand while saying, "This is a cow," thereby establishing the convention. Furthermore, in the linguistic practices of elders, people grasp the convention residing in the intention of another through the process of inclusion and exclusion (*āvāpodvāpa*). Just as in the linguistic practices of the Karṇāṭas and others, even though a convention is required for the purpose of learning the relationship [of a name] such as "Aryan," this principle must necessarily be accepted. Therefore, since words possess denotative power solely by virtue of convention (*samaya*), there is no inherent (*svābhāvika*) relationship.
Furthermore, because there is no restriction regarding specific locations, the relationship is not inherent.

Furthermore, because there is no fixed rule regarding specific regions—as for example, the word *cora* denotes a "thief" among the Āryans, but "rice" among the Draviḍas—if the relationship were inherent (*svābhāvika*), such lack of restriction would be impossible; for smoke never conveys fire in one place and water in another. Moreover, wherever a person establishes a convention for a word, that word is observed to convey that very object. If the relationship were inherent, however, it would be impossible for it to follow human will, just as smoke [conveys fire regardless of human intent]. Furthermore, we observe the naming of sons and others according to one's own will. Therefore, the relationship is indeed established; the claim that it is merely manifested by convention is also incorrect. If it is argued that only Vedic words have an inherent relationship with their meanings, we say no, because there is no evidence for this. Nor is there any distinction whereby the relationship between word and meaning would be inherent in one case and conventional in the other. This is especially true given the lack of distinction between nouns, verbs, prefixes, and so forth, in both cases. Now, if the relationship between word and meaning were purely conventional, it might be objected that it could not serve as the basis for linguistic usage everywhere—just as the convention of calling one's own son "Narasiṃha" does not apply universally, nor does the convention of calling curd "Bhavāmitra. But this is not so, because the objection is unproven (*asiddhatvāt*). There is certainly no universal application of usage everywhere, since the usages of Mlecchas and others are not recognized elsewhere.
Because linguistic convention has a beginning, the relationship is not inherent.

Furthermore, because all linguistic conventions (*vyavahāra*) have a beginning—just like the conventions concerning Nanda, Vikramāditya, Śrī Harṣa, and others—if they were beginningless, there would be no illustrative example. Even though they have a beginning, due to the influence of the authors of technical treatises (*samayakāra*) or some other cause, certain conventions become established in many regions and so forth while others do not; for instance, people today still employ only the names Rāma, Rāvaṇa, Yudhiṣṭhira, and so on, with their meanings well-known, but not the names of all men. Likewise, even among synonyms mentioned in lexicons (*nighaṇṭu*), some have meanings that are well-established in many scriptures and in the world, while others do not. This much, however, does not constitute a difference in the nature of the relationship between the natural and the conventional.

Furthermore, if convention were ineffective, then another [intrinsic relation] would be postulated. However, when the efficacy of convention is accepted even in a single instance, then in other cases as well, the denotative capacity of words will arise from convention alone; thus, the postulation of another relation is redundant. For there is no distinction here by which convention might be effective in some cases while another relation is effective in others.
[In an intrinsic relation, there would be an absence of the determination of meaning.]

It has already been stated that if the inherent relationship (*svābhāvikasambandha*) alone were efficacious everywhere, words would not function toward intended objects in the same way that smoke and other such signs do. If it is argued that each word possesses a relationship with all objects, then it would follow that the word "cow" (*go*) alone could convey the understanding of every object. If it is argued that this consequence does not arise because [the word] depends upon convention (*samaya*), then let convention suffice; what is the use of postulating an unproven inherent relationship that serves no purpose? If it is argued that a convention is not possible for what is unfit [to be related], we reply: surely the capacity (*yogyatā*) of words to denote and of objects to be denoted has already been explained.

Furthermore, if every word has a relationship with all possible meanings, and it becomes the cause for the cognition of a specific meaning only when restricted by a convention (*samaya*) created by a person, then Vedic words would have no capacity to convey meaning in the absence of an accepted author of such conventions. If, on the other hand, there were some author of conventions even in that case, then there would be no distinction whatsoever between what is human-made and what is not. Moreover, the doubt regarding the Vedas would remain unresolved—namely, whether the author of the conventions therein is flawed or virtuous—and consequently, the suspicion of invalidity (*aprāmāṇya*) would also persist; thus, the effort to establish their non-human origin (*apauruṣeyatva*) is futile.

{There is a lack of evidence for authorlessness}: Furthermore, there is no proof whatsoever for authorlessness. If it is argued that [the Veda is authorless] "because its author is not remembered," this is not so, because the reason is incongruous (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). If, on the other hand, what is intended is "because its authorship is not being remembered," even then there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*); for that which is eternal is neither something whose author is being remembered nor something whose author is not being remembered, but rather something that simply has no author at all. If, however, the intention is to express the state of having no author, then the inclusion of the term "not being remembered" is redundant.

Furthermore, there is an inconsistency [in your argument] due to dilapidated gardens, wells, and the like. If you argue that this applies only "provided there is no interruption in the tradition," even so, the reason remains inconclusive (*asādhāraṇa*). For there is no tradition whatsoever for eternal things such as space (*ākāśa*). Moreover, the non-remembrance of an author is observed even in the absence of a purpose—for instance, there are many verses and the like whose authors are not remembered, and for which even a tradition is not established; yet you yourself do not accept that these are of non-human origin (*apauruṣeya*).

This reason (*hetu*) is also unestablished (*asiddha*). For the followers of the *Purāṇas* remember that Brahman is the author [of the Vedas], stating: "The Vedas issued forth from his mouths," and "In every Manvantara, a different revelation (*śruti*) is ordained. Furthermore, in the passage "He who indeed imparts the Vedas," the Lord Rudra himself is established by the Veda as the author. Moreover, how could the various branches (*śākhā-bheda*) such as the Kāṇva, Mādhyandina, and Taittirīya—which are marked with the names of sages like the *Smṛtis* and *Purāṇas*—be without remembered authors? If you argue that a branch is marked with a sage's name because he saw or revealed it, and not because he composed it, this is the speech of one who is utterly deluded. To explain: if the branch was lost and seen by him anew, then there would be a contradiction with the uninterruptedness of the tradition (*sampradāya*) and a contradiction with the rejection of one who perceives supersensible objects (*atīndriyārtha*). If, on the other hand, it was not lost and was seen through the tradition, then it should be marked with the names of all the teachers by whom it was seen and revealed. Furthermore, what is the answer if it is said that even the scriptures of Buddha and others were seen or revealed by Buddha and the rest, but are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*)? If you say this contradicts your own tenets (*abhyupagama-virodha*), then since it declares their very human origin, how can it be a contradiction of your tenets? Moreover, the determination of reality does not depend on tenets, but rather on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). There is no specific means of knowledge here by which an author, though heard of in the Vedas, might be considered false or otherwise, while in the scriptures of Buddha and others he is not.

By this, the argument that "the study of the Veda must be preceded by another study of the Veda, because it is a study of the Veda, like the study of the present day," and so forth, is refuted; for the same logic applies equally to the study of the scriptures of the Buddha and others.
[This concludes the refutation of the *pariśeṣa* (residual) proof regarding the lack of human authorship.]

As for the claim that the Veda’s authority is established by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣataḥ*) because it is not of human origin—this is incorrect. First, its lack of authority cannot be characterized by non-origination (*anutpatti*), since we observe the arising of knowledge from it. Nor can its lack of authority be characterized by doubt (*saṃśaya*), because it does not produce doubts such as, "Should I offer the oblation, or not? Nor is its lack of authority characterized by error (*viparyaya*), because it remains unsublated in other places and times. Furthermore, there is no other definition of a lack of authority, for it is said: "Lack of authority is divided into three types: falsity, ignorance, and doubt. Moreover, since passages such as "The Puruṣa has a thousand heads" are *arthavādas* (explanatory or commendatory statements), the injunctions (*vidhi-vākya*) do not lose their authority on account of them. Furthermore, the operation of other means of knowledge regarding the subject matter of the Vedic injunction (*codanārtha*) has been refuted—namely, that perception is not a means of knowing *dharma* because it "perceives only what is present," and so forth. Thus, the claim that the Veda is not of human origin is itself untenable. For if that were so, one would have to accept the non-human origin and authority of such injunctions as: "One who desires heaven should pluck out his hair," "One who desires heaven should worship a shrine (*caitya*)," and "One who desires heaven should eat human flesh and kill Brāhmaṇas. Likewise, by the same logic, statements such as "The Jina is omniscient" would also have to be treated as mere *arthavādas*.

Now, one might object: "If the Vedas were of human origin (*pauruṣeya*), their status as *mantras* would be untenable; for a *mantra* is observed to bestow results when recited, whereas a human statement does not do so. Therefore, the Veda is not of human origin. This is not correct, because it would follow that the Śaiva Siddhānta and other such systems would also be non-human (*apauruṣeya*), since they too contain *mantras* that bestow results. If you argue that those [Śaiva] mantras are in fact Vedic, we say no; for they bestow results even upon Śūdras, and Śūdras have no entitlement (*adhikāra*) to the Vedas. And *mantras* do not bestow results upon those who lack such entitlement.

Furthermore, even vernacular mantras are seen to yield results. Since there are no vernacular words within the Vedas, it follows that Vedic mantras, like vernacular mantras, are of human origin. [Even though they are of human origin, mantras are composed only by those whose resolve is true.]

[Objection: "In that case, would not all persons be capable of composing mantras? [Response: No; because the capacities of all are unequal. For only those whose resolutions (*saṅkalpa*) are true are able to compose mantras. And the state of having true resolutions belongs to the Lord (*īśvara*) by virtue of the power of his innate sovereignty (*svābhāvikaiśvarya*). It belongs to the great seers (*maharṣi*) by virtue of the stability in non-violence, celibacy, truthfulness, and so forth, or by virtue of the power of austerity (*tapas*) and the like. Such power does not exist in other persons; therefore, not all possess the status of being composers of mantras. [This explains] the postulation of a composer even for that which has not been perceived.

Furthermore, if poetry were also a human creation, then either all men would be poets or none at all—this is an unprecedented logical argument. One might object: "We see a person composing poetry, but we do not see one composing a Vedic mantra. This is not so; for even the authors of mantras are seen through inference and scripture. Moreover, the perception of one who is not omniscient cannot encompass all things, such that the mere absence of such perception would entail the non-existence of what is unseen.

Furthermore, since no one is seen nowadays composing works such as the *Mahābhārata*, it would follow that those too are not of human origin. And what is the special quality of mantras by virtue of which they are considered uncreated, even though they consist of phonemes, words, and sentences? If you say the special quality is their production of results, we say no; for we observe the production of results through human means such as seals (*mudrā*), mandalas, and meditations (*dhyāna*).
[The mantras yield results solely through the convention (*samaya*) of the agent.]

Furthermore, the production of a result does not arise from the power of the sound [of the mantra] alone, because that would entail the consequence that whispered (*upāṃśu*) and mental (*mānasa*) recitations would be fruitless, that there would be no possibility of varying the time [of recitation], and that there would be no dependence on specific intentions regarding the injunction. Nor is this fault present if the production of the result arises from the power of the person [who recites]. For, by him, wherever and however a convention (*samaya*) has been made, the result is produced there accordingly through the maintenance of that convention, due to the force of its association with that [mantra]. Or rather, that very specific deity, maintaining that convention, bestows grace upon him, just like a king and so forth. Thus, just as with seals (*mudrā*) and mandalas, a mantra is also merely a matter of convention; and in this way, a difference in results is logically established from a single mantra according to the differences in the conventions followed. Otherwise, the result would be without distinction—just like the burning [caused] by fire—and there would be no such variation as: for one, success is immediate; for another, after a long time; for another, depending on celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and so forth; and for yet another, harm resulting from that very same [mantra].

Furthermore, it is observed that even a single syllable uttered by one who possesses knowledge of the ritual procedure (*samaya*) performs functions such as neutralizing poison, whereas other [syllables] do not. If [the mantra] were innate (*svābhāvika*), it would produce its own effect even when applied by those lacking that knowledge, just like fire. Therefore, the mantra is not non-human in origin either.
[In the case of the Veda being non-human in origin, its interpretation would be untenable.]

Furthermore, even the Veda, so long as it remains unexplained, does not convey its meaning, because [otherwise] we would never perceive it. And the explanation is a human product; if understanding arises from a human source, how can there be no suspicion of error? For humans are seen explaining the meaning of words even erroneously. If validity is accepted only through corroboration by other means of knowledge, then the postulation of the Veda’s lack of human authorship is useless, for its validity is established simply through corroboration by other means of knowledge—just as in the case of its explanations. Nor is that explanation itself eternal, nor does it consist of an uninterrupted tradition from time immemorial, since we observe extreme contradictions among the various explanations of the Vedas composed by the Sāṃkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others. There is no evidence whatsoever for the claim that one particular explanation is beginningless while all others are not. If the Veda were indeed without human authorship, then the meanings of its words would be entirely different [from those known to us]. Even among human languages, such as those of the Mlecchas and the Āryas, there is no identity of meaning; how much less could there be such identity for words that are supposedly non-human? Consequently, the suspicion that words such as *agnihotra* and *havana* might have entirely different meanings—such as "eating dog meat"—would never be dispelled. Furthermore, the Veda itself does not declare: "The meanings of these worldly words are exactly the same as mine. As for Jaimini and others who attempt to provide such an explanation, they do not become authoritative sources of knowledge, because they are human beings. Indeed, you do not admit that even Jaimini was a seer of supersensible objects, such that he could perceive the identity of meaning between worldly and Vedic words. How can the statement of one who speaks without having perceived this be authoritative? Even by means of context (*prakaraṇa*) and other factors, the meaning of a word is determined only when its conventional usage has been grasped in relation to several possible meanings. But since no Vedic word has ever had its meaning grasped anywhere [in common usage], it follows that, like the words of the Mlecchas, the Veda would result in being of entirely uncertain meaning.
But if it were of human origin, this fault would not apply.

But if [the Vedas] were of human origin, this fault would not apply. For he (the author), having set out with the desire to favor others, composed the Vedas using refined words (*saṃskṛta-śabda*) whose meanings were well-known, and then explained them himself, just like a modern author of a treatise. Consequently, others might also explain them through that same tradition. Furthermore, in cases of disagreement regarding the meaning of a word, one determines the meaning by means of context and so forth, just as in other sciences. If it is argued: "Even though it is perceptible, how can the Vedic word *agni* and so forth not have that same meaning as the common worldly word *agni*, since they are indistinguishable?"—then surely, if that were the case, how could it not also be of human origin when distinguished by a human [author]? Moreover, the meaningfulness of the common worldly word *agni* and so forth is pervaded by its being of human origin; how then can this Vedic word *agni* and so forth, while abandoning its human origin, be able to grasp that same meaning? For it must either accept both [human origin and that meaning], or reject both.

Furthermore, is the eternity of the sentence (*vākya*) being established, or that of the phonemes (*varṇa*)? It cannot be the sentence first, because it is not distinct from the phonemes—for there is no sentence consisting of sound that exists apart from the phonemes. This has already been demonstrated in detail previously: a word (*pada*) is a collection of phonemes, and a sentence is a collection of words. Moreover, a collection does not differ in reality; its distinction exists only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*). Even so, since conceptual construction is of the nature of cognition, it is indeed non-eternal. Nor is there any means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for the eternity of the sentence; rather, for its non-eternity, there is the inference: "because it is a sentence, like a worldly sentence. If, on the other hand, it is the phonemes themselves that are eternal—even if they were eternal, validity would not be established, because it would follow that all scriptures (*śāstra*) are authoritative, and it would follow that there could be no false speech. For the Vedic phonemes are not something else [distinct from worldly ones], otherwise it would follow that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) lacks validity.
The Vedic phonemes do not possess eternity by virtue of their sequential order.

Now, [the opponent claims: "In the Vedas, the sequence (*ānupūrvī*) of phonemes (*varṇa*) is eternal, but not elsewhere. This is not so; for since the sequence itself is of the nature of sound (*śabda*), it cannot be something distinct from the phonemes. Furthermore, if the sequence of phonemes were eternal, then because the prior-posterior relationship between the letter *a* and the letter *g* in the word *agni* would be eternal, the reversal [of that order] in words such as *gacchati* would be impossible. Nor is a plurality of phonemes admitted, such that one might say that in *gacchati* and other instances entirely different *a*s and *g*s are being denoted, and that—just as with the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains—it is impossible for their order to be otherwise. Even for produced things (*kṛtaka*) that possess a fixed causal transformation, a reversal of order cannot be effected; as, for example, in the case of the seed, sprout, leaf, and so forth, or the seasons, years, and so on. How much less so, then, could this apply to those whose nature is eternal and immutable? For a different state is not possible without the abandonment of the previous state; and if there is abandonment, there is impermanence (*anityatva*). Moreover, this sequence must be either spatial, like the line of ants, or temporal, like the sequence of growth in seeds, sprouts, and so forth. Neither of these two types is possible here, because all phonemes pervade all places and are eternal, like space (*ākāśa*) or the self (*ātman*). Nor is there any other way for there to be priority and posteriority. If it is argued that the priority and posteriority of the phonemes results from the priority and posteriority of their manifestation (*abhivyakti*), we say no; for this leads to the fallacy of falsity (*mithyātva*), since it would be a superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the properties of an external adjunct (*upādhi*), just like the superimposition of blue and other forms upon a crystal. Furthermore, just as the form of blue disappears when the adjunct is removed, the priority and posteriority of the phonemes would disappear upon the cessation of their manifestation; how then can they be considered non-human (*apauruṣeya*)?
Even though it exists as an beginningless stream, it is not eternal.

If it is argued that [the Veda] is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*) because it exists as an beginningless stream, we say no; for this leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To explain: even the customs of barbarians (*mleccha*), such as the marriage of mothers, as well as the statements of nihilists (*nāstika*) which deny the next world, the unseen results of action (*adṛṣṭa*), the self (*ātman*), and so forth, would consequently have to be considered not of human origin, since they too exist as beginningless streams. For even these can be set in motion by impressions (*saṃskāra*) instilled by others, and not otherwise; indeed, no one who has not had impressions instilled in them initiates a previously unknown practice. Even in the case of the first creation (*ādisarga*), every practice must be preceded by impressions instilled by the observation of a previous creation. Furthermore, you do not accept a "first creation," nor any "first person" who could initiate a previously unknown practice. Consequently, it would follow that all practices are not of human origin simply because they are beginningless. If it is argued that there is no fault because this is accepted [by us], then what is the merit in establishing such a lack of human origin? For it is for the sake of establishing its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the lack of human origin is desired; yet since that quality exists even in the statements of nihilists, it is not a valid proof [for the Veda].
The Refutation of Recognition as a Proof for the Permanence of Sound

Furthermore, as for the proof called *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) that has been stated to establish the eternity of all phonemes (*varṇa*) and words (*pada*), that too is no proof because it is unestablished (*asiddha*). For it is not the case that "the very same sound which was heard by me in Kāñcī is now being heard in Ujjayinī. [Objection: But surely there is recognition in the thought, "this very same *anuvāka* has been recited eight times"; likewise, recognition should be seen to apply individually to all words and phonemes. [Reply: No, because of the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of lamps and the like. [Objection: It is correct that a logical mark (*liṅga*) is not a proof when it deviates, but recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is presented as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And there is no fault of being inconclusive (*anaikāntikatva*) regarding direct perception, since even if a cognition of water and so forth is erroneous in one instance, it is accepted as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in another. Indeed, it is only where a cognition is sublated (*bādhyate*) that it is unfit to be a valid means of knowledge; yet recognition of sound is not sublated in another place, at another time, by another person, or in another state. [Reply: No, because recognition of sound is also sublated by both direct perception and inference. By direct perception, first of all, the production and destruction of sound are grasped in the thought, "In this place, sound has arisen; this clamor has been silenced by him. [Objection: The cognition [of production and destruction] is due merely to the presence or absence of manifestation (*abhivyakti*). [Reply: No; otherwise, the same consequence would follow for hair, nails, and so forth. For who could prevent someone from asserting that, even in those cases, eternity is accepted based on mere recognition, and that the notions of production and destruction are caused by manifestation and non-manifestation? Moreover, we never see the notions of production and destruction caused by manifestation and non-manifestation anywhere. On the contrary, recognition is seen in many cases due to similarity (*sādṛśya*). Furthermore, it would follow that all worldly sentences (*laukika-vākya*) are also eternal. Even there, recognition exists in the thought, "This sentence was uttered eight times," or "This verse was recited eight times. And if all sentences were eternal, the very same fault mentioned previously would apply.
The distinction between words arises from their being the means for inference by those who study them.

Furthermore, it is observed that even by means of a Vedic word, there is an inference of a specific person who has studied it from behind the scenes—such as "Devadatta is studying" or "Viṣṇumitra is studying. And that [inference] would be impossible if the word were not distinct [from the speaker]. For a staff, an umbrella, or the like, which are common to many people, cannot lead to the inference of a specific person when they are held up and displayed by someone at a particular time. Moreover, because differences such as intense, moderate, or faint are perceived, a permanent entity cannot possess qualities such as being more intense; nor is the perception of distinctions like intensity or faintness possible within a single, partless self.
Refutation of the Theory of the Manifestation of Sound (Śabdābhivyaktipakṣanirāsa)

If it is argued that [the difference in sound] exists due to the distinction between intense and weak manifestors (*vyañjaka*), is this state produced in the sound by the distinction between intense and weak manifestors, or is it merely the property of the manifestor being superimposed [upon it]? First, it is not produced [in the sound]. For no distinction can be made in an eternal entity by any cause whatsoever. Nor is a distinction of properties produced, because properties such as intensity (*tīvratva*) are eternal, since they possess the character of a universal (*sāmānya*) like "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*). If it is argued that only a distinction in manifestation (*abhivyakti*) is produced, we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of contradictory properties such as intensity and weakness in a single locus. Furthermore, if there were no distinction in the properties of intensity and so forth, a corresponding distinction in manifestation would be non-existent in reality and thus necessarily deceptive. If it is further argued that, just as the properties of a sword and the like are superimposed upon a face, the property of the manifestor is likewise superimposed upon the sound—we say no, because this is never observed. For a property of a sword, such as length, is superimposed only when it has been perceived by the same sense organ; it is not superimposed if unperceived or if perceived by a different sense organ. Since the nature of the air-conjunction (*vāyu-saṃyoga*) and other factors that manifest sound is itself unperceived, how could the superimposition of its properties be possible?
