Indeed, the properties of a *piśāca* or similar beings are never seen to be superimposed upon anything through sensory cognition, nor are the properties of color (*rūpa*) ever superimposed by the tactile sense (*tvag-indriya*).

Now, if it is maintained that some object perceivable by the ear—which possesses qualities such as intensity and is the manifestor of sound—is itself non-eternal, we say no; for that too is not distinct from sound. Indeed, the definition of sound is "that which is perceivable by the ear and possesses a universal" (*sāmānya*); and it is illogical for something possessing that definition to be a different entity from sound. If any [object] perceivable by the ear and possessing a universal were non-eternal, then the non-eternality of everything would be established, since there is no distinction [between them]. We shall state the fault regarding manifestation later on as well. {Refutation of Presumption (*arthāpatti*) regarding the Eternity of Sound}

As for what was stated—"Because perception is for the sake of another"—this, they claim, expresses an *arthāpatti* (presumption). How so? Perception is utterance, and that is for the purpose of another's comprehension; and that comprehension of meaning would occur only through the eternity of the word. For a word whose relationship [to its meaning] has been grasped perishes at that very moment; thus, because of its non-eternality and so forth, the word is heard only after the rule [of the relationship] has already ceased. Consequently, the comprehension of the word’s meaning would not be possible. Indeed, it is not logical for there to be comprehension of meaning from a word whose relationship has not been grasped. Therefore, by the fact that the comprehension of meaning cannot otherwise be accounted for (*anyathānupapatti*), it is understood that "the word is not non-eternal. This is not so; for even in the case of non-eternality, the capacity to convey meaning is established, just as it is with smoke and other such signs.

Furthermore, by this same logic, you must also accept the eternity and unity of the object (*artha*). Otherwise, how could the word "cow" (*go-śabda*), even when its relationship [to the object] has been grasped in the case of a *bāhuleya* (a dark-colored cow), produce a cognition for *śābaleya* (a spotted cow) and others if its relationship were not already grasped there? If it is argued that there is no fault because the universal (*sāmānya*) alone is both the meaning of the word and the logical mark (*liṅga*), we say no. For if the universal alone were the meaning of the word, faults such as the absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) have already been stated. Just as in the investigation of the relationship between the mark and the marked (*liṅga-liṅgin*), the investigation into the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) was established as pertaining only to the two possessors of the universal (*tadvat*), so too there is no fault in the relationship of signifier and signified (*vācya-vācaka*) between the two possessors of the universal. Moreover, just as you maintain that the status of being a logical mark belongs only to the universal, let the status of being a signifier likewise belong only to the universal. Since the relationship between signifier and signified will be grasped between two universals—just like pervasion—the argument from presumptive necessity (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted. Now, what is the universal in the word "cow"? It is the state of being the cause of the cognition "cow-word. That capacity by which all instances of the word "cow" become the causes of a single uniform cognition within themselves is the universal. Nor is there only one single word "cow," for it is well known to be divided into distinctions such as loud and soft, and this is consistent with the established fact of the distinction between pleasure and pain. Even if the universal does not exist directly among the individual words "cow," nevertheless, some kind of universal certainly exists there, just as in the case of "cook" and the like; for otherwise, a non-differentiated cognition regarding distinct things would not be possible, as has been stated. Therefore, since the capacity to signify is established for non-eternal words by relying on the universal, the eternity of words is not proven even through presumptive necessity.
The refutation of audibility as a proof for the permanence of sound.

As for the proof—namely, "Sound is eternal because it is audible, like the universal 'sound-ness' (śabdatva)"—that is not valid, because it is inconclusive (anaikāntikatva). To explain: a sequence such as "One desiring heaven should eat dog-meat, excrement, and so forth" is apprehended by the sense of hearing, yet it is not eternal. If you argue that this [sequence] is also eternal, we say no; for it would follow that it possesses authority (prāmāṇya) like the Vedic injunctions themselves. Furthermore, it would follow that one incurs sin (pratyavāya) upon transgressing its performance. Moreover, the reason is inconclusive due to the defects—such as incorrect pronunciation (visvara)—produced by the reciters of the Vedas; for if those too were eternal, the Vedas would be eternally afflicted by defects such as incorrect pronunciation.

Furthermore, [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to properties such as intensity and dullness, and because of the sounds of drums and the like; for even if those were eternal, there would be no perception of distinct sounds corresponding to each respective cause. Indeed, it is observed that a single manifestor can manifest many things, and many things can be manifested by a single manifestor. Consequently, there could be no inference of a specific cause based on a specific sound. Moreover, an imperceptible manifestor is never observed to be inferred by its manifested object, in the manner that a cause is inferred by its effect. Alternatively, if the non-eternality of some sound or some property of sound is admitted—on the grounds that there might be an inference of an imperceptible cause—then, in that case, the property of being audible (*śrāvaṇatva*) is itself inconclusive with respect to that very [non-eternal] instance. Furthermore, it must be stated that every proof for eternality is characterized by the fallacy of having its evidence superseded by a contrary fact (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).
The impermanence of sound is also apprehended by direct perception.

Indeed, the absence of sound is apprehended even by perception (*pratyakṣa*). For when the operation of the sense organ is present, there arises an indubitable and uncontradicted cognition that "there is no sound" or "the clamor has perished," provided that [the sound] was previously present; it does not arise when [the sound] is absent. This very same means applies even in the case of the perception of other objects. If it is argued that perception is untenable because of the absence of a relation (*sambandha*), this might be so: there is no relation such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*) between the sense organ and the absence of sound; therefore, the absence of sound is not apprehended by the sense organ. [Reply: No, for the relation called the qualifier-qualified relationship (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) exists. But of what is the absence of sound the qualifier or the qualified? The teachers say: of the ear-cavity (*karṇaśaṣkulī*). And the ear-cavity is apprehended by the tactile sense (*tvagindriya*); the qualifier-qualified relationship is seen even between things apprehended by different senses, as in the case of "a fragrant substance" and so forth. Therefore, it is not contradictory here either. Alternatively, let the location such as a house be the qualifier. For just as it is a qualifier of the sound, so too it is a qualifier of its absence; whatever is perceived as a qualifier or the qualified of an object is also [so perceived] in the case of its absence. The qualifier-qualified relationship is established by virtue of a specific cognition (*viśiṣṭapratīti*); therefore, wherever there is a specific cognition, the qualifier-qualified relationship is accepted even in the absence of spatial proximity (*deśādipratyāsatti*), as in the case of Devadatta [being qualified] by cows, fields, and so on, or by planets and constellations such as Śatru. Furthermore, its status as a cause of perception is established in the production of perceptual knowledge. It is not logical that because it is not a cause in one instance—like conjunction and the like—it should be a non-cause everywhere. Therefore, the impermanence of sound is apprehended even by perception.
{Establishing the non-eternality of sound by means of inference as well}:

Furthermore, sound is non-eternal because, while possessing a universal (sāmānyavat), it is an object perceived by the external sense organs of persons such as ourselves, like a jar, and because it is an object of cognition (viṣayatva), like color and so forth. Now, what is intended here by "being an object" (viṣayatva) is not merely "being knowable" (jñeyatva), which would render the reason inconclusive; rather, it refers to that object which, when apprehended through direct perception, produces attachment in some, aversion in another, or delusion in yet another—it is this [functional] objectivity that is intended here. And this does not deviate from non-eternality.
"Sound is impermanent because it possesses properties such as intensity.

For this reason also sound is impermanent: because it possesses properties such as intensity, like pleasure, pain, and so forth. For if these were properties of a manifestor, their being perceivable by the ear would be untenable; therefore, one should not suspect that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
"Sound is impermanent because, while being a real entity, it is an effect."

Furthermore, since sound is a real entity (*vastu*), it must be an effect (*kārya*) because it possesses the property of being produced, like a jar and so forth. If it is argued that this reason is unestablished (*asiddha*), we say no; for sound conforms to the properties of will (*icchā*) and effort (*prayatna*). First, regarding conformity to will: whatever kind of sound one desires to utter, that very kind it becomes. This rule does not apply to manifestation (*abhivyakti*); for instance, from a lamp brought forth with the intention of manifesting gold and such, one observes the manifestation of even things like snakes. Likewise, there is conformity to the properties of effort: from intense effort, the sound is intense; from weak effort, it is weak; and according to distinctions such as more intense or weaker, it becomes correspondingly so. Furthermore, it should be seen as conforming to the properties of striking a drum and so forth. Now, such conformity to the properties of effort and the like is impossible for that which is not an effect. Indeed, it is never observed that an object manifested—such as a jar—is perceived differently due to differences in the manifesting agent (like a lamp) or differences in its properties. If it is claimed that sound’s status as an effect is unestablished simply because it is perceived as following the properties of an effect, then how can the status of intellect (*buddhi*), jars, and so forth, as effects be established? For in their case too, one could argue: "Since intellect, jars, and so forth are perceived only where they are manifested by the eyes, clay, sticks, and so on, despite their being pervasive and eternal, there would follow the absurd consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the absence of the conventional usage of 'effect' and 'non-pervasiveness'. Therefore, because sound is enhanced by the excellence of its causal factors (*kāraka*), just like a jar, it is a product (*kṛtaka*); and because it is a product, it is non-eternal (*anitya*) and non-omnipresent (*asarvagata*).
[The impossibility of the occasional perception of sound if it were eternal:

Furthermore, if sounds were by nature unperceivable—like space and so forth—they would never be perceived at any time. If, however, they were by nature perceivable, they would be perceived at all times, since there could be no causes for non-perception such as obstructions. If it is argued that "non-perception is due to the absence of a manifestor," we say no; because the nature of such a manifestor cannot be determined. [The refutation of conjunction as a manifestor of sound.]

If it is argued that it is a particular conjunction, we say no; for sound is perceived even when a particular conjunction of wood and axe has long since ceased. Furthermore, it is not logical for the manifest to be perceived once the manifestor has ceased, just as [light] is not perceived when the conjunction with a lamp has ceased.
[Thus, conjunction cannot be the manifestor because neither its reaching nor its non-reaching is possible.]

And because of the impossibility of [the sound] reaching or not reaching [the sense organ]: if conjunction were the manifester of sound by depending upon reaching the sense organ, then, since the conjunction with a drum or similar object does not reach the ear, it would not be a manifester of sound. If it is argued that there is no non-reaching because the sense organs are all-pervading (*vyāpaka*), we say no; for then it would follow that people situated in all locations would perceive [the sound]. If it is argued that there is no consequence of perceiving everything because perception of that object occurs through the modification of the sense organ into the form of the object when it is situated in a suitable location (*yogyadeśa*), we say no; for "suitability of location" cannot exist apart from the sense organ and its reaching [the object], and so forth. Furthermore, since the proof of the Sāṃkhya system depends upon the establishment of the existence of the effect in the cause (*satkāryavāda*) and the Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*), and since that [system] will be shown to be untenable according to the logic to be stated later, their method of procedure is likewise untenable; therefore, it is not further elaborated as a prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Furthermore, if conjunction independent of the attainment of the sense organ were the manifester of sound, then it would follow that it would manifest [sound] for all persons. By this, the argument that the disjunction of bamboo slivers and so forth is the manifester of sound is also refuted.
[The fault regarding the manifestation of what is dependent and what is non-dependent.]

Furthermore, is manifestation that which is dependent [on a substrate], or that which is independent? If it is the manifestation of the dependent, then it follows that, like a universal (*sāmānya*), it must manifest together with its substrate. If you argue that—just as in the case of odors and so forth—it manifests even when the substrate is not manifested, we say no; for odors and the like are impermanent, and they are produced by their productive causes precisely as things capable of being perceived. It is never observed that anything previously incapable of perception becomes manifested upon reaching the sense organ when its substrate remains unmanifested. Even in the case of the touch of perspiration, because of contact with the wind, the previous state ceases and a distinct state arises along with its substrate; thus, there is no manifestation of something persisting while its substrate is manifested later on.

The manifestation of that which is non-pervasive is illogical. Suppose, then, that there is manifestation of that which is non-dependent. Even in that case—does it belong to something non-omnipresent or to something omnipresent? If a non-omnipresent thing is manifested, then the rule that "sound is manifested wherever the manifesting agent, such as the striking of a drum with a stick, occurs" would not hold; for a non-pervasive entity, like a jar or similar objects, cannot exist everywhere. Indeed, when those seeking to manifest a jar or the like bring forth a lamp wherever they may be, the manifestation of the jar does not necessarily occur in every such place.
The manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of even that which is all-pervading (*vyāpaka*) is untenable.

If there were manifestation of the all-pervading, then since all sounds would occupy the same location, it would follow that they are manifested simultaneously, just like jars and other objects situated in one place. Furthermore, it would follow that [the sound] is perceived by all persons, because it is manifested only when connected with the sense organs of all persons, given its all-pervasive nature as an indivisible whole (*akhaṇḍātman*). If it is argued that this is inconclusive (*vyabhicāra*) due to the case of universals (*sāmānya*), we say no; for those [universals] are manifested only upon the manifestation of their own substrates (*svāśraya*). However, you yourself do not accept that sounds possess such a state of being dependent on a substrate (*āśritatva*).

But surely, even on the theory of production, it would be impossible to perceive sound because it is not reached by the ear when it has manifested in the location of the drum or other source; no, for it is perceived once it has reached the ear through a series (santāna).
[Suspicion regarding the impossibility of the series:]

But surely, the series of sounds (*śabdasantāna*) is untenable because it has been refuted by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For instance: if a sound were to produce another sound in the very same portion of space occupied by itself, then the production of sound at the location of the ear would never occur. On the other hand, if it produces sound in a portion of space distinct from that occupied by itself, then let the sound produced at the location of the drum and so forth be produced directly at the location of the ear; what is the use of producing sound in the intervening spaces?

Furthermore, because there would be no cause for the cessation of the series, it would follow that even a sound produced in another continent could be heard, since its series would reach the ear. Moreover, a sound does not initiate another sound, because it is a sound, like the final sound. There is no evidence, however, for its being an initiator. [This concludes the refutation thereof.]

To this it is replied: First, as for the question—does sound produce another sound in the portion of space occupied by itself, or in a portion distinct from it? Of these, the first position is not accepted. As for the second position, what was said—that it should produce [sound] only in the location of the auditory organ, rather than producing sound in the intervening space—is incorrect; for even so, the continuity of the series (*santāna*) is established. Indeed, a sound produced from a sound is called a "series of sounds. Therefore, a series is logically possible even when there is the production of only a single sound. Furthermore, this is possible because it is like the production of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); just as the motion of an arrow or similar object does not produce another conjunction in a portion of space already occupied by a prior conjunction, nor in an excessively distant place, but rather in a place adjacent to that, and from there, a series of conjunctions is produced in successive stages in distant places; in the same way, sound also produces another sound in a place adjacent to itself, neither in the space occupied by itself nor in a distant place.

If it is argued that because space (*ākāśa*) is partless, proximity to its parts is untenable, we say no; for "parts" are merely conceptual constructs (*upādhi*) produced by conjunctions that do not pervade their substratum. In this regard, sound arises in a portion of space delimited by the conjunction of a drum and space; from that sound, another sound arises in a portion of space delimited by the conjunction with a corporeal substance proximate to the drum; and from that, yet another sound arises in a portion of space delimited by the conjunction with a corporeal substance immediately following that substance. Thus, the production of sound should be understood as depending upon successive conjunctions with corporeal substances in proximity to one another.

As for the argument that it is incorrect because there is no possible cause for the cessation of the continuum (*santāna*), that too is incorrect; for its cessation occurs just as the continuum of karma ceases. For example, in the case of arrows and the like shot into the sky, their motion initiates subsequent motions in degrees of intensity (taratama), until finally, when the motion becomes extremely feeble, it no longer initiates further motion and thus the continuum of that motion ceases. Likewise, sound also initiates [subsequent sounds] in degrees of intensity, such as loud, soft, and softer, until finally, when it becomes extremely feeble, it no longer initiates further [sounds] and thus the continuum of that sound ceases. Consequently, one standing near a drum hears the sound loudly, while one standing at a distance hears it softly; one who is very far away hears it even more softly, and one who is extremely distant hears it most softly. Such a gradation of hearing—loud, soft, and softer—is not possible if sound were eternal.

As for this proof—"Sound does not initiate sound, because it possesses the nature of sound (*śabdatva*), like the final sound"—if the first and subsequent sounds are taken as the subject (*pakṣa*), there is sublation by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhitatva*). For the status of being "first" and so forth is not possible for that which does not initiate [another sound]. Furthermore, regarding the thesis-meaning that "no sound whatsoever is non-initiating," there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because the final sound is indeed non-initiating. If the thesis is that "all [sounds] are non-initiating," there is no corroborative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Even if something other than the final sound is taken as the subject, there is sublation by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject, because it is unestablished that anything other than the final sound is non-initiating. Moreover, it is untenable because it is sublated by the means of valid cognition that apprehends the example; for the "finality" of a sound is not established in the absence of a continuum (*santāna*).

The inference that establishes the continuity of the series (*santāna*) is also incorrect in its claim that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for sound being the producer of [another] sound. For instance: sound perceived by the external senses of persons such as ourselves is the subject (*dharmin*); "produced from something of its own kind" is the property to be proven (*sādhya-dharma*); because, while being perceptible by the external senses of persons such as ourselves, it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*), like the color and other qualities of a composite whole (*avayavin*).
[This is established] through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) as the proof for the continuity of the series of sounds.

Furthermore, a series of sounds (*śabdasantāna*) is inferred because perception would otherwise be inexplicable. For the auditory organ does not grasp an object that has not reached it, since it is an external sense faculty, and because [otherwise] there would be the undesirable consequence of perceiving all sounds simultaneously. Moreover, reaching [the object] is not possible without a series. Indeed, a sound does not come and reach the auditory organ, because, being formless (*amūrta*), it is devoid of motion. Nor does the auditory organ go and reach the sound, for the very reason already stated. Furthermore, even the physical location of the auditory organ is not perceived as moving at that time. Therefore, perception occurs only through a series by means of which the sound reaches the auditory organ.

But surely, since perception can be accounted for in another way as well, the existence of a continuum (*saṃtāna*) is not established. For instance: all sounds exist as pervasive [entities], like space. They are perceived by the auditory organ when it is assisted by the refinement (*saṃskāra*) of the air. In that process, the air impelled by the speaker's intention moves toward the location of the ear, displacing the stagnant air in all directions. By this, the obstructing air is pushed aside, and once that has been displaced, the word "cow" is perceived. Alternatively, the very conjunction of the air impelled by the intention to speak with the location of the ear is what manifests the sound; thus, one should understand that even the air impelled by the striking of a drumstick against a drum serves to manifest sound. This is not so, because their eternity is unproven. Indeed, this mechanism would be plausible only if the eternity and pervasiveness of sounds were established. And the impossibility of that has already been stated due to the lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, impermanence has been proven. Once that is established, the postulation of a continuum of sounds is the superior view; the postulation of a mere manifester (*vyañjaka*) is not.
The absence of the manifesting air is established through the non-perception of touch.

Furthermore, the postulation of wind is untenable because its characteristic marks, such as touch, are not perceived. For if wind were to arrive at the location of the ear with speed, then its mark—namely, touch, or the sound of a whistling breeze, or the trembling of grass, hair, and the like—would necessarily be perceived. Moreover, that wind which is incapable of even touching grass and such things would, due to its weakness, be repelled by even a slight counter-wind; consequently, the sound of a drum would not be heard when facing a headwind. If it is argued that the wind produced by the impact of the drumstick on the drum arrives having overcome the counter-wind due to its strength, then in that case, the counter-wind together with the grass and other objects would also return [with it], just like one ram being driven back by another.

Furthermore, sound produced by the impact of air would also be heard [by everyone], yet this is not observed at all; therefore, the postulation of manifesting air is untenable. Moreover, if air possessed the capacity to manifest sound, then any air whatsoever, without distinction, would manifest all sounds—just like light and visible form. For instance, although lights that manifest visible forms are produced by specific causes such as the intention of a person or grass and wood, there is no distinction between them: a light produced by anyone manifests all specific visible forms situated within a suitable range. Likewise, since there is no distinction among airs even when they are produced by specific causes, an air impelled by anyone would manifest all sounds; for all [airs] are omnipresent and thus occupy the same location.

In the claim that "the ear, conditioned by air, perceives sound," there too the restriction [of its function] is untenable; for, as in the case of the eye conditioned by light, collyrium, and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence that it would perceive everything.
[This is another formal argument regarding the fact that sound is not something manifested.]

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is also presented here: the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is not something that requires a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) for the sake of perceiving objects that are perceivable by the same sense organ and occupy the same location, because it is a sense organ, just like the visual organ (*cakṣus*). However, in the view that the refinement belongs to the object (*viṣayasaṃskārapakṣa*), sounds must be made the subject of the argument: sounds do not require a specific refinement, because while being perceivable by the same sense organ, they are simultaneously connected with the sense organ, just like jars and other objects situated in the same place.
[Here follows the suspicion of the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) and its refutation.]

If it is argued that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because the flame of fire is manifested in boiling oil and similar substances through a different kind of latent impression (*saṃskāra*), we say no; for such manifestation is unproven. For manifestation is considered only of that which already exists; however, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the prior existence of the flame. By this, the manifestation of the sensation of heat by water in lime and the like, as well as the manifestation of odor in earth, are refuted. Furthermore, the distinction [of the reason] has been established by the fact that things about to arise are not perceived in the same location and are not perceived simultaneously with their connection to the sense organ; therefore, there is no inconclusiveness.

If it is argued that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) because even when a white color is manifested by a weak light, specific colors such as black are not manifested, we say no; for there is no dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*). For what is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the absence of being manifested by a specific manifestor (*pratiniyatavyañjakavyaṅgyatva*); thus, only those things that *are* manifested by specific manifestors constitute the dissimilar instances. Now, specific colors do not possess the property of being manifested by specific manifestors, because all specific colors are manifested by a light that manifests the color black. White, however, although it is a non-luminous color, has a nature of slight luminosity and therefore does not depend on a particular kind of light. Nevertheless, this does not amount to its being manifested by a specific manifestor.

Others, however, adopt the qualification "having attained a common property" (*samānadharmāpannatva*) in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*). That is not correct, because it would result in the qualification being unestablished (*asiddha*). For letters such as *ka* and *kha*, which are non-producers (*akāraka*), do not possess a common property. Indeed, in the absence of difference (*vaidharmya*), there would be identity of the phonemes. If, on the other hand, all sounds possess a common property by virtue of being "sound-ness" (*śabdatva*) even when there is a difference [in other respects], then even specific forms such as white and black would likewise have a common property by virtue of being "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) despite their differences; how then could the fallacy of inconclusiveness be avoided? If, moreover, what is intended by "common property" is the state of lacking the distinction between a primary flame and a secondary flame (*anujvālā*)—that is, being neither subtle nor gross—then the qualification is not unestablished. For if, upon the manifestation of *ka*, *kha* is not manifested due to its subtlety, then upon the manifestation of *kha*, the manifestation of *ka* should follow, just as when a mustard seed is manifested, the *bilva* fruit situated in that same place is manifested. Or, if *kha* is not manifested upon the manifestation of *ka* because it is a secondary flame, even so, the manifestation of *ka* would necessarily follow upon the manifestation of *kha*; just as when a black form is manifested, a white form is manifested. Thus, if an existing sound were manifested, the unavoidable consequence would be its simultaneous perception. Therefore, one must accept the perception of a non-eternal sound that has arrived through a series (*santāna*), for in that case there is no fault.
The suspicion that the same fault applies even to the position of origination.

But surely, even if [the letters] are non-eternal, the same fault applies: for the air impelled for the sake of the letter *ka* would produce all the letters as well, because it is indistinguishable from the air that produces other letters, since there is no difference in their non-existence therein. If you argue that, despite this lack of difference in non-existence, the air impelled for the sake of the letter *ka* is capable of producing only *ka* and not another letter—then the rebuttal is the same: despite this lack of difference in existence, the air impelled for the sake of manifesting the letter *ka* is capable of refining only *ka* and not another letter. Thus, the solution is equal.
The refutation thereof.

That is incorrect, because there is a difference between a producer (*kāraka*) and a manifester (*vyañjaka*). For a restriction is observed in the case of a producer, but not in the case of a manifester. To illustrate: that very same collection of producers, such as the lump of clay and the wheel, when directed by the intention of a potter, produces specifically a bowl or specifically a jar; however, a manifester such as a lamp or the eye is not restricted by anyone’s intention to manifest only that specific object intended by them. Furthermore, in our position the winds function as producers, whereas in your position they function as manifestors; how then can the objection and its rebuttal be considered equal? Therefore, all sounds are impermanent. Thus, it is established that the authority of the Veda does not derive from its eternity, but rather from its being spoken by a reliable person (*āpta*).

"The inclusion of comparison (*upamāna*) and the others occurs within these three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) alone. Within these very [three], comparison, presumption (*arthāpatti*), possibility (*sambhava*), non-existence (*abhāva*), tradition (*aitihya*), and so forth are included. Therefore, there are only three means of valid cognition. In this regard, comparison—such as "as is a cow, so is a gavaya"—is included within verbal testimony (*śabda*), because it consists of a sentence, like the sentence "Bring fire," and so forth. If, however, there were a distinction based on the form of comparison, then there would follow a distinction in the means of valid cognition even due to the distinctions between injunction (*vidhi*), explanatory passage (*arthavāda*), restatement (*anuvāda*), and so on; consequently, there would be an infinity of means of valid cognition. [Furthermore,] the comparison accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas is actually memory (*smṛti*).

Now, it might be argued that when one wandering in the forest sees the body of a *gavaya*, the cognition that arises—"My cow is similar to this"—is accepted as *upamāna* (analogy). And since its inclusion within any other [means of knowledge] is impossible—because perception and the like cannot operate with respect to a cow staying at home for someone situated in the forest—this is not so; for it has already been previously experienced through perception. At that time, this is merely a memory: "My cow is similar to this. Furthermore, you yourself do not accept that the instrument of memory can be a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If it is argued that this is because similarity has not been previously apprehended, this is not so; for the individual cow (*gopiṇḍa*) qualified by similarity was indeed perceived previously. Why? Because similarity is capable of being perceived, just like the horns and other features. Or, if it were admitted that similarity is incapable of being perceived, then it would never be perceived, like the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*). Consequently, for one who perceives a gavaya and later sees a cow, the cognition "this is similar to that" would not occur.

Furthermore, there arises this cognition as well: "This [animal] is similar to my cow. Now, this [cognition] is not produced by the sense organ alone, nor by the sense organ assisted merely by the memory of the individual body [of the cow]; for it would then be produced even by the sense organ of a forest-dweller, or by one assisted merely by the memory of the body of a buffalo or other such animal. If you argue that it is produced by the sense organ assisted by the memory of a specific individual body, then surely it must be admitted that there was a prior perception of the individual body qualified by similarity to a *gavaya*. Otherwise, there could be no memory of a specific individual body, since memory is impossible regarding what has never been seen. If you say that even upon perceiving something qualified by similarity through mere resemblance, there is an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*)—since one might likewise perceive a buffalo or other animal as qualified by mere resemblance—[we reply: if you claim that seeing its similarity is untenable because there is no cognition of it when the *gavaya* itself is not seen, we say no; for that perception is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*). Indeed, by means of non-conceptual perception, the similarity residing in the body of the cow was apprehended prior to the sight of the *gavaya*; therefore, there is no misconception regarding that apprehension, just as there was no misconception regarding the apprehension of "cow-ness" at the time of first perceiving the body of a cow.

[Objection: But surely, since there is the cognition of "similar to this" as a qualifier of the gavaya, how can it be considered memory? For if that were so, even determinate perception (*savikalpapratyakṣa*) would result in being memory, because they share the same logical status. [Reply: No; for that [memory-status] is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If she (the cow) were not similar to this one, then this one would not be perceived as similar to her, because similarity resides in both members of the relation. Yet this one is indeed perceived as similar to her; therefore, she too is similar to this one. There is also a formal argument (*prayoga*): the cow is similar to this [gavaya], because it delimits this [gavaya] by means of its own similarity; whatever delimits something by means of its own similarity is seen to be similar to it, just as one brother is similar to another brother.

Furthermore, if it were a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For instance, cognitions such as "the object previously seen was grosser than this," "longer than this," or "shorter than this" cannot be considered analogy (*upamāna*), because analogy does not have similarity as its object. Nor can they be subsumed under perception (*pratyakṣa*) and the other means of knowledge, since their status is identical to that of analogy. Consequently, the fixed number of means of valid cognition would be compromised. Therefore, such cognitions must be included within presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) or inference (*anumāna*). As for their being memory (*smṛti*), this is due to the fact that the object was previously perceived by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-pratyakṣa*). To illustrate: when asked by another, "How do you know that while standing here, that cow was similar to this one?", one points out exactly as follows: "I saw it previously through direct perception. This same principle should be understood to apply to cognitions such as "that [object] is gross or long."

{The possibility of conceptual recollection even from non-conceptual experience} If it is argued that because recollection conforms to the form of its experience, a conceptual recollection is untenable when arising from a non-conceptual experience, we say no; for even in the case of non-conceptual experience, a conceptual recollection regarding universals such as absence, grossness, length, and so forth, is observed due to the power of auxiliary factors. Indeed, it is not proper to either enjoin or prohibit what has been observed or inferred.
{The analogy of the old Naiyāyikas}

Others maintain that the purpose of analogy (*upamāna*) is the comprehension of the relationship between a name and the object named (*saṃjñāsaṃjñisambandhapratipatti*). For instance, having heard that a certain animal called a *gavaya* is used in a particular sacrifice, someone seeking it hears a forest-dweller say, "A *gavaya* is like a cow. Having set out in search of the *gavaya*, he sees in the forest an animal with a dewlap that resembles a cow and comprehends, "This is a *gavaya*. Similarly, having heard the statement, "As is a stalk of beans (*māṣastamba*), so is the *māṣaparṇī* plant; as is a stalk of mung beans (*mudgastamba*), so is the *mudgaparṇī*," one who has formed a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) perceives its similarity upon seeing it and, recognizing that medicinal herb, fetches it for medicinal purposes. Other objects of analogy should likewise be understood from common worldly experience. In this regard, analogy is the knowledge of similarity produced by the sense organ, assisted by the memory generated by the latent impression produced by the knowledge arising from the [initial] statement; and the result of that is the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the named.

That refutation is also incorrect, because the comprehension of the relationship between the name and the object had already arisen prior to the authoritative statement; thus, upon seeing the *gavaya*, there is merely the recollection of that [relationship]. For instance, when asked by someone, "How do you know this is a *gavaya*? one gives the answer, "I understood it from the words of a forest-dweller," and not, "I know it through comparison (*upamāna*).
Furthermore, its status as a distinct means of valid cognition is not established, precisely because it is not mentioned separately.

For instance—everywhere, those engaged in worldly practice are observed to employ a reference to three means of valid cognition (pramāṇas), saying: "I see a jar through direct perception," "I know fire by means of smoke," or "I understand heaven through scripture"; however, cognizers are never seen employing a reference to analogy (upamāna) in such a way. Therefore, analogy is not a separate means of valid cognition.
[Even when the object to be named is unperceived, there is the comprehension of the name.]

If it is argued that the comprehension of the relationship between a name and the named object is impossible when the *gavaya* has not been seen, we say no; for such comprehension is observed even in the case of Śakra and others who are not perceived by the senses. Furthermore, the application of a name is seen in some cases even regarding objects like a son who are not present to the senses; how much more so, then, the act of grasping that name? If it is argued that this is improper due to the absence of a cause—namely, that while there exists a cause for the grasping of names in the case of Śakra and others, such as his thousand eyes, no such cause exists for the *gavaya* and its kind—we reply: no. Even here, the name "gavaya" is taught by taking its similarity to a cow (*go*) as the cause. If it is asked: "Is it not the case that the property of being a *gavaya* (*gavayatva*) itself is the cause for the application of the name 'gavaya,' and if that property is not grasped, how can the name be applied? We reply: But surely the property of being a *gavaya* is also understood from that very sentence.
Like Citralekhā and others, analogy (upamāna) is not a separate means of valid cognition.

For example, someone instructs another by showing the form of a painting and so forth, saying, "A camel is like this; an elephant is like this. Or else, one instructs [the learner] regarding a camel by describing specific measurements such as its neck, and regarding an elephant by describing specific measurements such as its tusks. At that time, the person being instructed understands both "camel-ness" and "elephant-ness" from the sentence alone. Indeed, when the designations "camel" and "elephant" are taught by way of the specific features of the neck, tusks, and so on, it is not the case that the understanding of those [features] does not occur; nor is there any possibility of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) being involved therein.
The refutation of the view that analogy is a means of valid cognition whose application is unassailed.

But surely, while the cognition derived from the sentence was obscured, it becomes established through comparison by being delimited by the specific object bearing the name (*saṃjñin*). What, then, is this "obscuration"? It cannot be error (*bhrānti*), because it is not sublated at a later time or otherwise. Nor can it be doubt (*saṃśaya*), because, unlike the case of a post or a person, it is not experienced as having the nature of a conceptual oscillation (*vikalpa*). If this cognition—"The *gavaya* is similar to a cow"—were a doubt or an error, it would follow that the comparison (*upamāna*) based upon it would likewise be so. And if it is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), how can it be "obscured"? If it is argued that "obscuration" consists in the failure to establish the specific object bearing the name, we say no; for it would then follow that cognitions of the self, the internal organ, atoms, merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, would also be obscured. For even in those cases, the cognition produced through inference or scripture does not take the form "this is the self," "this is the mind," "this is an atom," or "this is merit. Rather, the cognition takes such forms as: "that in which desire and the rest are inherent is the self"; "that from which there is no simultaneous production of cognitions is the mind"; "that than which nothing smaller exists is the atom. In that case, what is the difference between this cognition [of the *gavaya*] and those others, such that one is called obscured and the other unobscured?
Even on account of the sentence "As is a cow, so is a gavaya," comparison is not a separate means of valid cognition.

Now, one might object: "In a case where the convention is established as 'that which possesses similarity to a cow is a *gavaya*, and its name is *gavaya*,' let there be no need for comparison (*upamāna*) as a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). But when the statement is 'as is the cow, so is the *gavaya*,' then from that [statement] only similarity is understood, not the relationship between a name and the named; therefore, comparison is required for that purpose. If the relationship is not understood from the statement, then the statement is useless; for even one who has not heard the statement perceives mere similarity through the eye aided by the memory of the cow, yet no cognition of the relationship arises from that. Therefore, in the statements "as is the cow, so is the *gavaya*," "such a thing is called a *gavaya*," and "the name *gavaya* belongs to such a thing," only a single meaning is perceived. Just as in the case of the soul (*ātman*), whose existence is inferred from desire and other qualities, and where statements such as "desire and other qualities have the soul as their name" establish only the relationship between a name and the named. Otherwise, if a convention were made simply as "this is a cow," then the cognition that "the word 'cow' is the name for this" would require another means of valid cognition here as well, since the underlying logic is the same.
Nor is it the case that analogy [is required] for the sake of understanding the specific [relation], namely, that "the word *gavaya* is the name for this [animal]."

It might be argued: "The specific understanding that 'the word *gavaya* is the name for this [animal]' did not arise previously from the sentence; therefore, analogy (*upamāna*) is required for that purpose. If that is so, then even in the case of the sentence "This is a cow," the understanding that "another such animal is also a cow" has not yet arisen; thus, another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) would have to be stated for that too. Furthermore, regarding another individual body, the cognition that "the word *go* is its name" does not arise from the previous sentence; therefore, a separate means of knowledge must be asserted for every individual body in order to cognize the relationship between the name and the named. Likewise, even if the word is not explicitly uttered, the intention of both the speaker and the listener is exactly the same: "The word *go* is the name for all such things. If it is argued that this understanding arises through implication (*sāmarthya*), then the same applies here as well: from the statement "A *gavaya* is similar to a cow," both parties intend that "the word *gavaya* is the name for an object similar to a cow," and it is through implication that the understanding occurs in this way. For in common worldly usage, due to a particular context, one observes speech that is otherwise than the actual intention—for example, "Eat poison" or "Do not eat in his house. Thus, even when something is stated otherwise, the listener grasps the speaker's true intention. Regarding the phrase "or through implication" (*sāmarthyāt*): "implication" refers to presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). When it is said, "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*," it follows by implication that "the name *gavaya* belongs to an object similar to a cow. Alternatively, the word "implication" may refer to intuition (*pratibhā*), or to a mental flash (*ūha*), or to capacity (*śakti*). Therefore, even in the conventional designation "this is a cow," the name for the entire class of cows is understood. And the name *gavaya* belongs to that which is qualified by similarity to a cow, just as it is when it is stated, "As is a cow, so is a *gavaya*."
Resolution of Contradictions with the Sūtras

If analogy (*upamāna*) were not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then for what purpose was it stated separately in the sūtra: "Perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition"? This is not a fault, because they are mentioned separately by virtue of their specific purposes, just as examples (*dṛṣṭānta*) and fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*) are mentioned separately from the means of valid cognition and the points of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). If it is argued that the sūtra concerning the classification [of the senses] is intended solely to exclude a number less than or greater than [the actual count], whereas the sūtra listing them in sequence (the *daṇḍaka-sūtra*) is not, we say no; for the fact that there are only three types of means of valid cognition has already been established by the sūtra on the nose and other [senses], which demonstrates the fallacy [of a different number].
The purpose of the author of the Sūtra in mentioning the means of valid cognition known as comparison (upamāna) separately.

And it has already been stated that there is no fixed restriction to twenty-four types in either the *Jāti-nigrahasthāna-vibhāga-sūtra* or the *Sūtra* itself. Therefore, just as certain *jātis* are mentioned separately so that confusion may not arise from the diversity of their formulations, and for the sake of understanding the methods of refuting them, they are stated individually; likewise, *upamāna* is stated separately on account of its specific purpose (*prayojana*). That purpose must then be stated, and it is stated as follows: the purpose is the establishment of the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*).

In the *Parīkṣā*, the validity of verbal testimony (*śabda*) was established through such statements as “by the aphorism on Mantra and Āyurveda” and “no, because of the deficiency in the means [of action], the agent, and the act. Yet, one might object that no utility for comparison (*upamāna*) is heard there either; this is not so. In that context, the validity of a specific type of word was established by way of removing defects such as falsehood. However, by mentioning comparison separately, the validity of verbal testimony is established through a different manner of addressing objections. How so? [It is] by way of certain objections raised against the validity of verbal testimony.

Some say: if sound has as its object perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*), it is merely repetitive (*anuvādaka*) and not a valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇya*). And if it does not have those as its objects, it is non-expressive (*avācaka*) because the relationship [between word and meaning] cannot be grasped. For instance, since the referent of a word (*padārtha*) is not established through perception or inference, the relationship with the word cannot be grasped. If the referent is established by the word itself, is it by that very same word? Or by another word? If it is by that very same word, there is the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). If the referent is established by another word, the same fault applies, and there is the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Alternatively, the word is applied to the sentence-meaning (*vākyārtha*): having expressed the meaning through the sentence, the word is conventionally designated (*saṅketyate*) therein.

That too is incorrect; for the meaning of a sentence (*vākyārtha*) is merely the syntactic connection (*anvaya-mātra*) of words whose meanings are already well-known (*prasiddha*). Those meanings are well-known, and they are what are "stepped upon" (*padyante*), hence they are called "words" (*padāni*). The meaning residing in a sentence is merely their connection. Alternatively, those things whose meanings are well-known are "words with well-known meanings" (*prasiddhārthāni*); they are called "words" because one steps by means of them (*ebhiḥ padyate*). The sentence is merely their connection, and that itself is the "meaning of the sentence" (*vākyārtha*). Furthermore, since an unknown meaning cannot be understood even from a sentence, it is said to be "merely a connection. Therefore, word does not possess authority (*prāmāṇya*). Such was the objection raised by some.
The utility of demonstrating analogy is for the purpose of refuting that [position].

In order to refute that [objection], analogy (*upamāna*) is stated separately for the purpose of providing an illustration. Just as for one who seeks a specific object but has not previously perceived a *gavaya*, the relationship between a name and the thing named is established by means of a statement called "analogy," based upon the well-known similarity to a cow; so too, in the case of the word "Śakra" and its referent, it is established by taking some basis (*nimitta*). Nor is there any logical impossibility even in what is observed. For it is indeed observed that even regarding an object not established through perception and other means, the cognition of the relationship between a word and its referent is produced by a sentence based on a basis such as similarity. Therefore, it is not the case that a word lacks authority because it is non-expressive when its object is not within the scope of perception and other means. Furthermore, even when the object is within the scope of perception and inference, it does not lack authority due to being a mere restatement (*anuvādaka*), because we have demonstrated the convergence (*samplava*) of the means of knowledge, and because [verbal testimony] produces the cognition of a specific meaning in dependence upon context and other factors. This has been explained in detail in the investigation of this very sentence. Consequently, the separate mention of analogy in the enunciation-sūtra (*uddeśa-sūtra*) is for another purpose; thus, there is no contradiction with the sūtra.
Even according to the *Lakṣaṇasūtra*, analogy (*upamāna*) is not a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Although it was taught separately, its inclusion [within other means] or its purposeful utility cannot be easily understood unless it is defined; therefore, its definition is also stated: "Analogy is the means of establishing the object to be established (*sādhya*) through well-known similarity. That very statement which results from a known or recognized similarity as its cause—such as "as is a cow, so is a *gavaya*"—is the means of establishing the object to be established; that is, it is the instrument (*sādhana*) or indicator of the relationship between a name and the thing named (*saṃjñā-saṃjñi-sambandha*).

Alternatively, the object of knowledge is the cognition of the relationship between the name and the named; the means of accomplishing that [cognition], the sentence which brings it about, is *upamāna*. And thus, even from the definition-sūtra, no *upamāna* distinct from verbal testimony (*śabda*) is perceived. Nor is there any fault in this interpretation, such that one would have to provide a different explanation. For in common worldly usage, it is well known that the sentence itself is the *upamāna*, in the sense that "by this [sentence] something is compared.
{Even from the perspective of critical examination, it is not a separate means of valid cognition.}

This explanation is also confirmed by critical examination (*parīkṣā*). For instance, the sūtra of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "Comparison (*upamāna*) is not established because of absolute, general, or partial similarity. First, comparison is not established through absolute similarity; for it does not occur that "as is a cow, so is a cow. Nor is it established through general similarity; for it does not occur that "as is a horse, so is a buffalo. Nor is it established through partial similarity; for everything is not compared with everything.

To this, the subsequent Sūtra states: "Since comparison is established through well-known similarity, the aforementioned defect does not arise. If comparison were unestablished because of absolute, partial, or general similarity, then its establishment must be stated otherwise. Or, if it is unestablished even otherwise, then it must be stated that comparison is indeed established [through the remaining way]. That too contradicts observation, for "comparison is established through well-known similarity. This is because it is observed in every respect: therein, through absolute similarity—by means of one action, another action is compared, such as "the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa was like the battle between Rāma and Rāvaṇa. Also through general similarity—the comparison of a *gavaya* by means of a cow. However, the similarity of a buffalo in terms of the arrangement of its limbs and so forth is not well-known; therefore, there is no comparison of it. But for that which has well-known similarity in terms of form or strength, there certainly is a comparison: "As is the form or as is the strength of this cow, such is that buffalo. Also through partial similarity—for instance, when there is a desire to know only the form: "As is a mustard seed, so is Mount Meru. Therefore, the claim that comparison is unestablished due to absolute, general, or partial similarity is an untenable defect. Thus, even from the perspective of examination (*parīkṣā*), it is understood that comparison is indeed a specific kind of verbal testimony (*śabda*). If this is so, is it not improper to examine this separately from the examination of verbal testimony? No; for although it is included [within verbal testimony], there is a reason for examining presumption (*arthāpatti*) and non-existence (*abhāva*) separately. The purpose of a separate examination is to demonstrate the inclusion of that which is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) within [another] means of valid cognition. The purpose of its separate enumeration has already been stated, and that too would not be appropriate for something that has not been examined. Therefore, a separate examination is not improper.
The negation of inclusion is the object of inference.

The inclusion of analogy (*upamāna*) within inference alone has been refuted, but its exclusion from being included within scripture (*āgama*) is not [refuted], for it exists exactly as it is heard [in the scriptures]. Thus, the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) states: "Analogy is inference, because the non-perceived is established by means of perception. Just as there is the establishment of the non-perceived fire by means of the perceived smoke, so too is there the establishment of the non-perceived *gavaya* by means of the perceived cow; therefore, analogy is indeed inference. In this regard, there is no explicit sūtra providing a rebuttal, yet one exists by implication; for the opponent anticipates that very intention: "If it is argued that analogy is for the sake of another (*parārtha*),"—that which establishes an imperceptible object through invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is called inference; and analogy does not function by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth, but rather by the force of the authority of a reliable person (*āpta*). "If you think that analogy functions by taking up a similarity well-known to both parties, in order to produce a cognition in another who is well-known to both, based on that well-known similarity"—having thus anticipated the intention of the author of the sūtras, the opponent states the refutation: "No, because there is also a determination (*adhyavasāya*) by oneself. For even for the speaker, a determination certainly arises from the analogical statement; therefore, analogy is not exclusively for the sake of another. Regarding this, considering the objection to be without substance, the author of the sūtras said nothing at all. It is not said that the speaker’s determination does not occur; rather, that [statement] is not an analogy for him. Since he has already understood its meaning from another source, he does not utter the sentence for his own understanding, but only for the sake of another. [Objection: But an inferential statement is also uttered only for the sake of another; therefore, there is no distinction between analogy and that. To this he says: "There is no lack of distinction, because the establishment of analogy is due to the application of the word 'thus' (*tathā*). For analogy is applied precisely as: "As is the cow, so is the *gavaya*"; here, however, the property of the subject and so forth are not stated as they are in inference. Nor does inference proceed in the manner: "As is smoke, so is fire. Therefore, there is no lack of distinction between analogy and even inferential reasoning for the sake of another. Thus, it is understood from the sūtras of examination (*parīkṣā*) that analogy is indeed a specific type of scripture.
The Refutation of Objections Concerning the Examination of the Tetralemma (Catuṣṭva)

If it is argued that there is a contradiction with the examination of the fourfold nature [of the means of knowledge], we say no; for its purpose is to refute the suspicion that there might be five or more. Thus, by the statement, "No, because tradition (*aitihya*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), and probability (*sambhava*) are valid means of knowledge," the opponent has indeed proposed an excess [of means]. And he states the refutation of that very point: "There is no refutation, because tradition is not different from verbal testimony (*śabda*), and because presumption, probability, and non-existence (*abhāva*) are not different from inference (*anumāna*). Just as in the examination of the fivefold nature of the sense organs, only a deficiency was refuted—so that the acceptance of an excess is not contradicted because it is established by valid means—likewise, only an excess of means of knowledge was refuted; therefore, the acceptance of their threefold nature is not contradicted because it is established by valid means. Furthermore, the conventional usage of "fourfoldness" should be understood as being like the conventional usages of the sixteen categories of objects, the five sense organs, or the twenty-four principles (*tattvas*).

Now, if the author of the Sūtras intended for analogy (*upamāna*) to be included within verbal testimony (*śabda*), why was its inclusion not stated just as that of tradition (*aitihya*)? Or why was the triad of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) never mentioned anywhere? No; this is because such is the nature of this very author of the Sūtras: that he does not state even his own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) in certain places, in order to make known that only those disciples who possess an excellence of power in reasoning (*ūha*) and so forth have the primary qualification for this [work]. Just as the sixfoldness of the sense organs (*indriya*) is not mentioned yet is nonetheless intended by him, so too, when fallacies were raised against reasons such as "having a beginning" (*ādimattva*) on the grounds of the non-existence of a jar, universals, and the eternity [of sound], the Commentator (Vātsyāyana), having himself provided the refutation, asked: "But why is no Sūtra heard from the author of the Sūtras on this point? and said this: "It is the habit of this blessed author of the Sūtras that in many sections he does not establish two opposing sides; he thinks that one ought to understand the truth from the established doctrine of the treatise (*śāstra*). The established doctrine of the treatise is inference (*anumāna*)—which is designated as 'reasoning' (*nyāya*)—possessing many branches according to the nature of the object. Likewise, after stating, "Doubt arises from the twofold nature of knowledge and ignorance," and "There is no doubt in that case, because it is well-established by the previous reason," the author of the Sūtras did not state a Sūtra to support the whole (*avayavin*) and so forth—which had been rejected by arguments such as "because it does not reside in its parts either entirely or partially"—yet this does not mean that the whole and so forth are unestablished. Furthermore, by first laboriously establishing the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) which stand in the place of lamps, he makes this known: that even what is not explicitly stated by these [Sūtras] must be understood after investigation. If, however, only what is stated in the Sūtras were to be accepted as established by command, then one would not perform investigation. Therefore, even what is stated in the Sūtras must be accepted after investigation. And it has been investigated that it is not possible for analogy to be a separate means of knowledge. Thus, it is settled: analogy is included within verbal testimony.

{The Proposition that Presumption is Included within Inference} Presumption (*arthāpatti*) is also included within inference because it establishes the cognition of an object by means of the power of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). {Presumption as accepted by the Bhāṭṭas}

What is this presumption (*arthāpatti*)? "When an object known through the six means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), being otherwise impossible, leads one to postulate a new fact, that is cited as presumption."

In this regard, when an effect such as a blister is perceived immediately following contact with fire, the cognition of the fire’s burning power—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—is *arthāpatti* preceded by perception (*pratyakṣapūrvikā*). When a general property is inferred and the cognition of its specific instance—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—occurs, it is *arthāpatti* preceded by inference (*anumānapūrvikā*). When a general property is understood through verbal testimony and the cognition of its specific instance—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—occurs, it is *arthāpatti* preceded by verbal testimony (*śabdapūrvikā*). When a specific cow is cognized through comparison (*upamāna*) and the cognition of its capacity for tasks such as carrying and milking—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—occurs, it is *arthāpatti* preceded by comparison (*upamānapūrvikā*). When the eye is cognized through the necessity of accounting for the cognition of color, and the cognition of its power to produce knowledge—which cannot otherwise be accounted for—occurs, it is *arthāpatti* preceded by *arthāpatti* itself (*arthāpattipūrvikā*). And when the external existence of a living person is cognized through the necessity of accounting for his absence from the house while alive, it is *arthāpatti* preceded by non-existence (*abhāvapūrvikā*).
{The refutation of its status as a separate means of valid cognition}

On this point, they say: the burning power of fire is a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*), and that is apprehended by perception itself; therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is useless here. Furthermore, presumptive testimony preceded by inference has already been refuted. As for the claim that "the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) is grasped only between two things possessing a property (*tadvat*)," when establishing the meaning of words as being those very possessors of the property, the objection that even presumptive testimony preceded by verbal testimony is improper has already been raised. Presumptive testimony preceded by comparison (*upamāna*) is also improper, since comparison is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Likewise, presumptive testimony preceded by non-existence (*abhāva*) is also improper, because non-existence cannot be established as a separate means of valid cognition according to the reasoning to be stated later.

If it is asked, "From what source is the cognition of an external existence? [the answer is] from inference (*anumāna*). For instance: Devadatta exists in an external location, because, while being connected with life, he is not perceived in the house, like a person seen elsewhere. If the connection with life were unestablished, even presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) would be impossible; likewise, the presumptive testimony that establishes the absence of a person staying in one place in another place is also nothing but inference. To explain: all locations under dispute are devoid of Devadatta, because they are distinct from the location occupied by Devadatta, like a location adjacent to him. If it is argued that there is a counter-inference (*pratyanumāna*) stating: "Those locations occupied by Devadatta are distinct from locations other than those adjacent to him," this is not sound, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of the moon and other such objects, and because it is sublated by non-contradictory speech. Likewise: this Devadatta eats at night, because, while lacking the attainment of nourishment through daytime eating or elixirs, he is corpulent, like a person admitted by both parties to eat at night. If the qualification [of the reason] is unestablished, then presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is also untenable. The cognition of the eye's power to produce its own cognition is an inference based on an inference (*anumitānumāna*); the inference of the instrument (*karaṇa*) is from the nature of action (*kriyātva*), and the inference of the power is from the nature of the instrument. Now, it may be objected that power is never perceived directly; as it has been said:

"The powers (*śakti*) of all entities fall within the scope of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). [To this we reply: If the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) were established by inference alone, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, the apprehension of power is not inferential. If power is not grasped through invariable concomitance, then how could it be known even through presumptive testimony, like a *piśāca* demon and so forth? For when it is said, "it is not otherwise possible," it is understood that "it is possible only when [the power exists]"; and this very thing is invariable concomitance, since it consists of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Indeed, as long as such possibility is not understood, "impossibility otherwise" cannot be understood. And when both are understood, the invariable concomitance has been grasped.
The refutation of the view that [the capacity] is merely an arthāpatti (presumption) for the sake of establishing its own efficacy.

If it is argued that where there is no apprehension of concomitance (*anvaya*) even in a general form, there *arthāpatti* (presumption) is a distinct means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), we say no; for there is a lack of any illustrative example (*udāharaṇa*). [Objection: But surely *śakti* (potency) itself is the example. [Reply: No; because potency, being of the nature of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, is in some cases perceptible (*pratyakṣa*). To explain: if the power to burn and so forth were non-different from fire and the like, then since fire and the like are perceptible, that power would also be perceptible, or else there would be a contradiction with its non-difference [from the perceptible]. Now, if it is different [from fire], is it the cause of burning and so forth, or not? If it is not the cause, how could it be understood through the "otherwise-unaccountability" (*anyathānupapatti*) of burning? This would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is the cause, is it alone, or accompanied by fire and the like? If it is alone, then surely fire and the like would be non-causes; consequently, the conception of the cause would be exactly the opposite. If it is accompanied by fire and the like, then surely potency is nothing other than the auxiliary cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*); and yet every auxiliary cause is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). [Objection: Not every auxiliary cause is potency, but rather a specific one. [Question: What is this distinction here? [Reply: If it is the state of not abandoning [the substratum] (*ajahadvṛttitva*), then the generality (*sāmānya*) such as "fire-ness" (*agnitva*) or a quality (*guṇa*) such as heat (*auṣṇya*) would be the potency. If the distinction is "being the last," even so, potency is not something other than conjunction and the like. Furthermore, does the auxiliary cause denoted by the word "potency" possess another potency or not? If it does not, or if it exists as non-different [from itself], then one should not speak of a further potency for fire and the like either, since the logic is the same. If there is yet another potency for potency, then the auxiliary potency is not "the last" one, because there is no further "last" potency beyond it. Therefore, just as there is a mutual relationship of auxiliarity among causal factors (*kāraka*), so too should the state of possessing potency be regarded.

{There is no postulation of a distinct power (śakti) even on account of obstructions and the like.} Now, it may be argued: since the effect such as burning is not observed even when there is contact with fire due to obstruction by mantras and the like, it follows that power is not a general auxiliary cause such as contact. Therefore, why does the effect such as burning not occur even in the view that there is a power other than those [general causes]? If you say, "Because the power is obstructed," we say no; for this is the same in the case of the general [causes]—the obstruction is equal even in the view that power consists of contact and the like.

[Objection: In that case, how can the dependence of the capacity (*śakti*) upon that [cause] be known without the impossibility of the effect otherwise (*kāryānyathānupapatti*)? For it is not possible for any deity or human being to perceive, through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), the absence of all obstructing factors—such as the employment of mantras, meditations, or medicinal herbs—in any particular instance. Furthermore, the primary status of a cause consists in its completeness (*sākalya*); and since that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it is not observed anywhere and thus cannot be grasped even through inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, the cognition of both primary causality and unobstructed capacity occurs only through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). [Reply: No, because *arthāpatti* is not distinct from negative-only inference (*kevalavyatirekyanumāna*). For when a positive example (*anvayadṛṣṭānta*) is unavailable for a specific probandum (*sādhya*), and the relation of pervaded and pervader (*vyāpyavyāpakabhāva*) is established by a means of valid cognition that excludes the contrary (*vipakṣabādhakapramāṇa*), there it is called negative-only inference. This very form exists here as well. To explain: if fire were entirely devoid of unobstructed capacity, it would not produce effects such as burning, because there is a contradiction between the presence of capacity and the non-performance of the effect due to obstruction. The understanding of this contradiction is derived from observing the non-production of the effect when there is obstruction by any one of the factors, such as mantras.

And the obstruction applies only to the capacity known as "fitness" (*yogyatā*), not to the final capacity. For the final capacity is the completeness of the causal factors (*kāraka-sākalya*); an obstruction of that is impossible, because the effect arises immediately thereafter. Or, if the effect does not arise, there is no completeness—since the absence of obstruction is itself a cause, and when an obstruction exists, that [absence] is non-existent; how then could there be completeness? Therefore, an obstruction is possible only for the capacity known as fitness. And since that [obstruction] stands in contradiction to the arising of the effect, the arising of the effect leads, by the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), to the cognition of the absence of an obstructor. Likewise, since the effect is not observed to arise even when a single causal factor is missing, causality is understood to reside in the totality [of factors]. That in the absence of which the effect still arises is not a cause at all. And if something is a cause, how could the effect arise when it is deficient? Thus, by the force of the negative concomitance of the arising of the effect, one cognizes the completeness of its own causes. Therefore, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is not distinct from the purely negative inference (*kevala-vyatirekin*); "presumptive testimony is the purely negative inference" is merely a difference in terminology. If it is argued that it is not an inference because of the absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), we say no, for then even the purely positive inference (*kevala-anvayin*) would have to be a separate means of knowledge due to the absence of negative concomitance.

Furthermore, it has been stated that the definition of inference is the capacity to establish an object by the force of inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). By this, presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*) is subsumed; how then could it be a separate means of knowledge? The absence of a positive example (*anvaya-dṛṣṭānta*), however, is merely a minor point of dissimilarity. If a separate means of knowledge were established on that basis alone, then since there are also minor points of dissimilarity among the various divisions of perception (*pratyakṣa*) and so forth, it would follow that they too would be separate means of knowledge. Therefore, it is established that presumptive testimony is indeed inference because it establishes an object by the force of inseparable connection. {The statement that probability (*sambhava*) is also included within inference}

Probability (*sambhava*) also is nothing but inference (*anumāna*), because it conveys an object by virtue of the power of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).
