Probability is the cognition that what is capable of filling a *droṇa* measure is necessarily capable of filling an *āḍhaka* measure, as well as the cognition that what falls within a number such as one thousand necessarily falls within a number such as one, two, or three. How is there invariable concomitance here? Because the larger quantity has the smaller quantity as its constituent aggregate; for in the absence of the smaller, the larger is impossible. {Non-existence (*abhāva*), moreover, is included within these three [means of knowledge].}

However, non-existence (*abhāva*) is included within the [other] three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the case may allow; for instance, just as the existence of the Kauravas and others is established through scripture, their non-existence is likewise observed to follow from the presence or absence of that very scripture. In such cases, the postulation of a separate means of valid cognition is untenable. Furthermore, the cognition of the absence of color and other qualities in the self (*ātman*) and similar entities arises from inference. Likewise, by the falling of water, fruit, and so forth, the absence of an obstructing force to gravity is inferred. Similarly, in the examples illustrating the various types of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), the inference of non-existence should be understood. The cognition of the absence of a jar on the ground and similar surfaces arises from perception (*pratyakṣa*), because it follows the presence or absence of the operation of the senses, just like the cognition of the palm of the hand and such.
Is it not the case that elsewhere this principle of "arising when that exists" (tadbhāvabhāvitva) is ultimately restricted [to perception], since it has been stated:
"Having apprehended the existence of the object and having remembered the counter-correlate,
the mental cognition of non-existence arises independently of the senses"?

[Objection: "Because the apprehension of the object (*vastu*) and the cognition of absence (*abhāva*) are produced so rapidly, their sequence is not perceived, just as in the case of the perception of the trembling of a tree and the subsequent inference of wind. [Response: No, because there is no proof (*pramāṇa*). There is no proof whatsoever for the claim that immediately after the apprehension of the object, there arises a non-sensory cognition (*anakṣaja-jñāna*) consisting of the thought "it is not there. By mere assertion, one might even deny the perceptual nature (*pratyakṣatva*) of color-form (*rūpa*) and the rest; for in that case too, one could say: "In the apprehension of the locus (*āśraya*) of color-form and the like, or in the apprehension of their existence and nature, the operation of the sense-organ (*akṣa*) is exhausted; therefore, the cognition of color-form and the rest occurs entirely independent of the senses. [Objection: "Even if the cognition of color-form and the rest were directly produced by the senses (*sākṣād-akṣaja*), there would be no sublation (*bādhaka*); moreover, since the common experience 'I see color-form with my eye' exists, its sensory origin is accepted. [Response: If that is so, then there is likewise no sublation to the sensory origin of the cognition of absence; for there is also such an experience: "With my very eye, I see that there is no jar here."
Establishing the connection of the sense faculty with non-existence.

If it is argued that "the absence of a relation is the subverting factor here," this might be so: for a sense organ becomes a grasper of an object only when it is related to it, and there is no relation whatsoever between the sense organ and non-existence (*abhāva*). Indeed, non-existence possesses neither conjunction (*saṃyoga*) nor inherence (*samavāya*); because these are absent, relations such as "inherence in what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktasamavāya*) and others are also impossible. Therefore, the cognition of non-existence is not born of the senses (*akṣaja*). This is not so, because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*) for both your own position and the opposing position. First, in your position, there is no conjunction or inherence for anything at all. However, for the eyes and other senses, a relation called "capacity" (*yogyatā*) with their respective objects is accepted. And that capacity is understood through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for sensory experience. Furthermore, since the sensory experience of the ground and the absence of a jar is indistinguishable, the relation called "capacity" between the ground and the absence of the jar is established by the sense organ as well. In my position too, a relation between the sense organ and non-existence—such as "being a qualifier of what is conjoined" (*saṃyuktaviśeṣaṇabhāva*)—has been shown in the section on direct perception (*pratyakṣapariccheda*). If it is argued that "for that which lacks conjunction, inherence, and so forth, the relation of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*) is impossible," we reply: this rule has not been accepted by you, nor by me; therefore, even independent reductio arguments (*svatantraprasaṅgasādhana*) are untenable. For even in the absence of relations such as conjunction, the relation of qualifier and qualified is accepted on the basis of specific cognitions (*viśiṣṭapratyaya*); otherwise, cognitions such as "one who possesses cows" (*gomān*) would not occur. If it is argued that "if there were a conjunction of the sense organ with the owner of cows, then there would be the consequence of perceiving the cow even when it is obstructed or distant, due to the relation of being a qualifier of what is conjoined," this is not sound. For the power of a cause is determined by observing its effect; and there is no rule that whatever has power or lack of power in one instance must have power or lack of power in all instances. Indeed, just as the eye produces the cognition of color-ness (*rūpatva*) and so forth through the relation of "inherence in what is conjoined" when there is contact with a mere finger, it does not likewise produce the cognition of a hand or the body [in that same instance]. For entities possess diverse powers, and the power of a particular thing resides only in a particular place.
Because it lacks a distinct characteristic (*viviktalakṣaṇābhāvāt*), non-existence (*abhāva*) is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*).

Indeed, because it lacks a distinct characteristic, non-existence is not a separate means of valid cognition. For, just as the characteristics of perception, inference, and verbal testimony have been stated to be mutually exclusive, there is no such characteristic for non-existence that distinguishes it from perception and the others.
[This addresses the objection regarding the definition favored by the Bhāṭṭas and its refutation.]

It is not that it does not exist, because it has been said: "Where the five means of valid cognition do not arise with respect to the nature of an entity, there the status of non-existence as a means of valid cognition serves to ascertain the existence of that entity."

In that case, by what means is the absence of the five means of valid cognition (*pramāṇapañcakābhāva*) apprehended? If it were by the absence of the objects of cognition (*prameyābhāva*), then there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): as long as the absence of the object of cognition is not established, the absence of the five means of valid cognition is not established; and as long as the latter is not established, the absence of the object of cognition is not established. If the absence of the five means of valid cognition is itself cognized by another absence of the five means of valid cognition, then that too must be cognized by yet another absence of the five means of valid cognition, and that by another—leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it is claimed that the absence of the five means of valid cognition is accepted as the determiner of the absence of the object of cognition even while remaining unknown—just like the sense organs—that is not so; for it would follow that it could also determine [the absence of objects] during states such as intoxication or fainting. If it is argued that this consequence does not arise because [the absence of the means of cognition] depends upon the perception of the locus and the recollection of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), we say no; for it would then follow that when a specific place is grasped through inference or scripture, and one recalls a jar or the like, the absence of that jar would be cognized. Furthermore, it would follow that when a house or similar object is perceived from a distance by the eye, one would ascertain the absence of the specific qualities of taste and so forth belonging to gems, jewels, medicinal herbs, and the like that are remembered to be there. It would also follow that when a house is perceived in the dark by the sense of touch, one would ascertain the non-existence of specific substances present there that are being remembered. If it is argued that perception itself is the determiner of absence, provided it depends upon proximity to the location, a specific sense organ, light, and so forth—for such is the totality of conditions (*sāmagrī*) observed for perception—then we reply: if, even in the absence of those [other means], the capacity of absence to function like a logical mark (*liṅga*) were observed anywhere, then its status as a separate means of valid cognition might be justified. For instance, inference proceeds when the reason (*hetu*) and other factors are grasped through some means of valid cognition; likewise, if the absence of a specific substance or a specific quality such as color were perceived when the ground or such is grasped through some means of valid cognition, then absence would be a separate means of valid cognition. However, if a distinct capacity is not determined, then granting it the status of a separate means of valid cognition would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).
The cognition of the non-existence of something located in another place is memory.

As for what was stated here—"Having seen a place such as the ground and gone to another location, when one sees a previously unknown counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), one then realizes its absence, thinking: 'This object does not exist in that place'"—that is incorrect; because the absence is already perceived at the very time the place is perceived. Furthermore, upon seeing the counter-positive, there occurs only a memory due to the awakening of its latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Indeed, when questioned, "How do you know?", one does not reply, "I know by means of the absence of the five instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)," but rather, "I remember: he was not there. The recollection that "he was not seen there" means the same as "his absence was seen"; for instance, if one merely remembers the place and sees the counter-positive, doubt still arises: "That place was indeed seen, but it was not observed by me—does it exist there, or does it not?"
The refutation of the requirement for the apprehension of an object as distinct from its counter-correlate.

It might be argued: "Non-existence (*abhāva*) becomes a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by depending upon the apprehension of an object as distinct from its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); therefore, when there is no cognition of such distinction, even if there is the apprehension of the mere object, the ascertainment of non-existence does not occur therein. [We reply: Then by what is that distinction apprehended? If it is by perception (*pratyakṣa*), then how is it that non-existence is not apprehended by perception? For the distinction is characterized as non-existence. If, however, it is apprehended by non-existence itself, there follows the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). To explain: as long as there is no apprehension of the distinction, so long non-existence is not a means of valid cognition; and as long as non-existence is not a means of valid cognition, so long there is no apprehension of the distinction.

It is maintained that non-existence is apprehended by indeterminate perception (*nirvikalpakapratyakṣa*); what offense has been committed by determinate perception (*savikalpaka*) such that its apprehension is not accepted? If it is argued that determinate perception is not possible without the cognition of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), this is true; nevertheless, when all non-existences have been apprehended by indeterminate perception, subsequently, whenever the auxiliary conditions—such as the recollection of a counter-correlate—are present for a particular instance, the apprehension of that instance by determinate perception certainly occurs.

[Objection: In that case, when one subsequently perceives a previously unknown counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) in another location, how can there be a determinate perception (*savikalpaka-pratyakṣa*) of its absence in a place not currently present? Furthermore, memory is not tenable, because the relation between them has not been previously experienced—just as one who, having seen a cow in isolation, later sees its owner elsewhere, cannot remember, "I saw this cow [here]. [Reply: No; for the absence has already been grasped previously through mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) precisely as being related to that [place]. This is understood from the impossibility of explaining the memory of a qualified object otherwise, and from the grasping of such things as "this is larger than that" or "this is more gross than that," which is like the grasping of a pervasion (*vyāpti*). Alternatively, one grasps the absence's relation to that [place] only afterwards. Nor is that absence non-perceptual at that time due to its being non-present, since the absence exists even near the counter-positive, and because there is no difference [in status] from [the perception of] "cowness" (*gotva*) and so forth. Consequently, just as one first sees "cowness" as unqualified by any other individual (*piṇḍa*), and later sees it as qualified by another individual, and then remembers it as qualified by that [other individual] in the first individual as well—"I saw this similarity there"—so too, having grasped the absence near the counter-positive as delimited by it, one remembers it—even though it was perceived elsewhere—as delimited by that very [counter-positive]: "This object was not there. Therefore, absence is not a separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

{The Rejection of Tradition as a Separate Means of Knowledge} Tradition (*aitihya*)—defined by some as a succession of rumors whose original speaker is unspecified, such as "A yakṣa dwells here in this banyan tree"—is held by some to be a distinct means of knowledge. However, if it is not false, then it is subsumed under verbal testimony (*śabda*). Even if there is no mention of a reliable authority (*āpta*) due to a lack of necessity, its nature as a form of verbal testimony does not thereby cease to exist.
{The Rejection of Gesture as a Separate Means of Knowledge}

Others, however, maintain that there is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) called "gesticulation" (*ceṣṭā*). What, then, is this gesticulation? Gesticulation is the movement of the body and its limbs produced by effort. It is accepted as a means of valid cognition because it conveys a specific intention of a person and a specific meaning through the force of conventions established in the science of drama (*nāṭyaśāstra*) and through the force of worldly conventions. Thus, it does not differ from scriptural testimony (*āgama*), since it possesses the same defining characteristics. If it were not of the nature of verbal expression, then written characters would also have to be considered a separate means of valid cognition, as the same logic applies. However, if gesticulation conveys effort and so forth by way of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāvitva*), it should be regarded as inference (*anumāna*). Therefore, it is established that there are exactly three means of valid cognition.
The purpose of the means of valid cognition.

What follows from this? For liberation is not established by this much alone. Indeed, the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*) is sought through the comprehension, by means of the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), of some object—whether it be something to be abandoned, something to be acquired, or the means for achieving that. Regarding this [object], some consider it to be Primordial Matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth; others consider it to be selflessness (*nairātmya*) and so forth. Because of such conflicting views, one who is in doubt asks: "But what is to be known (*pramātavya*) by these instruments of valid cognition? It is replied: "The object of knowledge (*prameya*). However, Primordial Matter and the like do not even possess the status of being objects of valid cognition; therefore, knowledge concerning them is not a means to the highest good because it is erroneous.
{The Definition of the Categories of Objects of Cognition}

The question "What is its definition? is untenable, because it has already been stated that the object of valid cognition (*pramā*) is the cognizable (*prameya*). This is not so, because the question concerns a specific type of cognizable. In the *Daṇḍaka-sūtra*, that which was designated by the term "cognizable" must now have its definition stated. That is said as follows: that object whose knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), by virtue of being useless for any other knowledge, becomes a factor for the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*), whereas false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) extends transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*)—that is the cognizable. That alone is to be known in its true nature and constantly cultivated. However, even things such as the number of insects are not the cognizable, because knowledge of them is useless for the supreme good. And that [cognizable] is fourfold: 1. that which is to be abandoned (*heya*); 2. that which brings it about; 3. absolute abandonment (*hāna*); and 4. the means thereto.

{The twelvefold objects of knowledge} Now, the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are divided into twelve kinds in the Sūtra; thus says the Sūtra: "The self, the senses, the body, the objects of the senses, cognition, the mind, activity, defects, rebirth, fruit, suffering, and liberation are the objects of knowledge. The word "tu" (but/however) functions as a qualifier, meaning that although there are other objects of knowledge, this is a specific enumeration of the [primary] objects of knowledge. Its twelvefold nature is also understood from its definition, because the definitions of these twelve are stated. (1) The Self (*ātman*).

In this regard, the definition of the self (*ātman*) is: "Desire, aversion, volition, pleasure, pain, knowledge, and so forth, are the marks (*liṅga*) of the self. Or rather, how desire and the rest serve as marks of the self, we shall explain later. Furthermore, that [desire, etc. is also a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) of it, because of its exclusivity (*asādhāraṇatva*). If it is argued that it is not a definition because it does not pervade liberated selves (*muktātman*), we say no; for this has already been examined. Just as the possession of action (*kriyāvattva*) is a defect [as a definition] of substance (*dravya*) due to its non-pervasiveness, so too it has already been examined whether or not such non-pervasiveness is a defect in the case of desire and the rest. (2) The Body.

"The body is the substratum of movement, the sense organs, and objects. In common usage, the word *ceṣṭā* (movement) is conventionally established for a specific type of action, as in "he runs" (*adhāvati*) or "he leaps" (*laṅghate*). That body is the ultimate whole (*antyāvayavin*) in which such movement inheres. Being the substratum of the sense organs does not mean being the locus of their inherence; rather, it means that the state of the sense organs is affected by their benefit or injury through the body; thus, the body is the substratum of the sense organs. It is also the substratum of objects: only when the body exists do all objects, within the portion of the self delimited by it, produce pleasure, pain, and so forth.
(3) The faculties and the determination of their function as apprehenders of objects.

"The sense organs—the nose, tongue, eye, skin, and ear—[arise] from the elements. This sūtra is for the purpose of a specific enumeration and for the purpose of a specific definition; however, the general definition has not been stated. Since the application of the term "sense organ" (*indriya*) [occurs] even through conventional usage (*paribhāṣā*), it should be understood by oneself. In this context: the *ghrāṇa* is that by which one smells; the *rasana* is that by which one tastes; the *cakṣus* is that by which one sees (*caṣṭe*); the *sparśana* is that by which one touches (*spṛśati*). And because it is the locus of the skin-sense, it is metaphorically designated as "skin" (*tvak*) for the sake of common usage. The *śrotra* is that by which one hears (*śṛṇoti*). Thus, in this regard, there should be seen a group of six sūtras: five for the purpose of specific definitions and one for the purpose of a specific enumeration.

He says "from the elements" (*bhūtebhyaḥ*) in order to exclude their being derived from the *ahaṃkāra*. One might suspect that since the *ahaṃkāra* is also denotable by the word "element" (*bhūta*) and possesses the three *guṇas*, the plural number would still apply; therefore, he says: "The elements are earth, fire, air, and ether. In that context, the fact that four [of these] are the causes of the sense organs, while for ether it is a specific portion that has the nature of a sense organ, is the essential point; thus the term "element" is used figuratively. Alternatively, the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is understood with respect to its connection with the ear-cavity (*karṇa-śaṣkulī*). Consequently, there is no contradiction in using the ablative case in the sense of a causal source (*nimitta-pañcamī*) in the phrase "from the elements. For if they were established as having a single material cause (*ekaprakṛtitva*), it would be impossible to account for their restricted objects of perception, as there is no supporting example (*dṛṣṭānta*). However, if they have diverse material causes (*nānāprakṛtitva*), the previously mentioned example of the lamp and so forth applies. Therefore, the five external sense organs are elemental (*bhautika*).

(4) *Arthāḥ* (Objects): "Smell, taste, visible form, touch, and sound—the qualities (*guṇa*) of earth and the other [elements]—are the objects (*artha*). The very fact of being for the sake of those [faculties] is here the definition of objects. Furthermore, the classification of objects is into "earth and the others" and "qualities. Here, by the term "quality," there is an inclusion of everything that is dependent and every qualifier. Consequently, whatever is an object of the sense faculties, whether it be an entity (*bhāva*) or a non-entity (*abhāva*), all of it is an object. Moreover, the body should be understood as a "body" (*śarīra*) because it is the locus of movement and so forth and is the seat of experience (*bhoga-āyatana*), and it should be understood as an "object" (*artha*) because it is an object of the sense faculties.
The purpose of the separate mention of odor and the other [objects].

The separate mention of smell (*gandha*) and the others is for the purpose of making known that they are the primary causes of the defects (*doṣa*). For while each of these—smell and the rest—individually possesses the capacity to cause a defect, other substances, qualities, and so forth, even when assisted by smell and the others, do not have such power to generate a defect. To illustrate: attachment, aversion, and the like arise toward flowers, trees, and so on, which are assisted by smell; toward specific foods, which are assisted by taste; toward dancing, large breasts, abundant hair, and so on, which are assisted by form; toward beds and such, which are assisted by touch; and toward flutes and the like, which are assisted by sound. Furthermore, in the case of pleasure (*rati*) and the rest, one should observe, as applicable, that they are assisted by five [objects], four, three, or two. Likewise, even the non-existence of things such as separation from the beloved becomes a cause of defect when its form is characterized by memory or mental superimposition (*āropa*). Thus, there is no contradiction with the two aphorisms: "The objects, form and the rest, which are the causes of the defects, are produced by conceptualization (*saṅkalpa*)," and "But the conceit of a whole (*avayavin*) is caused by those [defects]."
(5) Intellect (*buddhi*)

"Buddhi, upalabdhi, and jñāna are not different in meaning. Buddhi is the first transformation of *pradhāna*; *upalabdhi* is experience characterized by the arising of a reflection for the *puruṣa*; and *jñāna* is the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) into the form of an object. To refute this view, the definition was stated even in terms of synonyms. What more need be said regarding the assumption of distinct meanings for words such as *pratīti*, *avagama*, and *vijñāna*? In that case too, the answer is the same: these are merely synonymous terms. Furthermore, this very *buddhi*, when turned away from its causes of defect through discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), is the cause of liberation; and when not so turned away, it is likewise to be known as the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*).
(6) mind

"The non-simultaneous production of cognitions is the mark (*liṅga*) of the mind (*manas*). Since that which is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*) cannot be defined otherwise, a mark—which serves as its definition—is stated for the mind just as it is for the self (*ātman*). For the nose and other [senses] as well, the cognition of smell and so forth is likewise their mark and definition. To begin with, the self, because of its all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), is connected with all the sense organs. The sense organs too are connected with their respective objects on occasions such as looking while one is awake; nevertheless, cognitions of smell and so forth do not arise simultaneously, as we observe a lack of simultaneous engagement (*vyāsaṅga*). In this context, that whose presence or absence results in the production or non-production of a cognition is the mind. The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: the self, the sense organs, the objects, and so forth, require another auxiliary factor for their sequential conjunction, because even when they are present together, they produce effects sequentially—just as the colors and other factors that produce a variegated pattern require a brush (*varṇaka*) or similar tool. Because the term "mark" is expressed without a compound, the Sūtra provides another mark: pleasure and so forth are determined by a sense organ, because they are objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), like color and other [sensory qualities]. Since no capacity is perceived in the external senses to determine pleasure and so forth, that sense organ which determines pleasure and the rest is the mind. Furthermore, the fact that cognitions such as memory, inference, verbal testimony, and doubt are preceded by an instrument—or preceded by a sense organ—is established because they are cognitions, just like cognitions produced by the eye and other [senses]. Since desire and so forth are also actions, once it is established that they must be preceded by an instrument, one seeks the proof of the mind through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*). Alternatively, the fact that desire and so forth are not born from the external senses may also be proven by the reason that they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self.

{The purpose of mentioning the mind separately}: If the mind is also a sense-organ (*indriya*), for what reason was it mentioned separately? Some say it is because of its difference in nature (*vaidharmya*)—such as having all things as its object and not being composed of the elements (*abhautika*). Others, however, say: since the activity of all the sense-organs is rooted in the mind, the conquest of all the sense-organs is accomplished only through the conquest of that [mind]; therefore, the mind was mentioned separately to make known that one who desires liberation (*mumukṣu*) must exert great effort in conquering the mind. {7} Activity.

"Activity (*pravṛtti*) is the undertaking of speech, intellect, and body. The meaning is that activity is verbal, mental, and physical operation. Here, the term "intellect" (*buddhi*) refers to the mind (*manas*), by way of etymological derivation as an instrument (*karaṇa*). This threefold activity is further divided into two types based on the distinction between what is enjoined and what is prohibited. The fruit of such activity is merit or demerit. Its subtle distinctions cannot be fully enumerated, though its gross forms are demonstrated in the treatises on Dharma. {(8) Faults (*doṣa*):}

"The defects have the characteristic of incitement (*pravartanā*). This means that they are characterized by—that is, they have as their intrinsic nature—the fact that they incite a person toward both what is enjoined and what is prohibited; thus, desire, hatred, and delusion are "incitement. Others, however, explain it thus: incitement is the state of being a cause for engagement, a quality residing in desire and the rest that is self-cognizable; those [defects] which have that as their characteristic mark are so described. In every respect, it is understood from the statement, "Their threefold division exists because desire, hatred, and delusion are distinct entities," that desire and the others alone are called defects. (9) Rebirth (*pretyabhāva*).

"Rebirth (pretyabhāva) is re-arising. Having abandoned the body and so forth previously acquired, the soul's acquisition of another body and so forth is rebirth; the meaning is "birth after death. The word "again" (punar) indicates that this arising of the soul—characterized by a specific connection with a body and so forth—is not beginningless [in the sense of being first], but has never been a first occurrence. The meaning is that all such occurrences are "again," and never "first"; therefore, this rebirth is beginningless. Furthermore, rebirth is taught separately from the body and the senses in order to make known that there is no end to it except through liberation (apavarga), and for the purpose of cultivating the contemplation of the intensity of suffering inherent in birth and death.
(10) The fruit.

"An object produced by activity and defects is the result (*phala*). Activity and defects are those previously mentioned; an object produced by them through some mediation is the purpose, or result. For there are two kinds of purpose: that which is to be avoided and that which is to be accepted. Among these, that which is to be avoided is suffering (*duḥkha*) of many varieties, distinguished as primary and secondary. That which is to be accepted, however, is pleasure (*sukha*), distinguished as primary and secondary for the ignorant; but for the wise, everything is to be avoided, because even pleasure is established as being a cause of suffering. Thus say the knowers of the inner self: "To the discerning person, all is suffering. In this context, the result is taught separately from suffering in order to cultivate equanimity toward both pleasure and suffering, since they are acquired through one's own karma.

(11) Suffering (*duḥkha*): "Suffering is characterized by affliction" (*bādhanālakṣaṇaṃ duḥkham*). That which is characterized by affliction—that is, whose intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is affliction—is suffering in the primary sense. However, with respect to its secondary sense, that which has affliction as its characteristic—such as the body and so forth—is described in that way. Affliction (*bādhanā*) means pain (*pīḍā*) or torment (*santāpa*).
(12) Liberation (*apavarga*).

"Liberation (apavarga) is the absolute release from that. Therefore, liberation of the self is the perpetual cessation—the state of being forever severed—from that suffering which is divided into primary and secondary types. Thus, it has been stated that the objects of valid cognition (prameya) are of twelve kinds according to their distinct characteristics, and not merely fourfold. {The refutation of the doubt regarding the twelvefold nature of the objects of valid cognition}

True; it has been stated that [the objects of knowledge] are of twelve kinds. However, even those twelve kinds, when contemplated in their fourfold form as "to be abandoned" (*heya*) and so forth, become the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*); therefore, they are said to be fourfold. The author of the Sūtras, however, considering this fourfold nature to be logically established, did not state it explicitly. For indeed, unless the forms of "to be abandoned" and so forth are determined, the cessation of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) regarding the body and other things—by means of which arises dispassion (*vairāgya*) and the ultimate liberation (*apavarga*) from them—is not possible; moreover, the twelvefold classification is itself included within these four categories.

{The secret of why fourfoldness is not explicitly stated in the Sūtra}: If this is so, why did the author of the Sūtra not state that there are exactly four categories? It is not so; it is because [the Sūtra] aims to refute the views of others. In this regard, the view of the Sāṃkhyas is as follows: "That which is to be abandoned is suffering, consisting of the activity of *rajas*; the cause of what is to be abandoned is the conjunction of the seer and the seen; its cause is ignorance (*avidyā*); from the absence of that [ignorance] comes the absence of conjunction, which is abandonment; the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the seer results from that; and the means of abandonment is unshakable discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*)."

And for the Śākyas, the four noble truths—1. suffering (*duḥkha*), 2. its origin (*samudaya*), 3. cessation (*nirodha*), and 4. that which is called the path (*mārga*)—are intended as knowledge for the sake of liberation. In this context: 1. Suffering consists of the aggregates (*skandha*) of those in saṃsāra—the five aggregates: form (*rūpa*), perception (*saṃjñā*), feeling (*vedanā*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), and mental formations (*saṃskāra*). Regarding these, because of the statement that "form is a collection of primary elements (*bhūta*) and derivative matter (*bhautika*)," even taste and the other [sensory objects] are called the aggregate of form. That by which an object is expressed is "expression" (*abhilāpa*); pleasure, pain, and so forth are "feeling"; the aspect of cognition is "consciousness"; and the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of purity and so forth are "mental formations. The fact that these constitute saṃsāric existence and have suffering as their intrinsic nature has been established by the Śākyas in detail; it is not stated here for fear of excessive length in the text. 2. Its cause is the origin (*samudaya*). Thirst (*tṛṣṇā*)—characterized by the intense grasping born from the deep-seated attachment to self and what belongs to the self regarding the body, the senses, the locus [of the self], and so forth—is the primary cause and thus the origin. 3. For one who is free from thirst, there is no engagement even with silver, kingdoms, and the like, though they may be brought about by ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and so forth; therefore, the abandonment of all suffering is cessation (*nirodha*). 4. The means to that [cessation] is the knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*), which is the path (*mārga*). Thus, even in the doctrine of the opponent, the knowledge of the fourfold set beginning with what is to be abandoned is accepted as the cause of liberation. It is for the purpose of refuting that view that the distinction of the Self and so forth has been introduced.
The sequential assistance for the knowledge of the self and so forth.

In this regard, when self-knowledge exists, there arises a longing for the next world, and not otherwise—as we shall explain. Furthermore, when there is knowledge that [the body] is distinct from the self, the notion of "self" regarding that [body] ceases; consequently, one does not perform violence and the like for its sake. Having recognized the body as a locus of suffering, attachment toward it ceases. Even when the causes of defects are present, if the senses do not function, no defect arises; whereas if they do function, a defect necessarily arises. Thus, having understood the nature of the senses, one strives for their withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*). Striving thus, one abandons the notion of things being desirable once they are understood to be causes of suffering through transformation—like the ripening fruit of a tree—and cultivates dispassion (*vairāgya*). Having understood that false notions of reality are the cause of *saṃsāra* while true notions are the cause of liberation, one causes false notions to disappear through discriminative discernment (*parisaṃkhyāna*) and nourishes the notion of reality through practice. The purpose of separately including the mind has already been stated. And having known that active tendencies (*pravṛtti*), by way of generating merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, are the root of suffering, one avoids them. "Activity does not lead to rebirth for one whose afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted"—thus, having understood the nature of the defects, one exerts great effort toward their destruction. The purpose of fully knowing rebirth and its fruits has been stated. Suffering must also be understood for the sake of cultivation (*bhāvanā*). Having realized that the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is permeated by suffering, one becomes detached from it, just as one is from honey mixed with poison. And having understood that liberation (*apavarga*) is unsurpassed, infinite, utterly pure, and the cessation of all suffering, one strives solely for its sake. Thus, since the cultivation of the knowledge of reality is useful even in these twelve forms, the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) are said to be twelvefold. And for the sake of concise cultivation, its fourfold nature is now stated:
{The Investigation of Suffering}

In this context, "that which is to be abandoned is future suffering. For past [suffering] is not to be abandoned because it has already been discarded; nor is present [suffering] capable of being abandoned, since it has already reached the state of experience and is abandoned only through that very experience. Therefore, those who know reality consider only future suffering to be [the object of abandonment], not the present. Indeed, present internal and other forms of suffering cannot be avoided by means of a pure path free from violence and the like; rather, by avoiding [suffering] through the sequence of non-violence and so forth, they avoid only the infinite future suffering. Furthermore, there exists a specific means for the avoidance of future suffering, which has been demonstrated in the *Duḥkha-sūtra* and will be demonstrated further below. Therefore, only future suffering is to be abandoned.
The twenty-one divisions of suffering.

And that suffering is of twenty-one kinds: the body, the six sense organs (*indriya*), the six objects (*viṣaya*), the six cognitions (*buddhi*), pleasure, and pain. If it is asked how the objects are six, it is said: for the five [organs] beginning with the nose, the five objects such as odor are stated primarily. The sixth organ is the mind (*manas*); that which, being experienced by it, becomes the cause of pleasure or pain, is the sixth object. If it is asked what that is, distinct from the six cognitions of pleasure and pain, some say it is memory and volition (*saṅkalpa*), while others say it is sleep, laziness, and so forth. Or, it is the capacity to produce pleasure, pain, and so on, within the specific region of the self delimited by desire and the like, or the state of being the locus of the movement of the organs and their objects. The organs, the objects, and their cognitions are called "suffering" precisely because they are instruments of suffering.

{An Examination of the Manner in which Pleasure is of the Nature of Suffering} Pleasure, however, is suffering because it is accompanied by suffering. The meaning of "accompaniment" (*anuṣaṅga*) is inseparability: one who desires to experience pleasure must necessarily experience suffering; and one who wishes to avoid suffering must necessarily abandon pleasure, because it is impossible to abandon them while keeping them distinct.

Others, however, say: there exists a mutual relationship of producer and produced between pleasure and pain. For just as pleasure does not arise from food, drink, and so forth without the pains of hunger, thirst, and the like—such that even the pain of hunger and so on serves as a cause of pleasure—likewise, without the pleasure derived from affection for specific bodies, senses, and objects, pain does not arise either from separation from them or from contact with their opposites; thus, pleasure itself is a means to pain. Therefore, it need not be stated as something distinct from the object [of experience].

This is not so, because suffering arises even in the absence of pleasure from such things as sword-strokes. Furthermore, an object is a cause of suffering only while it is being experienced; pleasure is not like that, for rather, suffering is experienced through the departure of pleasure. For this very reason, all worldly beings are deluded by the thought, "Upon the attainment of pleasure, suffering will cease. This is because, just like the pleasure derived from experiencing the fruit of karmic maturation (*vipākaphala*), every pleasure derived from the enjoyment of sense objects becomes a cause of extremely intense suffering in its transformation (*pariṇāma*). Therefore, it is said that "pleasure is indeed suffering" for the purpose of prohibiting attachment to all pleasures and their means, and for the purpose of prohibiting aversion toward sufferings and their means, so that one may cultivate equanimity toward both. Suffering—consisting essentially of affliction, oppression, and torment—is suffering in the primary sense itself.

{The Investigation of the Cause of Suffering} The specific causes that bring about even those twenty-one types of suffering are ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*), as well as merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
{Ignorance}

In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cognition of the object correctly demonstrated by those who truly know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*) as being contrary [to reality]; its latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is also called ignorance. That which pertains to the self, beginning with the body and ending with liberation, is the "inner self" (*adhyātma*). Those who discern that according to its true nature are the "true knowers of the inner self. By them it was demonstrated:
"A skeleton-pillared [body], bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood, covered with skin, full of foul odors, and filled with urine and feces..."

"One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is possessed by old age and sorrow, a dwelling place for disease, afflicted, full of passion, and impermanent"— thus it is said. But for those blinded by passion, there is a cognition contrary to that.
By whom were women created? They are like jars of nectar, like heaps of happiness, and like treasuries of delight.

And so forth. In this way, one should understand that those blinded by passion, hatred, and delusion regarding [the objects] beginning with the self and ending with liberation possess perverted cognition. Furthermore, what was briefly illustrated in the Sūtra on Suffering is here designated as ignorance (*avidyā*). [Craving (*tṛṣṇā*)...]

"Thirst is the longing for rebirth. Just as one who is free from thirst does not engage with specific foods and drinks mixed with poison—even if he has a firm resolve for them—or with the property of others—even if he has a firm resolve for it—being thus non-engaged, he is not joined with misfortune. But one seized by thirst engages even while knowing [the danger]; he is also joined with misfortune. Likewise, he who has a grasping for the body, the sense-faculties, and so forth, acts in such a way that, longing even for another birth, he is joined with various desirable and undesirable places, bodies, sense-faculties, and so on, for the sake of becoming reborn. However, if even a delusion should arise in some way for one who is free from thirst, nevertheless, because he does not engage due to his freedom from thirst, he does not enter into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Therefore, thirst is also a cause of suffering.

If it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) is therefore incapable [of producing action], we say no; for even one who is free from craving, if he is ignorant, lacks the capacity to avoid suffering from snakes and the like even while acting, and thus lacks capacity in other respects as well. One who is free from craving is not able to remain motionless, because such is the nature of living beings (*prāṇidharma*). Even when action is inevitable, the wise man, by discerning and proceeding through the avoidance of violence and so forth, does not incur future suffering.
[Thus, merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) are the causes of suffering.]

Furthermore, according to the principle stated in the *Duḥkha-sūtra* and from the sūtra: "Among these, delusion (*moha*) is the most evil, because the others do not arise in one who is not deluded," it is certain that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the primary cause of suffering. Even when ignorance and craving have ceased, the arising of suffering is observed due to the impact of cold, wind, disease, and so forth; therefore, merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*) are also determined to be causes of suffering. Now, one might object: "Merit is the specific cause of happiness; how can it be a cause of suffering? No, for even happiness has been described as being of the nature of suffering. That merit which is a cause of happiness by way of procuring the body, sense organs, objects, and so on, is here stated to be a cause of suffering, because it is the cause of great suffering through some slight mediation. However, that merit which is produced by pure means such as devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-bhakti*), the limbs of yoga (*yoga-aṅga*), and other practices performed without desire for results—which is the cause of the happiness of knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*), tranquility (*śama*), and contentment—is not a cause of suffering even through mediation; rather, it is the very cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*). And thus, for that purpose, it is said: "The refinement of the self (*ātma-saṃskāra*) is achieved through restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*), and through yoga by means of the methods of inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*)."
{An Analysis of Killing}

Abandonment (*hāna*) is the cessation of suffering. Even when one practices the means taught in the treatises on dharma, adharma, artha, kāma, and medicine, there occurs an abandonment known as the cessation of internal and other forms of suffering; however, to exclude that [temporary cessation], the term "absolute" (*ātyantika*) is employed. For even for one who has attained the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and so forth, there is no absolute abandonment of suffering, since scripture declares that there is a return [to saṃsāra] due to the exhaustion of merit (*dharma*), and because of scriptural accounts of mutual subjugation, conflict, and the like. But for one who has attained liberation (*apavarga*), because ignorance, craving, and the rest—the causes of suffering—are absolutely eradicated, there is never, in any way, a connection with suffering.

{The means of cessation}: The means for that absolute cessation of suffering is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Regarding its status as the means, the very same reasoning already stated in the *Duḥkha-sūtra* applies. What is the object of the knowledge of reality that serves as the cause for liberation? It has the self (*ātman*) as its object. [Objection: But was it not stated that it has the twelve objects of cognition (*prameya*) as its object? [Response: True; however, it is said to have the self as its object in order to make known the primacy of the self. For this very reason, it is mentioned first. {Definition of the Self}

Although its nature is eternal, all-pervading, immovable, and stainless, it appears in a degraded form—being born, dying, existing in specific locations, coming into being, and ceasing to be; as well as being full of passion, hatred, delusion, and suffering—due to its association with the ten factors beginning with the body. However, when one abandons these faulty things, from the body to suffering, through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) alone and becomes solely devoted to the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*), then, manifesting in its own true nature of eternity and so forth, it attains liberation (*apavarga*) and remains in its own self, utterly stainless. Therefore, liberation is mentioned at the end, because beyond that there is nothing further to be abandoned or attained, and all activity has ceased. Even in the Veda, it is taught that the Self alone must be known with the utmost effort, as it is said: "The Self, indeed, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon."
It should be heard from the statements of the scriptures and reflected upon through reasonings;
having reflected, it should be constantly meditated upon—these are the causes for realization.
Thus [it is said]: "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow.

That Self is of two kinds—the Supreme (para) and the Lower (apara). Both of these must be known by one who seeks liberation. Accordingly, it has been stated: "Two Brahmans are to be known: the Supreme and the Lower," and so forth.

{The Definition of the Supreme Lord} In this context, the Supreme Self is the Blessed Maheśvara. His defining characteristics are: being distinguished by supreme sovereignty; being untouched from beginningless time by the worldly attributes of passion, aversion, delusion, suffering, and so forth; possessing beginningless omniscience; and being the creator of the entire universe. How is he, who possesses such characteristics, to be known? Through inference and through scripture. {Inference as a Means of Valid Cognition Regarding the Lord}

In this regard, inference is first stated: that which is the subject of dispute has an intelligent cause, because it comes into being after not having existed, like cloth and so forth. If it is argued that the subject (*pakṣa*) is doubtful because the specific nature of the locus (*dharmin*) is not specified, we say no; for by specifying the object of dispute, the specific nature of the locus is established, since the subject of the argument is precisely that locus regarding which there is dispute. If it is argued that there is indeed uncertainty because dispute takes many forms, we say no; for by specifying the particular property to be proven (*sādhya*), its specific nature is established, just as one determines a specific caste such as Brāhmaṇa by mentioning a specific action such as eating. The term "subject of dispute" refers only to that [locus] where the proponent accepts the quality of having an intelligent antecedent while the opponent does not accept it; it does not refer to space or cloth. If it is argued that the example is unestablished due to a contradiction with their own tenets—since even the fact that cloth and so forth have an intelligent antecedent is unestablished because the intelligent being is not the agent—we say no; for agency belongs to the intelligent being alone, because activity proceeds from a body and so forth impelled by the intelligent being. Indeed, one who is independent is called an "agent. A body and so forth lack independence because they follow the intention of a person, and because agency is not observed in a dead body and the like.
The Sāṃkhya objection and its refutation.

If it is argued that this is because we observe non-conscious substances such as milk acting independently for the sake of the growth of calves and so forth, we say no; for there is no absence of deviation from the probandum (*sādhya*). For if this were so, every logical reason (*hetu*) would be subject to deviation. Furthermore, if the conscious being were not the agent, there would be contradiction with both inference and scripture. To explain: even in the world, upon seeing specific works such as those of the sciences or arts, one infers a specific knowledge in their creator. And it is only for those devoid of such knowledge that there is a lack of agency. In the scriptures as well—such as the Vedas, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas—the agency of the knower alone is heard of. From statements such as "The learned man should sacrifice," it follows that agency regarding dharma and other matters belongs to the conscious being alone. Now, if it is argued that agency in the sciences, arts, and so forth belongs only to the non-conscious *buddhi*-principle—which possesses knowledge, desire, and effort—and not to the conscious being, this is merely the manifestation of great delusion, to claim that the possessor of knowledge is non-conscious. That which is the substratum of knowledge, desire, and the like is indeed the Self (*ātman*); we shall demonstrate that there is no conscious being other than that. Moreover, it has been established that terms such as *buddhi*, *upalabdhi*, and *jñāna* are synonyms.
The Mīmāṃsaka objection and its resolution.

But another says: "If it is claimed that some mere cause possesses a presiding agency (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*), then since this is established by the actions (*karman*) of all living beings, you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). This is first of all an incoherent statement, a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). When the probandum (*sādhya*) is "being preceded by an intelligent being" (*buddhimatpūrvakatva*), what relevance is there in raising the objection of *siddhasādhana* regarding insentient actions? If it is argued: "How is it that an effect such as a mountain, produced by actions performed by an intelligent being, is not itself preceded by an intelligent being? We say: No, because of a failure to understand what is intended to be said. For by "preceded by an intelligent being," we mean that which is directly produced by an intelligent being, and not merely that which is produced through a causal chain. Even an action, though preceded by an intelligent being, does not perform its own effect until it has been presided over by a conscious agent who knows its power. Indeed, a pot or similar object made by an intelligent being cannot perform its own function independently of an intelligent presiding agent. If it is argued: "Because [the argument] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the body of that very agent; and if that body also requires another intelligent cause, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)," we say: No, because there is no proof for the existence of a body belonging to God (*Īśvara*). Nor does the non-establishment of a body lacking proof entail the non-establishment of the agent, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, for one who attempts to prove the connection with a body solely on the basis of being an agent, there is the consequence of contradicting one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*), since you do not accept that [God] is an agent. The "reductio ad absurdum" (*prasaṅgasādhana*) is also improper, because the reductio is sublated by the root inference and because its locus (*āśraya*) is unestablished.
The objection regarding the activity of God and its resolution.

But surely, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*), one who is bodiless possesses no activity at all; and for one devoid of activity, agency (*kartṛtva*) is untenable, or else it would follow that even the liberated soul is an agent. What is this "activity"? If it is characterized by [actions such as] throwing upwards and so forth, then because of its incorporeality, no such [action] belongs to any soul, and it would follow that every soul is a non-agent. For throwing upwards and other such actions are primarily the business of the body alone; likewise, agency too would primarily belong to the body and not to the soul. Consequently, it would follow that an action performed by one person is experienced and enjoyed by another, which would result in the adoption of the doctrines of the Sāṃkhya school and others. If, however, "activity" is defined as the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātvartha*), then that exists even for incorporeal things such as space (*ākāśa*). But for liberated souls, there is neither a capacity produced by action and so forth nor an innate capacity; thus they lack agency. The Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), however, possesses an innate capacity characterized by supreme sovereignty; therefore, he possesses agency. And such a capacity is inferred from specific effects.
"In the inference for God (*īśvarānumāna*), the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*) and the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddhatā*).

Now, it might be argued that in this way, in the inference for a specific creator, the example would lack the property to be proven and the reason would result in being contradictory (*viruddha*). As it has been said:
"If the superintendence of a potter and the like is admitted in the case of a jar and so forth..."
There would be no state of being presided over by a Lord; if it did exist, there would be a lack of the probandum.
And if the example were established in that manner, there would be a contradiction of the reason.

The meaning of this is as follows: If it is admitted that the potter’s supervision is present in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), then there would be no supervision by God (*Īśvara*); consequently, the example would lack the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). If, on the other hand, it is admitted that supervision by God is also present, even so there is still the fault of lacking the property to be proven; for it is only when both [parties] agree upon the presence of a quality that something can properly serve as an example. Nowhere is supervision by God agreed upon by both parties, such that the example would not be devoid of the property to be proven. Furthermore, when the example is established in this way, not only does the example lack the property to be proven, but the logical reason (*hetu*) itself becomes contradictory (*viruddhatā*). For whatever property the reason is pervaded by in the example, it establishes that very object through the force of that pervasion. And in the case of examples such as a jar, a non-divine, embodied, perishable agent possessed of passion and the like is observed; therefore, by the power of pervasion, one arrives at the conclusion that even in the subject to be proven (*sādhya*), the agent must be of exactly that same nature.
{The refutation thereof}

This is merely a statement by one who has not understood the nature of the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). For instance, is the charge of "deficiency of the probandum" (*sādhyahīnatva*) and so forth raised with respect to the probandum as expressed by the words, or with respect to the probandum as encompassed by the [proponent's] intention? In the first case, there is no fault of deficiency of the probandum and so on. For the state of being preceded by God (*īśvarapūrvakatva*) is not the probandum expressed by the word; rather, what is [expressed] is the general property (*sāmānya*) of being preceded by an intelligent agent (*buddhimanmātra*). And since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with such a general probandum is well-established, how can there be any room for the charge of deficiency of the probandum and so forth? If, however, it is said with respect to the probandum as encompassed by the intention, then it follows that all inferences would suffer from deficiency of the probandum and so on. For in all inferences, the specific object which is the content of the cognition is encompassed by the inferrer’s intention. Indeed, a featureless generality is never the object of either cognition or practical activity, because it is already established [prior to inference] and because it is incapable of burning and so forth. Nor is possession of fire established by mere fire, because it is impossible to prove possession of fire when that fire is separated by space and time. Nor is it established by mere place, because that would be futile. Therefore, the proponent’s intention is: "this place possesses fire by means of that [specific] fire. And thus, since a pervasion of the probans with such a specific probandum is impossible, inference would fail to function. Consequently, those seeking fire would have neither cognition nor practical activity directed toward a specific place and so forth based on that inference. Furthermore, because inference does not convey a previously unknown particular, it would follow that it lacks authority (*aprāmāṇya*), like memory, since it apprehends what is already grasped. Moreover, regarding the part that is established as new, no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) is perceived in the example; thus, the charge of deficiency of the probandum and so forth follows. Therefore, because it contradicts the specific [particular] encompassed by the intention, it follows that all inferences would lack authority, and thus the status of being a proponent of inference as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is lost. As for the proponent of non-authority, the contradiction has already been explained at length previously, during the refutation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) beginning with "because a means of knowledge is not figurative" (*pramāṇasyāgauṇatvāt*). As for what was also said—that the reason, as seen to be pervaded by this or that [property] in the example, conveys that very [property]—that too is incorrect. For smoke, though seen in the kitchen and so forth as related to pots and the like, does not convey pots and the like as well. If it is argued that smoke is not invariably connected (*niyata*) with pots and the like, and therefore does not convey them, then what is this "invariable connection"? We do not understand what is meant by the claim that it is nothing other than non-existence (*abhāva*). If it is simply inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*), then there is no such invariable connection between "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) and "having a non-divine creator" (*anīśvaratva*) and so forth. Let there be no cognition of that [specific creator] either; for "divine" and "non-divine" are specific qualities of the agent, and the pervasion is through the general, not the specific. Fire is not the pervader of smoke by way of such qualifiers as "causality" and so forth. [Objection: But surely, from a specific kind of smoke, even a specific kind of fire such as that from a forest fire is cognized by one who knows it. [Reply: True; here too, one who knows the pervasion between the qualified [particulars] certainly cognizes a specific agent from a specific effect. However, one who is ignorant of the pervasion between particulars does not cognize a specific fire such as a forest fire even from smoke; nevertheless, he infers mere fire.

It might be argued: "Smoke in general is not pervaded by specific qualities such as being produced by a *tāraṇa* fire; yet, even if one cannot infer those specific qualities from smoke in general, it is correct to infer fire. However, the effect in general is pervaded by specific qualities such as having a non-divine body; therefore, since one does not perceive these specific qualities like non-divinity from the mere fact of being an effect, it is not correct to infer a creator. This is not so. For if the effect in general were indeed pervaded by specific qualities such as non-divinity, then wherever an effect is observed, there would be the establishment of a creator endowed with those specific qualities—just as fire is established from smoke. But this is not the case. Indeed, a creator like us is not capable of producing effects such as the earth; and if he is incapable, how can he be inferred as their creator? Furthermore, pervasion is not established merely by observing a connection in a single instance (*dṛṣṭānta*), for otherwise it would follow that [the fallacious reasons] such as "being an effect" or "not being hot" would also be valid. Nor is it logical that the proof of the creator's agency should fail simply because specific qualities like non-divinity are not established; for it is not the case that because fire is not proven to be "not hot" on account of its being an effect, its impermanence is also unproven. Or, it is not logical that because atoms are not proven to have specific qualities like impermanence on account of being the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the manifestation of color and so forth, their possession of color and so forth is also unproven. Indeed, if a specific quality such as "having a body" were established, the reason would be incompetent due to the deficiency of the condition of having an uncontradicted subject (*abādhitaviṣayatva*). But there is no deficiency in any part of the reason used to establish the mere existence of a creator, such that it would be incompetent even in that regard. How, then, is the specific quality of divinity established? It has been stated that the same reason, supported by proofs that negate opposing positions through the force of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), becomes a *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative) when it is restricted to the scope of specific qualities such as omniscience. Otherwise, the mere generality of a creator for the earth and other things could not be established.
The designation "Lord" (Īśvara) refers to the creator of the earth and other elements.

But how, again, is the existence of God established even when one does not recognize the specific effects produced by Him? It is because of the distinctness of the effects (*kāryavailakṣaṇyāt*). Just as, for example, even when one does not recognize the specific smoke produced by *agaru* (aloe wood), upon perceiving smoke that is distinct from the specific smokes produced by grass and such, one infers a fuel that is likewise distinct from grass and such; and having learned the name "agaru" for it from a reliable person (*āpta*), one understands it as such, or else one assigns it another name oneself. In the same way, perceiving the earth and other effects which are distinct from the specific effects produced by beings like ourselves, one infers a creator who is distinct from beings like ourselves; and having learned the name "Īśvara" (God) for him from a reliable person, one understands it as such, or else one assigns it another name oneself.

If it is argued that although a substance as minute as an atom has not been seen, it has nevertheless been seen by others, whereas Īśvara has not been seen by anyone—if so, how do you know that he has not been seen by anyone? For you certainly do not know the perceptions of all living beings. Furthermore, if it has not been seen even by one who possesses invisible sense organs (*indriya*), then there could be no inference regarding him either. Nor does the fruit of heaven, hell, and so forth arise from the action alone, because since action is momentary, it lacks the capacity to initiate a result in another birth. As for the claim that [the action] remains after becoming subtle, how is this understood, given that it has not been seen by anyone? If you say it is through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), we say no; for presumptive testimony is included within inference. Likewise, the sense organ is not the physical locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) itself, because the moon and other objects are perceived even when they are not in contact with the eyeball. And it has already been stated that there is no perception of what is not in contact. By the example of the eye, it should be understood that the other sense organs as well are distinct from their physical loci. Furthermore, since it has been established that the sense organs consist of earth, water, and so forth, the sense organ is therefore not the locus. Consequently, just as there is an inference of the completely imperceptible karma and the sense organs by means of the signs of pleasure and the like, and the perception of form and so forth, so too is there an inference of Īśvara by means of effects such as the earth and other things.

Just as properties of the example—such as being a manifestor (*vyañjaka*)—are not attributed to the visual organ (*akṣa*) and so forth, so too properties of the example such as "not being the Lord" (*anīśvaratva*) should not be attributed to the Lord (*īśvara*). Since the consequence of [absurd] increases (*utkarṣa*) and so forth, as well as [the fallacies of] reasons contradictory to the specific property (*viśeṣaviruddha*), apply equally to all inferences, inference is not invalidated by them; otherwise, it would follow that all inference would be invalid. It might be argued: "If, in all inferences, the specific property of the probandum (*sādhyaviśeṣa*) is rejected by increases, decreases, and reasons contradictory to the specific property, then—in the absence of the specificities of the organs of action, fire, and so forth—the specificities of smoke and the like, which consist in the perception of pleasure, pain, form, and so on, would not be possible. But here, in the case of the negation of specificities such as omniscience (*sarvajñatva*) and the rest, what is not possible such that its negation would be a non-negation?"

In this case, an effect such as the earth and so forth is simply not tenable. For an effect cannot arise without a cause, because it has been stated that "there would be either eternal existence or non-existence," and so on. Nor can an effect be produced from causes that are themselves insentient, because it is impossible for insentient things to act spontaneously. For if they were to act by their own nature, there would be the consequence of non-cessation; furthermore, there would be the consequence of threads and other materials acting spontaneously, since there is no distinction [in their lack of sentience]. [Only a sentient being can be the supervisor of the insentient.]

Karma, too, because it is insentient, possesses neither spontaneous activity nor the capacity to instigate action. For an insentient cause cannot be the supervisor (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of sentient beings, as there would be no distinction [between them] and such a supervisor is never observed. Furthermore, if the supervisor were insentient, its activity would be devoid of intention; consequently, the effects produced by what is supervised by it—such as the patterns of woodworms—would not possess a nature restricted to specific locations and so forth. Indeed, a sentient cause, regulated by a particular intellect, is capable of producing the specific arrangements of parts among stationary and moving things, whether external or internal, and whether belonging to restricted or unrestricted classes. For it is only from materials and instruments supervised by an intelligent being that we observe the restriction of the arrangement of parts in the various forms of stationary and moving species, such as in the case of paintings and the like. Thus, the materials and instruments under dispute produce their effects only when supervised by an intelligent being, because they are insentient, just like the materials and instruments used for a painting.

If it is argued that the status of living beings (*jīva*) as the presiding agents (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) over earth and the other elements is not possible because [the world] is already established as being presided over by the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) alone, and thus what is already proven is being attempted to be proven—[we reply: no; because prior to the production of the body, that [enjoyer] is insentient and lacks independence. Indeed, the self (*ātman*) does not ever create a body and so forth for the sake of undergoing the suffering of the womb and the like. Even when it possesses sentience and independence, its knowledge does not extend to the objects of the bodily fluids, impurities, the constituent elements (*dhātu*), or unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). For if one were to act even after knowing the power of the unseen merit/demerit and so forth, there would never be any obstruction to one's will.

Furthermore, he does not know how to construct even his own body with its specific arrangement of bones, marrow, semen, blood, and so forth, nor the particular channels through which these circulate. Nor is he able to digest food daily for the sake of bodily growth by transforming it into the states of nutrient-essence (*rasa*), waste (*mala*), and constituent elements (*dhātu*), separating the nutrients and other components individually, and circulating them to their respective locations via the specific channels. By this, the agency of the parents is also refuted; for it is not logical that they possess agency over that [body] in the absence of knowledge, desire, and effort directed toward it, as that would lead to the absurd consequence of everyone being the agent of everything. If agency were granted merely by existence, it would follow that even space and the like would be agents. For in both common worldly usage and in the scriptures, only one who acts by knowing and employing the materials and instruments according to their own will is renowned as an independent agent. It is only when materials and so forth are regulated by the knowledge, desire, and effort of such an agent—though they themselves are insentient—that it is logical for them to serve as the cause of a specific arrangement and so on, and not otherwise, as is the case with mere lumps of clay. Therefore, He who regulates the materials, instruments, and so forth—even those that are subtle and located internally or externally within the stationary and moving worlds—by means of His knowledge, desire, and effort, is the Blessed Lord, the Sovereign (*Īśvara*).
The absence of a body for the Lord.

For this very reason, he is also devoid of a body and so forth. For if he were embodied, he would be directly perceived—just like a potter—while performing an action upon stationary objects and the like by means of his hands and other limbs. Furthermore, because there would be no room for hands and such within the extremely subtle internal cavities, the circulation of sap and other fluids would be impossible; consequently, changes in form, the growth of parts, nourishment, and so on would not occur. Moreover, even if suffering and the like were present, their suppression [of pleasure] would obstruct his power, and due to the constancy of such states, the actual production, growth, and so forth of stationary beings and others would not take place. Thus, one who is not the Lord and is joined with a body and so forth is unable to produce even effects such as bodies or trees, let alone effects such as the earth and mountains.

**The Proof of the Product-Nature of the Earth and Other Entities:** The product-nature (*kāryatva*) of the earth, mountains, and so forth is perceived through their possession of parts (*sāvayavatva*). This is because that which possesses parts is incompatible with permanence, and because we observe the destruction of one part through digging and other such means. It is incorrect to claim that the whole is not destroyed even when its parts are destroyed, for that would entail the absurd consequence that the whole remains undestroyed even when all its parts have perished. Furthermore, as it has been said: "If its activity is not postulated to be like that of a potter..."
How can an insentient entity conform to that desire?
The manner in which atoms and so forth come into being.

If it is postulated that this Lord lacks activity—such as the lifting of hands and so forth—as a potter or similar agent does, then how do atoms and other such entities proceed from his activity? It is not logical that their movement occurs through his mere will; for we do not observe that the movement of sticks and other tools occurs solely by the will of a potter. Nor is it appropriate to argue that they act like ministers and others who follow the will of a king; for ministers and the like proceed after having ascertained the king’s intention from some source. But the nature of atoms and such is insentient; how could they perceive his will? And if they do not know it, how could they proceed in accordance with his will?

To this it is replied: Is it intended here to establish that the activity of atoms and so forth is accidental (*ākasmikī*), or that it has for its cause actions (*karman*) and the like unguided by a conscious being (*cetana*), or rather that it has for its cause the operation of a person possessing a body and other organs? First of all, no activity whatsoever is accidental, because that would entail the absence of any regularity regarding place, time, and so forth. Nor does it have for its cause actions and the like unguided by a conscious being, because such a thing is not observed in the case of lumps of clay and the like, and because the spontaneous activity of insentient things like *karman* and their status as causes for the activity of others have already been refuted. Furthermore, the activity of the material causes (*upādāna*) of immobile things and the like, even if caused by the operation of a person possessing a body and so forth, has just now been refuted. Therefore, by the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*), and because the fundamental inference is free from defects such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), it is established that the activity of atoms and the like proceeds solely from the will of God (*Īśvara*). However, because a potter possesses limited power (*vyāhata-śakti*), the activity of the staff and other tools does not proceed from his mere will. As for what was said—that how can an insentient entity conform to His will—that is not so; for although the body and its parts are insentient, we observe their activity through conformity to the will of the self (*ātman*). Indeed, when one is impelling one's own body, one does not do so by means of another body. If it is argued that the body is offered to the person for enjoyment by means of *karman*, and therefore it acts under the influence of that [person’s] will, let it be so; nevertheless, since the atom and the like are insentient, their activity does not proceed from mere will, and thus the charge of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) against this [argument] is avoided. Just as you have stated this distinction regarding [the nature of] entities, so too have we stated a distinction regarding the characteristic of the will of God.
