Moreover, the object is also presented as something to be enjoyed by means of karma alone. Why does it not proceed [into action] by mere will, just like the body? If it is argued that the body is presented by a karma of such a nature, whereas the object is not presented by a karma of that same nature, then in that case, the will of the Lord is of such a nature, while that of the potter and others is not; therefore, the movement of atoms and so forth proceeds from the will of the Lord alone and not from the mere will of the potter via the stick and other tools—what is contradictory in this?

Moreover, certain masters of meditation are seen to move even objects such as sticks, like a puppet-master, by mere intention alone. For this reason as well, it is not impossible that the movement of atoms and other entities proceeds from the will of God. Furthermore, a gradation of power is observed among men; thus, it is possible for someone to possess such capacity that they can impel everything by their mere will.
[Like karma, God’s sovereignty is likewise independent.]

And what is this delusion of the disputants, by which they accept the independent causality of *karma*—despite its lack of prior perception—which is even contradictory, yet do not accept it for the Blessed One, even though it is established through numerous scriptures and reasonings? Furthermore, *karma* is not of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), such that it could know, "I have been performed by him," and having made itself suitable for the experience of that very person's body and so forth, offer itself up. Nor is the body of the nature of consciousness, such that it could know, "I have been offered up by this very *karma*," and proceed according to its will like a servant.

{The Cause of the Disparity between Karma and the Supreme Self} Now, one might object: by the scriptural injunction "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," the person's status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is established; yet that capacity for all actions to produce enjoyment is not possible without dependence on a body. Furthermore, the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhogyatva*) occurs only when [the world] conforms to his will. Therefore, by the presumption based on the meaning of the revealed text (*śrutārthāpatti*), the Veda is inferred to be the expounder of this entire [system]. And there is no means of valid cognition whatsoever that establishes that atoms conform to the will of God. {The Refutation of That}

This is incorrect, because the very person by whom this injunction—"One desiring heaven should sacrifice"—is given, he alone will bestow the fruit upon the performer of that action, just like a king and so forth. Therefore, the argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*) is exhausted and does not establish that the ritual act (*karman*) is the cause [of the result]. Furthermore, the human origin of the Veda has already been established.

Furthermore, just as the subsistence of actions in a subtle form, their capacity to produce the *apūrva*, and their causality toward the body and so forth are postulated on the basis of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), why is it not likewise postulated—on the basis of scriptural presumptive testimony—that they are presided over by an intelligent agent? For otherwise, how could insentient action, being unaware of its own agent, deliver its fruit to that very person? Even if that were its inherent nature, it would produce the fruit immediately upon its own origination, like the light of a lamp. However, this undesirable consequence does not apply if there is dependence upon the will of an intelligent being, because, like a king or similar authority, there is no fixed temporal restriction for such a will.

The claim that there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to demonstrate that atoms conform to the will of God is likewise a mere blind impulse; for an inference has already been stated, and scripture (*āgama*) will be mentioned later. Furthermore, the atoms and other entities under dispute conform to the will of someone, because they possess activity, like a garment or similar objects. He whose will they conform to is the Blessed Lord, the Supreme Ruler. Indeed, by virtue of his innate power of supreme sovereignty, all things—which are as if fashioned from his own body—proceed in accordance with his will. Since we and others lack such sovereignty, it is our very bodies that have come to conform to the will [of another] due to the force of karma presided over by Him; what contradiction is there in this?
{The refutation of the reason "knowability" (prameyatva) as a proof for the absence of being an agent of earth and so forth}:
As it has also been said:
"But for one who asserts knowability that is non-contradictory by perception and other means..."
Who indeed would postulate that which is capable of precluding existence?

This too is incorrect; for even if knowability (*prameyatva*) and the like were properties of both the existent and the non-existent, the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) would not be established. For if a property of an existent is used to prove non-existence, it would be a contradictory reason (*viruddha*). On the other hand, a property of non-existence would be unestablished (*asiddha*) if the subject (*dharmin*) itself is unestablished. If the subject is established as existent, the reason is sublated (*bādhitaviṣaya*); if it is established as non-existent, the reason such as knowability is redundant (*vyartha*). A property common to both, however, is simply inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). Therefore, a property such as knowability does not prove non-existence.

Now, if attributes such as being the creator of the world are negated by means of [the reason] "being an object of knowledge" (*prameyatva*), then the existence of the subject (*dharmin*) itself is not thereby negated; for the existence of fire is not negated simply because its attribute of coldness is negated. If you argue that, by implication (*sāmarthyāt*), the existence of the subject is here negated, we say no; this is due to the fallacy of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*). For when a subject does not exist, the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) cannot be established for "being an object of knowledge" and so forth. And if that is unestablished, how can there be any power of proof (*gamakatva*)? Furthermore, "being an object of knowledge" is unestablished even in its own nature; for it is not logical for God, who is not perceived by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), to possess the status of being an object of knowledge. If He were perceived by a *pramāṇa*, how could there be a negation of His being a creator and so forth? Since His very nature is established precisely through the proof of His being a creator and so on, the negation of being a creator for one who is already known in the form of a non-creator would be purposeless. Thus, the subjecthood belongs to that which is accepted by the opponent. If you argue that because it is accepted by the opponent, its "being an object of knowledge" is not unestablished, we ask: is that acceptance by the opponent a *pramāṇa* or not a *pramāṇa*? If it is a *pramāṇa*, then the negation of being a creator and so forth is sublated by that very same [acceptance], since the opponent accepts Him only as qualified by being a creator and so forth. If, on the other hand, it is not a *pramāṇa*, then how is there no fallacy such as the unestablished locus? From where have you determined this distinction—that the opponent’s acceptance of "being an object of knowledge" is based on a *pramāṇa*, while his acceptance of "being a creator" is based on what is not a *pramāṇa*? There is no difference between the two cases regarding the perception of being accepted by the opponent. If you argue: "I do not desire the establishment of either being a creator or being an object of knowledge. Rather, since the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of 'being an object of knowledge' with 'not being the creator of the world' is observed elsewhere, I urge the consequence (*prasaṅga*) that for one who desires Him to be an object of knowledge here as well, He must follow as a creator," we say no; because the scope of the *prasaṅga* is sublated by the inference from effect (*kāryānumāna*). If you claim that the sublation of the scope is equal in both cases, we say no. The *prasaṅga* does not depend on the inference from effect, yet its property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) remains unestablished; whereas the inference from effect does not depend on the *prasaṅga*, yet its *pakṣadharmatva* is established independently. How, then, can these two be equal? If they were equal, it would follow that God is both a creator and a non-creator, which is impossible to maintain, given the contradiction between being a creator and being a non-creator in a single locus.

Furthermore, such a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga) applies equally to all inferences; for instance, for one who accepts that the eye and other sense organs are objects of knowledge (prameya), it follows that they would not be sense organs; for one who accepts that the person (puruṣa) is an object of knowledge, it follows that he would not belong to the next world; and for one who accepts that fire is an object of knowledge, it follows that it would not produce this smoke. Thus, the consequence is the total abolition of all inference. [The non-contradiction between being the creator of the world and being an object of knowledge.]

Furthermore, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and such properties as being the creator of the world; for if there were such a contradiction, it would follow that the acceptance of being an object of knowledge entails the exclusion of being the creator of the world. If it is argued that there is a contradiction characterized by non-coexistence—just as between pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) and atomicity (*aṇutva*)—because they are never observed together in a single locus, we say no; for a contradiction cannot be apprehended without the prior cognition of both terms. If it is argued that a contradiction is understood even when not observed elsewhere—as in the case of having horns measuring ten million *yojanas* and being an object of knowledge—we say no; for here too, a contradiction is unestablished. Let such a horn belong to someone in some place; what contradiction is there? There would be a contradiction if one were to claim that such a horn belongs to something of the same genus as those horned animals previously observed. Likewise, if one were to accept that the creator of the world belongs to the same genus as those agents and knowers previously observed, then there would be a contradiction. However, since we accept that God (*Īśvara*), who is distinct from potters and the like, is the creator of the world, there is no contradiction.
The refutation of other arguments for the denial of God as well.

By this [reasoning], fallacious arguments such as "God is not the creator of the earth and so forth, nor is he their knower everywhere, because he is a person" or "because he is a speaker," and so on, are shown to be incorrect. Likewise, the following is also incorrect: "The effect consisting of the earth and so forth does not have God as its creator, because it is an object of cognition (*prameyatva*), because it is other than what is constructed by persons like us, like space (*ākāśa*)," and so on. This is because, while a specific negation may imply the admission of the remainder through logical force, it would lead to the consequence of contradicting one's own established tenets (*apasiddhānta*) if another creator were thereby established; furthermore, there is no proof of a contradiction between being an object of cognition, being other than what is constructed by persons like us, and having God as the creator. [These arguments suffer from] either a doubtful inconclusiveness (*sandigdhānaikāntikatva*) or a doubtful non-sublation of the subject (*sandigdhābādhitaviṣayatva*). Moreover, since the inference based on the effect (*kāryānumāna*) is more powerful, all these reasons for denying God must be seen as invalid due to their subjects being sublated. For a contradiction has been demonstrated in the production of effects such as bodies and the like without an intelligent cause; therefore, those [other arguments] lack even a doubtful inconclusiveness. Thus, because it is faultless, the inference based on the effect is more powerful.

[The objection: "How can there be activity for the creation of the world on the part of one whose desires are fulfilled? [Response: Indeed, those who act with foresight engage in activity solely for the purpose of acquiring what is desired and avoiding what is undesired. If the Lord were to act in that same manner, He would follow after unfulfilled desires, which would entail the consequence of His not being the Lord, just like ourselves and others. Furthermore, if His activity were for something that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), He would simply be acting without foresight, because He would be performing an action that does not serve a human purpose. Thus it is said: "For Him who is creating the world, what desired object could possibly remain unaccomplished?"
Even a fool does not engage in action without having a purpose in mind.
"In the same way, if there were activity [of the world] due to its consciousness, what would be gained? If activity were for the sake of play, its fulfillment of purpose would not be impaired;
for if there were manifold exertion, there would indeed be much greater suffering. Thus.
{Refutation of that [objection]}:

Is this [argument] presented for the purpose of refuting the inference of a Lord (īśvara), or is it an independent proof (*svatantra-sādhana*) for the purpose of refuting the Lord? It cannot be for the purpose of refuting the inference, because that [inference] has already been established as being free from defects such as being unproven (*asiddha*), and thus, being irreproachable like the inference of smoke, it is impossible to refute. Or, if it were defective, then that very defect should have been stated; what is the use of this irrelevant [argument]? For no defect whatsoever in the reason (*hetu*) is demonstrated by this.

Now, he has stated this proof for the purpose of refuting a creator god (*īśvara*): "The Blessed Lord is not the creator of the world, because he lacks any visible or invisible motive, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*). Here too, if the subject (*dharmin*) is not cognized, then the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*). If, however, it is cognized, then it is sublated by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends it. Furthermore, how the properties of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and so forth are established based merely on what is accepted by the opponent has already been explained in detail previously.

Furthermore, those who understand inference maintain that the activity of inference for others (*parārthānumāna*) proceeds with the desire to produce a certainty in others that is identical to one's own certainty. Therefore, only a reason whose presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*) and other criteria have been ascertained by oneself should be employed for another; otherwise, if it were not established for oneself, the proponent would not even exist. For there is no such thing as an unlearned person who can act as a teacher.

Furthermore, how is it ascertained that this [reason] has been accepted by the opponent? If you say "from the treatise," no; for at the time of the debate, the treatise is not an authoritative means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*). Or, if it were an authoritative means of knowledge, then the probandum (*sādhya*) would also be established from it just like the reason, since there is no distinction between them. If you say that the reason is established from the words of the opponent, then what follows now? Immediately after the statement of the thesis (*pakṣa*), must this person ask the opponent: "What, indeed, is the reason well-known to you? And if he does not state it because of ignorance or some other cause, how can the reason be established from him?

Regarding the purpose of the Lord’s activity: nevertheless, this must be investigated—why does the Blessed One engage in activity? Some say it is for the sake of favoring others (*parānugrahārtham*). Since favoring others cannot be accomplished without first producing abodes, bodies, sense organs, and so forth, He also creates such things as abodes. But there is no purpose whatsoever for His own self; indeed, by virtue of His great majesty (*mahānubhāvatā*), being capable [of all], He engages in activity solely for the sake of others.
[Objection: The Lord would produce only happiness and not suffering.

[Objection: "In that case, let him produce only happiness; for a person of great power (*mahānubhava*) does not engage in producing delusion, suffering, and so forth for others, just like a physician. [Reply: No; for that [power] is established precisely through non-engagement. It might be thought: "Just as even a physician of great power produces suffering by means of burning, cutting, harsh medicines, and so on, for the sake of curing diseases such as tumors and swellings, so too does the Lord (*Īśvara*) produce even suffering for the sake of curing the disease of unrighteousness (*adharma*). But this is not so. Why? Because that [power] is established precisely through non-engagement. When the Blessed One does not engage in the production of undesirable states and so forth, nor in presiding over unrighteousness, then unrighteousness does not produce the suffering of disease. Furthermore, why would he cause unrighteousness to be committed? For a person of great power who has engaged for the sake of cessation would not cause that [unrighteousness] to be committed again; if he did, he would be like a bad physician. Nor is it possible for there to be engagement in what is not prescribed or the arising of unrighteousness for one who is not presided over by the Lord. [Objection: "He engages even in unrighteousness for the sake of exhausting the unrighteousness caused by that [initial act]. [Reply: If its exhaustion were otherwise impossible, then its non-exhaustion would simply be the logical course. For in exhausting it, unrighteousness increases; in exhausting that increase, unrighteousness increases again, and in exhausting that, yet again—thus there is a great calamity. [Objection: "Peace will come later. [Reply: Since peace has not occurred throughout incalculable millions of births, what hope is there that it will occur later? Furthermore, even a physician acts after knowing the distinctions and determining the diagnosis. But since the Blessed One is omniscient, it is not fitting for him to engage with those who are incurable.
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: whoever exerts himself for the sake of accomplishing whatever is intended by another is said to be "engaged for the sake of another" (*parārtha-pravṛtta*). Now, happiness is intended by all transmigrating beings due to beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*); and the Lord, exerting himself to accomplish that [happiness], causes even unrighteousness (*adharma*) to be performed as a necessary consequence (*anuṣaṅgataḥ*). For otherwise, happiness caused by the enjoyment of sense objects would not be possible. Furthermore, as long as the unrighteousness that obstructs merit (*dharma*) has not ceased, happiness will not arise from that merit; therefore, for the sake of accomplishing the happiness caused by that [merit], he first presides over the very unrighteousness that obstructs it and then removes it by means of its fruit, since otherwise its removal would be impossible. However, in the case of one for whom removal is possible through means such as expiation (*prāyaścitta*), because such a person has arisen as one capable of removal in that way, he causes the removal to occur precisely in that manner. Thus, although engaged for the sake of another, he also produces the suffering of hell and so forth as a necessary consequence. In this way, for those revolving in the wheel of saṃsāra through the longing for happiness, when he encounters a cooperative cause for the production of the seed of engagement in the path to liberation for someone at some time in some way, then—having produced that seed—he sets that person upon the path to liberation as well. Thereafter, setting them in motion through practice in every birth, he thins out the formative tendencies (*saṃskāra*) that are causes of saṃsāra, and extends the formative tendencies that are causes for the means to liberation, until he leads them to final release (*mokṣa*). Therefore, there is no contradiction even in accepting his engagement for the sake of others.
In the activity of the Lord, even his own self-interest is possible.

Alternatively, [the Lord] acts solely for his own sake. If one asks, "What is that purpose of the Blessed One?", it is precisely the creation of the world and so forth. If one asks, "How so?", even the attainment of happiness and the absence of suffering—how can these be a purpose? If it is because a person acts for their sake and because they desire them, then since the Blessed One also acts for the sake of creating the world and so forth and because he desires it, that very thing is his purpose. If one asks, "For what reason does he desire that?", one might ask, "For what reason does a person desire happiness? This is quite trivial. Therefore, whatever object one acts with reference to, because that is what one desires, it is the purpose. Nor does it follow that one who acts for his own sake is not the Lord (anīśvara) due to having unfulfilled desires; for only he whose wishes are not accomplished as intended is said to have unfulfilled desires. But since for the Blessed One those things are accomplished exactly as intended, how could there be unfulfilled desires?
Or rather, the activity of the Lord is inherent in his nature.

Alternatively, [the Lord] acts by His very nature (*svabhāva*), just as the sun: just as the sun illuminates the world by its very nature, and once the world is illuminated, living beings experience the variety of pleasure, pain, and so forth in accordance with their own karma; likewise, the Blessed One (*bhagavān*) also brings about the arising, maintenance, and destruction of the worlds by His very nature. And He joins living beings with pleasure, pain, knowledge, ignorance, and so on, in accordance with their respective karma. Nor is there any contradiction with consciousness in acting by way of nature, since even among conscious beings, a restriction based on nature is observed. For even in a learned person, a restriction of activity toward useless things such as tearing grass is observed, which establishes the existence of a restriction based on nature. If it is argued that this is a "passion" (*vyasana*), then this is indeed a passion for the Blessed One as well—namely, that although He possesses unsurpassed knowledge and sovereignty, whenever there are causal conditions for certain entities, He presides over those causes and brings those entities into being. Furthermore, because that passion has not arisen from anything else, it is called His "nature."

Nor does there exist a contradiction with His sovereignty when He produces an effect corresponding to unperceived causes such as material substrates (*upādāna*), for we observe that even those who are independent produce effects that correspond to their material substrates and other factors. Indeed, independence is defined as being the employer of causes whose capacities are perceived; and this [independence] exists in the case of Maheśvara. Just as the Lord’s authorship of effects such as the earth is possible, so must the Lord be accepted as being of such a nature, since He has been established as faultless by the force of the inference from effects. {The existence of the one Lord is also established through scripture (*āgama*).}

From scripture (*āgama*) as well, it is determined that the Blessed One alone possesses the power to produce the entire world, as it says: "Rudra is one; there is no second," and "He who, like the sun, rules these worlds by his sovereign powers.
"Of him neither effect nor instrument is found;
neither equal nor superior to him is seen."
"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold;
and his knowledge, strength, and action are inherent."

Thus ends the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. Likewise, in all the Upaniṣads as well, it is established that knowledge of the Self, characterized by attributes such as being the creator of the universe, is the cause of liberation. For instance: "He who has eyes on all sides, and faces on all sides, arms on all sides, and feet on all sides"; "With his two arms and with his wings, He hurls [the worlds] together"; and "The one God, generating heaven and earth. Furthermore, it says: "O Gārgī, by the command of this Imperishable (Akṣara), heaven and earth stand held apart. Manu and others also say:
"One should know that Supreme Person as the ruler of all, subtler even than the subtle, golden-hued, and attainable through the intellect in the state of dream.
"He, pervading all beings with his five forms..."
"It perpetually causes [beings] to whirl like a wheel through birth, growth, and decay," and so forth. Thus,
there is no lack of authority in the statements of scripture regarding the realization of such [truths].

One should not conclude that these [scriptural passages] lack authority regarding the cognition of their own subject matter (*svarūpa*), for it is logically consistent that sentences which establish the nature of what is pure or impure, as well as those which establish the nature of heaven, hell, and so forth, along with the nature of their means and constituent parts, possess authority. Indeed, without the cognition of a thing’s own nature, neither its adoption nor its avoidance is possible; otherwise, if one were to act toward one thing when another has been cognized, there would be the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If it is argued that because they are subordinate to injunctions (*vidhi*) and prohibitions (*pratiṣedha*), these texts have as their purpose the instigation of activity and cessation, rather than having the nature of the object itself as their aim—this is not so. For without the cognition of the nature of the object, the activity and cessation determined by those [injunctions and prohibitions] would be impossible. Indeed, no sensible person would admit that statements such as "the horn of a hare" possess authority or have as their purpose the instigation of activity and cessation even if they were subordinate to an injunction. Therefore, although [passages like] "The Self, verily, is to be seen" are subordinate to an injunction, statements concerning the world-creator, omniscience, and so forth, must be taken as having exactly the reality of their objects (*yathārthatva*), because they have the nature of the object itself as their aim, just like statements concerning clarified butter as a sacrificial post (*ghṛtayūpa*) and the like.
The purpose of self-knowledge is liberation.

As for what was said—that knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) is enjoined for the purpose of engaging in sacrifice, but not for the sake of liberation because it is not so stated—that is incorrect. Once the authority of the Veda is established, those who seek results proceed to perform the *agnihotra* and other rites even without knowledge of the Self; or rather, the Self is known through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). However, if the Veda lacked authority, there would be no engagement even if there were an injunction for the knowledge of the Self. Therefore, knowledge of the Self is not enjoined for the purpose of engaging in sacrifice, but rather for the sake of liberation, because it is so stated in other passages, such as: "I know this great Person, refulgent like the sun, beyond darkness," and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for going. Furthermore, its being for the sake of sacrifice is not heard in any other passage either, and thus it is merely a baseless assumption. Therefore, just as in the case of "One should offer the *agnihotra* as long as one lives," its connection with a fruit mentioned in another passage must be understood according to the maxim "whatever has a connection with a purpose [is connected to that]," and so forth. Otherwise, an injunction that is fruitless would not be performed by anyone and would thus be useless. If it is argued that it is performed to avoid sin (*pratyavāya*), we say no, because that too is not stated [in scripture]. Moreover, in this way, there would be the fault of abandoning what is explicitly stated and assuming what is not. Therefore, knowledge of the Self is enjoined for the sake of liberation.

Furthermore, when the question arises as to what properties that self (ātman) is to be seen as possessing, the previously mentioned statements such as "formless, tasteless, odorless," and so forth, are connected [to this context]. Thus, even by virtue of contradicting scripture (āgama), the reasons for negating God (īśvara) should be understood as lacking authority.
{The Refutation of the Proof for God’s Omniscience}

By this same reasoning, one should understand that arguments such as "the Lord’s cognition is not omniscient because it is a cognition like ours" are either contradicted by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādhitatva*), or suffer from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*). For if the Blessed One were not omniscient, the production of infinite effects would be impossible; this is because the production of effects cannot occur from insentient causes that are not presided over, and because one who has not ascertained the capacities of the causal factors cannot act as a presiding agent. Furthermore, it has been stated that once he is established as the knower of the material causes and so forth of all effects, his omniscience is proven.
{The Bhaṭṭa objection and its refutation} And thus, as for what was said—
"An omniscient being is not currently perceived by people such as ourselves"—
"Nor can there be the conceptualization that 'he did not exist,' just as [one cannot conceive] a negation [of something non-existent].
For how could he be known even by those cognizers of his own time as 'this one is omniscient,' when they themselves lack the cognition of his knowledge and its objects?"

The claim that "one who is not omniscient cannot know the Omniscient One" is thus refuted; for even though they lack the direct cognition of His knowledge and its objects, worldly people and His disciples recognize Him through His expertise in the scriptures, arts, and so forth. Otherwise, their engagement in hearing the scriptures and other such activities for the sake of acquiring knowledge would not occur. Just as one who is unacquainted with the scriptures and such recognizes an expert in those scriptures by his actions and authoritative words, so too do those who are not omniscient recognize the Omniscient One. [This concludes the rebuttal of the doubt regarding the non-cognition of the first creation.]

As for what was said—that there is an ignorance of the first creation, and that if such ignorance were known, it would contradict the beginninglessness of *saṃsāra*—that is merely the manifestation of extreme dullness. For one does not become blind simply by not seeing a horn on the head of a donkey. One who perceives everything that exists does not have his omniscience impaired even by the non-perception of the first creation and so forth, which do not exist. Furthermore, [the objection] regarding the tasting of a foul flavor is also improper. For when someone perceives a specific taste, smell, or the like through their senses, they experience the association with pleasure, pain, attachment, aversion, and so forth; in that case, there is the designation of "tasting" and the defect caused thereby. But for the Blessed Lord, there is no cognition born of the senses, nor is there anywhere attachment or aversion, nor anything pure or impure. Rather, whatever exists exactly as it is, He knows it as such through His eternal knowledge, according to such scriptural statements as, "He sees without eyes."
The perceptual nature of the knowledge of the Lord.

If it is asked how there can be the conventional usage "he sees" in the absence of the eye, it is through metaphorical designation (*upacāra*). The purpose of this metaphor is to remove the suspicion that his cognition might be indistinct; the basis (*nimitta*) for the metaphor is visual cognition, and the common property (*sādharmya*) is the fact that God’s cognition has a direct (*aparokṣa*) form. For indeed, to him every object is directly perceived, just like the palm of one's own hand. By this, the conventional usage of "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) is also explained: God’s cognition is not primary perception because it lacks the capacity to produce a valid means of knowledge (*pramā*), nor is it perception by virtue of being produced by a sense organ (*akṣaja*), since it is eternal.
The proof of the eternality of God's knowledge.

If it is asked, "Whence [is] its eternity?", it is from inference (*anumāna*) and scripture (*āgama*). Among these, the inference is as follows: "The cognition of the Supreme Lord is eternal, because it is a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of an eternal substance that is a distinct entity from the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of smell, dharma, and sound, just like the color and other qualities of the atoms of water and so forth. The meaning is this: the inherent causes of smell, dharma, and sound are earth, the supreme self (*paramātman*), and space (*ākāśa*); [the cognition is eternal] because it is a quality of an eternal substance that is distinct from those. In this context, the term "quality of an eternal substance" is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) by means of qualities such as those of water and other effects produced by transformation (*pākaja*); the term "specific quality" is included to exclude deviation by means of qualities of eternal substances such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and the like. Nevertheless, there would still be deviation by means of qualities produced by cooking (*pākaja*), by the specific qualities of the non-supreme self, and by sound; to exclude these, the qualification "smell, dharma, etc. is employed. Now, one might object: "The supreme yogi is a distinct entity from the inherent causes of smell and so forth, and his specific quality is cognition, yet that [cognition] is non-eternal; thus, the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is not so. For a thing is not a cause merely by the fact that it "is acting"; rather, it is also [a cause] by the fact that "it will act" or "it has acted. As the experts in grammar state: "Verbal suffixes whose time is not specified apply to all three times. Consequently, there is also common usage such as "this effect has been produced from that cause," and because it is well-established that inference regarding cause and effect can have past and future objects as its domain.

Thus, the meaning of this passage beginning with "smell is a non-quality" (*gandho 'dharmaḥ*) is as follows: the knowledge of the Supreme Lord is eternal, because, while residing in earth, ether, and transmigrating souls, it is a specific quality of an eternal substance, like the color and other qualities of the atoms of water and so forth. If it is argued that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*) due to the will and effort of the Supreme Lord, we say no; for by this very same reason, the eternality of those two is also established, and thus there is no deviation from the probandum (*sādhya*).
[The establishment of the substratum of eternal knowledge through pure negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).]

Or rather, the reason (*hetu*) is one of pure negative concomitance (*kevalavyatirekī*). For instance: "The Blessed Lord is the substratum of eternal knowledge, because He possesses unsurpassed agency; the dissimilar example (*vaidharmyadṛṣṭānta*) is ourselves and others. If it is argued that the subject (*pakṣa*) has an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇa*), we say no. It is precisely because the qualification is unestablished that the reason is one of pure negative concomitance; for if the qualification were established, there would also be positive concomitance (*anvaya*). Furthermore, for one who accepts "unestablished qualification" as a logical defect, the establishment of eternity in space (*ākāśa*) and so forth through inference would be impossible for an opponent who maintains that everything is non-eternal. Nor is it the case that eternity is not apprehended by the perception of ourselves and others in some instances, since existence (*sattā*)—both beginningless and endless—is manifested by perception. [Objection: Non-eternity is observed in things such as jars, and that [non-eternity] is denied in the case of space and so forth; therefore, how can eternity be established? [Reply: If you say it is established "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*), what is this so-called "implication"? Indeed, there is no means of cognition other than inference distinct from perception and scripture. If "implication" is simply inference, then if eternity is established even from that, how is it not a case of "unestablished qualification"? Moreover, in this case too, the state of not being the substratum of eternal knowledge is observed in ourselves and others, and that is denied in the case of God; and upon that denial, the establishment of being the substratum of eternal knowledge follows by implication. If this is so, the formulation of the thesis (*sādhyanirdeśa*) should be: "The Blessed Lord is not one who is not the substratum of eternal knowledge. What is the difference here? Even in this formulation, the meaning is the same, because two negations result in an affirmation.
{The doubt regarding the non-establishment of pervasion and its refutation}

[Objection: But surely, since no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) has been established between being the substratum of eternal knowledge and unsurpassed agency, it is incorrect to say that the cessation of unsurpassed agency follows from the cessation of being the substratum of eternal knowledge. For otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that the cessation [of agency] would follow even from the cessation of being the substratum of eternal suffering and so forth. Consequently, just as being the substratum of eternal knowledge is established by means of unsurpassed agency, so too would being the substratum of eternal suffering be established. This is because there is no difference between the two cases regarding the observation of non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*) in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*). [Response: This is not so. For, through the means of valid cognition that refute opposing views (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of unsurpassed agency by being the substratum of eternal knowledge is established within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself—according to the maxim of "not seeing a crow on the bank of the Kākatīrā. However, it is not the case that [the pervasion] is established in this way by being the substratum of eternal suffering and so forth; for even in the absence of such [suffering], unsurpassed agency is possible. Indeed, unsurpassed agency is defined as the capacity to produce all effects at all times without exception, and that is not possible for one who is overcome by even a mere trace of suffering and the like, much less for one who is overcome by eternal suffering, hatred, and so forth. Likewise, one should not raise the objection that being the substratum of a hare's horn and the like would be established [as a consequence]; for the contradiction of unsurpassed agency with the absence of such things is not established.
Without being the substratum of eternal knowledge, the status of being the creator of the world is impossible.

Furthermore, such unsurpassed agency is not possible without being the substratum of eternal knowledge; for it has been stated that the agency of the entire world and all other effects is impossible for one who is either insentient or non-omniscient. Moreover, the omniscience of the Blessed One must be accepted as uninterrupted throughout beginningless and endless time, because here we observe the continuous production of infinite effects, such as mobile and immobile beings. And that state of having all things as its object at all times would not occur if knowledge were caused. Indeed, a continuous stream (*santāna*) delimited by prior and subsequent time is not possible for causal complexes (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) that produce effects of a single form and are free from defect; for since impermanent things necessarily undergo increase, decrease, and so forth due to their dependence on other factors for the acquisition of their own nature, a continuous stream of knowledge produced by such a complex—being subject to these fluctuations—cannot be established as unsurpassed and devoid of limits.

If one accepts a cause for God’s knowledge, one must accept only that whose causal capacity has been observed. For instance, the capacity of the body and the sense organs to produce knowledge is as certain as that of smoke and fire [to produce cognition], and the capacity of ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and so forth to produce the body and its like is also certain—just as [the capacity of those factors] to produce pleasure and the like is certain. Therefore, for one who desires that knowledge be non-eternal, it follows that one must accept all the attributes of transmigrating beings (*saṃsārin*). Consequently, supreme agency and omniscience are contradicted; and because of that contradiction, the production of the world is also contradicted.
Knowledge is eternal because of the absence of a body and other such factors.

If it is argued that the body and the senses of the Blessed One are eternal, we say no; for there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*) and because it contradicts reason (*yukti*). Furthermore, if one accepts their eternity in this manner, one would also have to accept that his wife and so forth are eternal. It is also unreasonable to claim that the body consists merely of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the like, because [such a collection] lacks the status of being the substratum of movement, the senses, and objects. A body is defined as the locus of experience (*bhoga-āyatana*), and the Blessed One has no such locus of experience. If it is argued that this contradicts the scriptures (*āgama*) which teach that he possesses a physical form (*mūrti*) composed of earth and other elements, we say no; for those [scriptures] function through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*), since [the form] follows his mere will just as a body does. Otherwise, even the sacrificer (*yajamāna*) would be a "body. Moreover, it is not logical for a conscious being to be a body. Likewise, the eternity of the senses is also untenable, because space (*ākāśa*) and the mind (*manas*) are also considered senses when they are assisted by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and they cease to be senses when that assistance is absent. Furthermore, neither merit (*dharma*) nor demerit (*adharma*) exists for the Lord (*Īśvara*), as that would contradict his state of being beyond transmigratory existence (*asaṃsāritva*). And there is no evidence for the existence of merit alone. Since the alternatives of eternality and non-eternality are impossible—were it eternal, let knowledge itself simply be eternal, which avoids the fault of conceptual complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*); were it non-eternal, there would be a contradiction with his being the agent of universal destruction and so forth, since the production of suffering in others and the like is a cause of demerit. As for the claim that ignorance alone is the cause of demerit and that, due to its absence, there is no demerit even in specific cases—that is incorrect; for scripture prescribes a more severe penance for one who knowingly commits a forbidden act. If it is argued that demerit does not arise in one whose defects (*doṣa*) have been exhausted, then merit also does not arise for him, as the evidence is equal in both cases. Thus, since the body and other factors that produce knowledge are absent, the Blessed One’s knowledge must be eternal.

[Objection: But since mere cognition (*jñāna*) is invariably non-eternal, how can the eternity of anything be established? Or, if it were established, no one could establish the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of anything with anything else, because that would lead to a lack of confidence in all cases. [Reply: This is not so. For it is only cognition that possesses excellence (*sātiśaya*) which is observed to be invariably non-eternal, not that which is unsurpassed (*niratiśaya*), just like largeness (*mahattva*) and atomicity (*aṇutva*). Furthermore, by those very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) between being the locus of eternal cognition and being an unsurpassed agent—which refute opposing arguments—the proofs for non-eternality, such as "being cognition," "being a specific quality of an omnipresent substance," and so forth, must be regarded as invalid, because they are sublated. Indeed, there is no contradiction whatsoever between being cognition, being a specific quality of an omnipresent substance, and so on, on the one hand, and eternity on the other, such that a contradiction could be demonstrated between unsurpassed agency and the opposite of eternal cognition. Thus, the invariable concomitance of "being cognition" and the like with non-eternality cannot be established. Nor is the establishment of invariable concomitance achieved merely by the non-observation [of the reason] in the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), because that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, non-observation elsewhere is not itself a contradiction; otherwise, it would follow that largeness and atomicity are also contradictory to eternity. Nor is there a lack of contradiction even if the Supreme Lord’s cognition lacks the causes whose capacity is observed [in the world], provided it arises from another cause; for the contradiction of an effect arising from another cause when the capacity of the observed causes is absent is established by perceptual evidence (*dṛṣṭapramāṇa*), as in the case of fire and smoke. Otherwise, it would follow that even for the earth and so forth, there would be no contradiction in an effect arising from other causes even in the absence of an agent whose capacity regarding material causes (*upādāna*) and so on is observed. Consequently, if the existence of God himself is not established, of what could one consider the cognition to be eternal or non-eternal? Therefore, because the inference from effects such as the earth is more powerful, the fact that its agent is untouched by attributes such as suffering and non-omniscience—characteristics of ourselves—is inferred from the impossibility of explaining otherwise his production of infinite effects unconditioned by direction, space, and time. Similarly, the absence of agency dependent upon non-eternal cognition, a body, and so forth, is also inferred. Thus, the scripture says: "Brahman is Truth, Cognition, and Infinite" (*satyaṃ jñānam anantaṃ brahma*); and by passages such as "He has neither effect nor instrument" and "Without hands or feet," the Lord's cognition is shown to be uncreated and His agency to belong to the partless (*niṣkala*). From this very fact, the eternity of will (*icchā*) and effort (*prayatna*) is also established, since their production is impossible in the absence of a body and so forth. Although they are one in terms of eternity, their distinction and their existence throughout the three times (*traikālika*) are figuratively attributed based on the difference in their effects, just as cognition is distinguished by the difference in its objects. Whatever has not been stated here regarding the resolution of objections raised by others and the refutation of opposing views should be sought in the *Nityajñānaviniścaya*, and other points should also be inferred by oneself.
{The Buddhist objection} But another says:
"An eternal means of valid cognition does not exist at all, because validity consists in the comprehension of a real entity."
"Because it is not permanent due to the impermanence of the objects of knowledge, and because it arises sequentially;
because there is no production from a permanent [cause], and because dependence is impossible;
and because it cannot be assisted in any way—even if [the cause] were impermanent, there would be no validity."

There is no eternal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because validity consists in the apprehension of a real entity (*vastusat*). If indeed the apprehension of a real entity constitutes validity, one might ask: why is eternality not [the case]? He replies: because that apprehension of a real entity is non-permanent due to the impermanence of the objects of knowledge (*jñeya*). For when an object has not yet arisen or has already perished, its apprehension is not tenable. Granted that knowledge may be impermanent due to the impermanence of its objects, one might argue that the knower (*jñātṛ*) is indeed eternal. To this he replies: because there is an incompatibility between the production of sequentially arising knowledge and an eternal [subject]. The meaning is that sequential origination is impossible from an eternal thing, which possesses a single, unchanging nature. Nor can there be sequence through a succession of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), because dependence [upon such causes] is untenable for an eternal entity. Since an eternal thing cannot be assisted, dependence upon another is not logical. Even if the Lord’s knowledge were impermanent, it could not possess validity, because it would still be in no way assistable. For one who is assisted by someone in some way teaches out of compassion for the sake of assisting others; such a person becomes a means of valid cognition for the world. But the Lord does not possess this kind of proficiency (*vyutpatti*). Indeed, one who is unimpaired does not become a scholar (*paṇḍita*).
The refutation of that [objection] is as follows:

To this it is replied: First, as for what was said—that there is no eternal means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—if by that you mean that an eternal instrument of valid cognition is denied, then that is not so, because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and other such instruments of valid cognition are eternal. However, regarding the claim that nothing exists eternally in the state of a causal complex (*sāmagrī*), this is a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), provided that the internal organ and the rest are admitted to be non-eternal. If one simply says "there is nothing eternal at all," the inclusion of the term "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is redundant. Furthermore, if the eternity of the means of valid cognition itself is being denied, that too is a case of proving what is already established. Moreover, it has been stated that the knowledge of God (*īśvara-jñāna*) is directly both the means of valid cognition and its result.

Now, if it is argued that there is no eternal, non-contradictory knowledge at all, that is incorrect; for the non-contradiction of the Supreme Lord’s knowledge is established by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its existence. Furthermore, the negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*) was previously established, and by that very [inference], the [opposing view] is sublated by the statement beginning with “because the objects of knowledge are impermanent,” and is thus untenable. Nor is it the case that a cognition’s having an object as its domain occurs solely through being produced from that object, such that the sequential occurrence of the object would necessitate a sequential occurrence of the cognition. Accordingly, it was established in the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*) that even an object that is not a cause can be an object of cognition. Nor does the fact that something which is not a cause can be an object entail that everyone would be omniscient; for the cognitions of transmigrating beings arise with restricted objects, being determined by specific causal complexes (*sāmagrī*) such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth. For this very reason, it is logical that the Supreme Lord’s knowledge has all things as its object; since there is no regulating factor for the restriction of an object when [knowledge] is without a cause, the fact that the Supreme Lord’s knowledge has all things as its object is an inherent property (*svābhāvika-dharma*), and like the properties of being omnipresent or non-omnipresent belonging to space or atoms, it does not admit of further questioning.
Even though there is equality in being the object of a single eternal cognition, there is still the distinction of [time] such as past and so forth.

But surely, if a single eternal cognition has all objects as its domain, there would be the undesirable consequence that even past and future objects are present, because they would be the objective supports (*ālambana*) of that single cognition—just like the constellation Kṛttikā and others. This is not so. Indeed, the cognition of a yogin, though single, has as its domain objects belonging to the past, future, and present by virtue of the power of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), yet this does not entail that all objects are present. Or, for example, things connected by a single universal called "existence" (*sattā*) do not possess a single location or a single nature, because that would contradict perception and other means of valid knowledge. In that case, when certain objects move to another place, they do not go along with existence, nor do they become separated from existence. Even while being connected to that [single] existence, they do not fail to abandon their previous locations and so forth—this has been established in detail during the proof of the universal (*sāmānya*). Likewise, there is no connection to a single time for those objects connected by the single cognition of the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*). Thus, a future object, becoming present through the efficacy of its own causes while being the object of the Supreme Lord’s cognition, does not abandon its very nature of being [future]; rather, it does not lose its connection to the Lord’s cognition. When, abandoning its present nature, it enters into a state of being past, it does not lose its connection to the Lord’s cognition. Such being the case, whatever object, having abandoned a previous property—whether of the nature of existence or non-existence—attains another property, all of that attains it while indeed remaining connected to the Supreme Lord’s cognition, just like its connection to existence.
The distinction between the relation with existence and the relation with the knowledge of the Lord.

However, this is the distinction: existence (*sattā*) has with existent things (*sad-bhiḥ*) a relationship called inherence (*samavāya*), characterized by the relation of substrate and superstrate; therefore, it does not have a relationship with past or future objects. But the knowledge of Maheśvara has with all objects whatsoever a relationship characterized by the relation of object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*); and since that [relationship] exists even with past and other such objects, this was established in the definition of perception (*pratyakṣa*). Thus, it is the object itself that becomes variously different, not the knowledge of the Lord. For that [knowledge], although possessing a single nature, is designated as being variously different because it is conditioned (*upadhīyamāna*) in various ways by objects that are themselves becoming variously different—just like a mirror or a crystal. Therefore, the Lord’s knowledge is not rendered unstable by the impermanence of its objects, nor does its non-contradictoriness (*avisaṃvāditva*) cease.
Regarding the conventional usage of terms such as "the object has been seen" despite the fact that [the cognition] does not produce knowledge of the Lord (*īśvara*):

if the Lord’s cognition does not operate upon the object, nor is it produced from the object, nor possesses its nature, then how can it be said that the object is "seen" by him? This is not so; for it has been stated that an object is said to be "seen" by him precisely because it is connected to him, just like objects of the past or future. {The objections of Dharmakīrti and Prajñākaragupta, and their refutation}
As it has also been said:
"A relationship is established through positive concomitance preceded by negative concomitance;
how can there be the possibility of a relationship for that which is eternal and lacks negative concomitance?"
That too has been refuted by establishing the relationship between past and future objects and the cognitions of them, as well as between a universal and its possessor.
As for what was said:
"A word produced from the perception of all objects is the designator of everything."
"A restriction based on the speaker's intention is not logically possible for that which is eternal."

That too is incorrect. For a word uttered by someone does not become the designator of as many objects as that person possesses knowledge of. Furthermore, knowledge itself is not the intention to speak (*vivakṣā*), since some people who possess knowledge are observed to be observing a vow of silence. [The opponent argues: "The Lord’s will regarding all his activities is eternal; even though its production depends on place, time, material causes, and so forth, it functions by its very nature without error. Consequently, the effect also occurs without error regarding place, time, and so forth. Therefore, the claim that ‘the restriction of the intention to speak is not possible for an eternal entity’ is also incorrect; for even eternal entities such as substance, quality, and universal are perceived through valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as having specific, restricted natures. [Response: This too is incorrect, because one does not perceive a word being produced from a speaker who possesses knowledge of a certain number of objects. Nor is it logical that a word uttered by someone becomes the designator of only those objects of which that person has knowledge. Furthermore, the intention to speak is not identical to knowledge, since we observe some individuals who, despite possessing knowledge, maintain a vow of silence. Moreover, the claim that the Lord’s will regarding all his actions is eternal—functioning naturally without error even when its arising depends on place, time, material causes, and so forth—and that for this reason the effect likewise occurs without error regarding place, time, and so forth—is also untenable. This is because even eternal things, such as substances, qualities, and universals, are apprehended by valid cognition as having restricted natures. Thus, the argument fails.

As for what was said—"one does not become wise merely by being unimpaired"—that too is refuted precisely by the non-acceptance of [the soul's] being either eternal or non-eternal, for the Blessed One’s wisdom is innate.

[Objection: But if he does not experience passion (*rāga*) and so forth, how can he know their antidote? And if he does not know it, how can he be an authoritative source (*pramāṇa*) when teaching? On the other hand, if he does experience passion and so forth, it follows that he is possessed of passion and the like, and therefore he would simply be a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). [Reply: This is incorrect. For one does not become possessed of passion merely by knowing it; rather, one becomes so through its inherence (*samavāya*) [in oneself]. Otherwise, it would follow that even in the state of Buddhahood, he would still possess passion and the like, or else he would lack omniscience (*sarvajñatva*). As for what was said here: "One who knows the reality of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted, as well as the means for their abandonment and attainment..."
"He who is accepted as an authority is not one who knows everything;
let him see far away or not, but let him see the desired truth.
If it were the seer of the distant who were the authority, then we would worship vultures!"

Therefore, the Buddha’s omniscience consists merely in the vision of the four noble truths. Even so, if he does not experience passion and the like, how can there be a vision of the truth of suffering? Or, if he does experience them, how is it that he does not possess passion and the like? [This concludes the refutation of the objections raised against the position of an eternal Īśvara.]

Furthermore, the Buddha consists of the four noble truths because he has attained them through the experience of those four. If there were no such experience, how could he who does not even know the fourfold set be an authority (*pramāṇa*)? If it is argued that he knows them sequentially, this is not so, because it is impossible for a single [consciousness] to have sequential knowledge. Moreover, at the time of experiencing the Path (*mārga*), does he have the experience of Cessation (*nirodha*) or not? If he does, then since they are mutually contradictory by nature, there would be no engagement in the practice of the Path. If he does not, then likewise there would be no engagement in the practice of the Path, because its purpose would not be perceived. If it is argued that he engages after knowing [the truths] through inference or instruction, then even from inference and so forth, if the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [object] does not arise [in consciousness], how can there be knowledge of it? If it were possible, then even in the case of perception, there would be knowledge of it even when its aspect does not arise, as there would be no contradiction. Furthermore, the view that perceptual knowledge possesses the form of the object (*arthākāratva*) has been refuted in detail. Therefore, the Blessed One, like a bystander, perceives the passions and so forth residing in other selves, yet he himself does not possess them.
As it has also been said: "He possesses such a power of granting boons that,
even when devoid of ritual practice, he bestows sovereignty upon the seeker."

"Now, if that power does not exist at all, how could there be another [power] for it either?"—this too is incorrect; because whatever power belongs to any other cause is determined precisely by the production of its effect, just like the power of fire to burn grass and so forth, or the power to soften rice grains. Therefore, wherever and in whatever manner the manifestation of an effect is observed, the Lord's power is understood to exist there in that same manner.
As for what he also said:

"From what cause has such a power as that come to him? How can it be understood that this is his very nature? This too is incorrect, because it has been stated that his power, being inherent, is to be inferred from its effects. Now, if such a power belongs to God without a cause, why does our own kind not possess such a power? To this, the answer must be given by way of the very nature of things: when it is the case that fire possesses the power to burn while space and so forth do not, who is to be questioned about this? As for what was said—

"If, when an intrinsic nature has been established through direct perception, one should raise an objection, then this is the appropriate response: there is no irrationality regarding what is perceived."

"Otherwise, having said something else and being rendered speechless by the opponent, one might remain after stating a reply such as 'by the very nature of things' (*vastusvabhāvaiḥ*); consequently, everyone would be a victor. This [objection] is also incorrect. Just as in the case of what is established by perception (*pratyakṣa*), this reply is entirely logical when directed against one who questions even that which is established by inference (*anumāna*) and the like regarding its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Otherwise, this reply would not be stated when directed against one who questions the intrinsic nature of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), liberation (*apavarga*), and so forth, such as their specific relationship between means and ends (*sādhana-sādhya*). Merit and demerit are distinguished by their intrinsic natures of producing happiness, suffering, and so on in future lives; yet such natures are not established anywhere by perception. Consequently, even in that case, such an inquiry could be made: "Why is it that from this particular means (*sādhana*) there arises merit, and not demerit or a sky-flower (*khapuṣpa*)? Or: "Even within the causal succession (*hetuparamparā*), why does the capacity (*śakti*) come to belong to this [cause] alone, and not to another? In this way, an inquiry can be made in all cases. Therefore, the only appropriate inquiry is: "By what means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa) is such an intrinsic nature determined? But when an intrinsic nature is established by a means of valid cognition, an inquiry is simply untenable. For the such-like intrinsic nature of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) is established by the force of the inference from effects (*kāryānumāna*); therefore, an inquiry into that is improper.
{Dharmakīrti’s objection to the inference of God} Now,
that very inference is not tenable, as he said: "In the cases of [an object] remaining still and then moving, specific structures, purposeful action, and so forth..."
"Either the desired conclusion is established, or it is unestablished; or else there is doubt regarding the example."

"The material cause and so forth are presided over by an intelligent being, because they function after having remained [inactive], like a staff and other such tools. The effects such as the earth are produced by an intelligent agent, because they are characterized by a specific configuration, like a house and other structures. The efficient causes such as *dharma* proceed while being presided over by an intelligent being, because they perform purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), like a pot and other objects. In arguments such as these, if the probandum (*sādhya*) is intended as a general property, then there is the "establishment of what is already accepted" (*iṣṭasiddhi*), meaning that what is already proven is being proven. If, however, the presiding of God (*īśvara*) is the probandum, then there is "non-establishment" (*asiddhi*), meaning the probandum is absent from the example. Or else, there is doubt regarding the example, because the presiding of God is not certain in the case of a staff and the like. Alternatively, there is doubt, which is to say the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*), due to that very God himself; for He too functions after having remained [inactive], yet He is not presided over by anyone else, as that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, the property of being characterized by a specific configuration is also inconclusive due to that same God—since there is no specific configuration apart from the entity itself, and the nature of being an entity (*vastutva*) exists in God as well. Likewise, the property of performing purposeful action is also inconclusive due to that very God.

{Refutation thereof} To this it is said: as for the claim that this is a "proving of what is already established" (*siddhasādhana*), that is incorrect; for among those who do not accept a Lord (*anīśvaravādin*), no agent of the earth and so forth, nor a presiding controller of their material causes and so on, is established, such that there would be a proving of what is already established.
{Doubt regarding the sentience of karma and its refutation}

Now, it might be argued that the Buddhists, who maintain that the diversity of the world arises from karma, do not deny the existence of an agent (*kartṛ*) in general. Nor can it be claimed that [the argument] proves what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because karma is insentient (*acetana*); for according to the statement, "volition (*cetanā*) is mental action," it is not established that anything other than that [volition] is sentient. Furthermore, if even a sentient being were controlled by another sentient being, it would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This too is incorrect; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the claim that karma is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Thus, we shall explain that the self (*ātman*) alone is sentient due to its connection with consciousness, and that karma, being a different entity, is not sentient. Moreover, does that karma possess complete knowledge of the material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth, or not? If it does, then the difference is merely nominal. If it does not, how can it be an agent? For one who lacks knowledge of the capacities of the threads and other materials is not able to weave a cloth. Even a sentient being who is unskilled in a particular field is able to accomplish a task when proceeding under the guidance of another's intellect, but not otherwise. By this, the following [position] is also refuted, which he [the opponent] has stated:
"If volitional action alone were the cause of activity,
then even when it is being examined, no further examination of that [cause] would be required."

Indeed, "ascertainment" (*nirūpaṇa*) is said to be the thorough knowledge of the capacities of the material cause and so forth with respect to the effect. And that [ascertainment] does not belong to *karman* (action), because it would follow that *karman* itself would be the Lord (*īśvara*). For he who, having ascertained that "this is capable of this, but this is not capable of that," proceeds toward the production of the world—he alone is the Lord. Since a potter and others proceed toward the production of a jar and so forth only after ascertaining the capacity of its material cause and so forth, there is no lack of an example. If it is argued that if the potter and others possess independence (*svātantrya*), it contradicts such statements as "this living being is ignorant and lacks mastery," we say: no; for we do not admit independence in all respects. Indeed, his independence is well-known insofar as he is the impeller of the staff and other tools; and it is in that limited sense that he serves as an example.
The Refutation of the Notion that Īśvara is Impelled by Another.

As for what was said—that "like a potter and others, God too would have to be impelled by another, leading to an infinite regress"—that is incorrect. For it is logical that one who acts while being ignorant of something is impelled there by another who possesses knowledge of it. However, God is not ignorant of anything, because He is omniscient. Furthermore, as for the claim that "the establishment of omniscience depends on the establishment of His being an agent, and His being an agent depends on His omniscience, resulting in a circular argument," that is also incorrect. For when one infers an agent who is knowledgeable about the material cause and so forth from an effect such as a temple, there is no room for the fault of circularity.

{The impossibility of God being the instigator of unrighteousness} Now, if God is omniscient and omnipotent, why does He instigate ignorant people toward improper conduct? For in this way, by causing them to perform what is unfit, He would appear to be lacking in discernment. If one were to argue that He is indeed discerning because He makes them experience the fruit of unrighteousness as something appropriate [for their state], this is not so; because—"He indeed causes living beings to engage even in the commission of unrighteousness."
"How could he, having caused [beings] to perform what is improper, then cause them to engage in what is proper?

[The opponent argues: "Having caused them to commit evil, he causes them to engage in the Dharma in order to turn them away from it. What kind of "acting with foresight" (prekṣāpūrvakāritā) is this on the part of the Blessed One? This results in the following: "I shall wash it off and then discard it.
"If his activity is for the sake of mere play, how can there be acting with foresight?"
"One person experiences momentary satisfaction, while another is deprived of life.
Furthermore:
"If all other treatises arise from the conceptualization of a Lord,"
"How can that which teaches both the true and the false be an authoritative source (pramāṇa) on account of its giving [benefits]?

"It is a great marvel that even that which teaches the false is considered an authoritative source because of its giving. Now, if it is argued that false scriptures are not created by Īśvara, then likewise other effects would also not be created by Īśvara.
{Refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: First, as for the question of what impels ignorant people toward improper conduct—that is not a valid objection, because it has already been examined. This was examined [in the section on the Lord’s activity]: how the Blessed One, even when inducing people to act contrary to *dharma*, does not become an instigator of what is improper. Furthermore, regarding the point that his activity is for the sake of sport (*krīḍā*), that is refuted by our very acceptance of it. For the sport of the Blessed One is not for the sake of pleasure, as in the case of kings and others; rather, it is a particularity of his nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*), like the play of children. The example of children is given due to a certain similarity. [Objection: "If he is free from passion and so forth, he would fall into a state of indifference (*audāsīnya*)."

Is it not the case that for one who is free from passion and the like, equanimity alone is appropriate? If, however, he attains equanimity through the sovereign power of the world's karma, then how can he be the Lord (*īśvara*) when he is dependent on the karma of others? Furthermore: "For the virtuous, indifference alone is appropriate toward the sequence of actions of the wicked;
for the virtuous, applying caustic to a wound is not the conduct of the good."

"Now, if this very sequence is of such a nature that it reveals itself and acts toward its own production, then this nature of the sequence cannot be prevented by me; therefore, people should act therein as is appropriate. This is not so; for:
"He who has no mastery even over himself is clearly not the Lord.
How could there be a lack of mastery over the world, whose activities are determined by its own karma?"

{That refutation}—this too is incorrect. For instance: [the opponent claims] "It is logical that one who is free from passion and the like should be indifferent. Is this a *prasaṅga-sādhana* (reductio ad absurdum) or an independent (*svatantra*) proof? If it is stated as an independent proof—"The Blessed One is indifferent because he is free from passion and the like, just like a liberated person"—then, in that case, a property (*dharma*) must be established for the sake of proving the inseparable connection (*avinābhāva*). Since that [property] is understood only through inference based on effect (*kāryānumāna*), how can indifference be established? Or, if it is not so understood, the reason (*hetu*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddha*).

Now, if a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*) is being made for the sake of establishing indifference on the part of one who accepts that [the Lord] is free from passion and the like, we say no; because that [position] is sublated by the inference from effects such as the earth and so forth. For it has already been stated that the production of the infinite effects, such as mobile and immobile beings, is not possible if the Blessed One were either possessed of passion and the like or indifferent. As for what was said—"How can the Lord be dependent on the karma of others?"—that is not so, because we do not accept it. For it is the insentient that is dependent on the sentient, but the sentient is not dependent on the insentient, according to the analogy of the weaver and the threads and so forth. Furthermore, the Lord does not become dependent on karma merely by performing an effect in accordance with karma. For a weaver and the like, who produces cloth and other things in accordance with threads and so forth, are not said to be dependent on those threads and so forth.

[Objection: Well then, just as a weaver or the like, even when the threads and other materials are present, does not produce the effect—the cloth—because his purpose has already been fulfilled; so too, why does the Lord not remain indifferent even while karma and other factors exist, since his purpose has been fulfilled? [Reply: We do not know; he alone should be asked: "O Blessed One, why are you not indifferent? As for us, perceiving the effects and understanding the agent accordingly, we do not deserve censure. Furthermore, it was previously stated that [the Lord] acts for the sake of others (*parārtham*). Even regarding how one who acts for the sake of others can still be the cause of suffering and so forth, this has already been explained; therefore, the objection beginning with "it is like applying salt to a wound" (*na kṣatakṣāranikṣepaḥ*) is also improper.

{Dispelling the Doubt Regarding the Lord’s Lack of Sovereignty} Even regarding the position that [the world] proceeds by its own nature (*svabhāva*), what was stated—"He is not even master over himself," and so forth—is also untenable. For it is not the case that, being a master, he would commit an error concerning reality such as permanence or impermanence; nor does his mastery cease simply because he does not act. Indeed, mastery and supreme sovereignty consist precisely in being the agent of infinite effects, such as the earth and so forth. {The Lord’s Authorship of the Scriptures}

As for the statement beginning with “other treatises” (*śāstrāntarāṇi*), that too is incorrect; for it is not admitted that all treatises were directly composed by Īśvara. And whatever treatise is spoken directly by Īśvara is indeed true; therefore, because he provides instruction in truth, the Blessed One is indeed a valid authority (*pramāṇa*). Because he is the cause and agent of everything by way of presiding over the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) which is the cause of false cognition and so forth, he is also called the author of all treatises. But it is not the case that one who gives false instruction is [an authority] in this way; for example, those who teach unreal objects through causes such as dreams or magical illusions are called givers of false instruction, but those who merely employ the means for those [illusions] are not.
There is only one creator of the entire world.
