But is it not the case that for even a single effect, one creator is seen, and yet many are also seen? Likewise, for many effects, there may be one or many creators. How, then, is it understood that the Lord alone is the sole creator of the entire universe, and not many non-Lords? It has been stated in this regard: he who employs visible causes and is himself not employed by them is called an independent creator. Furthermore, it is impossible for a non-Lord to exercise the function of an employer based on prior observation with respect to atoms, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth, as well as the internal parts of the earth, mountains, bodies, and the like. In that case, even if there were many non-Lords who were the creators of the earth and other things, they would be like countless infants constructing a particular palace.

If you maintain that there are indeed many lords who are the creators of the earth and so forth, then you fall into the error of contradicting your own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). Furthermore, while refuting one [creator], to then accept many reveals a remarkable skill in avoiding what is undesirable. Moreover, do those lords possess sovereignty, omniscience, and unsurpassed power, or not? If they do, then what is the purpose of postulating multiple lords? It would be redundant. If they do not, then there must be some other master who governs them; otherwise, how could they act toward the production and so forth of the world at all times without conflict?

{The doubt regarding the impossibility of a single eternal God being an agent} Now, it may be argued that since we observe degrees of excellence in qualities, it is logical that even those who were previously incapable may later attain capability through specific application; however, how can there be proof for an absolutely distinct [being] whose nature consists of inherent capacity and is devoid of any [external] accompaniment, because no means of accomplishment is possible for such a one? To this he says:
"Let it be established that 'the agent is the maker' based on the connection with configuration (*saṃsthāna*)."
"But how could there be any established reality for that which is devoid of causes and qualities?
"If reality were inherent by its own nature, the world would be inherently so;
that this [world] belongs to that one alone is clearly the work of a Lord."
Furthermore:
"The attainment of lordship by a lord must come from another;
that [lordship] of the other must likewise come from yet another; thus, a lord is not inherent by nature."

"If there is an increase in qualities such that the state of Śakra or Brahmā is possible, then even the status of Īśvara is attained; thus, there is no abiding eternal Īśvara. (This is its refutation.)

To this it is replied: If God were not at all the creator of the earth and so forth, then everything stated [in the scriptures], such as “entities are created by a creator due to their connection with a specific configuration,” would be entirely untenable. On the other hand, if He does exist, there is no dispute regarding His existence; rather, the dispute concerns His eternity. Furthermore, we do not first prove that the earth and so forth are preceded by an eternal God, but rather that they are preceded by an intelligent agent in general. Therefore, it has been stated that the proof of God follows by the force of an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context), because one who is not God lacks the capacity for the production of the earth and so forth. Once God is established in a general sense, His eternity is subsequently investigated. And since that has already been investigated previously, the claim that “the reality [of the world] is due to its being inherent” and so forth is also untenable.

Moreover, this argument is unprecedented: that if the sun has the nature of illuminating and heating the world, the world itself would possess that same nature. If you argue that the sun does not possess such an inherent nature, then the same logical consequence applies: even if the world has specific causes, it would still follow that the world is caused by those very factors. Furthermore, we have already established at length that even eternal entities, such as "cowness" and "horseness," possess a fixed nature.

The statement beginning with “the lordship of the Lord” is also untenable; for it is either sublated by the inference from effects such as the earth—which apprehends the subject (dharmin)—or else it suffers from the fallacy of an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddhatva).
[Even if knowledge and so forth were possessed of excellence, they would be inherent in the Lord.]

As for the claim that “there is an excellence of qualities” and so forth, that too is incorrect; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of the excellence of Śakra and others apart from scripture (*āgama*), and scripture is not a valid authority for you. Or, if its validity were accepted, then by that very [scripture] an eternal Lord (*īśvara*) would also be established. Furthermore, the Buddha’s scripture is not a valid authority for us. Moreover, if—even for one who is not a Lord—there were an excellence resulting from the practice of yoga, asceticism, and so forth, as in the case of Śakra and others, then there would not be the constant production and destruction of innumerable mobile and immobile beings, because [such excellence] would overcome the arising of non-virtue such as violence; this has already been stated.

Now, one might object: "If someone were to reject the idea that the excellence of knowledge and so forth arises from practice (*abhyāsa*) along with its logical concomitance (*anugama*), how could they not also reject it when it exists as an inherent nature (*svābhāvikatva*) without such concomitance? For if one robs even a village, one certainly has no expectation of protection in the forest where there is no refuge. This is incorrect. We do not reject the excellence of knowledge and so forth that arises through degrees due to practice, for that is accepted in the case of yogis. Furthermore, the inherent nature of the Creator's knowledge and other qualities is established by the force of the impossibility of explaining his effects otherwise, just as the atomicity and magnitude of atoms and space are established. If, however, you reject that which lacks logical concomitance, then you would also have to reject momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) and the like. If it is argued that in those cases, since the concomitance is established by subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*), it is established here too for that very reason—even though momentariness and identity-with-the-entity are grasped by perception, there is no certainty, and thus the subverting evidence merely removes the delusion regarding them—then we ask: how can one who says that the same applies here, where the earth and so forth are grasped by perception as being preceded by an agent endowed with eternal sovereignty, yet there is no certainty and the subverting evidence merely removes the delusion regarding that, be refuted? For the objection and the response are identical."

{The avoidance of faults regarding the reasons such as "having existence after abiding":} Thus, in the case of [reasons] such as "having existence after abiding," "specific configuration," or "purposeful activity," there is neither the proof of what is desired nor the lack of proof [of the reason], because in the example—the staff and so forth—the presiding of an intelligent agent is established. However, with respect to a specific property to be proven (*sādhyaviśeṣa*), there would be a lack of proof in the example for all inferences; by this, doubt regarding the example is also refuted, because the general property to be proven (*sādhyasāmānya*) is certain.

As for the claim that "doubt constitutes inconclusiveness," that too is incorrect; for it is only appropriate to point out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) when there is a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) admitted by both parties, and you do not admit the existence of God. Furthermore, it is impossible for that which is insentient—such as time or space, which lacks discrimination—to act after having remained stationary; however, a sentient being, having personally understood the causes such as place and time as well as the purpose [of the action], can indeed act even while remaining stationary, and thus there is no contradiction. {The refutation of the inconclusiveness of "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*) with respect to God.}

The claim that "configuration (*saṃsthāna*), even if non-specific, is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to God" is merely a manifestation of delusion. For in the world, it is not established that mere substance (*vastumātra*) is known as a specific configuration; rather, a specific configuration is said to be a specific conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) of parts. And since the specific conjunction of parts and the whole (*avayavin*) have been proven, it is incorrect to say that there is no configuration apart from atoms. Furthermore, one must necessarily admit that even atoms appear in forms such as triangular, quadrangular, or circular due to some excellence (*atiśaya*); otherwise, there would be no correspondence (*avisaṃvāda*) to that appearance. That excellence by which the appearance of triangles and so forth occurs is itself the specific configuration. Since that does not exist in God, how can the Blessed Lord also be a specific configuration? As for the further incorrect claim that "the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) is also inconclusive because of that very same [reason]," that too is incorrect, because causal efficiency when qualified [by its nature] is not inconclusive. For the causal efficiency of an insentient effect does not deviate from being produced by an intelligent agent; indeed, neither insentience nor the state of being an effect applies to the Blessed Lord.
{The suspicion that [the world] is not preceded by deliberation regarding its effects, and the refutation thereof}:
As for what was said—
"Because non-deliberateness is observed in respect to objects..."
"It is the doctrine of those who know logic that the cause [of such things] is insentient: 'The causality of non-intelligent entities is not logical;
what is the use of goats and the like forming pellets from dung and such?'"

That too is incorrect; for in the absence of a cause involving deliberate reflection, teeth might as well grow from the eyes and other [faculties], and a tongue might even emerge from the anus and so forth, because their respective causes would be indistinguishable.
[Furthermore,] the rolling of goat dung and similar objects into balls also serves a specific purpose.

If it is asked, "What is the purpose of an intelligent being in forming balls from the dung of goats and the like?"—the purpose is precisely the production of the fruits of karma caused by that, since at the time of excretion, pleasure or pain arises for the goats and others due to that specific kind of dung. By this, the purpose in creating the variegated patterns of jujube-fruit thorns, peacock feathers, moonlight, and so forth, should also be understood. In those cases too, there must necessarily be pleasure or pain, or seeing or touching; therefore, how can one who presides over the diverse karma of living beings and produces corresponding results be said to act without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakāritva*)? Or, let it be granted that the effect is purposeless; even so, there is no non-establishment (*asiddhi*) of the Lord, because the inference for Him is faultless. Just as toys such as elephants, horses, and chariots made by children, though purposeless, are not created by insentient causes alone, so too are the earth and other elements. Indeed, it is not logical that a reason free from defects such as unestablishedness (*asiddhatva*) should fail to prove the probandum (*sādhya*). If the defect of unestablishedness or the like were present, then that very defect should be stated; what is the use of another alternative that is not a constituent part of the proof (*asādhanāṅga*)?

{The suspicion that the reason, such as "arrangement" (*sanniveśa*), is unestablished (*asiddha*):} But surely, the fault of being unestablished also exists here, because arrangement and so forth—which are pervaded by an intelligent supervisor—are not perceived in the case of the earth and other such things. Thus he says:
(ka) "That [arrangement] which is established as following the presence or absence of a supervisor..."

"Therefore, that which is inferred from such [features] as the arrangement [of parts] is appropriate. Even when the act of creation is not observed, one infers an agent in the case of various structures like palaces and the like. If such an arrangement and so forth were present in the earth and other [elements], then an inference of a supervisor based on that would be appropriate. However, since we observe an arrangement and so forth that is dissimilar to those [man-made objects], an inference of a supervisor is not appropriate; thus he says:
"Of that which is established [as having an agent] in the case of a distinct object, [there can be no inference] for what is not distinct [from it] merely because of the identity of the word."
"Inference is not tenable [in this case], just as [fire] is not inferred from a pale substance.

When a distinction is observed among objects—such as in the case of a jar and the like, where a specific characteristic well-established by its particular shape and so forth, characterized by being presided over by a person, exists—it is not tenable to infer that same characteristic residing in the earth and other elements based merely on their non-difference due to the similarity of the word "shape" (*saṃsthāna*).
For indeed, an inference of fire does not arise even from vapor and the like simply because they share the similarity of the word "pale" (*pāṇḍu*).

If it is argued that the inference of fire proceeds from paleness because it is not sublated by perception, whereas the inference of God is not sublated and therefore its occurrence is logical—this is not so, because:
"(g) An inference does not proceed merely on the grounds that 'it is not sublated.
It is stated that its occurrence is due to the observation of a [logical] connection."

(gha) "Otherwise, because a potter produces some transformation of clay such as a jar and so forth, it would follow that an anthill is also his creation. (ṅa) If it is argued that the non-perception of a potter is the subverting factor here, then what perception is there in the case of God? Therefore, because there is no similarity of substance—as there is between a jar and an anthill—inference is not tenable. If it is argued that even in the absence of a commonality of substance, inference will occur simply through the recurrence of the word [‘creation’], that is incorrect, because:
(ca) "Because a word is commonly established as referring to a different class [of objects],
it is not logical to use it as a means of proof [for another], just as the presence of horns does not prove that goats and the like possess 'cowness' (*gotva*).
Since [words] are dependent upon the speaker's intention, where could the referents of words actually exist?"
"But if the object were established through its mere absence, then everything would be established for everyone.

(cha) Furthermore, just as the Blessed One is endowed with qualities such as eternity and omnipresence, so too is space; in that case, why is this distinction made—that God alone is the cause and not space? And if causality is postulated based on mere existence, then when Caitra’s wound heals due to his connection with medical treatises and medicines, why is causality not postulated for a tree stump, which is likewise unrelated? If it is argued that the tree stump is not a cause because no operation is perceived therein, then the same applies to God as well.
"Without a difference in intrinsic nature, even causal activity is not tenable;
because that which is eternal lacks differentiation, its capacity [to act] is difficult to establish.
Furthermore—
(Ña) "When X exists only when Ys exist, if one postulates something other than those [Ys] as the cause of X, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases.
Therefore, let whatever [effect] arises from whatever [cause] arise from that very [cause].
"It is certain that some [arise] from volition and some from other [causes].
{The refutation of that [position]}

(ka) To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that if the kind of arrangement and so forth seen in palaces and the like were exactly the same in the case of the earth and so forth—that is not correct. For even though there is a mutual difference in configuration among those various things such as monasteries, palaces, and jars, there is no deviation from their being preceded by a conscious agent. Now, if you say that in all those cases one forms the cognition that they are "made" despite seeing no activity [on the part of an agent], whereas one does not do so regarding the earth and so forth; then, is it now the case that the earth and so forth are simply non-products (*akārya*)? Indeed, it cannot be said that something is a product if it is not perceived as such through its being made. And if it is perceived as being made, why would one not form the cognition that it is "made"? Furthermore, not everyone forms the cognition that even palaces and the like are "made"; rather, just as in the case of ancient palaces and the like, only those who recognize the pervasion (*vyāpti*) form the cognition that they are "made," while those who are ignorant of the pervasion form the cognition that they are "unmade"—so too it is with the earth and so forth. Thus, there is no distinction whatsoever.

If it is argued that the notion of being created by a person arises with respect to things like palaces but not with respect to things like the earth, [we ask: for whom does it not arise? For those who have established the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*), or even for those who lack the memory of the pervasion (*vyāpti*)? First, for those who have established the invariable concomitance and whose memory has not failed, the notion of being created by a person certainly does arise; for even in common worldly experience, there is the recognition that the variety of the world was fashioned by some Creator. However, for those who are confused regarding the grasping and recollection of the pervasion, the notion of being created by a person does not arise even in the case of certain palaces and such. Yet, this much alone does not mean that those things are not created by a person. Furthermore, in this way, the notion of being created by a person does not arise even with respect to the Vedas for both common people and the Mīmāṃsakas; consequently, the reasons such as "being a sentence" (*vākyatva*) adduced to prove their being created by a person would be unestablished (*asiddha*) in that case as well.

Furthermore, even for the sake of establishing impermanence, the proof consisting of "being produced" (*kṛtakatva*) and so forth would be unestablished (*asiddha*). For that which is seen in jars and the like—namely, being produced—is not present in sound in the same way, since [sound] is not something graspable by the ear. Therefore, this is merely a difference between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the inference (*dārṣṭāntika*), which is common to all inferences and does not specifically invalidate the inference of God.

As for the argument that "like a white substance," that is incorrect; for regarding whiteness, when used to establish fire, there is either an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntikatva*) or a contradiction with the object of the inference (*bādhitaviṣayatva*).

Furthermore, as for the argument beginning with "it is not the case that [the inference] is not sublated," that is incorrect; because we do not accept it. Indeed, we do not say that the operation of inference occurs solely on account of non-sublation, but rather because of the apprehension of five or four characteristics, such as the property of being a feature of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*).

(gha) Furthermore, regarding what was stated—"otherwise, by a potter," and so forth—what is intended by the meaning of the word "potter" (*kumbhakāra*) there? Is it some conscious agent whose specific qualities are not intended to be expressed, or is it a person endowed with the collection of instruments such as the wheel? What follows from this? In the first case, nothing is contradicted, because even anthills and the like are admitted to be preceded by a conscious agent. In the second case, however, there is also a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), because we observe the production of anthills and the like even when no specific person endowed with the collection of instruments such as the wheel is perceived.

(Ṅa) Furthermore, as for the claim that "the Lord also does not exist because he is not perceived," that is incorrect; for it is the non-perception of a perceptible object (*dṛśyānupalambha*) that establishes non-existence, not mere non-perception (*anupalambhamātra*), since otherwise it would follow that even merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and so forth, do not exist due to their non-perception.

(C) As for what was also said—"In that case, even unseen *karman* need not be postulated; why then this entry into the knee of the void [of logic]? For if, having postulated *karman*, another Lord is postulated, and then yet another beyond that, there would be an infinite regress"—that too is incorrect. Since *karman* lacks the capacity to employ [its causes] preceded by a full knowledge of their causal powers, it is logical that it requires a presiding controller, just like a lump of clay and so forth. Through its supervision, the causal factors—whose powers are already observed, such as the potter and others—are employed according to his will. How then could there be an infinite regress, since he does not require another presiding controller equal in knowledge and power? If it is argued that he requires one with superior knowledge and power, and thus there is an infinite regress, we say no; because he does not require more than those within the scope of his own training and experience.

Nor does an infinite regress follow even if there is dependence on a superior [agent], because it ceases upon reaching that which is unsurpassed. For when another possesses neither superior knowledge nor superior capacity, he is endowed with unsurpassed knowledge and capacity and thus does not require another supervisor; therefore, the infinite regress is averted. There is no proof for one who attempts to establish an infinite regress by refusing to accept the unsurpassed, and there is a contradiction with the production of effects. Consequently, whoever is ignorant of a certain thing requires another who knows it in that regard, but one who already knows it does not require yet another who knows it.
Regarding the cause for beautiful, ugly, or intermediate configurations:

if, then, effects such as the earth and mountains were created by an intelligent being, why is their configuration not exceedingly beautiful? In that case, one must admit that an intelligent creator exists for those regions of the earth and mountains, as well as for specific things such as bodies and trees, whose configurations are exceedingly beautiful.

Furthermore, among the various specific works produced by any wise person, such as paintings and the like, not all of them possess an exquisite form. For just as a discerning artist, desiring to produce a variegated work, creates some with an excellent form and others with a mediocre form; so too the Blessed One, though omniscient, creates a world of diverse forms. Alternatively, just as bodies and sense organs, the Blessed One also creates the earth and other elements in accordance with the karma of sentient beings—there, because of the abundance of merit (*dharma*) among the gods, He creates their earth and so forth with an exceedingly beautiful form; but because of the abundance of demerit (*adharma*) among the denizens of hell, He creates their earth and so forth with an unattractive form. This place called the earth and its mountains is the abode for those living beings who possess the remaining fruits of their experienced merit and demerit; therefore, He created it as the cause for the various modes of pleasure and pain for them.

(cha) Furthermore, as for the two verses beginning with "That which is well-known in another class [of objects]," etc., that too is incorrect. For it is not the case that, just as the word *go* (cow) functions with respect to nine distinct objects such as speech and so forth without any single common cause, so too does it function with respect to earth and the other elements. If indeed there were no single, objective universal (*sāmānya*) characterized by "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) existing in both jars and the like, as well as in earth and the like, then how could "being an effect" be established through its "configuration" (*saṃsthāna*), and "impermanence" through "being an effect"? There is no distinction here whatsoever such that, while the mere similarity of the word "effect" would not be unestablished (*asiddha*) in earth and the like when proving impermanence, it would be unestablished when proving "having an intelligent supervisor" (*buddhimad-adhiṣṭhātṛpūrvakatva*). In both cases, the jar and the like are the very same example; just as the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of "being an effect" by "impermanence" is well-established there, so too is the pervasion by "having an intelligent supervisor. Thus, let there be establishment or non-establishment for both. Nor is there any distinction among insentient things such that only the causes of chariots and the like—being insentient—are never set in motion without an intelligent supervisor, whereas the causes of earth and the like, though insentient, are set in motion even without an intelligent supervisor.
Even regarding universals such as eternality, the agency belongs to Īśvara alone, and not to space and so forth.

Furthermore, as for the objection: "Even though there is no distinction regarding eternality, omnipresence, and so forth, why is this distinction made that God alone is the cause and not space?"—that too is an unexamined matter, because the distinction has already been demonstrated through the inference from effects. For in the case of examples such as a jar, it is well known among both worldly people and investigators that the agent is indeed an intelligent being, and not space; therefore, when the earth and other things are the objects of proof (*sādhya*), it is established that the agent is indeed an intelligent being. That very being is God, since it has been stated that a non-God lacks the capacity for that task. By this, the argument beginning with "due to the connection with scriptures, medicines, and so forth" is also refuted. Even if the causality of a post (*sthāṇu*) in cases such as the healing of a wound is not postulated due to a lack of evidence, why should the causality of the Blessed One in the earth and other things not be postulated? For here too there is no lack of evidence, nor is God perceptible, such that his lack of connection to the effects like the earth could be grasped as being like that of a post.
{The Refutation of the Suspicion that a Devoid-of-Activity Īśvara is an Agent}

Now, suppose it is thought: "It is not logical for that which is devoid of activity (*nirvyāpāra*) to be a cause, and activity on the part of God is not possible without a difference in his nature (*svabhāvabheda*). What is the meaning of "without a difference in nature"? Does it mean without a difference in auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), or without a difference in attributes (*dharma*), or rather without a difference in essence (*ātman*)? In this regard, if the intended meaning is "without a difference in auxiliary causes," then that is unproven (*asiddha*); for even God certainly possesses a difference in auxiliary causes. We shall explain later how, even when producing an effect that is not of His own form, there is no futility of the auxiliaries. If the intended meaning is "without a difference in attributes," that too is unproven; for in the Blessed One, a mutual difference among attributes such as omniscience, being the creator of the world, and eternity is established. If the intended meaning is "without the destruction of attributes," that too is unproven; for the destruction of attributes such as conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is logically possible. If it is argued that activity is not possible without the destruction of all attributes, that is also incorrect; for when all attributes are destroyed, an activity already commenced cannot exist. If the meaning is "without a difference in essence," then does the essence of God not differ from another, or does it not differ from itself? It is illogical to say it does not differ from another, because that would entail monism (*advaita*), and we shall refute monism later. If it does not differ from itself, then since no other causal agent (*kāraka*) differs from its own self either, there could be no activity; consequently, the entire world would be without a cause. If the difference in nature means the destruction of one's own self, and activity is not possible without that, then is activity possible for that which has been destroyed? Or is it that activity is possible upon the cessation of a non-productive nature and the arising of a productive nature, but not for that which is eternal? This point we shall refute in the refutation of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
The capacity of an eternal entity is not difficult to infer.

(Jha) As for the claim that "because an eternal entity lacks exclusion (*avyatirekitva*), its capacity is difficult to infer," that is incorrect; for its capacity is established by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends its existence, as it has already been stated that the production of effects such as the earth and so forth is otherwise impossible. Furthermore, although universals such as "cowness" (*gotva*) are eternal, their capacity has been demonstrated in detail with respect to the inclusive and exclusive cognitions of "cow" and the like. Therefore, the capacity of an eternal entity is not difficult to infer.
The refutation of the doubt that an effect might be preceded by either a conscious or an unconscious agent.

(Ña) Even as for the argument beginning with “when these exist,” that too is incorrect; for it would entail the consequence that karma and so forth need not even be postulated. Indeed, when fathers and others exist, karma, craving, and the like are not observed to be the causes of the body and so forth that come into being; therefore, even if those [karma and craving] were postulated, there would still be a lack of stability regarding the causes. If you argue: “Having observed the efficacy of karma, craving, and so forth in one case, it is understood through inference in other cases as well,” then why is it that, having observed the efficacy of an intelligent supervisor (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) in one case, he is not also understood through inference in other cases? If you say: “Let it be understood where it has been observed, but not in the case of the material causes and instruments such as the earth,” then [we reply]: let it be understood in the case of karma, craving, and so forth only where their efficacy has been observed, but not in the case of the embryonic body and so forth. If you say: “Because there is no difference in terms of being a body, it is understood in the case of the embryonic body and so forth as well,” then [we reply]: because there is no difference in terms of being insentient (*acetana*), why is it not also understood in the case of the material causes and instruments such as the earth? If you say: “The efficacy of a mere intelligent supervisor may be understood, but not that of Īśvara, because he is unobserved,” then [we reply]: if that is so, let the efficacy of mere karma, craving, and so forth be understood, but not that of something produced in another life, because that too is unobserved. If you say: “The production in another life is established by the efficacy of the cause of the embryonic body and so forth,” then [we reply]: if that is so, the establishment of Īśvara-hood follows from the efficacy of an intelligent supervisor of the material causes of the earth and so forth; thus, there is no distinction whatsoever. Therefore, since it is established that all effects are preceded by an intelligent agent, the claim that some things arise from a conscious source while others arise from something else is also incorrect.

{The objection that action is redundant if God is the cause, and its refutation}: Now, if God were the cause, action would be useless; or, if action were the cause, God should not be accepted [as the cause].
For it is said: "If, having disregarded action and the like, [God] alone were to be the cause..."
Otherwise, it would follow that everything could be the cause of everything.

This is incorrect. For it is not the case that the potter’s causality is rendered useless by the wheel, the staff, and so forth, such that the potter would be the cause of jars and other objects only after disparaging the wheel and other tools; nor is he not the cause at all if he does not disparage them. Furthermore, they are apprehended by different means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). To explain: God is perceived through the inference of being preceded by an intelligent agent, whereas karma is perceived through the diversity of births and so forth. Indeed, a diverse effect is seen to arise from diverse causes, as in the case of a painting and the like; and likewise, the effects consisting of birth and so forth are observed to be diverse. [The diversity of birth: [The diversity of birth: The diversity of birth is as follows: some are born in a state of suffering, others in a state of happiness; some are short-lived, others long-lived; some are weak, others strong; some are ugly, others beautiful; some are of low caste, others of high caste; some are ignorant, others wise; some are poor, others wealthy; some are of low status, others of high status; some are born in hell, others among animals, others among hungry ghosts, others among gods, and others among humans. Such is the diversity of birth. And this diversity of birth cannot be produced by non-intelligent causes such as material elements (*bhūta*) or karma alone. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since karma is non-intelligent, it cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from karma, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements alone. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements are non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements and karma together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements and karma are both non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from both material elements and karma, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, and time together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, and time are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, and time, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, and nature (*svabhāva*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, and nature are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, and nature, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, and chance (*yadṛcchā*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, and chance are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, and chance, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, and destiny (*niyati*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, and destiny are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, and destiny, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, and the self (*ātman*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, and the self are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, and the self, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, and primordial matter (*prakṛti*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, and primordial matter are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, and primordial matter, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, and the Lord (*īśvara*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, and the Lord are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, and the Lord, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, and the supreme soul (*paramātman*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, and the supreme soul are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, and the supreme soul, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, the supreme soul, and the individual soul (*jīva*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, the supreme soul, and the individual soul are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, the supreme soul, and the individual soul, which is God. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the diversity of birth cannot be produced by material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, the supreme soul, the individual soul, and the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) together. Why? Because we observe that a diverse effect arises from a diverse cause, as in the case of a painting and the like. Therefore, since the effect of birth is diverse, its cause must also be diverse. And since material elements, karma, time, nature, chance, destiny, the self, primordial matter, the Lord, the supreme soul, the individual soul, and the subtle body are all non-intelligent, they cannot produce diversity. Thus, there must exist an intelligent cause distinct from material elements, karma,

Birth, first of all, is diverse: for some it is birth into a noble family, for others into an ignoble one; for some it is with wealth, for others without wealth. It should also be understood as diverse through the gradations of caste, intelligence, character, physical form, deformity, and disease.
[The diversity of death]

Likewise, death is manifold: for some it occurs in the womb, for others immediately upon birth; it varies according to distinctions of time such as months or years, according to distinctions of suffering that range from long to even longer, and according to distinctions of auspicious or inauspicious causes. Nor can this diversity of birth and death be attributed to the diversity of the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth, because diversity is observed even when there is no difference in the causes such as food and the like. Since persons are diverse by their very nature, it is understood that the diversity of birth and so forth arises precisely from the diversity of the karma performed by them. If [the opponent argues] that the Lord exists as the presiding agent over these, just as He is the presiding agent over the diverse implements such as the loom, then how is the other [the individual soul] not rendered redundant?
{The suspicion that [the seed] is unchanging because it lacks causality, and its refutation}:
As it has also been said—
"By means of the transformation of its own nature, the cause [is the seed] in the production of the sprout..."
"Because when earth and so forth are processed, a specific quality is observed in them.
However, even though there is a transformation of nature in the case of Īśvara, he possesses no state of being processed; therefore, like earth and so forth, he is not a cause.
"Therefore, those things which are individually incapable, but in whose combination a quality is possible..."
"Their causality resides in their collection, not in a Lord (Īśvara) or the like, because there is no difference [between them and the collection]."

That too is incorrect, for a cause does not function solely through transformation (*pariṇāma*). To explain: the earth and other elements are observed to be causes—even while remaining unmodified—for supporting living beings who are standing, sitting, or walking, as well as for the production of cognition within themselves. Furthermore, a particular gem is seen to be a cause of cognition, pleasure, and so forth, even though it is motionless. If it is argued that since causality is established in certain effects by means of a transformation of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-pariṇāma*), everything must likewise be a cause in that same way because there is no distinction [between them], we say no; for that would entail the consequence of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and we shall refute momentariness later.
The establishment of the fact that insentient things are presided over by a conscious agent.

Why, when the causality of certain insentient things is established through their being presided over by a sentient being, is it not inferred that all such things are likewise [presided over], given that there is no difference in their insentience? For the non-existence of transformations such as earth or crystal is established because they are not perceived—since they meet the conditions for perception—but this does not apply to a presiding agent, because that is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). If it is asked: "Since a potter and the like are perceptible (*aindriyaka*), why is their non-existence not established by their non-perception?", we say: No; because a sentient being distinct from one's own body is not directly perceived. Only the body of the potter and so forth is perceptible; let its non-existence be established by its non-perception, but not that of another intelligent being distinct from it. If it is argued: "Once the absence of the body is established, the absence of this [agent] is also established, because an agent without a body is never perceived," then, in that case, a dead person would not initiate a new birth because he lacks a body, since such a thing is not observed. Nor does one initiate a new birth while still possessing a body, precisely because that is not observed; for it is never seen that the intellect (*buddhi*) leaves one bodily continuum and enters into another. If it is argued: "It is like the transition between the stages of childhood, youth, and so on," we say: No; for although there are differences in state, there is a single continuum, as evidenced by the fact that "the very same person lives. Conversely, however, the departure from a Buddha’s body and entry into a fetal body in another birth is nowhere seen. If it is argued: "Entry into another body is seen in dreams," we say: No; for that is false. If it were real, the cessation of breath and other vital functions in one who is asleep would be perceived by others. Furthermore, the production of an effect in a distant place from a material cause located elsewhere is never observed. Therefore, for those who merely restate what is observed, the establishment of a future world is difficult to achieve. Therefore, when a general cause is inferred from a general effect, a specific cause corresponding to that specific effect must also be understood; otherwise, there would be only an inference of the general. As for what was said—"Therefore, when [atoms] are individually incapable," etc.—that too is incorrect. Because even here, in the subject of the example such as a jar, the incapacity of sentient factors like the agent and the action when separate is observed; by that, it is inferred that even in the case of the earth and so forth, the capacity belongs only to the agent, action, and so on when they are combined. Whether those agents, actions, and so forth are eternal or non-eternal, pervasive or non-pervasive—it must be accepted that they are established exactly in such a way that the production of the effect is possible. Enough with this stubborn adherence to a false view.

{The Examination of the Lower Self} Thus, the Supreme Self has been determined; now the lower self is examined. That which is called the "lower" is the infinite experiencer of the fruits of saṃsāra. It must indeed be inferred as the substratum of specific effects such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth.

The meaning is that "beginning with cognition" (*buddhyādayaḥ*) refers to those starting with cognition and ending with knowledge, as well as those beginning with desire (*icchādayaḥ*). And so says the Sūtra: "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and knowledge are the marks of the self. However, according to the established reading of the Vaiśeṣika [text], it should be understood as "those for which cognition is the first" (*buddhir ādir yeṣām*). But how, then, is the self inferred by means of cognition and the rest? That is stated: cognition and the rest must be inherent in something, because they are effects or because they are qualities, like color and so forth. [Objection: Here, the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*), since it is not established that color and the rest reside in the self; furthermore, the reason (*hetu*) is contradictory (*viruddha*), because it is pervaded by the opposite of what is to be proven. [Response: This is not a fault, because the proof establishes merely that [the qualities] reside in some substratum in general.

{The Refutation of the Body and Other Entities as the Substratum of Cognition} If that is so, then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because it is accepted that cognition and its attributes reside in the body and the sense organs. This is not the case; for, first of all, against one who does not perceive that cognition and its attributes have any substratum at all, it is precisely their having a substratum that is being proved. Once that is established, the self (*ātman*) is proven by the refutation of the body and other entities as their substratum. To explain: the body is not the locus of cognition and its attributes, because it is an effect of the elements (*bhūtakāryatva*), like a jar and the like. {The example is not devoid of the property to be proved}.

[Objection: Is it not the case that the illustrative example (nirdarśana) lacks the property to be proven (sādhyahīna)? For it is impossible to apprehend jars and the like through perception as being devoid of intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth; and if they are to be apprehended only by means of inference, there would be the consequence of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). [Reply: No. If [intellect and the rest] were to have the elements (*bhūta*) as their substratum (*āśraya*), it would follow that they would be perceived by the many people who perceive those [jars], and there would also be the consequence of them being perceivable by the external sense organs (*bāhyendriya*). Indeed, it is never observed that qualities (*guṇa*) residing in the elements are perceivable by one fixed person alone, nor that they are perceivable by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) alone. Furthermore, there would be the consequence of their being perceived as long as their substratum is perceived, just like color (*rūpa*) and so forth; for it is not observed that specific effects of the elements undergo absolute cessation even while their substratum exists. If it is argued that this is "like beauty" (*lāvaṇya*) and so forth, we say no. This is because beauty and the like possess the nature of one or another among color, conjunction, or touch. Nor is mere color and so forth absolutely cut off even in a dead body.

Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that activity and so forth—which indicate the presence of cognition and the like—would be perceived even in objects such as jars, just as they are in living bodies, because there is no distinction between the two in their being the substrata of cognition and the rest. If it is argued: "In living bodies alone does cognition and the like possess the capacity to produce activity and so forth, not in jars and the like. Therefore, although cognition and the like exist in those [jars], activity and the like which indicate them are not perceived," we say: No. For if they are not perceived, there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the existence of mere cognition and the like [in jars]. If it is argued: "Nor is there any means of valid cognition for their non-existence," we say: No. Because such a thing is unestablished (*aprasiddha*). Indeed, where the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of activity and the like is never perceived at any time, there is no established proof for the existence of cognition and the like. Whether such a thing exists or not, as for that which is well-established as cognition and the like, its absence in jars and the like is certain, because not even one of the marks, such as activity, is ever perceived therein. Therefore, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is not devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyahīna*).

By this, the status of the sense organs and the mind as instruments (karaṇa) is effectively refuted with respect to their being the substratum of cognition and so forth. It should be understood that the deficiency of the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) regarding the absence of the property to be proven (*sādhya*) has been avoided. Thus, when it is established that [desire and so forth] are not qualities of the body, the senses, and so on, it is understood through the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) that the Self (*ātman*) is that in which these qualities reside.
[Furthermore, because desire and so forth occur in a specific sequence, they must indeed be dependent upon the Self.]

Furthermore, if these qualities—desire and the rest—were to arise with their substratum in the body, they would not appear in the sequence in which they are observed to arise. To explain: when pleasure is experienced by the self due to contact with an object of a certain kind, one sees an object of that same kind and desires to acquire it. This desire to acquire, arising from the synthesis of perceptions in one who perceives multiple objects, is the mark (*liṅga*) of the reality of the self. For a desire does not arise in one person through the synthesis of a perception of a cause of pleasure experienced by another.

Likewise, when the self has experienced suffering upon the encounter with a certain kind of object, it feels aversion upon seeing an object of that same kind. This aversion, arising from the synthesis of perceptions by one who perceives multiple objects, is a mark of the self. For its production through such a synthesis of perceptions would not be possible otherwise, since it is impossible for one person to synthesize what was seen by another. Nor can aversion arise in one person from the synthesis of perceptions of a cause of suffering belonging to another.

When an object of a certain kind is encountered, that which has been determined to be a cause of pleasure or a cause of pain—upon seeing an object of that same kind, one exerts effort for the sake of acquisition or avoidance, desiring to obtain it or to reject it. This effort, arising from the synthesis of perceptions by a single perceiver of multiple objects, is a mark of the self (ātman), according to the reasoning previously stated.

When one has previously experienced pleasure in the presence of a certain kind of object, pleasure arises upon the recollection of that same kind of object; this [pleasure] is a mark of the self (*ātmaliṅga*), produced from attachment born of the recollection of the experience of pleasure. For if it were merely a distinction in cognition restricted to a specific object, it would not occur, as in the case of another body.

Likewise, when one encounters an object of a certain kind that one has previously experienced as painful, even upon seeing such an object after a long time, suffering arises due to the mental association (*pratisandhāna*) with it; this suffering, which arises from aversion produced by the association resulting from the perception of its cause, is a mark (*liṅga*) of the self, for otherwise such a process of association and so forth would not be possible.

Furthermore, having perceived an object possessing qualities such as height and so forth, and while reflecting upon it with a desire for its specific details, one seeks to know them; thereafter, from the perception of those specific details, a definitive cognition (*nirṇaya-jñāna*) arises. This cognition, being apprehended as sharing a single agent with the reflection and the desire to know, is the mark (*liṅga*) of the self. For neither memory nor the synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*) of experiences occurs if [the self] has not seen [the object] or if what was seen by another is involved; in the absence of that [self], there would be no production of desire and the like, which share a single agent with those [cognitions]. {The demonstration of the lack of consciousness in the sense organs}

If it is argued that the self is not established because a single agent could exist even if the sense-faculties were the agents, we say no; for since the sense-faculties are manifold, their unity is untenable. Consequently, upon perceiving an object with one sense-faculty, there would be no recollection, recognition, and so forth regarding the objects of other sense-faculties; yet such things are observed. Therefore, desire and the rest are not functions of the sense-faculties.

Furthermore, since memory of an object is observed even when the sense faculty is impaired, and memory is not possible when the experiencer is impaired—lest it follow that there would be a common body for all—then, because actions would proceed according to divergent intentions, the body might at times fall into pieces.

Furthermore, just as in the case of different bodies, a fixed distribution of pleasure and so forth—which serves as an inferential mark for distinct consciousnesses—is observed even within a single body; moreover, there would be disagreement, and disputes and the like might occasionally arise, just as among several conscious beings residing in a single house; and even the relationship of student and teacher would be perceived in relation to a single body.

If it is argued that the sense organs are conscious because they have fixed objects, like a good householder, we say no; for precisely because they have fixed objects, they are insentient, like a lamp and so forth. Furthermore, there exists no conscious being with fixed objects regarding form and the other sense-objects who could serve as an example here.
[Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the absence of activity and cessation in the sense organs.]

Furthermore, there would follow the consequence of the absence of both engagement (*pravṛtti*) and withdrawal (*nivṛtti*). For a person engages in or withdraws from boiled rice and the like by inferring its taste and other qualities upon seeing it. Yet such an inference is not possible through the eye, nor through the tongue and so forth, because color, taste, and the rest are not perceived by one another, and thus their relationship has not been grasped by anyone. Moreover, [inference] is impossible for the sake of oneself or for the sake of another. The eye does not engage for its own sake, because it has not experienced its own purpose (the color). Nor can it experience taste and so forth even while engaging with them. Nor does it engage for the sake of the tongue and other senses, because the nature of the tongue and the rest is not known simultaneously with their objects. Nor is there activity belonging to the tongue and the rest themselves; for if they do not know the location and so forth, where could their activity be directed? Therefore, there exists a single perceiver or rememberer of color, taste, and the rest, distinct from the sense organs, who, having seen a color, infers the taste and so forth and thereby engages [with the object].

{The suspicion that the body is the self, and its refutation} In that case, let the body itself be [the self]; for it has been said: "The person is the body qualified by consciousness. What is this body? Are the parts [the body], or rather the whole? If they are the parts, then because of their multiplicity, the aforementioned defects—such as the impossibility of purposeful activity due to conflicting intentions—would follow. Furthermore, if the parts were cut into pieces, cognition and other qualities would be perceived in them through their own respective marks, just like color and so forth. For it is not the case that color, taste, and the rest are not perceived when the parts are cut into pieces.
The refutation of consciousness in the aggregate of parts.

Now, if that "body" is said to be a collection (*saṅghāta*), is it non-different [from its parts] or different? If it is non-different, then the parts themselves have merely been designated by another name; and the faults already mentioned apply there as well. If the collection is qualified by some particular property, even in this case the faults—such as the multiplicity of conscious entities—do not cease. If, on the other hand, the collection is different [from the parts], would it be of the nature of an arrangement (*saṃniveśa*) or a whole (*avayavin*)? In either case, because it perishes every day, the recollection and synthesis of objects experienced at different times would be impossible. For a specific conjunction (*saṃyoga-viśeṣa*) is designated by such terms as "arrangement," "accumulation," and "structure"; and that [conjunction] perishes every moment, otherwise the body’s nourishment, weakness, and so forth, resulting from the consumption or non-consumption of food and drink, would not occur. Furthermore, due to the destruction of the conjunction, the whole (*avayavin*) is also destroyed.

The continuum of the body, which is momentary by nature, moreover, persists by depending upon a cause that diminishes at every instant; it persists through a continuum consisting of the successive arising of similar [moments], just as a lamp persists by depending on oil, so too the body persists by depending on food. Therefore, though perishing at every moment and arising through a continuum, it is perceived and recognized just like a lamp.
[Thus,] due to the difference in states, there is also a difference in the body.

And thus, what has been stated by some—namely, that "only the states such as childhood and youth differ, but not the possessor of the states"—is refuted; for in this way, even the destruction of things like a lamp would not be established, since one could resort to the lazy argument that "even there, it is only the states that differ."

Furthermore, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would follow as a consequence: the states of the lump of clay, the pot, the shards, and so forth, are nothing other than the states of being manifest or unmanifest, gross or subtle, visible or invisible, and so on; and thus the non-duality of Pradhāna and Brahman and the like would be established, for these are merely the various states of a single entity such as earth, water, fire, air, and so on. Moreover, since these states cannot be defined as either different or non-different from that which possesses them, how can the Advaitin and the Sāṃkhya—standing with their feet firmly planted in this position—be refuted? Therefore, those who desire to maintain the doctrine of difference must accept difference based on the superimposition of contradictory attributes. And this [difference] exists in the body, because the attributes of childhood, youth, and so forth, as well as the difference in transformation, are contradictory. Thus, since the body is likewise unstable, it cannot possibly be the substratum for memory, recollection, and the like.
The causal relationship between the body and its continuum is untenable.

If it is argued that the production of memory and so forth regarding an object experienced by a previous body arises from the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) with the subsequent body, then is the previous body the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of the subsequent body, or the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), or rather the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)? What follows from this? If it were the inherent cause, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving all previous bodies even at the time of the old body, because there is no opposition between an inherent cause and its effect. Furthermore, nowhere is there the persistence of an effect once its inherent cause has ceased to exist.

Furthermore, two or more substances possess the status of being inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) with respect to a substance, but not a single one; for a substance supported by only a single substance is never observed anywhere. What follows from this? A substance cannot be a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because it is impossible for it to lack the status of being an inherent cause. That which is a cause proximate through one of the two types of proximity while not being a substratum of the effect is called a non-inherent cause. [This is the proximity of the non-inherent cause.]

Proximity (*pratyāsatti*), however, is characterized by causal co-inherence (*kāryaikārthasamavāya*) and co-inherence in the same object (*ekārthasamavāya*). For example, the proximity of the color and other qualities of the parts to the color and other qualities of the whole is characterized by causal co-inherence; and that of the contact with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇasaṃyoga*) and so forth to cognition (*buddhi*) and so forth is likewise [characterized by co-inherence in the same object].
[This establishes the status of desire and other qualities as having a material cause.]

If this is so, then it is incorrect for desire and the like to be efficient causes (*nimittakāraṇa*) in the initiation of effort and so forth, because they satisfy the definition of an inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). If you argue that this is not the case because their causal capacity has not been ascertained, then in the absence of such ascertainment of capacity, they cannot even be considered causes at all.

Now, it might be argued that while the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) possesses the capacity to produce all particular qualities of the self, such is not the case for desire and the rest; therefore, their status as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) is not accepted, because the conjunction with the mind (*manaḥ-saṃyoga*) alone is sufficient. This is not so, because without *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit), the efficacy of the conjunction with the mind cannot be determined. Or rather, let *adṛṣṭa* itself be the non-inherent cause.

Furthermore, one should not accept that gravity, fluidity, and so forth possess the status of an *asamavāyikāraṇa* (non-inherent cause) in the production of action, because corporeality (*mūrti*) alone is sufficient for this purpose. Indeed, no motion ever occurs in the absence of corporeality; thus, corporeality is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of both [action and cognition]. Nor is there any such rule that only one thing can be the inherent cause—let this discussion rest for now.

Therefore, the body is not the *asamavāyikāraṇa*. As for its being a *nimittakāraṇa* (efficient cause), memory and other such functions would not be possible, because it would follow that there would be memory even regarding objects experienced by one's father, grandfather, and so on.
A doubt concerning the continuity of the refinement of the body's constituent parts.

It might be argued as follows: "Unlike us Buddhists, for whom destruction is without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), rather, after the destruction of the whole (*avayavin*), another distinct substance is produced by the constituent parts (*avayava*) which remain in conjunction. In that case, just as when the color and other qualities residing in the previous body are destroyed, similar color and other qualities are produced by the colors and other qualities of those very parts; likewise, even upon the cessation of the dispositions (*saṃskāra*) of the previous body, a similar disposition is produced by the dispositions of its parts. Consequently, the occurrence of recollection and so forth regarding objects experienced in the previous body is possible in the subsequent body."
{The refutation thereof}

This is not the case. For in all composite substances (*kāryadravya*), the manifestation of form and other qualities is preceded by the qualities of their causes; therefore, as long as no other qualities manifest within the atoms (*paramāṇu*), it is logical that whatever composite is produced—even successively—by those atoms, will have manifestations of form and so forth that are similar to them. However, mental formations (*saṃskāra*) do not exist in this way within atoms, because they are not experiencers. If they were experiencers, the faults of a multiplicity of conscious entities and so on have already been stated. Furthermore, if the body were the experiencer, let the formation belong to that very body; [but it does not], because its parts are distinct from it.

Furthermore, the body of meat-eaters is also composed of the constituent parts of the bodies of rabbits, buffaloes, boars, and so forth. Consequently, if the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by those experiences were to arise, it would follow that there should be recollection and so on even regarding objects previously experienced [by those animals]. Alternatively, if you argue that the parts of the bodies of rabbits, buffaloes, and the like are destroyed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) through the impact of chewing and so forth, and therefore no latent impression persists; then, in that case, the parts of the bodies of infants and others are likewise destroyed down to their ultimate atoms by the ever-moving air, fire, water, and so on, and thus the persistence of their latent impressions is also untenable. Or, if there were no destruction of the parts of the bodies of infants and others, then fingers and other such members would always be perceived exactly as they were, and no specific changes resulting from wholesome food, medicine, and so forth would be observed. Therefore, since the body also perishes moment by moment, it is not logical for it to be the substratum of desire and the rest.

Furthermore, by the statement beginning with "due to the connection with memory practiced in a previous [life]," we shall explain that the substratum of desire and so forth is beginningless. Therefore, neither the body, nor the sense organs, nor the vital breaths, nor even the objects can possibly be the substratum of desire and so forth; for, like the body, the sense organs and the rest cannot themselves be beginningless.
{The mind, too, is not the substratum of desire and so forth.}

If it is argued that the mind (*manas*) should be the substratum of desire and so forth because it is eternal, we say no; for it too is an instrument (*karaṇa*), like an axe or a saw. If it is claimed that this is unestablished, we say no; for its status as an instrument is established by the very means of valid cognition that prove its existence. Furthermore, while the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the substratum of desire and so forth has been demonstrated, the atom-like nature (*aṇutva*) of the mind has been proven on the grounds that simultaneous cognitions are impossible. Indeed, if one were to accept the mind’s all-pervasiveness while maintaining its status as the substratum of desire, the dispute would be merely over a name. {The impossibility of cognition being the substratum of latent impressions (*vāsanā*):}

If it is argued that cognition itself, when perfumed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), is called the "mind" (*manas*), and that desire and so forth have that very [cognition] as their substratum—this is not so; for because cognition is unstable, it is logically impossible for it to be the substratum of latent impressions and the like. Indeed, it is observed that only what is stable can be perfumed by a perfumer. Furthermore, it must be connected [to the perfumer], just as cloth and the like are connected with flowers and so forth. Moreover, the status of being a substratum is observed only for things that are both stable and connected, such as walls and the like. However, cognition lacks stability, since it is destroyed by another cognition or by desire and the like. Therefore, cognition is neither perfumed by anything, nor is it the substratum of anything.
In the doctrine of momentariness, the relationship between the perfumed and the perfumer is untenable.

[Objection: But this illustration is unestablished (*asiddha*), for according to those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), nothing whatsoever is stable, nor does anything possess a [permanent] relation. For even in the case of cloth and the like, the latent impression (*vāsanā*) is simply a distinct arising from a preceding moment accompanied by flowers and so forth. Furthermore, the status of being a substratum (*āśrayabhāva*) belongs even to walls and such things; it is merely a specific kind of causal agency (*janakatvaviśeṣa*). [Reply: No, because here too there is an absence of an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭāntābhāva*). For among those who do not maintain momentariness, nothing is observed that is both unrelated and existing at a different time which is yet being impressed (*vāsyamāna*); nor is the status of being a substratum observed for anything that is both at a different time and unrelated.
The doubt that there is a continuum without any underlying substrate, like that of a seed and its sprout.

If it is argued that it is "like a seed and so forth"—that is, if you think: just as from a rice seed a sprout arises endowed with its specific potency, and from that [sprout] the leaves, stalks, and so on arise following that potency and produce only a rice seed and not a barley seed because they do not have anything else as their antecedent; likewise, from a particular preceding cognition, each subsequent cognition arises following the potency of the preceding cognition, producing a complete collection of all deposited potencies. And that which is the depositing of the potencies of the preceding cognitions into the subsequent cognitions is what is called "latent impression" (*vāsanā*). {Refutation thereof}

No; because [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). First of all, the destruction and production of seeds and the like without any continuity (*niranvaya*) is not established, nor is the transmission of the potencies of preceding cognitions into succeeding cognitions established. In the case of seeds and the like, there is indeed a persistence of subtle parts, just as there is a persistence of the parts of semen and blood. For example, when the parts of semen and blood cease in the mother’s womb, another composite whole (*avayavin*) is produced by those very persisting parts together with the parts of the nutrient essence (*rasa*). Even for one who has emerged from the womb, the persistence of the parts should be understood despite the cessation of the composite whole. Similarly, even upon the cessation of the seed and so forth, leaves, stalks, and the like are produced by those persisting parts together with the parts of the earth. In that process, the parts of the nutrient essence—stable and connected with the parts of semen and blood—are transformed (*bhāvyante*) by the parts of the seed and the parts of the earth. Being thus transformed, they initiate an effect that is not contrary to them. Likewise, the self (*ātman*) is transformed by preceding cognitions into something stable and connected. What is meant by this? A specific impression (*saṃskāra-viśeṣa*) is produced therein, and being thus transformed, it produces memory and the reconnection of experiences (*pratisandhāna*) inherent in its own nature, following the pattern of those cognitions. Thus, the Sāṃkhya procedure is not established for the Naiyāyikas, nor is the Naiyāyika procedure established for the Sāṃkhyas. Consequently, there is no example admitted by both parties in either position. Therefore, which side would achieve proof here? Proof belongs to that position where memory and the reconnection of experiences are logically possible. Memory is not possible for those who deny the self (*anātmavādin*), because what is seen by one cannot be remembered by another. Otherwise, an object seen by one person would be remembered by everyone. Just as for us there is an example admitted by both parties—namely, that an object experienced by one is not remembered by another, such as a different mental continuum (*santānāntara*)—you have no such example admitted by both. If you argue that there is an example in the fact that the very same experience is not seen to be the rememberer, we reply: let it be that the experience itself is not the rememberer. For it is the *experiencer* (*anubhavitṛ*) who is desired to be the rememberer, and the experience itself is not the experiencer, because it is illogical for the action and the agent to be one. Indeed, it is not reasonable to say "the cutting itself cuts. And if that which is the experiencer does not remain the same as the rememberer, what contradiction is there in saying that it will become so at a later time? Furthermore, if another were the rememberer even at a later time, it was already stated that this would entail the absurdity that other continua would also be rememberers.

If it is argued that there is no such undesirable consequence because of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), you might think: "This undesirable consequence would indeed arise if it were said without qualification that one person remembers what was seen by another; however, memory occurs despite the difference [of persons] due to the causal relationship. But while there is no causal relationship between cognitions belonging to different mental continua (*santāna*), and for that reason there is no memory in other continua, it is not the case that there is no causal relationship among cognitions within a single continuum, such that the subsequent cognitions would fail to have memory of the object experienced by the preceding cognition.

No, because there is no deception regarding their distinctness (*nānātva*). For it was stated that distinctness is the proof when memory is impossible; and that [proof] is not deceived even by the mention of the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*).
