Indeed, by mentioning the causal relationship, none of the faults—such as its being unestablished (*asiddha*) and so forth—is demonstrated, nor is the establishment of one's own position (*svapakṣasiddhi*) effected by this. It is not the case that memory arises from the causal relationship—in this regard, there is no example admitted by both parties. If it is argued, "It is like the redness in cotton," and it might further be thought:
"In whichever very continuum the latent impression of karma (*karmavāsanā*) has been deposited..."
"It bears its fruit in that very same place, just as redness [appears] in cotton. Thus it is said.

No; because proof and refutation are impossible. There is no proof, because there is an absence of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and so forth. Indeed, a positive concomitance such as "just as redness [occurs] in cotton" cannot exist, because there is no causal relationship [between the prior and subsequent cognitions]. Nor is there a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) such that "wherever there is no recollection, there is no causal relationship. There is no refutation either, because no [fallacies] such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) are raised. For it is not the case that recollection by subsequent cognitions regarding an object experienced by a prior cognition is impossible simply because [the latter] is different [from the former], like the cognitions in a different continuum. Thus, no defect whatsoever is established by the [example] "like redness in cotton" against this reason.
{The doubt that memory and experience lack a single common substratum}

If it is argued that this is because the method of elimination (*pariśeṣa*) has been shown to be unestablished (*asiddha*), it might be as follows: indeed, perception does not observe experience (*anubhava*) and memory (*smṛti*) to have a single substratum anywhere, by which we could establish that they both reside in the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, the method of elimination is unestablished, because there is no contradiction even in the case of memory [occurring in another] through the relation of cause and effect. Now, if it is said that memory is not observed when there is difference [of substrate], well then, it is the same in the case of identity, for memory is also not observed when there is identity. Moreover, one might say that when one thing is dyed, another is not seen to be dyed. But if that were so, then when a cotton seed is dyed, the cotton produced later in its continuum would not be red; therefore, one must admit that even in that case, the redness resides in the self, since the logic is the same.

Furthermore, even in your own position, the *sūtra* "because action is perceived as non-durable" establishes that cognitions perish very rapidly. Consequently, the object experienced by a particular experience has perished; how then could there be remembrance at a later time? If you say it is due to a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), no; for that [impression] is a different entity from the experience. For if a different entity were the cause of the remembrance of that object, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle. If you argue that, despite the lack of distinction in being different entities, only that impression which was produced by a specific experience generates the remembrance of that specific object—and thus there is no over-extension—then, if this is so, you too must admit that the causal relation itself is the regulator. Therefore, let that alone be the regulator; what is the use of postulating an internal, useless (*āntargaḍu*) self (*ātman*) as a cause?
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: As for what was stated—that the coexistence of perception and memory in a single substratum is not observed in any case—that is not so, because it *is* observed. For instance, one determines: "I am now remembering that object which I previously experienced," or "I, who was the experiencer, am the rememberer. Thus, one ascertains that perception and memory have a single, non-different self as their substratum, without depending on the recollection of a relationship between a mark and the marked (*liṅga-liṅgi-sambandha-smṛti*), nor on the instruction of a credible person (*āpta-upadeśa*). Nor is this an illusion, because there is no contradiction with reality. One who denies the perceptibility of pleasure and so forth should likewise be enlightened by this very reasoning. Similarly, the fact that recollection, desire, aversion, and so on share a single cause is grasped through perception: "That which I touched before, I see now"; "Having seen it, I myself desire it or I hate it"; "Desiring or hating it, I exert effort"; "Exerting effort, having attained that object, I have become happy or miserable. Thus, since memory, recollection, desire, and the rest—which have as their substratum the entity that shines forth in the cognition "I"—appear through perception, the self is therefore grasped even by perception. Indeed, the cognition "I" is neither doubtful nor erroneous, nor is it inferential or verbal.
Nor is the cognition of "I" based on the body, nor is the body its object.

For if the body were its object, there could be no such realization as: "In my childhood state I was ignorant, happy, or miserable, but now I have become learned, free from disease, or ill"; this is because the bodies of childhood and other stages are distinct. Indeed, one does not say, "I who was fair-skinned am now dark-skinned."

But surely there exists such cognition as "I am fat," "I am fair," and so forth; how could that have the self (*ātman*) as its object, given that properties such as fatness are impossible in it? Is the house set on fire simply because there are mice in it? Just because a cognition such as "the crystal is blue" cannot be considered valid does not mean that the cognition "the crystal is white" should likewise cease to exist. The cognition "I am fat" and so forth has the self as its object precisely by means of the body as a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). In this regard, if it arises concealing the difference [between the self and the body], then it is indeed erroneous, like the cognition "the crystal is blue. However, if one perceives it as "I am fat" in the sense of "I possess a fat body," then it is truly real.

There is indeed a cognition of difference regarding the body and so forth—such as "my body is stout" or "my body is thin," or "my body is fair" or "my body is dark. Likewise, [there are cognitions] such as "I have desire or aversion," "I have effort," "pleasure has arisen in me, or pain," and "through the grace of my teacher, I have obtained distinguished knowledge"; in this way, desire and the rest are also perceived as distinct. Similarly, cognitions such as "this is my eye" should be understood as grasping the distinction between the self and the sense organs.
The designation of a distinction between selves, such as "my self," is thus rendered consistent.

[Objection: But surely there is also this cognition, "my self" (*madīya ātmā*). If the self is thus cognized, then it is not proper to dispute what is already cognized, because that would contradict one's own words. [If you argue: "This is for the purpose of establishing an undesirable consequence"—that is to say, for one who accepts that in the case of "my body," "my sense organ," "my desire," and so on, the referent (*ālambana*) of the cognition "I" is something distinct from the body and the rest, it follows that in the case of "my self," the referent must likewise be something distinct from the self? [Reply: No; because it does not appear as such. For the cognition "this is my self" does not appear through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) in the same way as [the cognition of] "my body" or "my desire. Nor does the self appear through inference (*anumāna) as something other than the object of the notion of "mine" (*mat-pratyaya*), like a sense organ. Rather, having directly perceived the self as "I," one designates it as "self" for the sake of communicating to others by excluding other selves—the meaning being: "my self is none other than myself. However, when one wishes to designate the body or the sense organ by the word "self," then the expression "my self" is indeed a statement of difference; for the body and so forth are metaphorically designated as "self" because they assist the self, just like a servant.
Even though the perception of a difference between selves is erroneous, the perception of a difference between bodies is non-erroneous.

Furthermore, if the knowledge of the self (*ātmajñāna*) is erroneous because it is sublated by being distinct from the object of the notion "I" (*matpratyaya*), then why is the knowledge of the distinction between the body and so forth not also erroneous? For it is not logical that because the cognition of hair-threads and the like is erroneous in one instance, it must be erroneous in all instances; otherwise, there would follow the absurd consequence of there being no distinction between what is erroneous and what is non-erroneous. Therefore, just as the various bodies of the past, future, and present are distinct entities from the object of the notion "I" because they are unified by a single presiding subject through the synthesis [of experience] as "mine," so too the distinctions of desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition—belonging to the three times—are distinct from that single entity and possess that single agent as their cause, because they are unified as being related to a single subject through the synthesis "mine."

Furthermore, the distinct instances of desire and so forth must have a single, non-different substrate, because they are the objects of a single unifying cognition of "mine," just as spectators are the objects of a single unifying cognition of one dancer. By this inference, too, the fact that the distinct instances of memory, experience, desire, and so forth share a single substrate is established. Therefore, what was stated—that "a single substrate for experience and memory is never observed"—is incorrect.
[This concludes the refutation of the failure to establish the method of elimination (*pariśeṣāsiddhi*).]

As for what was also stated—"The *pariśeṣa* [inference] is unestablished because there is no contradiction even in the case of memory due to the existence of a cause-and-effect relationship"—that too is incorrect; for we observe memory and so forth even when the cognitions of a disciple, a teacher, and others stand in a causal relationship. If it is argued that "it is only when there is a single continuum (*ekasantānatva*)"; then, apart from the cause-and-effect relationship, what else is a continuum? Or, if such a continuum is accepted, it would be nothing other than the self (*ātman*) itself accepted under a different name.
[This is the meaning of "continuum" as established in common worldly usage.]

If it is argued that the causal relation itself—consisting of the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) and its effect—is what constitutes a continuum (*santāna*), we say no. This is because, since there is no distinction in their being merely causes due to the absence of any specific relation, the division between the material cause and other types of causes would be untenable. Just as for us, despite the lack of distinction in their status as producers, there is a division into inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes based on specific relations, we do not see any such basis for the division of causes into material and others in your view. If it is argued that whatever produces a continuum is the material cause, we say no, because this leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the status of being a material cause would depend on being a producer of a continuum, and the status of being a continuum would depend on being produced by a material cause. In common worldly usage, however, the convention of "continuum" applies to a causal relation between things of the same kind, such as "the Brahmin lineage" or "the Śūdra lineage. It is based on the well-known usage of these terms that we ourselves also employ the convention of "continuum" in cases such as sound or a lamp.
There is a fault in his acceptance of the Sugata's [teaching].

If this continuum (*saṃtāna*) is intended by you in this way, then how is it that the cognitions of the disciple and the teacher do not belong to a single continuum? For it is not the case that these [two sets of cognitions] lack a commonality of kind (*samānajātīyatva*), nor is there an absence of a cause-and-effect relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). Therefore, just as for the disciple, even cognitions long past are indirectly (*pāramparyeṇa*) the cause, and thus memory occurs regarding an object previously experienced; so too, the cognitions of the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), having arisen from birth onwards, are indirectly the cause, and thus memory should occur regarding an object experienced by him as well.

Furthermore, smoke, sound, and so forth would arise even without a material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*). For it cannot be asserted that these, either, have a cause of the same kind through an beginningless series. And if that were so, consciousness too would arise in the womb and elsewhere without a material cause; thus, there would be no other world (*paraloka*).

Now, if it is maintained that even heterogeneous material causes can serve as the substrate for smoke and sound, then in that case, let the body within the womb itself be the substrate for cognition; there is no need to postulate a cognition from a previous life. For a substrate is accepted according to what is observed; otherwise, one would have to postulate an infinite continuum even for smoke, sound, and so forth.
[The doubt regarding the non-arising of specific qualities due to lack of distinction, and its resolution.]

[Objection: But if the body were the material cause (*upādāna*) [of cognition], then because it is uniform, there would be no production of multiple distinct cognitions; for no distinction is possible among smoke, sound, and so forth, arising from that which is their undifferentiated material cause. [Reply: No; for even when the material cause is the same—such as a lute (*vīṇā*) and the like—a difference in sound is observed. If you argue that the difference here arises from the difference in effort (*prayatna*) and so forth, then in this case too, a difference in cognition will arise from the difference in the transformation of the humors (*rasa*, *dhātu*, etc. at every moment. Furthermore, the internal constituents of the body, such as bile (*pitta*) and wind (*vāta*), are not perceptible, such that their specific or non-specific states could be perceived; for those two are to be understood solely through their effects.
{The suspicion of reviving upon the removal of the cause of death, and its refutation}:

By this, that which was stated—namely, "given that death results from a certain imbalance of wind (*vāta*) and so forth, there follows the contingency of reviving once that [imbalance] ceases"—is also refuted. Since the cause of death itself exists internally and is cognizable solely through its effect, its cessation is likewise not imperceptible. For even in the case of external objects, the capacity or incapacity for causing death is not perceptible; this is because it does not manifest in poisonous substances whose power has been neutralized by mantras and the like, nor in curd and other substances into which the poisonous power has been transferred.

By this, that which was stated—namely, "Only from such a specific type of disease does one die and not another; therefore, even the imbalance of wind (*vāta*) and the other humors is not the cause of death"—is also refuted, because it is impossible to ascertain what constitutes "being of such a nature."

Furthermore, death cannot occur due to the cause of *karma* according to your position, because since *karma* is impermanent, it cannot function as a cause. If even that which has perished could serve as a cause, it would follow that liberation is impossible. If you argue that *karma* acts as the cause for a result at a fixed time through a succession of produced potencies—just as the redness [of dye] occurs in cotton—we say no; for even the example is unproven. For redness does not occur in cotton either if there is production and destruction without any continuity (*niranvaya*). What then? It occurs when there is a continuity of the constituent parts (*avayava*) such as the seed and so forth. Moreover, those who maintain that consciousness arises from the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavādin*) can also say this: "An action performed by someone, through a succession of produced potencies in the semen, blood, and so forth of the parents, bears fruit at some point in a certain person; however, the time of ripening (*vipākakāla*) is held by you also to be indefinite. Thus, the fault of "the acquisition of what was not done" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and other defects are equal for both sides.
Nor is there a restriction of memory even on the basis of the causal relationship between effect and cause.

If the restriction of memory and so forth were due to the relation of cause and effect, then it would occur according to a fixed order of stages and a fixed time, just as in the case of the seed, sprout, leaf, stalk, and so on. To illustrate: from a seed, through its connection with soil, water, and other factors, only the sprout arises at a specific time, and not any of the others such as the leaf or stalk. From the sprout, only the leaf arises, and not any of the others such as the stalk or the seed. From the leaf, only the stalk arises, either immediately following the observed time-order or after an interval of two or three months. However, there is no such fixed order of stages or fixed time for memory, experience, and so forth; therefore, the restriction of memory and the rest does not arise from the relation of cause and effect.

Furthermore, since all karmic impressions (*vāsanā*) reside in a single cognition through identity (*tādātmya*), it would follow that when there is a single maturation (*vipāka*), there must be the maturation of all [impressions]; or else, there would be a contradiction of their identity, just as in the case of a seed. If you argue: "This might be so—just as a seed, though consisting of multiple impressions such as the sprout, the stalk, and so forth, does not produce them all simultaneously, so too cognition, though consisting of multiple latent dispositions (*saṃskāra*), does not produce memory, pleasure, and the like all at once," we say: no, because this is not accepted. I do not maintain that a seed possesses separate powers for producing the stalk and so forth; rather, a specific seed is capable only of producing a specific sprout, and a specific sprout is capable only of producing a specific leaf. It is utterly illogical to claim that while cognition is endowed with diverse powers simultaneously, it does not produce diverse effects simultaneously.
Nor does the sequence of memory arise from the sequence of the power of cognition.

Now, if the possession of capacity belongs only to those cognitions that arise sequentially, then the production of memory and so forth must also occur sequentially. But does this capacity, as it arises sequentially, come from only the immediately preceding moment, or even from a distant moment? If it comes from only the immediately preceding moment, then the doctrine of a future life would be dismissed with a mere handful of water—there would be no depositing of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) capable of producing memory and so forth even for an experience separated by half a muhūrta, much less for karma performed in another birth. For in your view, there is no other referent for terms such as "merit" (*puṇya*), "demerit" (*apuṇya*), or "latent impression" (*saṃskāra*) than the capacity to produce pleasure, pain, death, and so on; and yet you maintain that this capacity arises only from the immediately preceding moment.

Now, if it is argued that capacity arises even from a moment that is temporally remote, we say no; for that which is separated by time cannot be a cause. However, since all experiences (*anubhava*) and their objects (*karman*) are causes through a mediated succession (*pāramparya*), it would follow that even a single experience could produce all capacities, and consequently, all its effects would arise simultaneously. That is precisely the refutation. [Objection: A doubt regarding the causality of the remote] But surely, even that which is separated by time is seen to be a direct cause, as it has been said:
"It is certain that the consciousness of one who has slept deeply arises at awakening due to prior experience, even though there is an interval of time.

For proficiency in memory and so forth is not possible without prior practice; therefore, because proficiency in memory, attachment, aversion, and the like is observed, it is established that such practice is the cause, even if it is temporally remote.

If it is argued that because a separated [cause] is non-existent, how can it possess causality, we reply that non-existence is equally true for the immediately preceding [cause] as well; however, at its own time, even a separated cause is indeed existent. If it is argued that only that which exists at the time of the production of the effect is the cause, then what is this "time of production"? Is it the very time of the effect, or is it prior to that? If it is the time of the effect, then since both would exist at one and the same time, the distinction between cause and effect would be untenable. If it is prior to the effect, then since the effect is non-existent at that time, how can there be its production? For a property cannot exist when its substratum (dharmin) is absent. Furthermore, it would follow that the production of that [effect] itself would be a cause, since there is no difference in its occurring at a time prior to it.

By this, the state of being "presently arising" (*utpadyamānatā*) is also refuted, because the terms *utpāda* (arising), *utpatti* (origination), and *utpadyamānatā* are synonyms. Therefore, the cause does not exist at the time of the effect, nor does the effect exist at the time of the cause; consequently, there is no mutual relationship between them either. For a relationship consists in dependence (*pāratantrya*); what dependence can there be for that which is already established? And what dependence can there be for that which is unestablished and non-existent in itself? Therefore, the conventional designation of "causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is based merely on the fact that [the effect] occurs when that [cause] exists. This "occurring when that exists" is simply the presence of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). Furthermore, since this does not exist even when there is a temporal interval, it follows that a cause may have ceased long ago.

{Refutation of that} This is untenable; for that which has ceased to exist is non-existent, and if that which is non-existent could produce an effect, then even things such as a rabbit’s horn would have productive power, since there is no difference in their non-existence. If you argue that it was previously destroyed and therefore produced that effect—such that when it exists it does not produce, but when it is absent it produces—this is a most excellent arrangement! It comes down to this: "While living I am powerless, but once dead, I shall father a son for you."

Furthermore, even if that which has ceased were to be a cause, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-cessation of the production of effects. For it is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), through numerous examples such as fire and smoke, that the cessation of the production of an effect occurs upon the withdrawal of the cause. However, if the production of an effect were to occur from that which has already withdrawn, then there would be the consequence of the continuous production of that effect, because there would be no obstruction to the power of that cause to generate it; for that which has withdrawn does not undergo withdrawal again. Nor can there be a non-production of the effect while the cause remains in that state, because otherwise there would be the consequence of non-production at all times. If it is argued that the cessation of the production of the effect occurs upon the withdrawal of its auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), we say no; for the auxiliary causes themselves, being withdrawn, would likewise function as causes, and the same logic applies. Furthermore, it has already been stated that that which has withdrawn does not undergo withdrawal again. Moreover, if the cessation of the effect occurred only upon the withdrawal of the auxiliaries, then the production of the effect would occur upon their withdrawal; consequently, the status of being the cause would belong to those [auxiliaries] themselves, not to the [previously] destroyed [cause], because the characteristics of a cause do not persist in that [destroyed entity]. If it is argued that my refutation is similar to that of the proponent of an eternal cause, we say no; for that would contradict the admission of a non-distinct power (*śakti*), and if one rejects the necessity of auxiliaries for an eternal entity, it would follow that the entity is disconnected [from any causal efficacy].

{The Rejection of Future Causality} By this, the causality of even the future is also refuted. Furthermore, if the future were a cause, it would follow that the effect takes up [the cause] for the sake of the completion of the cause; and this is contradictory. Now, one might object: "Its status as a cause certainly exists, for we do not deny the causality of that which exists prior [to the effect]. What then? It is said that, in view of its non-deviation from what is yet to be, it also possesses the nature of an effect."

And as for the claim that "that which is a material cause (*upādāna*) while being a cause will become an effect," what indeed is the distinction regarding the material cause? Is it not sufficient for it to be a material cause simply by virtue of its non-deviation [from the effect]? This too is incorrect; the mutual relationship of cause and effect has already been refuted. Furthermore, the inference of a cause has been established, and from that, the inference of the next world (*paraloka*) will follow. One must not, in opposition to that, transgress all established boundaries and admit that even a cause is an effect. [Only that which has come into being is a cause.]

For it is well known in all worldly treatises that whatever is employed for the sake of the production of something is the cause of that thing; yet this [future] form does not exist in what is yet to be. Therefore, only that which has already come into being (*bhūta*) is the cause of what is to be (*bhāvin*).

[Objection: But in that case, would it not follow that everything that has already come into being would be a cause? [Response: Causality belongs to that which is the object of an unerring [cognition]. [Objection: Is its priority in time [the criterion] when it is the object of an unerring [cognition]? [Response: That too is of little consequence; for instance:

If the state of cause and effect arises merely from the fact that [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists, then what contradiction is there? In that case, what is the purpose of the temporal sequence of prior and posterior? (The refutation thereof)

That is incorrect; for it would follow that even properties such as unconditionedness (*akṛtakatva*) and permanence (*nityatva*) would possess the status of cause and effect. If you argue that this is not the case because there is no difference in substance (*arthāntaratva*), that too is incorrect;

since if the state of being cause and effect were based merely on the fact of one thing occurring when the other occurs, then even in the absence of a difference in substance, there would be no contradiction in their being so related.

For there is no contradiction whatsoever in applying a name arbitrarily, such that the name "cause" would be applied only to a distinct entity (*arthāntara*) that acts as a pervader, and not to one that is not a distinct entity. Furthermore, it has already been stated that just as causality is not possible for [the cause] itself, so too causality is not possible for the past and the future.

As for the claim that "the effect does not exist at the time of the cause, nor does the cause exist at the time of the effect, and therefore there is no relation between the two," that is not correct, because momentariness is not admitted.

As for what was also said—that dependence constitutes a relation, and that this is not possible for either an established or an unestablished thing—that too is incorrect. For if an effect were not dependent on a cause, it would be causeless, and consequently, being independent of anything else, it would have to exist eternally or not exist at all. Or, if it does depend on a cause, how is there no dependence?
[Dependence exists] in both cases, whether [the cause] is established or unestablished.

Therefore, whether it be already established or not yet established, there is dependence (*pāratantrya*) in both states. To explain: if that which is unestablished were not dependent, then it would either remain eternally unestablished, or it would establish itself spontaneously without depending on the connection with specific place, time, and so forth. Consequently, that which is unestablished by its own nature is forcibly established by causes; thus, it is "dependent. For this very reason, it is called "the effect as non-existent" (*asatkārya*). If it is asked, "Why then are things such as a sky-flower not also established by causes?", we shall examine this later.

Even that which has been established possesses dependence, because it abides in its inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*). And this is observed even in the world: a servant, a son, or the like, though established, is dependent on others. If [the effect] were established as independent, it would never perish; therefore, there exists a relation, provided it is possible for one who maintains the doctrine of momentariness.
[In fact, the coherence of the causal relationship is possible only in the non-momentary doctrine.]

Now, one might object: even for those who maintain that things are non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*), it is the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) in its state of assembly that is the producer, and since that does not exist at the time the effect arises, how can there be a relationship between the produced and the producer? This is not so, because such a restriction is not admitted. This is not a fixed rule—that a relationship exists only between two things that are simultaneous—but rather, it is accepted according to what is observed. Indeed, the relationship between the produced and the producer is observed precisely in this way: that the effect follows immediately after the causal complex. However, we shall explain later that for the proponents of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavādin*), the very apprehension of this [sequence] is impossible; therefore, it is said that in their view, the relationship cannot be established.

Furthermore, a causal relationship (*janyajanakabhāva*) is not directly perceived even when there is a temporal interval, as it is in the case of things occurring immediately one after another. This is not so; for it is not the case that what has perished or what has not yet arisen can be a cause in a direct sense. Indeed, only when the cause exists in the state of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is there a direct relationship between cause and effect. Thus, the fact that only an existing thing possesses the capacity to produce, while the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryatva*), is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and is not contradictory. But what would be gained by postulating the status of a producer at the time the effect already exists? It would imply that an existing thing is produced by something non-existent—this contradicts both common worldly experience and the scriptures. Therefore, a perished experience or the like cannot be the producer of memory and so forth. Nor is the arising of memory and such possible without prior practice (*abhyāsa*). Consequently, a certain latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by prior practice remains without perishing; upon encountering a specific auxiliary condition (*sahakāriviśeṣa*), it produces memory, recollection, attachment, aversion, and so on. And it is logical that once that [impression] has ceased, memory and the like will not arise, even if other causes are present.
{The impossibility of mental formations for those who deny the self}:

For those who deny the self, however, since prior practice has ceased along with its mental formation (*saṃskāra*), how could memory and so forth arise? Furthermore, if there were persistence through a continuum, then upon the cessation of the stream of cognition, there would be either the cessation of that [self] or a contradiction regarding its identity. This is because that which is partless cannot undergo cessation by way of a part.

By this, the claim that even for those who deny the self (*anātmavādin*), a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of karma can serve as the cause for results in another life, is refuted. Since that [impression] is not distinct from cognition, it cannot cease through experience any more than the form of cognition itself ceases; nor can it cease due to any other cause. The conventional expression "cessation of the impression" occurs when a cognition arises devoid of that impression, because the impression produces the cognition. Furthermore, if the subsequent cognition possesses the form of its material cause (*upādāna*), then it must possess the very form of the impression; if it does not, then it would not possess the form of cognition either, because it is impossible for a partless entity to receive a form through a single part.

{There is no suspicion that cognition is caused by latent impressions (saṃskāra), as in the case of melted butter and the like.} If it is argued, "Like butter and so forth": suppose you think—just as butter, lac, gold, and the like become liquid through contact with fire and become solid again through contact with cold, yet the state of being liquid and so forth does not persist at all times like the form of the gold itself; likewise, even if the form of cognition persists, the latent impression does not persist at all times. {The refutation of that:}

No; because [that] is not accepted. I do not maintain the identity (*tādātmya*) of hardness, fluidity, and so forth, by which the example would be established. For it has been proven that the property (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) are distinct entities; therefore, it is logical that the substratum persists even when the property ceases. However, if there were identity, both persistence and non-persistence would be impossible. [Thus, for a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) distinct from cognition, neither being supported nor not being supported is tenable.]

Now, if the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is an entity distinct from cognition, is it dependent or independent? If it were independent, then it would initiate its own effects elsewhere as well, like the fruit of a tree—for example, just as fruits fallen from a tree produce their own subsequent series independently, so too these impressions, having abandoned the stream of cognition, would produce their own respective streams, or they would generate effects together with those arising in other streams, like a daughter who is radiant together with the sons of others.

If, then, the mental formation (*saṃskāra*) is that which is supported, its relation to the support must be stated—whether it be conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*)—but neither is accepted by you. If, however, the relation were one of identity (*tādātmya*), the relationship of support and supported would be untenable, for a relationship of support and supported is never observed with respect to one's own self. Furthermore, the relation of identity has already been refuted previously. If it is argued that the relationship of support and supported is simply the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), we say no; for even in the case of cause and effect, there would follow the consequence of their moving separately, as in the case of a tree and its fruit.
[This concludes the refutation of the doubt that the Self is the object of cognition because of the causal relationship.]

As for the argument that even the Naiyāyikas observe the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) alone to be the regulator [of cognition], and therefore let that be the case—what is the need for a self (*ātman*)?—that is not so; for us, the causal relation is the regulator precisely because it is restricted by the specific substrata of the universals (*jāti*). [This is the restriction of universals.]

In this regard, due to the restriction by specific genus (*jāti*), for example: from that which is qualified by the nature of rice-seed (*śālitva*) and seed-ness (*bījatva*), there arises an effect qualified precisely by the nature of a sprout (*aṅkuratva*) and rice-ness (*śālitva*); from that, [an effect] qualified precisely by the nature of a rice-leaf (*patratva*) arises; from that, [an effect] qualified by the nature of a rice-stalk (*nālatva*) arises; and so it should be understood for each subsequent stage. Furthermore, because the constituent parts of the seed persist, there is also a restriction of the substratum (*āśrayaniyama*). Likewise, from a specific prior practice (*pūrvābhyāsa*) comes a specific mental impression (*saṃskāra*); from that, a specific memory (*smṛti*); and from that, a specific synthesis (*anusandhāna*) and so forth. [Thus, the causal relation exists] through the restriction of the substratum.

Likewise, the restriction regarding the substratum is also established: wherever there is repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), there alone is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*); and wherever there is the latent impression, there alone occur memory, recollection, and so forth. Thus, this restriction is logically justified. [This explains the diversity of substrata for the cognition of redness and its latent impression.]

As for what was said—that redness must also be admitted to reside in the self—that is not so, because redness can be accounted for otherwise. Indeed, it was stated previously that the occurrence of redness is possible through the sequence of impressions (*vāsanā*) upon the constituents of the seed. If it is argued: "Just as the impression is produced in the soil particles—which are connected with the perfumed seed-constituents by acting as their auxiliaries—in the same way, the substratum of the impression produced by experience will produce its own impression elsewhere," [we reply]: no, because the multiplicity of the substrata of those impressions is not perceived. For the impression of redness is perceived as having many substrata, since its fruits are apprehended simultaneously; the impression of experience, however, is not like that. If it were so, then as in the case of cotton, there would be the production of an infinite number of continua from a single continuum. And just as many lamp-continua arise from a single lamp-continuum, and sometimes even the absolute cessation of all of them occurs, so too it might be here. Therefore, it is precisely because desire and the rest are restricted to a single substratum that there is the restriction to a single continuum and the restriction to sequential production.
The doubt concerning the impossibility of being the substratum for both existence and non-existence.

Now, would the substratum belong to that which is non-existent or to that which is existent? First of all, there is no substratum for the non-existent; for there is no substratum whatsoever for the horn of a donkey. One merely seeks the production of the non-existent from a cause; therefore, only a cause is possible for the non-existent, not a substratum. Nor is there a substratum for the existent, because it is of no service—nothing at all is produced by a substratum for that which already exists. If you say that its "stability" is produced, we say no; for neither a difference nor a non-difference [between the entity and its stability] is possible. If there were no difference, then the entity itself would be what is produced. Furthermore, the essential nature (*svarūpa*) is not itself the stability, because motion is observed even while the essential nature persists. Nor is it something distinct, for if stability were distinct from the entity, there would be an infinite regress of one stability after another. And how could a substratum be the cause of stability? For it is not logical that the cause of a jar should be the support of a cloth. Therefore, nothing is the substratum of anything.

{The refutation of that} This [position] is also untenable. As for the claim that "that which is non-existent has no substratum"—on this point there is no dispute. However, the claim that "even that which is existent has none" is not acceptable, because it is observed. For a substratum of that which is existent is indeed observed, whether as an inherent (*samavāyin*) or a conjoined (*saṃyogin*) one. In that regard, for qualities such as color (*rūpa*), a jar (*ghaṭa*) is the inherent substratum; for substances such as water, however, it is the conjoined substratum. And what is observed cannot be rejected even by a hundred logical alternatives (*vikalpa*).
{The relation of container and contained is untenable based on a mere collection of parts}.

If it is argued that the cognition of the relation between locus (*ādhāra*) and located (*ādheya*) occurs through mere conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), we say no; for such a construction is untenable whether based on what is perceived or what is unperceived. If it were a construction of something seen elsewhere upon something else—like the construction of a person upon a post—then the relation of locus and located would not be absolutely non-existent. If, on the other hand, it is argued that the construction arises from the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of words such as "primordial matter" (*pradhāna*) and so forth, that too is incorrect; for how could a purposeless construction occur only with respect to specific objects? If it is argued that the awakened latent impression produces the construction because of the perception of a specific object, then what is this "specificity" of the object? It must be that very relation of locus and located, whose absence prevents the cognition of being a locus or located from occurring even when the object is seen elsewhere. If it is argued that the locus is simply the cause of its arising—namely, that for things which perish moment by moment and arise in successive locations, their arising in the location of the material cause (*upādāna*) is produced by contact with a locus—and therefore the earth and so forth are called the "locus" of water and so forth because they bring about a specific state, and thus the locus is merely a specific cause—we say no, because momentariness is unproven. This [argument] might hold if momentariness were established, but we shall demonstrate later that it is unproven.
The determination of the relationship between locus and located (ādhārādheya-vyavasthā) occurs only in the theory of non-momentariness (*akṣaṇika-vāda*).

However, once non-momentariness is established and a distinction between property and property-possessor (*dharma-dharmin*) is admitted, one must necessarily accept the existence of the locus-located relationship for earth, water, and so forth; for there is no lack of validity in that cognition, as it is like the cognition of a blue crystal and the like.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "nothing whatsoever is produced by a substratum (āśraya) for that which already exists," that is incorrect. For it is not accepted that the cause itself is the substratum, such that if it were non-productive, it could not be a substratum. What then? It is through connection with the properties of the substratum; that is, through connection with properties such as priority and posteriority belonging to the substratum, like [the notions of] "prior" and "posterior. [That in which something else abides is its support (ādhāra).]

The cognition "this is here" is non-contradictory, and it is not tenable without the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*). Or rather, that by which the stability of something is maintained is its locus. Stability is the capacity to produce multiple effects in succession; and it has been stated that this [stability] occurs for wholes, qualities, motions, and so forth, through the power of their substratum. Now, is it not well known that stability is the cessation of motion? True; we too have explained it in this way, for when there is no locus, the very destruction of impermanent things is what constitutes "motion," and so forth.

If it is argued that if the substratum (*ādhāra*) were the cause of persistence (*sthiti*), then because sound, cognition, and so forth would have a permanent substratum, they would never cease to exist, we say: no; for the substratum becomes the cause of persistence only when accompanied by the absence of any cause for their destruction. However, due to the connection with a cause of destruction, there is no persistence even though the substratum exists. (This concludes the resolution of the problem of infinite persistence.)

As for what was said—that if stability were distinct [from the entity], then there would be another stability for that stability, resulting in an infinite regress—that too is incorrect; because, like luminosity (*prakāśa*) or existence (*sattā*), its very nature does not depend upon another nature of its own. For just as jars and the like are illuminated by a lamp, a lamp is not illuminated by another lamp. Or, just as among substances and so forth there arises the cognition "existent" (*sat*) due to existence (*sattā*), it is not so that within existence itself there is a cognition based on another existence.

Furthermore, as for the claim that the cause of stability (*sthitihetu*) cannot be the support (*ādhāra*) of another thing that possesses stability, we say no; because stability is an attribute (*dharma*) of that [thing]. For stability is indeed an attribute of the sustainer (*sthātṛ*); therefore, the cause of that [stability] is the support of the sustainer. However, a jar is not an attribute of a cloth. [Thus, it is not accepted that everything can be a support.]

In that case, it follows that sound and other such causes must be the substrata (*ādhāra*) of space and so forth, because sound and the rest are properties of space; [we reply: no, for this is not admitted. We do not say that whatever is a cause is necessarily the substratum of its property-possessor (*dharmin*); rather, that which is the specific cause for the persistence of something is its substratum. Well then, what is the specific cause for the persistence of the self, space, and so forth? None at all; for this very reason they lack a substratum—indeed, no substratum is possible for the self, space, etc., whether as a conjunct (*saṃyogin*) or an inherent (*samavāyin*). Or, if the term "substratum" is used merely for a cooperative cause (*sahakārin*), then according to your own position, it is not just any cause that is the material cause (*upādāna*) or the substratum, but rather a specific cause—as, for example, milk alone is the material cause of curd, and a bowl alone is its substratum. Similarly, for us, the substratum is a specific cause or a specific cooperative cause, and that is either a conjunct or an inherent one. For a thing is to be understood as a substratum only when it is related as a cause or a connector in the manner in which the usage of "substratum" is observed, but not in the case of unseen things like God and the like.
The doubt regarding the non-existence of persistence prior to origination, and its refutation.

Now, if the stability of an entity is produced by its substratum only afterwards, then prior to that stability, the entity would be non-existent; and how could stability, which has arisen as something distinct, belong to the entity? For there is no relation between them, such as identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). To this it is replied: if an entity possesses a stability characterized by immobility, or characterized by the successive acquisition of multiple auxiliary causes, let it be "non-existent" in relation to that [stability]; what is the fault in this? However, we do not accept the claim that stability—defined as actual existence—is produced only afterwards, because its existence is brought about precisely by the causes that produce it. Even in the absence of the relations of identity or causality, how can it be said that "this is the stability of the entity"? This too is incorrect, because the restriction to these two types of relations lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), and because the relation of identity has already been refuted. Therefore, just as in the case of universals (*sāmānya*) and so forth, stability also possesses some kind of relation.
Even in this position—that the substratum is the cause of persistence—there is no fault whatsoever;
[for instance,] the status of being the substratum of desire and so forth does not belong to the body and such.

Furthermore, it has been established that form and the other [sensory qualities] reside in a substance (*dravya*); likewise, desire and the rest must also have some substratum which, having experienced [an object] itself, remembers it; having remembered it, synthesizes [the experience]; having synthesized it, desires or hates it; and subsequently, exerting effort, experiences pleasure or pain. Moreover, how could that which engages in activity for the sake of the next world and which experiences the ripening of its own performed karma be unstable or characterized by such things as the body?

By this very [argument], momentariness is refuted—for if everything were momentary, it would be impossible to establish such things as the fact that memory is of precisely what was previously experienced by oneself. [Thus, non-momentariness is established through recognition.]

Furthermore, non-momentariness (*akṣaṇikatva*) is apprehended in crystals and other such objects by means of perception known as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). For, immediately following the operation of the senses, there arises a cognition grasping an object delimited by both prior and subsequent times, in the form "this very same crystal. Likewise, there occurs recognition that grasps the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) as delimited by multiple points in time, as follows: "I myself, who saw its sprout, now see its fruit."

If it is argued that [recognition] is erroneous, like the perception of a lamp-flame and so forth, we say no; for in this case there is no sublation (*bādhaka*). Furthermore, once error has been established as being due to sublation in one instance, it is not logical to assume error everywhere on the mere basis of a similarity with recognition, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). For example, since the cognition of water or [floating] hairs is seen to be erroneous in one case, it would follow that it is erroneous in all cases. Therefore, it is only that specific recognition which is sublated that can rightly be considered erroneous—just like the cognition of hairs and so forth—not every instance of recognition. {The Buddhists' Doctrine of Momentariness}
But is it not the case that every act of recognition is indeed erroneous, because it manifests a non-momentary form? And yet, there is no such thing as a non-momentary object. To this he says:
"Only that which performs a causal function is ultimately real here;
non-momentary things are unreal, because they are contradicted by [the impossibility of] successive or simultaneous [action]. (PV 3.3ab; PVin 2.55)

For instance: first of all, a manifold entity does not produce effects sequentially, because it possesses a single nature (*ekasvabhāvatvāt*). For that which has a single nature must produce, all at once, as many effects as it is capable of producing, since there can be no delay for that which is capable. If there were such a delay, even the production of the first effect would not occur. If it is argued that at the time of producing the first effect, it lacks the capacity to produce future effects, then in that case, those future effects could never arise from it, because it does not abandon its inherently incapable nature. If it were to abandon that nature, then there would be no identity between the cause of the prior and subsequent actions; and if there is such a difference, momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*) is established. Nor does it produce [effects] simultaneously, because its nature of bringing them about would never cease. Consequently, it would either produce causal efficiency continuously and simultaneously, or—if that nature were to cease—the aforementioned momentariness would follow. Furthermore, a single entity does not produce an effect sequentially by depending on a succession of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), because it is illogical to depend on that which provides no assistance. As it has been said:
If there were any effect whatsoever, then another [cause] would be required;
or if there were anything that performed an action, why would it require anything else? (PV 3.579) [For neither a distinct nor a non-distinct benefit is possible.]

And there is no assistance [rendered], because assistance that is either distinct or non-distinct is impossible. If the assistance is produced by the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*) as something non-distinct from the cause, then it follows that the cause itself is being produced; and thus the auxiliaries would be useless, since that nature [of the cause] was already established previously. If, on the other hand, the assistance is distinct, what is the relationship such that "this belongs to that"? In the case of identity (*tādātmya*), there is no distinction. Even in the case of origination from it (*tadutpatti*), if its production were independent of the auxiliaries, then why would the auxiliaries not be useless? If, however, it depends upon them, then another assistance must be postulated from that [cause] toward them, and as before, the dilemma of the distinct and non-distinct alternatives would follow, resulting in an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Therefore, dependence upon auxiliaries is not logical.
The impossibility of the conceptual distinction between the capable and the incapable.

Furthermore, because the conceptual alternatives of being capable or incapable are untenable: if the cause is capable, then it produces the effect by virtue of its own capability alone, and nothing is contributed by the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*). If it is incapable, it does not produce the effect even when auxiliary factors are present, just as a stone [cannot produce] oil. If you argue that it becomes capable when the auxiliaries are present, then it follows that the nature of incapacity has ceased and a capable form has arisen through the auxiliaries; and if that is so, it is impermanent. Thus, a cause that arises sequentially is what produces the effect sequentially, like a seed and so forth; there is no single, non-sequential entity whatsoever that can produce effects sequentially.
The application of inference regarding momentariness.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: that which is non-momentary does not exist, like a rabbit’s horn and the like. And all things exist; therefore, they are momentary. To establish the exclusion of existence from the non-momentary, the subverting reason (*bādhaka*) was stated: "because causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is impossible through either succession or simultaneity. Indeed, capacity (*śakti*) is the defining characteristic of an entity (*bhāva*), while the absence of all capacity is the defining characteristic of a non-entity (*abhāva*). This existence, characterized by capacity, is pervaded by the production of effects either successively or simultaneously. Therefore, the production [of effects] in such a manner, being excluded from non-momentary things, excludes existence—which is its own pervader—along with it. Consequently, there is no non-momentariness for that which exists.
Refutation of the Doctrine of Momentariness (Kṣaṇikavāda-nirāsa)

To this, we reply: If you intend to establish the non-existence of non-momentary things, then what is the subject (*dharmin*) here? If that very thing is the subject, it is illogical to prove its own non-existence. For when the subject does not exist, the reason lacks the property of being a predicate of the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), and without the property of being a predicate of the subject, there is no power of proof (*gamakatva*). Therefore, the thesis "non-momentary things do not exist" is stated. Alternatively, if the meaning of the thesis is that "existent things are not non-momentary," even so, how can the reason "because of the contradiction between succession and simultaneity" possess the property of being a predicate of the subject? If you argue that existence itself is the reason, which, by proving momentariness, proves the absence of non-momentariness—then still, since there is neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), how can it be a valid reason? It would be an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason, as it applies equally to the opposing position. If you say that positive concomitance exists in cases such as a lamp, we say no; because it is unestablished. For the momentariness of even a lamp is not established; as we shall explain later, a thing that has arisen awaits a cause for its destruction. If you say its power of proof lies solely in the force of negative concomitance, we say no; because there is also an absence of a counter-example based on dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). If you say that a rabbit's horn and the like serve as the example, we say no; because they are not objects of cognition. For that which cannot be presented even in its own form cannot be understood as being devoid of the properties of the probandum and the probans, and it is not logical for something that is not cognized to function as an example. If you say that its cognition certainly occurs through verbal testimony (*śabda*), is that [testimony] a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or not? If it is a valid means of knowledge, we say no; because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) based on identity (*tādātmya*) or causality (*tadutpatti*). For if there were such a connection, it would follow that it is a real entity (*vastu*), and thus a non-momentary entity would exist. If you accept its status as a valid means of knowledge despite the absence of a connection, then there is a contradiction with the principle that "there is no proof in the absence of an invariable concomitance" (*nāntarīyakatābhāvāt*), and so forth.

If, on the other hand, it is not a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇa*), then how can an unobserved example be established? Since that which is not cognized by a means of valid cognition could also exist in a counter-example (*pratidṛṣṭānta*), there is no establishment of even a negative example (*vyatirekadṛṣṭānta*). [Objection: This might be the case—the establishment of positive and negative concomitance occurs within the subject (*pakṣa*) itself through the power of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*). For instance, it has been stated that for a momentary entity, causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is contradictory with both succession and simultaneity. Therefore, existence, characterized by causal efficiency, is excluded from the non-momentary; and because there is no contradiction with causal efficiency in the momentary, it is concomitant with it.
{The refutation thereof}

That is incorrect, because contradiction cannot be apprehended unless that which is contradictory is itself apprehended. For there is no apprehension of the contradiction between fire and snow if one of the two is not apprehended. And if the non-momentary is apprehended as being contradictory to succession and simultaneity, then how can it be non-existent? For it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in the form of being an object of cognition. And if it does not perform such an action, how could it be cognized? For you do not accept that something which produces no other effect can be an object of cognition. Alternatively, if the non-momentary is not cognized at all, then how is its contradiction with succession and simultaneity understood? For contradiction does not exist by virtue of their own intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*); for if there were contradiction by way of intrinsic nature, it would follow that everything would perish.
There is no contradiction even with the conventional [truth] that is non-momentary.

If it is argued that the proof of contradiction is established by means of a non-momentary entity that is established conventionally (*saṃvṛtti*), then that which is conventionally established must be either real or conceptual. If it is real, how can it be non-existent? Or how could there be a contradiction with causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*)? For that which performs causal efficiency is called "real. If, on the other hand, it is conceptual, then is the contradiction with it real or conceptual? It cannot be real, because it would be a contradiction of a conceptual contradictory, like the contradiction of the son of a barren woman. If the contradiction itself is merely conceptual, then there is no ultimate contradiction between a non-momentary entity and causal efficiency—whether by way of succession or simultaneity. Consequently, even the establishment of the exclusion of existence from the non-momentary is not ultimately real; since existence is unreal in its exclusion, momentariness—which depends upon it—is likewise unreal. Thus, this addiction to the doctrine of momentary flux, which involves so much effort to plug a leak, has been destroyed in a single blow as if it were impossible.
The proof of the non-existence of successive things by means of non-succession, and its refutation.

It might be argued: "Since we observe a sequence of effects, such as sprouts, following a sequence of causes, such as seeds, the existence of successive things through succession is established; thus, even the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is proven. If this is your claim, how is this observation made? Is this sequence of effects from a cause that is itself successive, or is the observation made without any such determination? If the observation is that this sequence of effects arises only from a successive cause, how can that be when there is no ascertainment of the non-existence of non-momentary things? For an observation of the form "this alone [is the cause]" cannot be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) unless there is an ascertainment of the non-existence of other possibilities. Furthermore, non-existence is determined only through non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) of something that is perceptible. And if a non-momentary thing were perceptible, it would possess the capacity to be perceived in some instance.

Now, if the perception [of the effect] occurs precisely through non-determination—that the sequence of the effect follows from the sequence of the cause—then how can there be the certainty that "the sequential does not arise from the non-sequential"? For it is not possible, merely because one observes the birth of a son and so forth from a father and so forth, to conclude with certainty that such birth does not arise from karma and the like. [The doubt regarding the establishment of negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) by implication, and its refutation:]If it is argued that the certainty of negative concomitance is established by implication (*arthāt*), [we reply: No, for the same doubt would persist. That is, even if one perceives the absence of the effect when the cause is absent, the doubt remains: "Does this [absence of the effect] occur because the cause is absent, or because other causes are present? Therefore, just as in the case of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), the certainty of negative concomitance is also impossible without the observation of the causal capacity (*śakti*). Furthermore, since the causal capacity is not perceived, the certainty of negative concomitance is not established even by implication. Thus, the certainty of negative concomitance is not established even by implication. Consequently, the certainty of both positive and negative concomitance is impossible. Therefore, the certainty of the causal relationship is not established. Hence, the claim that "the cognition of the causal relationship is based on the observation of positive and negative concomitance" is untenable. (TS 1397–1400) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of inference (*anumāna*), then the following must be stated: Is that [inference] based on the observation of positive concomitance, or is it based on the observation of negative concomitance? First, it cannot be based on the observation of positive concomitance, because the causal relationship has not yet been established. Nor can it be based on the observation of negative concomitance, because negative concomitance is not established without the prior establishment of the causal relationship. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of inference, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). That is, that [inference] too would require another inference to establish the causal relationship, and that too would require another, and so on ad infinitum. Therefore, the claim that "the cognition of the causal relationship is based on inference" is also untenable. (TS 1401–1402) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of verbal testimony (*āgama*), then the following must be stated: Is that [verbal testimony] based on perception (*pratyakṣa*), or is it based on inference? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on inference, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of verbal testimony, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of verbal testimony" is also untenable. (TS 1403–1405) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of comparison (*upamāna*), then the following must be stated: Is that [comparison] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of comparison, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of comparison" is also untenable. (TS 1406–1408) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of presumption (*arthāpatti*), then the following must be stated: Is that [presumption] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of presumption, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of presumption" is also untenable. (TS 1409–1411) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of negation (*abhāva*), then the following must be stated: Is that [negation] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of negation, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of negation" is also untenable. (TS 1412–1414) Therefore, the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, the claim that "the cognition of the causal relationship is based on the observation of positive and negative concomitance" is untenable. (TS 1415) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of the nature of things (*svabhāva*), then the following must be stated: Is that [nature of things] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of the nature of things, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of the nature of things" is also untenable. (TS 1416–1418) Therefore, the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition. Consequently, the claim that "the cognition of the causal relationship is based on the observation of positive and negative concomitance" is untenable. (TS 1419) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of the exclusion of others (*anyāpoha*), then the following must be stated: Is that [exclusion of others] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of the exclusion of others, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of the exclusion of others" is also untenable. (TS 1420–1422) Therefore, the causal relationship is not established by any means of valid cognition. Consequently, the claim that "the cognition of the causal relationship is based on the observation of positive and negative concomitance" is untenable. (TS 1423) Alternatively, if the causal relationship is established by means of the non-apprehension of the apprehensible (*upalabdhy-anupalambha*), then the following must be stated: Is that [non-apprehension] based on perception, or is it based on verbal testimony? First, it cannot be based on perception, because the causal relationship is not an object of perception. Nor can it be based on verbal testimony, because the fault of infinite regress has already been stated. Furthermore, if the causal relationship were established by means of the non-apprehension of the apprehensible, there would be no distinction between the Vedic scriptures and other worldly treatises. That is, just as worldly treatises are not authoritative because they are composed by humans, the Vedic scriptures would likewise not be authoritative because they are composed by humans. Therefore, the claim that "the causal relationship is established by means of the non-apprehension of the apprehensible" is also untenable. (TS 1424–1426) Therefore, the causal

It might be argued: "Just as from the observation that smoke arises from fire, one gains the certainty that smoke does not arise from what is not fire, so too from the observation that sequential things arise from a sequence, one gains the certainty that sequential things do not arise from a non-sequence. This comparison is flawed. For in that case, even when other conditions are present, smoke is not perceived in the absence of fire, whereas it is perceived when fire is present; thus, since positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are established, the causal necessity is proven. However, in this case, even when the sequences are present, there is no observation that sequential things do not arise because of the absence of the sequence, by which the establishment of negative concomitance would occur.
Non-sequentiality is not non-existent.

Furthermore, since that which is perceived possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) characterized by perception, it is not non-existent; and it is logical to accept the nature of cause and effect as they are observed, rather than the undesirable consequence of everything being indistinguishable. For instance, although wood and other materials do not differ in their status as causes of smoke, they do not possess the nature of fire; and although ashes, sparks, and so forth do not differ in being produced by burning, they do not possess the nature of smoke. Therefore, although seeds and the like do not differ in their capacity to produce sprouts and so on, only the seeds and such are sequential, whereas God, rice, and the like are not. Likewise, although there is no difference in their arising sequentially, sprouts and the like do not arise from a single seed alone, whereas certain cognitions and so forth do arise [from it]. Similarly, a seed performs its various functions even sequentially because it is a cause, just like a wheel and other such things. In this way, the sequential agency of each individual entity, such as a sprout, must be established just like a wheel and so forth. Just as jars and other objects arise only sequentially from a single wheel, or the felling of trees from an axe, so too is anything else—such as a gem with a distinct nature—observed to perform its effects sequentially. If it is argued that these are not valid examples because they are equivalent to the point to be proven (*sādhyasama*), we reply: it is impossible for what is established by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) to be equivalent to the point to be proven. Otherwise, no example would ever be established, as the objection that "everything is equivalent to the point to be proven" would remain unrefuted everywhere.
The doubt that momentariness alone is what is apprehended by direct perception because of its being present.

But is it not the case that perception grasps only the present and does not determine its extension across prior and subsequent times, because such [extension] does not appear? For in perceptual cognition, an object does not appear as having a form that persists through prior and subsequent times; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of such an appearance even for one who sees something for the first time. Therefore, non-momentariness is not graspable by perception; rather, it is momentariness alone that is grasped even by perception. For an object that is unmixed with other moments is called "momentary," and that indeed appears in such a way. {Refutation thereof}

That too is incorrect; for if things appear for only a single moment, even the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) would not be possible, let alone the establishment of the production of successive effects from a successive cause. To explain: would the cognition of the causal relation belong to two objects, or to an object and its cognition, or rather to two cognitions?
[In the Buddhist system, the cognition of the causal relation between two objects is refuted.]

It cannot first be between two objects, because at the time of the cause the effect is not perceived, and at the time of the effect the cause is not perceived. Nor is the status of being an effect or a cause established for a single entity alone, since their nature is determined through the perception of their mutual relationship.

If it is argued that the very nature of a thing constitutes both its being an effect and its being a cause, even so, upon the apprehension of a single nature, how could there be the cognition that "this is the effect of that" or "this is the cause of that"? Furthermore, if they are not apprehended as being mutually related, there would be no inference of the cause from the effect, nor inference of the effect from the cause. Consequently, for those seeking to attain what is desired or avoid what is undesired, engagement in the means to achieve those ends and withdrawal from them would not occur; thus, even the treatises (śāstra) would fail to serve the purpose of human life (apuruṣārtha). {Nor can the causal relationship between two things be grasped through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka)}.

If it is argued that the determination of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established because [the effect] exists when that [cause] exists and does not exist when that [cause] is absent, we say no. For one who perceives only a single moment is unable to apprehend that "it exists when that exists. If it is argued that both are perceived sequentially, in whose sequence would there be perception? Indeed, no single entity persists through two moments such that there could be a sequential perception of it. Furthermore, even if two things arise sequentially, there can be no grasping of their relationship because they do not perceive each other's essential nature (*svarūpa*).
