If it is argued that the relationship is understood through conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), then what kind of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is this conceptual construction? For you have no valid cognition other than direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and inference (*anumāna*). Nor is this conceptual construction an inference, because it lacks the prerequisite of a three-featured logical mark (*trirūpaliṅga*). Nor is it direct perception, because it lacks the quality of being free from conceptual construction (*kalpanāpoḍha*). Furthermore, it cannot be a synthesizer of what was grasped by direct perception, since grasping occurs through direct perception and this [conceptual construction] is incapable of such grasping.

Furthermore, if causality were established merely by the presence of the effect when the cause is present, then since smoke and the like are observed to exist even when there is a donkey or similar animal, it would follow that the donkey and such are also causes of that smoke. If you argue that this consequence does not arise because the smoke exists even in the absence of that [donkey], this is not so; for how could a momentary instance of smoke, which occurs when that [cause] is present, also occur in its absence? It is impossible for what has already arisen to arise again. Indeed, other moments of smoke can occur even in the absence of a donkey; therefore, the donkey is not the cause of those [moments].
[Thus, the relation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is impossible even within a continuum.]

Now, if it is claimed that the causal relationship between the continuum (*santāna*) and its effects is established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), we say no; for the continuum is impossible apart from the moments (*kṣaṇa*). Or, if it does exist [apart from them], then the causal relationship belongs to that [continuum] alone. Furthermore, since the efficacy of the moments cannot be determined, they would follow as being non-existent, because a real entity (*vastu*) is defined by its capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*).

And since the continuum (*santāna*) is non-momentary, the causal capacity would have to be attributed to that which is non-momentary. If it is argued that the continuum itself is indeed momentary, we say no; for its capacity remains unestablished because neither positive concomitance (*anvaya*) nor negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) can be established for it. Indeed, positive concomitance is impossible for things that persist for only a single moment; and in the absence of that, negative concomitance is likewise unestablished, for you yourself have admitted that "what lacks positive concomitance lacks negative concomitance."

If it is argued that even there the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) is with respect to a continuum (*saṃtāna*), then indeed, in that case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), because that continuum, being itself momentary, would likewise depend upon another continuum.

Now, if it is argued that there is a positive concomitance (*anvaya*) when fire exists smoke exists in general, and a negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) when that [fire] is absent smoke does not exist—this is not so, because even here there is a lack of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). First of all, the positive concomitance is not grasped by perception (*pratyakṣa*), for perception grasps only the individual nature (*svarūpa*) of two things sequentially; it is not a cognizer of the relationship between producer and produced. For the cognition of this relationship does not occur through the mere cognition of fire, since otherwise it would follow that one could determine the status of smoke as being produced by fire simply by seeing fire, even without having observed positive and negative concomitance. Nor does the cognition of this relationship occur through the mere cognition of smoke, since otherwise it would follow that one could determine a thing as being produced by fire simply by seeing smoke, even without having observed positive and negative concomitance.

[Objection: "But surely, immediately after the perception of fire, the existence of smoke is perceived; therefore, fire is the cause and smoke is the effect. [Reply: No, for the same [objection] applies here as well. This immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is not grasped by the cognition of fire, nor by the cognition of smoke. For one cognition of an object cannot, by its own nature, grasp an immediate succession that has not been seen by another [cognition].
{The Refutation of the Various Ways of Expressing the Grasping of the Causal Relation}

Furthermore, how is the existence of the effect grasped from the existence of the cause? Does it arise from that alone? Or does it necessarily arise from that? Or does it arise from that as well as from something else? We see no other alternative here. In this regard, if it arises from that alone, then by implication it is understood that it does not arise from anything else. Even there, there are two alternatives: does it arise at this time, or at another time? If the view is that it arises from that alone at this time, then it would follow that at another time it does not arise from anything else. [Alternatively,] if the view is that even at another time it arises from that alone—this is not within the scope of perception. For even at this time, how can there be the cognition that "it arises from something else in another place"? Moreover, such a thing is not so, because there would be a lack of necessity in the causal relationship.

Nor is there a restriction that it arises from this alone, for it may not arise at all—either in another place, at another time, or occasionally; therefore, the understanding of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) does not proceed from perception.

If, on the other hand, the position is taken that it also arises from this, then by implication one understands the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) oneself—that it might also arise from something else—and thus there is no causal relationship, because positive and negative concomitance are unestablished.
[The impossibility of cognizing negative concomitance through non-perception.]

Now, if it is argued that this [non-existence] is understood through non-perception (*anupalambha*) in the sense that "it does not exist when this is absent," what is this non-perception? Is it perception (*pratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*)? It cannot be perception, because its object is a thing that is not connected with another moment; and how by that [perception] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) are not grasped has already been explained. Nor is inference itself non-perception. Why? Because inference is preceded by the grasping of positive and negative concomitance. If the grasping of positive and negative concomitance were by that very [inference], there would be the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*). If, on the other hand, it were by another non-perception, then for that too the grasping of positive and negative concomitance would require yet another non-perception, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).
The causal relation is not apprehended through perception and non-perception.

By this, the claim that the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is established through perception and non-perception (*pratyakṣānupalambha*) is also refuted. To explain: if by the term "perception and non-perception" only positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) are meant, then they cannot be establishing factors if they remain ungrasped; and it has already been stated how such grasping is impossible, whether by perception or by inference. If, on the other hand, it is claimed that it is perception itself—specifically that which grasps affirmation and negation—which is so described, that too is incorrect. It has been stated that neither the presence [of the effect] when the cause is present, nor the absence [of the effect] when the cause is absent, is grasped by perception. The causal relation must be understood through non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*); otherwise, there could be no inference of a cause from an effect. Perception, however, does not even operate across another moment, much less across the infinite varieties of space and time.

Nor can the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of affirmation and negation that arise subsequent to perception—denoted by the terms "perception" and "non-perception"—be considered [the means of knowing the causal relation], because they are not valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*). For you do not accept any conceptual construction other than inference as being a valid cognition. Nor can they be designated as valid cognitions on the grounds of arising subsequent to a valid cognition, because the perception that serves as their cause has already been refuted as being capable of grasping the relationship between cause and effect. Furthermore, neither perception nor the reason called "non-perception" can be denoted by the terms "perception" and "non-perception," because perception and inference cannot operate upon the same object simultaneously. There is no entry for even the inference called "non-perception" without the prior apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*); yet, if that very apprehension of concomitance were established by that [inference] itself, the fault of circular reasoning (*itaretarāśraya*) and so forth has already been stated. Therefore, the comprehension of the causal relation between two objects is not possible.
{The Refutation of the Causal Relationship between the Object and its Cognition}

Nor is a causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) apprehended between the object and its cognition, because they are identical. For there is no distinction here by which a causal relationship could not be established between two objects, yet could be established between a cognition and an object. Furthermore, that object which appears is intended to be merely a form (*ākāra*) of the cognition; and a producer-produced relationship cannot exist with respect to a form that is part of one's own nature, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. Moreover, an object distinct from that [cognition] is never perceived, since two forms of the object—one conjoined with cognition and one unconjoined—do not appear. Since the relationship is not grasped through perception, inference (*anumāna*) also does not operate. Nor can the causality of the object be established by the observation of the object's form, because the object's form is observed even in erroneous cognition.
The refutation of the claim that the cognition arises from an object possessing a form that corresponds [to it].

If it is argued that only a corresponding form arises from the object, how is this invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) established? Furthermore, is "correspondence" (*saṃvāda*) the performance of a purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), or the attainment of the object? Is either of these non-different from the cognition, or different? If they were different, there would be another undesirable consequence in the proof. If, however, they are non-different, there too there are two possibilities: is it that very same cognition, or something else? If the correspondence is that very same cognition arising again, then it would apply even to erroneous cognition, for erroneous cognition also certainly arises again and again; indeed, it is not the case that there is only one single instance of erroneous cognition.

{Refutation of Corroboration in the Buddhist System} Furthermore, there is the cognition of touch and so forth; that too is non-existent [as corroboration]. For there can be no corroboration of the cognition of one object by a cognition of a different object, because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). By what distinction, moreover, is corroboration said to exist between the cognition of the eye and so forth and the cognition of touch and so forth? Indeed, unlike the Naiyāyikas, you do not accept the apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching, nor do you accept that cognitions occurring at prior and subsequent times have a single object. Therefore, how could there be corroboration of a prior cognition upon the arising of another cognition?
{Satisfaction and doubt, and their refutation}

If it is argued that this is due to "satisfaction" (*paritoṣa*), such as follows: even when visual consciousness has arisen regarding an object such as water, there is no confidence (*anāśvāsa*) until there occurs a cognition of touch and so forth. When the cognition of touch and so forth occurs, satisfaction arises; then, because the lack of confidence ceases, there is the practical application of validity (*prāmāṇya-vyavahāra*). This is not the case, because satisfaction is not established as being invariably concomitant (*pratibandha*) with the object of the preceding cognition. For satisfaction arising from the cognition of touch and so forth produced by perception is never observed anywhere to be invariably concomitant with the truth of the visual consciousness. Nor is it so by means of inference, because inference cannot function in the absence of an established invariable concomitance. Furthermore, validity is not established from satisfaction alone if it is not invariably concomitant, for that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Moreover, satisfaction is possible even in dreams and similar states. Furthermore—

"If cognition is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), what is the purpose of satisfaction? If cognition is the means of valid knowledge, then the establishment of the object follows from that alone; what else will satisfaction accomplish? That which is not established by cognition cannot be accomplished even by hundreds of satisfactions. For what use is satisfaction, which is distinct from cognition? If it is argued that [satisfaction] is for the sake of establishing the object, how can one thing be established by another? If it is because of a relationship (*sambandha*), by what is that relationship established? If you say "by satisfaction itself," then in that case too the establishment of the relationship must be required, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If [the relationship] is established by cognition, then the object is established by that very [cognition], and satisfaction is redundant. Even in the position that the object is established through cognition, the same fault has already been stated.

By this, the non-liberation from objects is also refuted: if that [non-liberation] were a distinct entity from consciousness, then, like one who is satisfied [with a mere appearance], it would not establish the object. If it were not a distinct entity, then because it would be the cognition of its own form alone, like an erroneous cognition, it would not establish the object; thus it has been said. By this, memory, desire, aversion, and so forth are also refuted. Therefore, even the causal relationship between cognition and the object is not established. {The refutation of the causal relationship between two cognitions}

Nor [can the causal relation be established] because both cognitions consist merely in self-awareness (*svātmasaṃvinmātra*); for in your own system, one cognition does not know another cognition. Furthermore, there is no awareness of the effect at the time of the cause, precisely because the effect has not yet arisen; nor is there awareness of the cause at the time of the effect, precisely because the cause has already perished. And it has been stated that the apprehension of the relation of cause and effect does not occur through the awareness of a single form alone. As for satisfaction, liberation from fear, memory, and so forth, their refutation here should be understood by the very same logic previously stated; consequently, even the comprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is impossible, and thus the causal relation between two cognitions cannot be determined even through inference. Therefore, for those who maintain that only a single present moment is perceived, the causal relation is not apprehended in any way whatsoever; and since it is not apprehended, existence defined as causal efficiency (*arthakriyālakṣaṇa*) lacks proof and thus cannot serve as a valid reason (*sādhana*).

Likewise, the claim that the production of an effect is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity is also unestablished. [Objection regarding the possibility of causal relation through conventional reality: But even if, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no apprehension of a causal relation, it certainly exists conventionally (*saṃvṛtti*); and it is on that basis alone that inference proceeds. For from the perspective of ultimate truth, only emptiness remains; therein, the operation of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—which is the cause of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—does not exist. Therefore, the apprehension of the causal relation occurs only through conventional reality.

What, then, is this conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*)? Conventional reality is merely the conceit of cognition by means of another instrument of knowledge; the meaning is that conventional reality is simply the conviction regarding an object arising from the latencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless linguistic usage. For the meaning of "conventional" is the meaning of being cognized without investigation. Just as in some cases, such as with Devadatta, there is a conceit of having seen him even though he has not been seen—and that [conceit] ceases upon further reflection—so too this [object] is not the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). In the same way, all worldly transactional activity is exactly like this; thus, the entire world is mere convention. To explain: there is neither perception nor inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the apprehension of the relation of cause and effect through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The suspicion that the apprehension of the causal relation [occurs] through reasoning.

Now, the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is to be understood through reasoning (*tarka*) and valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). The definition of reasoning is: "The comprehension of an object for investigation [arises] from a connection that has not been previously perceived. For instance, the absence [of smoke] when that [fire] is absent is observed; however, the causal relationship between fire and smoke is not defined merely by such a rule. Furthermore, a causal relationship is not perceived together with the presence of one thing upon the presence of another. Yet, worldly people understand: "Because this exists, therefore this arises; therefore, this is the effect of that. This cognition arises either from reasoning or from presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). If this were not the effect, its arising from that would be impossible; thus, presumptive testimony consists in the postulation of an unperceived object.

{Refutation of that}: That is incorrect. For if the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) were an object of cognition, then its cognition would have to arise either through reasoning (*tarka*) or from something else. Yet, even by one who exerts effort, this [relation] is not perceived as a distinct form apart from the entities themselves. Nor is there any cognition [of it] based on the fact that "from this, that necessarily arises," because at that time only the existence of those two [entities] is grasped; thus, that is not the causal relation.

Now, if the rule [of causality] is understood through reasoning (*tarka*) or through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), on the grounds that this [effect] is perceived immediately after that [cause], then one might think: "Therefore, at other times as well, this [effect] must arise from this [cause] alone; otherwise, this very thing would not come to be. That is incorrect. Even if it is true that it is perceived from this [cause] now, from where does the cognition [that it will be so] at other times come? If you say, "It is exactly so," then a jar is also perceived immediately after a cloth; in that case too, it would be the same. If you say, "A deviation is observed here," then by that very fact there is a lack of confidence even in that [case]. If you say, "There is no such cognition of a lack of confidence," that is due to repeated observation by those who do not see far ahead. If you say, "Worldly convention is exactly like this," then if that is so, why is it that causal relations and the like are not established through conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*)? For a cognition whose reality has not been investigated is considered to be conventional reality. And if that is so, why should worldly convention not proceed in this very way? The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is not applicable to worldly convention, because it is established merely through the differentiation of mental dispositions (*adhimukti*), like the fixed conventions of a dream. Indeed, by investigating the ultimate truth, there would be the consequence of the total collapse of worldly convention; therefore, even in the position of momentariness, the relation of cause and effect is established through conventional reality.
The refutation of the misconception regarding the establishment of the causal relationship [of things] from the perspective of conventional reality.

This [position] is also untenable. For if the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) exists only conventionally (*saṃvṛttyā*), then everything would be merely conventionally existent (*saṃvṛtisat*), and nothing at all could be established as ultimately real (*paramārthasat*), because the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) would not be established for anything from an ultimate standpoint. If you say, "We accept this very point," then why do you not likewise accept the existence of universals (*sāmānya*), wholes (*avayavin*), conjunctions (*saṃyoga*), and so forth? If you argue that these lack causal efficiency even conventionally, we say no, because the appearance of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) is equal in both cases. To explain: wherever the eye operates, there the appearance of pillars and the like does not fail to occur, just as the appearance of hair-locks and such occurs to one with ophthalmia (*taimirika*). Thus, the apprehension of the causal efficiency of pillars and the like is established. Likewise, the cognition of the universal "cow" does not arise in relation to buffaloes and the like. Furthermore, the cognition of a whole, conjunction, and so forth does not arise in relation to mere atoms devoid of conjunction; thus, the causal efficiency of universals and the rest is also established. Moreover, if conventional reality (*saṃvṛtti*) is defined as a cognition whose true nature is not investigated, and if the establishment of the causal relation is accepted on that basis alone, then you must admit that the causal relation—well-known to all worldly practitioners—is actually restricted to non-momentary things. What is the use of subtle analysis in that case? For by means of subtle scrutiny, based on the aforementioned reasoning, the causal relation itself would be utterly destroyed. Even so, since [the causal relation] remains unestablished, momentariness cannot be proven through existence, nor can the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of causal efficiency by succession and simultaneity be established. Furthermore, even according to your own view, the apprehension of the causal relation is impossible through subtle scrutiny, because you do not accept the apprehension of one thing by another unless they are related. And since a relation (*pratibandha*) resides in two terms and is not grasped by perception—which grasps only positive concomitance (*anvaya*)—inference also has no scope there. In our view, however, there is no impossibility of apprehending the causal relation, because we do not accept the restriction that perception has only a single moment as its object. Indeed, in the context of establishing the apprehension of pervasion, it was demonstrated that even the perception of ordinary people like us can sometimes operate regarding past and future objects due to specific causes such as the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*). Otherwise, the cognition of the causal relation and so forth would be impossible. If you argue that this cognition arises solely from the beginningless habituation (*abhyāsa*) to worldly practice (*vyavahāra*), we say no, because there is no proof for this either. For one who maintains that only a single, unconnected moment is perceived, the entire chain—from beginningless habituation to worldly practice, to mental impressions (*vāsanā*), and finally to false cognition—is as lacking in authority as a tradition of blind men.

Just like the cognition of the relationship between cause and effect, the cognition of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like must be accepted as valid, because there is no contradiction [in experience].

For just as the validity of the cognition "this is the effect of that" is established precisely by the absence of contradiction, so too must the validity of the cognition "these were made by him in succession," "these were made by him simultaneously," and of recognitions such as "this is that very same crystal" and "I am that very same person," be accepted, since they share the same logical status (*tulyayogakṣematva*).

Now, if it is argued that even a non-corresponding (fallacious) recognition is observed, why is the cognition of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) not also seen to be non-corresponding? If you say, "That which is non-corresponding is not actually a cognition of the causal relation at all, because it lacks validity," then the same applies here: that which is non-corresponding is not actually a recognition. Because it is a mere semblance (*tadābhāsa*), even a mistaken recognition must necessarily be admitted to have similarity as its cause; otherwise, it would occur everywhere. Furthermore, it has already been examined that similarity is impossible [for us] since we do not admit a single, persisting entity. And if such an entity were admitted, how could everything be momentary?
{The answer to the question: "Does the effect arise sequentially or simultaneously?"}

As for what was said—"Does a non-momentary entity act successively or simultaneously?"—it acts in both ways according to observation: it acts simultaneously in those effects where there is simultaneous acquisition of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), and it acts only successively in those where there is successive acquisition of auxiliary causes. If it is argued that "if it produces effects of both forms (momentary and non-momentary), the auxiliaries would be useless," we say no; for it is only through their association that the effect is produced. If the non-momentary entity were to produce the effect even without them, then they would indeed be useless. If it is asked, "What benefit do the auxiliaries provide to it, such that without them it does not act?"—[the answer is: they produce the very effect; for if they were to produce something else, they would not be auxiliaries at all. To explain: if they were to produce that [non-momentary entity] itself, then they would be its producers, not its auxiliaries. If, on the other hand, they produce something else that is not its effect, how could they still be its auxiliaries? For things are called "auxiliaries" only when they produce a single effect together with that [entity]. Indeed, even in your own position, among form, light, mental attention (*manaskāra*), and so forth, which possess the status of auxiliaries, there is no mutual benefit other than their being the cause of a single effect. Nor is there a restriction of auxiliarity as in the case of things dependent on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), because even a cognition produced by light serves as an auxiliary to the production of a specific subsequent cognition. If it is argued that "that cognition, which has light as an auxiliary, is produced by the light," we say no: is it produced by the light alone, or together with the cognition? If you say "by the light alone," how can there be the arising of a cognition without the material cause (*upādāna*) of cognition? If it did arise, then the existence of a future life (*paraloka*) would not be established. If you say "together with the cognition," then if that cognition is also produced by the light, the continuum of light must be accepted as beginningless; and in that case, there would be contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*). If, however, it is not produced [by the light], then light is not a benefactor to that cognition; how then can there be the status of an auxiliary for that which provides no benefit? There is no such thing as an auxiliary for one who confers no benefit.
The determination of capacity and incapacity.

"Let it be granted that even one who provides no assistance can be a cooperative cause (*sahakārī*). Nevertheless, if its capacity (*śakti*) existed previously, why does it not act? If it did not exist, how could it act later if it remains incapable? And if it becomes capable later, how is there no difference between the capable and the incapable states, given that the superimposition of contradictory properties is the definition of difference? This is not so. For its "capacity" is simply the completeness of its cooperative causes, and its "incapacity" is the deficiency thereof. Thus, due to the deficiency of cooperative causes, it is said to be incapable beforehand; and due to their completeness later, it is said to be capable. The distinction between property (*dharma*) and property-bearer (*dharmin*) has been established; therefore, even when capacity arises, the possessor of that capacity does not necessarily arise, and even when capacity ceases, the possessor of that capacity does not necessarily cease, because there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*). If it is asked, "How can one thing be the capacity of another distinct thing?", [we reply: How is a self the capacity of itself? If you say "because of identity" (*tādātmya*), why is it not accepted [that they are related] through non-identity (*atādātmya*)? If it is argued that this would lead to the absurdity (*prasajyeta*) that everything is the capacity of everything, we say no. Just as light, though distinct from cognition, is not a cooperative cause for everything—since it arises in such a way due to the restriction of its own causes—so too the completeness of cooperative causes arises in such a way due to the restriction of its own causes, whereby capacity belongs only to some things and not to all.

Furthermore, it is not logical for a cause to produce an effect that is a different entity (*arthāntara*), for it would follow that everything could arise from everything. If you argue that "everything does not arise from that [cause], and therefore that is not the cause of everything," then from what does this [distinction] arise—that despite the lack of distinction in their being different entities, only some things arise from it and not everything? If you say, "This is simply the nature of things (*vastusvabhāva*)," then why do you cling so stubbornly to this misconception? Is it not also simply the nature of things that, despite the lack of distinction in their being different entities, only some things have the power to produce some specific things, and not everything has the power to produce everything?
The determination of capacities is like the relationship between producer and produced.

Just as, despite the lack of distinction in being separate entities (*arthāntaratva*), the causal relationship (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is perceived through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) only between those two things that possess specific, restricted natures; so too, despite the lack of distinction in being separate entities, the relationship of power and the possessor of power (*śakti-śaktimadbhāva*) is perceived through positive and negative concomitance only between the completeness of auxiliary conditions (*sahakārisākalya*) and the cause, which possess specific, restricted natures. For example, the completeness of auxiliaries such as light belongs specifically to the power of the eye, not to the nose and other senses; yet, in the production of the cognition of its own object, that power belongs specifically to the visible form (*rūpa*), not to odor and the like. To explain: it is observed that only the visible form produces a cognition within itself when there is the completeness of the eye, light, and so forth, but not when that completeness is absent. Therefore, it is not the power alone that is the cause, since the causehood of the possessor of power is also determined through positive and negative concomitance.
The determination of capacity and incapacity based on the difference in time.

As for what was said—that there is a distinction between the potent and the impotent due to the imposition of contradictory properties—that is not so, because there is no contradiction when there is a difference in time. For example, a crystal is motionless prior to the production of an action, and that very same [crystal] is subsequently in motion. If it is argued that this is not a valid example because it is yet to be proven (*sādhyatvāt*), we say no; for that which is established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be considered "yet to be proven. For if one were to say, "Thus, the distinction based on the imposition of contradictory properties is unproven," how could such a person be refuted? Therefore, in whatever way a lack of contradiction is observed between two properties, they must be accepted in exactly that way. Just as the same cause is potent with respect to its own effect but impotent with respect to another effect—so that potency and impotence do not contradict each other for a single entity due to the difference in their objects—likewise, even if there is a difference in potency due to a difference in time, there is no distinction in either case, because the non-difference of the possessor of potency is established by valid cognition.
Even though there is a difference in capacity, there is a distinction between that which is capable and that which is incapable.

Even if it is admitted that the power (*śakti*) is distinct from the possessor of power (*śaktimat*), nevertheless, there is no necessary distinction between the potent and the non-potent. Why? Because even in your own system, the rule that a difference in attributes necessitates a difference in the substratum is not established. Thus, while demonstrating the separate utility of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) even with respect to a single effect, it has been stated: "Just as for a jar produced from a lump of clay, a potter, a string, and so forth, its difference from things that are not of the nature of clay comes from the lump of clay; its specific configuration comes from the potter; and its distinct nature [from other jars] comes from the string, and its differentiated nature from the wheel. Therefore, the nature of clay does not come from the potter, nor does the specific configuration come from the clay. Likewise, in the case of visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), the character of apprehension (*upalambhātmatā*) comes from the preceding moment of cognition; the capacity to grasp form comes from the eye; and the conformity to the object's form comes from the object. Such is the intended meaning: the separate utility of auxiliaries is to be seen everywhere in this way. And just as there is no difference in the effect despite the difference in the natures such as "clay-ness" and so forth, so too there will be non-difference despite the difference in natures such as "potency" and "non-potency," because the uncontradicted ascertainment of oneness is the same in both cases, and because any subverting argument against the difference in natures is fallacious. Now, if one does not admit a difference in nature for anything that is of a non-different essence, then the statement regarding the separate utility of auxiliaries would be the prattle of a child or a madman. Furthermore, without separate utility, the fact that a specific effect is preceded by specific causes cannot be established, as it would follow that everything existing at all times—even the entire three worlds—would be a cause. Consequently, the inference of a specific cause from a specific effect would not be possible.
The words "exclusion of others" (*atadvyāvṛtti*), "capacity" (*śakti*), "property" (*dharma*), and so forth, have a single referent.

Now, if it is argued that a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāvabheda*) is postulated based on the difference in the exclusions of others, then why should we be deceived by mere differences in verbal expression? For no object other than the referent of the word "intrinsic nature" is denoted by the words "exclusion of others," "capacity," "property," or "form," since even in your own treatise, they are observed to be used interchangeably as having a single referent.

Now, if it is argued that even the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*) is stated only through conceptual construction (*kalpanā*), then that distinction between exclusions is indeed non-existent, because its nature is merely imagined, like the form of a snake and so forth in a rope and such things. Consequently, the relationship between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*) based on the distinction between exclusions would be entirely false; therefore, the distinction between the substratum (*dharmin*) does not follow solely from the distinction between properties (*dharma*).
[Distinction of essential nature due to distinction of time.]

Furthermore, as for this which was stated—that even at the time of producing the first effect, the non-momentary entity possesses the nature of producing subsequent effects because its essence is undifferentiated, and therefore it should produce all effects at the very time of performing the first action—this is untenable due to self-contradiction, like saying "the mother is barren. For how could that which has the nature of performing subsequent effects perform that [first] effect at the outset? If it were to do so, then it would not have the nature of performing subsequent effects. Indeed, that which has the nature of producing blue does not also produce yellow and so forth. Nor does the possessor of those natures differ on account of the difference between the natures of producing the first and subsequent effects, since it has been stated that a difference in nature is subject to deviation.

Furthermore, by whatever intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) form (*rūpa*) produces another form, it does not produce taste (*rasa*) and so forth by that same nature, because it would follow that taste and the rest would also possess the intrinsic nature of form. Consequently, every effect of form would be perceived by the eye. But this is not accepted; therefore, just as form produces only that [specific form] by its nature of producing another form, and produces only cognition (*jñāna*) by its nature of producing cognition—not form and the like—and produces only taste by its nature of producing taste, and generates only those two [smell and touch] by its two natures of generating smell and touch; in the same way, even a non-momentary entity produces only the first effect by its nature of producing the first effect, and not the subsequent ones. It generates only the subsequent effect by its nature of producing the subsequent effect, and not the first or the later ones. In this manner, specific natures should be understood for each successive effect occurring over an infinite duration of time.

It is also incorrect to say that only intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) are causes, and not the possessor of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvī*), because this would entail the consequence that even form (*rūpa*) is not a cause, since it is only intrinsic natures that possess causality.
[Suspicion regarding the single intrinsic nature of form:

Now, perhaps no distinction of intrinsic nature is admitted for form; rather, there is only a single such intrinsic nature by which it produces effects that are of different forms and in different locations. Thus, a distinction of intrinsic nature is merely imagined on account of that single, non-distinct intrinsic nature producing effects with distinct intrinsic natures.
{The refutation thereof}

[Objection: But surely, even another [opponent] who, in accordance with the production of multiple effects possessing sequential natures from a non-momentary entity that has an undifferentiated nature, imagines a difference in its nature, does not deserve censure. Furthermore, causality does not consist merely in being immediately antecedent, because it would follow that everything in the three worlds, being immediately antecedent, would be a cause. Therefore, only that which is operative in the production of an effect is a cause. Consequently, even a permanent entity, because its nature is to operate sequentially, acts in succession and is thus the cause of sequentially occurring effects. And the fact that a non-momentary entity has a nature of sequential operation is understood precisely from the perception of sequentially occurring effects—just as the nature of simultaneous operation is understood from the perception of simultaneous effects.

If it is argued that even the postulation of simultaneous activity for that which is partless is not tenable, [we reply]: if the cause of form and so forth produces multiple effects simultaneously even without simultaneous activity, then for us as well, there is no purpose in postulating successive activity. Because of its very nature (*tatsvābhāvyāt*), the non-momentary entity will produce effects in succession.
[Furthermore,] the fact that the nature of capacities and so forth is imperceptible does not render them unauthoritative.

Now, if a non-momentary entity has the nature of producing effects sequentially, why does that very nature not appear [to perception]? Who says that it does not appear? If it is asked: "Even if its effects do not appear, how can its nature as the producer of those effects appear?"—we say no. This is because the effects are distinct from that [entity]; thus, when they do not appear, let there be no appearance of the thought, "This is the producer of these. For when a qualifier is not apprehended, the cognition of the qualified does not arise. However, the entity is indeed apprehended in its own form (*svarūpataḥ*). Just as in your own view, even when taste and so forth are not apprehended, the visible form (*rūpa*) which produces them is still apprehended, since it is impossible for a partless thing to be apprehended by parts. Nor are taste and so forth apprehended by the eye. Furthermore, the weight of stones and the like is not apprehended by mere sight. Yet you do not maintain that it is distinct from them, nor that it simply does not exist. Moreover, even the aspect of momentariness and so forth does not appear when visible forms and the like are being apprehended, otherwise it would follow that inference is useless.
The logical parity between momentariness and non-momentariness.

If it is argued that the aspect of momentariness and so forth is indeed apprehended, but because that apprehension is not sharp, there is no ascertainment (*niścaya*) of it—then why is it not likewise imagined that even when the aspects of permanence, omnipresence, and so forth are apprehended, there is no ascertainment due to a lack of sharpness? Furthermore, a lack of sharpness in apprehension cannot be assumed in all cases. For it is not logical to claim that even objects such as "sky-flowers" are indeed apprehended, yet are not ascertained because the apprehension of them is not sharp. However, in the case of a nature characterized by successive production, there is sometimes ascertainment; therefore, it is reasonable to imagine a lack of sharpness in the apprehension of that [momentariness] in some instances, since the apprehensions of grass and the like possess sharpness through their resulting ascertainments.

If it is argued that because its nature is to produce effects sequentially, no simultaneous production of effects ever occurs from it, we say no; for with respect to those specific effects, its nature is indeed to produce them simultaneously.
[This resolves the contradiction by means of the distinction between objects.]

If it is argued that there is a contradiction between the natures of acting successively and acting simultaneously, we say no; for there is no contradiction because their objects are distinct, just as something can have the nature of being a cause with respect to one thing and the nature of not being a cause with respect to another. For example, fire and the like have the nature of being a cause in relation to their own effects, but they have the nature of not being a cause in relation to things that are not their effects. Similarly, an eternal cause possesses such a nature that it produces the arising of some things successively and others simultaneously. If it is argued that if an eternal entity possesses such a nature by its very essence, it would follow that it does not depend on auxiliary causes (sahakārins), we say no; for its nature is precisely such that it produces specific effects only when accompanied by others, and only simultaneously. If it is asked, "From where did this nature of the eternal arise?", the answer is: from its very eternity; it arose from nothing else. Oh, what scholarship is this of one who eats at dawn—to ask for a cause of an eternal, beginningless, and causeless thing!
The proof for permanence is recognition.

If we must certainly be questioned, then ask this: what is the proof for the existence of a permanent entity? In that regard, it has been stated that the means of proof which subverts the opposing position (*vipakṣabādhaka*) is negative inference (*vyatirekyanumāna*). If it is argued that, were the permanent to be causeless, its nature would necessarily apply everywhere due to the absence of a regulating cause (*niyāmakahetu*), we say no; for its permanence consists precisely in its being beginningless (*anāditva*). Indeed, a nature that occurs only occasionally is logically restricted by a regulating cause, but not one that is beginningless. The claim that an object’s restricted nature arises solely from a regulating cause is not a statement made by a seer (*ṛṣi*); rather, if it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), that is equally the case here as well. Thus, it has been demonstrated that even for causeless things such as "cowness" (*gotva*) and "horseness" (*aśvatva*), their specific, restricted natures are apprehended even by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, if recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) were invalid, the apprehension of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) would also be impossible, because the identity of a single genus or a single continuum would remain unestablished, and it has already been stated that the apprehension of a continuity between moments is not possible. Therefore, the validity of uncontradicted recognition must be accepted, just like other perceptions and inferential cognitions. Moreover, recognition regarding crystals and the like is not contradicted, since the refutations based on succession and simultaneity have already been answered.
Just as in the case of the body and so forth, recognition in objects such as crystal is not figurative.

If it is argued that, just as in the case of the body and so forth, recognition occurs even in the case of crystals and the like due to the non-apprehension of the distinction between successive similar productions, and thus appears to be non-false—this is not so; because no causes for production and destruction are perceived. For, whereas the cause of the body’s daily production, such as food and drink, and the cause of its destruction, such as the movement of its parts, are perceived through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), no such cause for the momentary production and destruction of a crystal or the like is perceived. Furthermore, the destruction of anything cannot be accidental, because like production, destruction is also observed to arise solely from causes, as established by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).
The suspicion that entities are momentary because destruction is causeless.

But surely, the cause of destruction has already been refuted by the arguments of incapacity and futility; for instance: if this entity has arisen from its own causes with a non-perishable nature, then it is impossible to destroy it—thus, the cause of destruction is incapable [of its task]. Indeed, that which has arisen from its own causes with a non-white nature cannot be made white by another cause. If, on the other hand, something else distinct from it is produced as "destruction," then what does that have to do with the original entity even when that destruction arises? For it is not the case that the entity is destroyed by the destruction itself. Nor can it be concealed, since it has arisen with an unconcealed nature; how could it be made to have a concealed nature? Indeed, a thing of a black nature is never observed to be made white by anyone.

Now, if the nature of perishing has arisen from its own cause alone, then destruction occurs by virtue of that very nature, and thus a cause of destruction is redundant. For whatever arises from its own cause with a certain nature does not require another cause for that state, just like luminosity, heat, or hardness. Indeed, lamps and the like, which possess the nature of luminosity and so forth, do not require another cause for their luminosity once they have arisen from their own causes. Therefore, an entity is independent with respect to its destruction. If it were dependent, there would be no rule of necessity regarding its occurrence, as in the case of dyeing a cloth; consequently, some produced things, such as jars, might even be eternal. Even if there are many causes of destruction, since their presence depends upon their own conditions, their presence is not necessary; thus, it is possible that something might not perish at all. For causes do not necessarily produce their effects, because of the possibility of deficiency or obstruction. As it has been said: [The original Sanskrit verse follows here. Thus it is stated: "If a thing is produced with a perishable nature, what use is a cause of destruction? For a thing produced with a certain nature from its own cause does not depend on another cause for that state, just like luminosity, heat, or hardness. Lamps and the like, having arisen from their own causes with the nature of luminosity, do not require another cause for their luminosity. Therefore, an entity is independent with respect to destruction. If it were dependent, there would be no certainty of occurrence, as in the case of dyeing a cloth; hence, some produced things like jars might even be eternal. Even if there are many causes of destruction, since their presence depends on their own conditions, their presence is not necessary; thus, it is possible that something might not perish. For causes do not necessarily bear fruit, due to the possibility of deficiency or obstruction. Thus it is said.
"Because destruction is causeless, it follows from [the object's] own nature;
for among phenomena that depend on other conditions, necessary occurrence is not observed.
Even when its causes are abundant, non-occurrence might happen in some cases."
The refutation thereof.

To this it is replied: As for the claim that [the cause] belongs to that which has a perishable nature or that which has an imperishable nature—that is not so; for it would entail the consequence of the total abolition of causes, since such a dilemma is possible in every case. To explain: does the cause have the nature of coming into being, or rather the nature of not coming into being? If the first position is held, then it comes into being by itself, because it possesses that very nature; thus the cause is redundant. In the second position, however, it is incapable, for that which has the nature of not coming into being—such as a rabbit’s horn—cannot be produced by anything. Causes such as cutting or burning should likewise be understood as untenable due to redundancy and incapacity, respectively, under the two positions of having that nature or not having that nature. And thus, since the possibility of rejecting all causes arises in this way, even the effort for the sake of liberation, such as listening to the scriptures and so forth, would be futile.
The suspicion that the causal relationship between fire and smoke might be unestablished.

Now, the presence of smoke when there is the presence of fire, and its absence when that [fire] is absent—this causal relationship (*hetuhetumadbhāva*) between fire and smoke, established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), is recognized by everyone in the world; it cannot be refuted even by a hundred arguments. Furthermore, if an entity were causeless, its connection with specific places, times, and so forth would not be possible. If this is so, then destruction (*vināśa*) as well—which possesses specific places, times, and so forth—cannot possibly be causeless. Moreover, causes of destruction are observed through positive and negative concomitance: for example, the mallet and so forth for a jar, and fire and so forth for wood.
But has it not been stated here: "Because destruction is invariably concomitant with mere existence, sound is impermanent;
if fire were to produce something other than itself, the wood would still be visible."

The meaning of this is as follows: destruction is necessarily concomitant with mere existence (*sattāmātra*); thus, its nature is simply existence itself. Therefore, for sound or anything else, impermanence arises precisely from the cause of existence and is not without a cause. Since that which has the nature of having been produced does not depend on any other cause, destruction is said to be "causeless. Even in the case of wood, destruction is not brought about by fire; what then? When the preceding [moment] ceases through its own inherent nature (*svarasa*), another [moment] governed by fire arises. Otherwise, if fire were to produce a different entity, the wood would still be perceived. For when one entity is produced from a different entity, the thing called "wood" is not seen to disappear; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the argument.
{The refutation thereof}

That too is incorrect. For if existence (*sattā*) and destruction (*nāśa*) were identical in nature (*tādātmya*), they would be perceived at all times, since there would be no contradiction with their own nature; and if there were a contradiction, there could not even be perception in a single moment, because that which is contradictory to it would be coexistent with it by virtue of being its very nature. Now, if it is argued that there is no contradiction with its own nature, but rather that this [entity] is produced from its own causes as something lasting for only one moment and is not perceived in another moment—just as it has been said: "Existence itself, characterized by a duration of one moment, is called destruction"—then, if this is so, its non-existence after the moment follows from the designation "lasting for one moment. In that case, how can there be identity (*tādātmya*) between two things produced successively, given that unity is impossible, as in the case of a seed and a sprout? Precisely for this reason, they have different causes, since a succession is impossible for two things born from the same causal complex (*ekasāmagryāpanna*).

Now, if this entity is a "perisher" (*naṃṣṭṛ*), then it will perish by itself. For what obstacle to its perishing could there be? If it is not a perisher, then it will certainly not perish. What is the meaning of "perisher"? Does it mean that it is essentially destruction itself, or rather that it is the agent of destruction? If, first of all, it is essentially destruction itself, then there would not even be the perception of it for a single moment, because perception is impossible for that which is indistinguishable from destruction. Or, if there were perception, there would have to be perception at all times, because it would not abandon its own nature. Or, if there were abandonment [of its nature], that itself would be the arising of destruction, since the definition of destruction is the abandonment of the entity's own nature. Furthermore, the identity of that [abandonment] with the entity is untenable, because affirmation and negation are contradictory as a single thing. For it is not logical that the very same thing both exists and does not exist, or that the very same thing is both persistence and non-persistence. If, on the other hand, it is said that the "perisher" is the agent of destruction, even so there is no identity between them, because they stand in a cause-and-effect relationship, like fire and smoke. This contradicts the admission that destruction is not an effect. Moreover, because it would not be of the nature of that [destruction] nor its cause, the claim that it is "inefficacious" (*akiṃcitkara*) would also be contradictory. If it is said that the "perisher" is "perishable" (*naśvara*), what is the meaning of "perishable"? Is it the nature of destruction, or the agent of destruction? In either case, the aforementioned fault applies.
The irrationality of [the view] that perceives [things] such as light.

The analogy of light and so forth is also untenable; for instance, in our view, the oneness of a lamp and its light is not established, nor is their having a single cause. For our established doctrine is that after the substance has arisen, qualities such as light arise from a different causal complex (*sāmagrī*). In your view, however, an entity such as a lamp is essentially identical with its color-form (*rūpa*) and other qualities—this is well known—and thus it is not logical for it to be its own destroyer. For destruction is said to be non-existence (*abhāva*). And existence itself cannot be non-existence, because the difference between the two is universally recognized by all people without contradiction, and because you yourself have stated the distinction between their definitions. Furthermore, there can be no cessation of existence even at the time of its arising, for if there were, it would follow that it lacks causal efficacy (*arthakriyāsāmarthya*) prior to its activity just as it does afterward. Or, if it were not destroyed, it would follow that it must persist later just as it did before, since its continued existence (*sthiti*) has not been negated. If you argue that it subsequently lacks all causal capacity, then surely that very lack is what is universally recognized in the world as "destruction," and since that occurs later, how can it be the destruction of the entity? It has already been stated that identity is impossible between two things that occur sequentially. Moreover, even if destruction were causeless, a restriction regarding its occurrence only later would not be possible.
Even for that which is dependent, its necessary occurrence cannot be established.

As for what was said—that if destruction were dependent on a cause, there would be no rule of its necessary occurrence, just like the dyeing of a cloth—that is not so, because [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For even that which is dependent is seen to have necessary occurrence, such as death and the like. Indeed, death is defined as the cessation of the vital breaths and so forth; it does not occur by its own nature alone, since the extinction of the continuum of a lamp and the like, the production of a dissimilar moment in a jar and the like, and the setting of the risen moon and so forth—such things necessarily occur after a certain time depending on specific causes. Therefore, there is no deviation [from the rule] even when there is dependence.
Establishing the fruitfulness of causes.

Furthermore, causal inference (*kāraṇānumāna*) has been established; therefore, the claim that "causes do not necessarily possess their effects" is also untenable. Nor is time here restricted as the cause of destruction; rather, it is simply that a produced thing perishes at some time from some cause. Consequently, although there may be an occasion when the hammer or other causes that bring about the cessation of a jar are subject to obstruction or deficiency, at another time the cessation of the jar will still occur through some other means. You too must necessarily accept this; otherwise, because death would depend upon other conditions, its invariable concomitance [with birth] would not exist. And if it did not depend on other conditions, all living beings would die immediately after birth. Yet no one who is born can possibly be immortal, since we observe that all living beings have the nature of dying. Therefore, the statement beginning with "even though the cause of that [destruction] is abundant" is also untenable.
Even though existence and non-existence are similar in being effects, they are not identical.

Furthermore, as for the argument beginning with "if another entity arises from fire," that is incorrect. Since existence and non-existence are mutually contradictory and characterized by the absence of identity, how could there be the perception of a piece of wood whose essence has perished, given that its very non-perception constitutes the cognition of its absence and the realization that "it does not exist"? For one who maintains identity (*tādātmyavādin*), however, it would follow that the wood which is actually being seen is simultaneously unseen and destroyed. Even if they are equally distinct entities (*arthāntara*), why is it that only a specific thing is the destruction of a specific thing? He alone should be questioned who asserts this. For we observe that the destruction of the wood arises specifically from fire, and not from space or other things. Nor is this destruction identical to the wood itself, because that contradicts direct perception and because it arises from something else. Furthermore, it is impossible for what has already arisen to arise again.
"Identity of nature does not follow merely from the similarity of being a different entity.

Nor is it logical to reject the specific nature of a perceived thing simply because of the mere similarity of its being a different entity. For it is not tenable to say that just as a jar does not illuminate a cloth and so forth, so too a lamp [does not illuminate] because there is no difference in their being different entities. And just as fire is not the cause for other things, let it likewise not be the cause for smoke and so forth, since there is no difference in their being different entities—such is the underlying intention [of the objection]. The reply to this is: "Because the inquiry into the essential nature (*svabhāva*) is no different in both cases."

Now, it might be argued that an entity (*bhāva*) which ceases by its own inherent nature does not require a cause of destruction at all, because such a cause would lack efficacy and because [the production of] an action is precluded. First of all, a cause of destruction that lacks efficacy cannot produce that [destruction] once the entity has already been established. Nor can it do anything for the entity when producing something else. Furthermore, since it produces neither that form nor another form, it is ineffective and thus not required. Moreover, due to the preclusion of action, they consider "destruction" to be the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the entity. Consequently, it follows that this so-called "cause of destruction" must produce non-existence. In that case, if non-existence were some kind of effect possessing an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then it would simply be an entity and could not be non-existence. Therefore, to say "it produces non-existence" means "it does not produce an entity."

[Objection: "Even if a negation of its activity were made, it would still be ineffective; why then is this even considered? [Response: This too is incorrect. For instance: does the destruction of an entity exist or not? If it does not exist, there would be the perception of the entity at all times, because its own nature remains in that same state. And if it is not in that same state, how can destruction not exist, since being in a different state is precisely what destruction is? Now, if destruction exists, is it non-different from the entity? If so, then there would be the consequence that the entity would not be perceived before [destruction] just as it is not perceived after, or else it would be perceived after just as it was perceived before, because no obstacle to its perception has arisen. And if such an obstacle were to arise, how could destruction, occurring later, not depend on another cause?

Furthermore, as for the argument that "if non-existence were an effect, then it would come into being and thus would be existence itself"—that is incorrect; for even when a different designation is applied due to a different cause, it is impossible to negate the actual state of the thing itself, just as one might apply the designations "consensus" and "stability" to what is actually "disagreement" and "instability."

As for the claim that "that which does nothing is not to be taken into account," that too is incorrect: how can something be "inefficacious" when it is causing an obstruction to the capacity of an entity? Furthermore, as long as there is no obstruction to its capacity, the consequence that it must continue to act even after [the supposed destruction] is as unavoidable as before.
Thus, there is no room for doubt regarding the lack of a relationship between destruction and the entity.

Now, what is the connection between the wood and the destruction produced by fire? It cannot be the relation of locus and located (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*), for if it were, one would expect to perceive them separately, as in the case of a bowl and curds. Nor can it be "origination from that" (*tadutpatti*), because destruction does not originate from the wood itself, nor does it originate from the fire alone. If you argue that it originates from the wood in dependence upon the fire, then what need has [the wood] for that [fire], since it gains no additional excellence (*atiśaya*)? Furthermore, when an effect arises, the cause is not said to be "destroyed" while remaining in its very same state. Destruction is indeed a distinct entity (*arthāntara*). If it is asked, "Why then is the wood not seen?", [we reply: what is this contradiction between the arising of a distinct entity and the perception of the wood, such that the wood is not seen simply because it is occupied by that other entity? Even so, it follows that there must be an obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) of that wood. But this is not tenable; for an obscuration would obstruct the act of seeing, but it cannot obstruct the functional capacities (*sāmarthya*) of a substance, such as its capacity for impact and so forth.
{The refutation thereof}

This [objection] is also incorrect, namely the claim: "What connection can there be with destruction? That is not so; for we do not accept connections such as the relation of substratum and superstratum (*āśrayāśrayibhāva*) and the like. Rather, the connection between existence and non-existence—which are characterized respectively by the negated object and its negation—is precisely that. Destruction is not a form of concealment (*āvaraṇa*); for by means of concealment, the power of perception is either obstructed or displaced. But by means of destruction, no obstruction or displacement of anything is produced; rather, destruction itself is the total displacement of all the capacities of the wood. And that [destruction] is brought about by fire and other such causes.
The suspicion that destruction itself might be destroyed.

Now, if destruction (*nāśa*) is also produced, then it too would be destructible because it is something created (*kṛtakatvāt*). Consequently, wood and the like would emerge once again. If you argue that this is not so—just as Caitra does not re-emerge when his killer is slain—we say no; for the killer is merely the cause of destruction. Indeed, the killer is not the destruction of Caitra itself, since we observe the two existing simultaneously. Furthermore, let there be no re-emergence of the wood once the fire and other causes of its destruction have ceased; however, destruction is simply the non-existence (*abhāva*) of the entity. When that non-existence ceases, what other course is possible for the entity, given that a positive affirmation (*vidhi*) is possible within a double negation?
{The refutation thereof}

No; because it is unestablished—the destructibility of destruction itself is not established at all. [Objection: But how can the admission of its production be unestablished? [Reply: No; because production occurs from a mere efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*). For only that which is produced from inherent, non-inherent, and efficient causes undergoes cessation once produced. Indeed, the properties of non-existence (*abhāva*) are the opposite of the properties of existence (*bhāva*); therefore, this rule applies to existent things: only that which is produced is destroyed, and only that which is produced is subject to destruction. However, this rule does not apply to non-existence; for instance, antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) perishes even though it is unproduced, whereas subsequent non-existence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), although produced, is indestructible. Furthermore, this consequence does not hold for those who maintain that destruction has a cause, because there is no rule of necessity regarding that which has a cause; for causes are not present in every case.
Even for destruction, there is the statement of its destruction.

Now, it is certainly not certain that there are no causes for the cessation of destruction in all cases. If this were so, let there also be a cessation of destruction in some instances. It is indeed heard that the bodies of Kāṣṭhakūṭapitṛ and others, such as Ātharvaṇa and Vasiṣṭha, which had perished and been reduced to ashes, reappeared through the grace of Maheśvara; and those who had died were brought back to life. Furthermore, certain specific effects, such as the light of a lamp, are seen to come into being again after having perished. In such cases, it is not known whether, upon the removal of that destruction, those very same things arise again, or whether other things similar to them arise. Nor is there any subverting argument against either alternative.
Even when suffering has ceased through its non-existence, the liberated one does not possess the state of being a sufferer.

If it is argued that when the cessation of suffering (duḥkha-nivṛtti) ceases for one who is liberated, there would follow the consequence of suffering once again, we say: no, because of the absence of a cause. For a cause that produces an entity is what removes its non-existence; however, for the liberated person, there is no cause that produces suffering, and therefore the absence of suffering does not cease. This is just as the prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) of a rabbit’s horn does not cease, due to the absence of any cause that could produce a rabbit’s horn. If it is argued that a rabbit’s horn, etc., is an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva) and not a prior non-existence, we say: no, because two kinds of non-existence are accepted. Thus says the Sūtra: “Because of the existence of non-existence prior to production” (*prāg utpatteḥ abhāvopapatteś ca*). The word *ca* (and) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), since mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is also included within prior non-existence. As for those who maintain that non-existence is fourfold, they explain the word *ca* as having a conjunctive meaning (*samuccaya*); even in their view, the cessation of prior non-existence is not necessarily required for the liberated person, because the prior non-existence of suffering and so forth does not cease [for them]. For if that were to cease, there would be the undesirable consequence of the arising of suffering and so forth even for the liberated person. Nor is this [non-existence of suffering] an absolute non-existence, because that would entail that it possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), like Īśvara, space (*ākāśa*), and so forth. Consequently, effort toward liberation would be useless. Therefore, there is no cessation of every instance of prior non-existence or destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*); rather, only that [non-existence] ceases for which there exist causes capable of producing its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). What contradiction is there in this?

{The suspicion that even the unproduced might perish}: But if this were so, there would be no fixed rule that every produced entity perishes while the unproduced never perishes; for some unproduced thing might perish due to some cause, and some produced thing might not perish due to the absence of a cause.
{The refutation of that}.

This might be so, provided that a cause for the cessation of even an unproduced entity has ever been observed by anyone, or if a cause for the cessation of a produced entity were never observed at all. To explain: first, regarding substance (*dravya*), the destruction of its parts and the destruction of their conjunction are established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as the causes of its cessation; yet neither of these two causes is possible for space (*ākāśa*), the self (*ātman*), and so forth, because they are partless (*niravayavatva*). However, since every produced substance possesses parts, the disjunction of parts from it must necessarily occur at some time or another due to some cause, just as in the case of a jar or similar objects. In this same manner, the possibility and impossibility of causes of destruction for the categories of produced and unproduced qualities (*guṇa*) and so forth must likewise be established through valid cognition.

{The suspicion regarding whether destruction has a cause or is causeless}: First, if destruction has a cause, it follows that it cannot be destroyed because there can be no cause to bring about its cessation; thus, its indestructibility is logical. However, if it were causeless, then the destructibility of all things would be unavoidable. If it is argued that it lacks destructibility because it is unproduced (*akṛtaka*), like the non-existence of a sky-flower and the like, then by that very logic, it would follow that it is beginningless (*anādi*). Consequently, like a sky-flower, an entity would never be perceived, because its opposite [destruction] would persist at all times. Furthermore, if there were no opposition between the entity and its destruction, the two would always coexist.
{Refutation thereof}: Now, this very point was anticipated and refuted by the Venerable [Vasubandhu] himself, since he stated:
"Even if destruction were causeless, because of the permanence of both the entity and its destruction..."

"If [you argue that] there is the consequence of coexistence, how can there be permanence for that which is non-existent? This is incorrect. For the conceptual distinction between permanent and impermanent is not possible regarding destruction (*nāśa*), because those two are properties of real entities (*vastu-dharma*) and because destruction is a mere nothingness (*akiñcit*). [To this we reply: That is untenable, because it is impossible for that which comes into being later to be a "nothingness. Alternatively, if it were not to come into being, an entity would never be destroyed; for something whose destruction is unestablished cannot be said to be "destroyed," just as in its present state. [In this context, "destruction" refers to the absence of the conventional usage of existence and the negation thereof.]

Here it is argued: "It is not that destruction does not exist at all; rather, there is no such thing as destruction that happens *to* an entity. The entity itself, persisting for a single moment, is destruction. One determines this [entity] to have a nature of non-intensity (*amandasvabhāva*) only subsequently, and not even upon its initial perception, because of a lack of clarity. It is determined later by virtue of that [subsequent state], by those of uneven intellect through the very observation of change. This too is inconsistent. For if destruction does not exist, why is it said: "But there is no such thing as destruction that happens to an entity"? Indeed, what is perceived as destruction is the destruction of the entity itself, and not of anything else. Nor is the entity itself destruction, because destruction has the characteristic of being the negation of the entity. For an entity is not perceived as "destroyed" in its own essential form (*svarūpa*).
The refutation of the claim that destruction lacks clarity.

As for what was said—that because of a lack of clarity even when there is perception, one does not determine [the object] beforehand—that is not so. If the very perception of the entity were the perception of its destruction, why would its clarity not exist? For if it were unclear, there would be no determination of the entity. Now, if it possesses clarity regarding the entity, is its object then distinct [from the entity], such that there is clarity in one case and a lack of clarity in the other? And if that were so, destruction would not be the entity itself. Nor does an entity abandon its own nature merely by being given the name "destruction"; and if its nature is not abandoned, how could it not be perceived as it was before?
The refutation of transformation as the nature of destruction.

The claim that [destruction occurs] "merely by the observation of modification" is also incoherent, because since destruction is a non-entity (*akiñcit*), modification is impossible. Furthermore, how can that which produces a modification be called a non-entity? If it is argued that the modification of an entity itself is the modification of its destruction, because the two are identical (*tādātmya*), we ask: does every modification of an entity establish its destruction, or only some specific one? If it is the former, it is not so, because it is not observed. For worldly people do not determine the destruction of an entity from whatever modification they observe its persistence. Regarding the latter alternative, however, only a certain specific state of the entity would be its destruction, like poison. Moreover, since things endure for only a moment (*kṣaṇasthāyitva*) and their non-persistence arises after that moment, how can it be said that there exists something which "becomes" the entity? [In other words, if the entity perishes at every moment, there is no distinct "destruction" that occurs to it.]
