It is consistent to say that an entity does not abide by itself.

But surely, even the absence of duration does not belong to that [entity], because the alternatives of being a different entity or not a different entity are impossible. Therefore, it must be that this entity possesses such an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) produced by its own causes, whereby it does not remain of itself. What is the meaning of "it does not remain of itself"? Does it mean that it remains in that very same state yet becomes unperceivable? Or does it mean that, independent of other causes, it undergoes destruction of its own accord? If you say it remains in that very same state yet becomes unperceivable, from where has this spell-less, drug-less magic been learned by the entity, such that it is sometimes perceptible and sometimes imperceptible to a person whose sense faculties and so forth remain in that same state, while it has neither arisen nor perished and there is no intervention or distance? For who could believe that an entity exists while in its present state, but later does not exist, and yet does not perish later? Now, if it is said that it undergoes destruction of its own accord later on, is that destruction a different entity (*arthāntara*) or not a different entity? Even in the doctrine of causeless destruction (*ahetuka-nāśavāda*), the fault is the same.

{Kīrti’s refutation of this doubt} Now, this too has been raised as a doubt and refuted, as he said: "Even if the existence of an entity were intrinsic, if this [following] alternative is considered, it is the same."
"Nothing happens to it; it simply ceases to exist.

Even if destruction were causeless, the conceptual alternatives of its being identical to or different from the entity would entail an equal fault. [Objection: If it is different, why is the entity not seen when something else arises? If it is non-different, then that very same entity exists, and thus it would certainly be seen. To this, the answer is: "Nothing happens to it," and so forth. For he does not say that this destruction or some other thing happens to the entity; rather, what happens is that the entity itself no longer exists.

For if one were to assert the existence of something for anyone, then existence would have been negated by that [negation]. And thus, while the negation of existence is the subject at hand, one would have stated something entirely irrelevant; for there is no such thing as the non-existence of something through the existence of another. [In that case,] this would be "non-existent" only if it did not exist by itself. {The demonstration of its irrationality}: This is a true objection, but it has not been refuted. For instance: if nothing happens to it, then even its negation does not happen; consequently, because its nature remains un-negated and stays exactly as it was, it would be perceived even before [the alleged negation].

[Objection: But was it not said that "it is that very same thing"? [Reply: True, it was said, but what was said is incorrect; for it is impossible to deny what has been observed by valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*). Indeed, it is not logical to say of fire perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) that "this is not fire at all. [Objection: It is perceived for only a single moment. [Reply: What is the cognition of that [thing] in the subsequent moment? [Objection: Nothing at all. [Reply: Then why is it not perceived? [Objection: Its own nature (*svabhāva*) is such that it is not perceived by itself. [Reply: In that case, it would not have been perceived even previously, like the horn of a hare (*śaśaviṣāṇa*). [Objection: The entity exists only later, having a nature that was unperceivable [previously]. [Reply: But if this is so, since the perceivable and unperceivable natures belong to different times, how can there be identity (*aikya*) between them?
Furthermore: "If non-existence does not exist later, what is intended by that existence?
That [existence] is also not a negation; if it is non-existence, what is being negated?"

That which is the non-existence of an entity after its existence is precisely what is called "destruction. Why is it not said that destruction is something other than the entity itself? If it is said that destruction belongs to the entity, yet it is not said that "it comes into being," then what is the fault in saying that it does come into being? If you argue that it would then simply be the entity itself, does the nature of an object change merely by virtue of being designated? If it is said that the entity is produced here, one might ask: from where does the production of a non-entity arise? It arises because it is occasional, just like the entity itself. If it were not occasional, then the non-entity would exist even during the state of its manifestation.

As for what was said—that "if one were to state the existence of something, then that existence would not have been negated by this [negation]"—that too is incorrect, because speech is merely indicative (*jñāpaka*). Indeed, nothing is either produced or negated by speech. Rather, just as a jar, which did not previously exist, is produced by potters and the like, so too that very same thing, which did not previously exist, is negated by a mallet and the like. This is well known even to cowherds and women, since there is no difference between the two cases regarding the cognition of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Now, suppose the intention is this: "If one were to state the existence of something, then the negation of existence would not thereby be made known. That is indeed true; if one were to state the existence of something else—the production of another entity—then the negation of existence would not have been expressed. But when one states the existence of the negation itself, how could that not be an irrelevant statement (*aprastutābhidhāna*) while the negation of existence is the subject at hand? It is only for one who says "nothing happens to it" that an irrelevant statement would follow when the negation of existence is the subject, because in that case the negation itself is not being stated.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "this [entity] is non-existent if it does not exist by itself," that too is incorrect. For how could something be non-existent when it is itself neither produced nor destroyed? Indeed, just as in the present state, one who has not produced passion is not himself impassioned—no such statement of this kind is accepted as authoritative by any intelligent person. Therefore, just as one who was previously unpas­sioned becomes impassioned only through the arising of passion due to other causes, so too one who was previously undestroyed becomes destroyed only through the arising of destruction due to other causes.
"It does not exist" is merely a description of a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*).

Now, is it not the case that this "it does not exist" (*na bhavati*) is a non-implicative negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), which does not denote the existence of anything at all? Otherwise, it would be an implicative negation (*paryudāsa*). But even that is not tenable, because nothing is being negated. For if something were to be excluded, then by its exclusion, something distinct from it would be touched upon; yet that is not the case here. When it is said that "destruction occurs in all cases," there is the cognition of the very existence of something. Thus, by this [statement], only the existence of another thing would be expressed, and not the mutual distinction between the two. And if there is no distinction, there can be no implicative negation. Consequently, because there is an absence of exclusion (*vyatireka*), there could be no positive concomitance (*anvaya*) either, since the latter is characterized by the persistence of a single nature. Persistence, moreover, would occur only if there were a distinction from what is other than that; but since that [distinction] does not exist, the world would be devoid of both activity and cessation. Therefore, when it is said that "the destruction of something occurs," it must mean that the thing itself simply does not exist.
{The refutation thereof}

This too is incorrect. For one who does not admit non-existence (*abhāva*), the aforementioned reasoning would entail that the world is devoid of both engagement and withdrawal (*pravṛtti-nivṛtti*)—a consequence that applies only to him, not to us. If non-existence were admitted, it must necessarily be accepted as having the characteristic of existence; otherwise, existence itself would be non-existence. Nor is negation established merely through a change of synonymous designations; for no distinct meaning is established by calling a jar (*ghaṭa*) a pot (*kalaśa*). Furthermore, there is no division of parts within a single essence such that one part alone could be the object of negation. And if negation were without an object, it would simply lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Consequently, the establishment of impermanence and other such properties would be unreal. However, if there is a distinction between existence and non-existence, those two terms will also be meaningful. There is indeed a distinction between *prasajya* (absolute) and *paryudāsa* (relative) negation: the object of *prasajya* is non-existence itself, whereas the object of *paryudāsa* is another positive entity. Moreover, the mutual exclusion of two existents is "mutual non-existence" (*itaretarābhāva*), for an existent, when delimited by that [exclusion], is said to be distinguished from other existents. Even though non-existence is likewise distinguished from existence, it is nevertheless not the object of *paryudāsa*, because even that which is distinguished from it still possesses the nature of its own non-existence.
The infinite regress of non-existence and its refutation.

Now, if mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is indeed a different entity from the positive thing (*bhāva*), then another mutual non-existence must be admitted to exclude that [first one], and yet another to exclude that one as well; thus, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Some say that there is no infinite regress, just as with the light of a lamp. We, however, observe this: an infinite regress is not admitted in cases where the infinite regress would contradict something perceived. And here, nothing perceived is contradicted. Insofar as the exclusion of a jar from cloth and other things is established by that very [exclusion] itself, the jar is proven to be excluded from cloth and so forth; in that case, nothing is undermined by an infinite regress of further exclusions. If it is argued that the object is not established as excluded because its capacity is exhausted by the apprehension of a succession of exclusions, we say no; for even in the case of particulars and qualifiers, the apprehension [of such a succession] is not admitted. Furthermore, the exclusion is grasped by a non-conceptual, variegated cognition (*mecakajñāna*), which also grasps the infinity of the exclusions.
The suspicion that exclusion is purposeless, and its refutation.

Is that entity excluded by its own nature (*svarūpa*), or is it not excluded? If it is excluded, then another exclusion is purposeless. If it is not excluded, there follows the consequence of the confusion of entities. What is the meaning of "by its own nature"? Does it mean "without exclusion," or "by a form distinct from exclusion"? It is not logical [to say] "without exclusion," because exclusion is an eternal property (*nityadharma*) of the entity. For when a property exists only occasionally, the substratum is designated as being otherwise in its absence; for example, a man is called "without earrings" (*akuṇḍalī*) in the absence of earrings, or "unperished" before destruction. Furthermore, an entity never exists devoid of exclusion from other entities, just as a cow does not exist devoid of cowness (*gotva*), nor fire devoid of heat. If, on the other hand, it is intended that "it is excluded by its own nature" means "by a form distinct from exclusion," then that is acceptable to us, since we admit difference (*bheda*). Nor, in this case, is exclusion purposeless; for even if a wealthy man is called "wealthy" by a form distinct from his wealth, does that make the wealth useless? Therefore, even mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is indeed a different entity from the positive thing itself.
{The Refutation of the Doubt that Cessation is a Positive Entity}:

As for what was said—that when it is stated that "cessation occurs everywhere," some positive entity (*bhāva*) is necessarily perceived—that too is incorrect. For arising (*utpatti*) is not the defining characteristic of a positive entity, such that cessation, being an occurrence, would thereby become a positive entity; for even space (*ākāśa*) and the like, which are characterized by non-arising, are nonetheless positive entities. Furthermore, arising is held to be the defining characteristic of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*) in the sense of the cessation of its own nature, and not in the sense of a connection with existence (*sattā*) for that which previously did not exist, nor in the sense of inherence (*samavāya*) in a cause. {The Demonstration of the Initial Existence of Cessation}

The cessation of its own nature (*svarūpa*) is also said to have a beginning. That cessation has a beginning precisely by way of its nature as non-existence (*abhāva*), because that form is not perceived at the time when the positive entity (*bhāva*) is perceived. And because it has a beginning, it possesses a cause. It is said that "cessation occurs" due to the mere similarity [of cessation] to having a cause and having a beginning; however, this much alone does not entail that it is a different kind of entity (*bhāvāntara*), nor does the mere fact of being a cause for purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) entail that it is a positive entity, since we do not accept the definition of a positive entity as you have stated. What then? Is the definition of a positive entity its "thingness" (*vastutva*)? "Thingness" is said to be a property that is common to substances and so forth, yet excluded from prior non-existence and the other types of non-existence. The distinction between existence and non-existence is based on whether they are conjoined with or not conjoined with that [thingness]. Alternatively, their distinction is based on the fact that one is the object of a cognition involving affirmation (*vidhi*) while the other is the object of a cognition involving negation (*pratiṣedha*).
The distinction between existence and non-existence is based on their being independent or dependent.

Or [it is because] there is the perception of both the independent (*svatantra*) and the dependent (*paratantra*). For instance—a positive entity (*bhāva*), being perceived as distinct from each of those possessing similar or dissimilar characteristics by means of its own property (*svadharma*), is discriminated as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," or "this is of one distinct nature," "that is of another distinct nature. But non-existence (*abhāva*) is not like this; even without the apprehension of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), it is characterized by its own property individually. Indeed, even in a single location, although the specific distinctions among the infinite varieties of non-existences might appear, they cannot be individually characterized. Therefore, since the determination of the perception of those specific instances occurs only through the apprehension of the counter-correlate, the perception of the dependent is the definition of non-existence; thus, non-existence is not simply a positive entity.
Even by the Buddhists, a difference in the defining characteristics of existence and non-existence is accepted.

Furthermore, you yourself have stated that there is a difference in the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of existence and non-existence; how then can they be one? The distinction between all things is established precisely through the difference in their characteristics. If, even on that basis, no distinction were established, then the distinction of anything from anything else would not be proven, leading to the consequence of non-duality (*advaita*). Is [the entity] here also omnipotent? It belongs to the existent (*bhāva*). If it comes into being later, then it must necessarily be admitted to have a different cause. If, on the other hand, it exists even previously, then the existent would not produce its effect even before; this is an unavoidable consequence. If it is argued: "The absence of all power is the negation of all modes [of activity], and it is illogical for such a thing to come into being," then does the absence of all power in the existent not exist at all now? In that case, the existent would be as capable as it was before. For when there is a double negation, the original meaning itself remains, just as in the case of "it is not a non-tree. This might be the case: only the negation of the existent is intended, but it is not intended that this [negation] arises from a cause; for according to you, a real entity must partake of either identity or difference. To that, the refutation has already been stated. However, for one who holds that nothing happens to the existent when it perishes, there is no room for the conceptual alternatives of identity or difference—for this alternative would apply only to an existent, since affirmation follows the nature of the real object.
{The possibility of a thing having the nature of non-existence}:

Even when one says, "this is the existence of the thing," it is in fact said that "it does not exist. For in this way, [the thing] is negated, since a positive affirmation is impossible within a negation. For this very reason, there is no cause whatsoever for its destruction; thus it is said:
"If any effect whatsoever were to exist, another [cause] would be required."
"What object that is incapable of producing anything—why would it depend on anything?
[The opponent argues: "For a cause exists only when there is an effect, and for that which is perishing, there is no effect.
This too is incorrect; for if the negation of an entity is occasional, how could it not have a cause? And if it were eternal, it has been stated that the entity would never be un-negated at any time.
The non-antagonism toward the conceptualization of identity and difference.

This dilemma of identity and difference causes trouble for you, but not for us. For if there is a distinction, we observe a variety of entities, and thus one might ask: what kind of property is it by which the destruction of a jar occurs? It is a property opposed to the jar, produced with a nature determined by its own causes. Once that [property] has arisen, how can it be said that the jar exists? If it is argued that even when an enemy such as a mongoose arises, the conventional usage of "existent" is still observed in relation to snakes and the like, we say no; this is because mongoose and the like are only metaphorically considered "opposing factors," since they bring about that [destruction], just like food or water. In reality, however, opposition belongs only to existence and non-existence themselves.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "this conceptual differentiation could only exist if there were an entity," that too is untenable because it contradicts your own words. For you have asserted the identity (*tādātmya*) of existence and non-existence; yet that is contradicted if one does not accept reality (*tattva*). Even if reality is accepted, the distinction between their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇabheda*) is contradicted. For how can there be reality, or even the indeterminability of reality, for that which is said to be differentiated by a difference in its defining characteristics?

As for the argument that it is improper—namely, that even by saying "non-existence comes to be," one has in fact said "existence does not come to be"—that too is trivial. For there is no disagreement regarding the expression itself; rather, the disagreement concerns the meaning. First, the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) must be examined: does it exist or not? Is it something distinct from existence or not distinct from it? For when a meaning is determined, its expression is appropriate whether as a qualifier of an action (*kriyā*), a qualifier of a factor of action (*kāraka*), or through a mediated connection (*vyavahitānvaya*). Yet in your view, there is no such thing as the meaning of the negative particle, because it is impossible for it to be either distinct or non-distinct from the meaning of the subsequent word. In the statement "existence does not come to be" (*bhāvo na bhavati*), what is being negated here? Is it the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*), the meaning of the noun (*nāman*), or both? If it is the negation of the verbal meaning, then the entity (*bhāva*) itself would not be negated; for when it is said, "Devadatta does not eat," the non-existence of Devadatta is not understood simply from the negation of the act of eating. If, on the other hand, it is the negation of the nominal meaning, even so, the un-negated action implies some substratum. Consequently, it would follow that there exists some thing called "the non-existence of non-existence. If it is the negation of both, then if this occurs at the time of the existence, it would mean that at the very moment existence comes to be, existence does not come to be. If, however, it occurs later, then since the two—the existence and the non-existence—would occur sequentially, their having different causes is established.

As for what was said—that "only when there is an effect does there exist a cause"—that too is incorrect. For if non-existence (*abhāva*) were not produced, the entity (*bhāva*) would remain in its very same state; how then could it be said to have perished? [Objection: But even if another thing (*arthāntara*) were produced, the entity would still remain in its same state. How then could it be said to have perished? [Reply: No; because the defining characteristic of an entity is its persistence in that state (*tādavasthya*), and once that statelessness (*atādavasthya*) has arisen, how can the entity be said to remain in its same state? For this very reason, it does not produce an effect either. For its non-existence consists in the absence of all causal capacities, not merely in being some other thing. [Objection: But since non-existence is defined by its distinction from all the properties of an entity, its production is not logical; for production is a property belonging only to an entity. [Reply: No; because properties such as knowability (*jñeyatā*) and so forth exist even in the absence of [positive] existence. Otherwise, it would simply be unknown. [Objection: How can there be an affirmation (*vidhi*) within a negation (*pratiṣedha*)? [Reply: Indeed, this negation belongs to the entity, not to itself. Even this absence of all capacities belongs to the entity alone, and not to itself independently, because it is capable of performing functions such as the perception of its own self. Just as light is the opponent of darkness alone, and not of itself.
{The conceptualization of the meaning of the sentence "it does not exist by itself"}:

What is the meaning of "it does not exist by itself"? (1) Is this non-existence itself [the entity]? (2) Or does it bring about its own non-existence? (3) Or does it not bring about existence? (4) Or does it do nothing at all? (5) Or does it do something by itself? (6) Or does it become a non-existent thing by itself?
(1) First of all, it is not possible for existence itself to be non-existence by itself, because of their contradiction.
(2) Nor does it bring about its own non-existence, because non-existence cannot be established as being either identical to or different from reality.

(3) Furthermore, if it does not bring about existence, then since the negation of one alternative implies the admission of the remaining possibility, it follows that it must bring about something else.

(4) Now, if it does not perform even the slightest action, does it remain indifferent? If you say "not at all," then how is it that it performs no action? If you say that although it performs no action it does not remain [static], then does it go to another place, another time, or another state? And if so, the entity would be pervasive across space and the like.

(5) Now, if it were nothing in itself, that would be illogical; for how can an object whose nature is blue and so forth, while being perceived, be said to be "nothing in itself"? If you say it becomes something later, is it still of that same nature even later, or is it of a different nature? If you say it is of that same nature, then it must have been nothing even before, since there is no difference in its nature. If you say it is not of that nature later and thus becomes something, from where did this non-blue nature arise later? For it was produced from its own cause as having that very nature, distinguished from what is not of that nature; how then could it become of a different nature even later? Indeed, a stone excluded from the nature of lightness can never become light.

(6) By this, the claim that "it becomes non-existent by itself" is refuted; for since it has arisen from its own causes as something excluded from non-existence by its very nature, how could it ever become non-existent? Therefore, this entity arises from its own cause with an existent intrinsic nature (*bhāvasvabhāva*), and it becomes non-existent only through another cause. Just as a white cloth, having arisen, becomes black only through another cause.

If that is the case, then it is simply the entity (*bhāva*) itself that becomes variously different, and there is no other non-existence (*abhāva*). No; for this would entail the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), and that [doctrine] is only tenable if the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryatva*). Furthermore, we shall explain the untenability of that [doctrine]. Moreover, if its prior nature is not abandoned, how can the entity become otherwise? For it would follow that its [prior] form would still be perceived. Or, if that nature is abandoned, then it is precisely that non-existence which has arisen subsequently, since its characteristic is the abandonment of that form—this is logical. And how can a non-existence that is being perceived not exist? If it is not perceived, then what is the object of the negation? For by the word "non-existent" (*asat*), that very thing is not denoted, because an entity has diverse aspects. Furthermore, the words "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) are not established as synonyms. Nor is it a different object (*arthāntara*); since that too would be a real entity (*vastu*), it would fall within the scope of affirmation (*vidhi*), and you do not accept that a non-entity (*avastu*) could enter the range of perception as something distinct from a real entity. Moreover, a negation without an object would be invalid (*apramāṇa*) alone; consequently, the negated entity would always exist, because the negation is not established through a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇataḥ*). Or else, there would be the consequence of negating everything, since mere speech that is not a valid cognition is possible everywhere. If it is asked: "How can a negation whose object is a different thing negate the entity?", then why does that which denotes the absence of that [entity] not negate it? Because existence and non-existence possess such a nature that by the affirmation of one, the other is negated.

{The Refutation of the Charge of Irrelevant Assertion} For this very reason, there is no risk of an irrelevant assertion; for in this way alone does the cessation of existence become the relevant subject—namely, if that cessation itself is what is expressed. Otherwise, there would not even be an occasion for the discussion of the cessation of existence, and thus the negation would be entirely useless, as its purpose would be absent.

If you say that the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpākāra*) is the object of negation, then do you now intend to follow this rule: "Whatever is suspected must be stated"? For how can the statement of a conceptual form—which is distinct from the real entity (*vastu*)—negate that entity? Indeed, when one thing is mentioned, another thing is not thereby negated. If the conceptual form is a non-entity (*avastu*), what connection (*sambandha*) could there be such that by its mention the entity would be negated? If you say the connection is characterized by the relation between the negatable and the negation, then our desired conclusion is established; for the dispute is merely over a name. Now, suppose some property of the entity is the object of negation. Is that [property] different from the entity or not? If it is different, then you have entered into our own position. If it is not different, then the entity itself would be the object of negation, which is not logical; for the meaning of "the pot exists" is not the same as the meaning of "the pot does not exist. If you say the object of negation is a particular state (*avasthāviśeṣa*) of the entity, no; for that too cannot be either different or non-different [from the entity]. If you say it is designated as such because it appears as if it were a separate object, then it is a superimposed object (*samāropitārtha*). In that case, the negation would likewise be invalid (*apramāṇa*). If you say that just as in the case of a rope, the difference [between the rope and a snake] is superimposed, but the object [itself] is not, then what is the object of the negation? Is it the object or the difference? If it is the object itself, then we have returned to the point that affirmation and negation share the same object. If it is the difference, then how is the negation not invalid due to having a superimposed object as its domain? If you say that even though the object is superimposed, it is not invalid because it is indirectly connected (*pratibandha*) to the real object—just like the cognition of a jewel in the luster of a jewel—then is the connection between affirmation and negation in a single object like that between the words "cloth" and "garment" (synonyms)? Or is it a connection to restricted objects like the words "white" and "black"? In the former case, how are they not synonyms? And if they are synonymous designations, how is the entity negated? In the second case, the difference between existence and non-existence is established, just as with white and black. If you say the connection is to a single object, as with the words "blue" and "lotus," no; for even there, it has been established that the difference lies in the qualifiers. Furthermore, if affirmation and negation were to operate upon a single object based on a difference of properties—as with the words "blue" and "lotus"—then their operation would not occur through the difference of place and time. It is not the case that "what was blue here before is the very same lotus later elsewhere. If you say it is like "active" and "inactive," no; for that would entail momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), and in momentariness, a succession of multiple properties cannot belong to the same self. Moreover, there would be a difference in causes, as in the cases of activity and inactivity. Now, if you say that the negation at another time and place has non-perception (*anupalambha*) as its object, since the non-existence of things is simply non-perception—what is this so-called "non-perception"? If it is the absence of perception, how can it be the object of the negation of a pot and so forth? For by mentioning the absence of one thing, another is not thereby negated, as that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Nor is the existence of anything established from non-perception. If you say it is the establishment of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), is it of usage with an object or without an object? If it is with an object, what is that object? That is precisely what we have begun to investigate. As for the proof of usage without an object, it has already been said that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, regarding that cognition "it does not exist" which establishes the linguistic usage of the absence of a pot and so forth: is it with an object or without an object? First, it is not a proof if it is without an object, because it is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*); for even when a pot exists, a false cognition "it does not exist" is seen due to some cause. If it is with an object, what is its object? It cannot be the pot itself, because it is separated by space and time and is the object of the cognition "it exists. Nor is it merely some other object, as that would lead to over-extension. If you say the object of the non-perception of the pot is the ground itself as distinguished from it, or that the ground itself is the non-perception of the pot, because that is the object of the linguistic usage of its absence—this is not so. The ground and such are not the object, because they are a different entity (*vastvantara*). When a different entity is presented or cognized, it does not mean the non-existence of the pot-entity is presented or cognized. For if that were so, the objection raised against the view that "destruction is merely a different entity" would be removed by yourself. Moreover, without the cognition of the distinction from that [pot], the apprehension of what is distinguished from it is impossible. Furthermore, the distinction from that is not the very nature of the ground, because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), just like the conjunction with it. If you say the conjunction with it is also the very nature of the ground, no; for a qualifier is a different object from the qualified (*viśeṣya*), like a staff and so forth. There is no proof whatsoever for their identity. If the object of the cognition and expression "the pot is not here" is the ground itself and not a pot-absence distinct from it, then the object of "the pot is here" would also be the ground itself. One need not postulate a pot distinct from it; let the ground alone, as qualified by the presence of the pot, suffice for both cases. But this is not logical. Therefore, just like the existence of the pot, the non-existence of the pot also appears on the ground as something distinct from it. In this way, the application of affirmation and negation becomes meaningful.
The nature of darkness as the absence of light.

In the absence of all light, it appears as "darkness" or "thick gloom" within one's own house and so forth. Yet, no other distinct entity (*vastvantara*) devoid of light is perceived there. Furthermore, since touch and the like are not objects of the eye, even if they are perceived by another sense organ as being devoid of light, this does not establish the non-existence [of light]; for otherwise, it would follow that even a blind person could discern the absence of light. For this very reason, the non-existence of light is not established even by the perception of a cognition devoid of light, because such a cognition is also not an object of the eye, and even a blind person possesses such a cognition. As for the form of the house and so forth, it simply does not appear due to the absence of light. If it is argued that darkness is merely a specific color appearing as "black," and that its perception as distinct from light is what constitutes the non-perception of light—this is not so; for a black color cannot be perceived without light. Moreover, such an appearance occurs even for one with eyes closed, yet the determination of the absence of light does not arise from that alone, as doubt is observed. However, when one opens the eyes and looks, then the determination of its absence becomes free from doubt. Just as the eye requires no other light for the perception of light, so too it does not require light for the perception of its absence. For whatever causal complex (*sāmagrī*) perceives a positive entity, that same complex perceives its absence. Thus, since identity between existence and non-existence is untenable, destruction must have a cause. Consequently, since no cause of destruction is perceived in things like crystal at every moment, they are not momentary; therefore, recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) in those cases is not erroneous. Likewise, recognition of the self (*ātman*), which grasps the single substratum of desire and the rest, is not erroneous, because it is not sublated. Thus, the substratum of desire and the rest is established as distinct from the body and so forth.
{An Investigation into the Dimension of the Self} What is its dimension? This is now investigated.

Some, first of all, consider [the soul] to have a dimension equal to a portion divided into hundreds of thousands of the tips of a hair. That is incorrect, because it would follow that pleasure, pain, and so forth could not be perceived throughout the entire body, since their substratum would be impossible to exist everywhere. If it is argued that it connects with all parts sequentially, we say no; for we observe the simultaneous arising of pleasure and so forth in all parts of the body. If it is argued that there is the conceit of simultaneity due to rapid movement, we say no; for a permanent entity cannot possibly move rapidly. At times, when it is situated in one place, the remaining parts of the body would be lifeless. Furthermore, while the soul is atomic, it is more reasonable to postulate its rapid movement. Moreover, there is no proof whatsoever for establishing the atom-like nature of the self.

It is also untenable that [the self] has the same dimensions as the body alone, because it would follow that the self possesses the properties of growth and decay due to the growth and decay of the body, and consequently, it would be non-eternal. Therefore, the *puruṣa* is all-pervading like space.
[This is the proof for the pervasiveness of the individual soul.]

If it is asked, "What is the proof for its all-pervasiveness? it is said: All other corporeal substances, with the exception of my own body, are conjoined with my self, because they are corporeal, just like my body. Furthermore, since qualities such as color and so forth—depending on their conjunction with their own substratum—act as causes for motion in another substratum (such as air) due to gravity and the like, [the self must be pervasive]. Likewise, it is heard in scripture that when the yogic power of *aṇimā* (atomicity) has manifested, the yogi indeed creates countless bodies together with their sense organs and simultaneously experiences enjoyments; this is possible only if the knower is all-pervasive, not if he were atomic or limited to the size of the body. For if the self were limited to the size of the body, it would be composed of parts and subject to destruction, since all substances other than all-pervasive atoms are observed to be composed of parts and perishable. Therefore, the self is all-pervasive, because, while not being the locus of atomic dimension, it is an eternal substance, like space.
The proof for the eternity of the individual soul.

If it is asked, "Whence comes its eternity? it is because it is beginningless (*anāditvāt*). If it is asked, "Whence is that [beginninglessness]? it is said: because a newborn infant exhibits joy, fear, and grief due to the continuity of memories from previous practice; and because there is a desire for breast-milk resulting from the habit of feeding after death. Indeed, the arising of joy, fear, grief, and so forth is not possible without the recollection of the means of pleasure and pain. And joy and the others are observed even in one who has just been born; by these, memory is inferred; by memory, mental impression (*saṃskāra*); and by mental impression, previous practice. Since such practice is not possible in this life, it is understood to belong to another birth, just as the joy and other states of one who has awakened from sleep indicate practice occurring on the preceding day.

[Objection: "In that case, then, there would be the undesirable consequence of remembering what was experienced in another birth, just as one remembers what was experienced on another day. [Reply: No; because that latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has been destroyed by the extremely intense suffering of death and so forth. Some say that because the impressions of joy, fear, grief, and so forth are exceedingly firm, they are not destroyed. We, however, say this: even when the impression exists, memory does not occur due to the absence of a cause for its awakening. Where memory does not occur despite the presence of causes for awakening, there the destruction of the impression must necessarily be postulated. [The causes for the awakening of impressions: 1. *Sahaja* (innate) impressions awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a cow awakening the innate impression of a gavaya. 2. *Āhita* (acquired) impressions awaken through the sight of an object associated with them, such as the sight of a teacher awakening the impression of his disciple. 3. Impressions of joy, fear, grief, and so forth awaken through the recollection of the causes of those states, such as the recollection of a festival awakening the impression of joy. 4. Impressions of learning awaken through the sight of the object of study, such as the sight of a book awakening the impression of grammar. 5. Impressions of skill awaken through practice, such as the practice of archery awakening the impression of skill. 6. Impressions of dreams awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a horse awakening the impression of a dream of a horse. 7. Impressions of the after-death state awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a chariot awakening the impression of the after-death state. 8. Impressions of the womb awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a mother awakening the impression of the womb. 9. Impressions of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a woman awakening the impression of the intermediate state. 10. Impressions of the previous life awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a village awakening the impression of the previous life. 11. Impressions of the future life awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a palace awakening the impression of the future life. 12. Impressions of the present life awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a field awakening the impression of the present life. 13. Impressions of the past awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of an old man awakening the impression of youth. 14. Impressions of the future awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a young man awakening the impression of old age. 15. Impressions of the present awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a healthy person awakening the impression of health. 16. Impressions of the dead awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a corpse awakening the impression of death. 17. Impressions of the living awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a living person awakening the impression of life. 18. Impressions of happiness awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a pleasure-garden awakening the impression of happiness. 19. Impressions of suffering awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a thorn awakening the impression of suffering. 20. Impressions of virtue awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a virtuous person awakening the impression of virtue. 21. Impressions of vice awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a wicked person awakening the impression of vice. 22. Impressions of merit awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a sacrifice awakening the impression of merit. 23. Impressions of demerit awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a slaughterhouse awakening the impression of demerit. 24. Impressions of dharma awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a temple awakening the impression of dharma. 25. Impressions of adharma awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a temple of a heretic awakening the impression of adharma. 26. Impressions of knowledge awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a scripture awakening the impression of knowledge. 27. Impressions of ignorance awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a false doctrine awakening the impression of ignorance. 28. Impressions of liberation awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a liberated soul awakening the impression of liberation. 29. Impressions of bondage awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a bound soul awakening the impression of bondage. 30. Impressions of the self awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a reflection awakening the impression of the self. 31. Impressions of the non-self awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a pot awakening the impression of the non-self. 32. Impressions of permanence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a mountain awakening the impression of permanence. 33. Impressions of impermanence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a flash of lightning awakening the impression of impermanence. 34. Impressions of eternity awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of the sky awakening the impression of eternity. 35. Impressions of non-eternity awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a tree awakening the impression of non-eternity. 36. Impressions of existence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a jar awakening the impression of existence. 37. Impressions of non-existence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a rabbit's horn awakening the impression of non-existence. 38. Impressions of unity awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a single atom awakening the impression of unity. 39. Impressions of plurality awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a forest awakening the impression of plurality. 40. Impressions of generality awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a cow awakening the impression of generality. 41. Impressions of particularity awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a black cow awakening the impression of particularity. 42. Impressions of inherence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a cloth awakening the impression of inherence. 43. Impressions of non-inherence awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a pot awakening the impression of non-inherence. 44. Impressions of substance awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of gold awakening the impression of substance. 45. Impressions of quality awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of color awakening the impression of quality. 46. Impressions of action awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of motion awakening the impression of action. 47. Impressions of universal awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of existence awakening the impression of the universal. 48. Impressions of particular awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of earthness awakening the impression of the particular. 49. Impressions of ultimate particularity awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of an atom awakening the impression of ultimate particularity. 50. Impressions of time awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a year awakening the impression of time. 51. Impressions of space awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a direction awakening the impression of space. 52. Impressions of mind awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a thought awakening the impression of mind. 53. Impressions of matter awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a body awakening the impression of matter. 54. Impressions of consciousness awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of cognition awakening the impression of consciousness. 55. Impressions of the unconscious awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of deep sleep awakening the impression of the unconscious. 56. Impressions of the waking state awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of an object awakening the impression of the waking state. 57. Impressions of the dreaming state awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of a dream-object awakening the impression of the dreaming state. 58. Impressions of the dreamless sleep state awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of deep sleep awakening the impression of the dreamless sleep state. 59. Impressions of the fourth state awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of the Self awakening the impression of the fourth state. 60. Impressions of the lower worlds awaken through the sight of similar objects, such as the sight of hell awakening the impression of the lower worlds. 6

What, then, are those signs (*nimitta*) from which the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) occurs? It is said: "From resolution" (*praṇidhānāt*). And so says the Sūtra: "From resolution, connection, repetition, characteristic, similarity, possession, support and supported, relation, immediate succession, separation, common purpose, opposition, attainment of excellence, intervention, pleasure and pain, desire, aversion, fear, longing, action, passion, merit, and demerit. Resolution (*praṇidhāna*) is the fixing of the mind through the desire to remember; it means concentration of the mind or one-pointedness. Having remembered an object in general, one who wishes to remember its specific details performs a resolution. Connection (*nibandha*), however, is the grouping of objects within a single composition. For objects grouped in a single composition become causes for mutual recollection, whether in their original sequence or otherwise. Alternatively, "connection" is the depositing of things to be remembered in a certain place, such as on a cloth, in a book, or elsewhere. Repetition (*abhyāsa*) is the recurrence of cognitions regarding the same object; from that comes the awakening of prior impressions and the production of an intensification of impressions. Indeed, even with slight repetition in the mastery of a text, the awakening of prior impressions is inferred, as in the case of one who has forgotten what was previously learned through practice. A sign (*liṅga*) is smoke and the like, which is a cause for remembering fire and so forth. A characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is a mark located on a part of an animal, such as a horn, which causes the remembrance of "cowness. Similarity (*sādṛśya*) is that found in paintings and the like, pertaining to lions and other such beings. Possession (*parigraha*) is the relationship between owner and owned. Support (*āśraya*) is a village chief, who causes the remembrance of those dependent upon him; by contrast, the "supported" (*āśrita*) is explained in the opposite sense. Relation (*sambandha*) is the mutual cause of remembrance among students, teachers, and others. From immediate succession (*ānantarya*): there is remembrance in sequence regarding things to be done. From separation (*viyoga*): whoever is separated from someone remembers that person. From common purpose (*ekakārya*): there is remembrance of another agent [of a shared task]. From opposition (*virodha*): from seeing one of two people desiring victory, there is remembrance of the other. From attainment of excellence (*atiśayaprāpti*): whoever has attained or is to attain excellence from something remembers that thing constantly. From intervention (*vyavadhāna*): [remembrance of] swords and the like by means of sheaths and so forth. From pleasure (*sukha*): one remembers the cause of that pleasure; and from pain (*duḥkha*), the cause of that pain. From desire (*icchā*) and aversion (*dveṣa*): one constantly remembers whom one desires and whom one hates. From fear (*bhaya*): one remembers that from which one fears. From longing (*arthitva*): one remembers that for which one longs. From action (*kriyā*): [remembrance of] a chariot-maker by means of a chariot. From passion (*rāga*): one remembers that object, such as a woman, in which one is impassioned. From merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*): there is remembrance even of things experienced in other births.

This sūtra is intended as an illustration, for the signs that serve as the causes of memory—which awaken latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)—are innumerable. All such signs become awakeners of latent impressions when assisted by merit (*dharma*) or demerit (*adharma*). Conversely, those factors which obstruct them fail to awaken them; for this very reason, only some individuals possess the memory of past births (*jātismara*), and not everyone. Thus, it is heard in tradition that for Jaigīṣavya and others, memory arose regarding thousands of previous births exactly as they were experienced, due to latent impressions assisted by the *dharma* born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*). In other living beings, however, memory regarding things experienced in other lives occurs only in a general sense, and not with respect to specific details of place, time, and so forth. This is because of the absence of a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭa-viśeṣa*) that assists the cause of specific memory, and because of the presence of obstructing factors. Furthermore, memory is observed in this manner: "I remember that I have seen this person somewhere," yet "I do not remember where or when I saw him. Likewise, "I do not remember where or when I ate this."

Now, one might object: if there is no memory such as "I saw this object in such-and-such a place or at such-and-such a time in another birth," then what is the proof that there is memory of the means of pleasure and other things experienced in previous births? To this it has been said: "Because of the occurrence of joy and so forth. For joy and the like do not occur with respect to specific objects that are the causes of pleasure or pain unless there is a recollection of their nature from previous experience. Likewise, even animals are observed through their symptoms to be overcome by grief due to the separation from offspring and so on. Furthermore, grief is inferred in a newborn infant by its crying; that too points to previous practice. Moreover, the fact that even a newborn infant approaches the breast out of a desire for milk is observed. Since the drinking of milk was not practiced in this life, it is understood that it occurs here because of practice in a previous birth, just as it occurs on subsequent days due to practice on the preceding day. Thus, when the practice in each successive previous birth is established through inference based on inference (*anumānānumāna*), the beginninglessness of the self (*ātman*) is proven.

"In that case, one might infer that cats and other such beings were also cats and so forth in their previous births; otherwise, how could there be such a restriction regarding their desire for mice and the like? This is indeed true, yet there is no rule that this must have occurred in the immediately preceding birth. Just as proficiency in sciences, arts, and the like indicates prior practice in a general sense, but does not indicate practice on the day immediately preceding, or on the third or fourth day, so too the proficiency of cats and others in seizing mice is not possible without prior practice—this much is inferred. As for that practice, let it have occurred in the immediately preceding birth or in a birth separated by many lifetimes; there is no specific reason [to prefer one over the other] in this matter.
The apprehension that prior mental impressions might perish, and its refutation.

[Objection: But surely the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the opposite of the suffering of death and [other] cognitions; how then can it persist when separated by many births, given that it is destroyed by the cognition of the counteragent (*pratipakṣajñāna*) in its various forms and by the suffering of death and so forth? [Reply: No, because there is no proof (*pramāṇa*). There is no proof for the claim that the latent impression is necessarily destroyed by the cognition of the counteragent and so on. As for forgetting, it is possible even when there is an obstruction caused by the latent impression produced by the cognition of the counteragent or by a particular unseen force (*adṛṣṭaviśeṣa*), just as the latent impression of a text or a craft is [obstructed] by a latent impression that is its counteragent. If, however, that latent impression were not actually perceived, then the effort required to grasp a new text or the like would be exactly the same as that required for something already grasped but forgotten. Furthermore, there is no such rule [of necessity]; therefore, it is not the case that [the impression] is destroyed solely by cognitions and the suffering of death. As for one who maintains that [the impression] is indeed destroyed, in his view, animals such as deer, boars, dogs, and cats would lack skill in the activities natural to their own species. For they have no teacher in this life. Moreover, we observe skill in those activities even among those raised together from birth. Nor is it the case that these animals belong to that same species in every single birth, since it is possible for them to be born sequentially through many different species due to the diversity of their specific karmas.
Only those formative forces belonging to the same class obtain their functional activity.

Granted that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) may persist through many births, nevertheless, it is not logical that impressions separated by many births should gain functional activity while being overwhelmed by impressions belonging to the immediately preceding birth. For it is not the case that a person whose impression produced by practice over many years generates memory, yet one whose impression is produced by practice over the immediately preceding days does not generate it. This is not so, because it has already been stated: here, the action known as wholesome or unwholesome (*śubhāśubha-karma*) is the primary cause for the awakening of latent impressions. Therefore, since it is from a specific action that the connection with a particular birth is determined, from that very [action] there is the gaining of functional activity for the impressions of that birth and the awakening of other impressions. Otherwise, that action would simply remain unexperienced. To illustrate: even in a birth as a dog, a pig, or the like, if the impressions of a Brahmin or similar status were to gain functional activity, then there would be no inclination toward consuming excrement or engaging in sexual intercourse. For in the case of a Brahmin or such, there is indeed hesitation regarding those things, not passion. Therefore, by the power of the action that causes a specific birth, only the impressions of that particular birth gain functional activity.
{The suspicion that *saṃskāra* is superfluous because of *karman*, and its refutation}:

If it is argued that the skill and proficiency of living beings in their own actions arise solely from the power of specific *karman*, so what is the need for *saṃskāra*? [We reply: Even if *karman* is accepted, the beginninglessness (*anāditva*) of the self (*ātman*) is not thereby negated. For there is no birth without *karman*, nor is there *karman* without birth.

Furthermore, it is not logical to deny the role of perceived causes even when [fear] has karma as its cause. This is indeed observed: that for whatever one has practiced, one possesses skill in that regard. Moreover, if there were no prior experience, then—just as frogs and the like do not seek to eat flies and so forth—one would likewise refrain from flies out of fear of snakes and the like. For a frog has not personally experienced death at the hands of a snake in this very life, such that the mere sight of a snake would cause it to tremble with terror. Therefore, fear arises only for one who remembers the cause of death, based on the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the experience of the suffering of death throughout many previous births. Similarly, among those born into the same family, such as Brahmins and others, we observe a varying degree of proficiency or lack thereof in certain matters; this too is accounted for solely by the diversity of latent impressions from previous births. Thus, through the inference of a succession of preceding births, the beginninglessness [of the cycle] is established. Consequently, because there is no cause for destruction—such as being produced (*kṛtakatva*)—it is established that the self (*ātman*) is eternal.

Now, one might ask: what is the purpose of self-knowledge (*ātma-jñāna*), for which such great effort has been made here? Its purpose is precisely the establishment of the next world (*paraloka*). For if that [self] is not established, then because the transmigrating subject (*paralokin*) is unestablished, the next world itself remains unestablished. Consequently, even a discerning person (*prekṣāvat*) would have no inclination toward heaven. Therefore, once the existence of the next world is ascertained through the existence of the transmigrating subject, there arises activity directed toward the next world; from that, the accomplishment of one's desired goal follows. Thus, because it is useful for engagement in the next world and because it is the cause for the destruction of demerit (*adharma*), self-knowledge is a limb of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). Furthermore, its status as the cause for the destruction of demerit is to be understood from such scriptural authorities (*āgama*) as: "The knower of the Self overcomes sorrow."
{The suspicion that the self is a cause of misfortune} Now, one who desires liberation should not cultivate knowledge of the self, because that is a cause of saṃsāra; and thus it has been said:
"In him who perceives a self, there arises a constant attachment of the form 'I am [this]' toward it."
"Out of affection, one craves pleasures; craving conceals the faults [of those pleasures].
The meaning is that craving, having concealed the faults, displays them as virtues. And from that:
"Perceiving virtues and being intensely desirous, one thinks 'this is mine' and takes up the means for their attainment."
"Therefore, as long as there is attachment to a self, so long is one a wanderer in saṃsāra.
When there is a self, there is the notion of 'other'; from the division of self and other, grasping and aversion arise.
Bound by these two, all faults are produced."

{Refutation of that} This is incorrect. For instance: is the cognition of a self with respect to the body and so forth the cause of saṃsāra, or is it [the cognition] with respect to something distinct from those? If it is the first position, then nothing is contradicted, since it is accepted that the cognition of a self in what is not-self is the cause of saṃsāra. But in the second position, there is no proof; for when the aforementioned thorough knowledge of the self exists, no one is seen to be subject to saṃsāra.

As for the claim that "affection for the self arises from the knowledge of the self," that too is incorrect. For it is not the case that wherever there is knowledge, there must be affection; there is no such universal concomitance (*vyāpti*), since affection is not observed even when one perceives grass, animals, and so forth. If you argue that there is no affection toward grass and such because they are not perceived as being useful to the self, then in that case, there is likewise no perception of the self as being useful to the self. Therefore, let there be no affection toward the self either. If you ask, "How can one who has affection for what is useful to the self lack affection for the self itself? we say: no, for affection toward things useful to the self occurs through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). When ignorance is cast off, however, there is no affection even for those things useful to the self.
Even the followers of the Sugata have accepted the knowledge of the self.

Furthermore, the entity that belongs to the next world is called the *ātman*. You have also made an effort to thoroughly understand it, yet this same fault remains even upon such an understanding. If you argue that the cessation of attachment results from the knowledge of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), we say no; for even in the position of momentariness, you yourself accept the existence of the relationship between benefactor and beneficiary (*upakāryopakārakabhāva*). Consequently, attachment certainly persists toward the infinite streams of existence (*santāna*) when they are perceived as having the nature of a self (*ātman*); otherwise, there would be no engagement in liberation (*mokṣa*). Therefore, the instruction to engage in the pursuit of liberation is useless; rather, it is precisely because of attachment to the self that one engages in the means to liberation just as one does in the means to pleasure.

Therefore, what was stated—"for whoever has affection for something, he is filled with joy by the pleasure of that thing, just as [one is] by the pleasure of a son and so forth"—is equally applicable to one's own continuum of consciousness.
[Thus, for those who deny the self, affection is untenable.]

Now, if those who profess the doctrine of no-self (*anātmavādin*) have no affection even for their own stream of consciousness (*jñānasantāna*), how could they have it for the streams of others? For it is not logical that one who has no affection even for their own self should have it for another. If you argue that there is affection for others due to compassion arising from great majesty (*mahānubhāvatā*), we say no; for this would entail that such a person acts without prior intelligence, being utterly deluded regarding their own interest. If you claim that the very act of working for the sake of others is the great man’s own interest, then he should also perform acts such as massaging the limbs of a courtesan, since the benefit of others is equally present there. If you say he does not do so because it would entail falling into hell and other lower realms, then surely his greatness of majesty would be truly great if he were to accept going to hell for the sake of others! Therefore, even for the proponent of no-self, affection certainly exists for their own stream of consciousness because they act to avoid their own suffering—just as people feel affection for their children and so forth. From that affection comes a thirst for happiness; from that, the Śākyan, by disregarding faults and perceiving qualities, becomes intensely thirsty and thinks, "This is mine," and thus takes up the means to achieve it. Because of this obsession with "mine," the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) does not cease even for a Buddha.

The statement, “the notion of ‘other’ regarding one’s own self,” and so forth, is also incorrect. For the faults of grasping (*parigraha*) and the like do not arise merely from the knowledge of the distinction between self and other; for even a Buddha possesses the mere knowledge of the distinction between others [and himself], otherwise he would not engage in giving instruction and the like. Furthermore, the cultivation of compassion (*karuṇā*) is accepted by you as the means for attaining omniscience. And compassion is not possible without the knowledge of the distinction between self and other. Indeed, the desire for others to be separated from suffering is preceded by the recollection of suffering in one's own self, and that is called pity (*kṛpā*). Therefore, the mere knowledge of the distinction between self and other is not the cause of craving, grasping, and so forth. What then? It is false conceptualization (*mithyā-saṃkalpa*); and thus the Blessed Vyāsa said:
"For if the objects of the senses were clearly conceptualized as being for one's harm,
then everyone moving within the range of the senses would be joined with misfortune.
(The refutation of the notion that the self is of the nature of a fault.)

First, this must be examined here: is it merely the designation "self" that is faulty here? Or is it the cognition "mine" or "I" that is faulty? Or is it the very object of that [cognition] that is faulty?
If the designation "self" is faulty, then we too shall employ another designation.

Now, if the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) is defective, how is it to be removed? Even for the proponents of momentary consciousness (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna-vādin*), the ego certainly exists; for we observe activity directed toward the attainment of the desired and the avoidance of the undesired, and there is the recognition: "I have experienced this," and "I know this. If it is argued that the ego arises from prior mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) even for one who maintains the doctrine of no-self (*anātmavāda*), and that it is removed through the practice of selflessness (*nairātmya*), this is not so; because there is no connection [between them]. It is logical that the cessation of the ego occurs through the practice of the absence of ego, just as the cessation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) occurs through the practice of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), or as the cessation of false knowledge occurs through the practice of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). But the self (*ātman*) is a different entity altogether; how, then, could the cessation of the ego occur through the practice of its non-existence? Otherwise, the cessation of the ego would result merely from the practice of being "devoid of intellect" (*nirbuddhatva*) by virtue of a mere statement.

Now, if it is argued that the self (*ātman*) is the object of the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), then as long as the self exists, the cessation of the ego-sense would not occur—no; for this is impossible according to both our own and others' views. First, in your view, an eternal entity cannot possess the capacity to produce anything at all. In our view, however, no single entity possesses such productive power; therefore, due to the absence of auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*), the ego-sense ceases even while its object—the self—persists, just as smoke ceases when fuel is absent even though fire persists. You too must necessarily accept this, otherwise, as long as the stream of cognition (*buddhisantāna*) does not cease, the ego-sense could not cease, since in your position the self is nothing other than cognition itself.

{The Refutation of the Defectiveness of the Knowledge of Eternality} Now, if it is argued that the knowledge of eternality and so forth is defective in this regard, that too is incorrect; because from the knowledge of non-eternality and so forth, there might still be engagement even in what is not to be done, out of a desire for self-preservation and the like. However, when one understands thus:
"Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new..."
"Likewise, casting off worn-out bodies, the embodied one enters into others that are new.
"Weapons do not cut this, fire does not burn this,
waters do not moisten it, and the wind does not dry it."

At that time, one becomes entirely indifferent toward the body and other such things. How, then, could there be attachment to them, aversion, and so forth? Accordingly, it has been stated in the *Prameyavibhāgasūtra* how the cognition of the body and so on as something to be abandoned arises from the knowledge of the reality of the self (*ātmatattvajñāna*). [This constitutes the proof that the knowledge of selflessness is the cause for the cessation of cyclic existence.]

The knowledge of selflessness (*nairātmyajñāna*) is indeed the cause of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), because it is a cognition based on error (*viparyayajñāna*), just like the determination of permanence in things that are impermanent. If it is argued that this is unestablished (*asiddha*), thinking: "The non-existence of a self has been established by proofs such as its being unproduced (*ajāta*); therefore, the knowledge of selflessness is not false," that is incorrect. For: "A property of an existent cannot exist when [the subject] is unestablished, nor can properties that deviate or depend on both [existence and non-existence]. How can that existence, which is a property contradictory to non-existence, be proven? (PV 1.191 = PVin 3.63; cf. TSP 504,19–20; NBhū 551,20–21; J 88,2–3)
The same fault applies even when proving non-existence, just as it does for existence.
[Regarding the doubt that words have conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as their object and its refutation:
But has this not already been stated here?
The referent of a word, established by conceptual construction arising from beginningless habitual tendencies, is a threefold locus of properties (dharmin) based on existence, non-existence, or both.

In that case, when there is no basis in an existent entity (*bhāvānupādāna*), the non-perception of the probandum (*sādhya*) is likewise the reason; it is not the non-existence of that very [probandum] itself, but rather the employment of the word [to express it]. Among these, the conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of blue and so forth has existence as its basis, because it is preceded by a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by the cognition of a specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). However, the conceptualization of a rabbit’s horn and so forth has non-existence as its basis, because it is preceded by a latent impression deposited by the cognition of non-existence. Furthermore, the conceptualization of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), formlessness (*amūrta*), and so forth, has both as its basis, since properties such as being an object of knowledge or being formless can pertain to both the existent and the non-existent. Thus, since the referent of a word is seen to be of three types, when there is doubt regarding that referent of words such as "self" (*ātman*), the fact of not having an existent entity as its basis is what is to be proven (*sādhya*); therefore, there is no fault such as the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddhatva*).

This too is incorrect. For it has already been established that words have real entities (*vastu*) as their objects, and it has also been refuted previously that they have conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*)—as connected to those entities—as their objects. Furthermore, on what basis is the fact that conceptualizations such as "the self" (*ātman*) do not have real entities as their material cause (*bhāvopādāna*) established? If you say it is because they are not perceived in that way, we say no; for that would be identical to the point to be proven (*sādhyaviśiṣṭatva*). Indeed, smoke does not have fire as its material cause simply because it is not perceived as such.

Moreover, even if a conceptualization of Mount Meru or Pātāla were to have those entities as its material cause, the non-existence of Mount Meru or Pātāla could not be determined merely by their non-perception.

Furthermore, since even the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of dharma, adharma, the Buddha, and so forth would have that [unreal mental construction] as their material cause (*upādāna*), they too would either be non-existent or the conventional usage of "existent" would be negated for them. If, however, there is an inference (*anumāna*) for their existence, then the negation of the conventional usage of "existent" is not appropriate in their case either; if this is so, then an inference has been established for the existence of the self (*ātman*) and other such things as well. Therefore, a negation here [of the self] is likewise untenable.
{The impossibility of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) if the self were eternal, and its refutation}

[Objection: But surely, because that which is eternal is unchanging, its connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth is untenable; or, if such a connection were possible, it would not be eternal. To this [the opponent] says: "What effect do rain and sun have on space? Their fruit is seen upon leather. If the self were like leather, it would be non-eternal; if it were equal to space, it would have no fruit. This too is incorrect. For, since the fault of "attaining what was not earned" (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and so forth has already been stated regarding non-eternality, it was previously explained that even the restriction to a single continuum (*ekasantāna*) is impossible. {The Doctrine of the Ārhata}

But another says: If the person (*puruṣa*) were eternal, because he would possess a single, unchanging nature, the succession of pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, and so forth would be impossible; the self would always be both happy and miserable, since that nature could not be destroyed. Nor is it the case that he is simply impermanent, for that would entail faults such as the arrival of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*). Therefore, only the position of non-absolutism (*anekānta*) is faultless. As it has been said: "O Lord, for those who are devoted to grasping at one-sided views and are thus enemies to themselves and others, there is neither wholesome nor unwholesome karma, nor indeed is there bondage or liberation anywhere."

And since the position of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda) is established by valid means of knowledge, he says: "A person, seeking a crown, a daughter, and gold, experiences grief, joy, and indifference— constituted by these three states— at the times of destruction, arising, and persistence."
He states that liberation does not result from the knowledge of the seven categories in an absolute sense:
"The soul and the non-soul, as well as influx and restraint,
likewise efflux and bondage, and liberation— this is held to be the [sevenfold] enumeration."
These [seven principles] have been proclaimed and should be fully understood as being characterized by the doctrine of *syādvāda*.
Through the knowledge of them, the soul is freed from the influx [of karma]; this is declared here to be liberation. (The Exposition of the Seven Principles)

<1> In this regard: "Because its intrinsic nature is consciousness (*cetanā*), the soul (*jīva*) is characterized by its modifications (*vikalpa*). The modifications of that consciousness are its synonyms: ignorance (*ajñāna*), pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), desire (*icchā*), and so forth; that which has these as its characteristics is the soul. <2> But that which is distinct from those is the non-soul (*ajīva*).
