<3> "Āsrava is characterized by the gateway for the influx of merit and demerit. It is called *āsrava* because it is like a flow (*āsrava*). What is the sense of this comparison? Just as the great ocean is filled day after day by the waters of rivers and other streams, so too is a living being incessantly filled by karmas that have entered through the gateways of false view and so forth; thus, the gateway of false view and so forth is *āsrava*.

"Restraint (*saṃvara*) has the characteristic of the cessation of the outflows (*āsrava*). It is called restraint because by means of it one is restrained. Just as there is no entry for a wicked person when a house is closed with a door-panel, likewise, when a person is restrained by the performance of wholesome deeds, there is no entry of karma characterized by merit and demerit—the cause of bondage. Because it closes the gateway for the influx of new karma, it is called restraint.

<5> “Nirjarā is characterized by the partial exhaustion of karma. Nirjarā is simply *nirjarā* (the act of wearing away). Just as poison whose potency has been neutralized by the power of mantras, medicinal herbs, and so forth, does not cause agitation, so too karma that has been acquired but whose essence (*rasa*) has been worn away by specific forms of austerity (*tapas*) does not yield the fruits of *saṃsāra*.

<6> “Bondage (*bandha*) is characterized by the mutual penetration and interpenetration of the self and karma. Bondage is like the act of binding. Just as a person bound by shackles or other fetters is rendered dependent and lacks autonomy, so too is one bound by the bondage of karma.

"Liberation is characterized by the total dissociation from karma. The meaning is that when there is independence—like being released from shackles and the like—a person becomes happy precisely by going to the desired destination.
{The nature of Syādvāda}

"Marked by *syādvāda* (the doctrine of manifoldness). This means: *syād asti* (in some sense, it exists), *syān nāsti* (in some sense, it does not exist), *syād asti ca nāsti ca* (in some sense, it both exists and does not exist), *syād avaktavyam* (in some sense, it is inexpressible), *syād asti cāvaktavyaṃ ca* (in some sense, it exists and is inexpressible), *syān nāsti cāvaktavyaṃ ca* (in some sense, it does not exist and is inexpressible), and *syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyaṃ ca* (in some sense, it exists, does not exist, and is inexpressible). This sevenfold formulation (*saptabhaṅgī*) is called *syādvāda*. Living beings (*jīva*) and other categories are to be understood as qualified by this. If one asks what the characteristics of this sevenfold formulation are, it is said: "The sevenfold formulation is the conceptualization of affirmation and negation, not contradictory [to each other], regarding a single object through the force of inquiry and by means of accepted valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). For example: "In some sense, it is a jar; in some sense, it is not a jar; in some sense, it is both a jar and not a jar; in some sense, it is inexpressible; in some sense, it is a jar and inexpressible; in some sense, it is not a jar and inexpressible; and in some sense, it is a jar, not a jar, and inexpressible."

"In this regard, the jar exists by its own nature (*svātman*), but does not exist by the nature of another (*parātman*). That which is the locus of the persistence of the cognition and designation of 'jar' is its own nature; whereas that which is the locus of the persistence of the cognition and designation of something else—such as a cloth or the state of being shards—is the nature of another. If the jar did not exist even by its own nature, then the conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) of 'jar' would not occur at all. Likewise, if it existed even by the nature of another, then the conventional usage of 'cloth' and so forth would also apply to it. Therefore, the jar exists by way of its own form (*svarūpa*), but does not exist by way of the form of another (*pararūpa*)."

The pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*) and non-pot-ness (*aghaṭatva*) presented through the aforementioned modes are not distinct from one another. For if they were distinct, there would be no persistence of their respective cognitions and designations; consequently, there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and so forth. But such is not the case; therefore, this entity consists of both natures. As it sequentially assumes the denotability of those terms, it is called both a "pot" and a "non-pot. If that entity which consists of both natures were called merely a "pot," then because it would not include its other nature, it would be unreal (*atattva*). If, on the other hand, it were called merely a "non-pot," then because it would not incorporate its own nature, it would be false (*anṛta*). A real entity is not merely that much [one-sided]. Nor is there any other word that expresses its state as consisting of both natures. Therefore, because it transcends the range of speech, it is said to be "inexpressible" (*avaktavya*). When it is indicated by way of presenting its pot-nature and by defining its nature as inexpressible, that very same object is expressed as: "It may be a pot and inexpressible" (*syād ghaṭaś cāvaktavyaś ca*). When it is to be taught by way of demonstrating its non-pot aspect as previously defined and by way of the path of expressibility, that very same object is expressed as: "It may be a non-pot and inexpressible" (*syād aghaṭaś cāvaktavyaś ca*). By virtue of presenting those two [natures] either successively or simultaneously, that very same object manifests with those designations and is thus expressed as: "It may be a pot, a non-pot, and inexpressible" (*syād ghaṭaś cāghaṭaś cāvaktavyaś ca*).
"In this way, the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī) should be applied to all objects. There is no object whatsoever that does not possess a sevenfold predication."

[Objection: "Is it not the case that because you do not accept exclusivity (ekānta), you necessarily arrive at the acceptance of non-exclusivity (anekānta)? Therefore, that itself is an exclusivity. How then can there be the sevenfold predication (saptabhaṅgī) in all cases? [Reply: No; for even in the case of non-exclusivity, one does not accept exclusivity. For instance: "It may be exclusive (syād ekāntaḥ); it may be non-exclusive (syād anaikāntaḥ); it may be both exclusive and non-exclusive (syād ekāntaś cānekāntaś ca); it may be inexpressible (syād avaktavyaḥ); it may be both exclusive and inexpressible (syād ekāntaś cāvaktavyaś ca); it may be both non-exclusive and inexpressible (syād anaikāntaś cāvaktavyaś ca); it may be both exclusive, non-exclusive, and inexpressible (syād ekāntaś cānekāntaś cāvaktavyaś ca). [This concludes the refutation of the Ārhata doctrine.]

To this it is replied: as for the statement beginning with "for those who are attached to the view of absolute certainty," that is incorrect; because the occurrence of wholesome and unwholesome actions and so forth is possible only within the framework of non-absolutism (*anekāntapakṣa*). To explain: if there were the absolute position that whoever is the agent of an action is also the enjoyer of its fruit, then the engagement of a discerning person in those actions for the sake of attaining the desired and avoiding the undesired would be logical. But under the doctrine of non-absolutism, it would follow that even what is done by one might be enjoyed by another. In that case, a discerning person would not engage even in acts such as eating; for even a naked ascetic (*nagnaśramaṇaka*) would obtain satisfaction from acts of eating performed by a king or others. Indeed, it would be an adherence to absolutism if [the result] did not occur [in the other].
The collection of faults in the position of non-absolutism (anekāntavāda).

Furthermore, by one who perceives the faults in both the eternal and the non-eternal and thus accepts the non-exclusive (anekānta) position, there would necessarily be an acceptance of both sides. And if those are accepted, then the faults stated for both positions also follow. Who other than a fool would know how to avoid these faults in such a way? Therefore, the self (*ātman*) is indeed eternal; it is said to be "happy" when happiness inherent in it arises, and "suffering" when suffering arises. Only the arising and perishing of pleasure, pain, and so forth belong to the self; the self itself is eternal. Nevertheless, it is designated as possessing that [quality] through each respective quality that arises or perishes, just as Caitra is designated as "staff-bearing," "earring-wearing," or "umbrella-holding"—or as "staff-less," "earring-less," or "umbrella-less"—due to his connection with or disconnection from a staff, earrings, or an umbrella.
{The refutation of the statement that Samantabhadra has a crown on his head}

The claim that "one seeking a bracelet, a crown, or gold" and so forth is also untenable. For in that case, there is indeed the destruction of the prior whole (avayavin) which was endowed with the universals (*jāti*) of being a bracelet and being gold; yet even upon its destruction, the universal itself is not destroyed, because—just like the universal of gold—the universal of being a bracelet is recognized (*pratyabhijñāna*) in another individual instance. Furthermore, since no subsequent substance endowed with the nature of a bracelet has been produced, one who seeks such a thing feels grief; and since the previous substance endowed with the nature of a crown did not exist [before] but now one endowed with that same universal has arisen, one who seeks that feels joy. However, because both the prior and subsequent wholes possess the connection with the universal of gold, one who seeks that remains neutral, just as when someone deposits goods in a merchant's house, and the merchant, having used them for his own purposes, returns them to him in that same state; consequently, that person experiences only neutrality.

The universal *suvarṇatva* (gold-ness), however, exists even in each individual part; therefore, even when that composite whole is destroyed, because the cognition of "gold" continues uninterrupted among the parts and in the immediately succeeding other composite whole, there arises the conviction that it has not been destroyed. Or, as in the case of a lamp, the water of the Ganges, and so forth, because something similar occurs in immediate succession, one thinks "this is that very same thing," and the seeker of that object maintains a state of indifference. Therefore, neither permanence nor impermanence belongs to a single entity. For impermanence is well known to be perishability, and permanence is non-perishability; since these two are contradictory, they cannot coexist in one place. Indeed, nothing appears that is both destroyed and not destroyed at once.

Even though there is the destruction of the form of the mat (*kaṭa*) and the production of the form of the crown (*mukuṭa*), while the goldsmith remains constant, nevertheless, in this case, the establishment of both permanence and impermanence for a single entity [is untenable], because the three forms do not possess mutually exclusive properties (*anyonyadharmāsaṃsarga*). Or, if there were such a commingling of properties (*saṃsarga*), then just as one who desires the bracelet would experience grief, so too would joy and indifference occur [simultaneously]. For this very reason, the three forms are not identical. If it is argued that even if they are distinct, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is impossible, we say no; for coreferentiality exists in respect to that which possesses those qualities (*tadvati*). Just as, despite the difference between a staff and an earring, there is coreferentiality in the person who is their substratum, expressed as "the man with the staff" (*daṇḍī*) or "the man with the earring" (*kuṇḍalī*). If, on the other hand, there were non-difference, then from the very perception of the form of the bracelet, there would also have to be the perception of the form of the crown and so forth, since it is impossible for perceived and unperceived forms to be one. Or, if they were one, there would be no distinction even between a donkey and a camel. If it is argued that there is indeed mutual difference among the successive states (*paryāya*), but not between the state and the possessor of the state (*paryāyiparyāyin*), we say no; for even in that case, difference is established because they are perceived through mutual exclusion. To explain: when a goldsmith is perceived in relation to an armlet (*keyūra*) and so forth, the form of the mat is not perceived; likewise, when the form of the royal seat or the mat is perceived, the goldsmith is not perceived. Therefore, due to the imposition of contradictory properties such as perception and non-perception, there is indeed difference, just as between a donkey and a camel.

{The suspicion that even difference is non-exclusive, leading to the absence of an example in the case of exclusivity}: Now, let it be granted that there is difference; nevertheless, it is incorrect to say that it is "difference alone," because [according to the Jaina view] it may be difference, it may be non-difference, it may be both difference and non-difference, it may be inexpressible, it may be both difference and inexpressible, it may be both non-difference and inexpressible, and it may be both difference, non-difference, and inexpressible. Thus, since the entire world is permeated by the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), there is no example whatsoever available for establishing an exclusive [position]. {The refutation thereof}.

[Objection: Surely the nature of the Jina—consisting of liberation, omniscience, and so forth—is absolutely distinct from the natures of donkeys, camels, pigs, and the like, which are extremely base. Thus, how can there be no example [for your position]? For you certainly cannot say: "The Jina in his state of liberation might be most base, he might not be most base, he might be both most base and not most base, he might be inexpressible, he might be both most base and inexpressible, he might be both not most base and inexpressible, or he might be both most base and not most base and inexpressible. If you claim that even here the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*) is accepted, then this—which is devoid of scripture and logic and is propounded out of mere rivalry—does not please the minds of the wise. If, indeed, you were at some time to worship a donkey, a camel, or a pig as if they were the Jina, and were to eat stones, excrement, and the like as if they were molasses, curd, and buttermilk, then the establishment of any absolute distinction would be impossible. For what excellence does the Jina possess that is not found in donkeys, camels, and the like? Or what is the baseness of donkeys, camels, and the like that is not found in the Jina, such that he alone is worshipped to the exclusion of donkeys, camels, and so forth? Likewise, what defect do stones, excrement, and the like have that is not found in molasses and the like? Or what excellence do molasses and the like have that is not found in stones and the like, such that molasses and the like are eaten while stones and the like are avoided? If you argue that there is indeed some excellence in these very things by virtue of which activity occurs toward them specifically, then there is no non-absolutism (*anekānta*) everywhere. If, on the other hand, your position is that there is absolutism in some cases and non-absolutism in others, then that wherein there is absolutism is your example. But for you, who maintain non-absolutism in all respects, no example exists anywhere for the proof of non-absolutism. For instance: whatever is different from X is absolutely different from X because it is a distinct entity, just like the Jina and so forth are [absolutely] different from donkeys, camels, and the like. [Objection: There is also non-difference here in the form of existence (*sattva*) and so forth. [Reply: No; for an example is employed only for that aspect whose absolute difference between the two is established. If, however, the absolute difference of anything is not established, then—due to the absence of any rule for distinguishing between means and non-means, or between what is edible and what is inedible—there would follow no restriction on anyone’s activity toward anything. This has already been stated.
{The Refutation of Flawless Speech}

Furthermore, as for this statement—"The jar exists by its own nature, but does not exist by the nature of another"—what follows from this? If it means that a single jar possesses multiple properties (*dharma*), then there is no dispute, since we also admit that even a single substratum (*dharmin*) can possess multiple properties consisting of both affirmation and negation. If, however, you mean that the jar consists of both existence and non-existence, what is the meaning of "consisting of both"? If it means that it possesses both properties, then, as stated, there is no dispute. But if you mean that the jar itself is the non-existence of anything other than itself, then surely you have accepted the Buddhist position, because of their assertion that "there is no exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) other than the excluded thing (*vyāvṛtta*). And the refutation of that has already been explained at length.
"The establishment of a real entity (*vastu*) depends upon valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and valid cognition exists only in the case of an exclusive doctrine (*ekāntavāda*).

[Objection: But in our view, there is indeed a distinction between existence and its opposite, non-existence, because we admit that things possess a dual nature. [Reply: No; for the reality of an object is not established by mere assertion. The existence of categories is established through valid cognition, yet you have not stated any valid cognition by which that dual nature could be established. We, however, have stated the valid cognition: if something is a different entity from another, it is a different entity from that other only in a non-exclusive sense (*anekāntena*)."

Furthermore, the intended absence of a cloth and so forth is not of the nature of a jar, because it is the absence of a cloth and so forth, like the destruction (pradhvaṃsa) of that [cloth]. How then does the appearance "the jar is not a cloth" arise? This is based on mutual non-existence (itaretarābhāva). But what is the relation between a positive entity and mutual non-existence? Even if there were a relation, the cognition "there is no cloth in the jar" would still occur. As for the question "what is the relation?", that is not a valid objection, because the answer has already been stated: it has been said here that there is a certain particular proximity between a positive entity and its corresponding absence, by virtue of which they are not perceived separately. In that case, let whatever name one wishes be applied to it.
The negation of the identity of existence and non-existence.

As for what was said—that even when there is a relation, there would be the cognition "the cloth does not exist in the jar," just as there is the cognition of the absence of a jar on the ground—that is incorrect. For, just as with positive entities (*bhāva*), a difference in cognition is logically established through a specific type of relation. Just as a difference in cognition is observed due to a specific relation between positive entities—such as the cognitions "there is indigo substance in the bowl," "the cloth is blue," or "the object is perceived"—it is understood that a specific relation of non-existence (*abhāva*) likewise serves as the cause for a difference in cognition. Indeed, in all cases, a specific cause is established by means of a specific effect.

Moreover, it has been stated that the non-existence (abhāva) is perceived as dependent upon another. Therefore, the cognition of the non-existence of a thing occurs in the same manner as its counter-positive (pratiyogin) is presented to the mind. Consequently, the non-existence of a jar—which is presented to the mind as being located on the ground—is perceived as if it were itself located on the ground, as in the thought, "There is no jar here. However, when that counter-positive is presented to the mind as being identical with the locus itself, then its non-existence also appears as having that very nature, as in "This cloth is not a jar. Thus, there is no identity between existence and non-existence.

{The Refutation of the Proof of the Non-Difference between Pot-ness and Non-pot-ness} As for what was stated— that pot-ness and non-pot-ness are not different from one another— that is the speech of one who is utterly deluded, because the non-difference of affirmation and negation is contradicted by the common experience of all people. {Even in the case of the prasajya and paryudāsa [negations], non-difference is untenable}.

Furthermore, non-difference is untenable even under the two alternatives of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) and relative negation (*paryudāsa*). First, regarding the alternative of absolute negation: "non-pot-ness" (*aghaṭatva*) would simply be the absence of pot-ness; yet that very thing cannot be its own absence. If it were so, the absence of a snake would be the non-snake itself, and consequently, one would experience fear from that absence just as from the presence of a snake. Moreover, there would be an identical perception of both places—one devoid of it and one not devoid of it.

Even in the case of the position of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), "non-pot-ness" is said to be something other than pot-ness, such as cloth-ness and so forth; and that is indeed distinct [from it]. For if there were no difference, then the cognition and designation of "cloth" would persist even with respect to pots and the like, and the cognition of "pot" and so forth would occur even with respect to cloth.
[For it is impossible for one thing to lack the nature of another through the nature of that other.]

It is also incorrect to say that "this [pot] is a non-pot by virtue of its nature as a cloth. For, in the first case, is the pot—which already exists—made into a non-pot by virtue of its nature as a cloth? Or is it merely made known as such? Regarding the first position, there is no proof. Indeed, just as a lump of clay is perceived being made into a pot by a potter and others, one never observes that very same thing being made into a non-pot by anyone, either at that time or at another. If it were a non-pot because it has perished, then at that moment it would not be a pot; therefore, it is not the case that the pot itself is made into a non-pot by virtue of its nature as a cloth. Nor is it merely made known as such, for that would entail the error of false cognition (*mithyājñapti*), like the cognition of silver in what is not silver. If it is argued that it is called a "non-pot" simply because it does not appear in the form of a cloth, we say no; this is contradictory. Precisely because it does not appear in the form of a cloth, it is for that very reason said to be a single entity, namely, the pot itself.

Furthermore, even where it is said that something possesses a dual nature by virtue of being the substratum for both properties, even there it does not possess those two natures in relation to its own self and another’s self, as in the case of "it is blue and it is a lotus. For it is not said that it is blue and a lotus *by way of another's nature*; rather, it is so stated only by way of its own nature. Likewise, the nature of being existent and non-existent must also be predicated only by way of its own nature. Existence or non-existence in another form is not primary; for gold and the like do not exist in the form of clay and the like, nor is a sky-flower non-existent in the form of a pillar and the like, since it is non-existent only by way of its own [impossible] nature. Thus, if entities were to possess a dual nature, then by way of its own nature a jar would be both a jar and a non-jar. Since its being a non-jar is merely secondary when it is a non-jar only by way of another's nature—just as a young brahmin might be called "fire" or a boy "lion"—that dual-natured thing is therefore secondary. Primarily, however, whatever is of a certain nature by way of its own nature is of that very nature alone.
The impossibility of possessing both natures by way of its own essential nature.

If it is argued that a thing is of a dual nature by its very essence, we say no; for this would result in the lack of a fixed distinction between desirable and undesirable natures, which in turn would lead to the impossibility of the worldly conduct of living beings. For just as the existence of pleasure and so forth is desired by living beings, so too is its non-existence undesired. And just as the existence of pain and so forth is undesired, so too is its non-existence desired. Consequently, if things such as the means to pleasure and pain were of a dual nature (both existent and non-existent) by their very essence, there could be no engagement in activity or withdrawal from it for the sake of attaining the former or avoiding the latter, because they would be established as both desirable and undesirable simultaneously. Furthermore, this cause of pleasure and so forth, being existent, would be engaged in producing its own effect, yet being non-existent, it would be unable to produce it. Even while failing to act, it would not attain liberation because it is existent. Thus, being pulled in opposite directions by existence and non-existence, what state would it reach? Alas, this poor wretch has fallen into an insurmountable calamity through the evil intellect of the naked mendicant!
The lack of definitive establishment regarding the words of the Tīrthaṅkaras and so forth.

Furthermore, is the word of your Tīrthaṅkara true or false? It is not tenable to say it is "only true," for that would entail the fallacy of an absolute doctrine (*ekāntavāda*). If, however, you maintain that even here there is the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*)—namely, "it may be true," "it may be false," "it may be both," "it may be inexpressible," and so forth—then the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-apramāṇa*) becomes untenable, because the doctrine of "may-be-ness" (*syādvāda*) applies without distinction to everything. Likewise, the practice of your Tīrthaṅkaras would also be such that it "may be contemptible," "may be non-contemptible," or "may be both. The same would apply to the practices of thieves and others; thus, there would be no distinction whatsoever. Consequently, the established order of influx (*āsrava*) and so forth would be untenable. For your own system maintains that only those with distinguished practice achieve restraint (*saṃvara*), shedding of karma (*nirjarā*), and liberation (*mokṣa*), whereas those with undistinguished practice incur only influx (*āsrava*) and bondage (*bandha*). If both types of practice—distinguished and undistinguished—are themselves indeterminate, being "both distinguished and undistinguished," then how can there be any established order regarding influx and the rest?
The lack of systematic order regarding the living beings and so forth.

Likewise, the distinction between the living (*jīva*) and the non-living (*ajīva*) is also untenable. For according to the doctrine of manifoldness (*syādvāda*), the living might be non-living, and the non-living might be living; how, then, could there be a fixed distinction between the two? If you claim that such a distinction exists despite being unfixed, does it exist in an ultimate sense, or are you merely deceiving us in this way? Indeed, no fixed distinction can be established unless one accepts the position of absolute [determination]. The very mode by which the determination of things is asserted is their real nature (*tāttvika-svabhāva*). That which has an undetermined nature is not real, because it is a distortion—just as the yellow color perceived in a crystal and the like is not its true nature. Therefore, in reality, an entity does not consist of both existence and non-existence.
The refutation of the view that an entity possesses the nature of both permanence and impermanence.

Nor is it of the nature of both eternal and non-eternal. For instance: if a substance such as the self (*ātman*) were eternal by way of its own substantial form (*paryāya*), then in reality it would be exclusively eternal; in that case, any non-eternality conceived through the non-eternality of its modes (*paryāya*) would be merely figurative. Furthermore, it is not logically tenable for it to be both destroyed and not destroyed by its very own nature. Moreover, all worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) of living beings is observed to be preceded by the certainty that "it is indeed destroyed," which too would not exist [under your view]. If it is argued that the self also possesses non-eternality in the form of pleasure and so forth, this is not so; for pleasure and the like are distinct from the self, and their distinctness has been established in the section refuting the Śākya (Buddhist) doctrine.

If it is argued that non-difference also exists, we say no; for non-difference is sublated by the very ascertainment of difference, as in the case of the moon and the sun. Moreover, if non-difference were real, then difference would be unreal, like the second moon perceived by one suffering from ophthalmia.

One who asserts that the *puruṣa* is eternal in one respect and non-eternal in another must be asked this: are those two aspects distinct from the *puruṣa* and from each other, or are they non-distinct? In the case of their being distinct, the *puruṣa* cannot possess both eternity and non-eternity by virtue of those two [aspects], because that would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of the principle. In the case of their being non-distinct, it follows that by the very same aspect through which there is eternity, there is also non-eternity; the refutation for that has already been stated. If they are both distinct and non-distinct, then too one must ask: is there distinction by the very same aspect through which there is non-distinction, or is it by a different aspect? If it is by the same, then the same refutation applies again. If it is by a different aspect, then an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) results. Consequently, there could be no certainty anywhere as to "this is exactly thus. In the absence of such certainty, the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which is to be accomplished through worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) preceded by that certainty, would not belong to anyone. Yet, we observe that for the intelligent, the human goal arises from activity preceded by certainty. Therefore, there is no such established rule regarding eternity, non-eternity, difference, non-difference, and so forth.
The impossibility of being both different and non-different according to the Mīmāṃsaka position.

In the Mīmāṃsaka position, however, the state of being both different and non-different (*bhinna-abhinnatva*) is untenable up to the end of the discussion on permanence. For in their view, the self (*ātman*) is held to be strictly eternal. It is not logical for that [self] to have identity (*tādātmya*) with impermanent things such as pleasure and so forth, because that would contradict its eternity and unity; or else, the plurality and impermanence of pleasure and so forth would be contradicted. Yet, there is no lack of identity either, since you admit the position of being both different and non-different. Nor is the position of non-difference [tenable], because the faults [of that position] have already been stated. Even when difference is admitted, you have not entirely abandoned the position of non-difference; therefore, under the position of non-difference, the consequence follows that the person (*puruṣa*) would be impermanent and manifold. Under the position of difference, however, this consequence does not follow—thus, you have entered into the Jina’s doctrine (*jinamata*).
The Refutation of the Universal Being Both Different and Non-different from Particulars.

By this, the view that the universal (*sāmānya*) is both different and non-different from the particulars (*vyakti*) is also refuted. For even in that case, to the extent that there is difference, to that same extent the properties of the universal and the particular would not coalesce; consequently, the universal would not possess such properties as eternality and pervasiveness. Alternatively, by virtue of the identity of the particulars with the universal, the particulars would incur [the properties of] eternality and so forth; and thus, lamps and other things, which are exclusively characterized by impermanence and non-pervasiveness, would no longer be perceived. If, on the other hand, the universal is absolutely different from the particulars in its nature as eternality and so forth, then it is not different from them in any way whatsoever. For that which constitutes the very form of the universal is precisely its being a distinct entity from the particulars; and since that [distinct entity] possesses properties such as eternality, it cannot be non-different [from the particulars]. Even if there were non-difference between the universal and the particular through some other essential nature (*svarūpāntara*), there would still be no [true] non-difference, because that other essential nature would not consist of the universal itself.
For two distinct things, there is no restriction regarding their spatial separation.

Now, if the universal (*sāmānya*) were absolutely distinct [from the particular], then it would sometimes be perceived even with a difference in location; this is not so, because [the universal] is not non-exclusive with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*) and other attributes. Or, for example, pleasure and the like are not perceived as having a difference in location from the body. Furthermore, if a difference in location were perceived by another difference in location, that difference in location would likewise be perceived by another difference in location, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Moreover, since atoms, space, and so forth lack a difference in location despite their mutual distinction, they would consequently be non-different. By this, the argument that there is a difference [between the universal and the particular] due to a difference in sense organs is refuted. However, a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) is indeed perceived between the universal and the particular, because of the cognition of differences in essential nature such as being eternal or non-eternal, and being inclusive or exclusive; enough of this digression. Thus, when an absolute difference between attribute (*dharma*) and substrate (*dharmin*) is established, the *puruṣa*—endowed with attributes such as eternity and omnipresence—is established as the substratum of knowledge and the rest.

{The Refutation of the Sāṃkhya Doctrine and its Rejection} Now, it may be objected that it is not logical for the *puruṣa* (spirit) to be the substratum of cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth, because that would entail [the *puruṣa*] being an effect of *pradhāna* (primordial matter). Whatever is permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion is entirely an effect of *pradhāna*, just like the objects such as sound and the rest. To this we say: no, because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*). For indeed, there is no valid evidence whatsoever for the existence of *pradhāna*. {Presentation of Evidence for *Pradhāna*}

The Pradhāna exists because of [the evidence of] (1) homogeneity (*anvaya*), (2) limited magnitude (*parimāṇa*), (3) activity (*śakti-pravṛtti*), and (4) the relationship of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), as well as (5) manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*). That which produces modifications (*vikāra*) or in which modifications are deposited is the Pradhāna, the fundamental cause. And that is determined from five points; for instance: (1) **From Homogeneity:** The proof of the Pradhāna is as follows: those entities under dispute are preceded by a single cause, because they share a common nature, like a jar, a bowl, and so forth. That which is the single cause is the Pradhāna.

(2) [The proof of Pradhāna] from finitude: Furthermore, because they are finite, like roots and so forth. For instance, in the case of rice, a limitation is observed among the interconnected parts—the root, sprout, leaf, stalk, joint, panicle, awn, husk, flower, pericarp, grain, and kernel. Likewise, there is a limitation of the various differentiated entities (bhedas) under consideration: the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the five gross elements, the five types of error, and so on. Therefore, these differentiated entities must also be joined together within some single cause; that in which they are joined is Pradhāna.

(3) *The primary cause is established by virtue of capacity.* Furthermore, because activity proceeds from capacity, the capacity capable of producing the effect is observed in all three times through examples such as the nature of clay. The capacity of the nature of clay is understood to reside in its own causes; the capacity of those causes likewise resides in their own causes, and so on, until one reaches that which has no further cause.
Thus, the primary cause is established by virtue of [the continuity of] activity.

By the word "power" (*śakti*), the effect itself is denoted as existing in an unmanifest form. Its transition into a manifest state is called "activity" (*pravṛtti*). Power exists even prior to activity, because we observe activity in things that have already acquired their own nature. It exists at the time of activity as well, because we observe its disappearance. It exists even after that, because we observe activity once again. Thus, since all manifest things proceed from this power, that power, which persists eternally, is called "Pradhāna" (the Primary Cause).
[The proof for Pradhāna follows from the relationship between cause and effect.]

For this reason as well, the Pradhāna exists, because the relationship of cause and effect is observed, as in the case of a chair and so forth. By the term "relationship of cause and effect," the relationship of benefactor and beneficiary (upakāryopakārakabhāva) is expressed. For it is observed that things existing in a relationship of benefactor and beneficiary originate from a single cause, such as a chair and its parts. Furthermore, there exists a mutual relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between the elements (bhūtas) as effects and one another, as well as between humans and so forth; therefore, these have a single cause. (5) [The proof of the Pradhāna] is by virtue of the diversity of forms (vaiśvarūpyāt).

For this reason also, Pradhāna exists, because of the perception of manifold forms (*vaiśvarūpya*), as in the case of milk and the like. For example: from milk comes curd; from curd, whey and clarified butter (*ghṛta*); from the consumption of that, nourishment; and from that, sons and so forth. Sometimes there is the decoction of a dead body; the decomposition of a putrefied body results in the state of worms. It is heard in the science of tree-life (*vṛkṣāyurveda*) that a putrefied body is used for the growth of trees. Thus, trees also have that [body] as their cause; from the tree comes fruit; from the fruit comes sap; from the consumption of that, nourishment and strength—all this exists in the milk, precisely because of the non-difference between cause and effect. In this way, the existence of immobile things in mobile ones, and of mobile things in immobile ones, occurs without the destruction of their respective classes. Thus, everything has everything as its essence. Due to the obstruction by place, time, form, and instrumental causes, there is no manifestation at the same time. This entire manifoldness of the mobile and immobile is the transformational product (*pāriṇāmika*) of water and earth. The transformation of water and so forth belongs to something else; that too belongs to another; that too to another; and that too to another, until there is a point of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) somewhere. And that wherein there is non-distinction is Pradhāna.

{Refutation of the Primary Proofs} All of this is untenable. First, as for the argument that [the effect] must exist because it is "endowed" (anvita), that is not so; for the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika), since persons (puruṣa) are also endowed with such qualities as consciousness (caitanya), existence (sattva), and knowability (jñeyatva). If, on the other hand, "being endowed" is intended to mean "being associated with the attributes of the cause," even then the example lacks the property to be proven (sādhyavikala), because it is unestablished that jars, bowls, and the like are preceded by a single cause.

Now, it might be argued: "Whatever particulars are permeated by something are seen to be of that very nature, just as pieces of sandalwood permeated by sandalwood-essence are not distinct from sandalwood; and just as jars and other objects permeated by clay are not non-clay in nature, so too all entities are permeated by pleasure, pain, and delusion; therefore, all are of the nature of pleasure and so forth. This is not so, because the reason is unestablished (*asiddhatvāt*). For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the fact that all entities are permeated by pleasure and the rest. [This concludes the statement regarding the pervasion of all entities by pleasure and so forth.]

But has it not been stated as a proof: "Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell—these five are all specific arrangements of the three [qualities], pleasure, pain, and delusion. Why? Because each set of five has a single common effect. The repetition [of the word "five"] is stated for the purpose of including the three pentads of the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types. The repetition should also be understood here in the phrase "because of having a single common effect."

In that regard, a single effect of the five *sāttvika* [transformations] is observed: serenity, lightness, elation, attachment, horripilation, and joy. To illustrate: upon hearing the words "A son has been born to you," his serenity arises and his senses become healthy. Lightness is the buoyancy of the body; elation is the state of being a giver of means for satisfaction; attachment is the power directed toward that [object]; horripilation is the bristling of the hair; and joy is happiness. This should be applied similarly to touch and the other [objects].

Likewise, among the five rajasic [senses], one function is observed: drying up, burning, breaking, stiffening, agitation, and aversion. In that regard, upon hearing the words "your son is dead," there occurs drying up, which is an intense longing for water; burning is suffering; breaking is the discharge of tears, sweat, impurities, and so forth; stiffening is the lack of knowledge regarding a remedy, such as thinking "what shall I do?"; agitation is restlessness; and aversion is the desire to act in a contrary manner. This should be applied similarly to touch and the other objects of the senses.

Likewise, a single effect is observed for the five [qualities] characterized by *tamas*: covering (*varaṇa*), depression (*sādana*), destruction (*apadhvaṃsa*), loathsomeness (*bībhatsa*), and dejection (*dainya*). Among these, upon hearing the words "your son is dead," there is *varaṇa*, which is the obstruction of action; *sādana* is despondency; *apadhvaṃsa* is the loss of luster or the disappearance of conviction; *bībhatsa* is a state of mutilated appearance; *dainya* is being intent on begging for anything at all; and *gaurava* is the incapacity to lift even one's own hand and so forth. This should be applied similarly to touch and the other objects. And since the five great elements, such as earth, are composed of these [objects] like sound and the rest, they too are merely particular arrangements of *sattva* and the other qualities. Likewise, the same effect—serenity and so forth—is produced by the thirteen instruments consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. Similarly, the same effect—serenity and so forth—is produced by the principles of illumination, activity, and restraint, which consist of the divine, human, and animal realms. Therefore, the entire world is merely an arrangement of pleasure and the other qualities.
{The refutation of that}

This too is incorrect. Even if sound and the other [objects] do indeed produce effects such as serenity (*prasāda*), what follows from their being of the nature of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth? For there is no necessary connection (*pratibandha*) here. But was it not stated: "Sound and the rest are of the nature of pleasure and so forth, because they produce serenity and the like, just like pleasure itself"? No; that argument is *kālātyayāpadiṣṭa* (vitiated by lapse of time). For if sound and the rest were of the nature of pleasure, it would follow that they are perceivable solely by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and it would further follow that deaf persons and others would not exist. Indeed, pleasure and the like are not things that cannot be grasped by those lacking the sense of hearing and so forth. Furthermore, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell would not have their respective objects grasped by specific senses, since they would possess a single nature. Moreover, it would follow that the cognition of pleasure and the like would occur without distinction, just like the cognition of blue and the like. Just as when an object has the nature of blue, there occurs for all observers of it an indistinguishable appearance of blue, so too, if an external object were of the nature of pleasure, then the appearance of pleasure and so forth would likewise be indistinguishable for all observers of it. In that case, there would be no such distinctions as: "in regard to that very same object, for one there is pleasure, for another pain, for one it is intense, for another it is mild," and so on. Therefore, sound and the rest are not of the nature of pleasure and the like.
{The Refutation of the View that Space and Other Elements are Produced from Sound and Other Qualities}

As for what was stated—that "these [elements] are composed of sound and so forth," and so on—that is conceived in exactly the opposite way. For it is space and the other elements that originate sound and the rest, and not sound and the rest that originate space and the others, because space and atoms are eternal. Furthermore, that which is originated by something else is not necessarily identical in nature to its cause. For if there were no difference, the very relationship of cause and effect would not exist, since activity toward oneself is a contradiction in both the established and unestablished states. Nor is there a rule of identity in genus between cause and effect, because even through direct perception we observe a difference in genus between the weaver, the shuttle, and the cloth. Nor is identity established between a genus and that which possesses the genus, such that there would be non-difference between cause and effect despite their sharing a single genus; for the absolute difference between a genus and its possessor has been demonstrated at length. Moreover, by virtue of being connected with *sattā* (existence), it would follow that all persons are one. And from that—

"The root-primal nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification; the seven beginning with the Great One (mahat) are both primal natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only a modification; and the person (puruṣa) is neither a primal nature nor a modification"—this accepted doctrine is contradicted [by your position].
Because they possess form and other [sensory qualities], earth and the other [elements] do not have the nature of pleasure and so forth.

Furthermore, because they possess properties contrary to those of form (*rūpa*) and so forth, earth and the other elements do not have pleasure (*sukha*) and the like as their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If it is argued that earth and the others are specific transformations (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) of pleasure and the like, are these [transformations] different from pleasure and the like, or non-different? If they were different, then—like the *puruṣa* (Spirit)—they would lack the three *guṇas*. If, however, they were non-different, then their possession of form and the like, as well as their perceptibility by the senses, would be contradicted, just as in the case of the *pradhāna*. If it is argued that when a different property (*dharma*) arises, the conventional designation "earth" and so forth applies to the *sattva* and the other *guṇas* themselves, then if that different property is distinct from them, they would—as in the case of the *puruṣa*—lack the three *guṇas*. And if it is non-distinct, then—as in the case of the *pradhāna*—the impossibility of fixed place and time would follow, as well as the consequence of there being no difference in essential nature (*svabhāva-vailakṣaṇya*). If it is argued that they are different in one respect and the same in another, this has already been refuted under the point that things cannot be "indefinable" in terms of being either identical or different. Moreover, this would lead to the refutation of earth and the other elements. If it is argued that [earth, etc. are "indefinable" (*anirvacanīya*) in terms of being either identical to or different from the principles (*tattva*), we say no; for this contradicts the accepted doctrine of twenty-five principles. Indeed, if intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest are not defined as being different from the *pradhāna*, the twenty-five principles are not logically established. Furthermore, since the mutual distinction between sound and the other objects, the sense organs, and earth and the other elements is established through the imposition of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmādhyāsa*), how can you fail to define their difference? Or else, you would have to fail to define the difference of the *puruṣa* as well. Moreover, although pleasure, pain, and delusion share the common property of having forms and so forth perceivable by a single sense organ, their absolute difference is admitted. Yet, although sound and the other objects possess the contrary property of being grasped by specific sense organs, you claim they are not absolutely different—oh, what "conformity to authority" this is! Even though sound and the others are perceived as entirely different from pleasure and the others by means of perception and other proofs, if non-difference were established based on some slight similarity, then monism (*advaita*) itself would be established, since a similarity exists even between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣas*. Therefore, the *pradhāna* is not established through positive concomitance (*anvaya*).
Refutation of the Cause of Dimensional Measure (parimāṇa)

Nor is there a non-establishment of [the reason] "limited magnitude" (*parimāṇa*). For if limited things were joined with a single cause, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) would be unestablished. As for roots, sprouts, and so forth, they arise sequentially from the parts of a rice grain (*vrīhi*) together with other constituent parts once the preceding parts have perished; there is no simultaneous conjunction in a single locus. Nor do they arise from a single [cause], since it is established that all effects are preceded by an agent, instruments, and material causes (*upādāna*). Furthermore, not even a single substance has a single material cause. If you mean that they are preceded by a material cause of the same genus (*jāti*), then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*), because we admit that the material cause is indeed of the same genus as the substance. However, a distinction between intermediate sub-species (*avāntarajāti*) among the material causes such as earth, water, and so forth, is perceived even through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, if you deny that, there would also be a contradiction with direct perception and other means of knowledge. Moreover, it is not established anywhere that pleasure (*sukha*) and the like possess the nature of a material cause, because they are qualities (*guṇa*). Thus, the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) is not established even by the reason of "limited magnitude."
By this, the argument that the Pradhāna is established through the relationship of beneficiary and benefactor is refuted.
[This concludes] the refutation of the argument based on the activity of potentialities (*śakti*).

Nor is the existence of *pradhāna* established by the operation of power (*śakti*). Who could believe that an effect exists, already situated within its causes, throughout all three periods of time? For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) whatsoever for the claim that sons, grandsons, and so forth already exist within the womb of a maiden even prior [to birth]. By this, the argument based on the cause of manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya-hetu*) is also refuted. If it is argued that these are established through the capacity of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*), we say no; because that very point is unestablished. Indeed, there is no means of valid cognition for the prior existence of an effect.
{The Doctrine of the Pre-existence of the Effect} Now, has it not been stated as a means of valid cognition:
"Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced; because there is the selection of a material cause; because everything is not possible from everything;"
"Because that which is capable does not produce [an effect] when lacking capacity, and because [the effect] exists as the cause, the effect pre-exists.

These are reasons based on the method of agreement (*avīta-hetu*). If that which is non-existent were produced, then even things such as a rabbit's horn would be produced; however, they are not produced. Therefore, the effect is indeed existent [prior to its production].

Furthermore, if the effect such as a cloth did not exist within the threads and other materials, then those seeking a cloth would not take up the threads and other materials, because those materials would be devoid of that effect, just like *vīraṇa* grass.

And if the cloth were already present within the threads, then every effect would arise [from them], since there is no difference in their non-existence; yet it does not so arise. Therefore, because of the absence of the production of everything from everything, it is certain that only that which exists in a particular place arises from that place.

Moreover, agency is accepted by everyone only for that which possesses power (*śakti*). And it is not logical for that which is devoid of power to be powerful. Furthermore, we do not perceive power as something other than the effect (*kārya*). Since the capable is what is produced, it is not logical for that which is non-existent (*asat*) to possess capability. Moreover, if something is the cause of another, the latter must arise from the former; and it is not tenable to say "this is the cause of that" when the effect does not exist. Therefore, the effect must indeed be existent. {Refutation of the Theory of Pre-existent Effect (*satkāryavāda*)} This too is incorrect—

As for the argument that "because that which is non-existent cannot be produced," that is not so, because the necessary connection (*pratibandha*) is unproven. Even if it is true that the non-existent, such as a rabbit’s horn, is never seen being produced, how does it follow that cloth and the like—which are also [claimed to be] non-existent—are not produced? For just as the non-existence and the state of not being produced of a rabbit’s horn and the like are established by means of perception and other valid cognitions (*pramāṇa*) in accordance with the consensus of all people, why is it not accepted that the prior non-existence and the state of being produced of cloth and the like are likewise established? Furthermore, why is it not accepted that the effect is non-existent on the grounds that "that which is non-existent cannot be produced"? In that case too, one could say this: "If that which is existent were produced, then even a person (*puruṣa*) and so forth would be produced; but they are not produced, therefore the effect is non-existent."
The refutation of the cause for grasping at appropriation.

As for what was said—that [the effect exists] because of the taking up of the materials—that too is incorrect, because it is contradictory. For if the effect already exists even prior [to its production], then no one would exert themselves toward its causes for its sake, since that would be useless; indeed, in the world, one who already possesses something does not strive for the sake of that very thing. Now, if it is argued that the fact that even an existing thing can be "made" is established by observing common usage such as "make me a back" or "make me hair," we reply: no, because that is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). In the case of the back, hair, and so forth, some other effect is actually produced; it is only the back, hair, etc., that are said to be "made" figuratively, and not directly, since they were already accomplished previously. Furthermore, it is impossible to produce what is already accomplished; in that case, the cause would be purposeless. If it is asked: "If a cloth that is non-existent is made from threads, why is it not also made from *vīraṇa* grass and the like? We say: no, because *vīraṇa* grass and the like lack the capacity (*sāmarthya*) for that. If it is argued that capacity itself is the effect, we say: no, because capacity is a property of the cause; how then could the effect, which arises later, be identical with that [capacity]? Moreover, the specific appropriation of particular causes occurs after one has recognized their suitability (*yogyatā*), and not because of the perception of the effect—for an unaccomplished cloth cannot be perceived. Furthermore, according to those who maintain the doctrine that "everything is of the nature of everything else," since the cloth exists even in *vīraṇa* grass and the like, why is the cloth not made from them? And why are they not appropriated by those seeking a cloth?

{Refutation of the possibility of everything arising from no cause} By this, the absence of the possibility of everything [arising] has also been answered. As it has been said: "That which is possible is produced, and that which is non-existent cannot be produced. How can that which exists be made possible? For neither *pradhāna* nor *puruṣa* can be produced by anyone.
Refutation of the Reason of Causal Existence (*kāraṇabhāvahetu*)

As for what was said—that [the effect exists] because of its being the nature of the cause—that too is subject to contradiction. For if the effect already exists even prior [to production], then what is to be done by the cause? And how can that which accomplishes nothing be a cause? Indeed, a relationship of cause and effect is not possible between conscious beings (*kṣetrajña*) themselves. If it is argued that the manifestation of the effect is produced by the cause, then if that manifestation is produced while being non-existent, it would follow that the effect is non-existent (*asatkārya*). If, however, the manifestation already exists, then the causal agents are rendered useless. If it is argued that the manifestation itself is further manifested, then one faces an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), whether that [second manifestation] is existent or non-existent. If existence is admitted in every case, then everything is always manifested, and thus the causal agents are indeed useless. By this, the distinction of reasoning based on the attainment of the operation of another property (*dharmāntara*) is refuted. Whatever purpose is stated for the causal agents, since all of that exists in every respect even prior [to action], the causal agents are simply useless. In whatever form the effect exists priorly, that form did not exist before but arises later from causes; so how is the effect not non-existent (*asat*)?

If one accepts the doctrine of Mādhava (the Sāṃkhya), however, there would be the total destruction of the Sāṃkhya system itself. How so? For if some property such as manifestation (*abhivyakti*) or something else were produced while being non-existent (*asan*), then reasons such as "because the non-existent cannot be produced" (*asadakaraṇāt*) would become invalid. Consequently, since the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryatva*) would not be established, the diversity of the world (*vaiśvarūpya*) and other principles would not be established, and thus the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and the rest would remain unestablished. Furthermore, there is no distinction here by which the production of a non-existent effect like a cloth could be impossible, while the loss of its own nature (*ātmahāna*) for that which is existent might be possible for some of its properties. Nor can it be said that nothing whatsoever ever becomes non-existent; for even by those who boast of their skill, some result must necessarily be asserted, which is unestablished and brought about by the causal factors. If nothing non-existent arises and nothing existent ceases, then the claim that "manifestation does not occur simultaneously due to obstructions caused by place, time, form, and instrumental causes" is also contradicted. For if manifestations always exist, why are they not simultaneous? If they do not exist [now], how will they come to be later? Likewise, if the obstruction by place and so forth exists, it would never cease, leading to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perpetual non-manifestation. On the other hand, if the obstruction is non-existent, then why is there non-manifestation? As for the argument that "in reality nothing is produced or destroyed, for the conventional usage of 'activity' and 'cessation' refers merely to the conjunction and disjunction of the *guṇas*; the designation of 'effects' is a metaphorical application (*upacāra*) based on a different arrangement of the *guṇas*—sattva and the others—just like a rope, a scale, or a string"—that is incorrect. Since we have already established that the whole (*avayavin*) is a distinct entity from its parts, and since conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is a distinct entity characterized by production and destruction, how can it be said that "nothing is produced"? Moreover, in the case of ropes and the like, because they possess form (*mūrtatva*) and parts, a different arrangement can be achieved through the movement of their parts. However, for the *guṇas*, because they are all-pervading (*vibhu*) and partless, a different arrangement is impossible, just as it is for the Self (*puruṣa*). Furthermore, disjunction (*viyoga*) is also untenable for all-pervading entities. Moreover, even if there were a specific arrangement of things devoid of color and other qualities, how could color and other qualities be perceived? For even when the air is arranged in a particular way, colors such as white are not perceived. Indeed, whatever the nature of the color and other qualities of certain things may be, those very same qualities are perceived even when those things are arranged differently, as in the case of black threads. Therefore, the conventional usage of "earth" and so forth does not apply to a mere arrangement of *guṇas*. For if the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) were the material cause (*upādāna*) of earth and the rest, they would not possess diverse forms and qualities, given that we observe that an effect-substance follows the form and qualities of its material cause. If one were to admit that the Primal Matter possesses diverse forms and qualities, then the name "Primal Matter" would simply be applied to atoms (*paramāṇu*), since it is impossible for a single substance to possess diverse forms and qualities, and because we observe that material causes are restricted to small dimensions and plurality. Furthermore, the fact that atoms are the substratum of pleasure and the like has already been refuted. Therefore, the Primal Matter does not follow as the substratum of pleasure and the like, nor does the Self follow as the Primal Matter. And if the Primal Matter were the substratum of pleasure and the like, the Self would be rendered devoid of any means of valid cognition (*niṣprāmāṇika*).

Now, it might be argued that an inference of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) from the object of enjoyment (*bhogya*) has been stated: "Prakṛti is subject to modification and is inseparable from an enjoyer, because it is an object of enjoyment, like rice and other such things. Likewise: "The eyes and other organs exist for the sake of another, because they are composite, like a bed and so forth. This is incorrect, because the very nature of enjoyment (*bhoga*) is unestablished. In the world, pleasure, pain, and the cognition thereof are well known as enjoyment; yet you maintain that these belong to the intellect (*buddhi*), which is an instrument (*karaṇa*). What, then, is the enjoyment of the *puruṣa* other than this? By this, the argument for [the organs] being for the sake of another is also refuted: for what purpose of the *puruṣa* is accomplished by the body and its constituents? For even merit (*dharma*) and the rest are held by you to belong to the intellect alone.
{Because human aims are of two kinds, there is the suspicion that the aim of another might be accomplished.}

Now, has it not been stated that the purpose of the *puruṣa* is twofold—the perception of sound and other objects, and the discernment of the difference between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*? By the former, experience (*bhoga*) is meant; by the latter, liberation (*mokṣa*). If it is asked how there can be experience, it is replied as follows: having perceived the intention of the intellect (*buddhi*), the senses transform into the form of their respective objects. Thereupon, the intellect undergoes a modification in the form of those sensory functions. However, the manifestation of consciousness does not occur within that mental modification of the intellect. Just as fire-flames are manifested in wood and other materials when they come into contact with the rays of the sun through a magnifying glass (*sūryakānta*), so too, when there is a conjunction of the object, the sense organ, and the activity of the mind, consciousness is manifested within the modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). This manifestation, which is a modification of the intellect, is called "experience" (*bhoga*). In this regard, according to the view of those who maintain that the instruments (*karaṇa*) are thirteenfold, the principle of the Great One (*mahattattva*) is denoted by the word "intellect" (*buddhi*). But for those who assert that the instruments are elevenfold, the mind (*manas*) itself is the intellect; as it has been said: [The verse follows: *“The intellect is the instrument of determination; the ego is the instrument of self-conceit; the five faculties of knowledge are the instruments of perception; and the five organs of action are the instruments of execution.”* Thus, in the system of those who accept eleven instruments, the mind alone is the intellect. It has been stated: [the verse continues].

"The Person, whose nature is indeed unchanging, causes the insentient mind— which bears his own reflection— to act through his proximity, just as an adjunct [colors] a crystal. When the intellect has transformed into the form of the Seer (the Puruṣa) in its state of isolation, that is said to be his experience."
"Just as the reflection of the moon arises in clear water.

This beginningless relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, characterized by the enjoyer and the enjoyed, is called bondage. Its root is non-perception (*adarśana*); therefore, it ceases through perception (*darśana*). Upon its cessation, the *puruṣa*, free from limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhi*) and pure by nature, is said to be liberated. As it has been said:
"One who knows the twenty-five principles, regardless of which stage of life (*āśrama*) he is devoted to..."
"Whether one has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, one is liberated; there is no doubt about this.
It is further stated:
"Upon the attainment of perfect knowledge, when dharma and the other [factors] reach the state of being non-causes..."
"The embodied one persists by the force of residual impressions, like the whirling of a potter's wheel;
once the separation of the body has been attained, because its purpose has been fulfilled and primordial matter (pradhāna) has ceased its activity,
he attains both the absolute and the ultimate state of liberation (kaivalya)."
"Just as the world engages in activities for the sake of satisfying its longing,
so does the Unmanifest engage for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.
Just as a dancer, having displayed herself on the stage, desists from her dance,"
"Having thus revealed herself to the Puruṣa, Prakṛti desists. By various means, she who is beneficent acts for the sake of the Puruṣa—
who is non-beneficent, devoid of qualities, and without purpose— even though he is without purpose."
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti),
which, once seen by the Spirit (puruṣa) thinking 'I have been seen,' does not again come into the sight of the Spirit.
Thus, because the two-fold purpose of the Spirit is accomplished in this way, it is not the case that [primordial nature] lacks a purpose for another.

{Refutation of that} This [position] is as untenable as chewing on the air—namely, that consciousness is manifested like a flame of fire. That is not so; for since the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted, the manifestation of even a flame of fire is logically impossible. Even under the theory of the pre-existence of the effect, the manifestation of something previously concealed is possible; however, in your view, there can be no concealment of consciousness, because you admit that it is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*). For even when the intellect (*buddhi*) is transformed into a specific form, there is no alteration of the consciousness's prior nature, as that would contradict its being unchanging.

Even if there were no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), if experience were admitted [for the Self], then experience would always occur without distinction; and in that case, what experience of the Person (*puruṣa*) could be produced by *pradhāna*? If it is argued that experience is simply the transformation of the intellect (*buddhi*) into the form of consciousness (*caitanya*), is that [transformation] caused by the Person or not? If it is caused by the Person, then the Person is not indifferent (*udāsīna*), because he is the agent of his own experience. If, on the other hand, even the transformation into action does not belong to him, and he is called "indifferent" despite acting merely through his presence (*sannidhi*), this is not so; for it leads to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). If agency belongs to one who is inactive merely through presence, then since selves are all-pervading and thus present everywhere, all selves would be the agents of all [actions]. Furthermore, liberated selves would also be experiencers, because there is no difference in their mere presence. Nor is it the case that one is an experiencer without actually performing the act of experiencing, for no one is known to be an experiencer while not performing the act of eating. Moreover, this would entail that liberated selves are also experiencers, as there is no distinction [between them and bound selves]. By this, the theory of the "arising of a reflection" is also refuted. Even though the nature of consciousness is the same for all persons and their presence is undifferentiated due to their pervasiveness, what determines the rule that the arising of a reflection occurs for only a certain person and not for all persons? If you say it is caused by distinctions such as afflictions (*kleśa*) and karma, we say no; for afflictions and the like are admitted to be modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).
{The impossibility of the relationship of owned and owner between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa)}:

Now, one might argue that even though [the experience] is a modification of the intellect (buddhi), it is metaphorically attributed to the person because of the restrictive rule of the relationship between owned and owner; for it is heard [in common parlance] that "the master is punished for the fault of the servant. This is not so; for an example of a completely indifferent being acting as an owner is nowhere established. On the contrary, there are examples such as kings and the like [who are active]. Furthermore, ownership is observed only in one who provides assistance, such as a servant. And the intellect is not able to provide any assistance whatsoever to the person, whose very nature is pure.

If it is argued that the intellect (*buddhi*) is beneficial because it reveals itself like a dancer, this is not so. For a dancer is said to "reveal herself" by producing the perception of her own self for the audience. However, the intellect does not produce anything at all for the person (*puruṣa*), since the person cannot be benefited in any way whatsoever. Furthermore, even a dancer cannot reveal herself to anyone who has no desire to see her. And those who do wish to see her, repeatedly directing their eyes out of a longing for pleasure, are themselves spectators; how then can they be called indifferent (*udāsīna*)? Therefore, experience (*bhoga*) is never established for one who is indifferent.

{The absence of bondage and liberation for the person} By this, liberation as well is refuted. Furthermore, liberation is said to belong to one who has a connection [to bondage], because of the absence of that [bondage]. And bondage is intended here to be ignorance, since it is said:
"By dharma there is upward movement; by adharma there is downward movement."
"Through knowledge comes liberation; from its opposite, bondage is held to arise.

From dispassion comes dissolution into primordial nature (prakṛti); from passionate attachment, the cycle of transmigration occurs. Through sovereignty comes lack of obstruction; from its opposite, the reverse of that [obstruction] results."

Furthermore, that ignorance, passion, and so forth are held to belong to the intellect (*buddhi*) alone and not to the *puruṣa*. How, then, can bondage, transmigration, and the like be possible for the *puruṣa* through ignorance and other factors produced by something else? For it is not logical that the virtuous should suffer bondage due to the offense of a thief, nor that thieves should obtain liberation from the merit performed by the virtuous.
[Objection: But surely bondage and the rest are attributed to the *puruṣa* only figuratively (*upacāra*), since it has been said:
"Nature binds herself to herself by means of the seven forms alone;
and she herself liberates the person from his purpose by means of a single form."

This is not so; for since there is no basis (*nimitta*), even metaphorical designation (*upacāra*) is untenable, and it has already been stated that the relationship of owner and owned is also untenable in your position. Furthermore, because neither difference nor non-difference is possible: first, the relationship of owner and owned cannot be distinct from *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, because you do not accept it as such; indeed, nothing apart from the *guṇas* and *puruṣa* is accepted by you. If, on the other hand, it were non-distinct, then since *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are indestructible, the relationship of owner and owned would also be indestructible; consequently, liberation would be impossible. [The refutation of the view that *prakṛti* acts once its purpose is fulfilled.]

This also refutes the claim that "Pradhāna does not function once its purpose has been fulfilled," because the cause for its functioning has not been severed. Alternatively, if there were a severance [of that cause], then Pradhāna itself would be severed, since it is non-different from that [cause]. By this, the cessation of desire (*autsukya*) is also refuted. Or, it is like the perception of sound and so forth: just as having accomplished the perception of sound and so forth, [Pradhāna] does not become one whose purpose is fulfilled—since the perception of sound and so forth is seen again—likewise, even after accomplishing the vision of the distinction between the Guṇas and Puruṣa, it would function again for that very same purpose.

It might be argued as follows: Having brought about the perception of sound and so forth, Nature acts for the sake of seeing the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*; but once that too has been accomplished, there is no further motive for activity—so why would she act? If this were the case, then having brought about the perception of sound and so forth, she should simply effect the vision of the distinction between the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*, since her eagerness toward those [sensory objects] has ceased; for what purpose does she bring about the perception of sound and so forth in birth after birth? For in this way, the activity of Nature would be devoid of any human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), since it does not accomplish that for which she set out. Nor is activity appropriate for the sake of perceiving sound and so forth, because there is no longer any eagerness for them, having already been accomplished in previous births. If you say that because she acts without foresight (*aprekṣāpūrvakāritva*), she accomplishes something else even when acting for another purpose, then—even though she acts for the sake of the transmigrating self—she might occasionally produce experience (*bhoga*) for a liberated self as well, due to her lack of discrimination.

The statement beginning with "having understood the intention of the intellect" is also untenable; because the sense organs are instruments—like an axe or similar tools—they cannot perceive intention, nor can they act on their own initiative.

It is also untenable for the intellect (*buddhi*) to be the locus of merit (*dharma*), knowledge, and so forth, because it is an instrument and insentient (*acetana*), like a spade or similar tools. If it is argued that the person (*puruṣa*) likewise cannot be the locus of merit and so on because he is sentient, like a liberated soul (*muktātman*), we say no; for this is contradicted by the very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that apprehend the subject and the example. Indeed, consciousness (*caitanya*) is not established from any source as being distinct from cognition (*jñāna*). It has been established that whatever possesses cognition also possesses pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit, and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*). Furthermore, even in the world, one who is separated from suffering and its causes is known as "liberated"; therefore, it must be accepted that for those who are not liberated, there exists suffering along with its causes—demerit, ignorance, and so forth.
