Thus, it is settled as previously stated: knowledge of the non-Self is a limb of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).
{The Exposition of the Knowledge of the Supreme Self} Now, the knowledge of the supreme self must be explained as a constituent factor of the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*).
{A Doubt Concerning Non-dual Knowledge as a Constituent Factor of the Highest Good}

But is it not the case that knowledge of the Self through the distinction of high and low is certainly not a means to the supreme good? Why? Because knowledge of difference is of the nature of ignorance (*avidyā*), like the knowledge of differences such as [the plurality of] the moon; and thus says the Śruti: "This is indeed one, not a second"; "From a second, indeed, fear arises"; "He goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity"; "All this, verily, is Brahman"; and:
"For him who knows, all beings have become the Self alone—for him who perceives this oneness, what sorrow or delusion can there be?"
"But he who perceives all beings in the Self alone,
and the Self in all beings, does not feel aversion toward anything.
For the single Self of all beings is established in every body."
"It is seen as one and indeed as many, like the moon in water.

Inference is also stated: the entire world is not different from the Supreme Self, because of its existence, knowability, and so forth, just like His own nature. Nor is there a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because that [perception] does not have difference as its object. As it has been said:
"The wise declare that direct perception is an affirmer, not a negator."
"Therefore, the scripture concerning oneness is not contradicted by that perception.

Furthermore, every cognition of difference that has become the subject of dispute is erroneous, because it is a cognition of difference, like the cognition of a difference in the moon and so forth. Non-dualistic cognition (*advaitajñāna*) is indeed the sublater of the cognition of difference, because it arises at a subsequent time, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl and similar objects. Non-dualistic cognition occurs after the thorough investigation of the meaning of the Vedas; however, the cognition of difference exists for everyone prior to that due to the power of beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*). Therefore, it is not the sublater [of non-duality], like the cognition of silver and the like.

Furthermore, if the three worlds are not apprehended [as distinct], how can a jar be perceived as distinct from them? For one who has not seen a horse cannot perceive a non-horse as distinct from a horse. How, then, is the difference between a jar and a cloth apprehended? If it is due to a difference in their defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), how is there a difference between those two characteristics themselves? If one resorts to a further difference in characteristics for that case as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If the difference is due to a difference in appearance (*pratibhāsa*), how is there a difference between the two appearances? If one resorts to a further difference in appearance for that case too, by what means can the resulting infinite regress be stopped? Moreover, there is the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*): as long as the jar is not perceived as excluded from the cloth, the cloth cannot be understood as excluded from the jar; and as long as the cloth is not perceived as excluded from the jar, the jar cannot be understood as excluded from the cloth. Furthermore, because there is no distinction in the perception of the form of "Being" (*sadākāra*), plurality is not logical for that which is perceived through a single form, as this would entail the undesirable consequence of destroying the conventional usage of non-difference (*abheda-vyavahāra*). If it is argued that plurality is perceived through forms such as "jar," is the form of the jar and so forth different or non-different from the form of Being? If it is different, then it is simply non-existent, because it is other than Being, like a rabbit's horn. Yet, the non-duality of reality is being considered. If it is non-different, then the form of the jar and so forth is nothing but the form of Being; how, then, can there be difference? Therefore, this appearance of difference is based on ignorance (*avidyā*), and that ignorance is indefinable in terms of being either identical to or different from Brahman. Thus, even in the doctrine of non-duality (*advaita*), the diversity of the world is not contradicted, because—like the diversity of objects perceived in a dream—it cannot withstand critical inquiry.

{Refutation of that} All of this is untenable. First of all, the proof of non-duality (*advaita*) by the force of scripture (*āgama*) is not valid; for scripture exists even on the side of dualism (*dvaita*). To that end, it is stated in the Śruti:
"Two birds, inseparable companions, cling to the same tree."
"One of them eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.
Likewise: "Two Brahmans are to be known—the higher and the lower," and so forth.
Similarly:
"Let us know him as the supreme Maheśvara among lords, the supreme deity among deities, the highest lord among lords, the God who rules over the worlds,
the one worthy of praise. Through ritual acts, the seers attained death, seeking wealth and desiring progeny."
"Then other wise sages attained immortality beyond [the results of] actions," and so forth. It is also stated in the Smṛti:
"But the Supreme Person is another, declared as the Paramātman (Supreme Self)."
"The immutable Lord, having entered the three worlds, sustains them"—
and so forth. [Thus,
there is consistency of non-dualistic statements within duality.]

In that regard, within the dualist position (*dvaitapakṣa*), those statements which express non-duality (*advaita*) are to be explained as being meaningful with reference to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). One must see that this entire world is indeed the one Supreme Brahman. Furthermore, because the whole world is presided over by Brahman or created by Brahman, it is said, "All this, indeed, is Brahman. In this manner, other statements are to be explained without contradiction. However, for one who holds the view that there is nothing whatsoever second, statements expressing duality would necessarily become invalid (*apramāṇa*); for even figuratively (*upacāreṇa*), no meaning is possible for them, due to the absence of any basis for such figurative usage. Moreover, there is no logical principle (*nyāya*) whereby some statements in a single scripture (*āgama*) are authoritative while others are not. If it is argued that both [types of statements] are authoritative through a division of their respective domains—duality existing in the state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsārāvasthā*) and non-duality in the state of liberation (*mokṣāvasthā*)—that is incorrect; for if duality is not admitted, the very possibility of transmigratory existence is untenable. For that which is the Supreme Self does not possess a form consisting of a physical body and so forth, nor does it transmigrate among gods, humans, and animals due to association with passion and the like, since scriptural passages such as "For him, neither activity nor instrument exists" establish that it is eternally devoid of form and the like, and is free from transmigratory existence. If it is argued that the occurrence of transmigratory existence is possible as a modification (*vikāra*) of that [Self], we say no; for the position of transformation (*pariṇāmapakṣa*) has already been refuted.
The establishment of cyclic existence and liberation through the powers of knowledge and action.

It might be thought thus: the power (*śakti*) of that Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is twofold, characterized as action (*kriyā*) and knowledge (*jñāna*). Among these, from the power of action, first, *pradhāna* (primordial matter) arises; and from *pradhāna*, the manifold expansion of transformations such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and so forth. There is no difference between cause and effect; therefore, there is no difference between *pradhāna* and the rest from the power of action. Furthermore, there is no difference between power and the possessor of power (*śaktimān*); hence, the entire universe has Brahman as its self. From the power of knowledge, however, the individual selves (*jīvātman*) arise, and they too are not different from Him. For those [individuals] who, having arisen through the force of ignorance (*avidyā*), possess attachment and the like, there is *saṃsāra*. Among them, those individuals who, while still possessing ignorance, go to dissolution in the Supreme Brahman—they, like the powder of a frog, because their seed-state is not burnt, are born again; then, through the connection with attachment and the like, there is *saṃsāra* once more. But those who, having burnt the seed of *saṃsāra* called the latent impression of duality (*bhedavāsanā*) by the fire of knowledge characterized by the stabilization of non-dual contemplation, dissolve into Brahman—for them, because the seed is burnt, there is no return. Thus says the Śruti: "Desiring, or then not desiring—he who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is the Self, whose desire is attained—for him the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart; right there they are completely dissolved. Being Brahman, he attains Brahman. Likewise: "They say he does not see, for he becomes one; they say he does not hear, for he becomes one," and so forth.
{The refutation thereof}

But that is not so. Why? Because the position of transformation (*pariṇāma*) has been refuted. For there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for something devoid of form and other qualities to transform into the form of color and so forth. Furthermore, because the pre-existence of the effect in the cause (*satkārya*) has been negated, the non-difference between cause and effect is also refuted. Moreover, the difference between power (*śakti*) and the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) has been established. And it has been stated that an immaterial thing cannot be the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of a material thing. Therefore, Īśvara is not the material cause. The scriptural passage beginning with "Being Brahman itself... praises the excellence of yoga. A yogin is said to be "Brahman itself" because, through supreme excellence, he is as utterly pure as Brahman. The meaning is that being in such a state, he perceives the Supreme Brahman. Regarding the phrase "he becomes one," a simile should be understood here: a yogin established in the Supreme Brahman does not perceive even a second self. Thus, by becoming as if one with it, he is said to "become one. Alternatively, by entering into the class of those who are liberated, he is said to "become one. However, an actual unification of things that are substantially distinct is never possible.

[Objection: Is it not observed that water and other substances merge—water merges with another body of water, a lamp with another lamp, clay with another piece of clay, and ghee, oil, and so forth with other ghee, oil, and so forth? [Reply: This is not so; for even in the case of water and the rest, a real merging (*ekībhāva*) is not established. What then? When they are joined with another, their unity is only figuratively attributed because they initiate a single composite whole, or simply because no separation is perceived. Furthermore, if one were to admit a merging of selves as in the case of water and so forth, then the destruction of the selves would likewise occur. Therefore, there is no non-duality (*advaita*) even in the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). As for those who do not accept the transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the Lord (*Īśvara*), in their view the Lord cannot be the cause, because of the absence of an effect—for it is not logical for something to be a cause if it does not produce an effect. Nor does he create himself, because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself. Moreover, the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) would be untenable, since the Lord is eternally liberated and because there is no bondage apart from him. If it is argued that the Blessed One’s agency consists solely in being the instigator of ignorance (*avidyā*), we say no; for even that is untenable on the non-dualist position. Indeed, the status of being an instigator of ignorance is observed only when plurality exists, as in the case of a magician who, through the application of mantras and herbs, causes ordinary people to engage in ignorance known as erroneous cognition. And in the absence of difference, of whom would there be ignorance? What is the definition of ignorance? For what reason does the Lord instigate it? And what is knowledge (*vidyā*)? If it is the very nature of Brahman, then since knowledge would exist eternally, the arising of ignorance could never occur. For when knowledge is present, ignorance finds no room, due to the contradiction between their coexistence; or, if there were no contradiction, ignorance would never be destroyed, and thus liberation would be impossible.

{The Refutation of Ineffability} The rejection of ineffability—defined as being neither identical nor different—is also untenable. For by the negation of identity, difference is established; or by the negation of difference, non-difference is established. How, then, could there be ineffability in either case? Since the mass of hair (*keśoṇḍuka*) is definable as being different from the cognition [of it], thus the theory of misapprehension (*viparītakhyāti*) is supported. Furthermore, the refutation of its ineffability in terms of being both existent and non-existent has already been made therein, as it was stated that an existent thing appears as different in terms of place, time, and form.

Nor is ignorance (*avidyā*) merely the hair-tuft; rather, it is the cognition appearing as that [hair-tuft]. Since that [cognition] possesses the nature of arising and perishing, how could it not be distinct from the immutable Brahman? Furthermore, the beginninglessness of ignorance is relative to its continuous flow (*pravāha*); otherwise, there would even be a contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, since ignorance itself is impossible when non-duality (*advaita*) is real, Vedic statements expressing difference—even with reference to a difference created by ignorance—cannot possibly be meaningful. {Refutation of the claim that direct perception and inference are sublated}

By this, that which they say—namely, "Because perception and inference are seen to be subject to subversion (*upaplava*), whereas the Vedas are not, there is no subversion of non-duality as propounded by them through perception and inference"—is also discarded, because subversion is demonstrated by the Vedic sentences themselves. Furthermore, if perception were subject to subversion, how could the establishment of the Vedas occur? And from Vedas that are not apprehended, there can be no comprehension of their meaning. Moreover, the human origin (*pauruṣeyatva*) of the Vedas has been established; therefore, their authority rests solely upon being rooted in perception. If inference is also subject to subversion, then in the event of disagreement regarding the meanings of words and sentences, how could there be a definitive determination? How could there be certainty regarding contradictory or non-contradictory interpretations? And how could there be a determination of the validity or invalidity of one's own and others' statements? As for what was said—"They say that perception is an affirmator (*vidhātṛ*)" and so forth—that too is incorrect, because perception was established as a negator (*niṣeddhṛ*) as well during the discussion on its inclusion among the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, just as the absence of a jar and so forth on a ground is grasped by perception, mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*) is also grasped by perception. Thus, following the presence or absence of the operation of the senses, the cognition of the mutual difference between things is seen to occur without contradiction by anyone in the world, just like the cognition of the existence of jars and such. Consequently, even by perception, the knowledge of non-duality is subverted, just like the cognition that "there are a hundred elephants on the tip of a finger."
Refutation of the inference that the cognition of difference is erroneous.

As for what was stated—that the cognition of difference under dispute is erroneous because it is a cognition of difference, like the cognition of the difference between [two] moons—that too is incorrect; for [the reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the cognition of difference between knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*). If it is argued that this [latter cognition] is also indeed the subject of the thesis (*pakṣa*), then does it follow that there is now only ignorance and no such thing as the knowledge of reality at all? If so, how can non-duality (*advaita*) be established? If non-duality were established by means of an erroneous cognition, then the establishment of difference would also follow from it, since there is no distinction [between them]. If, on the other hand, the cognition of non-duality is not erroneous, then it must be understood as distinct from the erroneous; and since the apprehension of that distinction is itself not erroneous, how is there not an inconclusiveness [of the reason]?

And what is the meaning of the "reason" (*hetu*)? Is it the very same as the meaning of the "thesis" (*pratijñā*), or is it something different from it? If it is the very same as the thesis, then there would be a redundancy of meaning and a lack of distinction from that which is to be proven; for it is not the case that one says, "There is fire here because of fire. If, on the other hand, the meaning of the reason is indeed distinct, then there is a contradiction with non-duality (*advaita*). Likewise, if the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is also the very same as the thesis, then it cannot be a prover because it is unestablished, and there is the fault of redundancy. If one accepts their difference, however, there is a contradiction with non-duality. And what is the meaning of the "thesis"? Is it the very meaning of the Sūtra beginning with "the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge," etc., or is it something other than that? If the meaning of the Sūtra concerning the means of knowledge and so forth is itself the thing to be proven, then it is proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If it is something other than that, then again there is a contradiction with non-duality.
The Refutation of the Inference that Non-dual Knowledge Sublates the Knowledge of Duality.

As for what was also said—that non-dual knowledge (*advaitajñāna*) is indeed the sublater (*bādhaka*) of dualistic knowledge because it arises subsequent to it, like the cognition of mother-of-pearl and so forth—that too is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). For example, the cognition "there are a hundred elephants on the tip of my fingernail," which arises after hearing the words of an unreliable person, does not sublate the prior cognition of their absence. Furthermore, it has been stated that since the relationship between the means of proof and the object to be proven, or the teacher and the taught, is not possible within non-duality, one who desires non-duality must simply maintain silence. [Even when the three worlds are not perceived, the cognition of difference is still possible.]

As for the objection that—if the three worlds are not apprehended by it—how can a jar be perceived as distinct from them? That is not so; because even without the apprehension of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), the absence (*abhāva*) manifests in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpakabuddhi*). And regarding absences that have been apprehended, it has been stated that in whatever way the cognition of a counter-correlate arises, in that very way there occurs a mere recollection (*smṛti*) through its conceptualization: "That object which was seen by me does not possess this nature"—thus is recollection observed to occur without any contradiction. Therefore, even if the three worlds are not apprehended by non-conceptual knowledge, the jar is indeed apprehended as distinct from them; subsequently, by means of the sense organ assisted by the recollection of the jar, a conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*) is produced in the form "the cloth is distinct from the jar. Consequently, the fault of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśraya*) does not apply. Furthermore, the difference between objects such as a jar and a cloth situated in one place is apprehended simultaneously, just like [the difference] between two fingers; therefore, there is no mutual dependence in this case either.
The determination of the apprehension of difference arises from the distinction between the appearance of characteristics and the [underlying] reality.

As for what was asked—whether difference [between objects] arises from a difference in their definitions (*lakṣaṇa*) or from a difference in their appearances (*pratibhāsa*)—that is not so, because the answer has already been stated. It was stated right at the beginning that in a case of doubt, difference is understood through a difference in definitions. Furthermore, in every instance, there is no cause for doubt; therefore, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even if difference were based on a difference in appearance, there would still be no infinite regress. For it is not maintained that the determination of the difference between objects depends upon the apprehension of a difference between appearances, such that an infinite regress would result. What then? A single cognition in which the difference of objects appears is called a "difference in appearance. And it has been established in the discussion refuting the theory of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-nirākaraṇa*) that even if that [cognition] is not apprehended, its object is not thereby unapprehended.
The Refutation of Non-duality Established through the Six Aspects of Reality.

As for the argument that “there is no distinction because the cognition of the form of existence (*sadākāra*) is identical,” that is not correct, because the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are equal. For by the very same means of valid cognition through which the non-distinction of the cognition of the form of existence is understood, by that same means of valid cognition the distinction in cognition through specific forms—such as place, time, parts, qualities, actions, universals (*jāti*), and so forth—is indeed manifested. If it is argued that this is because the specific forms cannot be established as being either different or non-different from the form of existence, we ask: what is this “form of existence”? Is it existence itself (*sattaiva*), or is it that which possesses it (*tadvān*)? If it is the universal existence (*sattāsāmānya*), then the specific forms are indeed distinct from it, since the distinction between a universal and that which possesses it has been established. Nor does this entail their non-existence like a hare’s horn; for while a hare’s horn lacks a connection with existence, the specific forms in question do possess such a connection. If, on the other hand, the “form of existence” is said to be that which possesses existence, then the specific forms of place, time, and so forth are not distinct from the form of existence. Even so, let the unity of the class (*vargaikatva*) be established due to the non-distinction of the form of existence, but not the unity of the individual (*vyaktyekatva*). For it has already been stated that establishing the unity of individuals contradicts perception and other means of knowledge. Thus says the Sūtra: “The absolute unity of number is unestablished, due to the impossibility and possibility of the means of valid cognition. If there were no possibility of a means of valid cognition, there would be no establishment [of anything], as it would follow that all doctrines are established. And if there is the possibility of a means of valid cognition, then the distinction between the knower (*pramātṛ*) and so forth is established; as it has been said: “In these four categories, reality is fully encompassed. Furthermore, regarding the claim that “this entire appearance of difference is based on ignorance (*avidyā*),” a means of valid cognition must be stated here as well. For no object is established by mere words, as it would follow that all doctrines are established. And by the statement of a means of valid cognition, the distinction between the person to be instructed and the instructor, and so forth, becomes unavoidable.
{Monism of Sound and its Refutation} By this, the monism of sound (*śabdādvaita*) is refuted, as they say:
"Brahman is without beginning or end, the essence of sound, which is the imperishable syllable."
"From which the process of the world evolves in the form of objects.
"There is no cognition in the world that exists without the accompaniment of words;
everything appears as if permeated by them, for all is established in speech."

Whatever is permeated by something else is not distinct from it, just as jars and other objects permeated by clay do not have a nature other than clay. Or, whatever is a transformation of something is not distinct from it, just as the moon in water is a transformation of the [actual] moon, and every object is a transformation of sound, because it appears in the form of sound. Therefore, every object has sound as its essence. Sounds, too, are permeated by all phonemes (*varṇa*); phonemes are permeated by vowels (*svara*); and vowels are permeated by the single resonance (*nāda*). Thus, the entire world is one, having sound as its essence. Precisely because they proclaim non-duality (*advaita*), there is no difference between the doctrines of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*), the non-duality of Brahman (*brahmādvaita*), the non-duality of sound (*śabdādvaita*), and so forth. Apart from differences in the method of establishing their positions—establishing the non-duality of consciousness in one way, the non-duality of Brahman in another, and the non-duality of sound in yet another—the difference among the proponents of non-duality lies only in this; however, there is no difference even within non-duality itself. Accordingly, for the purpose of refuting all proponents of non-duality, the author of the *Sūtra* stated only a single aphorism: "The Sāṃkhya position is not established as an absolute [truth]," and so on. Because the pre-existence of the effect (*satkārya*) is refuted, the reality of sound does not undergo transformation into the forms of touch and the other [sensory qualities].
{The Refutation of the Perception of Difference Arising from Ignorance}

Nor can the perception of difference occur through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), for ignorance is defined as false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). And that [false knowledge] differs by way of differences in place and time, differences in causes (*nimitta*), and by way of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everyone would always perceive errors such as [illusory] hairs everywhere; furthermore, there would be the consequence that true knowledge (*tattvajñāna*) would never arise, due to the absence of a cause. If a cause does exist, then because of the difference between the cause and its effect, non-duality (*advaita*) is contradicted. If it is argued that even in that case, difference arises from ignorance itself, then in this way, true knowledge would not arise from anything at any time in reality, and thus liberation (*apavarga*) would be impossible. Moreover, if true knowledge and liberation have ignorance as their cause, there is the consequence that they are unreal (*avāstava*), like a mass of hair seen by a person with ophthalmia; consequently, like other treatises, the treatise on non-duality would also result in being useless for the human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) in reality.
The impossibility of liberation for Brahmā.

Furthermore, for whom is liberation (*mokṣa*) considered? It is incorrect to say that it belongs to that very Brahman, because Brahman is by its very nature liberated (*svabhāvamukta*). Alternatively, if [Brahman] were subject to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*), then no one would ever be liberated; consequently, since neither liberation nor its means would be perceived by anyone, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of their not being taught. And if they were not taught, how could there be any engagement with them? Moreover, if even while engaging [in practice], one single person were liberated, there would follow the destruction of transmigratory existence itself, because no other transmigrating being would be possible. If it is argued that the conceit of self (*ātmābhimāna*) exists due to the power of ignorance (*avidyā*), has ignorance not been destroyed even upon final release (*apavarga*)? Nor is there any other self besides the liberated one who could possess ignorance. If it is argued that individual selves (*jīvātman*) exist, are they different from [the one Brahman] or non-different? If they are different, then there is a contradiction with [the doctrine of] oneness (*ekatva*). If, however, they are non-different from the liberated one, then how can there be transmigratory existence for individual selves?
{The impossibility of a distinction in the form of individual souls, like the moon in water}:

By this, the [analogy] "like the moon in water" is also refuted. For just as when the moon is eclipsed by Rāhu, the moon in the water is not perceived anywhere, so too when liberation is attained through the Supreme Self, the transmigrating soul is not perceived anywhere.

Furthermore, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the distinction between pleasure, pain, and so forth would be impossible. Just as the form of the moon situated in the sky is perceived to be exactly the same for all moons reflected in water, and there is no distinct arrangement of forms for each individual reflection, so too, whatever pleasure, pain, knowledge, desire, or the like belongs to one's own self, that very same thing would belong to everyone. Thus, the distinction of pleasure and so forth for each individual person would be untenable. If it is argued that this distinction exists due to the difference in bodies, we say no; because such a distinction is not observed. Even when there is a difference in bodies—such as in childhood, youth, and old age—no such distinction is observed. One continues to connect with the pleasures, pains, scriptures, and other experiences previously experienced in former bodies even in the body of old age, thinking, "I had this pleasure."

{Refutation of the Analogy of the Space within a Jar} By this, the examples of the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa*) and the space within a hut (*maṭhākāśa*), and so forth, are refuted. Furthermore, just as the space within a jar becomes liberated only upon the cessation of the jar, so too the person delimited by the body would become liberated only upon the cessation of the body; thus, liberation would result without effort. Consequently, the scripture on liberation (*mokṣaśāstra*) would be rendered useless.
{Refutation of the Latent Impressions of Ignorance}

If it is argued that even when the body has ceased, there remains a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) caused by ignorance and so forth, and that for the portion of the Self delimited by that [impression], which is as if separate, there is transmigration (*saṃsāra*), we say: no, because the alternatives do not hold. For is that impression produced by the body spatially limited like the body itself, or is it all-pervading like the existence of space? In the first case, the impression produced by the body located in Citrakūṭa would produce a future birth only in that very same place where the portion of the Self delimited by it was acted upon, and the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth would also occur only there, because another location is not delimited by that impression. If it is argued that the impression is mobile and thus delimits other locations as well, we say: no, because since the impressions of ignorance, merit, and so forth are devoid of action, their movement is impossible. Furthermore, having gone to a liberated location, it might delimit that as well. And if it were to delimit that, it would follow that the liberated one would again become subject to transmigration. If it is argued that while remaining in its own place, the impression produces its effects in other locations too, then it would likewise produce them in the liberated location as well—thus the same undesirable consequence follows.

Now, if the *saṃskāra* were all-pervasive like the existence of space (*ākāśasattā*), then all regions of the self would be pervaded by it; thus, no region whatsoever would be free [from it]. By this, the illustration of the gem and the thread is refuted, because this case shares the same fault as the examples of the pot and space, and so forth. Therefore, there is not one and the same self in all bodies.
{The Refutation of the Illustration of the Spark from a Fire}

Now, [the opponent claims: "Just as sparks fly from a heated iron ball, countless individual souls (*jīvātman*) arise from the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*); there is a systematic distinction among them regarding saṃsāra, liberation, knowledge, and so forth. This is not so; for it has already been established that even those selves who undergo saṃsāra are beginningless. Furthermore, if they were produced [de novo], they would necessarily be impermanent, and consequently, there would be no world beyond (*apara-loka*).
{Refutation of the Analogy of the Ocean Water}

If it is argued that, like water from the ocean, they emerge from that very source and dissolve back into it, this is not so; for it would follow that Brahman, like the ocean, possesses parts and other such defects. Furthermore, the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) has been refuted; therefore, no supporting example is established for the position that dissolution is a transformation (*pariṇāma*). [The suspicion that ignorance (*avidyā*) might be the individual soul (*jīva*), and its refutation.]

Now, if it is argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) itself is the individual self (*jīvātman*), and that its beginninglessness, its incalculability, and its state of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāritva*)—along with the cessation of that [ignorance]—constitute liberation (*mokṣa*), then it must be stated: "To whom does that [self] belong? First of all, as has been said, it cannot belong to Brahman. If it is argued that it is like the extinguishing of a lamp, then who is it that exerts effort for that purpose? If it is the individual self itself, no; because the cessation of the self is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). For why would the individual self, whose very nature is ignorance, cause itself to cease? Furthermore, there is no means for its cessation. Knowledge (*vidyā*) certainly does not arise in the individual self, which consists of ignorance, due to their mutual contradiction. Nor can it arise in Brahman, because [knowledge] is eternal therein. Nor is the absolute destruction of ignorance possible through any other means. And there is no such thing as ignorance other than false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*). Since it has been established that all knowledge is dependent [on a substrate], it must be stated: "Ignorance belongs to whom? It has already been stated that this is impossible for either Brahman or a part thereof. For if they had a single substrate, the distinction (*vyavasthā*) regarding pleasure, pain, memory, and so forth, would not be possible, since we observe a continuity of experience even when the bodies are different. If it is argued that this is like the lack of continuity regarding experiences in the womb-body, no; because in that case, the impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the cause of memory has either not yet arisen, has perished, or has been suppressed. If it is argued that the same applies to other [successive] bodies, no; because that would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-memory [in those cases as well]. Yet, we observe a teacher’s recollection of the meaning of the scriptures and so forth. From this, it is understood that his impression remains un-suppressed. Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence of memory occurring for the student and others as well, because the self is one, just as in the case of childhood and other bodily states. Therefore, because the distinction of pleasure, pain, memory, and so forth is observed for each body, the self is manifold. [Objection: But even in your view, since all selves are omnipresent, they exist in every body; thus, the distinction [of experience] is untenable, and the subtle body (*liṅga*) of all persons would be perceived in a single body. [Reply: No; the distinction is established by the restriction of unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). That body which is produced by a specific unseen force created by someone becomes the locus of experience for that person alone. For other selves, however, their existence therein is merely by way of proximity, not by way of being the controller. Therefore, there is no undesirable consequence of perceiving the subtle body of all in a single body. Thus, it stands: the transmigrating selves are innumerable, while the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is indeed one. Hence, there is no contradiction even if some attain liberation by means of the supreme meditation. Therefore, since the knowledge of the Supreme Self as distinct from the individual selves is a means to liberation as an auxiliary to the meditation on the Supreme Self, it has been stated that the Supreme Self is to be known as an entity different from the individual selves.
The injunction for meditative worship.

What, then, is the method for its worship? It is stated: that method of worship is the practice performed for the sake of attaining the destruction of afflictions (*kleśa*) and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). By whatever means the afflictions known as attachment, aversion, and delusion are destroyed, and one-pointedness of mind directed toward Maheśvara is attained—that means being practiced is called the method of worship of the Supreme Lord, because of the statement: “And through yoga, by means of the methods of the internal discipline. The means taught even in treatises such as those of Patañjali should be adopted provided they do not contradict our own scripture. In this regard, according to the principle of system-building (*tantrayukti*), the maxim holds: “The opinion of another is accepted if it is not prohibited. Therefore, means consisting of ignorance, such as the initiation involving the giving of gold and so forth, are not included here, because they lack the capacity to destroy attachment and the other afflictions. Furthermore, it was discussed in the *Duḥkha-sūtra* that as long as the afflictions are not destroyed, the cessation of transmigratory existence is impossible. It was also discussed that knowledge other than the knowledge of the twelvefold objects of cognition is not the means. Moreover, the knowledge of the twelve objects of cognition is not capable of removing attachment and the rest merely by its arising alone without assistance; rather, it must be accompanied by the practice of the methods of yoga.
{An Exposition of the Two Types of Yoga}

Yoga is twofold, distinguished by the states of being emergent (*vyutthita*) or non-emergent (*avyutthita*). Among these, in the state of emergence, one should practice *kriyā-yoga*, characterized by austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and devotion to the Lord (*īśvara-praṇidhāna*). Thus it has been said: "Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute *kriyā-yoga*; its purpose is the attenuation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the cultivation of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Here, the order of the items has been reversed from the sequence of their purpose; however, in the *Pātañjala-sūtra*, the reading is "for the cultivation of meditative absorption and for the attenuation of the afflictions. In this context, austerity (*tapas*) is the endurance of internal and other forms of suffering. Internal suffering (*ādhyātmika*) is that which pertains to the body and mind independently of external causes; suffering caused by beings such as humans and animals is external (*ādhibhautika*); and suffering caused by divine agencies, such as cold and heat, is celestial (*ādhidaivika*). When one endures these three types of suffering through the practice of restraint with a tranquil disposition, performing the accumulation and exhaustion of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it is called austerity. From the subsequent accumulation of merit, there arises an excellence of faith and other qualities that serve as the cause for the engagement in yoga. Furthermore, from the exhaustion of demerit comes the pacification of obstacles such as disease, despondency, doubt, negligence, and laziness; consequently, the undisturbed mind becomes concentrated in meditative absorption (*samādhi*).

[Objection: Surely mental distraction arises from sufferings; therefore, one who seeks yoga should not perform austerity (*tapas*). Furthermore, the accumulation and destruction of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) occur through recitation (*japa*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), and so forth. There is no authoritative evidence for austerity being a means [to these ends]. [Response: This is not so. For how can one who is overwhelmed by madness, lust, and the like perform recitation, withdrawal of the senses, and so forth? Therefore, he must perform austerity. Just as the gross impurity of a garment is removed by a gross means, while the subtle [impurity] is removed by a subtle means, so too the gross impurity of the self is first removed by a gross means, and subsequently the subtle [impurity] is removed by subtle means such as recitation and withdrawal of the senses.

{The proof for austerity being a means to dharma} As for what was said—that there is no proof that austerity is a means for the accumulation of dharma and so forth—that is not so, because it is established by scripture. And thus says Manu:
"All this, whether divine or human happiness, has its root in austerity."
"The wise have declared austerity to be the middle [path], while those who perceive the Vedas have declared austerity to be the end.
Even those who have committed great sins, as well as others who have performed forbidden acts,
are liberated from that defilement by means of well-performed austerity alone."
Whatever sin people commit through their mind, speech, or body,
those whose wealth is austerity quickly wash it all away by means of austerity alone.

Although austerity (*tapas*) may also have heaven and other such things as its fruit, nevertheless, when assisted by auxiliary factors such as specialized knowledge and dispassion (*vairāgya*), it brings about clarity of mind (*cittaprasāda*) with only slight mediation. Once the mind is clarified, one should complete the austerities and observances (*niyama*), such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* fast, and then practice the limbs of yoga itself. However, for one who is already capable of withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*) and the other limbs due to the power of austerity performed in previous births, austerity is not prescribed, because its purpose has already been accomplished.
{The Exposition of Kriyā-yoga}

Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the repeated practice of a mantra denoting the Lord (*īśvara*). The term "tranquil" (*praśānta*) is included to exclude those mantras denoting the Lord that serve as causes for minor supernatural powers (*kṣudrasiddhi*); rather, one must remain solely devoted to the Supreme Self. Alternatively, self-study is the practice of the meaning of the Yoga scriptures for the sake of knowledge. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the continuous reflection and contemplation upon the reality of the Supreme Lord through intense devotion, or worship by means of hymns, recitations, flowers, and so forth, or the dedication of all actions to the Supreme Teacher. It is also the recitation of the *praṇava*, which denotes Him, and the meditation upon its meaning. This very practice—characterized by austerity, self-study, and the like—is called "yoga" because it is the cause of the yoga of action. And this yoga of action, when cultivated, brings about *samādhi* and attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*).
The afflictions.

What, then, are the afflictions (*kleśa*) here, and how many are they? It is said: in brief, the afflictions are attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and delusion (*moha*). For these afflict the person by being antagonistic to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and by being the cause of falling into cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Among them, attachment is characterized by incapacity; aversion is characterized by intolerance; and delusion is a false cognition. Now, Patañjali states: "Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life are the afflictions. Therefore, why are egoism (*asmitā*) and clinging to life (*abhiniveśa*) not mentioned here? No; because they are impossible [in this context] and because they are included within these very three. To explain: the definition of egoism is stated as "the appearance of identity between the power of the seer and the power of seeing. Its meaning is as follows: "The Puruṣa is the power of the seer, and the intellect (*buddhi*) is the power of seeing. Egoism is like the attainment of a single nature by these two; when there is a state of non-differentiation between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the enjoyed—which are absolutely unmixed—enjoyment is conceived. For when their own true natures are attained, there is only isolation (*kaivalya*). This [egoism] is refuted by the negation of the Pradhāna (primordial matter) and by the negation of enjoyment. Furthermore, the knowledge of non-differentiation regarding things that are distinct is simply ignorance (*avidyā*); it is not a separate entity called egoism. Likewise, the definition of clinging to life is: "Clinging to life is a natural flow that persists even in the wise. This is the fear of death—the thought "May I not cease to be," or "May I continue to exist"—which occurs in every living being from the moment of birth. Because its nature consists of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) rooted in the experience of the pain of death since beginningless time, it is called a "natural flow. And just as it is seen in those who are utterly ignorant, it is perceived as persisting even in the wise, who know the prior and subsequent limits of existence. This too is included within delusion or aversion. Since death is inevitable, the hope for life takes the form of the notion "this is that," and thus it is delusion. It has been stated that even for the wise, delusion such as confusion of directions can occur due to internal defects. The fear of death is simply the inability to endure the pain of dying; therefore, it is not distinct from aversion. If it were distinct merely on account of some difference, then there would be the undesirable consequence of having to list envy, anger, jealousy, pride, arrogance, and so forth separately, and thus the restriction to three types of affliction would not hold. Therefore, the affliction is indeed threefold. Accordingly, the Sūtra says: "In that regard, there are three groups, because attachment, aversion, and delusion have different objects. Now, the threefold nature of the defects (*doṣa*) has been mentioned; are the afflictions something other than those? Indeed, the author of the Sūtras used the word "affliction" (*kleśa*) in the passage "For one whose afflictions are destroyed, there is no activity leading to rebirth," referring to the defects themselves. These afflictions, becoming attenuated day by day by the wise who practice the yoga of action (*kriyāyoga*), are perceived even through direct perception. Just as the yoga of action is a cause for the destruction of afflictions, so too are the limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*); therefore, they too should be practiced with great effort.
The factors of yoga.

What, then, are those limbs of yoga (*yogāṅga*), and how many are there? It is said: "The eight limbs are restraint (*yama*), observance (*niyama*), posture (*āsana*), breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*). The meaning is that these limbs are the means of accomplishment. If it is asked, "What other yoga is there besides *samādhi* such that *samādhi* would be its limb?"—the answer is that *samādhi* itself, when it has reached its ultimate excellence, is *yoga*; for that [ultimate] *samādhi*, the preceding *samādhi* is the limb, just as the word "beginning" implies the middle and the end. Alternatively, every degree of excellence in *samādhi* is *yoga* by virtue of being produced by a prior *samādhi*, and it is a limb by virtue of producing a subsequent degree of excellence. If *samādhi* arises from *samādhi* alone, then surely only one limb would result, and thus one should not say "there are eight limbs. This is not so; because the subsequent ones are established only upon the establishment of each preceding one. For restraint is not established if observance is not established; posture is not established if observance is not established; breath control is not established if posture is not established; withdrawal of the senses is not established if that is not established; concentration is not established if that is not established; meditation is not established if that is not established; and absorption is not established if meditation is not established. Therefore, all eight are limbs of yoga.

(1) Definition of the Yamas: "In that regard, the *yamās* are the causes of purity and increase for a person, which are not restricted by place, time, or circumstance. Purity (*śuddhi*) is the destruction of demerit (*adharma*), and increase (*vṛddhi*) is the accumulation of merit (*dharma*). Alternatively, purity is the stainlessness of the mind (*citta-vaimalya*), and increase is the excellence of yoga (*yogotkarṣa*). Those causes of these [purity and increase] which are unrestricted by place and so forth—meaning they are practiced in every place, at every time, and in every circumstance—are the *yamās*, such as non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the rest.

[Objection: But surely even non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) and the like are practiced by some according to restrictions of place and so forth—for instance, "I shall not commit violence at a sacred site," or "I shall not [commit violence] on all days," or "I shall not kill living beings except in a state of war. [Reply: No; for even non-violence and the like are observances (*niyama*) precisely because they depend upon place and other such factors. For this very reason, from an ultimate standpoint, the householder and others do possess observances. It is said that "an ascetic (*yati*) is one who is endowed with restraints (*yama*). If it is asked, "In the absence of restraints, how can there be the accomplishment of observances for the householder and others?", [we reply: No; for there is no contradiction in the accomplishment of observances that bring about the fulfillment of those duties which impel one toward action. Indeed, the duty of an ascetic consists in cessation; therefore, for one whose restraints have not fallen away, the observances—which are the causes of that [cessation]—are not accomplished.
(2) Examination of Determination (*niyama*)

"Restrictions regarding specific ritual actions (*kriyāviśeṣa*) are causes of merit that depend upon place, time, and state. Among these, circumambulating a deity depends on place; the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsana*) depends on time; however, the act of recitation (*japa*) depends merely on a state of purity. Regarding the attainment of an excellence of merit, there is an infinite dependence on place and so forth, as it is heard in such scriptural passages as "in the presence of Śiva," and so on. Thus, other specific ritual actions are also restrictions by virtue of their dependence on place and the like. However, according to the intention of Patañjali, the definition of *yama* and *niyama* should be understood as follows: *yamas* are characterized by abstention (*nivṛtti*), while *niyamas* are characterized by engagement (*pravṛtti*). Accordingly, it has been said: "Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possessiveness are the *yamas*. Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) are the *niyamas*."

(3) Definition of Posture (*āsana*): "Posture is the binding of the instruments for the sake of conquering the afflictions that obstruct the practice of yoga. The afflictions that obstruct the performance of yoga are diseases and the like; for it is taught that their conquest comes from the conquest of posture. Here, the "instruments" (*karaṇa*) are the limbs of the body, such as the feet; their "binding" (*bandha*) is their regulation for the sake of achieving *prāṇāyāma* and other practices. Thus, posture means sitting firmly and comfortably. It is of many kinds, such as the lotus posture (*padmaka*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), and so forth. (4) Definition of Breath Control (*prāṇāyāma*): [The text follows: "Breath control is the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. This is the restraint of the flow of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). It is of three types: external (*bāhya*), internal (*antara*), and stationary (*stambha*). External breath control is the expulsion of the breath beyond the nostrils; internal is its drawing back into the abdomen; stationary is the suspension of both movements. Each of these is practiced with specific measures of time, space, and number, and each is fourfold according to its mild, medium, and intense degrees, as well as the state beyond measure (*atīta*). Through this, the covering of the light is destroyed, and the inner light becomes manifest. Furthermore, when the mind is fixed on a single object, the conjunction of the mind and the senses with their objects is called "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*). By this, the senses do not experience contact with their objects, even when in proximity; thus they become as if devoid of objects. From this arises supreme mastery over the senses. When the senses are restrained by withdrawal, the afflictions, actions, and their latent impressions no longer taint the mind. Therefore, one should practice withdrawal. By this, the yogi attains complete mastery over the senses. Even while the senses are engaged with their objects, the yogi's mind remains unattached, like a lotus leaf in water. This is the perfection of withdrawal. From this, the yogi gains the power to enter another's body. When the mind is withdrawn from all objects and fixed upon a single point, that is "concentration" (*dhāraṇā*). The continuity of concentration is "meditation" (*dhyāna*). When that very meditation shines forth as the object alone, devoid of the form of the meditator, it is "absorption" (*samādhi*). These three—concentration, meditation, and absorption—applied to a single object are called "samyama. By mastering samyama, knowledge born of intuition arises. When samyama is applied to the moments of succession, there is knowledge of past and future. By applying samyama to the relationship between the sign (*liṅga*) and the signified (*liṅgin*), there is knowledge of all things. By applying samyama to the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is knowledge of the *puruṣa*. By applying samyama to the *vairāgya* (detachment), there is knowledge of the past and future lives. By applying samyama to the *pratibhā* (intuition), there is knowledge of everything. By applying samyama to the *sūrya* (sun), there is knowledge of the cosmic systems (*lokas*). By applying samyama to the *candra* (moon), there is knowledge of the arrangement of the stars. By applying samyama to the *dhruva* (pole star), there is knowledge of their motion. By applying samyama to the *nābhi-cakra* (navel center), there is knowledge of the constitution of the body. By applying samyama to the *kaṇṭha-kūpa* (pit of the throat), there is cessation of hunger and thirst. By applying samyama to the *kūrma-nāḍī* (tortoise channel), there is steadiness of the body. By applying samyama to the *mūrdhajyotis* (light at the crown of the head), there is knowledge of the celestial beings (*siddhas*). By applying samyama to the *hṛdaya-puṇḍarīka* (lotus of the heart), there is knowledge of the mind. By applying samyama to the *saṃskāras* (latent impressions), there is knowledge of previous births. By applying samyama to the *pratyaya* (present cognition), there is knowledge of the minds of others. By applying samyama to the *rūpa* (form) of the self, there is disappearance of the bodily form. By applying samyama to the *parigraha* (grasping), there is knowledge of the subtile elements. By applying samyama to the *sthūla-svarūpa-asmitā-anvaya-artha-vattva* (grossness, essential nature, egoism, inherence, and purposefulness) of the elements, there is mastery over them. From this mastery, the elements and their products follow the will of the yogi, like a wish-fulfilling gem. By applying samyama to the *grahaṇa-svarūpa-asmitā-anvaya-artha-vattva* (perception, essential nature, egoism, inherence, and purposefulness) of the organs, there is mastery over them. From this mastery, the organs function according to his will. Furthermore, there is the power of rapid action like the mind. By applying samyama to the *prakṛti-vikāra-prakāśa-kriyā-sthiti-śīlatva* (the nature of the primary cause and its modifications, consisting of illumination, activity, and inertia), there is mastery over the *guṇas*. From this mastery, he perceives the distinct nature of the *puruṣa* and the *guṇas*. By applying samyama to the *puruṣa*, there is knowledge of the *puruṣa*. From this, the *puruṣa* is seen in its own nature, free from the qualities of the *guṇas*. By applying samyama to the *samyoga* (union), there is the destruction of the covering of the light. From this, the light of wisdom shines forth. By applying samyama to the *vivekakhyāti* (discriminative discernment), there is the destruction of the seeds of bondage. Then, through the final *kaivalya-pratyaya* (cognition of isolation), the *saṃskāras* born of *kaivalya* destroy the *saṃskāras* born of discriminative knowledge. When those too are destroyed, the *saṃskāras* born of detachment arise; then the mind, having fulfilled its purpose, returns to its own *prakṛti*. At that time, the *puruṣa*, being pure and established in its own nature, is called "liberated. End of the Second Chapter. The Third Chapter begins: "Now, the supernormal powers (*siddhis*) are described. By practicing *prāṇāyāma*, the impurities of the mind are removed, and the light of wisdom becomes manifest. *Prāṇāyāma* is the cessation of the movement of inhalation and exhalation. It is of three types: external, internal, and stationary. External is the expulsion of the breath beyond the nostrils; internal is its drawing back into the abdomen; stationary is the suspension of both movements. Each is practiced with specific measures of time, space, and number, and each is fourfold according to its mild, medium, and intense degrees, as well as the state beyond measure. From this, the covering of the light is destroyed, and the inner light becomes manifest. Furthermore, when the mind is fixed on a single object, the conjunction of the mind and the senses with their objects is called "withdrawal" (*pratyāhāra*). By this, the senses do not experience contact with their objects, even when in proximity; thus they become as if devoid of objects. From this arises supreme mastery over the senses. When the senses are restrained by withdrawal, the afflictions, actions, and their latent impressions no longer taint the mind. Therefore, one should practice withdrawal. By this, the yogi attains complete mastery over the senses. Even while the senses are engaged with their objects, the yogi's mind remains unattached, like a lotus leaf in water. This is the perfection of withdrawal. From this, the yogi gains the power to enter another's body. When the mind is withdrawn from all objects and fixed upon a single point, that is "concentration" (*dhāraṇā*). The continuity of concentration is "meditation" (*dhyāna*). When that very meditation shines forth as the object alone, devoid of the form of the meditator, it is "absorption" (*samādhi*). These

Prāṇāyāma is the cessation of the movement of the air residing within the body, characterized by inhalation and exhalation. Having assumed a comfortable posture in a secluded, windless, solitary, and noiseless place, one should perform the various types of *recaka* (exhalation), *pūraka* (inhalation), and *kumbhaka* (retention). This [control] must be mastered very gradually, like a lordly forest elephant. Just as a lordly forest elephant, when subdued gradually through training, provides great benefit, whereas if seized by force without training, it causes only destruction; so too, the vital air (*vāyu*), when subdued gradually through practice, destroys all unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the impurities such as passion, and leads one to Yoga. But if it is overcome and suppressed by force without practice, it causes only misfortune, such as abdominal tumors caused by wind (*vātagulma*).

(5) Definition of Pratyāhāra (Withdrawal): Pratyāhāra is the complete withdrawal of the mind from objects that cause effort toward meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For when the mind is withdrawn, the senses are also withdrawn. Why? Because the activity of the senses has its root in the mind. For one who is devoted to pratyāhāra, mastery over the senses and the attainment of *samādhi* occur; it is not otherwise. (6) Definition of Dhāraṇā (Concentration):

"Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a place. What is the place here? And what is the binding of the mind to a place? Some say that the place is a limb of the body, such as the feet and so forth, or an external place, such as the solar orb and so forth. We, however, say that the Supreme Self alone is intended here as the "place," because those established in the desire for liberation are engaged in its worship. For it is heard in scripture that the fruit of concentration on the feet and other limbs is the attainment of the worlds of Viṣṇu and so forth. The binding of the mind—that is, the intellect—is said to be its concentration, which is the making of it motionless through effort; this is called "concentration. {(7) Definition of Meditation (*dhyāna*):}

In that context, *dhyāna* (meditative absorption) is one-pointedness (*ekatānatā*). In that very place where concentration (*dhāraṇā*) occurs, a continuous flow of cognitions (*pratyaya*) directed toward the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), which is not interrupted by any other intervening cognition, is *dhyāna*. Although it is stated there as "one-pointedness," because the word "of the mind" (*cittasya*) is understood from the preceding context, it is understood as "one-pointedness of the mind. And for the mind, one-pointedness is precisely its function of producing a continuous flow of similar cognitions.
(8) Definition of *samādhi* (concentration).

That very meditation (*dhyāna*) is called *samādhi* when, due to the absence of contact with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it becomes as if empty of its own nature—which consists of the appearance of only the form of the object of meditation—just as a crystal [appears empty] through association with conditions. Alternatively, *samādhi* is defined as the state of the mind remaining fixed in one place alone, like a lamp in a windless spot, resulting from the excellence of meditation. And that *samādhi*, characterized by the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*), brings about a corresponding gradation in the excellence of the light of wisdom, according to the degree of its own intensity.

Thus, these limbs of yoga should be practiced by one seeking liberation with extreme application for the sake of perceiving Him, relying upon supreme detachment characterized by a lack of interest in everything—contemplating the various kinds of sufferings, such as excess, decay, destruction, bondage, and affliction, found in all states from Brahmā downwards—and relying upon supreme devotion toward Maheśvara due to the perception of His absolutely transcendent qualities. Then, having attained the highest excellence of *samādhi*, in a very short time, he perceives directly the Blessed One, Śiva, whose nature is incomparable and who is unerring. Having seen Him, he attains the unsurpassed good known as liberation (*apavarga*). And so it has been said:
"When men shall roll up space like a piece of leather,
only then will there be an end to suffering, provided they have not known Śiva.
"Only by knowing Him does one go beyond death."
And so forth.

If it is asked why liberation does not result from another [view] because there is no difference in their being the Self (*ātmatva*), we say: no; because another is not the cause of all things that arise—for indeed, even if there were another Self, it would not be the cause of all produced entities. If it is argued that space (*dik*) and time (*kāla*) are also non-distinct [from the Self] because they too are the efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of all produced entities, we say: no; because this lacks proof. [Now, a doubt arises as to whether time and space actually possess proof.]

Is it not the case that the lack of a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇakatva*) is unestablished? For time (*kāla*) has as its inferential mark (*liṅga*) the cognitions of priority and posteriority, simultaneity and non-simultaneity, and slowness and quickness; since these cognitions, which are distinct from previous cognitions regarding their objects, arise when no other cause is possible, that which is their cause is time. It is the cause of the conventional usage of *kṣaṇa*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *kalā*, *muhūrta*, *yāma*, day-and-night, half-month, month, season, solstice, year, *yuga*, *kalpa*, *manvantara*, dissolution (*pralaya*), and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*); and it is the cause of the production, subsistence, and destruction of all actions, because they are designated by it. And although it is one only, due to the distinction of its marks, it is metaphorically treated as manifold according to the differences in action—like the intellect (*mati*) or like a cook (*pācaka*). Because it possesses qualities and is not dependent on anything else, it is a substance (*dravya*).

Likewise, space (*dik*) is characterized by the notions of "east," "west," and so forth. Taking a corporeal substance as a limit, it is that from which there arise these ten notions regarding corporeal objects alone—such as "this is to the east of this," "this is to the west of this," "this is to the south of this," and so on. It is a substance (*dravya*), because it possesses qualities (*guṇavattva*) and because it is non-dependent (*anāśritatva*). Although space is one due to the lack of distinction in its characteristics, it is metaphorically designated as "ten directions" through the divisions of "east" and so on, based on the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of the conjunctions with the sun. Similarly, due to the association with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), it is metaphorically designated as having ten parts through the divisions of Indra’s quarter and so forth. Furthermore, the fact that space is the cause of the production of all effects and so on is understood from the very designation [of it as such].
{The refutation thereof}

To this it is replied: If the probandum (*sādhya*) is merely that [the cognitions] are preceded by some cause in general, then there is the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*), because they are indeed preceded by causes such as God (*Īśvara*). However, if the probandum is that they are preceded by a cause distinct from the elements (*bhūta*), the self (*ātman*), the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), and their qualities (*guṇa*), etc., then there is no corroborative instance (*dṛṣṭānta*). Now, one might argue that establishment by elimination (*pariśeṣa*) is intended, since it was stated [in the commentary]: "Of these," and so forth. The meaning is that for those simultaneous and other cognitions regarding objects such as cloth, the preceding cognitions—namely the cognitions of cloth characterized by qualifiers such as action, quality, and universal—are of a different nature than the simultaneous and other cognitions; thus, in their production, no cause other than time (*kāla*) is possible. This is not so, because elimination itself is unestablished (*asiddha*).
{The fact that space and time have their purpose fulfilled by the Lord (Īśvara)}:

For instance—the Blessed Lord Īśvara is indeed the efficient cause (*nimitta*) of all effects consisting of knowledge and ignorance. And the organs of action and so forth exist as far as possible. Now, if it is argued that since the Lord and others are common causes even in the cognitions of cloth and the like, there would follow the consequence of non-distinction among those cognitions if they were caused by Him alone—[we reply: no, because [the case] is the same. For you also accept that space and time are the efficient causes of all things that arise; therefore, even if they were the causes, the consequence of non-distinction would likewise follow.

[Objection: "But surely, it is only in cognitions such as 'simultaneous' that time is the specific cause, and only in [cognitions] such as 'prior' and 'posterior' that direction is the specific cause; whereas in all other effects it is a common cause. Therefore, the consequence of non-distinction does not follow. [Reply: No, because their essential natures differ. For there is no difference in the essential nature of either time or direction with respect to a particular effect. And if they were the cause of all effects through an undifferentiated essence, like Maheśvara, how could they be specific causes in some instances?

Now, it might be argued that the nature of a single entity is accepted in such a way that it serves as a common cause for the production of some things and an uncommon cause for others. Even so, there is no purpose served by the postulation of time; let the nature of Maheśvara himself be postulated in that manner, for his status as the cause of the world has already been established. However, there is no proof for the direction and time being the causes of all effects. [This concludes the refutation of those who designate them as such.]

But was it not said that "it is because of its designation"? True, it was so said; however, what was said is incorrect. For there is no universal rule (vyāpti) that whatever designates something must be its cause, since things such as a crow or a stick are designated as belonging to a house or a person even though they are not their causes. Furthermore, we observe that even production and so forth are designated by means of color and other qualities—as in: "the white has been produced," "the white remains," or "the white has perished."

An expression by means of a word ending in the third or seventh case is also seen even when that [word] is not the producer, as for example: "Devadatta’s son was born with a dark complexion and large eyes"; "the wandering mendicant stands [distinguished] by his topknot"; "the man died [distinguished] by his vomiting blood"; or "a stake arose in my assembly hall," "Caitra stands in the assembly hall," and "he died in the assembly hall"; and such expressions as "a son was born when my brother arrived" or "rain fell when you arrived."

Now, if it is maintained that time is the cause specifically of particular cognitions such as "simultaneous" and so forth, this is not so; for it would entail the impossibility of the cognition of simultaneity. To explain: when a collection of effects is produced at one time, it is called "produced simultaneously. If time were a single entity, then because all actions would arise at the same time, nothing would be produced non-simultaneously, and there would follow the impossibility of the conventional usage of "long" and "quick. Indeed, that which is produced over a long duration is called "produced after a long time," and that which is produced in a short duration is called "produced quickly. Both of these [distinctions] would be untenable if time were a single entity.
{The impossibility of a difference in time due to a difference in limiting conditions (upādhi)}:

Now, it was argued that a difference in time occurs due to a difference in limiting conditions, as in the case of a jewel or a revolving firebrand; but what, then, is this difference in limiting conditions here? If it is said to be simply a difference in action (*kriyā*), then surely even in the case of "done simultaneously," there is indeed a difference in action; why, then, does the cognition of non-simultaneity not arise?

If it is argued that the distinction between successive actions is the cause for the conventional usage of "non-distinction of time," then what is the meaning of "successive occurrence"? It means non-arising simultaneously. What is the meaning of "non-arising simultaneously"? It means non-arising at one and the same time. But in this case, there is the consequence of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): as long as the distinction of time is not established, the succession of actions—characterized by their arising at different times—is not established; and as long as the successive occurrence of actions is not established, the distinction of time based on the difference of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) cannot be established. Therefore, the meaning of the word "time" is actually a certain property of action, synonymous with "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). The conventional usages such as "lava," "nimeṣa," and so forth, should also be understood as referring to collections of those [moments], just like the usages of "two," "three," etc., regarding collections of single units, or like the usages of "karṣa," "pala," etc., regarding collections of weights. In this way, conventional usages such as "this is simultaneous," "produced after a long time," "produced quickly," or "produced immediately" become logically possible.
The refutation of the confusion between the higher and the lower.

By this, the confusion between "prior" (*para*) and "posterior" (*apara*) is refuted. How so? "Posteriority" resides in the youth who is the substratum of spatial posteriority, while "priority" resides in the elder who is the substratum of spatial priority; this is the confusion of prior and posterior, and that too would be impossible if time were a single unity. For just as an object separated by many parts of the earth or parts of light is called "distant" and "prior," whereas one separated by few is called "near" and "posterior"; likewise, an object separated by many moments or days-and-nights is called "distant" and "prior," while one separated by few is called "near" and "posterior. Furthermore, the state of being "many" or "few"—like gravity or dimension—is based on relative dependence (*apekṣā*), and thus it would be impossible if time were a single unity.
The refutation of time as having the nature of an action.

Nor is action itself time, because it is a qualifier of that [action], like dimension and so forth. Just as for these [objects] there is one dimension, yet for these [same objects] there is a distinctness of dimension (*parimāṇatva*), so too for these [actions] there is one time, yet for these [same actions] there is a distinctness of time (*kālatva*); such is the cognition. In this regard, just as minuteness, largeness, and so forth are specific types of dimension, so too are moments (*kṣaṇa*), instants (*lava*), and so forth, specific types of time. For instance: that dimension beyond which no smaller dimension exists is "atomicity" (*paramāṇutva*); likewise, that time beyond which no shorter time exists is a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*). And thus, because their defining marks (*liṅga*) are not distinct, it is incorrect to claim they are one; for otherwise, it would follow that weight, dimension, and so forth are also one, since the objection and its refutation are identical.

{The Refutation of Time’s Status as a Substance} Its status as a substance is also refuted by this very same argument. Since time appears as a qualifier of action—just like dimension and so forth—its lack of dependence [on another substrate] is unestablished. Alternatively, let it be that even dimension and the like are qualifiers precisely because they are independent. Nor do we perceive [in time] qualities such as color, as we do in the case of a staff or similar objects, even though it serves as a qualifier of a qualifier. That is not so, for it also possesses qualities. Furthermore, if [substancehood were established] merely by having number and so forth, then universals and the like would also absurdly follow as being substances because they possess qualities. Therefore, time is not a substance.

{The Refutation of the Substantiality of Space (Dik):} By this, the substantiality of space (*dik*) is also refuted. Because space possesses the properties of material substances—just like length, shortness, and so forth—and because cognitions qualified by those [properties] occur only with respect to material things. As for the tenfold division of space, even if it were real, what contradiction would there be?

Now, one might object: "If [direction] were real, then just as Prayāga is to the west of Vārāṇasī, it would likewise be so in relation to Kānyakubja. This is not so, because [the relationship] is not invariable; for properties such as proximity and remoteness are accepted as being real. And it is not the case that Prayāga is proximate to Pratiṣṭhāna in the same way that it is proximate to Kānyakubja. Therefore, the manifestation of properties such as "eastern" and so forth occurs in dependence upon specific causes. Enough of this digression. Thus, space and time do not serve as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*) of all produced things.

Moreover, if it were intended that time or space—which possess knowledge of the primary material causes (*upādāna*) and so forth—is the cause of the world, then Maheśvara himself would simply have been mentioned under another name. However, if they were insentient (*acetana*), they could not be objects of worship; thus, the vision of them could not be a means to the highest good (*śreyas*). For a sentient being—such as a royal sage (*rājarṣi*) and others—is observed to be occasionally pleased when beheld daily with humility, and thereby bestows grace according to one's capacity.
