An insentient thing or an incapable being cannot do so. Therefore, liberation arises solely from the vision of Śiva. {The Definition of the Nature of Liberation}

What, then, is this liberation (*mokṣa*)? Some first describe it thus: liberation is the soul’s abiding forever like space, upon the total destruction of all its specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*), during the state of cosmic dissolution (*saṃhārāvasthā*). Why? Because pleasure and pain are inseparable; since there is no abandonment of one without the arising of the other, [the soul would remain bound]. Furthermore, the activity of discerning persons (*prekṣāvat*) is not for the sake of pleasure alone, because activity is observed even for the purpose of avoiding pain such as that from thorns. Nor is this scripture commenced for the sake of a sensualist, such that there would be no inclination toward liberation which is devoid of sense-objects; rather, it is directed toward those who are utterly weary of suffering, for the purpose of annihilating suffering. This is because, due to the assault of the threefold suffering, they desire only its cessation.
"The manifestation of happiness in liberation" is the view of the Nyāya school.
Others, however, say that because it is a state of delusion—like states such as fainting—it is not appropriate for those with discernment to engage in it there; as it has been said:
"It is not right for us to seek happiness for the sake of abandoning suffering; rather, [the cessation of suffering] is better, since happiness is of the nature of suffering."
"For no one who knows the true nature of things would act for the sake of establishing delusion.
"I would rather choose the state of a jackal in the lovely Vṛndāvana than go to that objectless liberation which Gautama desires."

Furthermore, just as pleasure is desired and pain is undesired during the state of saṃsāra, so too in the state of liberation, the cessation of pain is desired while the cessation of pleasure is undesired. Since the result would involve an equal expenditure [of effort], engagement in that [liberation] is improper. As it has been said: "A wise person should not undertake tasks that are endless, fraught with difficulties, yield results equal to the cost, and are impossible."
Therefore, since the activity of discerning persons cannot otherwise be accounted for, the experience of bliss must be admitted for the liberated one.

As for the claim that activity is observed even for the sake of avoiding suffering, that is not so; for no such example exists for an activity whose sole purpose is the avoidance of suffering. To explain: since the enjoyment of pleasure is impossible when suffering is present, even the removal of suffering from thorns and the like is for the sake of enjoying pleasure; thus, the example is dissimilar. Furthermore, the state of being inseparable from suffering applies only to sensual pleasure, not to eternal [bliss].
Regarding the proof for the existence of happiness in liberation:

if it is asked, "How is the attainment of the enjoyment of happiness by the liberated one established? we reply: indeed, it has been stated that this is established through presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*). Furthermore, it is established through scripture (*āgama*). For it is said:
"That ultimate happiness which is beyond the senses is to be grasped by the intellect."
One should indeed recognize that as liberation, which is difficult to attain for those of undisciplined self.
"Brahman's form is bliss, and that is manifested in liberation," and also: "Brahman is consciousness and bliss.
[The conventional usage of the term "happiness" does not apply to the mere absence of suffering.]

If it is argued that this word "pleasure" (*sukha*) refers merely to the absence of suffering (*duḥkhābhāva*), we say no; for neither a primary nor a secondary sense is possible here. First of all, the mere absence of suffering is not pleasure in its primary sense. For if that were so, there would be no distinction in bliss resulting from the cessation of the suffering of hunger through any kind of food whatsoever, nor would there be a distinction in bliss resulting from the cessation of the suffering of desire through any young woman whatsoever. Yet, in reality, a distinction in pleasure is indeed perceived arising from specific qualities of fragrance, form, and sound. If it is argued that even in those cases the suffering of longing (*autsukya-duḥkha*) is what ceases, we say no; for even in the absence of longing, a distinction in pleasure is perceived when specific sounds and other objects are encountered.
That is not so; pleasure is simply the absence of suffering.

Or rather, the word "pleasure" is applied to the absence of suffering by way of metaphorical usage, as when one says, "I have become happy upon the removal of a burden. It cannot be that liberation is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha), for if that were the case, it would follow that wise people would not engage in its pursuit. For indeed: "Even the absence of suffering is not desired as a human goal unless it is itself cognized."
"For a wise person is never seen to act for the sake of states such as fainting.

Furthermore, one who thinks, "Since there is an absence of obstacles to the removal of suffering from carrying heavy loads and so forth, happiness will arise even from the arrival of pleasant breezes and the like," applies the conventional designation, "I have become happy. This basis for such a designation does not exist in liberation. Moreover, the word "happiness" does not apply—even figuratively—to the absence of suffering when it is not being experienced.
[Note: There is indeed experience even in the state of fainting.]

If it is argued that [the term "pleasure"] would still apply even in the state of fainting, just as the word "pleasure" applies in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), we say no; for there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) to establish the absence of consciousness in that case. Indeed, the absence of one thing is apprehended by means of the consciousness of another, but by what is the absence of consciousness itself apprehended? If it were apprehended by consciousness itself, then how could consciousness be said not to exist? And thus, due to the total absence of all consciousness, even the logical mark (*liṅga*) cannot be understood as being related [to that absence]. Therefore, even through inference, there is no comprehension of the absence of all cognitions in one who is in deep sleep.
In deep sleep, there is bliss and the awareness of that bliss.

Furthermore, because one recalls, "I slept happily," it must be admitted that both pleasure and its cognition existed for the one in deep sleep. This same reasoning applies even regarding previous days; for if it is argued that one infers the absence of experience from the mere non-perception of the memory of suffering and then figuratively uses the expression "I slept happily" for the fact that "I slept free from suffering," this is not so. For the non-perception of a memory is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) in establishing the absence of an experience, and furthermore, there is no subverting evidence against the memory of the experience of pleasure.

Now, if knowledge exists in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), then what is the distinction between that state and liberation (*mokṣa*)? It is said that the state of deep sleep is characterized by the absence of all cognition; it cannot be otherwise, for a distinction [between the two] would not be established. To explain: the waking state is characterized by cognition produced by the external senses. That state in which, while the external senses are inactive, there occurs a recollection of external objects as if through cognition produced by the external senses, is the state of sleep (*supta*). That state in which, for one whose collection of senses has ceased and who is devoid of all conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there is a cognition manifesting as mere bliss, is the state of deep sleep. And in that case, does this bliss appear as eternal, or is it produced by a specific quality (*dharma*) assisted by sleep? Therefore, the metaphorical application of "bliss" to the non-perception of suffering is nowhere well-known. Furthermore, since there is no subverting factor (*bādhaka*) against the primary meaning, we do not see any reason to regard the scriptures that assert the existence of bliss in liberation as having a figurative meaning, whereby we might accept a secondary sense.
In the state of saṃsāra, there is an absence of the manifestation of eternal happiness.

If it is argued that because pleasure and its perception are eternal, there would follow the consequence of no distinction between the states of liberation and saṃsāra, we say: no. Just as a wall or similar object acts as an obstacle to the relationship between the eye and a jar, so too in the state of saṃsāra, demerit (adharma), suffering (duḥkha), and so forth exist as obstacles to the relationship between pleasure and its perception. Upon their destruction, in the state of liberation, the connection between pleasure and its perception occurs, just as the connection between the eye and a jar occurs when a wall or such has been destroyed. A wall or the like was cited merely as an example of something that opposes a relationship; it is not that demerit and the rest act as physical obstructions like a wall, for since they are formless (amūrta), it is impossible for them to obstruct two things located in different places. Rather, from the statement, "And that [pleasure] is manifested in liberation," it is understood that when all demerit and the rest have ceased, there occurs a manifestation characterized by a specific relationship between pleasure and its perception. Therefore, even if one speaks of demerit and the rest acting as obstructions in a figurative sense, there is no fault. Consequently, due to this specific manifestation, there is no lack of distinction between liberation and saṃsāra.
The relationship between eternal bliss and its experience, though itself non-eternal, does not perish in liberation.

If it is argued that because that relation is produced (*kṛtaka*), it would follow that it could sometimes perish, we say no; for this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) due to the case of destruction (*pradhvaṃsa*). If it is argued that [the reason applies] only when there is substantial reality (*vastutve sati*), we say no; for [the relation] is not established in the case of substances (*dravya*) and so forth, since it exists immediately [after them]. Or, if it were included within those [categories], then the relation of its cognition with universals (*sāmānya*), inherence (*samavāya*), and absences (*abhāva*) would not exist. If it is argued that by the power of the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth, the object is the causal factor (*kāraka*) of the action, and the cognition produced by it is the subject (*viṣayin*), we say no; for this would entail the absence of a relation between eternal divine cognition (*īśvarajñāna*) and objects, and it would also entail the absence of a relation between the cognition of people like us and past or future objects. Therefore, even if the relation between eternal bliss and its cognition were produced, it must be eternal precisely because there is no cause for its destruction.
The bondage of one who possesses passion for eternal pleasure is not of the nature of the self.

[Objection: Is it not the case that because passion (*rāga*) consists of bondage, one who is engaged with passion for eternal bliss is not liberated? [Reply: No; for passion is characterized by its power over objects. That which is attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*) toward objects such as sound and so forth, which are the means to pleasure, is called "passion. For that indeed consists of bondage, since it is the cause of *saṃsāra* by way of engaging in the acquisition, preservation, and so forth, of those objects. But even if there is passion for eternal bliss, nevertheless, it is the cause precisely for engaging in the means to liberation, which is the cessation of the acquisition of all objects and so forth; otherwise, that bliss could not be attained. For that [eternal bliss] is not something to be accomplished through objects, nor is it something that perishes, such that—for the sake of objective pleasure—one would have to engage repeatedly in violence and the like for its sake. Therefore, there is no consequence of bondage.

Furthermore, since hatred (*dveṣa*) is likewise of the nature of bondage, one who exerts himself out of hatred for the suffering of saṃsāra would not be liberated. If, on the other hand, he has no hatred toward that [suffering] at all, then how could he avoid the cause of saṃsāra?

Furthermore, for one who is impelled even by a passion for the absolute absence of suffering, liberation would not occur. If it is argued that there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding the absence of suffering, why then does one long for it? If you say that this occurs even without passion, then he likewise has no passion for eternal happiness; thus, that too would be sought even without passion—this is quite trivial. Therefore, passion characterized by the desire for the glitter of sense-objects is meritorious; because it is the cause of meritorious activity, it is a cause of bondage, but not mere longing. Hatred (*dveṣa*) also is not merely the desire to abandon [something], but rather... [the rest of the sentence is omitted in the source].
The third chapter in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*, a compendium of arguments composed by the venerable teacher Bāsarvajña, is completed. This work is now finished.
